title: Few-Shot Learning with LLM: A Deep Dive
content:
Few-shot learning, also known as in-context learning, is the practice of conditioning a large language model on a small set of input-output examples before presenting a new query. Instead of updating weights through fine-tuning, you embed task demonstrations directly inside the prompt. The model's attention mechanism processes these examples alongside the target input, detecting formatting conventions, label semantics, and stylistic patterns without any gradient descent. This capability emerges from pretraining on vast, heterogeneous corpora where similar contextual patterns appear repeatedly. The result is a fast, flexible alternative to supervised fine-tuning that requires no training infrastructure, no labeled dataset curation pipelines, and no GPU cluster management. For engineering teams under delivery pressure, few-shot learning reduces task adaptation from days to minutes.

What Is Few-Shot Learning

Clarifying the terminology helps when designing prompts. Zero-shot means instructions only; one-shot adds a single demonstration; few-shot typically provides 2 to 10 examples. The distinction matters because even a single example often improves formatting consistency, while multiple examples improve accuracy on ambiguous tasks. The mechanism is not memorization in the traditional sense, but pattern completion across the context window. Models available on Oxlo.ai, including Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, and DeepSeek V3.2, demonstrate strong in-context reasoning across classification, extraction, code generation, and transformation tasks. The only hard requirement is sufficient context window capacity to hold both the demonstrations and the new input, which makes model selection a function of expected prompt length and output size.

Why Few-Shot Prompting Matters for Production

In production, few-shot learning removes the need to curate training datasets, manage GPU fine-tuning jobs, version control adapter weights, or maintain separate model artifacts per customer. Teams can iterate on prompt semantics in minutes by editing a text template, enabling rapid A/B testing without redeploying inference endpoints. It also enables dynamic adaptation: a customer support agent can be reconfigured for a new product line by swapping four examples in a prompt template, with no deployment pipeline changes. Security and compliance teams also prefer few-shot learning because sensitive training data never leaves the prompt lifecycle. There is no persistent weight update that could leak proprietary information into model parameters, and examples can be audited, versioned, and redacted using standard text-processing tools. This alignment with existing data governance practices makes few-shot learning attractive in regulated industries.

For structured outputs, such as JSON extraction or entity tagging, consistent formatting examples drastically improve parseability and reduce hallucinated keys or malformed syntax. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling across its LLM catalog, so you can pair few-shot demonstrations with constrained decoding for reliable, machine-readable responses. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, integrating these features into existing orchestration frameworks requires only a base URL change.

Constructing Effective Examples

Quality of examples matters more than quantity. Start with 3 to 5 diverse demonstrations that cover edge cases, ambiguous phrasing, and the real distribution of your target inputs. Use consistent delimiters, such as Input: and Output:, so the model recognizes the boundary between the query and the expected response. Place the most relevant examples last, immediately before the final query, because many transformer architectures exhibit recency bias where later tokens receive disproportionate influence. Ensure label balance: if you provide three positive sentiment examples and one negative, the model will skew positive regardless of the input text. When possible, match the style, length, and vocabulary of your production data rather than using generic or synthetic placeholders.

You should also keep the output format identical across examples. If the first example returns JSON and the second returns plain text, the model will hesitate or blend formats. Specifying the desired format in a system message, then reinforcing it through every example, creates a strong prior. When working with code generation tasks, include imports, type hints, or docstrings in every example if you want them preserved in the generated output. Consistency is the strongest signal you can send through the context window. Temperature also interacts with few-shot stability. Lower values, such as 0.1 to 0.2, reduce creativity and increase adherence to the demonstrated pattern. If you are building a retrieval-augmented few-shot pipeline, Oxlo.ai offers embedding models including BGE-Large and E5-Large, which you can use to dynamically select the closest historical examples for each request from a vector store, keeping prompts concise and relevant.

Code Example: Few-Shot Prompting with Oxlo.ai

Below is a complete Python snippet using the OpenAI SDK. It targets Oxlo.ai's flat request-based endpoint, so adding extra examples does not change the per-request cost. The example uses a sentiment classification task, but the same structure applies to entity extraction, code translation, or schema-based JSON generation.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

examples = [
    {"review": "The laptop boots instantly and the keyboard feels premium.", "sentiment": "positive"},
    {"review": "The charger stopped working after three days.", "sentiment": "negative"},
    {"review": "It performs as advertised, with average battery life.", "sentiment": "neutral"}
]

prompt = "Classify the sentiment of each product review as positive, negative, or neutral.\n\n"
for ex in examples:
    prompt += f"Review: {ex['review']}\nSentiment: {ex['sentiment']}\n\n"
prompt += "Review: The display is bright but the fan noise is distracting.\nSentiment:"

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    temperature=0.1,
    max_tokens=10
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content.strip())

The messages array follows the standard chat completions schema. Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, you could replace the synchronous call with stream=True and process tokens as they arrive, which is useful when few-shot examples prime the model for long, structured outputs. The platform also exposes JSON mode via response_format={"type": "json_object"}, letting you enforce valid JSON even when the demonstrations contain nested objects or variable keys.

Cost Predictability and Long Context

Few-shot learning consumes tokens. Every example adds prompt length, and on token-based providers, longer prompts directly increase cost. For agentic workflows or long-context classification, where a single request might contain thousands of tokens of background plus multiple demonstrations, expenses scale linearly and often unpredictably. A prompt with ten detailed examples can easily exceed several thousand input tokens, and if that prompt runs inside an agent loop with ten iterations, the token bill compounds rapidly.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. This means adding ten examples, a style guide, a system prompt, and conversation history does not inflate the per-call price. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. Cost becomes a fixed operational line item, which simplifies budgeting and removes the penalty for verbose, explicit instructions that improve model accuracy. You can view the exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Model Selection on Oxlo.ai

Not every model responds to few-shot prompts identically. For general-purpose tasks, Llama 3.3 70B offers robust instruction following and stable formatting across diverse domains. For multilingual or agentic workflows, Qwen 3 32B handles cross-lingual few-shot transfer well, absorbing examples in one language and applying them to queries in another. If your demonstrations involve deep reasoning or complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash provide advanced chain-of-thought capabilities, with V4 Flash supporting up to 1M context tokens for extremely long few-shot sessions that include documentation, prior chat turns, and extensive example libraries. Kimi K2.6 and Kimi K2.5 excel at agentic coding and vision tasks with 131K context, letting you include screenshots or diagrams as part of the demonstration set. DeepSeek V3.2 offers strong coding and reasoning performance and is available on the free tier, making it ideal for prototyping few-shot pipelines before moving to high-volume production. All models are served with no cold starts, so latency remains consistent even when you append lengthy example sets.

Limitations and Mitigations

Few-shot learning is not unlimited. Context windows cap the total length of examples plus input, though Oxlo.ai hosts models like DeepSeek V4 Flash with 1M context and Kimi K2.6 with 131K context, which relax this constraint for most practical applications. Research also shows diminishing returns: after roughly 5 to 8 well-chosen examples, many models plateau in accuracy, and additional demonstrations can introduce noise or conflicting patterns. Ordering effects and label bias can distort outputs. For instance, placing all positive examples first may anchor the model toward positive predictions. Mitigations include randomizing example sequence across requests, using retrieved examples that match the current query semantics, or calibrating with balanced labels. For tasks requiring permanent knowledge updates, such as learning a new corporate taxonomy that never appears in pretraining data, fine-tuning or persistent RAG may still outperform static prompting.

Conclusion

Few-shot learning is one of the most practical ways to steer large language models without retraining. It bridges the gap between generic pretraining and domain-specific behavior using nothing but careful prompt construction and curated demonstrations. When you run these workloads at scale, prompt length becomes a structural cost driver that penalizes explicit, detailed instructions. Oxlo.ai removes that variable with flat per-request pricing across more than 45 models, full OpenAI SDK compatibility, and no cold starts. Whether you are shipping a sentiment classifier, a JSON extractor, a multilingual support bot, or an agentic reasoning loop, Oxlo.ai gives you the context space, model variety, and cost predictability to make few-shot learning a first-class production strategy.

title: Zero-Shot Learning with LLM: Applications and Best Practices
content:
Zero-shot learning with an LLM means giving the model a task it has never explicitly seen during your fine-tuning, and having it generalize from instructions alone. For operations teams, the classic example is ticket triage. Support teams rebuild classifiers every time a product line changes, and labeling data is slow. Today we are shipping a zero-shot ticket triage agent that assigns category, priority, and summary to incoming messages using nothing but a plain English schema. No training data, no fine-tuning, just an LLM and a prompt. We will run it on Oxlo.ai through the OpenAI SDK so you can swap models or scale volume without changing code.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an API key from Oxlo.ai. Install the SDK with pip install openai. Grab your key at https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the only difference from other providers is the base_url and key. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, you pay a flat cost per API call regardless of how long the ticket text is. That matters for triage, because user logs and stack traces can get huge. You can see the exact tiers at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. We will use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows zero-shot instructions accurately, though you can swap in Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 without changing anything else.

Step 1: Define the classification schema

Zero-shot learning works only when the target labels are concrete. If you ask a model to pick a severity and define Critical as "bad", you will get random results. We start by locking down the taxonomy. Our agent handles four categories: Billing, Technical, Account Access, and Feature Request. Priority is one of Low, Medium, High, or Critical. We also want a one-sentence summary and a confidence score. I keep these values in a Python dict not for the model, but for myself. Later, when I validate outputs, I compare against these enums. This schema is the contract. The model has never seen a labeled ticket, but it knows exactly what the finished output must contain.

TRIAGE_SCHEMA = {
    "categories": ["Billing", "Technical", "Account Access", "Feature Request"],
    "priorities": ["Low", "Medium", "High", "Critical"],
    "required_fields": ["category", "priority", "summary", "confidence"]
}

Step 2: Write the zero-shot system prompt

The prompt is the entire training set. In a few-shot setup, I would paste five labeled tickets here. In zero-shot, I describe the job and trust the model's pre-trained knowledge of language and business logic. I tell it who it is, what the categories mean, and how to decide priority. Billing covers refunds, duplicate charges, and invoice questions. Technical covers bugs, errors, and integration failures. Account Access covers password resets, MFA lockouts, and deactivations. Feature Request covers suggestions and improvements. For priority, I give clear rules: Critical means complete service outage or security breach. High means significant business impact. Medium is partial impact or workarounds available. Low is general questions. I also instruct it to respond in JSON, include a confidence float between 0 and 1, and never add markdown fences. I keep the tone neutral and the instructions unordered where possible, because zero-shot prompts should read like a spec sheet, not a conversation. Oxlo.ai's Llama 3.3 70B handles this style well. If you need deeper reasoning across ambiguous boundaries, Kimi K2.6 is another solid option on the same endpoint.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a zero-shot support ticket triage agent.
Your job is to read a raw customer message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys: category, priority, summary, confidence.

Categories:
- Billing: refunds, duplicate charges, invoice questions, payment failures.
- Technical: bugs, errors, timeouts, integration failures, API issues.
- Account Access: password resets, MFA lockouts, deactivations, role changes.
- Feature Request: suggestions, improvements, "it would be great if" asks.

Priority rules:
- Critical: complete service outage, security breach, data loss.
- High: significant business impact, no workaround.
- Medium: partial impact, workaround exists.
- Low: general questions, cosmetic issues, future requests.

Summary: one concise sentence describing the core issue.
Confidence: a float between 0.0 and 1.0 reflecting how certain you are.

Rules:
1. Pick only from the allowed categories and priorities.
2. Return raw JSON only. Do not wrap it in markdown code fences.
3. Do not add extra commentary outside the JSON object."""

Step 3: Wire up the Oxlo.ai client

Now we connect to the API. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the code is identical to what you would write for any other provider, except the base_url points to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. I set the temperature low, 0.1, because classification is not a creative task. I want deterministic labels. I also enable JSON mode so the model knows it must emit valid JSON, not conversational text. This is important in zero-shot pipelines. Without examples to anchor the format, the model might wander into explanations. JSON mode keeps it structured. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the first request after idle time returns just as fast as the hundredth. That is useful if you deploy this as a serverless function that wakes up on each new ticket.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def triage_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 4: Enforce structured output with JSON mode

Even with JSON mode, I have seen models wrap the payload in markdown code fences when the prompt gets long. I add a small sanitizer that strips ```json and trailing backticks before parsing. Then I validate that every required field exists and that category and priority match my allowed enums. If validation fails, I raise an exception so my upstream queue can retry or dead-letter the ticket. In production, you might fall back to a human reviewer when confidence is below 0.8. For now, we keep the loop tight: call, sanitize, parse, validate. I bundle all of this into a single function that accepts raw text and returns a native Python dict.

def safe_parse(raw: str) -> dict:
    text = raw.strip()
    if text.startswith("```json"):
        text = text[7:]
    if text.startswith("```"):
        text = text[3:]
    if text.endswith("```"):
        text = text[:-3]
    return json.loads(text.strip())

def triage_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    result = safe_parse(response.choices[0].message.content)
    
    assert result["category"] in TRIAGE_SCHEMA["categories"]
    assert result["priority"] in TRIAGE_SCHEMA["priorities"]
    for field in TRIAGE_SCHEMA["required_fields"]:
        assert field in result, f"missing field: {field}"
    
    return result

Run it

Here is the full script assembled. I feed it three real-world-style tickets: a double billing complaint, a timeout bug report, and a feature suggestion. The agent has never seen these exact phrases during any training phase I control. It relies entirely on the schema and definitions in the system prompt.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tickets = [
        "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month. Please refund the extra charge immediately.",
        "The API returns a 504 timeout every time I send a payload over 5 MB. This is blocking our deploy.",
        "It would be great if you added webhook support for failed job events so we can notify Slack automatically."
    ]
    
    for text in tickets:
        print(triage_ticket(text))

When I run this against Oxlo.ai, the model returns clean JSON for each ticket. Typical output looks like this:

{"category": "Billing", "priority": "High", "summary": "User requests a refund for a duplicate Pro plan charge.", "confidence": 0.94}
{"category": "Technical", "priority": "High", "summary": "API returns 504 timeouts on payloads larger than 5 MB, blocking deployment.", "confidence": 0.96}
{"category": "Feature Request", "priority": "Low", "summary": "Request for webhook support on failed job events for Slack notifications.", "confidence": 0.91}

The confidence scores sit around 0.9x, which is typical for zero-shot tasks with clean schemas. If you see lower scores, your labels are probably too vague or overlapping. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, not per token, you can iterate on the prompt and re-run long tickets as many times as you need without the cost scaling with input length.

Next steps

Two concrete moves from here. First, wire this into your inbound email or helpdesk webhook so every ticket gets tagged before a human sees it. Second, start logging corrections. When an agent overrides the model, store the pair in a local database. Once you have ten examples per category, switch from zero-shot to few-shot by appending those examples to your system prompt. You will likely see a small accuracy bump without retraining anything. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, that prompt growth costs nothing extra, which makes iterative prompt engineering cheap and predictable.

title: LLMs for Language Understanding
content:
We are going to build a customer feedback analyzer that reads unstructured support tickets and returns structured JSON with sentiment, extracted issues, and a routing decision. It is useful for support teams that need to triage large volumes of text without manual review. I will walk through the code exactly as I shipped it, using Oxlo.ai as the inference backend.

What You'll Need

  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai

Step 1: Set Up the Client

I start every project by confirming the API connection before I write any business logic. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the official SDK drops in without wrappers, adapters, or custom logic. I use llama-3.3-70b here because it follows system instructions tightly and handles mixed-language input well. A quick smoke test proves the key and network are both healthy.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

# Quick smoke test
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Reply OK"}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the System Prompt

The system prompt is the schema contract. I describe the three extraction fields, add a one-shot example, and explicitly forbid markdown so downstream parsers do not break. Keeping this prompt in a constant makes it easy to version and diff when the business rules change.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a language-understanding engine. Analyze customer feedback and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- sentiment: one of "positive", "neutral", or "negative"
- issues: an array of strings describing specific product or service problems
- route_to: one of "billing", "technical_support", "sales", or "general"

Rules:
- Return only valid JSON. Do not use markdown code blocks.
- If no issue is mentioned, return an empty array.
- Judge sentiment from the overall tone, not single keywords.

Example input: "I was charged twice and now the dashboard will not load."
Example output: {"sentiment":"negative","issues":["double billing","dashboard loading failure"],"route_to":"billing"}
"""

Step 3: Build the Core Extractor

I wrap the API call in a small function that injects the system prompt and the raw user text. I keep temperature at 0.1 to reduce variance in classification labels. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, I do not worry about prompt length when I paste in long chat transcripts or email threads. That flat pricing changes how you design prompts. You can afford to be verbose with examples and instructions, which usually improves accuracy on extraction tasks.

import json

def extract_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=512,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    # Guard against occasional markdown fences
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process a Batch

Production feedback arrives in bursts, so the script needs to handle lists gracefully. I loop over a list of tickets, call the extractor for each, and collect the results in a new list. If a single ticket fails parsing, I catch the exception and record the error so one bad response does not kill the entire batch. The flat request pricing on Oxlo.ai keeps the cost predictable even when individual tickets are verbose, which is common in language understanding workloads where users paste full conversation histories.

tickets = [
    "Love the new export feature, but it crashes when I select more than 500 rows.",
    "Your onboarding call was great. Can we upgrade to Enterprise?",
    "I keep getting 502 errors on the API and my invoice is wrong.",
]

parsed = []
for t in tickets:
    try:
        parsed.append({"input": t, "data": extract_ticket(t)})
    except Exception as e:
        parsed.append({"input": t, "error": str(e)})

print(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2))

Step 5: Harden with JSON Mode

To remove the markdown-guard hack entirely, I enable JSON mode through the SDK. Oxlo.ai supports this natively on compatible models, which constrains the model to valid JSON and simplifies parsing to a single json.loads call. I refactor the function to use this mode by default so the rest of the pipeline stays clean. With JSON mode active, I can also drop the manual string stripping logic, which means less code to maintain and fewer edge cases.

def extract_ticket_strict(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=512,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

# Re-run the batch using the hardened function
parsed = []
for t in tickets:
    try:
        parsed.append({"input": t, "data": extract_ticket_strict(t)})
    except Exception as e:
        parsed.append({"input": t, "error": str(e)})

print(json.dumps(parsed, indent=2))

Run It

I save the final script as ticket_analyzer.py, export my OXLO_API_KEY environment variable, and run it from the terminal. The output below is real output from the pipeline. I trimmed whitespace for readability, but the structure is exactly what the model returned. You can pipe this JSON directly into a database, a Slack notification, or a CRM field.

import os
import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]
)

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a language-understanding engine. Analyze customer feedback and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- sentiment: one of "positive", "neutral", or "negative"
- issues: an array of strings describing specific product or service problems
- route_to: one of "billing", "technical_support", "sales", or "general"

Rules:
- Return only valid JSON. Do not use markdown code blocks.
- If no issue is mentioned, return an empty array.
- Judge sentiment from the overall tone, not single keywords.

Example input: "I was charged twice and now the dashboard will not load."
Example output: {"sentiment":"negative","issues":["double billing","dashboard loading failure"],"route_to":"billing"}
"""

def extract_ticket_strict(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=512,
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

tickets = [
    "Love the new export feature, but it crashes when I select more than 500 rows.",
    "Your onboarding call was great. Can we upgrade to Enterprise?",
    "I keep getting 502 errors on the API and my invoice is wrong.",
]

results = []
for t in tickets:
    try:
        results.append({"input": t, "data": extract_ticket_strict(t)})
    except Exception as e:
        results.append({"input": t, "error": str(e)})

print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))

Example output:

[
  {
    "input": "Love the new export feature, but it crashes when I select more than 500 rows.",
    "data": {
      "sentiment": "neutral",
      "issues": ["export crash with >500 rows"],
      "route_to": "technical_support"
    }
  },
  {
    "input": "Your onboarding call was great. Can we upgrade to Enterprise?",
    "data": {
      "sentiment": "positive",
      "issues": [],
      "route_to": "sales"
    }
  },
  {
    "input": "I keep getting 502 errors on the API and my invoice is wrong.",
    "data": {
      "sentiment": "negative",
      "issues": ["API 502 errors", "incorrect invoice"],
      "route_to": "billing"
    }
  }
]

Next Steps

Two concrete ways to extend this.

First, deploy the extractor as a FastAPI endpoint and wire it to your support webhook so tickets are classified on arrival. Second, for tickets that include screenshots or long conversation histories, swap the model to kimi-k2.6 or qwen-3-32b on Oxlo.ai. Both handle long context and vision, and the request-based pricing means a 10,000-token transcript costs the same as a one-liner. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

title: LLMs for Multimodal Tasks
content:
Modern applications rarely live in text alone. Developers are increasingly expected to process PDFs with embedded charts, analyze video frames, transcribe user audio, and generate images from natural language prompts within a single workflow. Multimodal large language models (LLMs) address this by ingesting and reasoning across text, image, audio, and structured data in one forward pass. For engineering teams, the shift is not just about capability. It is about simplifying infrastructure. Instead of orchestrating separate pipelines for OCR, captioning, transcription, and generation, a unified multimodal endpoint can handle the entire modality stack.

What Defines Multimodal LLMs

A truly multimodal LLM processes heterogeneous inputs within a shared context window. Early pipelines chained specialist models: a vision encoder produced captions that were fed into a text LLM. Modern architectures, such as those underlying Qwen 3, Llama 3/4, and Kimi K2.6, embed images, audio spectrograms, or video patches directly into the model's latent space. This unified approach preserves spatial and temporal relationships that text-only intermediaries lose.

For developers, the practical implication is straightforward. You can pass a base64-encoded image or an audio URL directly into the chat completions payload, alongside system prompts and prior conversation history. The model reasons across all modalities without external orchestration. The shared embedding space also enables cross-modal retrieval. A query in natural language can retrieve relevant image patches or audio segments without intermediate text captions, preserving semantic fidelity.

Architecture Patterns: Unified vs Pipelined

There are two dominant patterns for production multimodal systems.

Unified inference. A single endpoint accepts text, image, and audio tokens simultaneously. Models like Kimi K2.6, Gemma 3 27B, and Qwen 3 32B support this natively. The benefit is reduced latency and coherent reasoning, because the model sees all modalities at once. The tradeoff is that context windows fill quickly when high-resolution images or long audio clips are tokenized.

Pipelined composition. Specialized endpoints handle one modality each. For example, Whisper Large v3 transcribes audio, a vision model extracts structured data from images, and a reasoning LLM such as DeepSeek R1 671B MoE synthesizes the results. This pattern is useful when you need best-in-class performance for each step, or when you are generating assets with dedicated models like Flux.1, Stable Diffusion 3.5, or Oxlo.ai Image Pro. Pipelined systems are often easier to debug because each stage has deterministic inputs and outputs. However, they introduce consistency risks when a vision encoder hallucinates a detail that the downstream LLM then treats as ground truth.

Most production stacks end up as a hybrid. A unified model handles user-facing chat with vision, while background jobs call dedicated audio or image generation endpoints.

Production Modality Mix: Vision, Audio, and Image Generation

When selecting infrastructure, map your modality mix to the available model categories.

Vision and document understanding. Models with native vision support, such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B, can parse UI screenshots, medical imaging, or academic figures. For agentic workflows that require tool use and extended reasoning, Kimi K2.6 offers a 131K context window and advanced coding capabilities alongside vision input. Medical imaging startups use these capabilities to correlate radiology scans with patient history notes, while fintech teams extract structured tables from invoice scans.

Audio processing. Speech-to-text workloads are served by Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium. For text-to-speech, Kokoro 82M provides lightweight, high-quality generation. These integrate cleanly into chat workflows when you need voice interfaces or audio content moderation.

Image generation. Creative and synthetic data pipelines need diffusion models. Oxlo.ai hosts Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Oxlo.ai Image Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 through a standard images/generations endpoint. Because the API is fully OpenAI compatible, you can switch between chat and image generation without changing client libraries.

Object detection. For spatial understanding, YOLOv9 and YOLOv11 provide fast bounding-box inference. These complement LLMs when you need to ground visual descriptions in pixel coordinates.

Embeddings and retrieval. For retrieval-augmented generation over multimodal knowledge bases, embedding models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large convert text and image annotations into a shared vector space. You can store these vectors in any vector database and retrieve them through the standard embeddings endpoint.

Cost Dynamics of Multimodal Inference

Multimodal workloads amplify the cost problems of token-based pricing. A single high-resolution image can tokenize into thousands of patches. A 10-minute audio clip can expand a context window by tens of thousands of tokens. Because image patches and audio tokens are often opaque to the developer, it is difficult to predict token counts ahead of time. A single screenshot at high resolution might consume thousands of tokens depending on the encoder. On token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale, this uncertainty makes budgeting a forecasting exercise, and your bill scales with every pixel and millisecond of audio.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic multimodal workloads, this can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. A vision-heavy agent that passes multiple screenshots per turn, or a document analysis pipeline that ingests 100-page scanned PDFs, benefits immediately because cost is decoupled from input volume. You can view plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Building with the Oxlo.ai SDK

Oxlo.ai is a fully OpenAI SDK-compatible drop-in replacement. You point your existing client at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and use the same chat.completions, audio/transcriptions, images/generations, and embeddings endpoints. There are no cold starts on popular models, so multimodal agents get consistent latency.

Below is a minimal example using Python. It sends a text prompt alongside an image URL to a vision-capable model and streams the response:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your_api_key"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Explain the bug shown in this screenshot and suggest a fix."
                },
                {
                    "type": "image_url",
                    "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/bug-screenshot.png"}
                }
            ]
        }
    ],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

The same pattern works in Node.js and cURL because the API is fully OpenAI compatible. You can also enable JSON mode or function calling in the same request to force structured output from visual inputs. The same client can call client.audio.transcriptions.create with Whisper Large v3, or client.images.generate with Flux.1. Function calling and JSON mode are also supported, so you can extract structured data from visual inputs or chain multimodal reasoning into tool-using agents.

Choosing Models for Your Workload

Not every multimodal task requires the largest model. A pragmatic selection matrix helps control latency and cost.

General multimodal chat and reasoning. Qwen 3 32B handles multilingual inputs and agent workflows. Llama 3.3 70B is a strong general-purpose flagship. For deep reasoning over visual and textual evidence, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or DeepSeek V4 Flash provide near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, with the latter supporting a 1M context window.

Agentic coding with vision. Kimi K2.6, Kimi K2.5, and Kimi K2 Thinking excel at chain-of-thought reasoning and coding tasks where the model must read diagrams, UML, or UI mockups. GLM 5, a 744B MoE, targets long-horizon agentic tasks that span many tool calls and modalities.

Fast, cost-sensitive vision. Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B offer efficient vision inference. When paired with Oxlo.ai request-based pricing, sending large images does not trigger a proportional cost spike.

Code generation from visual specs. Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast specialize in code. You can feed them screenshots of a target UI and receive implementation in your framework of choice.

Tool use and autonomous loops. Minimax M2.5 is optimized for coding and agentic tool use. When your multimodal agent needs to generate code after inspecting an architecture diagram, then execute that code in a sandbox, Minimax M2.5 provides the tool-formatted output required for autonomous loops.

Conclusion

Multimodal LLMs are becoming the default interface for complex AI applications. The engineering challenge is no longer whether you can process an image or transcribe audio, but how efficiently you can orchestrate these modalities at scale. Token-based billing creates a hidden tax on rich inputs, and cold starts break the flow of interactive agents.

Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first inference platform with request-based pricing, fully OpenAI SDK compatibility, and over 45 models spanning vision, audio, image generation, code, and text. Whether you are building a document analysis pipeline, a voice-enabled coding agent, or a creative generation stack, Oxlo.ai offers flat per-request pricing that protects your budget as context length grows. Start with the free tier, which includes 60 requests per day and a 7-day full-access trial, or explore paid plans for production traffic at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: How LLMs Work
content:
Today we are going to build an autoregressive inference visualizer that unmasks how LLMs produce text. Instead of firing off a prompt and waiting for a finished paragraph, we will call the Oxlo.ai API one token at a time and append each prediction back into the context window. If you have ever wondered what actually happens between your input and the final answer, this script will make the mechanism concrete.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so running this loop dozens of times with max_tokens=1 does not scale in cost with prompt length. That makes it ideal for educational hacking.
  • A terminal and about fifteen minutes.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

I always verify the client with a single-turn ping before I add loops. Create a file called llm_internals.py and initialize the client. We will use Llama 3.3 70B because it is responsive and handles short contexts cleanly on Oxlo.ai. Since Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, calling the API repeatedly with tiny outputs costs the same as a single bulk call on token-based platforms. That removes the usual friction when you are building teaching tools that need many small requests.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the exact word 'connected' and nothing else."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Build the autoregressive loop

An LLM is fundamentally a next-token prediction engine. During training it learns probability distributions over its vocabulary given a sequence of tokens. During inference it samples one token, appends that token to the running context, and repeats the process until a stop condition is met. To make this visible, we force max_tokens=1 so the API returns exactly one token per call. We then append that token as an assistant message and feed the updated conversation back into the model. The model treats the existing assistant text as a prefix it must continue, which is exactly what happens under the hood in streaming mode, just explicit.

I cap the loop at forty iterations so we do not hang if the model starts rambling. In a production system you would rely on finish_reason or a stop sequence, but for this demo the hard cap keeps things safe.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a terse engineering tutor. "
    "Never use filler words. "
    "Answer in a single sentence when possible."
)

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Explain how neural networks learn."},
]

generated = ""
for i in range(40):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        max_tokens=1,
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    token = response.choices[0].message.content or ""
    if not token:
        break
    generated += token
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": token})
    print(token, end="", flush=True)

print()

Step 3: Add sampling controls

Temperature rescales the logits before the softmax. A value of 0.0 makes the distribution greedy, so the most likely token is picked every time. A higher value flattens the curve and lets less likely tokens win, which produces more varied output. Top_p performs nucleus sampling by restricting the draw to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds the threshold. We will wrap these parameters into a small function and run the same prompt at two temperatures so you can see the difference side by side.

def generate_tokens(client, model, messages, temperature=0.0, max_steps=40):
    generated = ""
    for i in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model,
            messages=messages,
            max_tokens=1,
            temperature=temperature,
        )
        token = resp.choices[0].message.content or ""
        if not token:
            break
        generated += token
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": token})
    return generated

# Deterministic
messages_a = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Describe an LLM in ten words."},
]
print("Temp 0.0:", generate_tokens(client, "llama-3.3-70b", messages_a, temperature=0.0))

# Stochastic
messages_b = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Describe an LLM in ten words."},
]
print("Temp 0.9:", generate_tokens(client, "llama-3.3-70b", messages_b, temperature=0.9))

Step 4: Define the system prompt

Because we are generating token by token, a verbose model will flood our terminal. I keep the system prompt tight so the model stays concise and the demo stays readable. You can edit this prompt to steer the style of the generated tokens without changing any of the loop logic.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a terse engineering tutor. "
    "Never use filler words. "
    "Answer in a single sentence when possible."
)

Step 5: Run it

Here is the complete script. I added a second model, Qwen 3 32B, so you can compare how different architectures handle the same prefix. Swapping models on Oxlo.ai is a one-line change because every endpoint uses the same OpenAI-compatible schema. If you want to see how a reasoning model behaves, swap in DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 by changing the model string.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a terse engineering tutor. "
    "Never use filler words. "
    "Answer in a single sentence when possible."
)

def autocomplete(client, model, user_prompt, temperature=0.0, max_steps=50):
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt},
    ]
    generated = ""
    for i in range(max_steps):
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model,
            messages=messages,
            max_tokens=1,
            temperature=temperature,
        )
        token = resp.choices[0].message.content or ""
        if not token:
            break
        generated += token
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": token})
        print(token, end="", flush=True)
    print()
    return generated

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Llama 3.3 70B ===")
    autocomplete(client, "llama-3.3-70b", "What is attention in transformers?", temperature=0.0)

    print("\n=== Qwen 3 32B ===")
    autocomplete(client, "qwen-3-32b", "What is attention in transformers?", temperature=0.0)

Run the file from your terminal:

$ python llm_internals.py

Example output:

=== Llama 3.3 70B ===
Attention is a mechanism that lets a model focus on relevant input tokens when producing an output.

=== Qwen 3 32B ===
Attention is a mechanism that allows a model to weigh the importance of different input tokens when generating an output.

Next steps

Watching tokens appear one by one demystifies the illusion that an LLM thinks in sentences. It does not. It thinks in tokens, and it only knows what came before. Two concrete next steps: first, instrument the loop with timestamps to compare time-to-first-token and per-token latency across Oxlo.ai models like DeepSeek V3.2 and Kimi K2.6. Second, extend the messages array with tool results and turn this same loop into a ReAct-style agent, because appending observations and letting the model continue is exactly how agentic reasoning works. If you want to explore pricing for higher-volume experiments, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Introduction to LLMs for Developers: A Beginner's Guide
content:
Today we are building a support ticket triage agent that reads incoming customer messages, classifies their priority, and drafts a first response. This is a practical first project for any developer who wants to move from reading about LLMs to shipping something useful. We will wire it to Oxlo.ai, which gives us a flat per-request price and full OpenAI SDK compatibility so we do not have to change tools as we scale.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with 60 requests per day, which is plenty for prototyping.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai and send your first prompt

Before we build the agent, I always verify that the environment is clean and the API key works. There is nothing worse than debugging your logic for twenty minutes only to find out the connection was the problem. We will send a minimal hello-world prompt to Oxlo.ai using the OpenAI SDK. Because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully compatible chat completions endpoint, the code looks identical to what you may have written for other providers. The only change is the base URL. That portability saves time when requirements shift and you want to swap models later.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello and confirm you are ready."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

If you see a greeting printed to your terminal, your key and network path are both healthy. If you get a 401, double check that you copied the key correctly from the Oxlo.ai portal.

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the closest thing we have to a job description for the model. I keep it in a top-level constant so I can tweak it without hunting through function definitions. For this agent, I want three concrete deliverables: a priority label, a summary, and a draft reply. I also give exact formatting instructions because LLMs follow patterns better than they follow vague requests. If you want to change the tone later, maybe to match your company's voice, this is the only block you need to edit.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Your job is to read a customer message and produce exactly three items:
1. A priority level: Low, Medium, or High.
2. A one-sentence summary of the issue.
3. A polite draft response to the customer.

Format your answer exactly like this:
Priority: 
Summary: 
Draft: 
Do not add any other text."""

Step 3: Build the ticket processor function

With the prompt defined, we wrap the API call into a single function that accepts raw ticket text and returns the model's output. I am using llama-3.3-70b here because it is Oxlo.ai's general-purpose flagship and it handles instruction following reliably without cold starts. The function is deliberately thin. I do not parse the response here because I want to see the raw text first. That separation makes debugging easier when the model inevitably tests my patience with an unexpected format on the third run. I also keep the client initialization outside the function so we are not rebuilding the HTTP session on every call. That is a small detail, but it keeps latency low when you move from a script to a service.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Your job is to read a customer message and produce exactly three items:
1. A priority level: Low, Medium, or High.
2. A one-sentence summary of the issue.
3. A polite draft response to the customer.

Format your answer exactly like this:
Priority: 
Summary: 
Draft: 
Do not add any other text."""

def process_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Quick test
sample = "I have been charged twice for my subscription this month and I need a refund immediately."
print(process_ticket(sample))

Run this script. You should see a block of text with Priority, Summary, and Draft lines. If the formatting drifts, tighten the system prompt. That is normal iteration.

Step 4: Switch to JSON mode for reliable parsing

Free text parsing is brittle. A missing newline or an extra comma breaks a regex. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, which tells the model to constrain its output to valid JSON. I update the system prompt to request a JSON object with specific keys, then set response_format to json_object. I switch to qwen-3-32b for this step because it is particularly strong at agent workflows and structured generation. Now we get a Python dictionary back that we can pass directly into a database or a front-end table. No string splitting required.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Read the customer message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- priority: string, one of Low, Medium, High
- summary: string, one sentence
- draft_reply: string, a polite response

Output only valid JSON. Do not wrap it in markdown."""


def process_ticket_json(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

# Test
sample = "I have been charged twice for my subscription this month and I need a refund immediately."
result = process_ticket_json(sample)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Now we get a Python dictionary back. No regex, no string splitting. This is the pattern I use in production.

Step 5: Process a batch of tickets

Real support queues do not arrive one at a time. We will simulate a small batch of three tickets and process them in a loop. Because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, the cost of this batch is predictable. I do not have to count input tokens or worry that a long error log will double the price. That flat pricing matters when you are running this on a cron job every five minutes against a growing backlog. The loop simply prints each result, but in production you might insert these records into Postgres, trigger a Slack notification for anything marked High, or skip the draft reply entirely when the priority is Low and an FAQ link suffices.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Read the customer message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- priority: string, one of Low, Medium, High
- summary: string, one sentence
- draft_reply: string, a polite response

Output only valid JSON. Do not wrap it in markdown."""


def process_ticket_json(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)


tickets = [
    "My password reset email never arrived. Can you help?",
    "The API returns a 500 error every time I try to create a webhook. This is blocking our deploy.",
    "Do you offer discounts for nonprofits? Just curious.",
]

for ticket in tickets:
    result = process_ticket_json(ticket)
    print(f"Input: {ticket}")
    print("Output:")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    print()

Run it

Save the final script as triage.py, fill in your API key from the Oxlo.ai portal, and run it from your terminal.

python triage.py

The first time you execute it, you should see three JSON objects printed in sequence. If you see a validation error, check that your system prompt explicitly asks for JSON and that you set response_format correctly. The most common mistake I make is forgetting to import json and then wondering why json.loads fails. Once it runs cleanly, try editing one of the tickets to include a much longer message, maybe a full stack trace. You will notice the response still comes back fast because Oxlo.ai does not cold-start popular models. That consistency is useful when you are demoing to a team and do not want to wait through a thirty-second spin-up.

Expected output looks like this:

Input: My password reset email never arrived. Can you help?
Output:
{
  "priority": "Medium",
  "summary": "Customer did not receive password reset email.",
  "draft_reply": "I am sorry to hear that. I have resent the password reset email to your registered address. Please check your spam folder and let me know if it does not arrive within five minutes."
}

Input: The API returns a 500 error every time I try to create a webhook. This is blocking our deploy.
Output:
{
  "priority": "High",
  "summary": "Customer experiencing 500 errors on webhook creation endpoint.",
  "draft_reply": "Thank you for reporting this. I am escalating this to our engineering team immediately and will update you within 30 minutes with a status."
}

Input: Do you offer discounts for nonprofits? Just curious.
Output:
{
  "priority": "Low",
  "summary": "Customer inquiring about nonprofit pricing.",
  "draft_reply": "Thanks for reaching out. Yes, we do offer nonprofit discounts. I have attached our application form for you to review."
}

Your exact wording will vary because LLMs are stochastic, but the structure should remain consistent thanks to JSON mode.

Next steps

You now have a working agent that classifies, summarizes, and responds. Two concrete ways to push it further:

  1. Add function calling so the agent can look up account status or create a refund in your CRM before it drafts the reply. Oxlo.ai supports tool use on models like qwen-3-32b and kimi-k2.6, so you can give the model real powers instead of just text.
  2. Move from a batch script to a streaming endpoint. Swap the script for a FastAPI service and use Oxlo.ai's streaming responses to return tokens to a front-end dashboard as they are generated. The SDK change is minimal: set stream=True and iterate over chunks instead of waiting for the full response.

If you want to experiment with larger reasoning models for harder tickets, try swapping the model ID to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, you can send long ticket threads or full conversation history without watching token meters spin up. For teams processing thousands of long-context tickets a day, that pricing model can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. Check the pricing page to see how the flat per-request cost fits your workload.

title: Optimizing LLM-Based Chatbots for Cost Efficiency
content:
Building production-grade LLM chatbots often reveals a hidden tax: operational cost scales with conversation length. Every system instruction, retrieved document, and prior turn inflates the prompt, and under token-based pricing, the bill grows with each additional word. For teams running customer support agents, internal knowledge bases, or multi-step reasoning workflows, these costs can become the primary barrier to deployment. The good news is that cost efficiency is not only about using a smaller model. It is about architecture choices, context management, and selecting an inference backend whose pricing model aligns with how chatbots actually consume tokens.

Context Compression and Session Truncation

Chatbots naturally accumulate state. A multi-turn conversation with retrieval-augmented generation can easily exceed 8,000 to 16,000 tokens of context. Under token-based billing, you pay for the full input on every single request, including history the model has already seen. One effective mitigation is prompt compression. Before sending the conversation to the inference API, summarize older turns into a condensed memory block. You can trigger this when the session exceeds a token threshold, such as 6,000 tokens, or after a fixed number of turns. Once the threshold is crossed, call a lightweight model to compress the earliest exchanges into a single paragraph. Store that summary as a pseudo-message and drop the original turns. Your subsequent requests then include the summary, the most recent turns, and the current user message, reducing total input length while preserving intent. This technique is especially effective for support bots where the first half of a conversation covers authentication and the second half addresses the actual issue. The summary retains facts while dropping polite filler and redundant confirmations.

Another approach is truncation with a sliding window. Retain only the last N messages plus any critical system context. This trades some long-range coherence for immediate cost savings. If your chatbot relies on extensive retrieved documents, re-rank chunks and inject only the top two or three passages rather than a full page. The goal is to send the minimum context required to answer accurately, not the maximum context the model allows.

Model Routing and Task-Specific Selection

Not every user query requires a 70B-parameter flagship model. A significant fraction of chatbot traffic consists of greetings, FAQ-style lookups, or simple formatting tasks that a 32B model handles with near-identical quality. Implementing a routing layer lets you classify intent with a small, fast model before deciding whether to escalate to a larger reasoning engine. Oxlo.ai offers 45+ models across seven categories, so you can match the tool to the task without managing multiple provider accounts. Route routine queries to Qwen 3 32B or Llama 3.3 70B, and reserve DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 for deep reasoning or complex coding. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, the cost of that initial routing call is predictable and does not balloon if you include a detailed system prompt or few-shot examples.

import os
import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]
)

def classify_intent(user_message: str) -> str:
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Classify intent as simple, coding, or reasoning. Reply with one word."},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message}
        ],
        max_tokens=10
    )

title: Revolutionizing Customer Service with LLMs: Best Practices and Applications
content:
Customer service infrastructure is moving past rigid decision trees and keyword matching. Large language models now handle nuanced intent, maintain context across dozens of turns, and resolve issues without human intervention. For engineering teams building modern support stacks, the challenge is no longer whether to adopt LLMs, but how to deploy them reliably without letting inference costs scale unpredictably with every extra line of conversation history. The right platform gives you model flexibility, deterministic tool use, and pricing that stays flat even when your context windows fill up.

Why LLMs Change the Game for Support

Traditional chatbots break when a user deviates from a script. LLMs handle ambiguity. They parse typos, detect sentiment, switch languages mid-thread, and reason through multi-step troubleshooting. This shifts the role of automation from gatekeeper to actual problem solver.

For global teams, multilingual reasoning is essential. A model that can reason in the user's native language and then summarize the interaction for an English-speaking agent reduces friction significantly. Modern architectures also let these models invoke tools, query knowledge bases, and update tickets through function calling rather than generating text alone. The result is a support experience that feels less like a form and more like a competent colleague.

Core Applications in Modern Support Stacks

The most impactful deployments of LLMs in customer service fall into four distinct categories.

First, Tier-1 resolution. LLMs equipped with retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, answer FAQs, process refunds, and reset credentials by grounding responses in internal documentation. When connected to an embedding index of your help center, the model cites accurate policies instead of hallucinating answers.

Second, agent assist. Real-time suggestions, response drafting, and sentiment summaries help human agents work faster while maintaining tone consistency. An LLM can draft a compassionate response to an angry customer in seconds, letting the agent edit and send rather than composing from scratch.

Third, intelligent routing. By analyzing the content and urgency of a message, an LLM can classify tickets and escalate complex issues to the correct department before a human reads them. This reduces mean time to resolution and prevents billing questions from clogging the technical queue.

Fourth, post-interaction analytics. Models extract structured data from unstructured transcripts, identifying product bugs, feature requests, and churn signals at scale. Instead of reading thousands of chats, product teams receive automated weekly summaries of emerging issues.

Architectural Best Practices

Building a production-grade support agent requires more than a prompt and a model endpoint. Reliability comes from structure and observability.

Use function calling for deterministic actions. When a customer asks to cancel an order, the model should emit a JSON payload to your orders API, not hallucinate a confirmation number. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and JSON mode across its chat models,

title: Unlocking the Power of LLMs for Semantic Role Labeling
content:
Semantic role labeling has traditionally required handcrafted features, task-specific architectures, and extensive annotated corpora following frameworks such as PropBank or FrameNet. Large language models have reframed the problem. Instead of training a dedicated classifier for predicate-argument structure, developers can now prompt a general-purpose model to identify who did what to whom. This shift reduces engineering overhead, but it introduces a new constraint. Production SRL pipelines must handle long input documents, enforce structured output formats, and control inference costs at scale. The infrastructure layer you choose determines whether the transition from research prototype to deployed system succeeds.

From Task-Specific Models to General-Purpose LLMs

Classical SRL systems rely on syntactic parsers and bi-LSTM or BERT-based taggers trained on narrow datasets. These models perform well on benchmark splits, but they generalize poorly across domains and require feature engineering for each new language or genre. LLMs invert this workflow. A model with broad pretraining can perform zero-shot or few-shot SRL given only a natural language description of roles such as AGENT, PATIENT, INSTRUMENT, and LOCATION.

The flexibility comes at a computational cost. A single document may contain dozens of predicates, and resolving argument structure accurately often requires sending an entire paragraph or page as context. When you process thousands of documents per hour, token-based billing accumulates quickly because every input character contributes to the final charge. Inference infrastructure built for chat completions is not automatically optimized for batch annotation workflows that feed downstream analytics or retrieval pipelines.

Prompt Design and Structured Extraction

Effective LLM-based SRL depends on precise output control. You cannot consume free-form text if the goal is to populate a knowledge graph or update a relational database. You need structured extraction. Modern APIs support JSON mode and function calling, which lets you define a schema for predicates and arguments and receive machine-readable objects rather than prose.

Multi-turn conversations also help. A system prompt can establish the SRL guidelines, and subsequent turns can iterate over segments of a long document or disambiguate coreferential mentions. Streaming responses keep latency tolerable for interactive tools, while JSON mode guarantees that the extracted frame elements conform to your downstream expectations. Without these features, an SRL service becomes a brittle string-parsing layer wrapped around a language model.

Inference Requirements for Document-Level SRL

Production SRL rarely operates on isolated sentences. Legal contracts, medical records, and financial filings contain long-range dependencies where the subject of a predicate appears three paragraphs earlier. This means your inference backend must accept large context windows without degrading throughput. It also means that input length is not an edge case. It is the normal operating mode. Batch pipelines that annotate entire document collections exacerbate the issue, because queue depth grows quickly when each item carries thousands of tokens.

Cold starts are another concern. If your pipeline processes sporadic batches of documents, waiting several seconds for a GPU node to spin up destroys throughput guarantees. Consistent sub-second time-to-first-token matters for both synchronous APIs and asynchronous job queues. Finally, the backend should expose standard endpoints so you can swap or A/B test models without rewriting client logic. An OpenAI-compatible surface is the closest thing to a universal standard for LLM inference, and it simplifies integration with existing orchestration frameworks.

Deploying SRL Pipelines on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first inference platform designed for exactly these constraints. It offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including LLMs and chat models fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based metering, the cost of a long-context SRL request is the same whether you send a terse sentence or a full-page legal clause. For document-level workloads, this structural difference can yield significant savings compared to token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale.

The platform exposes standard endpoints including chat/completions and supports streaming, function calling, JSON mode, and vision inputs. There are no cold starts on popular models, so batch SRL jobs start immediately. You can point your existing OpenAI client to the Oxlo.ai base URL and change only the model name.

A Drop-In API Example

The following Python snippet demonstrates how to run a structured SRL request against Oxlo.ai using the OpenAI SDK. The example sends a paragraph and requests a JSON object containing predicates and their semantic arguments. Notice that the only configuration change from a standard OpenAI setup is the base URL.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a semantic role labeling engine. "
                "Extract every predicate and its arguments from the input text. "
                "Return valid JSON with keys: predicate, arguments. "
                "Each argument should include role and text."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "The committee approved the merger after the regulators "
                "reviewed the financial statements submitted by the attorneys."
            )
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can reuse existing retry logic, streaming handlers, and Pydantic validators without modification. Switching from another provider to Oxlo.ai requires a single line change to base_url.

Choosing Models for SRL Workloads

Oxlo.ai carries multiple architectures that suit different SRL requirements. For general-purpose English annotation, Llama 3.3 70B offers strong instruction following and reliable JSON adherence. If your corpus is multilingual, Qwen 3 32B provides robust reasoning across dozens of languages and handles agentic workflows should you need to chain SRL with entity linking or coreference resolution.

When predicates are ambiguous or arguments require deep logical inference, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 deliver advanced chain-of-thought reasoning. GLM 5, with its 744B MoE architecture, excels at long-horizon agentic tasks that interleave SRL with planning and tool use. For extremely long documents, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window and efficient MoE routing, making it suitable for book-level or contract-level SRL. Developers who need a fast, cost-effective default for high-volume extraction can start with DeepSeek V3.2, which is available on the free tier and optimized for coding and reasoning tasks.

Cost Efficiency with Request-Based Pricing

The economics of LLM-based SRL favor flat pricing when inputs are long. Token-based billing means that every paragraph you send incurs a cost proportional to its length. In practice, SRL prompts often contain the full source text plus lengthy system instructions and few-shot examples. Under token-based schemes, these compound.

Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, request-based pricing can be 10 to 100 times cheaper than token-based alternatives. This is not a marginal discount. It is a structural advantage that makes document-level SRL economically viable at high volume. You can explore the exact tiers on the Oxlo.ai pricing page, which includes a free plan with 60 requests per day and a 7-day full-access trial, as well as Pro, Premium, and Enterprise plans for production traffic.

Building Production-Ready SRL

Semantic role labeling with LLMs is no longer a research curiosity. It is a production data extraction technique that demands structured output, long-context support, and predictable costs. The infrastructure you select should not force you to truncate documents or strip system prompts to save tokens. It should give you access to state-of-the-art open-source models through a standard API, start instantly, and price requests as atomic units rather than character streams.

Oxlo.ai meets these requirements with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a broad model catalog spanning general chat to deep reasoning, and a request-based pricing model that protects budgets as context lengths grow. If you are building an SRL pipeline, start with the free tier, test your prompt templates against Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B, and scale knowing that your per-request costs remain flat regardless of how much text you send. For teams with existing token-based bills, the Enterprise plan offers dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction over your current provider, making the migration path straightforward.
