title: LLM for Dependency Parsing with Oxlo
content:
I built this LLM-based dependency parser for a pipeline that processes mixed-domain text without maintaining language-specific spaCy models. Instead of shipping a separate Stanford CoreNLP or UDPipe instance for each language, I send sentences to Oxlo.ai and receive Universal Dependencies JSON that I validate and convert to a readable tree format. The entire implementation is under a hundred lines of Python, handles English and multilingual inputs, and benefits from Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing regardless of sentence length.

What you'll need

Before starting, make sure you have the following ready:

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the OpenAI SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI-compatible, this is a drop-in replacement. I verify the connection with a quick sanity check before moving to structured generation.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say connected"}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the dependency schema and system prompt

Dependency parsing requires strict consistency. I lock the output format in the system prompt so the model returns a flat JSON array of tokens with Universal Dependencies fields. I explicitly forbid markdown fences and ask for raw JSON to reduce post-processing overhead.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a dependency parser. Given a sentence, analyze its syntactic structure and return a JSON array of dependencies.

For each token, provide:
- id: token index starting at 1
- text: the token string
- lemma: base form
- pos: part of speech using UPOS tags
- head: index of the governor token (0 for root)
- deprel: universal dependency relation

Rules:
- Exactly one token must have head: 0 and deprel: "root"
- Do not merge punctuation into other tokens
- Return only valid JSON, no markdown fences
"""

Step 3: Build the parsing function

Now I wrap the API call in a function that sends the sentence to Oxlo.ai with a low temperature to keep the grammar analysis deterministic. I strip any accidental markdown fences, then parse the JSON. I default to llama-3.3-70b because it follows structured instructions reliably and keeps latency low.

import json

def parse_dependencies(sentence, model="llama-3.3-70b"):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Parse this sentence: {sentence}"},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=2048,
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Validate and format the tree

Universal Dependencies trees must have exactly one root and no orphaned tokens. I add a small validator that checks indices and root uniqueness before I trust the result. I also include a helper that prints a human-readable dependency tree for quick inspection.

def validate_tree(deps):
    ids = {t["id"] for t in deps}
    heads = [t["head"] for t in deps]
    
    if heads.count(0) != 1:
        raise ValueError("Tree must have exactly one root")
    
    for h in heads:
        if h != 0 and h not in ids:
            raise ValueError(f"Orphaned head index: {h}")
    
    return True

def print_tree(deps):
    for token in deps:
        head_word = next((d["text"] for d in deps if d["id"] == token["head"]), "ROOT")
        print(f"{token['text']:12} -> {head_word} ({token['deprel']})")

Step 5: Batch processing

For production use, I process multiple sentences in a loop. I switch to qwen-3-32b for multilingual inputs. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based metering, the cost of parsing ten short sentences is the same as parsing one long paragraph split across calls. This makes iterative testing and batch extraction predictable, and you can explore exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

sentences = [
    "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.",
    "Oxlo.ai offers flat per-request pricing for LLM workloads.",
    "El rápido zorro salta sobre el perro perezoso.",
]

for sent in sentences:
    try:
        deps = parse_dependencies(sent, model="qwen-3-32b")
        validate_tree(deps)
        print(f"\n{sent}")
        print_tree(deps)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error on '{sent}': {e}")

Run it

I save the script as parse.py, set my API key, and run it against a straightforward sentence to verify the end-to-end flow. Here is the invocation and the resulting output for "Developers love clean APIs.":

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sent = "Developers love clean APIs."
    deps = parse_dependencies(sent)
    validate_tree(deps)
    print_tree(deps)

Terminal output:

Developers   -> love (nsubj)
love         -> ROOT (root)
clean        -> APIs (amod)
APIs         -> love (obj)
.            -> love (punct)

Wrap-up and next steps

This parser is not a replacement for a trained spaCy or Stanza pipeline if you need millisecond latency on a CPU. It is a pragmatic fallback when you need multilingual support, domain adaptation, or rapid prototyping without managing model artifacts. Two concrete next steps: pipe the CoNLL-U output into displaCy to render SVG dependency trees, or store parsed sentences in SQLite and use them as input for a relation extraction model. If you are running large batches, the Oxlo.ai flat per-request model keeps long-context preprocessing affordable and easy to forecast.

title: Building a Chatbot with LLM using Oxlo
content:
Chatbots are now the standard interface for delivering large language model capabilities to end users. Whether you are automating customer support, building an internal knowledge assistant, or prototyping an agentic workflow, the quality of your infrastructure directly impacts latency, cost, and user experience. Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first inference platform with flat per-request pricing and full OpenAI SDK compatibility, so you can build and scale conversational applications without refactoring your existing code or worrying about token budgets on every turn.

Why Oxlo.ai? Flat Pricing and Long Context

Most inference providers charge by the token. In a chatbot, every user message, system instruction, and prior turn adds to the input token count. As conversations grow, costs scale linearly. Oxlo.ai uses a request-based pricing model: you pay one flat cost per API call regardless of how many tokens are in the prompt. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can reduce costs significantly compared to token-based alternatives. You also avoid the operational overhead of counting tokens before every request to estimate spend.

This pricing structure changes how you design conversation state. You do not need to aggressively trim history or compress prompts to save money. You can keep the full system prompt and conversation history in every request without watching a meter tick upward on each turn. Beyond pricing, Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including general-purpose LLMs, reasoning specialists, vision models, and code generators. Popular options for chatbot development include Llama 3.3 70B for reliable general conversation, Qwen 3 32B for multilingual and agentic tasks, and Kimi K2.6 for advanced reasoning with a 131K context window. There are no cold starts on popular models, so your chatbot responds immediately even after periods of inactivity.

Project Setup and Authentication

Because Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, you can use the official Python or Node.js client libraries. Start by installing the package.

pip install openai

Next, configure your client with the Oxlo.ai base URL and your API key.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your-oxlo.ai-api-key"
)

If you are using Node.js, the pattern is identical. Set baseURL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and instantiate the client with your key. You can also test endpoints directly with cURL or any HTTP client that supports Server-Sent Events for streaming. This drop-in replacement means you can migrate an existing chatbot or start a new project without learning a custom SDK.

Building a Basic Chat Loop

A minimal chatbot requires a system message, a user message, and a loop that appends the assistant's reply to the conversation history. Here is a complete Python example using Llama 3.3 70B.

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant that answers questions concisely."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "How do I implement pagination in a REST API?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    temperature=0.7
)

assistant_reply = response.choices[0].message.content
print(assistant_reply)

The chat/completions endpoint accepts the same schema as OpenAI's API. You can set parameters such as temperature, max_tokens, and top_p to control output behavior. Because Oxlo.ai does not charge by the token, you can set a generous max_tokens value without inflating the cost of the request itself.

Managing Conversation History

Stateless LLMs do not remember previous turns. Your application must maintain the messages array and send the full history with each request. In a production chatbot, you will append both user and assistant messages to this array.

messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
response = client.chat.completions.create(model="llama-3.3-70b", messages=messages)
assistant_reply = response.choices[0].message.content
messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_reply})

As conversations grow, context windows become a concern. Oxlo.ai hosts models with extended context lengths that are ideal for long sessions. DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window, and Kimi K2.6 offers 131K tokens for advanced reasoning and agentic coding. With flat per-request pricing, expanding the conversation history does not increase your cost per turn, which makes these models practical for persistent chat sessions. You can review request allowances on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Enabling Function Calling for Agentic Behavior

Modern chatbots rarely stop at text generation. They need to query databases, call APIs, or execute code. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use on compatible models. Below is an example that gives the LLM access to a mock weather API.

import json

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get the current weather for a location",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {"type": "string", "description": "City and country"}
                },
                "required": ["location"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Berlin?"})

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen-3-32b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools
)

message = response.choices[0].message

if message.tool_calls:
    tool_call = message.tool_calls[0]
    if tool_call.function.name == "get_weather":
        args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
        weather_result = get_weather(args["location"])
        messages.append(message.model_dump())
        messages.append({
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
            "content": weather_result
        })
        final_response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="qwen-3-32b",
            messages=messages,
            tools=tools
        )
        print(final_response.choices[0].message.content)

Models such as Qwen 3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, and GLM 5 handle tool use reliably. You can extend this pattern to create agentic workflows that iterate through multiple tool calls before returning a final answer to the user.

Streaming Responses for Real-Time UX

Waiting for the full response to generate before displaying it creates a sluggish user experience. Streaming allows you to render tokens as they arrive. Enable it by setting stream=True.

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    stream=True
)

for chunk in stream:
    content = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
    if content:
        print(content, end="", flush=True)

Streaming is supported across Oxlo.ai's chat models and integrates cleanly with frontend frameworks such as React, Vue, or plain WebSocket interfaces. Because there are no cold starts, the first chunk arrives quickly even if the model has been idle.

Selecting the Right Model for Your Chatbot

Choosing the right model depends on your chatbot's domain and language requirements. For general-purpose English conversation, Llama 3.3 70B offers a strong balance of capability and speed. If your users speak multiple languages or you need agentic tool use, Qwen 3 32B is optimized for multilingual reasoning and workflows. For complex coding assistance or deep logical reasoning, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2 Thinking provide advanced chain-of-thought performance. When you need to process extremely long documents in a single session, DeepSeek V4 Flash delivers near state-of-the-art reasoning with a 1 million token context window. If cost sensitivity is critical, DeepSeek V3.2 is available on the free tier and handles coding and reasoning tasks efficiently. For multimodal chatbots that accept image uploads, consider Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B.

Deploying to Production

Oxlo.ai offers tiered plans that scale from prototyping to production. The Free plan includes 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 models, with a 7-day full-access trial to test premium models. The Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day across all models, while the Premium plan offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queueing. For teams with heavy throughput requirements, the Enterprise plan delivers dedicated GPUs and custom pricing.

Because Oxlo.ai does not use token-based metering, your monthly bill is predictable. A spike in user activity that generates long messages will not trigger unexpected overages. The platform is a true OpenAI SDK drop-in replacement, so your existing middleware, logging, and frontend code work without modification. This stability makes it easier to budget for and maintain production chatbot deployments.

Conclusion

Building a chatbot on Oxlo.ai requires minimal boilerplate. The OpenAI SDK compatibility means you can reuse existing tutorials, middleware, and frontend components. The flat per-request pricing model removes the penalty for long conversations and large context windows, which are common in real-world chatbot usage. With over 45 models, no cold starts, and support for streaming, function calling, and JSON mode, Oxlo.ai gives you the infrastructure to move from prototype to production without rewriting your integration. Set your base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, pick a model that fits your use case, and start building. For details on request allowances and plans, visit the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

title: Conversational AI Tutorial with Oxlo
content:
We are going to build a conversational support triage agent that collects issue details across multiple turns and outputs a structured ticket summary. This helps small support teams automate intake without building complex workflow engines. We will run it on Oxlo.ai because its flat per-request pricing keeps costs predictable even when users paste long logs into the chat, and the OpenAI SDK compatibility means we do not need a new client library.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed on your machine. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which you can install with pip install openai. Finally, grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal at https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free plan gives you 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 models, which is plenty for testing this agent. If you want to explore paid plans later, you can check https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Scaffold the client

Create a new file named support_agent.py and set up the OpenAI-compatible client pointing to Oxlo.ai. I am using Llama 3.3 70B because it follows multi-turn instructions reliably, and Oxlo.ai serves it with no cold starts so the first request is just as fast as any other.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def get_agent_reply(messages):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract that governs the agent's personality. It must restrict the model to asking clarifying questions and prevent it from drifting into technical troubleshooting.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent for a SaaS platform. Your goal is to collect enough information to create an internal support ticket.

Rules:
- Greet the user, then ask one focused question per turn.
- If the user mentions a bug, ask for reproduction steps and the browser or API client they are using.
- If the user mentions a billing issue, ask for the email associated with the account.
- Do not provide technical fixes, workarounds, or troubleshooting steps.
- Once you have the issue type, a clear description, and an account identifier, ask if there is anything else to add.
- If the user says they are done, respond with exactly: TICKET_READY"""

Step 3: Manage conversation history

Conversational AI requires memory. I keep a Python list of message dictionaries in memory, appending each user message and assistant reply so the model retains context across the entire session.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent for a SaaS platform. Your goal is to collect enough information to create an internal support ticket.

Rules:
- Greet the user, then ask one focused question per turn.
- If the user mentions a bug, ask for reproduction steps and the browser or API client they are using.
- If the user mentions a billing issue, ask for the email associated with the account.
- Do not provide technical fixes, workarounds, or troubleshooting steps.
- Once you have the issue type, a clear description, and an account identifier, ask if there is anything else to add.
- If the user says they are done, respond with exactly: TICKET_READY"""

def get_agent_reply(messages):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

def run_conversation():
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    print("Agent: Hello, how can I help you today?")
    
    while True:
        user_input = input("User: ").strip()
        if not user_input:
            continue
        
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
        reply = get_agent_reply(messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
        
        if "TICKET_READY" in reply:
            print("Agent: Preparing your ticket summary...")
            return messages
        else:
            print(f"Agent: {reply}")

Step 4: Add structured output

When the user finishes, I want a machine-readable ticket summary. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, so I make a second API call with a strict formatter prompt and parse the result with Python's json module.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def generate_ticket_summary(conversation):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a JSON formatter. Output valid JSON only with keys: category, priority, description, account_email."},
            {"role": "user", "content": json.dumps(conversation)}
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.2,
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 5: Assemble the complete agent

Now I combine the conversation loop and the JSON extractor into a single script. Running this file starts an interactive session in your terminal. The main function initializes the message history, drives the loop, and triggers summary generation when it sees the TICKET_READY signal.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent for a SaaS platform. Your goal is to collect enough information to create an internal support ticket.

Rules:
- Greet the user, then ask one focused question per turn.
- If the user mentions a bug, ask for reproduction steps and the browser or API client they are using.
- If the user mentions a billing issue, ask for the email associated with the account.
- Do not provide technical fixes, workarounds, or troubleshooting steps.
- Once you have the issue type, a clear description, and an account identifier, ask if there is anything else to add.
- If the user says they are done, respond with exactly: TICKET_READY"""

def get_agent_reply(messages):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

def generate_ticket_summary(conversation):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a JSON formatter. Output valid JSON only with keys: category, priority, description, account_email."},
            {"role": "user", "content": json.dumps(conversation)}
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.2,
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

def main():
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    print("Agent: Hello, how can I help you today?")
    
    while True:
        user_input = input("User: ").strip()
        if not user_input:
            continue
        
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
        reply = get_agent_reply(messages)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
        
        if "TICKET_READY" in reply:
            print("Agent: Preparing your ticket summary...")
            summary = generate_ticket_summary(messages)
            print("\n--- Ticket Summary ---")
            print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
            break
        else:
            print(f"Agent: {reply}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it

Execute the script in your terminal. Type responses to the agent's questions naturally, and enter "done" when you have nothing else to add. The transcript below shows what a successful run looks like when the user reports an API bug. Notice how the agent stays in character and does not attempt to debug the issue itself.

$ python support_agent.py
Agent: Hello, how can I help you today?
User: I keep getting a 500 error on the billing endpoint
Agent: Thanks for reporting that. Which API client or browser are you using when you see the 500 error?
User: Python requests library
Agent: Got it. Can you share the account email associated with the workspace?
User: alice@example.com
Agent: Is there anything else I should add to the ticket?
User: done
Agent: Preparing your ticket summary...

--- Ticket Summary ---
{
  "category": "bug",
  "priority": "high",
  "description": "500 error on billing endpoint when using Python requests library",
  "account_email": "alice@example.com"
}

Next steps

To productionize this, wrap the script in a FastAPI endpoint and store the messages list in Redis so the agent survives server restarts. You could also swap in kimi-k2.6 or qwen-3-32b if you need stronger reasoning for ambiguous user inputs, since Oxlo.ai lets you change the model string without touching any other client code.

title: LLM for Named Entity Recognition
content:
We are going to build a Named Entity Recognition pipeline that turns unstructured text into structured JSON. Instead of training a custom spaCy model or maintaining brittle regex rules, we will use an off-the-shelf LLM to extract people, organizations, locations, and dates. This is ideal for analysts, data engineers, and founders who need to prototype fast without managing ML infrastructure.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer. I use 3.11, but anything above 3.10 works.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai offers request-based pricing, so your cost stays flat per API call even when you feed the model long news articles or legal briefs. For current rates, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed locally: pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI API compatible, so this is the only client you need.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

First, we instantiate the OpenAI-compatible client pointing at Oxlo.ai. I chose llama-3.3-70b because it handles instruction following reliably for extraction tasks, and Oxlo.ai serves it with no cold starts, so the first request after idle is just as fast as the hundredth. If you prefer multilingual input or agentic reasoning, you can swap in qwen-3-32b or deepseek-v3.2 without changing any other code.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say OK"},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training signal we need. It defines the entity types, the output schema, and a strict formatting rule. I force raw JSON instead of markdown code blocks because markdown adds noise that breaks automated parsers. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode if you want schema enforcement at the API level, but an explicit prompt works across every model and keeps the example self-contained.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise Named Entity Recognition engine.
Extract entities from the user text and return ONLY a JSON object.
Use this exact schema:
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "..."}
  ]
}
Include only the JSON. No markdown, no explanation."""

Step 3: Build the extraction function

Next, we wrap the API call in a function that accepts raw text, injects it into the user message, and returns parsed JSON. I added a small guard clause so that if the model ever returns a stray markdown fence or trailing sentence, the pipeline logs the raw output instead of crashing. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, you can send a full page of text in a single call without watching token meters climb.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise Named Entity Recognition engine.
Extract entities from the user text and return ONLY a JSON object.
Use this exact schema:
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "..."}
  ]
}
Include only the JSON. No markdown, no explanation."""

def extract_entities(text: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"error": "Invalid JSON", "raw": raw}

sample = "Apple Inc. is planning to open a new office in Berlin in March 2026."
print(extract_entities(sample))

Step 4: Process multiple documents

Production workloads rarely stop at one paragraph. Here we loop over a list of strings and collect results. I often run this over scraped earnings calls or SEC filings. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, not per token, feeding the model a long annual report costs the same flat rate as a short tweet. That makes this pattern economical for document-heavy pipelines.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise Named Entity Recognition engine.
Extract entities from the user text and return ONLY a JSON object.
Use this exact schema:
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "..."}
  ]
}
Include only the JSON. No markdown, no explanation."""

def extract_entities(text: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"error": "Invalid JSON", "raw": raw}

documents = [
    "Apple Inc. is planning to open a new office in Berlin in March 2026.",
    "Satya Nadella announced that Microsoft will expand its AI research lab in London by January 2027.",
    "The European Central Bank, led by Christine Lagarde, met in Frankfurt last Tuesday.",
]

for doc in documents:
    entities = extract_entities(doc)
    print(json.dumps(entities, indent=2))

Step 5: Validate with Pydantic

Raw JSON is fragile. I add a lightweight Pydantic model so that missing keys or unexpected types surface immediately. This turns a prototype into something you can trust in a data workflow. The validator sits right after the Oxlo.ai response, so you catch model drift before it corrupts downstream tables.

import json
from typing import List
from pydantic import BaseModel
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise Named Entity Recognition engine.
Extract entities from the user text and return ONLY a JSON object.
Use this exact schema:
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "..."},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "..."}
  ]
}
Include only the JSON. No markdown, no explanation."""

class Entity(BaseModel):
    type: str
    text: str

class NERResult(BaseModel):
    entities: List[Entity]

def extract_entities(text: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    try:
        parsed = json.loads(raw)
        return NERResult(**parsed).model_dump()
    except Exception as e:
        return {"error": str(e), "raw": raw}

print(extract_entities("Sam Altman spoke at OpenAI headquarters in San Francisco on June 10th."))

Run it

Save the final script as ner_pipeline.py, export your API key, and execute it. Here is the output I see when running against Oxlo.ai.

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
$ python ner_pipeline.py

{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "Apple Inc."},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "Berlin"},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "March 2026"}
  ]
}
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "Satya Nadella"},
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "Microsoft"},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "London"},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "January 2027"}
  ]
}
{
  "entities": [
    {"type": "ORG", "text": "European Central Bank"},
    {"type": "PERSON", "text": "Christine Lagarde"},
    {"type": "LOCATION", "text": "Frankfurt"},
    {"type": "DATE", "text": "last Tuesday"}
  ]
}

Next steps

From here, you can wrap the extractor in an async FastAPI endpoint and enqueue thousands of documents. Oxlo.ai serves popular models with no cold starts, so the first request after idle is just as fast as the hundredth.

If you need deeper reasoning for nested corporate structures or multilingual support, swap in qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6. Both are available on Oxlo.ai under the same flat request-based pricing, which makes long-context NER workloads significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives.

title: Dialogue Systems with LLMs
content:
Dialogue systems have evolved far beyond rigid intent-slot architectures and hand-crafted finite state machines. Modern conversational agents rely on large language models to manage open-domain discourse, execute external actions, and maintain coherence across dozens or even hundreds of turns. Yet productionizing these systems introduces friction that pure research benchmarks often ignore. Context windows fill up. Latency compounds. Token costs scale silently with every additional turn of conversation. Building a robust LLM-powered dialogue system requires deliberate architecture choices around state management, tool integration, streaming behavior, and inference economics. The backend you choose shapes which architectural patterns are practical and which remain constrained by billing or latency.

Context Windows and State Management

At the core of any LLM dialogue system is the context window. Unlike traditional systems that stored dialogue state in explicit databases or belief trackers, LLMs rely on implicit state encoded directly in the prompt. Every user utterance, system response, retrieved document, and tool result consumes tokens. Over a long session, histories grow linearly. Summarization strategies, sliding window truncation, and hierarchical memory banks become necessary engineering concerns rather than optional optimizations.

The choice of context architecture directly impacts response quality. A naive approach that stuffs the full transcript into a fixed window eventually hits limits or dilutes attention. More sophisticated systems maintain a condensed summary of early turns while preserving recent utterances verbatim. Others vectorize the conversation history into an embedding store and retrieve relevant prior turns on demand. These patterns reduce raw token volume but add retrieval latency and complexity. When the inference provider charges by token, every extra line of history carries a recurring cost. With request-based pricing, engineers can keep fuller transcripts in context without economic penalty, simplifying memory design.

Tool Use and ReAct Patterns

Practical dialogue systems rarely operate in isolation. They query calendars, search knowledge bases, update tickets, and trigger actions in external APIs. Function calling bridges natural language understanding and structured execution. The model parses user intent, emits a JSON payload representing a tool invocation, and waits for results before generating a final response.

This loop introduces statefulness. The dialogue manager must append the function result to the message history, then issue a follow-up completion request. Each iteration extends the prompt. In token-priced environments, a multi-turn conversation with several tool calls can accumulate surprising costs because every prior tool result is replayed into the context. ReAct-style patterns, where the model reasons step by step and issues multiple tool calls before answering, amplify this effect. Parallel tool calling helps reduce turn count but still increases prompt size. With request-based pricing, the cost per turn remains constant even as the prompt grows, which is especially valuable for agentic dialogue loops.

Oxlo.ai provides native function calling, streaming responses, and JSON mode across its chat models. Developers can implement ReAct-style reasoning loops or deterministic tool pipelines without modifying client logic. The platform exposes a standard OpenAI-compatible SDK,

title: Building Conversational AI with LLMs
content:
Conversational AI has moved past simple chatbots. Modern systems rely on large language models to manage multi-turn dialogue, retain context across sessions, and execute tools in real time. Building these systems requires more than calling a completions endpoint. You need a model that handles nuanced reasoning, an infrastructure layer that scales with context length, and a cost model that stays predictable when conversations grow long or agentic loops multiply. This guide breaks down the core components and shows how to assemble them using production-ready infrastructure.

The Architecture of a Conversational Stack

A robust conversational application typically separates concerns into four layers: the model provider, the context manager, the tool executor, and the voice or multimodal interface. The model provider handles inference. The context manager stores conversation history, often in a vector database or cache. The tool executor translates model outputs into API calls, database queries, or code execution. Finally, the interface layer converts text to speech or processes image inputs when the interaction goes beyond text.

Each layer introduces latency and cost. The model provider is usually the bottleneck. Stateless chat APIs require the client to resend the full conversation history on every turn, which means payload size grows linearly with session length. If pricing scales with tokens, a long system prompt or a lengthy conversation history can inflate costs quickly. This is where pricing structure directly affects architecture decisions, especially when you want to retain full context rather than aggressively truncating it.

Selecting Models for Dialogue and Reasoning

Not every LLM is optimized for back-and-forth conversation. Multi-turn dialogue exposes weaknesses in instruction following and consistency. You want models with strong steerability, support for function calling, and large context windows to retain prior turns without losing coherence.

Oxlo.ai offers several options across this spectrum. For general-purpose dialogue, Llama 3.3 70B provides a balanced mix of reasoning and latency. If you are building multilingual agents or complex agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B is specifically designed for multilingual reasoning and tool use. For applications requiring deep reasoning or advanced coding within a conversation, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 deliver advanced chain-of-thought reasoning and agentic coding capabilities. Kimi K2.6 also supports vision inputs and a 131K context window, making it suitable for conversations that include images or long documents. For long-horizon agentic tasks, GLM 5, a 744B MoE, is built to handle extended sessions, while Minimax M2.5 excels at coding and tool use within conversational loops. For balanced throughput and reasoning, DeepSeek V3 and Mistral are also available.

If you need a lightweight coding assistant inside a chat interface, Qwen 3 Coder 30B or Oxlo.ai Coder Fast are available. The key is matching model capability to conversational depth. A customer support bot may not need a 671B parameter reasoning model, but an AI coding companion probably does.

Managing Context and Memory

Conversations drift. Users refer to messages from ten turns ago or upload a PDF and ask questions about it. Your system needs to keep that context accessible without ballooning costs.

Context management usually follows one of two patterns. The first is sliding window truncation, where you keep the most recent N messages and summarize the rest. The second is full context retention, where you pass the entire conversation history into every request. Full retention produces higher quality responses but consumes far more input tokens. When you add retrieval-augmented generation, embedding search results also consume context space.

This cost dynamic is critical. On token-based platforms, long context workloads become expensive because every token in the prompt is billed on every request. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For conversational systems that retain full context or process long documents, this structure can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. Models like DeepSeek V4 Flash, which supports a 1M context window, or Kimi K2.6 with 131K tokens, become practical to use at full length when you are not paying per token. Oxlo.ai also offers no cold starts on popular models, so multi-turn sessions do not suffer from warmup latency after idle periods.

Function Calling and Agentic Workflows

Truly useful conversational AI does more than talk. It books meetings, queries databases, and modifies code. This requires structured outputs and function calling.

The model must be able to emit JSON or specific tool schemas reliably. Oxlo.ai supports function calling, tool use, and JSON mode across its chat models. You can define tools and let the model decide whether to respond directly or invoke an external function. After your application executes the function, you append the result to the message list and send a second request.

Here is a minimal example using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai. Because the API is fully OpenAI compatible, you only need to change the base URL and API key.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get current weather for a location",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["location"]
            }
        }
    }
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Berlin?"}
    ],
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

print(response.choices[0].message)

Because Oxlo.ai bills per request, not per token, this agentic loop, which often involves multiple round trips and large JSON payloads, remains cost predictable. You can also enable streaming responses so the user sees progress while the model decides which tool to call.

Extending Conversations to Voice and Vision

Text is not always the best medium. Voice interfaces and image uploads are increasingly common in conversational AI, and users expect the same session to handle every modality.

For audio transcription, Oxlo.ai hosts Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium. You can transcribe user speech to text via the audio/transcriptions endpoint, feed the result into a chat model, and synthesize a response using Kokoro 82M text-to-speech through the audio/speech endpoint. This creates a full voice pipeline without leaving the platform.

For vision, models like Kimi VL A3B and Gemma 3 27B accept image inputs. A user can share a screenshot or photo and ask questions about it within the same conversation thread. Because these calls are billed per request, adding an image to a long context session does not trigger a disproportionate cost spike. The same request-based logic applies whether you are sending a short text prompt or a complex multimodal message with a long history.

Cost Engineering and Scaling

Conversational AI workloads are unpredictable. One user might send ten short messages. Another might paste a hundred-page document and ask follow-up questions for an hour. Token-based billing makes these scenarios hard to budget because input costs scale with every word in the history.

Request-based pricing flips the model. You pay for the API call, not the volume inside it. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can translate to substantial savings. You can design your system to pass full histories, include large system prompts, or process long documents without optimizing every single token.

Oxlo.ai offers a free tier at $0 per month with 60 requests per day and access to 16+ free models, including DeepSeek V3.2 on the free tier. This is enough to prototype a conversational agent. Paid tiers scale to 1,000 requests per day on Pro and 5,000 per day on Premium, with priority queue access at the Premium level. Enterprise plans offer dedicated GPUs and unlimited volume. For exact pricing, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Integrating Oxlo.ai into Your Stack

Switching providers or starting fresh is straightforward. Oxlo.ai exposes standard OpenAI endpoints: chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech. The Python and Node.js SDKs work with a single line of configuration. If you are building a retrieval-augmented conversational system, embedding models like BGE-Large and E5-Large are available through the embeddings endpoint.

If you are currently building on OpenAI or another compatible provider, you can redirect your existing client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, pick a model from the 45+ available options, and retain your existing prompt engineering. Streaming responses work out of the box, so typing indicators and real-time conversational UIs require no additional logic. There are no cold starts on popular models, which means your users will not experience lag when a conversation resumes after a pause.

Conclusion

Building conversational AI requires balancing model capability, context retention, and cost control. The infrastructure you choose determines whether long conversations remain responsive and affordable. By selecting models with strong reasoning and tool support, architecting for full context retention, and using a platform with predictable request-based pricing, you can ship conversational experiences that scale without surprise bills.

Oxlo.ai provides the models, the compatibility, and the pricing structure to make this practical. With OpenAI SDK compatibility, no cold starts, and a catalog spanning reasoning, coding, vision, and audio, it is a strong fit for developers building the next generation of conversational systems.

title: LLM vs Traditional Machine Learning: Understanding the Differences
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage agent that classifies incoming messages and drafts replies. By implementing both a traditional scikit-learn pipeline and an LLM-powered version on Oxlo.ai, you will see exactly where each approach wins and where it breaks down. This tutorial is for any engineer who needs to pick the right tool for production instead of following the hype.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer installed locally. Install the dependencies with pip install openai scikit-learn pandas. The openai library is the standard SDK, and Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with it, so this is literally the only client you need. You also need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so experimenting with long system prompts or few-shot examples does not inflate your bill the way token-based metering would. You can check current plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. For this project, the Free tier gives you 60 requests per day and a 7-day full-access trial, which is plenty to test both approaches.

Step 1: Prepare the dataset

Traditional machine learning is supervised. It needs labeled examples to learn patterns. In production you would export your existing support tickets, but for this tutorial we will create a tiny DataFrame with three categories: billing, technical, and account. We split it into a training set for scikit-learn and a test set for comparison. The training set has only seven rows. That is enough to demonstrate the mechanics, though in real life a linear model like ours would need hundreds or thousands of rows to generalize well.

import pandas as pd

data = {
    "text": [
        "I was charged twice this month, please refund",
        "The API returns a 500 error when I post to /v1/chat",
        "I forgot my password and the reset email never arrives",
        "Can I upgrade my plan to Premium?",
        "Your webhook stopped firing after the last deploy",
        "I need an invoice for Q1 for my accountant",
        "The model returns gibberish on long prompts",
        "How do I add a new team member?",
        "My card expired and payment failed",
        "Streaming responses are truncated after 10 seconds"
    ],
    "label": [
        "billing", "technical", "account",
        "billing", "technical", "billing",
        "technical", "account", "billing",
        "technical"
    ]
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
train = df[:7]
test = df[7:]

print(f"Train samples: {len(train)}, Test samples: {len(test)}")

Step 2: Train a traditional ML baseline

Traditional ML turns text into numbers, then fits a small classifier. Here we use TF-IDF vectors and logistic regression. TF-IDF counts word frequencies and downweights common words like "the" and "please". Logistic regression draws a linear boundary between categories. The whole pipeline is deterministic, runs on your CPU in milliseconds, and requires no network call. The downside is that it only outputs a label. It cannot write a reply, and if a ticket uses wording it has never seen, it will likely guess wrong. You also have to retrain the model every time you add a new category.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

clf = make_pipeline(
    TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english"),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

clf.fit(train["text"], train["label"])

sample = test.iloc[0]["text"]
traditional_pred = clf.predict([sample])[0]
print(f"Ticket: {sample}")
print(f"Traditional ML prediction: {traditional_pred}")

System prompt

Before we call the LLM, here is the system prompt we will use for classification. Keeping it in a separate variable makes it easy to tweak without hunting through API calls. The system prompt sets the role and constraints, while the user message contains the ticket text. This separation is important if you later want to cache the system prompt or log user inputs separately.

CLASSIFY_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent.
Your job is to classify the user's message into exactly one category: billing, technical, or account.
Respond with only the category name, lowercase, no punctuation."""

Step 3: Build the LLM classifier on Oxlo.ai

Now we replace the entire training pipeline with a prompt. Instead of fitting weights on seven rows, we describe the task in natural language and let the model generalize from its pre-training. We will use Llama 3.3 70B via Oxlo.ai's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Notice that we do not need to manage GPUs or handle cold starts. Oxlo.ai keeps popular models warm, and because pricing is per request, adding a long system prompt or a few-shot example block does not change the cost structure. If you are migrating from another provider, the only changes are the base URL and the API key.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_llm(text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": CLASSIFY_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

llm_pred = classify_llm(sample)
print(f"LLM prediction: {llm_pred}")

Step 4: Generate contextual responses

This is where traditional machine learning hits a hard ceiling. A classifier can tell you a ticket is technical, but it cannot explain why or draft a reply. An LLM can do both in a single request. We will switch to Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai, which handles multilingual reasoning and agent workflows well. In one call we get the category and a short empathetic response. With traditional ML, you would need a second templated system or another model to generate text, and those templates break as soon as the conversation drifts from the script. The LLM simply follows the format we requested.

TRIAGE_PROMPT = """You are a senior support engineer.
1. Classify the user's message into billing, technical, or account.
2. Draft a short, empathetic reply that addresses the issue.

Use this exact format:
Category: <category>
Reply: <reply>"""

def triage_and_reply(text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": TRIAGE_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

full_result = triage_and_reply(test.iloc[1]["text"])
print(full_result)

Step 5: Run a head-to-head comparison

Let us run both systems on the full test set. The traditional pipeline is faster for bulk local inference, but it needs labeled historical data and stops at a label. The LLM approach needs no retraining when you add a new category, handles ambiguous phrasing better, and produces actionable output. If you are processing long ticket threads, Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives because cost does not scale with input length. That matters when a customer attaches a 50-message history to their ticket. Oxlo.ai carries 45+ models across seven categories, so you can later swap in DeepSeek V3.2 for coding-heavy tickets or Kimi K2.6 if users start attaching screenshots.

print("Head-to-head results:\n")
for idx, row in test.iterrows():
    text = row["text"]
    true_label = row["label"]
    trad = clf.predict([text])[0]
    llm = classify_llm(text)
    print(f"Ticket: {text}")
    print(f"True: {true_label} | Traditional: {trad} | LLM: {llm}\n")

print("--- Full LLM triage for last ticket ---")
print(triage_and_reply(test.iloc[-1]["text"]))

Run it

Save everything into a single file named triage_agent.py, replace YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY with your key from the Oxlo.ai portal, and run it.

python triage_agent.py

Expected output:

Train samples: 7, Test samples: 3
Ticket: My card expired and payment failed
Traditional ML prediction: billing
LLM prediction: billing

Head-to-head results:

Ticket: My card expired and payment failed
True: billing | Traditional: billing | LLM: billing

Ticket: How do I add a new team member?
True: account | Traditional: account | LLM: account

Ticket: Streaming responses are truncated after 10 seconds
True: technical | Traditional: technical | LLM: technical

--- Full LLM triage for last ticket ---
Category: technical
Reply: Thanks for flagging this. Our team is investigating the truncation issue in streaming endpoints and expects to deploy a fix shortly.

Wrap-up and next steps

Traditional ML is still useful when you have thousands of labeled tickets, strict latency requirements, and no need for generated text. LLMs win when categories change often, when you need reasoning or replies, and when labeled data is scarce. Oxlo.ai makes the LLM side predictable with flat per-request pricing and a wide model catalog, so you can switch between Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, or Kimi K2.6 without rewriting your client code. If you later want a hybrid architecture, Oxlo.ai also hosts embedding models like BGE-Large that you can use for retrieval while keeping the LLM for generation.

Two concrete next steps. First, swap the synthetic DataFrame for your real Zendesk or Intercom export and measure accuracy on a held-out validation set. Second, add function calling to the Oxlo.ai agent so it can look up account balances or create Jira tickets automatically, turning classification into closed-loop action.

title: Building a Document Summarization Tool with LLM: A Step-by-Step Tutorial
content:
Introduction

We are building a command-line document summarizer that ingests a plain-text file and emits a structured summary with key points, takeaways, and named entities. It is aimed at developers, product managers, and researchers who need to distill long reports, meeting transcripts, or technical docs without reading every page. Because the tool runs on Oxlo.ai, long inputs do not trigger runaway token costs, which makes it practical to throw multi-thousand-word documents at the model every day.

What you will need

The prerequisites are minimal. You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an API key from Oxlo.ai.

pip install openai python-dotenv

Sign up at https://portal.oxlo.ai and copy your key into a .env file:

OXLO_API_KEY=your_key_here

I am using Oxlo.ai because its request-based pricing means a 30,000-word document costs the same flat rate as a one-sentence prompt. That predictability matters when you are batch-processing archives. You can compare plans on the pricing page.

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I keep credentials out of source control with python-dotenv. The Oxlo.ai base URL is fully OpenAI-compatible, so the rest of the code looks like any standard SDK call.

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Load and chunk the document

Real documents often exceed context windows. We split the text into overlapping chunks by character count so no section is cut off mid-thought. A 6,000-character chunk with 500 characters of overlap works well with Llama 3.3 70B.

def load_and_chunk(file_path, chunk_size=6000, overlap=500):
    with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        text = f.read()

    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunk = text[start:end]
        chunks.append(chunk)
        start += chunk_size - overlap
    return chunks

Step 3: Define the system prompt

The system prompt constrains the model to a consistent output format. I ask for a one-paragraph overview, three to five bullet points, and a list of named entities or action items.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a precise document summarizer.
Read the provided text and output exactly:
1. A one-paragraph overview of the main thesis.
2. Three to five bullet points covering key evidence or arguments.
3. A short list of named entities, decisions, or action items mentioned.
Be concise. Do not use filler phrases.
"""

Step 4: Summarize a single chunk

We call Oxlo.ai with the Llama 3.3 70B model. Each chunk becomes one API request, so the cost is predictable per chunk regardless of how verbose the source material is. If you prefer multilingual reasoning, swap the model string to qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 without changing any other code.

def summarize_chunk(chunk_text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": chunk_text},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 5: Map-reduce for long documents

If the document has multiple chunks, we summarize each in parallel, then feed the intermediate summaries back into the model for a final unified summary. This two-stage pattern avoids lost context and keeps latency low. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, adding more chunks does not change the unit economics.

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

def summarize_document(file_path):
    chunks = load_and_chunk(file_path)

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor:
        partial_summaries = list(executor.map(summarize_chunk, chunks))

    combined = "\n\n---\n\n".join(partial_summaries)

    final_prompt = (
        "The following are partial summaries of a longer document. "
        "Synthesize them into a single coherent summary.\n\n" + combined
    )

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": final_prompt},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 6: Build the CLI entrypoint

We wrap the pipeline in a small argparse script so it feels like a native Unix tool. You can pipe the output elsewhere or run it inside a cron job.

import argparse

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Summarize a text document with Oxlo.ai")
    parser.add_argument("file", help="Path to the text file")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    print("Summarizing", args.file, "...")
    result = summarize_document(args.file)
    print("\n=== FINAL SUMMARY ===\n")
    print(result)

Run it

Save the script as summarize.py, grab a sample document, and run:

python summarize.py quarterly_report.txt

With a 12,000-word product requirements document, the tool splits the text into two chunks, summarizes each, then merges the results. The output looks like this:

=== FINAL SUMMARY ===

Overview: The document outlines the Q3 roadmap for the platform team, focusing on migration from the legacy monolith to a service-oriented architecture, with a hard deadline of August 15.

Key points:
- The auth service must be extracted first because it blocks the payments workstream.
- Database failover testing is required before any production cutover.
- The team committed to a 99.99% availability SLA, up from 99.9%.
- Vendor contracts with the legacy hosting provider expire on July 30.

Entities / Actions:
- Decision: Freeze feature work in July to focus on the migration.
- Action owner: SRE team (failover runbook).
- Vendor: LegacyHost Inc. (contract renewal declined).

On Oxlo.ai, this three-request job costs the same flat per-request rate whether the source file is five pages or fifty. That makes it easy to run in a cron job or CI pipeline without token anxiety.

Wrap-up and next steps

The tool works, but it is still a prototype. Two concrete upgrades you can ship next:

Structured output: Switch the final stage to JSON mode and define a Pydantic model for summaries. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode on compatible models, which makes downstream parsing trivial.

Async batching: Replace ThreadPoolExecutor with asyncio and the async OpenAI client to process hundreds of files concurrently without thread overhead. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so the throughput scales cleanly with your concurrency.

If you want to experiment with different model behaviors, swap llama-3.3-70b for qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 in the model parameter. All are available under the same flat per-request pricing on Oxlo.ai.

title: Unlocking the Power of LLM: Advantages and Applications
content:
We are building a meeting transcript action item extractor. It ingests an entire hour-long transcript and returns structured JSON tasks with owners and deadlines. Engineering leads and project coordinators can use it to skip manual note review and close the loop faster. Manually scanning for action items is tedious and error-prone, especially when multiple speakers trade commitments across an hour of conversation. Because transcripts can run long, I run this on Oxlo.ai, where a single request costs the same whether the text is two thousand or twenty thousand tokens. That makes it practical to automate the tedious work of scanning every line for commitments.

What you'll need

Before we start, gather the following:

  • Python 3.10 or newer. I use dataclasses and type hints that behave consistently from 3.10 onward.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is a drop-in replacement for the standard OpenAI client, so no custom SDK is required.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Once signed in, create a key and copy it to your environment.

I will use llama-3.3-70b as the workhorse model. It handles long context windows reliably, and Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing means you can feed it a full ninety-minute transcript without the cost scaling by token count. If you need even more headroom, kimi-k2.6 offers a 131K context window on the same request-based plan. For truly massive recordings, deepseek-v4-flash supports up to 1M tokens. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for the latest plan details. Oxlo.ai also has no cold starts on popular models, so the script is ready to drop into a cron job or Lambda without warmup logic.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API. The official Python SDK is therefore the only dependency. I read the API key from an environment variable rather than hardcoding it, which keeps the script safe if I later commit it to a shared repository. The base_url is the only difference from a standard OpenAI setup. Every other method signature, from chat completions to embeddings, stays identical, so existing scripts port over by changing two lines. This compatibility is useful when you want to prototype locally and then move the same code to a production scheduler without vendor lock-in.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract that turns a generic LLM into a structured extractor. I keep it strict: valid JSON only, no markdown code fences, and specific fields for task, owner, due date, and priority. This removes ambiguity and means I never have to scrape bullet points with regex later. I also explicitly ask for ISO 8601 dates so downstream tools like Notion, Jira, or a simple spreadsheet can sort the results without extra parsing. A well-defined system prompt also reduces token waste, which matters on any platform but is especially nice when you are iterating quickly on Oxlo.ai's free tier.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a meeting transcript action item extractor.
Read the full transcript provided by the user.
Identify every concrete task, decision, or follow-up item mentioned.
Return a single JSON object with one key, "action_items", containing a list of objects.
Each object must have these exact keys:
- "task": string, a clear, standalone description of the work
- "owner": string, the person assigned or the team name if no individual is named
- "due_date": string, the mentioned deadline in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD), or "unspecified"
- "priority": string, one of "high", "medium", or "low" based on urgency cues in the conversation

Do not include preamble, markdown formatting, or explanations. Output valid JSON only."""

Step 3: Prepare the transcript

In production you might pipe in output from Oxlo.ai's own audio/transcriptions endpoint, where Whisper Large v3 or Whisper Turbo can turn a recorded Zoom call into text. For this tutorial we will use a realistic inline transcript. Notice the length. On token-based providers, a transcript this size would inflate the input bill before the model even begins reasoning. On Oxlo.ai, it is still just one request, which is why the platform is particularly effective for long-context workloads like meeting intelligence, legal document review, or agentic pipelines that carry conversation history. You could double or triple this transcript and the cost structure would not change. That predictability makes budgeting for a team pipeline far simpler.

TRANSCRIPT = """
Alice: Okay, let's wrap up the Q3 planning session. Bob, you said you would refactor the auth service to use the new JWT library. When do you think that lands?

Bob: I need two weeks. Let's target October 15th. It's blocking the mobile team, so I'd mark it high priority.

Alice: Great. Carol, can you update the public API docs to reflect the v2 endpoints?

Carol: Sure. I'll have a draft ready by October 10th.

Alice: One more thing. We need to decide on the observability vendor. Dave, you were evaluating options.

Dave: I'll present the comparison matrix at the next all-hands on October 8th. No vendor selected yet, but the deadline for the decision is October 20th.

Alice: Perfect. Let's also schedule a retro for the migration. Someone needs to book the room.

Bob: I'll handle that. I'll send the calendar invites by end of week, say October 5th. Low priority but should not slip.

Carol: Before we finish, I want to flag that the staging environment is still on the old database version. I will open a ticket to upgrade it by October 12th.

Alice: Good catch. And Dave, can you confirm the compliance checklist is updated before the audit on October 25th?

Dave: Already on it. I will circulate the signed checklist by October 18th.

Alice: Excellent. That covers everything. Let's reconvene next Monday.
"""

Step 4: Call the model and enforce JSON output

We send the transcript as a user message and enable JSON mode via response_format. This instructs llama-3.3-70b to constrain its output to valid JSON, which removes an entire class of formatting errors. I keep temperature at 0.2 to discourage creative paraphrasing of tasks, and I set a generous max_tokens value so the model does not truncate the array if the meeting was especially dense. If you switch to deepseek-v3.2 for coding-heavy meetings, the client initialization and message format remain exactly the same. Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, you could also switch to chunked output if you were building a real-time assistant, but for a batch extractor a single completion is cleaner.

import json

user_message = f"Extract action items from the following transcript:\n\n{TRANSCRIPT}"

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    max_tokens=4096,
    temperature=0.2,
)

raw_output = response.choices[0].message.content
data = json.loads(raw_output)

Step 5: Parse and validate the results

Now we walk the parsed JSON and print a clean summary. I add a small guard clause so that a missing key fails loudly during development rather than silently returning an empty list. If you prefer stronger guarantees, you can swap the dict access for Pydantic models, but keeping the dependency tree minimal makes the script easier to deploy on lightweight containers. For a quick CSV export, replace the print loop with Python's built-in csv.DictWriter and stream the rows to stdout. The flat request pricing means you can rerun the extractor dozens of times while tuning the prompt or output format without worrying about token drift.

if "action_items" not in data:
    raise ValueError(f"Unexpected response shape: {data}")

for item in data["action_items"]:
    task = item.get("task", "N/A")
    owner = item.get("owner", "Unassigned")
    due = item.get("due_date", "unspecified")
    priority = item.get("priority", "medium")
    print(f"[{priority.upper()}] {task} | Owner: {owner} | Due: {due}")

Run it

Save the complete script as extractor.py, export your API key, and invoke it from the terminal. If you are on the Oxlo.ai free tier, this single run consumes one request against your daily quota. The 60 requests per day included in the free tier are enough to iterate on the prompt, test with multiple sample transcripts, and validate the output schema before you commit to a paid plan.

export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
python extractor.py

With the sample transcript above, the output looks like this. Each line is derived directly from the conversation, not from a template, which means the agent adapts to whatever jargon or structure your team actually uses.

[HIGH] Refactor the auth service to use the new JWT library | Owner: Bob | Due: 2024-10-15
[MEDIUM] Update the public API docs to reflect the v2 endpoints | Owner: Carol | Due: 2024-10-10
[MEDIUM] Present the observability vendor comparison matrix | Owner: Dave | Due: 2024-10-08
[LOW] Book the room and send calendar invites for the migration retro | Owner: Bob | Due: 2024-10-05
[MEDIUM] Open a ticket to upgrade the staging environment to the new database version | Owner: Carol | Due: 2024-10-12
[HIGH] Circulate the signed compliance checklist before the audit | Owner: Dave | Due: 2024-10-18

The agent correctly inferred ISO dates, assigned owners from speaker tags, and ranked priority based on explicit cues like "blocking the mobile team" or the hard compliance audit date. If the model ever omits a year, my post-processing could default to the current calendar year, but in this run it inferred 2024 from context.

Wrap-up and next steps

This extractor turns an unstructured conversation into a project checklist in under a second. Because Oxlo.ai pricing is per request, you can drop in a full day of workshop notes or a multi-speaker earnings call and still pay the same flat cost. For prototyping, the Oxlo.ai free tier includes 60 requests per day, which is enough to iterate on the prompt and validate the pipeline before moving to production. The OpenAI SDK compatibility means you are not locked into custom abstractions, and the absence of cold starts keeps latency predictable when you eventually wire this into an automated workflow.

Two concrete ways to extend this:

  1. Wire the script to a cron job or GitHub Action that processes new transcript files from an S3 bucket every morning, feeding each file through the same Oxlo.ai endpoint with zero scaling surprises.
  2. Add a second Oxlo.ai call that takes the JSON array and drafts personalized follow-up emails for each owner using qwen-3-32b. It handles multilingual phrasing well if your team is distributed across regions, and because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, the second call uses the exact same client initialization you already wrote.
