title: Building a RAG Pipeline: A Step-by-Step Tutorial
content:
We are going to build a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that answers questions over a private text corpus. Instead of trusting an LLM to hallucinate facts, we will ground every response in actual source documents using Oxlo.ai embeddings and chat models. The pipeline ingests raw text, embeds it, retrieves the best chunks for a query, and synthesizes a cited answer. If you have ever needed to add a knowledge base to an agent without fine-tuning, this is the pattern to use.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. You also need a text file to search. I will use a hardcoded internal wiki snippet in the examples, but you can point the loader at your own markdown, JSON, or PDF text extract.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

We will use the OpenAI SDK as a drop-in client. Point the base_url to Oxlo.ai, set your API key, and instantiate the client once. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI API compatible, the only difference from other providers is the base URL and the model names. I will use llama-3.3-70b for generation and bge-large for embeddings.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

CHAT_MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"
EMBEDDING_MODEL = "bge-large"

Step 2: Chunk the source documents

RAG works best with small, coherent chunks rather than full pages. I split on double newlines to preserve paragraph boundaries, then enforce a maximum character limit. This keeps each chunk semantically focused while still giving the model enough context to reason about. Overlapping chunks can help when a thought spans two paragraphs, but for this runbook example simple boundary splitting is enough.

def chunk_text(text, max_chars=800):
    paragraphs = [p.strip() for p in text.split("\n\n") if p.strip()]
    chunks = []
    current = ""
    for p in paragraphs:
        if len(current) + len(p) < max_chars:
            current += "\n\n" + p if current else p
        else:
            if current:
                chunks.append(current)
            current = p
    if current:
        chunks.append(current)
    return chunks

raw_doc = """
Oxlo.ai On-Call Runbook

The Oxlo.ai inference platform runs on a request-based pricing model.
Each API call costs one flat fee regardless of prompt length.
This makes it cheaper than token-based providers for long-context workloads.

Supported models include Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, and DeepSeek V3.2.
All endpoints are OpenAI SDK compatible.
There are no cold starts on popular models.
"""

chunks = chunk_text(raw_doc)
print(f"Produced {len(chunks)} chunks")

Step 3: Build the embedding vector store

We send each chunk to the Oxlo.ai embeddings endpoint and cache the vectors in memory. Using the same embedding model for both ingestion and retrieval is critical, otherwise the vector spaces will misalign and similarity search will return irrelevant results. For this tutorial I store everything in a numpy array and compute cosine similarity manually so you can see the math. In production you would write these vectors to Postgres with pgvector or to ChromaDB.

import numpy as np

def embed_texts(texts):
    response = client.embeddings.create(
        model=EMBEDDING_MODEL,
        input=texts
    )
    return [item.embedding for item in response.data]

chunk_embeddings = embed_texts(chunks)
chunk_embeddings = np.array(chunk_embeddings)

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

Step 4: Retrieve relevant context

When a user asks a question, we embed the query using the same bge-large model, score every stored chunk with cosine similarity, and return the top three matches. Limiting the context to three chunks keeps latency low and ensures we stay within the context window. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, longer prompts do not increase cost, so you can experiment with larger top_k values without worrying about token meter creep.

def retrieve(query, top_k=3):
    query_vec = embed_texts([query])[0]
    query_vec = np.array(query_vec)
    scores = [cosine_similarity(query_vec, vec) for vec in chunk_embeddings]
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[-top_k:][::-1]
    return [chunks[i] for i in top_indices]

user_question = "How does Oxlo.ai pricing work?"
retrieved_chunks = retrieve(user_question)
print("\n--- Retrieved chunks ---\n")
for c in retrieved_chunks:
    print(c[:200] + "...")
    print()

Step 5: Define the RAG system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between retrieval and generation. I inject the retrieved chunks into a template that explicitly forbids hallucination. Keeping the prompt strict means the agent will say it does not know rather than inventing pricing or model details that are not in the source text.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise technical support agent.
Answer the user's question using ONLY the context provided below.
If the context does not contain the answer, say "I don't have that information."
Do not make up facts, prices, or features.

Context:
{context}
"""

Step 6: Generate the grounded answer

With the context injected, we call the chat completions endpoint. I set temperature to 0.1 because factual consistency matters more than creativity here. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, you can pass large context blocks without watching metered costs climb. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

def answer_question(query):
    context_blocks = retrieve(query)
    context_text = "\n\n---\n\n".join(context_blocks)
    prompt = SYSTEM_PROMPT.replace("{context}", context_text)

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=CHAT_MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": prompt},
            {"role": "user", "content": query},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

answer = answer_question("How does Oxlo.ai pricing work?")
print(answer)

Run it

The main block ties retrieval and generation together. It prints the intermediate context so you can verify that the retrieval step is actually pulling the right passages. Seeing the raw chunks makes debugging much easier when you move from a toy example to a real document store.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    question = "Which models does Oxlo.ai support?"
    print(f"Question: {question}\n")

    context = retrieve(question)
    print("Retrieved context:")

title: Introduction to LLM: Explaining the Basics
content:
We are going to build a working support agent that classifies incoming tickets and drafts a first response. This is the same pattern I use to triage questions before they hit a human team. If you are new to LLMs, this project will show you how system prompts, messages, and streaming actually work without hiding the wiring.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10+
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier gives you 60 requests per day across 16+ models, which is plenty for this tutorial. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI API compatible, so the standard SDK is all you need.

Step 1: Scaffold the script and connect to Oxlo.ai

I always start by verifying the client can reach the API and return a heartbeat response. Create a file named support_agent.py and initialize the OpenAI-compatible client pointing at Oxlo.ai.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, are you there?"}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the invisible instruction set that shapes every reply. I treat it like a runbook I would hand to a new hire.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a tier-1 support agent for a developer tools company.
Your job is to:
1. Classify the user's issue into one of: Billing, Technical, or Account.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic first response.
3. If technical, ask for one specific piece of information needed to escalate.

Rules:
- Keep responses under 120 words.
- Never make up refund amounts or policy details.
- Always offer to loop in a human if the user is frustrated."""

Step 3: Handle a single ticket

Now we wire the system prompt and a sample ticket into a single completion call. This is the simplest useful unit of an LLM application.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a tier-1 support agent for a developer tools company.
Your job is to:
1. Classify the user's issue into one of: Billing, Technical, or Account.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic first response.
3. If technical, ask for one specific piece of information needed to escalate.

Rules:
- Keep responses under 120 words.
- Never make up refund amounts or policy details.
- Always offer to loop in a human if the user is frustrated."""

ticket = "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month and I need the extra charge reversed immediately."

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": ticket},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 4: Add multi-turn memory

Real conversations have context. I keep a message list in memory and append each exchange so the model can reference earlier details, and because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, I do not have to truncate history to save money.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a tier-1 support agent for a developer tools company.
Your job is to:
1. Classify the user's issue into one of: Billing, Technical, or Account.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic first response.
3. If technical, ask for one specific piece of information needed to escalate.

Rules:
- Keep responses under 120 words.
- Never make up refund amounts or policy details.
- Always offer to loop in a human if the user is frustrated."""

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month."},
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
)

assistant_reply = response.choices[0].message.content
print("Agent:", assistant_reply)

messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_reply})
messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "The charge was on April 2nd and again on April 3rd. Both for $79."})

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
)

print("Agent:", response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 5: Stream the response

Waiting for the full response to buffer feels slow. I enable streaming so words arrive as they are generated, which is a one-line change in the SDK.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a tier-1 support agent for a developer tools company.
Your job is to:
1. Classify the user's issue into one of: Billing, Technical, or Account.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic first response.
3. If technical, ask for one specific piece of information needed to escalate.

Rules:
- Keep responses under 120 words.
- Never make up refund amounts or policy details.
- Always offer to loop in a human if the user is frustrated."""

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "My API keys keep returning 401 errors after I rotated them this morning."},
]

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    stream=True,
)

for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="", flush=True)
print()

Step 6: Build a small CLI loop

Finally, I wrap everything in an interactive loop so you can type tickets and watch the agent reply in real time. This is the same pattern I use when prototyping before hooking up a web framework.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a tier-1 support agent for a developer tools company.
Your job is to:
1. Classify the user's issue into one of: Billing, Technical, or Account.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic first response.
3. If technical, ask for one specific piece of information needed to escalate.

Rules:
- Keep responses under 120 words.
- Never make up refund amounts or policy details.
- Always offer to loop in a human if the user is frustrated."""

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("Support agent ready. Type a ticket or 'quit'.")
while True:
    user_input = input("> ")
    if user_input.lower().strip() == "quit":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    stream = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        stream=True,
    )
    reply = ""
    for chunk in stream:
        if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
            text = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
            print(text, end="", flush=True)
            reply += text
    print()
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

Run it

Save the final script as support_agent.py, replace YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY with your actual key, and run it. You should see the prompt appear immediately. Because Oxlo.ai serves popular models with no cold starts, there is no warmup delay.

python support_agent.py

Try pasting in a sample ticket.

> I was charged twice this month.
Billing Issue: I am sorry to see the duplicate charge. I can escalate this to our billing team right now. Can you confirm the last four digits of the card on file so they can locate the correct invoice?

Notice how the agent classifies the ticket and asks for a specific follow-up detail. If you continue the conversation, it remembers the thread because we keep appending to the messages list.

Next steps

This script is the skeleton of nearly every LLM application: a system prompt, a growing message history, and a loop. To put it into production, I would persist the conversation state to Redis or SQLite, then expose the loop behind a FastAPI endpoint so your helpdesk can POST tickets to it.

If you expect technical questions that need deep reasoning, swap llama-3.3-70b for deepseek-r1-671b or kimi-k2.6 without changing any other code. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, adding a long system prompt or a multi-turn conversation history does not inflate your cost the way token-based billing does. You can explore models and plans on the Oxlo.ai pricing page. The free tier is more than enough to prototype, and the flat per-request model makes long-context support agents cheap to run at scale.

title: Deploying LLM Models: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Deploying large language models in production requires more than calling a chat endpoint from a notebook. You need to think about inference engines, hardware provisioning, scaling behavior, and cost structures that can vary wildly between token-based and request-based billing. Whether you are running a fine-tuned Llama 3.3 70B on dedicated GPUs or routing traffic to a managed API, the architecture decisions you make early determine your latency budget, your monthly bill, and your ability to serve agentic workflows that fire dozens of long-context requests in a single session.

Self-Hosted Inference: Control at a Cost

Self-hosting gives you full control over weights, quantization, and scheduling. Common stacks include vLLM for continuous batching, Text Generation Inference for Hugging Face ecosystems, and llama.cpp for CPU-constrained environments. These tools let you serve models like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Qwen 3 32B on hardware you manage.

But the operational overhead is steep. Serving a 70B parameter model at FP16 requires roughly 140 GB of VRAM, which pushes you into multi-GPU nodes or aggressive quantization to INT4 or INT8. That compression can degrade reasoning quality on complex coding or math tasks. You are also responsible for GPU driver compatibility, CUDA version alignment, and KV cache memory management. Cold starts are common if you scale to zero to save on idle GPU costs, and queuing logic must be built in-house. For teams without dedicated ML infrastructure engineers, self-hosting can shift engineering hours away from product features and toward cluster maintenance.

Managed API Integration: Offloading Infrastructure

Managed providers abstract away the stack. You send an HTTP request and receive a streamed response. The provider handles model weights, driver updates, and autoscaling. This is the fastest path to production for startups and enterprise teams that want OpenAI SDK compatibility without maintaining a Kubernetes cluster for inference.

The trade-off is typically billing complexity. Most managed providers bill per token, which means your costs scale linearly with prompt length. For applications that pass large codebases, PDFs, or multi-turn agent contexts into the prompt, token-based bills grow quickly. You also need to verify feature parity. Not every provider supports function calling, JSON mode, or vision inputs on every model, which can force you to maintain multiple client implementations or add latency-heavy middleware.

Oxlo.ai and Request-Based Pricing

Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first alternative with request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based billing because a 50,000-token prompt costs the same as a 500-token prompt.

Oxlo.ai runs 45+ models across seven categories, including Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek V4 Flash with a 1M context window, Kimi K2.6 for agentic coding, and vision models like Gemma 3 27B. The platform also offers code models such as Qwen 3 Coder 30B, audio models including Whisper Large v3, and image generation endpoints. Everything is fully OpenAI SDK compatible across Python, Node.js, and cURL, so switching from another provider is usually a single line change.

title: Best API for Long Context Inference
content:
Long context inference has moved from research curiosity to production requirement. Software agents that iterate over large codebases, legal teams analyzing discovery documents, and support systems referencing years of ticket history routinely send prompts that exceed 32K, 100K, or even 1 million tokens. When your input grows, token-based billing grows linearly, turning a promising architecture into a budget risk. Choosing the right API means looking past marketing claims about context windows and examining how pricing, latency, and model availability interact at scale. The best long context API is not always the one with the largest window. It is the one that lets you use that window without economic penalties.

The Token Pricing Trap

Most inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, bill by the token. You pay for every input token and every output token. For short prompts, this feels intuitive. For long context, it becomes a structural problem. A single request with a 128K token prompt and a 512 token response still incurs charges for the full 128K input, even if the model does minimal work.

Agentic workflows compound the issue. A tool-calling loop that appends context every turn increases prompt size incrementally. After ten turns, you may be paying for the same background context ten times over. Token pricing does not care that 90% of your prompt is a static system message or a retrieved document chunk. It counts everything. The result is a budgeting paradox: the more context you give the model to improve accuracy, the more you pay for every single call. This discourages the exact technique, retrieval-augmented generation, that makes large language models useful on private data. Teams often resort to aggressive chunking or truncation, which reduces quality, just to keep token costs under control.

What to Look for in a Long Context API

When you evaluate APIs for long context workloads, look beyond the maximum context length listed on a model card. Consider these factors:

  • Validated context depth. Some APIs accept 128K tokens but degrade in accuracy or speed after 32K. Look for providers that serve models known to maintain performance across the full window.
  • Pricing model. Token-based billing penalizes long inputs. Request-based or flat-rate pricing decouples cost from prompt length, which is critical for agents and retrieval-augmented generation.
  • Cold starts. If an API spins down GPUs between requests, your first long-context call can take tens of seconds. Consistent latency matters for interactive applications.
  • Model breadth. You may need a reasoning specialist for one task and a vision model for another. A single endpoint that hosts diverse architectures saves integration time.
  • SDK compatibility. Rewriting client code for every provider is friction. Drop-in replacement for the OpenAI SDK is the closest thing to a standard.
  • Feature parity. Streaming, function calling, JSON mode, and vision input should all work without custom wrappers.

Throughput matters because long prompts take more time to prefill. You need an API that allocates sufficient compute to handle large KV caches without queueing your requests behind slower workloads. Ask providers whether they throttle context length or charge premium rates for windows above a certain threshold. Some token-based APIs quietly shift to higher per-token tiers once you cross 32K or 64K, making the cost curve steeper than it first appears.

Oxlo.ai and Request-Based Pricing

Oxlo.ai is a developer-first inference platform built around a simple idea: one flat cost per API request, regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers, Oxlo.ai does not scale charges with input size, so Oxlo.ai is significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads.

Because the price is per request, sending 200K tokens costs the same as sending 2K tokens. This predictability removes the tension between adding more context and controlling spend. You can pass entire codebases, long transcripts, or extensive tool histories without watching a meter run.

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK. There are no cold starts on popular models, and features like streaming, function calling, JSON mode, and vision input are all supported. No cold starts means your first request of the day returns as fast as your hundredth. For agents that wake up in response to user events, this is essential. You cannot afford a long warmup when a human is waiting for an answer.

title: Best Practices for LLM Model Interpretability in Conversational AI
content:
We are going to build a transparent customer support triage agent that explains its own routing decisions in plain English before it acts. This gives operators an audit trail they can inspect instead of a black-box classification. It is essential for any conversational AI system that touches real users and needs to meet compliance or quality standards.

What you'll need

Before we write any code, make sure you have the following ready.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier includes DeepSeek V3.2 and more than a dozen other models you can use for prototyping.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai

Step 1: Capture a complete audit log for every turn

Interpretability is impossible without a record. Before we call any model, we need a lightweight logger that records the raw prompt, the user message, the full response text, and a timestamp. I write these to a newline-delimited JSON file so I can replay any decision later with standard command-line tools like jq. I choose JSONL over a structured database for now because each line is independent. If a parser bug corrupts one record, the rest of the file is still readable. This single file becomes the source of truth when a stakeholder asks why a conversation was routed a certain way two weeks later.

import json
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

AUDIT_LOG = Path("triage_audit.jsonl")

def log_turn(system_prompt: str, user_message: str, raw_response: str):
    entry = {
        "timestamp": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),
        "system_prompt_hash": hash(system_prompt) & 0xFFFFFFFF,
        "user_message": user_message,
        "raw_response": raw_response,
    }
    with AUDIT_LOG.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(entry, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")

Step 2: Design a system prompt for explicit reasoning

The model cannot explain itself if we do not ask it to. I force a structured chain-of-thought by requiring the model to emit its reasoning inside <thinking> tags before it produces any JSON. This separates the deliberation from the decision and gives us a human-readable narrative we can surface in a dashboard without exposing raw JSON to non-technical staff. I also constrain the output to a strict JSON schema so the downstream automation does not break when we integrate with Slack, Jira, or an internal CRM.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a transparent support triage agent. Your job is to read a customer message and decide which team should handle it.

Allowed teams: Billing, Technical, Account-Security, General-Support.

Before you output your final answer, explain your reasoning step by step inside <thinking> tags. Consider:
1. What is the user's core intent?
2. Which team has the expertise to solve this?
3. How confident are you (High, Medium, Low)?

After your reasoning, output exactly one JSON object with no markdown formatting:
{
  "team": "<team_name>",
  "confidence": "<High|Medium|Low>",
  "reasoning_summary": "<one sentence>",
  "required_actions": ["<action1>", "<action2>"]
}

If the message is ambiguous, state the ambiguity in your thinking and set confidence to Low."""

Step 3: Parse the response into structured parts

Raw text is hard to query and dangerous to pass straight into business logic. I use a small parser that extracts the thinking trace and the JSON decision block into a native Python dictionary. If the model ever fails to produce valid JSON, the parser raises immediately so we fail loud rather than silently routing a ticket to the wrong team. I keep the original raw text inside the result so the audit trail remains complete even if we later change the parsing logic. In production you might replace the regex with a constrained mode or JSON schema validator, but this is enough to ship and iterate.

import json
import re

def parse_triage(raw_text: str) -> dict:
    # Extract the thinking trace
    thinking_match = re.search(r"<thinking>(.*?)</thinking>", raw_text, re.DOTALL)
    thinking = thinking_match.group(1).strip() if thinking_match else None

    # Extract the JSON block
    json_match = re.search(r"\{.*\}", raw_text, re.DOTALL)
    if not json_match:
        raise ValueError("No JSON decision block found in model response")

    decision = json.loads(json_match.group(0))

    return {
        "thinking": thinking,
        "decision": decision,
        "raw": raw_text,
    }

Step 4: Call Oxlo.ai with full observability

Now we wire the logger, the prompt, and the parser together into a single triage function. I use Oxlo.ai here because its request-based pricing means I can pass the entire system prompt and a long ticket thread in the context window without watching token costs climb. For long-context workloads, that flat per-request model makes thorough observability affordable. You can see the exact pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. I set temperature to 0.1 because routing decisions should be deterministic, not creative. I picked qwen-3-32b because it handles multilingual reasoning and agent instructions reliably, and the usage object is preserved so we can later correlate prompt size with confidence scores.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def triage(user_message: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    log_turn(SYSTEM_PROMPT, user_message, raw)

    result = parse_triage(raw)
    result["model"] = response.model
    result["usage"] = response.usage.model_dump() if response.usage else None
    return result

Step 5: Add a confidence gate for escalation

Interpretability is only useful if it changes behavior. We wrap the triage function with a simple gate that automatically escalates any Low-confidence decision to a human reviewer. The gate surfaces the model's exact thinking in the escalation ticket so the human does not start from zero. This closes the loop between seeing why the model hesitated and acting on that information. You can extend this pattern to trigger on missing required actions, unrecognized team names, or spikes in token usage that might indicate a confused model.

def triage_with_escalation(user_message: str) -> dict:
    result = triage(user_message)
    confidence = result["decision"].get("confidence", "Low")

    if confidence == "Low":
        return {
            "status": "ESCALATED",
            "human_note": (
                f"Low confidence triage. Model reasoning: {result['thinking']}"
            ),
            "audit": result,
        }

    return {
        "status": "ROUTED",
        "team": result["decision"]["team"],
        "actions": result["decision"]["required_actions"],
        "audit": result,
    }

Run it

Here is how we call the finished agent with a deliberately ambiguous message that touches both billing and security, plus the output you should expect. If you try a clearer message, such as a simple refund request, you will see a ROUTED status with high confidence instead.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    msg = (
        "I was charged twice last month and now I cannot log in. "
        "I think someone else is using my account because I see devices I do not recognize."
    )

    outcome = triage_with_escalation(msg)
    print(json.dumps(outcome, indent=2))

Example output:

{
  "status": "ESCALATED",
  "human_note": "Low confidence triage. Model reasoning: The user mentions both a duplicate charge and unrecognized account activity. While Billing handles the duplicate charge, Account-Security must handle the potential breach. Because two teams are equally relevant and the issues are intertwined, confidence is Low.",
  "audit": {
    "thinking": "The user mentions both a duplicate charge and unrecognized account activity...",
    "decision": {
      "team": "Account-Security",
      "confidence": "Low",
      "reasoning_summary": "Potential breach takes precedence, but billing issue is unresolved.",
      "required_actions": [
        "Freeze account",
        "Initiate billing review"
      ]
    },
    "raw": "...",
    "model": "qwen-3-32b",
    "usage": {
      "prompt_tokens": 312,
      "completion_tokens": 128
    }
  }
}

Wrap-up and next steps

That is the core of an interpretable conversational AI pipeline. From here, you have two concrete paths. First, feed the triage_audit.jsonl file into a small Streamlit or Grafana dashboard that plots confidence distributions over time so you can spot when the model starts to drift on certain topics. Second, swap in Oxlo.ai's DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 when you need deeper reasoning on complex edge cases, or prototype against DeepSeek V3.2 on the free tier. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, the only change is the model string.

title: Comparing LLM Inference APIs for Conversational AI Customer Support
content:
Conversational AI customer support systems operate under a strict set of constraints. Response latency must stay low across thousands of concurrent threads. Agents must retain context from earlier turns, attached order histories, and retrieved knowledge base articles. They must also invoke external tools to update CRM records or check shipping status. The inference API powering these systems determines whether you hit these constraints predictably, or whether costs and latency scale in ways that break your margin structure. Most providers today offer broad model catalogs and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, but their pricing architectures diverge significantly when applied to real support workloads.

What Support Workloads Actually Need

Support bots are not simple chat completions. A single customer turn might include a system prompt, a multi-turn conversation history, a few-shot example block, and retrieved context from a vector store. That easily pushes input token counts into the thousands or tens of thousands. If the model then calls a function to query an order database before generating a final response, the total compute path grows even longer.

Engineering teams should evaluate inference APIs on four concrete dimensions. First, context window capacity and the cost of filling it. Second, function calling accuracy and latency. Third, pricing predictability when input length varies. Fourth, SDK compatibility to minimize integration overhead.

The Standard Token-Based Model

The majority of inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, use token-based billing. You pay for input tokens and output tokens, often at separate rates. This model aligns cost with raw compute, and it works well for short, uniform queries.

For conversational support, it introduces volatility. A frustrated customer might paste a long email thread. An agentic workflow might embed ten retrieved documents into the prompt. Each of these scenarios balloons the input token count, and your bill scales linearly with that growth. If your support bot handles voice transcripts or image inputs, the tokenization complexity increases further. Teams often end up building elaborate prompt truncation and compression pipelines just to keep token costs manageable, adding technical debt to the system.

Oxlo.ai and Flat Request-Based Pricing

Oxlo.ai takes a different approach. It charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For customer support workflows where input context is inherently long and variable, this changes the cost structure entirely. A request containing a compressed ticket history, a knowledge base retrieval, and a system prompt costs the same as a short greeting.

This is not merely a pricing nuance. It removes the engineering tax of token optimization. You can pass full conversation threads, maintain richer few-shot examples, and give the model more retrieved context without watching a meter run on every input token. For agentic support flows that chain multiple tool calls and reasoning steps, the predictability compounds. For long-context agentic workloads, request-based pricing can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives, a gap that widens as you pass more retrieved documentation and conversation history into each turn.

title: LLM Inference API Security Considerations for Conversational AI
content:
Conversational AI applications handle sensitive user dialog, PII, and business logic through third-party inference APIs. Any gap in the security model between your application and the model provider exposes you to prompt injection, data exfiltration, and uncontrolled spend. This post breaks down the concrete controls developers should enforce at the API layer, and how a request-based inference platform like Oxlo.ai fits into a defensive architecture.

Transport Layer and Authentication

Every request to an inference API must transit over TLS 1.2 or higher. Verify that the provider uses valid certificates and that your HTTP client enforces certificate verification. If your infrastructure supports mutual TLS, use it between your application servers and any internal proxy. This prevents unauthorized internal services from reaching the inference endpoint even if they are already behind your firewall. Authentication should rely on revocable API keys stored in environment variables or a secrets manager, never committed to version control.

Oxlo.ai exposes a standard REST endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 that is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. This means you can reuse existing security patterns from the OpenAI ecosystem without custom adapters. A typical Python client setup looks like this:

import openai
import os

client = openai.OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

Because Oxlo.ai is a drop-in replacement, you can keep your existing key-rotation logic, proxy configurations, and secret-management workflows intact. Additionally, Oxlo.ai serves popular models with no cold starts, so your connection timeouts and retry policies remain stable and predictable.

Input Validation and Prompt Injection Defense

Never forward raw user input directly to a language model. Implement server-side validation with length limits, character allowlists, and semantic filters. For conversational interfaces, treat every user message as untrusted data. Use a system prompt to define boundaries, but do not rely on it as your only defense.

Structured generation helps constrain the attack surface. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling, which let you enforce output schemas. When the model must return valid JSON or invoke a registered tool, you gain a parseable boundary that makes anomalous output easier to detect and reject. Function calling is particularly effective for conversational AI because you can define rigid tool specifications. If the model deviates from the schema, your parser rejects the response before it reaches the user. This turns a generative endpoint into something closer to a typed API boundary.

If your conversational AI accepts images, apply the same scrutiny. Oxlo.ai supports vision inputs through models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B. Validate file types, strip metadata, and enforce size limits before passing bytes to the API.

Output Guardrails and Data Loss Prevention

Model outputs can contain hallucinated credentials, toxic content, or leaked context from system prompts. Apply a post-processing layer that scans responses for PII, secrets, or policy violations before displaying them to the user.

Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, so your guardrail pipeline can operate on partial chunks rather than buffering the entire completion. This reduces latency and lets you abort a response as soon as a policy violation is detected. For example, if a regex matcher finds a sixteen-digit number mid-stream, you can terminate the connection and log the event immediately.

Rate Limiting and Abuse Mitigation

Conversational AI endpoints are attractive targets for automated abuse, credential stuffing, and model exploitation. Implement client-side rate limiting with exponential backoff, and ensure your provider enforces hard quotas. Use token-bucket or sliding-window rate limiters in your application tier before traffic reaches the provider.

Oxlo.ai offers predictable daily request caps across its plans: 60 requests per day on the Free tier, 1,000 per day on Pro, and 5,000 per day on Premium. These quotas act as structural circuit breakers. Combine your gateway rate limiters with Oxlo.ai’s built-in daily caps, and you create a two-layer defense: your gateway throttles burst traffic, while the platform enforces the absolute ceiling.</

Why Model Selection Matters for Support Automation

Support conversations are not simple single-turn prompts. A typical interaction includes previous messages, order details, knowledge base articles, and policy clauses. That context can span thousands of tokens before the model ever generates a response. If the backend charges by the token, costs scale linearly with conversation length. If the model lacks a sufficient context window, accuracy degrades as the session grows. The best support stacks optimize for three variables. First, instruction following: the model must stick to a support script, respect tone guidelines, and avoid hallucinating policy. Second, context efficiency: it needs to reason over long transcripts without losing track of the user's original issue. Third, tool use: modern support bots query CRMs, create tickets, and escalate to humans via function calling. You need a platform that exposes these capabilities without adding latency or cold-start overhead.

JSON mode ensures that structured outputs, such as escalation payloads or satisfaction surveys, parse correctly on the first try. title: LLM Inference API Pricing Models Comparison for Conversational AI
content:
Conversational AI workloads are notoriously difficult to budget. A customer support bot that handles multi-turn dialogue, a coding assistant that iterates on long file contexts, or an agentic system that chains multiple tool calls all share one trait: the number of tokens consumed per interaction can vary by an order of magnitude. Most inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, structure their pricing around input and output tokens. While this model is straightforward for single-turn prompts, it introduces significant cost volatility for ongoing conversations. As context windows grow and agents loop over lengthy prompts, token counts balloon, and so does the bill.

The Mechanics of Token-Based Pricing

Token-based billing splits costs across two dimensions: the tokens you send (input) and the tokens the model returns (output). Providers typically charge separate rates for each, with premium models commanding higher per-million-token fees. For a simple classification task with a 50-word prompt and a 10-word response, this model is predictable. The cost scales roughly with usage, and developers can estimate spend by counting tokens in advance.

However, the model assumes that input size remains relatively stable. In conversational AI, every turn appends the full or partial conversation history to the prompt. A dialogue that starts as a 500-token request can grow to 8,000 tokens or more by the tenth turn. If the application uses retrieval-augmented generation with large document chunks, or if the model generates lengthy chain-of-thought reasoning before responding, the output token volume also surges. The result is a bill that increases non-linearly with conversation depth, making capacity planning an exercise in guesswork.

Why Conversational AI Breaks the Token Model

Modern chat applications are no longer simple question-and-answer interfaces. They maintain state across turns, inject system prompts, include tool definitions, and prepend retrieved context. Each of these elements adds tokens to the input side. On the output side, reasoning models such as DeepSeek R1 or agentic frameworks may emit extensive scratchpad content before producing a final answer.

For engineering teams, this creates a budgetary mismatch. A conversation that feels like a single user interaction might consume 15,000 input tokens and 4,000 output tokens. Under token-based pricing, that single interaction is billed as a large batch job. When multiplied across thousands of daily active users, the cost delta between a short query and a long-context session becomes the dominant line item in an AI infrastructure budget. Teams are forced to choose between truncating history, compressing prompts, or absorbing unpredictable costs.

Request-Based Pricing: A Fixed-Cost Alternative

An alternative approach is to decouple cost from token count entirely. Request-based pricing charges a flat fee per API call, regardless of how many tokens are in the prompt or the response. For conversational and agentic workloads, this model aligns costs with business value. A user sends a message, the system responds, and the transaction is billed as one unit. Whether the context window is 1,000 tokens or 100,000 tokens, the price remains the same.

This structure is particularly effective for long-context workloads, multi-turn agents, and any pipeline where input length is outside the developer's direct control. It removes the penalty for maintaining full conversation history, for passing large codebases to a coding assistant, or for using models with extended context windows. Instead of optimizing prompts primarily to save money, engineers can optimize them for accuracy and user experience.

Matching Models to Use Cases

Pricing models in the LLM inference market are not one-size-fits-all. Token-based billing works for simple, stateless calls, but conversational AI is increasingly stateful, long-context, and agentic. Selecting a large language model for conversational AI is no longer a simple matter of picking the highest score on a public leaderboard. Production chat systems, voice agents, and support bots operate under strict latency budgets, context window requirements, and cost constraints that vary wildly between a single-turn FAQ and a multi-turn agent that calls external tools. The right choice depends on mapping conversation patterns to model capabilities, then validating that combination against real user traffic. This guide outlines practical criteria for making that decision, and where platforms like Oxlo.ai fit into a modern selection strategy.

Evaluate Core Dimensions, Not Just Benchmark Scores

Public leaderboards measure aggregate reasoning or coding ability, but conversational AI has its own success metrics. Start by ranking your requirements across four dimensions that directly impact user experience.

  • Latency and throughput: Time to first token and inter-token latency determine whether a dialogue feels natural. High-traffic customer support bots often need sub-second first-token responses, which favors efficient architectures or distilled variants.
  • Context fidelity: Multi-turn conversations accumulate history, system prompts, and retrieved documents. A model must maintain coherence across thousands of tokens without losing track of user intent or instruction boundaries.
  • Tool use reliability: Agentic workflows require consistent function calling signatures and JSON output. A model that excels at chat may still fail on parallel tool calls or schema adherence.
  • Language and modality coverage: If your users switch languages mid-conversation or share screenshots, you need multilingual reasoning and vision support, not just strong English prose.

Benchmarks like MMLU are proxies, not guarantees. Prioritize models that score well on instruction-following and conversation-specific evaluations, then confirm behavior on your own transcripts.

Map Conversation Architecture to Model Classes

Not every turn in a conversation demands the same capability. Architect your stack by matching conversation patterns to model classes, rather than sending every query to a single heavyweight endpoint.

For straightforward, single-turn Q&A or routing decisions, a general-purpose flagship such as Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B provides fast, high-quality responses with broad multilingual coverage. These models handle polite refusal, style control, and short context windows efficiently.

When the dialogue shifts to agentic workflows, long-horizon planning, or complex coding, you need reasoning-optimized models. Design for Fallbacks and Model Routing

Conversational AI is now central to customer support, internal tooling, and autonomous agents. But every chat completion request carries risk: prompt injection, data exfiltration, credential leakage, and toxic output. Securing your LLM inference pipeline requires more than a single API key. This post covers concrete practices you can apply today, whether you are calling a self-hosted model or a managed provider like Oxlo.ai.

Authenticate Every Request with Scoped Credentials

API keys are the primary attack surface for any inference endpoint. Rotate them quarterly, store them in a secrets manager or environment variables, and never commit them to version control. Scope keys by environment so a development key cannot access production data. If your provider supports it, use IP allowlisting and separate keys for different service accounts.

Oxlo.ai uses standard bearer token authentication over HTTPS, and it is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK. This means you can drop Oxlo.ai into existing credential management workflows without custom adapters or proprietary client libraries.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
)

Enforce TLS and Pin Your HTTP Client

All traffic to an LLM inference API must use TLS 1.2 or higher. Verify server certificates, reject insecure redirects, and pin your client to expect a valid HTTPS connection. Oxlo.ai serves all endpoints, including chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, and audio/transcriptions, over HTTPS. If you are building a conversational AI product that processes sensitive user queries, configure your HTTP client to verify hostname matching and disable legacy cipher suites.

Sanitize User Inputs Against Prompt Injection

Prompt injection remains the most common and dangerous vulnerability in conversational AI. Treat all user input as untrusted. Use allowlists for expected characters, enforce length limits, and separate system instructions from user data with clear delimiters. For agentic workflows that use tool use or function calling, implement human-in-the-loop approval before destructive actions.

Oxlo.ai supports function calling, multi-turn conversations, and JSON mode across models such as Qwen 3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, and DeepSeek R1 671B MoE. These features expand capability, but they also expand attack surface. When using tool use, validate all arguments server-side before executing local code. Never let an LLM directly construct SQL, shell commands, or file paths without parameterized guards.

import re

def sanitize_input(text: str, max_len: int = 4000) -> str:
    # Remove control characters and limit length
    cleaned = "".join(ch for ch in text if ord(ch) >= 32)
    return cleaned[:max_len]

user_message = sanitize_input(untrusted_input)

Filter Outputs and Validate Structured Responses

Even benign prompts can generate harmful, biased, or PII-laden responses. Implement a secondary moderation layer that scans completions before they reach the user. If you rely on JSON mode for structured data extraction, validate the response schema with Pydantic or a similar library before acting on the data. A malformed or adversarial JSON payload can trigger deserialization bugs or logic errors in your application.

Oxlo.ai offers JSON mode on its LLMs and chat models. Validate every JSON response against a strict schema to prevent unexpected fields from reaching your business logic. For high-stakes domains like healthcare or finance, consider adding a deterministic rules engine after the LLM layer to enforce hard constraints.

Maintain Audit Logs Without Retaining PII

Logging is essential for debugging and compliance, but raw chat logs are a liability. Log request metadata such as timestamp, model name, status code, and latency. Redact message contents if they contain personally identifiable information. Use hashed or pseudonymized user identifiers instead of raw emails or phone numbers.

Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, your billing and usage records reflect request counts rather than token volumes. This simplifies cost auditing and reduces the sensitivity of usage metadata, since there are no per-token logs that might leak prompt or completion length.

Implement Rate Limiting and Abuse Detection

Protect your inference endpoints against enumeration attacks, credential stuffing, and cost-based abuse. Apply per-user and per-IP rate limits, and use exponential backoff for retries. Monitor for anomalous patterns, such as sudden spikes in request volume or repeated schema violations that may indicate automated probing.

Oxlo.ai offers tiered plans with daily request quotas, which act as a natural ceiling on spend. Enterprise customers can negotiate dedicated GPU pools for isolated, predictable throughput and additional queue controls. Review the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Understand Data Retention and Provider Policies

Before sending user data to any inference provider, review their privacy policy and data retention terms. Confirm that prompts are not used to train future models unless you have explicitly opted in. For regulated industries, ask about SOC 2, GDPR, or HIPAA alignment.

When using Oxlo.ai, review the platform's privacy policy to confirm that data handling meets your compliance requirements. For the highest assurance, Enterprise plans offer dedicated infrastructure that keeps traffic logically separated from other workloads.

Extend Security to Multimodal Inputs

Conversational AI is no longer text-only. Vision inputs and audio transcriptions introduce new vectors: malicious EXIF data, steganography, or adversarial audio samples. Oxlo.ai supports vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B, plus audio transcription via Whisper Large v3 and text-to-speech via Kokoro 82M.

Sanitize files before upload: strip metadata, transcode to a standard format, validate MIME types server-side, and reject oversized payloads. Never pass raw file bytes directly into downstream systems. If you are using image generation endpoints like Oxlo.ai Image Pro or Flux.1, apply the same content filters to prompts that you apply to chat inputs.

Secure Your SDK and Dependency Chain

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so you likely consume the official openai Python or Node.js package. Pin your dependency versions in requirements.txt or package-lock.json. Audit your supply chain regularly with tools like pip-audit or npm audit. Because Oxlo.ai requires no custom client libraries, your attack surface remains minimal and transparent. You do not need to install an obscure wrapper that may lag behind security patches.

Build Secure Conversational AI with Oxlo.ai

Security for LLM inference is defense in depth: scoped credentials, TLS enforcement, input sanitization, output filtering, audit logging, rate limiting, and provider due diligence. Oxlo.ai fits naturally into this stack. Its OpenAI-compatible API means you adopt standard security patterns without vendor-specific workarounds. Its request-based pricing removes token-count surprises from your billing while supporting long-context and agentic workloads securely.

title: LLM Inference API Comparison for Language Understanding Tasks
content:
Choosing an inference API for production language understanding tasks is rarely about finding the largest model. It is about matching context window requirements, latency constraints, and cost structure to the actual shape of your workload. Most comparisons rank providers by throughput benchmarks or model availability, but they rarely address how pricing mechanics affect long-document analysis, multi-turn agent loops, or batch classification jobs. If your application processes lengthy articles, legal contracts, or extended conversational histories, the token economics of your provider matter more than the headline model name.

What Language Understanding Tasks Actually Require

Language understanding covers a wide spectrum. Named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and semantic search typically send short prompts and expect structured outputs. Document summarization, contract review, and research synthesis demand tens of thousands of input tokens per request. Agentic workflows that maintain tool state and conversation memory compound that volume across multiple turns.

These workloads share one trait: input length dominates cost. When a provider bills by the token, every retrieved document chunk, system prompt, and few-shot example inflates the bill before the model generates a single completion token. The result is that a task with modest output requirements but heavy context can become disproportionately expensive.

Token-Based vs. Request-Based Pricing

The majority of inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, operate on token-based pricing. Under this model you pay for both prompt and completion tokens. For language understanding tasks involving long inputs, costs scale linearly with context length. A single request with a 128K context window can cost significantly more than the same request with a 4K window, even if the model's answer is only a few sentences.

Oxlo.ai approaches this differently with request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For long-context workloads, this can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives because the price does not increase when you add more documentation, conversation history, or retrieved passages to the prompt. If your pipeline sends large contexts repeatedly, the difference in monthly spend is substantial.

Rather than estimating token counts for every prompt template, you can budget by request volume. This predictability is useful for teams running batch classification or document analysis where input size varies wildly between calls. You can see the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

API Compatibility and Integration Friction

Switching inference providers usually involves rewriting client code, retesting error handling, and revalidating JSON mode behavior. Most engineering teams want a drop-in replacement rather than a migration project.

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, and you can use the existing Python, Node.js, or cURL patterns without changing request shapes. This matters for language understanding pipelines that rely on structured outputs, function calling, or streaming responses. The example below sends a long document for classification using the standard chat completions endpoint:

    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",

        {"role": "user", "content": "PASTE_FULL_CONTRACT_TEXT_HERE"}

title: Optimizing LLM Model Performance for Real-Time Language Understanding
content:
Real-time language understanding demands more than benchmark accuracy. In production, latency, throughput, and cost predictability determine whether an AI feature feels instantaneous or broken. Users expect chat interfaces to stream responses within milliseconds, voice agents to parse intent without perceptible delay, and agentic workflows to execute tool chains in rapid succession. Achieving this requires optimizing every layer of the stack, from model weights and serving infrastructure to API pricing mechanics. The following strategies target the specific bottlenecks that degrade responsiveness, with practical implementation details you can verify immediately.

Identify Latency Bottlenecks Beyond Model Size

Most discussions about inference speed focus on parameter count, but production latency is rarely that simple. Inference splits into two distinct phases: prefill and decode. During prefill, the model processes the entire input prompt in parallel to build the key-value (KV) cache. During decode, it generates tokens autoregressively, a step that is usually memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. This means a short prompt followed by a long output can still feel slow because each new token requires loading the full model weights and the growing KV cache across the GPU memory bus.

For real-time applications, you must minimize both phases. Keep prompts concise by retrieving only relevant context, and prefer architectures that handle long sequences efficiently. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can reduce active parameters per forward pass, lowering memory pressure. On Oxlo.ai, models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash and DeepSeek R1 671B MoE leverage sparse activation to deliver high-quality reasoning without loading the entire dense weight set on every token. Similarly, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window through an efficient architecture, making it suitable for long-document understanding without the proportional slowdown you might expect from legacy dense models.

Serving Optimizations for Sub-Second Response

Model architecture is only half the equation. How the inference engine serves requests matters just as much. Continuous batching, also known as in-flight batching, allows the server to process new requests as soon as slots free up, rather than waiting for an entire batch to finish. This keeps GPU utilization high and average latency low under concurrent load.

Speculative decoding offers another lever. A smaller draft model generates candidate tokens quickly, and the larger target model verifies them in parallel. When the draft model is sufficiently accurate, this effectively reduces the number of expensive forward passes required. Quantization to formats such as FP8 or INT8 further reduces memory bandwidth, though you should validate output quality for your specific domain after quantization.

Infrastructure consistency is equally critical. Cold starts, where a model must be loaded into GPU memory after a period of inactivity, can inject seconds of unpredictable latency into an otherwise fast pipeline. Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, which means your real-time pipeline maintains a steady latency profile without warmup penalties. This is essential for voice agents and interactive coding assistants where any stutter destroys user trust.

Right-Size Models for the Task

A common mistake in building real-time systems is defaulting to the largest available model for every request. Not every classification, extraction, or routing decision requires a 70B parameter flagship. In many cases, a 32B or even a 9B model delivers equivalent accuracy with far lower latency.

Oxlo.ai provides 45+ models across seven categories, giving you the latitude to match model capacity to task complexity. For general multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B offers strong performance at a fraction of the inference cost of larger dense models. For coding tasks that demand fast autocomplete or iterative debugging, Oxlo.ai Coder Fast and DeepSeek V3.2 provide specialized weights optimized for low-latency generation. For vision-language tasks that must resolve visual inputs in real time, Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B are available without requiring a separate image processing pipeline.

Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based metering, experimenting with these model swaps is cost-predictable. You can route simple queries to smaller models and escalate complex reasoning to larger ones without watching input token costs scale unpredictably. This tiered routing pattern is a proven architecture for keeping p95 latency low.

Use Streaming and Structured Output

Perceived latency often matters more than absolute latency. Streaming responses let you emit tokens to the client as they are generated, which makes the interface feel responsive even if total time-to-last-token is unchanged. Always enable streaming for user-facing chat or voice pipelines.

Structured output, including JSON mode and function calling, reduces downstream parsing overhead and eliminates the need for fragile regular expressions. When a model returns a well-formed tool call or schema-compliant object, your orchestration layer can act immediately rather than sanitizing free-form text.

Oxlo.ai supports streaming, JSON mode, and function calling through a fully OpenAI SDK compatible API. Switching your existing client requires only a base URL change:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this in JSON with keys: title, summary."}
    ],
    stream=True,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

This pattern gives you immediate first-token visibility and deterministic output structure, both of which are non-negotiable for real-time agents.

Cache Prompt Context and Reuse Embeddings

Prefill time scales with prompt length. If your application sends a large system prompt, few-shot examples, or lengthy conversation history on every request, you are paying a latency penalty repeatedly. Cache static components whenever your inference provider supports it, and use embeddings to retrieve only the minimal relevant context needed for each query.

For retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, embedding latency becomes part of the critical path. Oxlo.ai offers embedding models including BGE-Large and E5-Large, which you can query through the same OpenAI-compatible SDK. By keeping embedding inference and chat completion on the same platform, you reduce network hops and simplify authentication.

In multi-turn conversational interfaces, prune messages that fall outside the relevant context window. Sending ten turns of history when only the last three are semantically necessary adds prefill compute with no accuracy benefit. A disciplined context window policy directly translates to faster user responses.

Cost Predictability at Scale

Real-time workloads are rarely composed of single, isolated requests. They are high-frequency streams: a voice agent processing audio chunks, a coding assistant generating diffs on every keystroke, or an agentic loop chaining tool calls. Under token-based pricing, costs scale linearly with input length, which means long-context retrieval, full conversation history, or detailed system prompts directly inflate your bill.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives because your cost does not grow as you add more context or history to each request. You can include comprehensive retrieved documents, maintain full conversational state, or send large structured inputs without the cost anxiety that typically accompanies token metering.

This pricing model also simplifies capacity planning. A fixed per-request cost lets you map user sessions directly to infrastructure spend, which is far easier to forecast than variable token rates. For teams building real-time products, that predictability is an architectural advantage. You can review the exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Conclusion

Optimizing LLMs for real-time language understanding is a systems problem. You need to minimize prefill and decode latency through efficient architectures and serving optimizations. You need to right-size models, stream responses, and cache context aggressively. And you need an infrastructure layer that guarantees consistent performance without cold starts, alongside a pricing model that stays predictable under the high-frequency, long-context conditions typical of real-time applications.

Oxlo.ai addresses these requirements with a developer-first inference platform that offers 45+ models, OpenAI SDK compatibility, no cold starts on popular models, and flat per-request pricing. Whether you are routing simple queries through Qwen 3 32B, streaming structured JSON from DeepSeek V4 Flash, or embedding retrieval context with BGE-Large, the platform is built to keep latency low and costs transparent.

title: Using LLM for Language Translation in Language Learning Tasks
content:
I built a small CLI tool that acts like a patient language tutor. Feed it a sentence in Spanish, Japanese, or French and it returns a natural translation, a literal breakdown, grammar notes, and a difficulty rating. It is for self-directed learners and teachers who want to know why a phrase works, not just what it means. The whole thing runs against Oxlo.ai using the standard OpenAI SDK, so the setup is minimal.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • A sentence or passage you want to study

Step 1: Set up the client

I chose Qwen 3 32B for this project because Oxlo.ai lists it as a strong multilingual model with good reasoning and agent workflow support. Since Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, I do not need a special client library. I just point the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and use my existing OpenAI patterns. If you want to experiment later, Oxlo.ai also offers Llama 3.3 70B and Kimi K2.6, which you can drop in by changing a single string.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
)

Step 2: Design the system prompt

The system prompt is the entire product. I do not want a raw translation. I want the model to behave like a tutor sitting next to me. I ask for five sections: a natural translation, a literal breakdown, grammar notes, alternative phrasings, and a CEFR difficulty level. I keep the instructions imperative and short so they survive a low-token response.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a concise language tutor. When the user provides a sentence, respond with these exact sections:

1. Natural Translation: A natural English translation.
2. Literal Breakdown: Word-by-word or clause-by-clause literal mapping.
3. Grammar Notes: Two to three short bullets explaining key grammar points.
4. Alternative Phrasings: Two other ways a native speaker might express the same idea.
5. CEFR Level: Estimate the difficulty as A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, or C2.

Be brief and practical."""

Step 3: Build the translation function

I set temperature to 0.3 because I want the grammar notes to stay consistent across repeated quizzing. If the temperature is too high, the model might invent colloquialisms that do not match my textbook. I also cap max_tokens at 1024. That is enough for a single sentence and its analysis, but it acts as a guardrail against runaway verbosity. The function accepts a string and returns the assistant's message content. This is the core loop I run during my morning study session.

def translate_for_learning(sentence: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": sentence},
        ],
        temperature=0.3,
        max_tokens=1024,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

user_message = "El clima está muy agradable hoy."
print(translate_for_learning(user_message))

Step 4: Add structured JSON output

Raw markdown is fine for the terminal, but I wanted structured data I could import into Anki or Notion. I created a JSON mode variant by appending format instructions to the system prompt. I keep the same client and model, but I lower the temperature to 0.2 to reduce creative formatting that might break parsing. I parse the result with Python's built-in json module. If the model ever wraps the JSON in markdown backticks, I strip them before parsing.

import json

JSON_PROMPT = SYSTEM_PROMPT + (
    "\n\nReturn your response as a single JSON object with keys: "
    "natural_translation, literal_breakdown, grammar_notes (list), "
    "alternatives (list), cefr_level. Do not wrap the JSON in markdown fences."
)

def translate_json(sentence: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": JSON_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": sentence},
        ],
        temperature=0.2,
        max_tokens=1200,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

card = translate_json("Demain, je vais essayer de courir dix kilomètres.")
print(json.dumps(card, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))

Step 5: Batch process a passage

Single sentences are useful, but real language input is paragraphs. I added a chunking helper that splits a long passage on word boundaries and sends each chunk through the same JSON pipeline. Here is where Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing changes the math. On token-based platforms, a long paragraph can cost significantly more than a short sentence because you pay for every input and output token. Oxlo.ai charges one flat rate per request. That means a 250-word paragraph costs the same as a five-word sentence. For learners working through blog posts, news articles, or book chapters, this removes the anxiety of racking up token fees on long-context inputs. I keep chunks around 100 words to give the model enough context for coherent grammar notes without making each request too heavy.

def translate_passage(passage: str, chunk_size: int = 100) -> list[dict]:
    words = passage.split()
    chunks = [
        " ".join(words[i : i + chunk_size])
        for i in range(0, len(words), chunk_size)
    ]
    results = []
    for chunk in chunks:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="qwen-3-32b",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": JSON_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": chunk},
            ],
            temperature=0.2,
            max_tokens=1500,
        )
        raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
        if raw.startswith("```"):
            raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
        results.append(json.loads(raw))
    return results

passage = (
    "La inteligencia artificial está cambiando la forma en que aprendemos idiomas. "
    "Los modelos de lenguaje pueden ofrecer traducciones instantáneas, "
    "pero también explicaciones gramaticales detalladas que antes requerían un tutor humano."
)
cards = translate_passage(passage, chunk_size=50)
for c in cards:
    print(c["natural_translation"])

Run it

I save everything in a file named tutor.py, swap in my real API key, and run python tutor.py from my terminal. When I feed it a Japanese sentence, the model returns a clean breakdown that I can read in one screen. Here is what the output looks like.

Natural Translation: The cat is sleeping on the chair.
Literal Breakdown: Neko (cat) ga (subject marker) isu (chair) no (possessive/location) ue (top) de (at) neteimasu (is sleeping).
Grammar Notes:
- "Ga" marks the subject, not the topic.
- "Ue de" combines "ue" (top) and "de" (location particle) to mean "on top of."
- "Neteimasu" is the progressive form of "neru" (to sleep).
Alternative Phrasings:
- Isu no ue de neko ga nete iru.
- Neko ga isu no ue ni neteimasu.
CEFR Level: A2

Next steps

If you want to productize this, two directions are obvious. First, wrap the translate_json function in a FastAPI endpoint so a teacher can POST classroom sentences and get back structured study cards that feed directly into a flashcard app. Second, add a daily review loop that resurfaces the grammar_notes from your highest CEFR-level cards each morning. You can reuse the exact same Oxlo.ai client and just swap the system prompt to act as a drill instructor. Because the platform has no cold starts on popular models, the API responds immediately even if your study app has sporadic usage. For pricing details on running this at scale, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Building Conversational AI Systems for Tech Support with LLM
content:
Building a production conversational AI system for technical support requires more than wrapping a chat interface around a large language model. Support conversations are inherently stateful, context-heavy, and frequently multimodal. Users paste log files, attach screenshots of error dialogs, and expect the system to query internal knowledge bases, create tickets, and escalate issues without losing track of prior turns. For engineering teams, this means designing for long context windows, reliable function calling, and inference costs that remain predictable as conversation depth and attachment size increase. The infrastructure choices you make at the inference layer directly determine whether your agent can maintain coherence across a twenty-turn debugging session or collapse under latency and token bills.

Architecture Overview

A production-grade tech support stack typically combines retrieval-augmented generation with agentic orchestration. Incoming queries are embedded and matched against a vector store of documentation, runbooks, and resolved tickets. The LLM then acts as a router: it decides whether to answer directly, call a search tool, request clarification, or invoke an action such as creating a Jira issue or resetting a service flag. Because support threads can accumulate thousands of tokens across system prompts, conversation history, retrieved chunks, and raw logs, the inference layer must handle large prompts efficiently. The retrieval step itself can leverage Oxlo.ai’s embeddings endpoints, using models such as BGE-Large or E5-Large to encode documentation and ticket history into vectors. Cold starts are unacceptable when a user is waiting in a live chat window, and billing must remain transparent as context grows.

Model Selection

Not every support interaction requires the same model capacity. A password reset or billing question runs well on an efficient generalist, while a distributed systems outage demands deep reasoning and code analysis.

Oxlo.ai offers a catalog of over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all exposed through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. For standard conversational flow and multilingual agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B provides strong reasoning and tool-use capabilities. Llama 3.3 70B serves as a reliable general-purpose flagship for high-volume chat workloads. When a ticket involves complex debugging, architecture review, or step-by-step reasoning, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 deliver advanced chain-of-thought performance and agentic coding skills. GLM 5, a 744B parameter MoE, is suited for long-horizon agentic tasks that require planning across many tool calls. For coding-specific support, Minimax M2.5 and DeepSeek V3.2 handle agentic tool use and code generation. If you need to process an entire codebase or a one-million-token log archive in a single prompt, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers an efficient MoE architecture with a 1M context window.
