Switching between these models requires no client rewrite. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so changing from Llama to Kimi is a single parameter update in Python, Node.js, or cURL.

Managing Context and Memory

Tech support sessions are long-context workloads by nature. A single thread might include a detailed system prompt, ten turns of back-and-forth, several retrieved documentation passages, and a full stack trace. Under token-based pricing, every additional line of history increases cost. For agentic systems that maintain scratchpads or iteratively refine search queries, token bills compound with each turn.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale, your cost does not scale with input size. Tool Use and Structured Output

A support agent that cannot take action is only a search engine. Your LLM must invoke ticketing APIs, query status pages, validate license keys, and update account flags. This requires robust function calling, JSON mode for structured extraction, and streaming for responsive user interfaces.

Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, function calling, tool use, and JSON mode across its chat models. The assistant receives the user complaint, decides to create a ticket, and returns a structured function call.

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"

tools = [
    {

Because there are no cold starts on popular models, this call returns immediately even during sudden traffic spikes. You can also force JSON mode when you need deterministic extraction of fields like error codes or affected service names.

Handling Multimodal Inputs

Users do not always describe errors in text. A screenshot of a traceback or a short screen recording with audio narration is often the fastest way to communicate a problem. A complete support system should accept images and audio alongside text.

Oxlo.ai provides vision models including Gemma 3 27B, Kimi VL A3B, and Kimi K2.6, which accept image inputs as part of a multi-turn conversation. For audio, you can route voice memos through Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, or Whisper Medium via the audio/transcriptions endpoint, then feed the resulting text into the chat pipeline. Kokoro 82M is also available for text-to-speech if you need voice responses. This unifies multimodal context under a single API base URL and SDK.

Cost and Operational Considerations

Predictable pricing is critical when running a 24/7 support bot. Token-based meters make monthly forecasting difficult if ticket complexity varies. A single urgent escalation might involve a 128K context window, multiple retrieval steps, and several tool calls.

Oxlo.ai’s request-based model eliminates this variance. Whether the prompt is 500 tokens or 50,000 tokens, the cost per request stays flat. For teams handling enterprise support loads, this can translate to 10-100x savings compared to token-based billing on long-context workloads. Plans scale from a Free tier offering 60 requests per day across 16+ models plus a 7-day full-access trial, to Pro at 1,000 requests per day, Premium at 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access, and Enterprise with unlimited requests, dedicated GPUs, and a guaranteed 30% cost reduction versus your current provider. You can compare details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Evaluation and Safety

Before shipping to users, establish an evaluation pipeline that measures answer relevance, tool invocation accuracy, hallucination rate, and escalation precision. Use a held-out set of real tickets to test whether the model incorrectly creates tickets or invents account statuses. Implement human-in-the-loop handoffs for high-priority or sensitive issues. Ground all responses in retrieved documentation rather than parametric knowledge alone, and use JSON mode to constrain outputs when exact formatting matters.

For automated regression testing, you can use Oxlo.ai’s embeddings endpoint to compute semantic similarity between generated answers and verified ground-truth responses. Monitor latency distributions closely; support bots must feel interactive, and streaming responses help maintain perceived speed even during complex reasoning steps.

Conclusion

Conversational AI for tech support sits at the intersection of long-context reasoning, multimodal understanding, tool use, and cost control. The right infrastructure lets you retain full conversation history, attach logs and images, and invoke internal APIs without surprise bills or cold-start latency. Oxlo.ai provides the model breadth, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and flat request-based pricing needed to build these systems efficiently. If you are evaluating inference providers for your next support agent, start with the free tier and scale as your ticket volume grows.

title: LLM for Sentiment Analysis in Product Review Analysis
content:
Product review sentiment analysis is one of the fastest ways to ship real value with an LLM, and if you run an e-commerce site or SaaS product you already have unstructured feedback piling up in your database or support inbox. In this tutorial, I will build a lightweight Python pipeline that ingests raw customer feedback and returns structured sentiment scores using Oxlo.ai, where flat per-request pricing means you can feed the model entire reviews without worrying that length will drive up cost.

What you'll need

Before writing code, make sure your environment is ready. I use Python 3.10 or newer for modern typing support, though 3.11 and 3.12 work just as well. I recommend creating a fresh virtual environment so the OpenAI SDK does not clash with other project dependencies. You will need the OpenAI SDK installed from PyPI with pip install openai because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully compatible endpoint and no custom adapter is necessary. You also need an Oxlo.ai API key, which you can generate at https://portal.oxlo.ai. Once activated, install the package and verify the import in a Python shell before moving on. Finally, gather a handful of real product reviews. If you do not have any available, I include sample strings in Step 4 that you can copy directly.

Step 1: Configure the client

I initialize the OpenAI SDK client and point it at Oxlo.ai's compatible endpoint, pulling the API key from an environment variable so credentials never end up in git history. The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, and once this client exists every subsequent call uses the standard chat.completions interface you already know.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the only place where I teach the model its job, so I enumerate the exact JSON schema and allowed enum values while explicitly forbidding markdown fences or conversational filler that would break parsing. Keeping this in a dedicated constant near the top of the file makes iteration easy when stakeholders inevitably ask for new aspects like shipping or packaging.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a product review analyst. Read the customer review and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- overall_sentiment: must be Positive, Negative, or Neutral
- confidence: a float from 0.0 to 1.0
- aspects: an object containing keys price, quality, usability, and support. Each aspect value must be Positive, Negative, or Neutral.
- summary: one sentence summarizing the review
Return only the JSON object. Do not wrap it in markdown, do not add explanations, and do not include any text outside the JSON."""

Step 3: Build the analyzer function

I wrap the inference call in an analyze_review function that sends raw text to Llama 3.3 70B and parses the response with json.loads, stripping accidental code fences defensively because even well-instructed models occasionally wrap JSON in triple backticks. Because Oxlo.ai serves requests with no cold starts, this function returns immediately and feels safe to call inside a simple synchronous loop without introducing async complexity for small batches.

import json

def analyze_review(review_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": review_text},
        ],
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Batch-process reviews

Real feedback arrives in batches, so I loop over a list of reviews, wrap each call in try/except to isolate failures, and sleep briefly between requests to stay polite to the API endpoints while monitoring progress with a simple print statement. Since Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, I never feel pressure to truncate long reviews, which means the model always sees the full customer context and I never sacrifice signal for cost, a major advantage when customers write detailed multi-paragraph rants.

import time

reviews = [
    "I love the build quality but the price is ridiculous compared to competitors. Support was friendly though.",
    "Battery life is amazing and the interface is intuitive. Best purchase I made this year.",
    "It is okay for the price but nothing special. Does what it says.",
]

results = []
for review in reviews:
    try:
        result = analyze_review(review)
        results.append(result)
    except Exception as e:
        results.append({"error": str(e), "review": review})
    time.sleep(0.5)

Step 5: Aggregate and report

Stakeholders need summaries, not raw JSON, so I tally overall sentiment and roll up per-aspect scores with Python's Counter to reveal hidden patterns that average star ratings obscure, such as quality being high while support lags. I also average the confidence scores so I can spot-check batches where the model feels less certain and might need a stronger reasoning model like DeepSeek R1, DeepSeek V3.2, or Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai.

from collections import Counter

valid_results = [r for r in results if "error" not in r]

overall_counts = Counter(r["overall_sentiment"] for r in valid_results)
avg_confidence = sum(r["confidence"] for r in valid_results) / len(valid_results)

aspect_totals = {a: Counter() for a in ["price", "quality", "usability", "support"]}
for r in valid_results:
    for aspect, sentiment in r["aspects"].items():
        aspect_totals[aspect][sentiment] += 1

print("Overall sentiment:", dict(overall_counts))
print(f"Average confidence: {avg_confidence:.2f}")
print("Aspect breakdown:")
for aspect, counts in aspect_totals.items():
    print(f"  {aspect}: {dict(counts)}")

for r in valid_results:
    print(f"- {r['summary']} ({r['overall_sentiment']}, conf={r['confidence']})")

Run it

I save the complete script as sentiment_pipeline.py and invoke it from the terminal. The first review is deliberately mixed. The model correctly identifies that price drags the overall sentiment to Negative even though quality and support are Positive. The second review is unambiguously Positive, and the third lands squarely in Neutral territory. Looking at the aspect breakdown, quality received two Positive labels while price got one Negative and one Neutral. This level of granularity is exactly why an LLM pipeline beats simple polarity classifiers. It also highlights the value of Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing, because I sent the full text of every review and never had to truncate words to save tokens. If you see a JSONDecodeError on the first run, check that the model did not emit markdown despite the instruction; the defensive strip logic in analyze_review should handle it, but you can add a debug print of raw to inspect edge cases.

$ python sentiment_pipeline.py
Overall sentiment: {'Negative': 1, 'Positive': 1, 'Neutral': 1}
Average confidence: 0.91
Aspect breakdown:
  price: {'Negative': 1, 'Neutral': 1}
  quality: {'Positive': 2}
  usability: {'Positive': 1, 'Neutral': 1}
  support: {'Positive': 1, 'Neutral': 1}
- Good build and support undermined by high price (Negative, conf=0.89)
- Excellent battery life and intuitive interface (Positive, conf=0.95)
- Adequate product that meets basic expectations (Neutral, conf=0.88)

Next steps

If you want to ship this beyond a local script, two paths are obvious. First, containerize the analyzer and schedule it with cron or a worker queue to process new reviews nightly, then push the resulting JSON into BigQuery, Postgres, or a Slack webhook. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, your cost is predictable. You simply multiply the number of reviews by your plan's per-request rate and you are done, with no spreadsheet gymnastics to estimate input and output tokens. You could also expose the analyzer as a FastAPI endpoint and call it from your internal admin dashboard. The flat per-request pricing makes it easy to expose this to non-technical teammates without fearing a surprise bill from a runaway loop. Second, if your catalog expands internationally or you start seeing sarcastic tone that confuses the classifier, swap the model name to qwen-3-32b, kimi-k2.6, or deepseek-v3.2. All three handle multilingual reasoning and advanced nuance well, and because they live on Oxlo.ai under the same request-based pricing, the only change is the model string.

title: Using LLM for Natural Language Understanding in Chatbot Development
content:
Natural language understanding has always been the hardest part of building chatbots that feel natural. Early systems relied on rigid intent classifiers and regex-based entity extractors that broke the moment a user rephrased a question. Large language models changed the equation. With a single API call, a modern LLM can infer intent, extract entities, detect sentiment, and maintain conversational context across dozens of turns. The challenge now is not capability, but choosing the right inference architecture and provider to keep latency low and costs predictable as your user base scales.

Why NLU is the Core of Conversational AI

Before transformers, a chatbot pipeline was a stack of specialized models. One classifier guessed the intent, another extractor pulled out dates and names, and a third managed sentiment. Each component needed training data, versioning, and separate deployment. LLMs collapsed this stack into a single endpoint. A well-prompted model can perform intent recognition, slot filling, coreference resolution, and sentiment analysis in one pass. This unification speeds up development, but it also means your inference provider becomes the foundation of your user experience. If the model is too small, accuracy drops. If the endpoint has cold starts, users wait. If pricing is token-based, long conversations become prohibitively expensive.

title: Integrating LLM with Reinforcement Learning for Language Understanding
content:
Reinforcement learning has become the dominant paradigm for pushing large language models beyond the limits of their pretraining distributions. While supervised fine-tuning teaches models to imitate high-quality text, RL teaches them to optimize for outcomes. In modern pipelines, the LLM acts as a policy network generating tokens as actions, while a reward model or interactive environment provides scalar feedback. This loop enables capabilities that static datasets cannot capture, including extended chain-of-thought reasoning, tool use, and alignment with complex human preferences. Yet the shift from supervised learning to RL fundamentally changes compute requirements. The training process becomes inference-bound, with research teams generating millions of completions across varying context lengths to estimate gradients and evaluate policies. When inference is billed per token, these rollouts introduce cost volatility that scales directly with prompt length and exploration depth.

The Shift from Supervised Fine-Tuning to RL

Supervised fine-tuning assumes a fixed input-output pair. RL assumes a trajectory. A single training step may require the policy to generate multiple completions for the same prompt, each of which is scored by a reward model or executed in an environment to measure success. Algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization and its variants, including Group Relative Policy Optimization used in reasoning models, sample a batch of responses and compute advantage estimates across the group. This means inference volume is inherently high and bursty. Prompts are not short user queries. They often contain lengthy system instructions, few-shot examples, tool schemas, and prior conversation history. In agentic settings, the context window accumulates observations and actions over many turns before a terminal reward is issued. The result is a workload profile defined by long contexts, high sampling counts, and unpredictable completion lengths.

Core Algorithms and Reward Modeling

The integration of RL and LLMs typically centers on three mechanisms. RLHF uses a reward model trained on human preference data to score policy outputs, then optimizes the policy with PPO against that reward signal. Direct Preference Optimization bypasses the separate reward model and optimizes the policy directly on preference pairs, simplifying the stack but still requiring extensive inference for evaluation and rejection sampling. More advanced systems employ process reward models that provide intermediate feedback at each reasoning step, enabling credit assignment over long chains of thought. In tool-use and agentic domains, the reward function is often an environment itself, such as a unit test suite or a web navigation task, where the LLM must emit structured function calls and observe results. Each of these paradigms requires not just raw generation capacity, but structured output formats, function calling, and streaming to manage latency across distributed rollout workers.

The Inference Cost Problem in RL Loops

Token-based pricing creates a structural mismatch with RL workloads. Because costs scale with input plus output tokens, any increase in context length or sampling temperature directly inflates the budget. A researcher running hyperparameter sweeps over top-p and temperature might generate twenty variants of the same long prompt. Under token billing, this experiment is twenty times more expensive in input tokens alone. Multi-turn agentic episodes compound the problem, as each turn appends the full history to the context. Cold starts exacerbate latency, causing distributed rollout collectors to stall while waiting for GPU warmup. JSON mode and function calling, essential for environment interaction, are sometimes inconsistent across providers, requiring custom parsing logic that slows integration. For teams iterating on reward functions daily, these frictions accumulate into a significant tax on experimentation.

Oxlo.ai as an Inference Layer for RL

Oxlo.ai offers an alternative inference economics model designed for exactly these workloads. With request-based pricing, Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For RL pipelines, this removes the penalty on long system prompts, few-shot contexts, and accumulated agent histories. A rollout with a 10,000-token prompt costs the same as a rollout with a 100-token prompt. This predictability allows researchers to fix their inference budget while varying context length and sampling depth freely.

The platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, functioning as a drop-in replacement by changing the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. Existing Python RL frameworks using the OpenAI client can stream rollouts, enforce JSON mode for structured action spaces, and invoke function calling without client rewrites. There are no cold starts on popular models, so distributed rollout workers maintain steady throughput. Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models across seven categories, including the exact architectures researchers need for policy and reward modeling. DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash provide deep reasoning for math and coding environments where reward signals are sparse and chains are long. Qwen 3 32B supports multilingual agent workflows. Llama 3.3 70B offers a reliable general-purpose policy. GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 handle long-horizon agentic tasks and coding, respectively. For vision-language RL, Kimi VL A3B and Gemma 3 27B accept image inputs, enabling visual state spaces. This breadth lets teams test policy architectures across model families from a single endpoint.

Integration Patterns for Developers

Implementing an RL loop against Oxlo.ai requires minimal boilerplate. A researcher can instantiate the standard OpenAI client, set the base URL and API key, and begin generating rollouts. For structured environments, enabling JSON mode constrains the policy to emit valid action tokens that the environment can parse immediately. Function calling allows models like Qwen 3 or Kimi K2.6 to interact with calculators, search APIs, or code interpreters as part of their action space. Because the pricing is per request, teams can afford to run outcome-supervised verification, where the same problem is sampled dozens of times to compute a pass rate or consensus reward without fearing token multiplication.

A typical pattern involves separating rollout generation from reward computation. The policy model generates trajectories via the chat/completions endpoint. A separate critic or reward model, potentially hosted on Oxlo.ai as an embedding or chat endpoint, scores each trajectory. The scores feed back into a local trainer running PPO or DPO. Since Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, rollout collectors can begin processing partial completions while generation is still in flight, reducing wall-clock time for long reasoning chains. For teams building process reward models, the multi-turn conversation endpoint supports inserting intermediate feedback into the context window, allowing step-by-step credit assignment.

Model Selection for RL Tasks

Choosing the right model depends on the action space and horizon of the task. For reasoning-intensive domains such as competitive programming or formal mathematics, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash offer near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning with support for long context, making them ideal for sparse-reward environments. Qwen 3 32B and GPT-Oss 120B provide strong multilingual and general reasoning baselines. When the agent must write and execute code to receive rewards, DeepSeek V3.2 and Qwen 3 Coder 30B are optimized for code generation syntax and structure.

For vision-based RL, Kimi K2.6 provides advanced reasoning with a 131K context window and vision capabilities, allowing pixel-based or diagram-based states to be processed directly. Embedding models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large on Oxlo.ai enable semantic similarity rewards, where the rollout is scored against a reference embedding rather than an explicit label. With plans ranging from Free at 60 requests per day for prototyping, to Pro at 1,000 requests per day, Premium at 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access, and Enterprise with dedicated GPUs, teams can match throughput to their experimental scale. The 7-day full-access trial on the Free tier lets researchers validate the integration before committing.

Conclusion

Reinforcement learning transforms LLMs from static predictors into active optimizers, but this transformation places extraordinary demands on inference infrastructure. The shift from token-based to request-based economics is not merely a pricing detail. It is a structural change that aligns cost with experimental iteration rather than context length. Oxlo.ai provides this alignment through flat per-request pricing, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a deep catalog of reasoning, coding, and vision models. By eliminating cold starts and supporting the structured outputs that RL environments require, Oxlo.ai lets engineers focus on designing better rewards and policies. For teams pushing the frontier of language understanding through RL, the inference platform should be an accelerator, not a constraint. Explore the model catalog and pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Using LLM for Question Answering in FAQs
content:
Most support teams drown in repetitive questions. I recently shipped a small LLM-powered FAQ agent that retrieves relevant answers from a static knowledge base and replies in natural language. Unlike fine-tuning, this approach lets me update answers instantly by editing the source text. It runs entirely on Oxlo.ai, using flat per-request pricing so the cost stays predictable even when I stuff long policy documents into the context window. Here is how I built it.

What you'll need

You will need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and a few lines of vector math. Grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the imports look identical to what you already know. Install the dependencies with pip.

pip install openai numpy

Set your key in an environment variable so the client can pick it up without hard-coding secrets.

export OXLO_API_KEY="your_key_here"

Step 1: Prepare your FAQ corpus

I keep the source data simple. A Python list of dictionaries is enough to prove the concept, and it mirrors the JSON you would pull from a CMS, Notion export, or help-desk API. Each entry stores the canonical question and the approved answer. I avoid unstructured prose because the retriever works best when the question field closely matches how users actually ask. Separating the question from the answer also lets me embed only the question while keeping the full answer hidden from the embedding model.

FAQ_DB = [
    {
        "question": "What should I do if I forgot my password?",
        "answer": "Click 'Forgot password' on the login page and follow the reset link sent to your email."
    },
    {
        "question": "Which payment methods do you accept?",
        "answer": "We accept credit cards, PayPal, and bank transfers in supported regions."
    },
    {
        "question": "How can I contact support?",
        "answer": "Open a ticket via the help desk or email support@example.com."
    },
]

Step 2: Generate embeddings for retrieval

To find the right FAQ entry, I embed every question using Oxlo.ai's embedding endpoint. I use the bge-large model because it handles semantic similarity well for short sentences. One API call sends the whole batch, which keeps latency low. I store the resulting vectors in memory alongside the text. In production you might cache these to a file or vector database, but a numpy array is fine for a few hundred entries. The embeddings are normalized, which means I can use a dot product later instead of a full cosine calculation.

import os
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

def embed_texts(texts):
    response = client.embeddings.create(
        model="bge-large",
        input=texts,
    )
    return [item.embedding for item in response.data]

faq_questions = [item["question"] for item in FAQ_DB]
faq_vectors = embed_texts(faq_questions)

Step 3: Build the retriever

When a user asks something, I embed their query with the same model and compute similarity against the stored vectors. Because the bge-large embeddings are normalized, the dot product equals cosine similarity. I return the index of the top match and its score. If the score ever drops below a threshold, I can trigger a human handoff or return a generic fallback. For now, I trust the top result and pass its answer text forward as the context block.

def retrieve(query_vector, vectors, k=1):
    similarities = np.dot(vectors, query_vector)
    top_idx = int(np.argmax(similarities))
    return top_idx, similarities[top_idx]

def get_context(user_question):
    q_vector = embed_texts([user_question])[0]
    idx, score = retrieve(q_vector, np.array(faq_vectors))
    return FAQ_DB[idx]["answer"], score

Step 4: Craft the system prompt

The system prompt constrains the agent to answer only from the retrieved context. I also instruct it to admit when it does not know. Keeping this as an editable constant makes it easy to tune tone or add compliance language later without touching the retrieval logic. I keep the instructions short because the model already has the answer. It just needs formatting rules.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a concise FAQ assistant.
Answer the user's question using only the provided context.
If the context does not contain the answer, say "I don't have that information."
Keep responses under three sentences."""

Step 5: Query the LLM with context

Now I feed the retrieved answer into the LLM. I use Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai because it follows instructions reliably for short-form Q&A. The call is a drop-in replacement for the OpenAI SDK. I inject the retrieved text into the user message so the model has grounding. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, I do not worry about the extra tokens in the context block inflating the bill. This matters when the FAQ answer is a full paragraph or when I later upgrade to retrieving multiple chunks.

def ask_llm(context, user_question):
    user_message = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {user_question}"

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 6: Wrap it in a function

I package retrieval and generation into a single answer_question function. This keeps the notebook clean and mirrors how I would deploy it as an API endpoint later. The function returns the generated string, and I can optionally log the similarity score for monitoring. If I need to switch to a different Oxlo.ai model later, I only change the model identifier in one place.

def answer_question(user_question):
    context, score = get_context(user_question)
    answer = ask_llm(context, user_question)
    return answer

Run it

I test with a question that is worded differently from the FAQ. The user says "I forgot my password, how do I get back in?" which does not match the canonical wording exactly. The retriever still finds the right entry because the embedding captures semantic meaning, and the LLM reformulates the answer naturally. I run the script from the terminal.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    question = "I forgot my password, how do I get back in?"
    print(answer_question(question))

Output:

Click 'Forgot password' on the login page and follow the reset link sent to your email.

Next steps

This pipeline is live, but there are two obvious upgrades. First, add streaming with stream=True so the user sees tokens appear immediately instead of waiting for the full response. Second, build a small evaluation set of paraphrased questions and measure recall. If the retriever misses, switch to a larger embedding model on Oxlo.ai or add a keyword fallback. If your FAQ grows into long policy documents, chunk them into passages and retrieve the top three. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, stuffing multiple chunks into the context window is cheap. For teams handling multilingual queries, swapping the LLM to Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai requires only a single string change. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for details on request-based plans.

title: Optimizing LLM Model Performance for Low-Latency Applications
content:
Low-latency inference is the difference between an AI product that feels instantaneous and one that feels broken. Whether you are building a voice agent, a coding copilot, or an autonomous reasoning loop, user perception is governed by two metrics: time to first token (TTFT) and time per output token (TPOT). Optimizing these requires more than just faster GPUs. It demands careful model selection, efficient client configuration, and an inference backend that does not introduce variance through cold starts or unpredictable token-based billing. This post covers the practical techniques that actually move the needle on latency, and how Oxlo.ai's infrastructure aligns with each of them.

Why Latency Matters in Production LLM Workloads

Human perception of conversation is unforgiving. Research on interactive systems suggests that delays above a few hundred milliseconds interrupt flow state. In LLM-powered applications, latency compounds. A coding assistant that streams tokens slowly breaks the developer's concentration. An agent that performs multiple tool calls in a loop can accumulate seconds of wait time per step. For real-time translation or voice synthesis pipelines, every millisecond of inference delay adds directly to audio latency.

Latency is not a single number. TTFT measures how long the model spends processing your prompt and beginning to emit a response. TPOT measures how fast subsequent tokens arrive. A model with a low TTFT but poor TPOT will feel snappy at first, then stall. A model with high TTFT but fast TPOT will feel sluggish before the text starts pouring in. Production optimization requires balancing both, which means attacking the problem from the model layer, the prompt layer, and the infrastructure layer simultaneously.

Choose the Right Model Architecture

The largest model is rarely the fastest for a given task. Dense parameter counts increase memory bandwidth pressure, and memory bandwidth is often the bottleneck in transformer inference. Modern architectures offer alternatives. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models activate only a subset of parameters per token, reducing compute without proportionally reducing capability. Smaller, task-distilled models can match large generalist performance on narrow domains while cutting latency dramatically.

Oxlo.ai hosts a range of architectures optimized for different latency profiles. DeepSeek V4 Flash is an efficient MoE with a 1 million token context window and near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, making it suitable for long-context tasks where you still need speed. Qwen 3 32B excels at multilingual agent workflows with a smaller active footprint than many 70B-class dense models. For pure coding speed, Oxlo.ai Coder Fast and DeepSeek V3.2 provide high throughput on structured generation tasks. Because Oxlo.ai exposes all of these through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, you can A/B test model swaps by changing a single string in your client code, with no architectural migration.

Quantization and Distillation Without Sacrificing Quality

Quantization reduces the numerical precision of weights and activations, which directly lowers memory bandwidth requirements. INT8 and FP8 formats can cut model size in half with minimal accuracy degradation on most reasoning and coding tasks. Distillation compresses knowledge from a large teacher model into a smaller student, yielding faster inference for domain-specific workloads.

The practical challenge with quantization is access. Not every provider hosts quantized variants, and self-hosting them requires significant DevOps overhead. Oxlo.ai offers quantized checkpoints of popular open models, including Llama 3.3 70B and DeepSeek V3.2, behind the same API. This means you can drop from a full-precision flagship to a quantized variant without rewriting your request logic. Additionally, Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing removes the financial friction from experimentation. On token-based platforms, testing a larger context or a bigger model immediately inflates cost. With Oxlo.ai, you pay per request, so benchmarking latency across model sizes and precisions does not require recalculating per-token economics. You can find plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Streaming and First-Token Latency

The most effective way to improve perceived latency is to stop waiting for the full response. Streaming delivers tokens to the client as they are generated, which masks TPOT and dramatically improves user satisfaction even when total generation time is unchanged.

Time to first token is where infrastructure behavior becomes visible. If your provider spins down GPUs during low traffic, you will encounter cold starts that add seconds to TTFT. Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, which means TTFT remains consistent whether you are sending the first request of the day or the ten-thousandth. For applications where variance is as damaging as mean latency, this stability is critical.

Enabling streaming with Oxlo.ai is identical to the OpenAI SDK pattern. You only need to change the base URL:

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize the attached logs."}],
    stream=True,
    max_tokens=256
)

for chunk in response:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True)

Notice that the client structure is unchanged. If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, you can evaluate latency improvements on Oxlo.ai by updating two configuration parameters.

Prompt Engineering as a Latency Tool

Prompt length is linearly correlated with prefill compute. Every token you send must be processed through every layer before the first output token can be emitted. Trimming redundant system instructions, removing duplicated few-shot examples, and compressing historical context are all valid latency optimizations.

On token-based providers, aggressive prompt trimming is often a cost-cutting necessity. Long inputs inflate the bill even when the output is short. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing inverts this incentive. Your cost is predictable per API call, so you can optimize prompts purely for speed rather than for token economy. If a longer prompt genuinely improves accuracy, you can use it without watching a meter run. When latency is the priority, you can trim aggressively without worrying that you are "wasting" tokens you already paid for. This decoupling of cost structure from input length is particularly valuable for agentic workloads that accumulate long conversation histories.

Batching and KV Cache Efficiency

While dynamic and continuous batching improve provider-side throughput, single-request latency is most affected by KV cache behavior. The KV cache stores key and value tensors from previous tokens so they do not need to be recomputed. In multi-turn conversations, an efficient cache reuse strategy can slash TTFT for follow-up messages because only the new user utterance needs full prefill computation.

You can maximize cache efficiency by keeping system prompts static and appending new messages rather than rewriting the entire conversation history. When using function calling or tool use, minimize the size of JSON schemas passed in the tools parameter. Large schemas increase prompt length and parsing overhead. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and JSON mode across its chat models, so you can constrain outputs structurally without adding custom parsing layers that increase end-to-end latency.

Infrastructure Choices That Remove Cold Starts

Serverless inference is convenient until it is not. Providers that aggressively scale to zero introduce multi-second cold starts that destroy interactive experiences. Even p99 latency guarantees are meaningless if the worst-case behavior is a full container spin-up.

Oxlo.ai does not cold-start popular models. The platform keeps inference warm, which protects tail latency and makes benchmarking reproducible. For teams with strict latency service-level objectives, Oxlo.ai's Enterprise tier offers dedicated GPUs. This removes noisy-neighbor contention and provides guaranteed isolation. Combined with priority queue access on Premium plans, Oxlo.ai gives you infrastructure options that map directly to latency requirements rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all serverless model.

Putting It Into Practice with Oxlo.ai

Here is a concise playbook for lowering latency in an application already using the OpenAI SDK.

First, redirect your client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and authenticate with your Oxlo.ai key. Second, select a model matched to your latency budget. Use DeepSeek V4 Flash or Qwen 3 32B for reasoning and agent tasks. Use Oxlo.ai Coder Fast or DeepSeek V3.2 for code generation. Use Kimi K2.6 or Llama 3.3 70B when you need maximum capability and can tolerate slightly higher TTFT. Third, enable streaming on every user-facing endpoint. Fourth, audit your prompts. Remove redundant text, use concise system messages, and leverage JSON mode to limit output length. Fifth, if you are building agents, keep tool schemas minimal and reuse conversation state efficiently.

Finally, measure. Latency optimization is empirical. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing means you can run large benchmark suites against live traffic without calculating token costs for every permutation. You pay per request, so profile TTFT and TPOT across models, quantization levels, and prompt strategies until you hit your target. If you need higher throughput or dedicated resources, the Pro, Premium, and Enterprise plans scale with your traffic. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for the full breakdown.

Conclusion

Low-latency LLM inference is a system design problem, not a single configuration toggle. It requires the right model architecture, efficient quantization, streaming client logic, disciplined prompt design, and an inference backend that does not punish you with cold starts or unpredictable scaling. Oxlo.ai addresses these requirements through a broad catalog of efficient open-source models, flat per-request pricing that removes cost barriers to optimization, and infrastructure engineered for consistent performance. If you are optimizing for speed, start by changing your base URL and measuring the results. The data will tell you where the latency went.

title: Building Conversational AI Systems for Sales Support with LLM
content:
Sales teams generate massive amounts of unstructured text. Call transcripts, email threads, proposal documents, and CRM notes contain the context needed to close deals, but most organizations lack the infrastructure to surface insights in real time. Large language models have made conversational sales support feasible, yet production systems demand more than a simple chat interface. You need models that reason across long documents, execute functions against external APIs, and maintain coherent multi-turn dialogue without unpredictable cost spikes. Building this correctly means choosing an inference backend that supports long context, tool use, and predictable economics.

Core Architecture for Sales Support LLMs

A reliable sales support assistant requires three layers: memory, retrieval, and action. Memory preserves context across a conversation so a rep does not need to repeat deal history. Retrieval grounds the model in factual product knowledge, pricing sheets, and past customer interactions, usually through a vector store queried via embeddings. Action lets the assistant interact with the outside world through function calls to CRMs, calendar APIs, or inventory systems.

Each layer imposes distinct load on your inference provider. Retrieval-augmented generation often injects thousands of tokens of context into every prompt. Multi-turn sales conversations can accumulate lengthy thread histories. Action layers require low-latency, deterministic outputs, especially when the model must emit valid JSON or precise function arguments. If your provider charges by the token, every retrieved document and every turn in the thread directly inflates the bill. Your provider needs to handle all three layers without throttling, cold starts, or pricing that punishes you for including necessary context.

Selecting Models for Reasoning and Agent Workflows

Not every sales task needs the same model. A general question about product features requires different capabilities than drafting a complex custom proposal or debugging a pricing script. Oxlo.ai offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, giving you the flexibility to route queries to the right capacity instead of over-provisioning a single large endpoint.

title: Using LLM for Sentiment Analysis in Market Research
content:
Market research teams drown in open-ended survey responses. I built a small CLI tool that feeds customer verbatims to an LLM and returns structured sentiment scores, which cuts analysis time from hours to minutes. The whole thing runs against Oxlo.ai's request-based API, so a 500-response batch costs the same whether each answer is ten words or five hundred, with plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • pip install openai pandas. We only need openai for this tutorial, but pandas is useful when you move from hardcoded lists to real CSV exports.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Their flat per-request pricing is listed at https://oxlo.ai/pricing, and it means long survey responses do not inflate the bill the way token-based providers do.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

Before I write any business logic, I wire up the API client. I keep credentials in an environment variable so I do not accidentally commit keys to Git. The client constructor is identical to the standard OpenAI pattern; I only change the base_url to hit Oxlo.ai and supply my key. For this workload I default to llama-3.3-70b. It is a strong general-purpose model that follows structured instructions consistently, which matters when you are parsing JSON downstream. If you later switch to multilingual responses, you can change the string to qwen-3-32b without touching any other logic because Oxlo.ai exposes the same chat completions schema for every model.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the entire product specification. I instruct the model to adopt the persona of a market-research analyst, which biases it toward business language rather than casual chat. I also lock the output schema to four keys so that downstream code can rely on the shape. The confidence score is useful for filtering borderline cases before they reach a dashboard. I explicitly allow a Neutral label because survey respondents often state facts without praise or blame, and forcing a binary choice would degrade accuracy. Keeping the prompt in a module-level constant makes it easy to version control and A/B test later.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a market-research sentiment analyst.
Analyze the user-supplied survey response and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- sentiment: one of Positive, Neutral, or Negative
- confidence: an integer from 1 to 10
- topics: an array of up to three product themes mentioned (e.g., pricing, onboarding, reliability)
- explanation: one sentence describing why you chose this sentiment

Rules:
- If the response is purely factual with no emotional signal, choose Neutral.
- Do not include markdown formatting or commentary outside the JSON."""

Step 3: Build the single-response analyzer

I wrap the API call in a thin function so that the rest of the script does not need to know about LLM internals. The function accepts a single string, sends it as the user message, and parses the JSON response. I include a broad exception handler because LLM outputs can occasionally include a stray markdown fence or truncated string when the verbatim is messy. When that happens, I return a safe default so the entire batch does not crash. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the first request after idle time returns just as quickly as the tenth, which keeps the loop predictable.

import json

def analyze_response(survey_text: str):
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": survey_text},
            ],
        )
        raw = response.choices[0].message.content
        return json.loads(raw)
    except Exception as e:
        return {
            "sentiment": "Neutral",
            "confidence": 1,
            "topics": [],
            "explanation": f"Parse error: {e}"
        }

Step 4: Prepare a batch of survey responses

In production I read a CSV with pandas, but for a reproducible tutorial I use a hardcoded Python list. The five verbatims cover the spectrum: enthusiastic praise, mild indifference, a feature complaint, pricing appreciation, and a plain support question. This diversity lets you verify that the prompt is not collapsing everything into a single label. I loop over them and enrich each result dictionary with metadata so the final report preserves the original text for traceability. If you are processing a large export, you could add a small time.sleep between calls to respect rate limits, though Oxlo.ai's queues typically handle steady batches without throttling.

survey_data = [
    "The new dashboard is a game changer. I can finally see all my metrics in one place.",
    "It is okay. Nothing special but it gets the job done.",
    "I waited 20 minutes for the export to finish and then it crashed. Extremely frustrating.",
    "Pricing is transparent compared to competitors, which I appreciate.",
    "How do I reset my password? There is no link on the login page."
]

results = []
for idx, text in enumerate(survey_data, start=1):
    result = analyze_response(text)
    result["response_id"] = idx
    result["verbatim"] = text
    results.append(result)

Step 5: Aggregate and print the report

Raw JSON from the model is not a report. I use Python's standard collections.Counter to tally sentiments and surface the most frequent topics. This gives stakeholders an at-a-glance view of product health without requiring them to read individual responses. I also print the model's one-sentence explanation for every row so you can audit individual classifications during a read-out. That audit trail is critical in market research because clients often challenge automated findings. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, the cost of this batch is predictable: five API calls, regardless of how long the survey responses are. That makes budgeting for quarterly research spikes straightforward compared to token-based billing.

from collections import Counter

sentiments = Counter([r["sentiment"] for r in results])
topics = []
for r in results:
    topics.extend(r.get("topics", []))
top_topics = Counter(topics).most_common(5)

print("=== Market Research Sentiment Report ===")
print(f"Total responses analyzed: {len(results)}")
print(f"Positive: {sentiments.get('Positive', 0)}")
print(f"Neutral: {sentiments.get('Neutral', 0)}")
print(f"Negative: {sentiments.get('Negative', 0)}")
print("\nTop topics:")
for topic, count in top_topics:
    print(f"  - {topic}: {count}")

print("\nDetailed breakdown:")
for r in results:
    print(f"{r['response_id']}. [{r['sentiment']}] {r['explanation']}")

Run it

Save the complete script as sentiment_analyzer.py, export your key in the shell, and run it. The output below is exactly what I see on my machine. Your topic labels may vary slightly depending on model sampling, but the structure will match because the system prompt constrains the output format.

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
$ python sentiment_analyzer.py
=== Market Research Sentiment Report ===
Total responses analyzed: 5
Positive: 2
Neutral: 2
Negative: 1

Top topics:
  - dashboard: 1
  - pricing: 1
  - export: 1
  - metrics: 1
  - account: 1

Detailed breakdown:
1. [Positive] The user explicitly calls the dashboard a game changer.
2. [Neutral] The response is purely factual with no strong emotional signal.
3. [Negative] The user describes a crash and uses the word frustrating.
4. [Positive] The user expresses appreciation for transparent pricing.
5. [Neutral] The response is a factual support question without emotional language.

Next steps

This pipeline is already useful for weekly NPS exports, but two extensions make it production-grade. First, swap llama-3.3-70b for qwen-3-32b if you are processing multilingual surveys, since it handles mixed-language inputs without extra prompt engineering. Second, add a confidence threshold that flags anything below 7 for human review, which keeps the model honest when responses are ambiguous. You could also persist results to a SQLite database instead of printing to stdout so that trend lines emerge over time. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing makes both experiments cheap because you pay per survey row, not per word, which is ideal for long-form market research where respondents write detailed paragraphs. You can verify current plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Integrating LLM with Computer Vision for Image Understanding
content:
Image understanding has moved beyond bounding boxes and classification labels. Modern applications now demand systems that can interpret visual content, reason about spatial relationships, and communicate findings in natural language. Integrating large language models with computer vision makes this possible, whether through end-to-end vision-language models or composed pipelines that combine object detection with contextual reasoning. The infrastructure challenge is no longer just model accuracy. It is cost control, latency, and flexibility when high-resolution images and long textual prompts converge into massive token counts. Platforms that treat every input token as a metered event penalize multimodal workloads, because encoding an image into a language model can generate thousands of tokens before a single word of reasoning begins.

Unified Vision-Language Models vs. Composed Pipelines

There are two proven patterns for adding language understanding to visual data. The first is the unified vision-language model, which ingests images and text in a single forward pass and generates a coherent response. The second is a composed pipeline, where a dedicated computer vision model extracts structured information and a separate LLM reasons over that structured output.

Unified models are the fastest path to production. On Oxlo.ai, models such as Kimi K2.6, Gemma 3 27B, and Kimi VL A3B accept image inputs directly through the standard chat/completions endpoint. Kimi K2.6 brings a 131K context window, advanced reasoning, and agentic coding capabilities to visual tasks, making it suitable for document analysis, UI interpretation, and complex scene description. Gemma 3 27B offers a strong balance of efficiency and visual comprehension for workloads that need lower latency. Because these models are fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can use the same multimodal request format you already know.

Composed pipelines shine when spatial precision matters. If your application requires exact coordinates, pixel-level localization, or reliable object counting, feeding raw pixels into a generalist VLM can produce vague or hallucinated locations. A better approach is to run an object detection model such as YOLOv9 or YOLOv11 on Oxlo.ai to generate structured bounding boxes and labels, then pass that JSON into a reasoning model like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Llama 3.3 70B, or Qwen 3 32B. The LLM receives clean structured data and produces narratives, compliance reports, or maintenance instructions without guessing where objects are located. Oxlo.ai hosts both the detection models and the reasoning models, so the entire pipeline can run against a single API base URL with consistent authentication and no cold starts on popular models.

Implementation: Calling Vision-Capable Models

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can send image inputs using the same Python or Node.js patterns you already use. The only changes are the base URL and your Oxlo.ai API key.

The following example sends a base64-encoded image to a vision-capable model along with a text prompt. You can use this pattern with Kimi K2.6, Gemma 3 27B, or Kimi VL A3B by selecting the appropriate model identifier in the request.

import base64
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]
)

def encode_image(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")

image_b64 = encode_image("diagram.png")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2-6",  # vision model identifier on Oxlo.ai
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Explain the relationships between the components in this architecture diagram."
                },
                {
                    "type": "image_url",
                    "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{image_b64}"}
                }
            ]
        }
    ],
    stream=False
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

This request uses the chat/completions endpoint, which supports multi-turn conversations, streaming responses, JSON mode, and function calling. If you are building an agent that must inspect an image and then invoke a tool, you can enable function calling in the same request. The model will reason over the visual content and emit structured tool calls just as it would from text input alone.

From Detection to Language: Structured Vision Pipelines

For applications that demand measurement accuracy, safety compliance, or robotic interaction, a unified VLM may not provide the geometric reliability you need. In these cases, start with an object detection model. Oxlo.ai offers YOLOv9 and YOLOv11, which return precise bounding boxes, class labels, and confidence scores.

After you receive the detection JSON, feed it into a reasoning LLM via the chat/completions endpoint. The following pattern illustrates how to bridge structured detections into natural language analysis without managing separate infrastructure providers.

# Structured detections from YOLOv11 via Oxlo.ai object detection
detections = {
    "objects": [
        {"label": "forklift", "bbox": [120, 340, 280, 560], "confidence": 0.97},
        {"label": "pallet", "bbox": [400, 500, 520, 640], "confidence": 0.91}
    ]
}

reasoning_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-r1-671b",  # reasoning model identifier on Oxlo.ai
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a warehouse safety analyst."},
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Flag any clearance violations based on these detections:\n{detections}"
        }
    ]
)

print(reasoning_response.choices[0].message.content)

By separating perception from reasoning, you reduce hallucination. The detector handles what is where, and the LLM handles what it means. Oxlo.ai lets you run both stages on the same platform, which simplifies routing, authentication, and logging.

Agentic Tool Use with Visual Inputs

Vision becomes significantly more powerful when the model can act on what it sees rather than merely describing it. By combining image inputs with function calling, you can build agents that inspect hardware, read dashboards, or analyze screenshots and then trigger downstream operations.

Oxlo.ai supports function calling, tool use, JSON mode, and streaming across its chat/completions endpoint. Models such as Kimi K2.6, GLM 5, and Minimax M2.5 are designed for agentic tool use and can process visual context while deciding which tools to invoke. For example, an agent monitoring a server room could receive a webcam frame, identify an overheating indicator light with a vision model, and call a temperature-adjustment function in the same turn. Because Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, the agent can maintain interactive response times even when switching between visual reasoning and tool execution.

JSON mode is especially useful here. When an agent must parse a complex form or diagram, you can request that the model return extracted fields as structured JSON rather than prose. This eliminates fragile regex parsing and lets downstream systems consume the output immediately.

Cost Control for Multimodal Workloads

Image understanding is expensive on token-based infrastructure. A single high-resolution image encoded as base64 can expand into thousands of tokens, and when you add system prompts, few-shot examples, and multi-turn conversation history, the input length grows rapidly. On token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, costs scale linearly with that input length.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of how long the prompt is or how large the image is. For vision workloads, this model can be significantly cheaper because the cost does not balloon when you increase image resolution, add explanatory text, or maintain extended conversation context. If you are running agentic workflows that pass images back and forth across multiple turns, the savings compound. For exact plan details, see the Oxlo.ai pricing page at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

The free tier offers 60 requests per day and includes a 7-day full-access trial, which is enough to prototype multimodal pipelines before committing to a paid plan. The Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day across all models, while Premium offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access. Enterprise customers can opt for dedicated GPUs and unlimited volume with custom terms, including a guaranteed 30% savings over your current provider.

Getting Started with Oxlo.ai

To integrate LLMs with computer vision today, create an account on Oxlo.ai and generate an API key. Set your OpenAI SDK base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and select a vision-capable model such as Kimi K2.6, Gemma 3 27B, or Kimi VL A3B. If your use case requires precise spatial data, complement the pipeline with YOLOv9 or YOLOv11 detection and route the structured output to a reasoning model like DeepSeek R1 or Llama 3.3 70B.

Because the platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can migrate existing multimodal code by changing two lines: the base URL and the API key. There are no cold starts on popular models, so your first request returns as quickly as your hundredth. With 45+ models across seven categories, streaming, and a pricing structure that rewards long-context vision workloads rather than penalizing them, Oxlo.ai provides the infrastructure to make image understanding economically viable at scale.

title: Building Virtual Assistants with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Virtual assistants have moved beyond rigid decision trees. Today's implementations rely on large language models that can parse ambiguous intent, maintain state across sessions, and invoke external tools to complete tasks. For developers, this means the assistant is no longer just a prompt wrapper. It is a distributed system where the LLM acts as a reasoning engine, orchestrating function calls, retrieving context, and generating responses in real time. Building one requires deliberate choices about model capabilities, memory architecture, and inference economics.

Architecture of a Modern Virtual Assistant

A production virtual assistant is typically structured in four layers. The interface layer handles user input, whether text, voice, or image. The orchestration layer manages conversation state, decides when to call tools, and routes outputs. The memory layer persists short-term context within a session and long-term knowledge across sessions, often through a vector database or structured cache. Finally, the inference layer runs the LLM that powers reasoning and generation.

Each layer introduces latency and cost. The inference layer is usually the dominant variable, so choosing a backend that minimizes cold starts and offers predictable pricing directly impacts user experience. Oxlo.ai provides a fully OpenAI SDK compatible API with no cold starts on popular models, which means your assistant can respond immediately even after idle periods. You can route all traffic through the standard chat/completions endpoint and consume embeddings, audio, and image generation from the same base URL, which reduces client-side complexity.

Selecting a Model for Assistant Workloads

Not every assistant needs the same reasoning profile. A customer support bot may prioritize low latency and multilingual output, while a coding assistant requires deep reasoning and large context windows. A personal productivity agent might need to plan across dozens of steps, demanding a model optimized for long-horizon tasks.

Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories, so you can match the model to the task without managing multiple providers. For general-purpose conversation and instruction following, Llama 3.3 70B is a reliable flagship. If your assistant runs agentic workflows or serves multilingual users, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for those scenarios. For complex reasoning or software engineering tasks, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 provide advanced chain-of-thought reasoning and agentic coding capabilities, with Kimi K2.6 also supporting vision inputs across a 131K context window. When you need long-horizon planning, GLM 5 is a 744B MoE model designed for extended agentic tasks. For coding-specific assistants, Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast offer specialized performance. If you want to test capabilities at zero cost, DeepSeek V3.2 is available on the free tier and handles both coding and reasoning.

Because Oxlo.ai exposes all of these through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, you can prototype with one model and swap to another by changing a single parameter. There is no custom client to rewrite.

Implementing Tool Use and Function Calling

Tool use is what separates a conversational bot from a virtual assistant. By defining functions in your API call, you let the LLM decide when to retrieve data, modify records, or trigger actions in external systems. Effective assistants often expose multiple tools, such as web search, database queries, calendar operations, or code execution.

Oxlo.ai supports function calling, JSON mode, and streaming, which are the primitives you need for interactive assistants. Below is a minimal Python example using the OpenAI SDK. The assistant can answer directly or call a hypothetical get_weather function based on user intent.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get current weather for a location",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "location": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["location"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant with access to weather data."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Berlin?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

message = response.choices[0].message
if message.tool_calls:
    # Execute the function in your environment, append the result,
    # and send a follow-up request to produce the final answer.
    pass

If the model returns tool calls, your orchestration layer can execute them in parallel, append the results to the message history, and send a follow-up request to generate the final user-facing response. This loop is the core of agentic behavior. You can enforce structured outputs with JSON mode when you need deterministic schemas for downstream processing, and you can stream the response to improve perceived latency.

Memory and Context Management

Assistants fail when they forget what the user said three turns ago. There are two memory problems to solve. Short-term memory is bounded by the model's context window. For long sessions, you may need to summarize earlier turns, compress dialogue, or drop less relevant messages while preserving key entities. Long-term memory usually requires an embedding database. You convert conversation history, user preferences, or external documents into vectors using an embedding model, then retrieve relevant snippets at query time.

Oxlo.ai offers embedding models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large through the /embeddings endpoint, so you can keep the entire retrieval pipeline on the same platform. For the chat backbone, models like DeepSeek V4 Flash support a 1M context window, which reduces the pressure to truncate sessions aggressively. Minimax M2.5 is another strong option when your assistant relies heavily on tool use and coding.

From a cost perspective, assistants are notorious for long system prompts and extensive message histories. Token-based providers scale charges with every input token, which means a detailed system prompt plus multi-turn history can become expensive quickly. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so adding more context to a request does not increase the inference cost. For assistant workloads with heavy context, this can make the architecture significantly more economical than token-based alternatives such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale.

Adding Vision, Audio, and Image Generation

Text is only one channel. A complete assistant should handle images, voice, and even generate visuals on demand. A user might upload a screenshot and ask for help debugging a UI, or send a voice note while driving.

For vision tasks, models like Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B accept image inputs through the chat completions endpoint. Kimi K2.6 extends this further with advanced reasoning over visual content. You can pass base64-encoded images or URLs in the message payload exactly as you would with the OpenAI schema.

For audio, Oxlo.ai hosts Whisper Large v3, Turbo, and Medium for speech-to-text via the /audio/transcriptions endpoint. For text-to-speech, Kokoro 82M delivers synthetic voice output through /audio/speech. If your assistant needs to generate images, the /images/generations endpoint supports Oxlo.ai Image Pro and Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, and Stable Diffusion 3.5.

Keeping these modalities on a single provider simplifies authentication, latency, and billing. You do not need to stitch together separate contracts for transcription, inference, and generation. The unified base URL means your backend can remain a thin orchestration layer rather than a patchwork of API clients.

Deployment, Scaling, and Cost Optimization

Virtual assistants often start as prototypes and graduate to high-volume production systems. Your inference provider should accommodate both stages without forcing you to rearchitect.

Oxlo.ai offers a Free plan at $0 per month with 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 free models, including a seven-day full-access trial. This is enough to validate tool-calling logic and multi-turn behavior before committing spend. When you are ready to scale, the Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day for $80 per month, and the Premium plan offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access for $350 per month. For teams running dedicated workloads, the Enterprise tier supplies unlimited requests, dedicated GPUs, and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction versus your current provider.

The central economic advantage is request-based pricing. Because you pay one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length, you can pass large system instructions, extensive conversation logs, or retrieved document chunks without watching token meters run. For long-context and agentic workloads, this predictability is a structural win over token-based pricing. You can verify current plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Additionally, full OpenAI SDK compatibility means your existing assistant code works with minimal changes. You point the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, swap the model name, and retain your streaming, function calling, and error handling logic. There is no vendor-specific DSL to learn. Because Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, your assistant remains responsive during sporadic traffic, a common pattern for internal tools or customer support bots.

Conclusion

Building a virtual assistant in 2025 means assembling a pipeline of reasoning, memory, tools, and modalities. The LLM layer is the most critical dependency, and it should offer broad model choice, native tool support, and pricing that does not punish you for rich context.

Oxlo.ai meets these requirements with a fully OpenAI SDK compatible platform, more than 45 models spanning chat, reasoning, vision, audio, and embeddings, and flat per-request pricing that favors the long-context sessions typical of assistant workloads. Whether you are prototyping on the Free tier or deploying a production agent with dedicated GPUs, Oxlo.ai gives you the models and the economic model to build assistants that actually scale.
