title: Building Conversational AI Systems for Language Learning with LLM
content:
We are going to build a conversational language tutor that adapts to the learner's proficiency, corrects mistakes in real time, and generates a structured review sheet at the end of each session. It is useful for edtech products or internal tools that need private, API-driven speaking practice. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, long multi-turn sessions with detailed system prompts do not inflate costs the way token-based billing would, which makes it practical to keep extensive conversation history in context. See pricing details here.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an active Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with the OpenAI client, so no extra adapters are required.

Step 1: Initialize the client

Oxlo.ai exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only changes are the base URL and the model identifier. I use llama-3.3-70b because it handles long instructions and multi-turn dialogue reliably.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

# Verify connectivity with a simple turn
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in Italian."},
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The prompt functions as the tutor's curriculum. I instruct it to stay in character, speak at an A2 level, and return strict JSON so our application layer can parse corrections automatically.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a patient Italian tutor for English speakers at the A2 level.
Rules:
1. Always reply in Italian using simple vocabulary and short sentences.
2. If the user makes a grammar or vocabulary error, note it briefly in English.
3. Return ONLY valid JSON with two keys: "reply" (your Italian response) and "corrections" (a list of strings explaining each error). Use an empty list when there are no errors.
4. Do not break character or write English inside the "reply" field."""

Step 3: Build the session class

State lives in a lightweight Python class that tracks the message history and a running list of mistakes. Keeping everything in memory is fine for a single session, and because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, we can afford to send the full history on every turn without worrying about length-based cost creep.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

class TutorSession:
    def __init__(self, client: OpenAI, system_prompt: str):
        self.client = client
        self.history = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}]
        self.mistakes = []

    def chat(self, user_text: str) -> str:
        self.history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})

        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=self.history,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )

        raw = response.choices[0].message.content
        data = json.loads(raw)

        reply = data.get("reply", "")
        corrections = data.get("corrections", [])

        if corrections:
            self.mistakes.extend(corrections)
            print("[Corrections]")
            for note in corrections:
                print(f"  - {note}")

        # Store the raw JSON in history so the model remembers its own corrections
        self.history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": raw})
        return reply

Step 4: Inject adaptive difficulty

If the learner accumulates three or more corrections, we dynamically soften the system prompt before the next turn. This mimics a human tutor who slows down when a student is overwhelmed.

    def chat(self, user_text: str) -> str:
        # Adapt difficulty based on accumulated errors
        if len(self.mistakes) >= 3:
            softened = (
                self.history[0]["content"]
                + "\nAdditional instruction: the learner is struggling. Use very simple words, short sentences, and ask easy yes or no questions when possible."
            )
            self.history[0] = {"role": "system", "content": softened}

        self.history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})

        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=self.history,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )

        raw = response.choices[0].message.content
        data = json.loads(raw)

        reply = data.get("reply", "")
        corrections = data.get("corrections", [])

        if corrections:
            self.mistakes.extend(corrections)
            print("[Corrections]")
            for note in corrections:
                print(f"  - {note}")

        self.history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": raw})
        return reply

Step 5: Generate a session review

After the conversation ends, we send the accumulated mistakes back to the model and ask for a grouped study sheet. This gives the user concrete homework and closes the learning loop.

    def generate_review(self) -> str:
        payload = (
            "The student made these mistakes during an Italian session:\n"
            + "\n".join(f"- {m}" for m in self.mistakes)
            + "\n\nCreate a concise review sheet. Group mistakes by topic, give the correct Italian form, and add one example sentence for each topic."
        )

        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": payload}],
        )

        return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 6: Add a CLI loop

To make the tutor actually usable, we add a small input loop that reads from stdin and exits when the user types "review" or "quit". This is the glue code you would later replace with a web socket or voice pipeline.

def run_tutor(client: OpenAI, system_prompt: str):
    tutor = TutorSession(client, system_prompt)
    print("Italian tutor ready. Type your message, 'review' for a summary, or 'quit' to exit.")

    while True:
        user_input = input("\nYou: ").strip()
        if user_input.lower() == "quit":
            break
        if user_input.lower() == "review":
            print("\n--- Review ---")
            print(tutor.generate_review())
            continue

        reply = tutor.chat(user_input)
        print(f"Tutor: {reply}")

    if tutor.mistakes:
        print("\n--- Final Review ---")
        print(tutor.generate_review())

Run it

Here is a complete script that wires everything together. I intentionally make beginner-level Italian errors so you can see the correction and adaptation logic in action. Run the file and watch the tutor slow down after the third mistake.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a patient Italian tutor for English speakers at the A2 level.
Rules:
1. Always reply in Italian using simple vocabulary and short sentences.
2. If the user makes a grammar or vocabulary error, note it briefly in English.
3. Return ONLY valid JSON with two keys: "reply" (your Italian response) and "corrections" (a list of strings explaining each error). Use an empty list when there are no errors.
4. Do not break character or write English inside the "reply" field."""

class TutorSession:
    def __init__(self, client: OpenAI, system_prompt: str):
        self.client = client
        self.history = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}]
        self.mistakes = []

    def chat(self, user_text: str) -> str:
        if len(self.mistakes) >= 3:
            softened = (
                self.history[0]["content"]
                + "\nAdditional instruction: the learner is struggling. Use very simple words, short sentences, and ask easy yes or no questions when possible."
            )
            self.history[0] = {"role": "system", "content": softened}

        self.history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})

        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=self.history,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )

        raw = response.choices[0].message.content
        data = json.loads(raw)

        reply = data.get("reply", "")
        corrections = data.get("corrections", [])

        if corrections:
            self.mistakes.extend(corrections)
            print("[Corrections]")
            for note in corrections:
                print(f"  - {note}")

        self.history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": raw})
        return reply

    def generate_review(self) -> str:
        payload = (
            "The student made these mistakes during an Italian session:\n"
            + "\n".join(f"- {m}" for m in self.mistakes)
            + "\n\nCreate a concise review sheet. Group mistakes by topic, give the correct Italian form, and add one example sentence for each topic."
        )
        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": payload}],
        )
        return response.choices[0].message.content

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
tutor = TutorSession(client, SYSTEM_PROMPT)

turns = [
    "Ciao, io sono Marco e io piace la pizza.",
    "Io ho venti anni e io lavoro in una ufficio.",
    "Che cosa fai nel weekend?",
]

for text in turns:
    print(f"\nUser: {text}")
    reply = tutor.chat(text)
    print(f"Tutor: {reply}")

print("\n--- Session Review ---")
print(tutor.generate_review())

Expected output:

User: Ciao, io sono Marco e io piace la pizza.
[Corrections]
  - "Io piace" is incorrect. Use "Mi piace" because "piacere" needs an indirect object pronoun.
Tutor: Ciao Marco. Mi piace la pizza anche io. Quale pizza preferisci?

User: Io ho venti anni e io lavoro in una ufficio.
[Corrections]
  - Drop the second "io". The subject pronoun is usually omitted in Italian.
  - "Una ufficio" is incorrect. Use "un ufficio" because "ufficio" is masculine.
Tutor: Ho venti anni anche tu? Interessante. Lavoro in un ufficio piccolo.

User: Che cosa fai nel weekend?
Tutor: Nel weekend leggo un libro o cucino. E tu?

--- Session Review ---
Italian Review Sheet

1. Verb "piacere"
   - Use indirect object pronouns: mi, ti, gli...
   - Example: Mi piace il gelato.

2. Articles and gender
   - "Ufficio" is masculine, so use "un ufficio".
   - Example: Lavoro in un ufficio moderno.

3. Subject pronouns
   - Italian often drops subject pronouns because the verb ending shows the person.
   - Example: Ho venti anni.

Wrap-up and next steps

This pattern gives you a stateful, adaptive tutor with structured output and a review loop in under a hundred lines of Python. Because Oxlo.ai pricing is request-based, you can send full conversation history every turn without the cost surprises that come from long context on token-based platforms. Two concrete next steps: persist self.mistakes and self.history to SQLite so learners can resume across sessions, or swap the model to qwen-3-32b on Oxlo.ai if you are building a Mandarin, Arabic, or other multilingual tutor where Qwen's reasoning strengths shine.

title: Unlocking Sentiment Analysis with LLM for Customer Feedback
content:
Customer feedback is noisy, unstructured, and often contradictory. Support tickets, app store reviews, and survey responses arrive in high volume, making manual review impossible at scale. Traditional natural language processing pipelines relied on lexicons or shallow classifiers that collapsed under sarcasm, domain-specific jargon, and multilingual input. The result was a false sense of accuracy. A dashboard might show seventy percent positive sentiment while your churn rate climbs, because the classifier could not distinguish between lukewarm approval and genuine enthusiasm. Large language models changed the mechanics of this entirely. By reasoning over context rather than counting keywords, they enable granular, aspect-based sentiment analysis that actually reflects what a customer intends to communicate. The remaining challenge is not model capability, but infrastructure. Running this at scale requires an inference backend that handles long contexts economically and does not punish you for detailed prompts.

Why Traditional Sentiment Analysis Breaks

Legacy sentiment tools typically map words to polarity scores. The result is a bag-of-words approximation that misses negation, conditional statements, and cultural nuance. A review that reads, "The onboarding was smooth, but the billing page is a nightmare," receives a neutral score even though the user is signaling churn risk. Agentic workflows compound the problem. When an LLM must read a full support thread, prior ticket history, and attached metadata to render a judgment, the input context grows quickly. Keyword systems cannot process this breadth, and smaller embedding classifiers lose thread-level dependencies. What you need is a reasoning model that can ingest the entire artifact and return structured, actionable labels. Furthermore, customer feedback rarely exists in isolation. A single star rating might accompany a paragraph of text, a product version number, and prior interaction history. A model that sees only the paragraph loses the causal chain. Modern pipelines therefore need to ingest structured and unstructured data together, which lengthens prompts and increases token counts well beyond the comfort zone of older APIs.

How LLMs Capture Nuance

Modern LLMs perform sentiment analysis as a reasoning task, not a lookup task. You can prompt a model to return JSON with fields for overall sentiment, specific feature complaints, emotional intensity, and churn probability, all in a single request. This collapses what used to be four separate ML pipelines into one API call. You can also use function calling to route negative feedback directly into a CRM trigger, turning the LLM into both classifier and actor. This level of integration is why API compatibility matters. If your inference backend requires a custom client, you inherit maintenance debt every time the pipeline evolves. Multilingual models such as Qwen 3 32B handle code-mixed text without separate translation steps. Reasoning models like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 can work through ambiguous phrasing by generating internal chain-of-thought before committing to a label. For batch analysis of short snippets, lighter models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash offer efficient inference with a one-million-token context window, letting you fit hundreds of reviews into a single prompt if needed.

Implementing Feedback Analysis with Structured Outputs

The most reliable way to integrate an LLM into a data pipeline is to enforce structured output. Below is a minimal Python example using the OpenAI SDK pointed at Oxlo.ai. The script sends a customer review to Llama 3.3 70B and requests a JSON object containing sentiment labels and reasoning.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

feedback = """
I love the new design, but the checkout flow crashed twice and 
I had to re-enter my shipping info. Not sure if I will order again.
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a sentiment analysis engine. "
                "Respond only with valid JSON containing keys: "
                "sentiment, key_issues, churn_risk, reasoning."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Analyze this feedback: {feedback}"
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    max_tokens=512
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Key details in this snippet: the base_url is set to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, making Oxlo.ai a drop-in replacement for any OpenAI-compatible client. The response_format parameter forces valid JSON, which eliminates regex parsing. You can extend this pattern by adding a system message that defines your taxonomy, such as "positive", "negative", "mixed", and "escalation_required". Keeping that taxonomy in the system prompt rather than the user prompt reduces token overhead on repeated calls, though with request-based pricing the length matters less for cost than it does for latency. Because Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, the first request after idle time returns as quickly as subsequent ones, a critical property for asynchronous pipelines that process feedback in bursts.

Model Selection and Context Windows

Not every sentiment task requires the largest model available. For straightforward English classification, Llama 3.3 70B provides an excellent balance of latency and accuracy. If your feedback arrives in Mandarin, Spanish, or Arabic, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for multilingual reasoning and agent workflows. When you need to analyze an entire customer conversation thread or a long-form product review, DeepSeek V4 Flash delivers near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning with a one-million-token context window. For organizations building agentic systems that classify sentiment and then trigger follow-up actions, GLM 5 or Minimax M2.5 offer strong long-horizon task execution. Oxlo.ai hosts more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories behind a single API key and endpoint, so you can A/B test models without rewriting client code. You can also experiment with vision models such as Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B if your feedback includes user-submitted screenshots. Audio transcription via Whisper Large v3, also available on Oxlo.ai, lets you analyze voice support calls before they ever reach a text classifier. This unified stack means your sentiment pipeline can mature from simple text classification to a multi-modal understanding system without swapping API contracts.

The Infrastructure Advantage: Flat Pricing for Long Context

The economics of high-volume sentiment analysis are often overlooked. Token-based providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, scale cost linearly with prompt length. A support ticket with ten messages of back-and-forth, plus internal CRM notes, can quickly consume thousands of input tokens. When you multiply that across every ticket in a queue, the monthly bill becomes unpredictable.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of how many tokens the prompt contains. For long-context workloads such as full-thread sentiment scoring, this architecture can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. You can include full conversation history, product metadata, and few-shot examples without watching the meter run on every additional token. This predictability is essential for agentic systems that may iterate over a feedback thread multiple times, refining labels or extracting sub-tasks. Each loop adds tokens, but under a per-request model the cost stays bounded.

Oxlo.ai also removes operational friction. There are no cold starts on popular models, so latency remains consistent whether you are processing a midday surge of app store reviews or a nightly batch job. The platform supports streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, and vision inputs, which means your sentiment pipeline can later expand to analyze screenshots or audio transcripts without changing providers. You can prototype on the free tier, which includes 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 free models, and then scale through Pro, Premium, or Enterprise plans as volume grows. For exact plan details, see the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Conclusion

Sentiment analysis is no longer limited by model intelligence. It is limited by how affordably and reliably you can run those models against real-world data. By using structured prompts, selecting the right model for the language and context length, and routing traffic to an inference platform built for long inputs, you turn customer feedback into a real-time signal. Oxlo.ai provides the fully OpenAI-compatible infrastructure, flat per-request pricing, and broad model catalog to make that transition practical from the first prototype to production scale. Whether you are scoring short survey responses or ingesting million-token customer histories, Oxlo.ai is a genuinely relevant backbone for modern feedback intelligence.

title: Integrating LLMs with Computer Vision for Multimodal Understanding
content:
Multimodal understanding has moved from research novelty to production requirement. Applications now expect models to process screenshots, charts, photographs, and video frames alongside text. A customer support agent that cannot read an uploaded image, or a coding assistant that ignores a UI screenshot, is no longer competitive. The challenge for developers is not simply finding a model that can see, but building an inference layer that makes vision workloads predictable, fast, and cost-effective at scale.

Most modern architectures fall into two camps. The first is a pipeline approach: a dedicated computer vision model extracts labels, bounding boxes, or OCR text, then feeds that structured data into a separate LLM. Oxlo.ai supports this pattern through object detection endpoints such as YOLOv9 and YOLOv11, which can isolate regions of interest before language reasoning begins. The second and increasingly dominant approach is the unified vision-language model, where image tokens are embedded into the same latent space as text and processed by a single transformer. This eliminates brittle intermediate parsers and lets the model reason holistically over both modalities. Both patterns are viable on Oxlo.ai, and both benefit from the platform's request-based pricing and OpenAI-compatible API.

Oxlo.ai's Multimodal Stack

Oxlo.ai offers native vision-language models that are fully accessible through the same OpenAI-compatible endpoints as its text models. Developers can route image inputs to Kimi K2.6, which supports vision, advanced reasoning, and a 131K context window, or to Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B for focused vision-language tasks. These models sit alongside Oxlo.ai's broader LLM catalog, including Qwen 3 32B for multilingual agent workflows, Llama 3.3 70B for general-purpose reasoning, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for deep reasoning, and GLM 5 for long-horizon agentic tasks.

Because every model is served through a single base URL with identical SDK semantics, switching from a text-only pipeline to a multimodal one is a parameter change, not an infrastructure migration. You do not need to manage separate inference clusters, custom image preprocessors, or alternate authentication flows. The same client instance that handles chat completions can accept image URLs and base64 payloads without modification.

Vision Inference with the OpenAI SDK

Because Oxlo.ai is a fully drop-in replacement for the OpenAI SDK, integrating vision takes minutes. The following Python example sends a base64-encoded image to a vision-capable model and requests a structured analysis.

import openai
import base64

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

def encode_image(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        return base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")

image_b64 = encode_image("diagram.png")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Extract the three main technical components shown in this architecture diagram and list their responsibilities."
                },
                {
                    "type": "image_url",
                    "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{image_b64}"}
                }
            ]
        }
    ],
    max_tokens=1024
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

This request uses the standard chat/completions endpoint. The image is passed as a content block within the messages array, exactly as you would with proprietary vision APIs. Oxlo.ai handles the image tokenization, preprocessing, and inference without exposing cold-start latency on popular models. You can also stream the response by adding stream=True, or force JSON output by setting response_format={"type": "json_object"} for downstream parsing. For applications that require tool use, you can attach the same function definitions you would use in a text-only workflow, and the model can decide to invoke external APIs based on what it sees.

Predictable Pricing for Multimodal Workloads

Vision inputs are notoriously expensive on token-based inference providers. A single high-resolution screenshot can expand into thousands of text-equivalent tokens, and costs scale with every pixel you send. For competitors such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, this means multimodal agent loops, video-frame batch jobs, and high-resolution document analysis become difficult to budget. Costs spike when users upload unexpected image sizes or when an agent iterates over a sequence of screenshots.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Whether you submit a short text query or a 4K screenshot with a 10,000-token system prompt, the cost is the same. For long-context and agentic vision workloads, this can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based billing. You can build document extractors that ingest entire PDF pages as images, or visual agents that operate over long screenshot sequences, without watching your inference bill scale nonlinearly. Detailed plans are available on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Structured Outputs and Agentic Patterns

Vision becomes significantly more powerful when combined with structured generation and tool use. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode across compatible models, which lets you turn unstructured images into structured records. For example, a receipt photograph can be converted into a JSON object with line items, tax, and total. A wireframe screenshot can be transformed into a component hierarchy for frontend code generation. A satellite image can yield geo-tagged annotations. By defining a JSON schema in your application layer and setting the response format accordingly, you get deterministic output shapes without brittle regex parsing.

title: LLMs for Natural Language Processing Tasks: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
I built a lightweight NLP analysis agent that turns raw text into structured sentiment, entities, and summaries in a single API call. It runs on Oxlo.ai, so the cost stays flat per request even when I throw long documents at it. In this guide, I will walk you through the exact code I use so you can ship your own pipeline this afternoon.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI Python SDK installed with pip install openai
  • A text editor and a terminal

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I keep everything in one file, nlp_agent.py. The first thing I do is import json and OpenAI, then instantiate the client. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only difference from a standard setup is the base_url. I pull the key from an environment variable so I do not accidentally commit it.

import json
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between my code and the model. I tell it exactly which fields to return, the format, and what to avoid. I keep the temperature low later on so the output stays deterministic and easy to parse. I do not rely on JSON mode here because a strict prompt with a small model like llama-3.3-70b is already highly reliable.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise NLP analysis engine.
Analyze the user text and return ONLY a JSON object with this exact structure:
{
  "sentiment": "positive|neutral|negative",
  "confidence": 0.0 to 1.0,
  "entities": [{"text": "...", "label": "PERSON|ORG|PRODUCT|LOCATION"}],
  "summary": "one sentence summary",
  "key_topics": ["topic1", "topic2"]
}
Rules:
- Do not wrap the JSON in markdown fences.
- If no entities are found, return an empty list.
- Keep the summary under 20 words."""

Step 3: Build the analysis function

This function is the workhorse. It takes a raw string, sends it to llama-3.3-70b, and parses the JSON response. I set temperature to 0.1 so the model does not get creative with the schema, and I cap max_tokens at 512 because the response is small. If the model ever drifts and returns markdown fences, my error handling surfaces it immediately so I can tighten the prompt.

def analyze_text(raw_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": raw_text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=512,
    )

    content = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(content)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        raise ValueError(f"Model returned invalid JSON: {content}")

Step 4: Add batch processing

In production, I rarely analyze one document at a time. This helper accepts a list of strings, loops through them, and aggregates the parsed results. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the loop runs at full speed without waiting for containers to wake up. That matters when you are processing hundreds of support tickets or news articles in one pass.

def analyze_batch(documents: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for doc in documents:
        result = analyze_text(doc)
        results.append(result)
    return results

Step 5: Persist results to JSONL

Downstream tools expect line-delimited JSON. This helper writes each result as its own line, with UTF-8 support for multilingual text. I prefer JSONL over CSV because the nested entity lists do not flatten cleanly into columns. I also print a confirmation so I know the write succeeded.

def save_results(results: list[dict], output_path: str = "nlp_output.jsonl"):
    with open(output_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for item in results:
            f.write(json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"Saved {len(results)} records to {output_path}")

Run it

Here is the entry point I use for local testing. I feed it a sample document about Oxlo.ai, run the batch, save to disk, and pretty-print the first record. When I run python nlp_agent.py, this is what I see.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample_docs = [
        "Oxlo.ai is a developer-first AI inference platform with flat per-request pricing. "
        "I switched from a token-based provider and cut my long-context costs dramatically. "
        "The API is fully OpenAI compatible and there are no cold starts."
    ]

    analyzed = analyze_batch(sample_docs)
    save_results(analyzed)

    for record in analyzed:
        print(json.dumps(record, indent=2))

Example output:

{
  "sentiment": "positive",
  "confidence": 0.95,
  "entities": [
    {"text": "Oxlo.ai", "label": "ORG"}
  ],
  "summary": "User praises Oxlo.ai pricing and API compatibility.",
  "key_topics": ["pricing", "API compatibility", "inference platform"]
}

Wrap-up

That is the entire agent. It is less than 80 lines of Python and replaces a patchwork of separate NLP services. Two concrete next steps: wire the analyze_batch function into a FastAPI endpoint so other services can POST text to it, or swap in qwen-3-32b if you need to process multilingual documents with the same flat per-request pricing. You can see how the plans scale at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Building Language Understanding Systems for Chatbots with LLMs
content:
Modern chatbots have moved far beyond keyword matching and rigid decision trees. Today, language understanding systems are built on large language models that parse intent, extract entities, maintain conversational state, and generate contextually relevant responses in a single inference pass. This unification simplifies application logic, but it also shifts complexity to the infrastructure layer. The platform you choose determines whether your chatbot can handle long dialogue histories, agentic tool use, and multimodal inputs without unpredictable cost explosions or cold-start latency.

Core Components of Language Understanding

At a high level, a chatbot's language understanding layer must solve four problems: intent recognition, entity extraction, context tracking, and response generation. LLMs can address all four within a single prompt, especially when you constrain their outputs. Structured generation modes, such as JSON mode, let you force a model to return labeled intents and slots rather than free-form text, which makes downstream routing reliable. Function calling extends this by allowing the model to emit tool invocations, turning natural language into structured API calls.

These capabilities demand more than a simple text-completion endpoint. You need streaming responses for real-time interfaces, multi-turn conversation support to maintain state across messages, and vision capabilities when users share screenshots or documents. An inference platform that exposes all of these features through a unified API reduces the surface area you must maintain.

Architecture Patterns for Production Chatbots

Production systems rarely send every user message straight to an LLM. Most implementations use a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline to inject relevant documentation or conversation history into the prompt, which grounds the model and reduces hallucinations. For complex tasks, agentic architectures let the model iterate: plan a step, call a tool, observe the result, and reason about the next action. Each loop adds tokens to the context window, and agentic workflows can quickly accumulate tens of thousands of tokens per request.

Another common pattern is multi-modal understanding. A customer support chatbot might need to read an image of an error message, transcribe a voice note, or embed a product description for semantic search. This means your infrastructure must serve not only chat models but also vision, audio, and embedding models from a single integration surface.

Selecting Models for Understanding and Reasoning

No single model is optimal for every understanding task. A general-purpose chatbot might prioritize low latency and broad knowledge, while an agentic coding assistant needs deep reasoning and tool-use proficiency. Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all accessible through a fully OpenAI compatible API. This breadth lets you route different user intents to specialized backends without managing multiple provider contracts.

For general conversational understanding, Llama 3.3 70B provides a strong balance of capability and throughput. If your chatbot handles multilingual users or agentic workflows, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for multilingual reasoning and tool orchestration. When the task requires deep reasoning or complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 deliver advanced chain-of-thought reasoning with support for long contexts up to 131K tokens. DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a one-million-token context window with efficient MoE architecture, making it suitable for chatbots that must ingest entire codebases or lengthy documentation in a single request.

Under traditional token-based pricing, used by providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, these long inputs directly inflate your bill. title: The Role of LLMs in Language Translation Tasks
content:
Machine translation has progressed from rule-based systems to statistical phrase models, and now to large language models. While earlier approaches excelled at narrow, high-volume language pairs, they struggled with context, tone, and domain-specific terminology. Modern LLMs treat translation as a reasoning task rather than a lookup problem, using broad context windows and in-context learning to preserve nuance across paragraphs. For engineering teams building localization pipelines, the shift to LLMs introduces new infrastructure requirements. Long documents, multi-turn refinement, and structured output formats push API costs and latency into critical path concerns. The platform you choose determines whether translation remains an expensive batch job or a scalable service layer.

Beyond Word Substitution: Why LLMs Change Translation

Traditional neural machine translation systems operate on sentence-level encodings. They maximize lexical overlap and fluency, but they discard document-level coherence. An LLM-based approach inverts this constraint. By attending to thousands of tokens in a single forward pass, a decoder-only model can resolve ambiguous pronouns, maintain consistent terminology, and adapt register to match audience expectations.

This capability is especially pronounced in low-resource languages and specialized domains. A model such as Qwen 3 32B, available on Oxlo.ai, is explicitly optimized for multilingual reasoning and agent workflows. Instead of translating sentences in isolation, it can ingest a full technical brief, recognize standardized jargon, and render it accurately in the target language. The improvement is not merely lexical. It is structural. LLMs preserve Markdown tables, inline code, and XML tags that fragment traditional translation pipelines.

Context Windows and Document-Scale Translation

Enterprise translation rarely involves single sentences. Legal contracts, clinical study reports, and software documentation can exceed tens of thousands of tokens. Processing these documents requires models with substantial context capacities. On Oxlo.ai, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window, while Kimi K2.6 offers 131K tokens and advanced reasoning. These capacities allow a complete document to sit inside the prompt, eliminating segmentation errors that occur when text is split across multiple requests.

From a cost perspective, context length exposes a fundamental mismatch in token-based billing. Providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale charge proportionally to input length. A 40,000-token legal document therefore incurs 40,000 input tokens before a single target word is generated. For high-volume localization, this scaling function becomes prohibitive. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For long-context translation workloads, this model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. You can verify current plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Prompt Engineering and Structured Output

Translation quality depends on prompt design. A well-formed system prompt acts as a style guide, enforcing terminology databases, tone constraints, and formatting rules. Few-shot examples embedded in the message history further steer output toward domain standards. For production pipelines, unstructured text responses are difficult to validate. JSON mode solves this by constraining the model to emit parseable objects.

Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, streaming responses, and multi-turn conversations across its LLM catalog. A typical pipeline might send a system instruction, a few-shot example pair, and a source segment, then require the model to return a JSON object containing the translated string, detected source language, and confidence score. Streaming responses further improve pipeline ergonomics. Rather than waiting for a full document translation to complete, downstream systems can begin processing paragraphs as they arrive, reducing end-to-end latency for user-facing interfaces. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, adopting these patterns requires only a base URL change. The platform exposes the familiar chat/completions endpoint, so existing validation logic and retry handlers remain intact.

Agentic Translation Workflows

Translation is increasingly an agentic task. A model does not simply map source to target in a single pass. It consults terminology glossaries, segments content by heading, and iteratively refines output based on reviewer feedback. Function calling enables this behavior. An LLM can emit a tool call to retrieve a preferred term from a customer-specific memory store, then incorporate that term into the next generation step.

For example, a model can call a terminology lookup tool when it encounters an ambiguous pharmaceutical term, then resume generation with the verified equivalent. This loop can repeat across multiple segments without losing track of stylistic constraints established in the system prompt. Models such as GLM 5, with 744B parameters and MoE architecture, and Qwen 3 32B are designed for long-horizon agentic tasks. On Oxlo.ai, these models are available without cold starts, so agent loops do not suffer from warm-up latency between tool calls. Multi-turn conversations allow the model to maintain state across a full editing session, applying consistent corrections across an entire document rather than forgetting prior instructions between API calls. Because Oxlo.ai exposes standard function calling and tool use patterns through the OpenAI SDK, building these loops does not require learning a proprietary API surface.

Implementing Translation Pipelines with Oxlo.ai

Integrating Oxlo.ai into a translation pipeline is straightforward for any team already using the OpenAI SDK. The following Python example sends a long-form source document to Qwen 3 32B and requests a structured JSON response. Note that the cost of this request is flat, even if the source text approaches the model’s context limit.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

source_text = """
[Insert long multilingual document here]
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are an expert translator. Translate the user's document from Japanese to English. "
                "Preserve all Markdown formatting and technical terminology. "
                "Respond in JSON with keys: translation, detected_language, word_count."
            )
        },
        {"role": "user", "content": source_text}
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

result = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(result["translation"])

Oxlo.ai offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including LLMs, vision, and embeddings. For translation specifically, Qwen 3 32B provides strong multilingual reasoning, Llama 3.3 70B serves as a general-purpose flagship, and DeepSeek V4 Flash enables document-scale jobs with its 1M context window. Model selection should match workload shape. For rapid prototyping of multilingual chat, the Free tier includes DeepSeek V3.2, which offers strong coding and reasoning capabilities at no cost. For production document translation requiring near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, DeepSeek V4 Flash or Kimi K2.6 provide the necessary context and accuracy. All are accessible through the same base URL and SDK.

Developers can start on the Free plan, which includes 60 requests per day across 16+ free models and a 7-day full-access trial. Production teams typically move to the Pro plan at $80 per month for 1,000 requests per day, or the Premium plan at $350 per month for 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access. Enterprise customers receive custom dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30% savings versus their current provider.

Cost Model Implications for Production Translation

When evaluating inference infrastructure for translation, total cost of ownership depends on input length distribution. If your pipeline processes short chat messages, token-based billing may appear economical. If it processes contracts, textbooks, or codebase documentation, input tokens dominate the bill. Because token-based providers scale cost linearly with prompt length, a single long-document translation can exceed the price of hundreds of short queries.

Oxlo.ai flattens this curve. One request costs the same whether you send 500 tokens or 50,000 tokens. For long-context and agentic workloads, this structural difference can yield 10-100x cost reductions compared to token-based billing. The predictability also simplifies budgeting. A localization team can translate a fixed number of documents per day without forecasting token inflation caused by verbose source material or multi-turn refinement loops.

Selecting Infrastructure for Translation at Scale

LLMs have redefined what is possible in machine translation, but model capability is only half the equation. Context windows, prompt controllability, and cost structure determine whether a translation pipeline is viable at production volume. Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first environment with flat per-request pricing, deep context models, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility. With no cold starts and support for streaming, JSON mode, and function calling, it is built for the document-heavy, agentic workflows that modern translation demands. If your current costs scale with every source token, moving to a request-based model is a direct lever for margin improvement. Review the latest plans and model catalog at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: LLMs for Dialogue Management: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
We are going to build a task-oriented customer support agent that tracks dialogue state across multiple turns. It extracts user intent, fills required slots, and decides when to escalate to a human. This pattern works for any conversational interface where context matters more than a single prompt.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai gives us flat per-request pricing, so running a two-stage pipeline on every turn does not explode in cost the way token-based billing would for long system prompts. You can find details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Define the dialogue state and system prompt

Every dialogue manager needs a schema. I use a plain Python dictionary to track what we know so far, and a strict system prompt tells the model how to read a conversation and emit a JSON update.

import json

# Our state schema
state_schema = {
    "intent": None,      # refund, troubleshooting, general
    "product": None,     # product name or model
    "issue": None,       # short description
    "escalate": False    # human handoff flag
}

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a dialogue state tracker for a tech support agent.
Read the conversation history and produce a JSON object that strictly follows this schema:
{
  "intent": "refund" | "troubleshooting" | "general" | null,
  "product": string | null,
  "issue": string | null,
  "escalate": boolean
}
Rules:
- Only set intent when the user clearly states it.
- Extract product names exactly as mentioned.
- Set escalate to true if the user asks for a human or expresses frustration.
- Do not guess. Use null if information is missing.
Output only the JSON object, with no markdown and no explanation."""

Step 2: Build the state tracker

I send the full message history to Oxlo.ai and parse the JSON response. I use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows structured instructions reliably, and keeping this as a separate function makes the agent easier to test in isolation.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def track_state(messages):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            *messages,
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    content = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    # Strip markdown fences if the model emits them
    if content.startswith("```"):
        content = content.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(content)

Step 3: Generate context-aware replies

Once we know the state, we generate a reply that acknowledges what we already know and asks for whatever is missing. This second call uses the same Oxlo.ai endpoint but with a different system prompt focused on being helpful and concise.

REPLY_PROMPT = """You are a helpful tech support agent.
You have access to the current dialogue state provided below.
- If the intent is missing, ask what the user needs.
- If the product is missing, ask which product they are using.
- If the issue is missing, ask for details.
- If all fields are filled, confirm the details and say you are looking up a solution.
Be concise. Do not make up facts."""

def generate_reply(state, messages):
    state_block = f"Current state:\n{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": REPLY_PROMPT + "\n\n" + state_block},
            *messages,
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Step 4: Connect the conversation loop

Now I wire the pieces together. The loop collects user input, appends it to the history, calls the tracker, and then calls the reply generator. I keep the history in OpenAI message format so it is portable across providers, but the calls stay on Oxlo.ai.

def run_agent():
    messages = []
    print("Support agent ready. Type 'exit' to quit.\n")

    while True:
        user_input = input("User: ")
        if user_input.lower() in {"exit", "quit"}:
            break

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})

        # Update state
        state = track_state(messages)
        print(f"[State] {json.dumps(state)}\n")

        # Generate reply
        reply = generate_reply(state, messages)
        print(f"Agent: {reply}\n")

        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_agent()

Step 5: Add a knowledge base lookup

A real agent needs to ground its answers. I add a small knowledge base dictionary and a lookup step. If the state has both product and issue, we inject the matching article into the reply prompt so the model can summarize real information instead of hallucinating steps.

KB = {
    ("smartplug-x1", "won't connect"): "Reset the device by holding the button for 10 seconds, then re-run the pairing flow in the app.",
    ("smartplug-x1", "overheating"): "Unplug immediately. Check that the load does not exceed 15 amps. Contact support for a replacement.",
}

def lookup_solution(state):
    key = (state.get("product"), state.get("issue"))
    return KB.get(key)

def generate_reply(state, messages):
    state_block = f"Current state:\n{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"
    kb_fact = lookup_solution(state)
    if kb_fact:
        state_block += f"\n\nKnowledge base entry:\n{kb_fact}"

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": REPLY_PROMPT + "\n\n" + state_block},
            *messages,
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Run it

Save the script as support_agent.py, export your key, and run it. Here is a sample session after the user reports a problem:

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
$ python support_agent.py

Support agent ready. Type 'exit' to quit.

User: hi my smartplug-x1 won't connect
[State] {"intent": "troubleshooting", "product": "smartplug-x1", "issue": "won't connect", "escalate": false}

Agent: Thanks for reaching out. I see you are having trouble connecting your SmartPlug X1. Let's fix this. Please reset the device by holding the button for 10 seconds, then re-run the pairing flow in the app. Let me know if it still does not appear.

User: it still doesn't work and I'm frustrated
[State] {"intent": "troubleshooting", "product": "smartplug-x1", "issue": "won't connect", "escalate": true}

Agent: I understand your frustration. Since the reset did not resolve the issue, I am escalating this to a human specialist who will contact you shortly. Is there anything else I can note for them?

Next steps

Swap in qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 if you need stronger multilingual reasoning or vision support for screenshots of hardware errors. For production, replace the in-memory messages list with a SQLite or Redis cache so conversations survive restarts. If you want to cut latency further, Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, which you can enable by adding stream=True to the chat.completions.create call and yielding chunks as they arrive.

title: Using LLM for Language Generation Tasks
content:
We're building a batch product description generator that turns raw product specs into polished marketing copy. If you manage an e-commerce catalog or a content pipeline, this eliminates the busywork of rewriting specs by hand. We will wire it straight to Oxlo.ai using the OpenAI SDK so every request benefits from flat per-request pricing, which keeps costs predictable even when you stuff long product specifications into the prompt.

What you'll need

Prerequisites are minimal. You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. You also need a CSV file named products.csv with the columns sku, name, and features.

Step 1: Set up the client and verify connectivity

I always test the endpoint before I write business logic. A quick health check saves you from debugging auth issues inside a larger script. This snippet initializes the Oxlo.ai client and makes a single call to Llama 3.3 70B to confirm your key is live.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Reply with OK if you are ready."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the only creative layer we need. I keep it strict so the model returns consistent copy and valid JSON without extra markdown.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a product copywriter. You write concise, engaging e-commerce descriptions.
Rules:
- Output only valid JSON.
- Use this exact structure: {"title": "...", "description": "...", "tags": ["...", "..."]}
- The title must be under 60 characters.
- The description must be two sentences.
- Tags must be lowercase and relevant.
- Do not include markdown code fences."""

Step 3: Write the core generator function

Now we wrap the API call into a clean function. It accepts raw product fields, builds a flat user message, and returns parsed JSON. Keeping the input structured means the model does not have to guess which field is which.

import json

def generate_description(sku, name, features):
    user_message = f"SKU: {sku}\nProduct Name: {name}\nFeatures: {features}"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Enforce JSON mode for reliable parsing

Raw string parsing is fragile. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, so we can set response_format to lock the model into valid JSON. This removes an entire class of formatting errors.

def generate_description(sku, name, features):
    user_message = f"SKU: {sku}\nProduct Name: {name}\nFeatures: {features}"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 5: Batch process a CSV catalog

Here is where we save real time. I read a CSV of products, loop through each row, call our generator, and write the results to an output file. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request instead of per token, we can feed long feature lists into the prompt without watching the meter spin on input tokens. That matters when your catalog includes items with ten or more bullet points. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing to compare plans.

import csv

def process_batch(input_path, output_path):
    with open(input_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as infile, \
         open(output_path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as outfile:
        
        reader = csv.DictReader(infile)
        fieldnames = ["sku", "title", "description", "tags"]
        writer = csv.DictWriter(outfile, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        
        for row in reader:
            try:
                result = generate_description(
                    row["sku"], row["name"], row["features"]
                )
                writer.writerow({
                    "sku": row["sku"],
                    "title": result["title"],
                    "description": result["description"],
                    "tags": ", ".join(result["tags"]),
                })
                print(f"Generated: {row['sku']}")
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Failed on {row['sku']}: {e}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_batch("products.csv", "descriptions.csv")

Create a sample products.csv to test:

sku,name,features
WB-001,Ultra-Trek Backpack,"40L capacity, waterproof nylon, laptop sleeve, ergonomic straps, reflective strips"
WB-002,Titanium Camp Stove,"weighs 45g, compatible with butane and propane, wind-resistant burner, piezo ignition"

Run it

Save the script as generator.py, place products.csv in the same directory, and run python generator.py. You should see output like this in your terminal almost immediately, because Oxlo.ai keeps popular models warm with no cold starts.

Generated: WB-001
Generated: WB-002

And descriptions.csv will contain structured records such as:

sku,title,description,tags
WB-001,Ultra-Trek 40L Hiking Pack,"The Ultra-Trek Backpack combines rugged waterproof nylon with a dedicated laptop sleeve, making it ideal for commuters and trail hikers alike. Ergonomic straps and reflective strips keep you comfortable and visible from dawn to dusk.","backpack, hiking, waterproof, 40l, travel"
WB-002,Titanium Ultralight Camp Stove,"Weighing just 45 grams, this titanium stove is built for gram-counting backpackers who refuse to sacrifice performance. Its wind-resistant burner and piezo ignition deliver reliable flames even when the weather turns.","camping, stove, ultralight, titanium, backpacking"

Next steps

Two concrete directions to take this next. First, swap the model to qwen-3-32b if you need descriptions in multiple languages without changing any other logic, since the Oxlo.ai endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible. Second, add a caching layer with SQLite so you do not pay for regeneration when the same SKU runs twice. Both are trivial to layer on top of the existing client.

title: Integrating LLM with Other Machine Learning Models
content:
Large language models excel at reasoning over unstructured text, but they are not always the most efficient tool for every subtask in a production pipeline. Classical machine learning models, such as gradient-boosted trees, logistic regression, or custom computer-vision classifiers, still offer superior speed, interpretability, and deterministic behavior for narrow, well-defined problems. The most robust AI systems rarely rely on a single model. Instead, they orchestrate LLMs alongside traditional ML components, using each where it is strongest. This guide walks through practical patterns for building these hybrid systems, with concrete code and a look at how Oxlo.ai simplifies the infrastructure behind them.

Why Combine LLMs with Classical ML

LLMs bring remarkable flexibility. They handle ambiguous user queries, generate human-readable explanations, and adapt to new formats with minimal prompting. However, that flexibility comes with trade-offs. Inference can be slower than a lookup table or a lightweight classifier, and stochastic outputs complicate tasks that demand strict consistency, such as fraud scoring or hardware anomaly detection.

Classical ML models thrive in these constrained environments. A calibrated logistic regression or an XGBoost ensemble trained on tabular features can return a probability in milliseconds with full auditability. By pairing these models with an LLM, you can route complex, open-ended questions to the language model while delegating structured, high-volume decisions to deterministic code. The result is a system that preserves accuracy without sacrificing the conversational or reasoning layer that users expect.

title: Building Virtual Language Assistants with LLMs
content:
A virtual language assistant is not a single model. It is a pipeline that turns user intent into structured action, maintains state across minutes or days, and responds in natural language or speech. Whether you are building a customer support bot, a hands-free coding companion, or a multilingual concierge, the stack breaks down into four parts: an input interface, a reasoning core, a memory layer, and an output interface. The difference between a prototype and a production assistant usually comes down to how well these parts integrate, and how predictably they scale once context grows.

Architecture of a Virtual Language Assistant

At minimum, a text-based assistant needs an LLM endpoint and a conversation buffer. A voice-enabled assistant adds speech-to-text (STT) and text-to-speech (TTS) stages. In practice, most useful assistants also need retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or a database for user memory, plus a tool router for function calling.

Latency budgeting matters. STT and TTS each add overhead, so the LLM layer must stream tokens to keep the interaction feeling immediate. You should also consider where to run guardrails. A moderation layer can sit between STT and the LLM to filter noise or sensitive content, and between the LLM and TTS to prevent hallucinated personal data from being spoken aloud. Load balancing across model sizes lets you route simple queries to a fast model and reserve heavy reasoning for complex tasks. Designing this up front prevents rework when you move from demo to deployed service.

Selecting Models for Multilingual and Agentic Workloads

The reasoning core sets the assistant's personality and capability. For general-purpose dialogue, Llama 3.3 70B offers a strong balance of instruction following and latency. If the assistant must reason through complex problems or long code blocks, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 provide advanced chain-of-thought reasoning. For long-horizon agentic tasks that require planning across many steps, GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 are purpose-built for tool use and extended workflows.

Multilingual support is often overlooked until later. Qwen 3 32B handles multilingual reasoning and agent workflows out of the box, which makes it a safe default if your users are not exclusively English-speaking. When the assistant needs to interpret images, vision models such as Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B can process screenshots or photos alongside text.

Do not forget the supporting cast. Embeddings like BGE-Large power semantic search over a knowledge base. For audio pipelines, Whisper Large v3 or Whisper Turbo handle transcription, while Kokoro 82M delivers fast text-to-speech. Oxlo.ai hosts all of these in one place, which removes the need to stitch together separate providers for speech, vision, and text.

title: Sentiment Analysis with LLMs: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Sentiment analysis is one of the first production workloads developers hand to an LLM because it outperforms classical NLP pipelines with almost no training data. In this guide we will build a Python CLI tool that classifies customer reviews into Positive, Negative, or Neutral labels using an off-the-shelf model from Oxlo.ai. The finished script runs against the fully OpenAI-compatible Oxlo.ai API and benefits from flat per-request pricing, so analyzing a thousand long reviews or verbose support tickets carries no token-based surprises.

What you'll need

The dependencies are minimal. You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an Oxlo.ai API key.

pip install openai

Grab your API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. I recommend exporting it as OXLO_API_KEY in your shell, though the snippets below keep the literal placeholder so you can copy and run them immediately. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with 60 requests per day, which is enough to prototype and test this classifier across the 16-plus models included at no cost. If you need more volume, the Pro plan unlocks 1,000 requests per day across all 45-plus models. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

Step 1: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training we do. It constrains the model to exactly three labels and removes punctuation so downstream parsing stays trivial. Keeping the prompt short also keeps request latency low, which matters when you later process batches.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment classifier. Analyze the user-provided text and respond with exactly one word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral. Do not explain your reasoning. Do not add punctuation."""

Step 2: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

Oxlo.ai exposes a standard OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint, so the OpenAI SDK works as a drop-in client. You change the base URL and API key, and leave the rest of your application code untouched. This also means any existing OpenAI-based utility you already have can be migrated by updating two constructor arguments. Because Oxlo.ai keeps popular models warm, you will not hit cold-start latency on the first request.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 3: Build the classify function

I wrap the API call in a small function that accepts a raw string and returns the label. I keep the function synchronous for clarity, but it is trivial to wrap in an async helper later if you move to a FastAPI service or a worker queue. I use llama-3.3-70b here because it is Oxlo.ai's general-purpose flagship and follows instruction formatting reliably at high throughput. If your reviews are multilingual, qwen-3-32b is a strong alternative on the same endpoint with zero code changes. For reasoning-heavy edge cases such as sarcasm, you can later swap to kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment classifier. Analyze the user-provided text and respond with exactly one word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral. Do not explain your reasoning. Do not add punctuation."""

def classify(text: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Step 4: Harden the parser

Even with a strict prompt, an LLM occasionally returns a lowercase label or an extra period. I add a small normalization layer that forces the output into one of the three allowed buckets and raises a clear error if the model hallucinates an unexpected string. This defensive step saves you from dirty data downstream.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment classifier. Analyze the user-provided text and respond with exactly one word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral. Do not explain your reasoning. Do not add punctuation."""

VALID_LABELS = {"positive", "negative", "neutral"}

def classify(text: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip().lower()
    if raw not in VALID_LABELS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected label: {raw}")
    return raw.capitalize()

Step 5: Process a batch of reviews

Real workloads never arrive one at a time. In production I usually read these from a CSV or a message queue, but the core loop stays identical. The snippet below iterates over a Python list of review strings, calls Oxlo.ai for each, and prints a simple TSV report. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, feeding long-winded reviews costs the same as short ones. This makes the flat pricing ideal for sentiment pipelines that ingest entire support tickets or forum threads without ballooning costs. If you are processing a backlog, the request-based model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context workloads.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment classifier. Analyze the user-provided text and respond with exactly one word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral. Do not explain your reasoning. Do not add punctuation."""

VALID_LABELS = {"positive", "negative", "neutral"}

def classify(text: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip().lower()
    if raw not in VALID_LABELS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected label: {raw}")
    return raw.capitalize()

reviews = [
    "The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked all day without plugging in.",
    "Shipping took two weeks and the box was dented. Not impressed.",
    "It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special.",
]

print("review\tsentiment")
for r in reviews:
    label = classify(r)
    print(f"{r[:50]}\t{label}")

Step 6: Evaluate with labeled data

To know if the classifier is production-ready, I compare its predictions against a small ground-truth set. You can build this set by hand-labeling twenty or thirty representative examples from your own data. The helper below calculates exact-match accuracy, which is usually sufficient for three-class sentiment. If you need deeper reasoning for edge cases such as sarcasm or mixed sentiment, swap the model to kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 without changing any client code. Both models excel at advanced reasoning and will pick up on subtle cues that simpler prompts miss. Because Oxlo.ai bills per request, running an evaluation on a hundred long examples is predictable and cheap.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment classifier. Analyze the user-provided text and respond with exactly one word: Positive, Negative, or Neutral. Do not explain your reasoning. Do not add punctuation."""

VALID_LABELS = {"positive", "negative", "neutral"}

def classify(text: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip().lower()
    if raw not in VALID_LABELS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected label: {raw}")
    return raw.capitalize()

labeled = [
    ("I love this product, best purchase ever!", "Positive"),
    ("Terrible experience, would not recommend.", "Negative"),
    ("The item arrived on Tuesday.", "Neutral"),
]

correct = 0
for text, truth in labeled:
    pred = classify(text)
    status = "OK" if pred == truth else "FAIL"
    if pred == truth:
        correct += 1
    print(f"[{status}] truth={truth} pred={pred} | {text[:40]}")

print(f"\nAccuracy: {correct}/{len(labeled)} ({correct/len(labeled):.0%})")

Run it

Save the script as sentiment.py, export your key, and run it. You can replace the labeled list with your own data by reading a CSV or a JSON lines file. Here is what the evaluation output looks like on my machine using
