title: Optimizing LLM Model Size for Efficient Inference
content:
Developers often assume that larger parameter counts guarantee better output quality, but in production inference, model size is a constraint to be managed, not a virtue to be maximized. Every additional billion parameters increases memory bandwidth pressure, latency, and infrastructure cost. Efficient inference is not about using the biggest model available. It is about matching the right architecture, quantization level, and context strategy to your actual workload. The platforms that make this experimentation painless are the ones that let you swap models, test routing logic, and scale context without rewriting billing forecasts.

Quantization and Weight Compression

The most direct way to shrink a model for inference is post-training quantization. Techniques such as INT8, INT4, AWQ, and GPTQ reduce the precision of weights and activations, which directly lowers VRAM requirements and increases throughput. Inference workloads are often memory-bound rather than compute-bound; the bottleneck is reading billions of parameters from high-bandwidth memory. Reducing precision means fewer bytes per weight, so the same memory bandwidth can deliver more tokens per second. A 70B parameter model at FP16 can consume more than 140 GB of GPU memory, while a well-quantized variant can run comfortably on a single server-class accelerator. The trade-off is a small accuracy degradation that is often imperceptible for classification, summarization, or retrieval tasks.

The operational burden of quantizing, validating, and serving these artifacts is not trivial. You must manage calibration datasets, handle format compatibility, and maintain separate inference containers for each precision level. Oxlo.ai removes this overhead by providing fully managed endpoints for dozens of open-source and proprietary models. Instead of maintaining your own quantized weights, you can route traffic to the appropriate endpoint and let the platform handle the serving stack.

title: Using LLMs for Question Answering
content:
We are going to build a knowledge-base question answering agent in Python. It retrieves relevant documents from an in-memory store and uses an LLM hosted on Oxlo.ai to generate grounded, accurate answers. This pattern works for internal help desks, product FAQs, and documentation search, and you can deploy it anywhere you can run Python.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need an Oxlo.ai API key. Create one for free at https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier includes 60 requests per day, which is plenty for testing. Finally, install the OpenAI SDK. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API, so the official SDK is the only client we need.

pip install openai

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

First, import the OpenAI SDK and instantiate a client aimed at Oxlo.ai. The base_url and api_key are the only differences from a standard OpenAI setup. I like to run a quick connectivity check with a lightweight greeting to confirm the key is active and the endpoint is reachable. Because Oxlo.ai keeps popular models warm, there are no cold starts, and the first request returns immediately.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"},
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Load the knowledge base

For a production system you might pull from a CMS or a vector store, but a plain Python list keeps this tutorial reproducible without any external dependencies. Each document has a title and content field. I have seeded five entries that cover common support topics. You can replace these with your own internal wiki pages, API docs, or policy PDFs later. I keep each entry under 100 words so the full context easily fits inside the prompt.

KNOWLEDGE_BASE = [
    {
        "title": "Refund Policy",
        "content": "Customers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, refunds are prorated based on usage.",
    },
    {
        "title": "API Rate Limits",
        "content": "Free plans include 60 requests per day. Pro plans include 1,000 requests per day. Enterprise plans offer unlimited requests.",
    },
    {
        "title": "Supported Models",
        "content": "Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models, including Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, DeepSeek R1 671B, Kimi K2.6, and GLM 5.",
    },
    {
        "title": "Uptime SLA",
        "content": "Premium and Enterprise plans include a 99.9% uptime SLA. Status updates are posted at status.oxlo.ai.",
    },
    {
        "title": "Pricing Model",
        "content": "Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing. One API call costs the same regardless of prompt length, which makes long-context workloads predictable.",
    },
]

Step 3: Build a retriever

Retrieval is the secret sauce of good RAG. Real pipelines use vector search, but a keyword overlap scorer is surprisingly effective for structured text and takes zero setup. The function tokenizes the query and each document into lowercase word sets, computes the intersection size, and returns the top_k matches. It is deterministic, fast, and easy to debug. I set top_k to 2 because five documents are small enough that the best two usually cover the intent. When you move to production, you can drop in an embeddings-based retriever without touching the LLM logic.

def retrieve_docs(query, kb, top_k=2):
    query_words = set(query.lower().split())
    scored = []
    for doc in kb:
        text = f"{doc['title']} {doc['content']}"
        doc_words = set(text.lower().split())
        overlap = len(query_words & doc_words)
        scored.append((overlap, doc))
    scored.sort(reverse=True, key=lambda x: x[0])
    return [doc for _, doc in scored[:top_k]]

Step 4: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the agent's instruction manual. It tells the model exactly what role to play, how to use the retrieved context, and what to do when the answer is missing. I keep the formatting explicit: a {context} placeholder that gets filled at runtime, and a hard rule to reply exactly "I don't have that information." This prevents hallucinations on out-of-scope questions. I also cap the answer length so responses stay scannable.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise support agent. Answer the user's question using ONLY the context below.
If the context does not contain the answer, reply exactly: "I don't have that information."
Be concise. Use two sentences or fewer.

Context:
{context}
"""

Step 5: Assemble the pipeline

Now we wire everything together. The answer_question function does three things in sequence. It calls retrieve_docs to fetch the best matches from KNOWLEDGE_BASE. It injects those matches into SYSTEM_PROMPT and formats a proper chat completion payload. Then it sends the payload to Oxlo.ai using llama-3.3-70b, a strong general-purpose model that follows system instructions reliably. If you need multilingual reasoning, you can swap in qwen-3-32b, or use kimi-k2.6 for advanced reasoning tasks. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, adding extra context chunks does not inflate the cost the way token-based billing would. That means you can experiment with larger context windows and more examples without watching a meter run. You can see plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

def answer_question(user_message):
    docs = retrieve_docs(user_message, KNOWLEDGE_BASE)
    context = "\n\n".join(f"Title: {d['title']}\n{d['content']}" for d in docs)
    system_content = SYSTEM_PROMPT.format(context=context)

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": system_content},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Run it

Save the full script as qa_agent.py and run it from your terminal. I have included three test questions. The first asks about refunds, the second asks about the model catalog, and the third asks for a phone number that we never provided. A well-behaved agent should answer the first two confidently and refuse the third. This sanity check proves that the system prompt is actually governing behavior and not just decorating it. Below is the output I get on my end. Your timestamps and exact wording may vary slightly, but the substance should match.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    questions = [
        "What is the refund policy?",
        "Which models does Oxlo.ai support?",
        "Do you offer phone support?",
    ]
    for q in questions:
        print(f"Q: {q}")
        print(f"A: {answer_question(q)}")
        print()

Example output:

Q: What is the refund policy?
A: Customers may request a full refund within 30 days of purchase. After 30 days, refunds are prorated.

Q: Which models does Oxlo.ai support?
A: Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models, including Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, DeepSeek R1 671B, Kimi K2.6, and GLM 5.

Q: Do you offer phone support?
A: I don't have that information.

Next steps

This agent is intentionally minimal so you can reason about every moving part. The obvious upgrade is replacing the keyword retriever with dense embeddings. Oxlo.ai offers embedding models like BGE-Large and E5-Large through the same OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can generate vectors and build a FAISS or pgvector index without changing providers.

Another upgrade is switching to a reasoning model such as DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 for multi-hop questions that require synthesizing several documents. Because Oxlo.ai pricing is flat per request, long-context RAG workloads and agentic tool loops stay predictable. You do not need to count tokens or worry about a massive prompt suddenly doubling your bill. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details.

title: Deploying LLMs on Edge Devices
content:
Edge deployment of large language models has moved from research curiosity to production requirement. Device manufacturers, robotics teams, and mobile developers are racing to reduce latency and preserve privacy by running inference locally on GPUs, NPUs, and even microcontrollers. Yet the gap between a quantized 3-billion-parameter model on a smartphone and a 70-billion-parameter reasoning engine in the cloud remains wide. Most production systems will not live entirely at the edge. They will live in the tension between on-device efficiency and cloud capability, which is exactly where an inference platform like Oxlo.ai becomes structurally relevant.

The Engineering Constraints of On-Device Inference

Running an LLM on an edge device is an exercise in resource starvation management. Consumer NPUs and mobile GPUs operate within strict thermal and power envelopes. A model that fits in a cloud GPU's 80 GB of HBM must be distilled, pruned, or quantized to INT4 or INT8 to squeeze into 8 GB or 16 GB of shared device memory. Even then, context windows shrink, generation latency increases, and output quality degrades on complex reasoning or coding tasks.

Frameworks like llama.cpp, ONNX Runtime, and Qualcomm QNN have made deployment technically feasible, but feasibility is not the same as utility. An edge model can handle intent classification, entity extraction, or simple summarization. It struggles with multi-step agentic reasoning, long-context synthesis, or code generation across large repositories. Teams that treat edge as a complete replacement for cloud inference often hit a capability ceiling within the first month of production.

Hybrid Architectures: Bridging Edge and Cloud

The pragmatic architecture is hybrid. The edge device handles preprocessing, caching, privacy-sensitive filtering, and lightweight inference. When the task exceeds local capacity, the device forwards a structured request to a cloud endpoint. This pattern is common in robotics, industrial IoT, and voice assistants, where local inference manages low-latency feedback loops and cloud inference handles planning, diagnostics, or open-domain dialogue.

Oxlo.ai operates as the cloud layer in this stack. With 45-plus models across reasoning, code, vision, and embeddings, it provides the heavy compute that edge silicon cannot accommodate. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based metering, the cost of a cloud call from an edge device is flat regardless of how much sensor data, conversation history, or log context you attach to the prompt. For edge workloads that naturally accumulate long inputs, this pricing model removes the cost unpredictability that complicates token-based budgeting.

Prototyping Cloud-First Before Edge Optimization

Engineering teams typically prototype the full-capability version of a product in the cloud, then optimize for edge deployment. Attempting to design edge constraints into the first iteration leads to premature optimization and degraded user experiences. A better workflow is to validate the application logic against high-capability cloud models, profile the latency and quality requirements, and only then decide which subtasks can be downgraded to an on-device model.

Oxlo.ai supports this workflow with full OpenAI SDK compatibility. You can point your existing Python, Node.js, or cURL client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and evaluate flagship models such as Llama 3.3 70B for general dialogue, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for deep reasoning, or Kimi K2.6 for vision-enabled agentic coding. There are no cold starts on popular models, so your prototyping loop remains tight. The free tier offers 60 requests per day across more than a dozen models, which is enough to validate architecture before committing to a paid plan. Once you identify the latency-critical path, you can replace a subset of calls with a local quantized model while keeping the complex reasoning path on Oxlo.ai.

Model Pairing Strategies for Edge and Cloud

Successful hybrid systems pair edge and cloud models by capability tier. The edge tier usually runs a small language model, perhaps 2 billion to 8 billion parameters, fine-tuned for routing, classification, or constrained generation. When the edge model detects a request requiring reasoning, tool use, or long-context memory, it escalates to the cloud tier.

Oxlo.ai offers explicit options for each escalation target. For multilingual agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B provides strong tool-use performance. For complex coding tasks, DeepSeek V4 Flash delivers near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning with a 1 million token context window. For vision pipelines where the edge device captures images but cannot run large vision-language models, Kimi VL A3B or Gemma 3 27B are available through the same API. The platform also covers embeddings with BGE-Large and E5-Large, so vector search can happen in the cloud if the edge index is too large to store locally. Function calling and JSON mode are fully supported, which means the cloud model can return structured tool calls that the edge device executes safely.

Why Request-Based Pricing Matters for Edge Workloads

Edge devices generate bursty, context-heavy payloads. A maintenance drone might stream a megabyte of telemetry and log data into a single diagnostic prompt. A voice assistant might append fifteen minutes of conversation history to maintain continuity. Under token-based billing, these long inputs create unpredictable cost spikes that make unit economics impossible to model at scale.

Oxlo.ai flips this dynamic with flat per-request pricing. One API call costs the same whether the prompt contains fifty tokens or fifty thousand. For hardware teams shipping devices that call the cloud, this translates to predictable cost of goods sold and simpler pricing for end customers. You can link to the pricing page at https://oxlo.ai/pricing to compare plans, but the structural advantage is clear: long-context and agentic workloads, which are common in edge-cloud hybrids, are significantly cheaper when cost does not scale with input length.

title: Building Recommender Systems with LLMs
content:
Recommender systems have traditionally relied on matrix factorization, two-tower neural networks, and dense embedding spaces. These approaches scale well for billions of interactions, but they struggle with cold-start items, nuanced contextual reasoning, and generating human-readable explanations. Large language models introduce a fundamentally different approach. Instead of learning static latent vectors, an LLM can ingest raw item metadata, user reviews, and interaction histories directly into its context window, then reason about relevance in natural language. The challenge is not architectural feasibility but inference economics. Recommendation prompts often contain thousands of tokens of user history, product descriptions, or catalog entries. When costs scale linearly with token count, long-context recommendation becomes prohibitively expensive. Oxlo.ai addresses this directly with flat per-request pricing, making it practical to pass entire interaction logs into the prompt without worrying about token meter tickers.

Architectures for LLM-Based Recommendation

There are three practical patterns for integrating LLMs into recommendation pipelines.

First, direct generation. The prompt contains a user profile, explicit preferences, and a candidate set of items. The model returns a ranked list with rationale. This works best for small catalogs or final-stage reranking where the candidate pool is under fifty items.

Second, retrieval-augmented ranking. A traditional retrieval layer, such as a vector database or approximate nearest neighbor index, narrows thousands of items down to a manageable shortlist. The LLM then acts as a reranker, scoring each candidate against the user’s stated or implicit preferences. This hybrid approach preserves the scalability of conventional recommenders while adding the interpretability and contextual nuance of a language model.

Third, agentic workflows. The LLM interacts with tools, such as inventory APIs, price filters, or user profile databases, across multiple turns. It might ask clarifying questions, refine constraints, or iterate on a shortlist. Agentic patterns produce highly personalized results, but they multiply the number of API calls and the total context length. With token-based billing, each tool-turn inflates cost because the full conversation history is resent. Oxlo.ai’s request-based model removes that penalty, so agentic loops cost one flat fee per turn regardless of how much context accumulates.

A Practical Implementation with Structured Output

Let us look at a concrete implementation. Suppose we want to recommend movies from a candidate pool based on a user’s viewing history. We need the model to return a parseable JSON array so our application can ingest the results reliably. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, so the integration requires only a base URL change.

import openai
import json

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

user_history = """
Recently watched: Dune: Part Two (liked), Oppenheimer (liked), Barbie (disliked).
Preferred genres: sci-fi, historical drama.
"""

catalog = """
1. Interstellar (sci-fi, 2014)
2. The Grand Budapest Hotel (comedy, 2014)
3. 12 Years a Slave (historical drama, 2013)
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a recommendation engine. Return only a JSON array of recommended items with fields: title, reason."},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"User history: {user_history}\nCatalog: {catalog}\nRecommend 2 movies and explain why each fits."}
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    temperature=0.3
)

recommendations = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(recommendations)

This pattern is immediately useful for content moderation, e-commerce, and media applications. The system prompt constrains the output schema, while the user prompt carries the dynamic data. Because Oxlo.ai offers models such as Llama 3.3 70B for general-purpose reasoning and Qwen 3 32B for multilingual workloads, you can select the right capacity for your catalog complexity without rewriting client code.

Managing Long Context and User Histories

Real-world user histories are not three lines. They are thousands of clicks, purchases, and dwell-time events spanning months. Compressing them into embedding vectors loses signal. Feeding them raw into an LLM preserves nuance but explodes token counts. On token-based platforms, a 32k or 128k token prompt incurs a massive input charge before the model generates a single recommendation token.

Oxlo.ai flips this constraint. With flat per-request pricing, the cost of a recommendation call is independent of prompt length. You can pass a user’s last fifty product reviews, full item descriptions, or even a structured JSON log of their session behavior without incremental cost. For extremely long documents, Oxlo.ai hosts models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash, which offers a 1 million token context window, and Kimi K2.6, which supports 131K tokens with advanced reasoning and vision capabilities. This means you can build recommenders that read entire user manuals, long-form articles, or video transcripts to judge relevance, not just skim metadata.

Agentic Recommendation Loops

The most sophisticated recommender systems do not guess. They investigate. An agentic LLM can call tools to check real-time inventory, apply business rules, or query a user profile graph. For example, a travel recommender might call a flight API, a hotel availability endpoint, and a weather service before presenting a curated itinerary.

Function calling is standard on Oxlo.ai. You define schemas for your tools, and models such as DeepSeek V3.2 or Minimax M2.5 can invoke them across multiple turns. The economic implication is critical. In a four-turn agentic loop where each request carries 8,000 tokens of accumulated context, a token-based provider bills for every token in every turn. On Oxlo.ai, each turn costs one request. If your application serves thousands of users simultaneously, that pricing model can reduce inference costs by an order of magnitude for agentic workloads. You can view exact plan details on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Evaluation and Guardrails

LLM recommenders are not immune to hallucination. A model might cite a nonexistent product feature or invent a user preference. Guardrails are essential.

First, constrain the output. Use JSON mode or regex validation to ensure returned item IDs exist in your catalog. Second, ground the model. Attach a retrieval layer so every recommendation references real, indexed items. Third, evaluate offline before deploying. Measure standard ranking metrics, such as NDCG or hit-rate, on held-out user histories. Fourth, log and audit. Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, so you can inspect partial outputs in real time and abort generation if the model drifts from the schema.

Temperature settings matter. Recommendation tasks benefit from low temperature, around 0.2 to 0.4, to reduce creative hallucination while preserving enough variability to avoid repetitive suggestions. If your use case requires vision, models such as Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B on Oxlo.ai can process product images as part of the recommendation context, letting you build multimodal rankers without a separate image embedding pipeline.

Selecting Infrastructure for Production

When you move from prototype to production, inference economics dominate the feasibility of LLM-based recommendation. Token-based providers bill for every input and output token. That model penalizes long contexts, rich metadata, and multi-turn conversations precisely where LLMs add the most value over traditional recommenders.

Oxlo.ai is a developer-first inference platform built on flat per-request pricing. One API call costs one request, regardless of whether you send a 500-token summary or a 100,000-token user history. The platform hosts over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including general reasoning, code, vision, and embeddings. All endpoints are fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, so switching from another provider to Oxlo.ai requires only changing the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai

title: LLM for Text Classification
content:
I recently shipped a ticket classifier that reads customer support messages and routes them to the correct team before a human opens the inbox. It runs on Llama 3.3 70B through Oxlo.ai, and because the platform uses flat per-request pricing, a two-sentence question costs the same as a two-thousand-word error log. In this tutorial, I will walk through the exact code so you can deploy your own version in under an hour.

What you'll need

You only need a few things to follow along.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key. Create one at https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier includes 60 requests per day and a 7-day full-access trial, which is plenty for testing.
  • The OpenAI SDK. Install it with pip install openai.

Step 1: Design the classification schema

Before writing any network code, I define the output shape. A classifier is only useful if it returns structured data your downstream tools can consume. I need four fields: a category for routing, an urgency level for prioritization, a short summary for the dashboard, and a confidence score so I know when to trust the machine. I describe these constraints in plain English inside the prompt rather than using a strict JSON schema, because I find Llama 3.3 70B handles natural instructions more reliably than nested object definitions.

CLASS_SCHEMA = {
    "category": "One of: Billing, Technical, Account, Spam",
    "urgency": "One of: High, Medium, Low",
    "summary": "A 10-word max description of the issue",
    "confidence": "An integer 1-10 representing model certainty"
}

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the entire product for a classifier. I do not fine-tune. I simply describe the job, list the allowed values, and forbid extra text. This keeps latency low and parsing trivial. I explicitly disallow markdown fences because they break simple JSON parsers in downstream scripts.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket classifier. Read the user's message and classify it.

Rules:
- category must be exactly one of: Billing, Technical, Account, Spam.
- urgency must be exactly one of: High, Medium, Low.
- summary must be 10 words or fewer.
- confidence must be an integer from 1 to 10.

Respond ONLY with valid JSON. Do not add markdown fences or explanations."""

Step 3: Build the classifier function

Now I wire the prompt to Oxlo.ai. I use the standard OpenAI client, but I point base_url to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. I set temperature to 0.1 because classification benefits from repeatability, not creativity. I also set response_format to json_object so the model knows it must produce valid JSON.

I chose Llama 3.3 70B because it is Oxlo.ai's general-purpose flagship. It follows system instructions tightly and runs without cold starts, so you can deploy this classifier behind an HTTP endpoint and not worry about latency spikes on the first request of the day. One practical note: support tickets often arrive with long stack traces or chat history pasted inline. On token-based providers, that length drives up cost. Oxlo.ai charges per request, so the price stays flat even when a user dumps a thousand tokens of context. That makes this architecture viable for high-volume queues.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_ticket(ticket_text: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Add confidence filtering and routing

Auto-routing everything is risky. I use the confidence score as a circuit breaker. If confidence is below 8, I send the ticket to a human triage queue. If it is 8 or above, I look up the inbox and route immediately. This pattern keeps humans in the loop for edge cases while removing the drudgery of obvious tickets. You should treat the threshold of 8 as a starting point, not a law. Measure your own accuracy on a labeled validation set and adjust up or down. In a production app you would pull the inbox mapping from a database, but a dictionary is enough for the tutorial.

def route_ticket(ticket_text: str):
    result = classify_ticket(ticket_text)
    
    if result["confidence"] < 8:
        return {"action": "human_triage", "reason": "low_confidence", "details": result}
    
    team_inbox = {
        "Billing": "billing@company.com",
        "Technical": "tech@company.com",
        "Account": "account@company.com",
        "Spam": "/dev/null",
    }
    
    return {
        "action": "auto_route",
        "inbox": team_inbox[result["category"]],
        "details": result,
    }

Step 5: Process a batch of tickets

In production, this code sits inside a worker that pulls from a message queue. For a local test, I use a plain Python list. I chose three tickets that cover a clear billing issue, a technical bug report, and ambiguous fluff that could confuse the model.

tickets = [
    "I was charged twice for my subscription this month. Please refund the extra $49.",
    "The API returns a 502 every time I send a request with more than 100 items in the batch.",
    "Hey, love your product. Just saying hi.",
]

for t in tickets:
    decision = route_ticket(t)
    print(json.dumps(decision, indent=2))

Run it

Save everything in a file named classifier.py, export your key, and run python classifier.py. Here is the output I get back from Oxlo.ai against the three test tickets.

{
  "action": "auto_route",
  "inbox": "billing@company.com",
  "details": {
    "category": "Billing",
    "urgency": "High",
    "summary": "Customer charged twice, requests refund",
    "confidence": 10
  }
}
{
  "action": "auto_route",
  "inbox": "tech@company.com",
  "details": {
    "category": "Technical",
    "urgency": "High",
    "summary": "API 502 error on large batches",
    "confidence": 9
  }
}
{
  "action": "human_triage",
  "reason": "low_confidence",
  "details": {
    "category": "Spam",
    "urgency": "Low",
    "summary": "Positive feedback, no action needed",
    "confidence": 6
  }
}

The first two tickets are unambiguous, so the model returns high confidence and we route them instantly. The third ticket is polite noise. The model is unsure whether it belongs to Account or Spam, so it assigns a low confidence score and we escalate to a human. That is exactly the behavior I want in production. You can verify the JSON is valid by piping it through jq or by asserting keys in a unit test. If the model ever returns malformed JSON, the json.loads call will raise an exception. In production, I wrap that in a try-except block that falls back to human triage rather than crashing the worker.

Next steps

If you want to harden this into a production service, here are two concrete moves.

First, integrate with your helpdesk. Replace the static tickets list with a webhook from Zendesk, Front, or a custom email parser. You can run this classifier on every incoming message without worrying about token count, because Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing stays predictable no matter how much context the user includes. You can view the exact plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Second, add a second pass with a reasoning model. If the classifier returns low confidence, you can escalate to DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 to analyze whether the issue is a known outage or a user error. Both models are available on Oxlo.ai through the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the code change is literally just the model string. This gives you a fast cheap first pass and a slow deep second pass, all on one platform.

Finally, consider logging every classification to a local file or data warehouse. Over time, that log becomes a dataset you can use to audit model drift or to refine your confidence threshold based on real error rates.

title: Integrating LLM with Other AI Models
content:
Building production AI systems rarely ends with a single large language model. Real applications combine reasoning, perception, generation, and retrieval into coordinated pipelines. A chatbot that answers questions about a video needs audio transcription, vision understanding, and text reasoning working in sequence. An autonomous coding agent needs a code model to suggest edits and a generalist LLM to plan the next step. Integrating these components behind a unified API surface reduces complexity, but only if the underlying platform exposes consistent interfaces across every modality.

Why Integrate LLMs with Specialized Models

Monolithic LLMs are generalists, yet specialization still wins on latency, cost, and accuracy for narrow tasks. A 70B parameter model can describe an image, but a dedicated vision model often does it faster and cheaper. Likewise, embeddings models such as BGE-Large or E5-Large produce retrieval vectors far more efficiently than asking a generative model to output structured feature lists. By routing inputs to the right specialist, you build compound systems that are more capable than any single model. The challenge is not deciding whether to integrate, but how to orchestrate multiple APIs without fragmenting your codebase into incompatible clients.

The Architecture of a Multi-Model Pipeline

Most multi-model applications follow one of three patterns. In sequential chaining, the output of one model becomes the input to the next. An audio file passes through Whisper Large v3 for transcription, then the resulting text feeds into Llama 3.3 70B for summarization. In parallel ensemble, several models process the same input simultaneously. You might run object detection with YOLOv11 and image captioning with Gemma 3 27B at the same time, then merge their outputs with an LLM. In router patterns, an initial model classifies the request and dispatches it to the appropriate specialist, such as sending coding queries to Qwen 3 Coder 30B or creative writing to GPT-Oss 120B. Regardless of the pattern, consistency matters. If every model requires a different SDK, authentication scheme, and response format, your orchestration layer becomes brittle. A single platform that exposes all specialists through one protocol lets you swap models or chain them without rewriting request logic.

Selecting Your Model Stack on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai provides 45 plus open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all served from a single base URL. This removes the need to manage accounts across disparate providers. For reasoning and chat, the lineup includes Qwen 3 32B for multilingual agent workflows, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for deep reasoning and complex coding, Kimi K2.6 for advanced reasoning and agentic coding with vision support, and Llama 3.3 70B as a general-purpose flagship. For long-context tasks, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a one-million-token context window with near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, while GLM 5 handles long-horizon agentic tasks at 744B MoE scale. When you need dedicated code generation, Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast provide targeted completions. Vision workloads can use Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B for image understanding. For creative outputs, Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Oxlo.ai Image Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 handle image generation. Audio pipelines can leverage Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium for transcription, plus Kokoro 82M for text-to-speech. Retrieval systems have access to BGE-Large and E5-Large embeddings, while YOLOv9 and YOLOv11 cover object detection. Because every model on Oxlo.ai is accessible through the same OpenAI-compatible endpoints, you can move from chat completions to image generations to audio transcriptions without importing new libraries.

Implementation Patterns with the OpenAI SDK

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. You point your existing Python or Node.js client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and use the same methods you already know. This compatibility extends across chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech. Below is a simplified sequential pipeline in Python. It transcribes an audio file, generates a summary with an LLM, and produces a cover image for the resulting report. ```python from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY" ) # Step 1: Transcribe audio with open("interview.wav", "rb") as audio: transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create( model="whisper-large-v3", file=audio ) # Step 2: Summarize with an LLM completion = client.chat.completions.create( model="llama-3.3-70b", messages=[{ "role": "user", "content": f"Summarize this transcript: {transcript.text}" }], stream=False ) summary = completion.choices[0].message.content # Step 3: Generate a cover image image = client.images.generate( model="flux.1", prompt=f"Abstract editorial illustration of: {summary[:200]}", n=1 ) print(summary) print(image.data[0].url) ``` The same client handles function calling, JSON mode, and streaming responses. If the summary step needs structured output, you can set `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` and define a schema in the prompt. If the pipeline requires tool use, you can attach function definitions to the chat call and let Kimi K2.5 or Minimax M2.5 handle agentic tool execution before the next stage runs.

Cost Control for Agentic and Long-Context Workloads

Token-based pricing penalizes long inputs. When an agent loops over a conversation history that grows with every turn, or when you feed a one-million-token document into DeepSeek V4 Flash, input tokens accumulate quickly on providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale. Costs scale linearly with context length, making iterative agent architectures prohibitively expensive. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can be 10 to 100 times cheaper than token-based alternatives because you are not metered on every word in the prompt or completion. There are no cold starts on popular models, so latency stays predictable even when you burst between transcription, embedding, and chat calls. The pricing structure is straightforward. The Free plan offers 60 requests per day across 16 plus models with a seven-day full-access trial. Pro provides 1,000 requests per day across all models. Premium raises the limit to 5,000 requests per day and adds priority queue access. Enterprise plans offer custom unlimited volume with dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction versus your current provider. For exact figures, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing. Because the unit of cost is the request, you can design pipelines that pass large contexts between stages without watching a meter spin. Send a full codebase to DeepSeek V3.2 for reasoning, embed the resulting chunks with E5-Large, and route retrieved passages back into Kimi K2 Thinking, all without inflating your bill through intermediate token counts.

End-to-End Example: A Multimodal Content Agent

Consider a content moderation and repurposing agent. It receives a user-uploaded video, extracts frames, detects objects, transcribes speech, and produces a structured safety report with synthesized narration. Using Oxlo.ai, the pipeline looks like this. First, sample frames from the video and send them to Gemma 3 27B for visual content analysis via the vision-capable chat completions endpoint. In parallel, submit the audio track to Whisper Turbo for fast transcription. Feed both the visual description and the transcript into Qwen 3 32B, using JSON mode to enforce a strict safety schema. Finally, pass the flagged summary to Kokoro 82M for text-to-speech via the audio/speech endpoint. All four stages use the same OpenAI client, the same authentication, and the same request-based billing model. There is no need to negotiate separate contracts for a transcription provider, a vision API, and an inference host. Oxlo.ai aggregates every modality under one roof.

Conclusion

Integrating LLMs with other AI models is now a standard engineering requirement, not an experimental niche. The complexity lies in orchestration, not in the models themselves. A platform that unifies chat, reasoning, code, vision, image generation, audio, and embeddings behind a single OpenAI-compatible API removes the integration tax. Oxlo.ai provides that unified surface, paired with request-based pricing that protects budgets as contexts grow and agents iterate. If you are building compound AI systems, you can standardize on one client, one base URL, and one predictable cost model.

title: Using LLM for Sentiment Analysis
content:
Sentiment analysis stops being a toy problem when you are staring at a CSV with ten thousand unlabeled customer reviews and a product manager asking for a theme breakdown by Friday. In this tutorial, I will build a practical Python analyzer that classifies text, extracts the dominant topic, and returns structured JSON using an LLM hosted on Oxlo.ai. The final script is under eighty lines, runs against any of Oxlo.ai's chat models, and costs the same per request whether the review is one sentence or ten paragraphs. That flat pricing matters more than it sounds, because sentiment often hides in the middle of a long support thread, and truncating context to save tokens usually makes the model dumber.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer. The script uses type hints and modern string formatting that older versions handle differently.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with this client, so there is no custom library to learn.
  • An active Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. You can start on the free plan to test the flow before upgrading.
  • A few sample strings to analyze. We will define those inline, but you can later point the script at a CSV or database.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the OpenAI SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai's base URL. Reading the API key from an environment variable keeps secrets out of source control and avoids the classic mistake of committing a key to GitHub. I default to llama-3.3-70b because it follows system instructions tightly for classification tasks, which means the JSON schema in the prompt is respected. You can swap in qwen-3-32b if you need multilingual support, or deepseek-v3.2 if you want to experiment on Oxlo.ai's free tier. For production workloads that mix languages, kimi-k2.6 is another solid option on Oxlo.ai with strong reasoning and a 131K context window.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between my code and the model. I tell it to act as a sentiment analyst, restrict labels to Positive, Negative, or Neutral, and require a confidence score between 0 and 1. I also ask for the main topic in five words or fewer so I can aggregate themes later without pulling in spaCy or NLTK. Keeping the schema strict and listing the keys explicitly means JSON mode rarely hallucinates extra keys or wraps the output in markdown code fences. I learned the hard way that if you do not explicitly forbid markdown, some models will return backticks and break your parser.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment analysis engine. Analyze the user-provided text and respond ONLY with a JSON object containing exactly these keys:
- "sentiment": one of "Positive", "Negative", or "Neutral"
- "confidence": a float between 0.0 and 1.0
- "topic": a string of five words or fewer describing the main subject
- "reasoning": one sentence explaining why the sentiment was chosen

Do not include markdown formatting, explanations outside the JSON, or any other text."""

Step 3: Build the analyzer function

This helper wraps the API call. I set response_format to JSON mode so the model is constrained to valid JSON, and I keep temperature at 0.1 to reduce variance between identical reviews. After the call, I parse the content with Python's built-in json module. If you prefer stronger type safety, you could validate the dict against a Pydantic model here, but for a quick script the direct parse is enough. I also add a short prefix to the user message, Review:, so the model knows the boundary between my instructions and the external text. Without that prefix, a clever user could theoretically prompt-inject by submitting text that looks like a system command, though the system prompt role usually mitigates that risk.

import json

def analyze_review(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Review:\n{text}"}
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process a batch of reviews

Real pipelines process lists, not single strings. I define a small list of sample customer feedback covering praise, frustration, and indifference. I loop through them, call the analyzer for each, and collect the parsed results. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, feeding longer reviews into this loop does not increase the cost per classification the way token-based pricing would. That means I can send full support transcripts instead of truncating them to save money, which usually improves accuracy because the model sees the complete context. For a hundred reviews, this script makes a hundred requests. If you need to scale past that, you can add a ThreadPoolExecutor or asyncio.gather, but for a prototype the sequential loop keeps the code obvious and the rate limits happy.

reviews = [
    "The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked all day without plugging in.",
    "Shipping took two weeks and the box was dented. Not acceptable for the price.",
    "It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special either way.",
    "Customer support refused to honor the warranty. I am extremely frustrated and will not buy again.",
    "Best purchase I made this year. The screen is gorgeous and the keyboard feels perfect."
]

results = []
for review in reviews:
    result = analyze_review(review)
    result["source"] = review[:60] + "..."
    results.append(result)
    print(result)

Step 5: Aggregate and report

Raw JSON is useful, but I want a summary I can paste into a Slack channel. I tally sentiment counts and surface the most frequent topics with Python's standard library Counter. This gives a stakeholder-friendly snapshot without spinning up a BI tool or exporting to a spreadsheet. You could easily extend this to compute an average confidence score and flag any result below 0.5 for human review. Another useful filter is to surface only Negative reviews with high confidence, because those are the tickets that need a response first. The topic strings act as lightweight tags, so you can route warranty complaints to the legal team and shipping complaints to logistics without maintaining a separate classifier for each category.

from collections import Counter

sentiment_counts = Counter(r["sentiment"] for r in results)
topic_counts = Counter(r["topic"] for r in results)

print("\n--- Batch Summary ---")
print(f"Total reviews: {len(results)}")
for sentiment, count in sentiment_counts.most_common():
    print(f"  {sentiment}: {count}")

print("\nTop topics:")
for topic, count in topic_counts.most_common(3):
    print(f"  {topic} ({count})")

Run it

Save the complete script as sentiment_analyzer.py, export your key, and run it. The script has no external dependencies beyond the OpenAI SDK and Python's standard library, so it should run anywhere. Here is the full file followed by the output I see on my machine. Your exact JSON values may shift slightly depending on the model temperature, but the structure and labels should remain consistent.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import json
from collections import Counter
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment analysis engine. Analyze the user-provided text and respond ONLY with a JSON object containing exactly these keys:
- "sentiment": one of "Positive", "Negative", or "Neutral"
- "confidence": a float between 0.0 and 1.0
- "topic": a string of five words or fewer describing the main subject
- "reasoning": one sentence explaining why the sentiment was chosen

Do not include markdown formatting, explanations outside the JSON, or any other text."""

def analyze_review(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Review:\n{text}"}
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    reviews = [
        "The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked all day without plugging in.",
        "Shipping took two weeks and the box was dented. Not acceptable for the price.",
        "It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special either way.",
        "Customer support refused to honor the warranty. I am extremely frustrated and will not buy again.",
        "Best purchase I made this year. The screen is gorgeous and the keyboard feels perfect."
    ]

    results = []
    for review in reviews:
        result = analyze_review(review)
        result["source"] = review[:60] + "..."
        results.append(result)
        print(result)

    sentiment_counts = Counter(r["sentiment"] for r in results)
    topic_counts = Counter(r["topic"] for r in results)

    print("\n--- Batch Summary ---")
    print(f"Total reviews: {len(results)}")
    for sentiment, count in sentiment_counts.most_common():
        print(f"  {sentiment}: {count}")

    print("\nTop topics:")
    for topic, count in topic_counts.most_common(3):
        print(f"  {topic} ({count})")

Run the script from your terminal:

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="your-key-here"
$ python sentiment_analyzer.py

Expected output:

{'sentiment': 'Positive', 'confidence': 0.95, 'topic': 'laptop battery life', 'reasoning': 'The user praises the battery life and all-day usage.', 'source': 'The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked a...'}
{'sentiment': 'Negative', 'confidence': 0.92, 'topic': 'shipping and packaging', 'reasoning': 'The user complains about delayed shipping and damaged packaging.', 'source': 'Shipping took two weeks and the box was dented. Not accept...'}
{'sentiment': 'Neutral', 'confidence': 0.78, 'topic': 'generic laptop function', 'reasoning': 'The user states the laptop works but expresses no strong feelings.', 'source': 'It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special either way.'}
{'sentiment': 'Negative', 'confidence': 0.97, 'topic': 'warranty support refusal', 'reasoning': 'The user is frustrated by the refusal to honor the warranty.', 'source': 'Customer support refused to honor the warranty. I am extrem...'}
{'sentiment': 'Positive', 'confidence': 0.96, 'topic': 'screen and keyboard', 'reasoning': 'The user calls it the best purchase and praises screen and keyboard.', 'source': 'Best purchase I made this year. The screen is gorgeous and ...'}

--- Batch Summary ---
Total reviews: 5
  Positive: 2
  Negative: 2
  Neutral: 1

Top topics:
  laptop battery life (1)
  shipping and packaging (1)
  generic laptop function (1)

Wrap up and next steps

From here, the obvious next step is to replace the inline list with a CSV reader so you can process an export from your support desk or app store reviews. If you start hitting rate limits, switch to Oxlo.ai's kimi-k2.6 model for advanced reasoning on ambiguous reviews, or run requests concurrently with asyncio to saturate your local bandwidth. Another useful upgrade is to add a Pydantic validator that rejects malformed responses and retries them. You can view current request allowances and model availability at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: LLM for Conversational AI
content:
We are building a conversational support agent for an electronics store that handles returns, order status questions, and basic troubleshooting. It maintains context across multi-turn dialogues and escalates to a human when it encounters issues outside its scope. If you are an engineer automating tier-1 support, this tutorial gives you a working agent you can adapt to your own product in under an hour.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which you can install with pip install openai. Finally, grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal at https://portal.oxlo.ai. I am using Oxlo.ai here because its request-based pricing means long system prompts and extended chat histories do not inflate costs the way token-based meters do. That makes a real difference when your production threads run twenty or thirty turns deep.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

First, we point the OpenAI SDK at Oxlo.ai. I am using Llama 3.3 70B as the backbone because it follows system instructions tightly and handles back-and-forth dialogue without drifting. This model is fully OpenAI API compatible, so the only change from a standard setup is the base URL and the key.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the most important part of a conversational agent. It acts as the agent's script, defining personality, available actions, and guardrails. I keep it concrete: the bot knows exactly three troubleshooting topics, it knows it cannot invent orders, and it has a clear escalation tag for anything risky. Vague prompts produce vague agents, so be specific.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are SupportBot for ElectroShop, an electronics retailer.
You can help with:
- Order status lookups (the user must provide an order ID like ORD-1234)
- Return initiations for items bought within 30 days
- Troubleshooting: TV not powering on, router blinking red, or headphones with no audio

Rules:
- Be concise, friendly, and professional.
- If the user asks about an order but gives no ID, ask for it.
- If the user is angry, remain calm.
- If the issue requires legal action, physical repair, or you cannot help, include the tag [ESCALATE] in your response and stop.
- Do not invent order details. If you do not have an order ID, you do not have data.
- Today's date is 2024-05-20."""

Step 3: Build the conversation loop

Conversation is stateful. If you send each message in isolation, the agent will forget the user's name, their order ID, and the problem they described two turns ago. We solve that by maintaining a messages list in memory. On every loop, we append the latest user message, call Oxlo.ai, and append the assistant reply back to the list. The model receives the full thread each time, so context persists naturally.

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("SupportBot ready. Type 'exit' to quit.")
while True:
    user_message = input("Customer: ")
    if user_message.strip().lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
        break

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
    )

    reply = response.choices[0].message.content
    print(f"Agent: {reply}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

Step 4: Add guardrails and escalation

Production agents need an off-ramp. If a user mentions legal action or demands a repair we cannot authorize, the bot must stop and hand over to a human. I encode this in the system prompt with the [ESCALATE] tag, then scan the model output for that string in Python. If it appears, we print a handoff message and break the loop. This keeps the automation from overstepping.

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("SupportBot ready. Type 'exit' to quit.")
while True:
    user_message = input("Customer: ")
    if user_message.strip().lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
        break

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
    )

    reply = response.choices[0].message.content

    if "[ESCALATE]" in reply:
        print("Agent: I'm connecting you with a human specialist now. Please hold.")
        break

    print(f"Agent: {reply}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

Step 5: Simulate a tool lookup

A support bot that cannot look up data is just a chatbot. We will simulate a backend order database with a plain Python function. If the user's message contains something that looks like an order ID, we call the function and inject the result into the messages list as a system message. This gives the model real facts to reference, which sharply reduces hallucination.

import re

def lookup_order(order_id):
    # Simulated backend
    return f"Order {order_id}: Shipped on 2024-05-18, ETA 2024-05-22 via FastPost."

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("SupportBot ready. Type 'exit' to quit.")
while True:
    user_message = input("Customer: ")
    if user_message.strip().lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
        break

    order_match = re.search(r"ORD-\d{4,}", user_message)
    if order_match:
        order_data = lookup_order(order_match.group(0))
        messages.append({"role": "system", "content": order_data})

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
    )

    reply = response.choices[0].message.content

    if "[ESCALATE]" in reply:
        print("Agent: I'm connecting you with a human specialist now. Please hold.")
        break

    print(f"Agent: {reply}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

Run it

Save the final script as support_bot.py, set your environment variable, and run it from your terminal. Below is a sample session I ran while testing the agent. Notice how it reads the injected order data, stays polite, and triggers escalation when the user threatens legal action.

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
$ python support_bot.py

SupportBot ready. Type 'exit' to quit.
Customer: hi, where is my order ORD-8842?
Agent: Your order ORD-8842 was shipped on May 18 and is expected to arrive on May 22 via FastPost. Let me know if you need anything else.
Customer: the tv arrived cracked
Agent: I'm sorry to hear that. Since the TV arrived damaged, I can initiate a return for you if it was purchased within the last 30 days. Can you confirm the purchase date?
Customer: I want to sue you
Agent: I'm connecting you with a human specialist now. Please hold.

Wrap-up

Oxlo.ai supports tool use, so you can register JSON schemas and let the model decide when to fetch real records. title: Optimizing LLM Model Performance
content:
Large language model performance optimization sits at the intersection of systems engineering and statistical efficiency. Every millisecond of latency and every gigabyte of GPU memory directly translates into user experience and operational cost. For teams shipping production workloads, the optimization problem is not simply about selecting the biggest model. It requires a stack-level approach: compressing weights, maximizing batch throughput, managing memory hierarchies, and aligning pricing models with actual usage patterns.

Quantization and Model Compression

Quantization reduces the numerical precision of model weights and activations, shrinking memory footprints and increasing inference throughput. Techniques like INT8 quantization, AWQ, and GPTQ allow a 70 billion parameter model to run on a single GPU without proportional accuracy loss. The trade-off is subtle: aggressive INT4 compression can degrade reasoning on math-heavy tasks, while INT8 often preserves performance for general chat and retrieval workloads.

On Oxlo.ai, model compression and quantization are handled at the infrastructure layer. Developers do not need to manually calibrate quantization schemes or maintain separate weight files. The platform serves models such as Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 3 32B in optimized formats, so you get the latency benefits of compressed inference without the devops overhead.

Batching and Continuous Batching

Throughput is often the bottleneck in high-volume services. Static batching, where requests wait until a fixed batch size is reached, introduces unacceptable tail latency for real-time applications. Continuous batching, popularized by systems like vLLM and ORCA, allows new requests to enter the processing queue as soon as others finish their generation phase. This interleaving of prefill and decode phases keeps GPU tensor cores saturated.

The challenge with continuous batching is memory management. Each request in flight requires its own key-value cache, and without careful paging, fragmentation wastes VRAM. Oxlo.ai eliminates this operational burden. The platform serves popular models with no cold starts, meaning the scheduling and paging logic is already warm and optimized. You send requests, and the infrastructure handles the batching dynamics.

KV Cache Management and Memory Optimization

The key-value cache is the dominant memory consumer during autoregressive decoding. For long-context models, it can dwarf the parameter memory itself. PagedAttention partitions the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, similar to an operating system’s virtual memory, which nearly eliminates fragmentation and enables efficient memory sharing. Prefix caching further accelerates multi-turn conversations and agentic workflows by reusing computed attention states across turns.

Long-context optimization is not merely a software trick; it is a product-level capability. Ox

title: Building a Voice Assistant with LLM
content:
Developers are replacing rigid intent-slot voice pipelines with large language models that handle ambiguity, context, and multi-turn dialogue in a single inference pass. A modern voice assistant is now a tri-modal loop: audio in, reasoning in the middle, and audio out. The challenge is not architecture theory. It is stitching together automatic speech recognition, low-latency LLM inference, and text-to-speech without ballooning costs or cold-start latency that kills conversational flow.

This guide walks through a production-viable stack using OpenAI SDK patterns, and shows where Oxlo.ai fits as the inference backend for both audio and language processing.

Architecture of a Modern LLM Voice Assistant

Most successful voice assistants today use a pipeline of three services plus lightweight orchestration.

  1. Voice Activity Detection and Audio Streaming: The client captures microphone input, often using a local VAD such as Silero, and streams audio chunks to the server only when the user is speaking. This reduces bandwidth and cost.
  2. Speech-to-Text: The server runs automatic speech recognition to produce a text transcript. For real-time assistants, you want partial results or fast full-file transcription under a few hundred milliseconds.
  3. LLM Reasoning and Tool Use: The transcript is injected into a chat completion call. The model may stream reasoning tokens, call external APIs via function calling, and format a natural-language response. JSON mode is useful if you need structured output for client-side rendering.
  4. Text-to-Speech: The response text is pushed to a TTS service, and audio chunks are streamed back to the client for playback.

Oxlo.ai covers the middle two stages natively, offering both audio transcription and speech generation alongside its LLM catalog through the same API key and base URL.

Handling Audio Input and Output on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai provides fully OpenAI-compatible endpoints for audio. For transcription, you can use Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, or Whisper Medium through the audio/transcriptions endpoint. These models accept standard audio formats and return text with optional timestamp granularity. For speech synthesis, Kokoro 82M is available on the audio/speech endpoint and generates natural-sounding speech suitable for conversational interfaces. Both endpoints use the same request shapes you would send to OpenAI, so existing client code needs only a base URL change.

Because Oxlo.ai does not impose cold starts on popular models, your voice assistant avoids the first-turn penalty that can add seconds to transcription or chat initialization. That consistency is critical when users expect immediate responses after speaking.

Selecting the LLM Brain

A voice assistant does not always need the largest model. It needs low time-to-first-token, reliable function calling, and tolerance for multi-turn context. Oxlo.ai offers several strong candidates across its 45-plus model catalog:

  • Llama 3.3 70B: A general-purpose flagship with solid tool-use support and broad knowledge. Good for open-domain assistants that answer general questions and execute commands.
  • Qwen 3 32B: Strong multilingual reasoning and agent workflow support. Use this if your assistant must switch languages or handle complex conditional tool chains.
  • Minimax M2.5: Optimized for coding and agentic tool use. Ideal for developer-oriented voice interfaces that generate or review code.
  • DeepSeek V3.2: A capable coding and reasoning model that sits on the Oxlo.ai free tier, making it a practical starting point for prototypes.

All of these models expose streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversation state through the standard chat/completions endpoint. You can swap models by changing a single parameter without rewriting client logic. If your assistant performs vision tasks, you can also route image inputs through models such as Kimi VL A3B or Gemma 3 27B using the same chat completion schema.

Wiring the Pipeline in Python

The following example uses the OpenAI Python SDK against Oxlo.ai. It transcribes user audio, streams an LLM response with a weather tool, and synthesizes reply audio. The pattern works identically in Node.js or cURL.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

# 1. Transcribe incoming audio
with open("user_audio.wav", "rb") as f:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-large-v3",
        file=f
    )

# 2. Stream chat completion with tool use
tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Get current weather",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful voice assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": transcript.text}
    ],
    tools=tools,
    stream=True
)

# Collect text chunks for TTS
reply_text = ""
for chunk in response:
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
    if delta.content:
        reply_text += delta.content
        # In production, stream chunks directly to TTS
        # to minimize latency instead of buffering fully.

# 3. Synthesize speech
speech = client.audio.speech.create(
    model="kokoro-82m",
    voice="default",
    input=reply_text
)

speech.stream_to_file("assistant_reply.wav")

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can adopt frameworks such as OpenAI Agents, LangChain, or raw SSE consumers without adapter layers. The stream=True flag returns tokens as they are generated, which lets you pipeline text chunks into Kokoro before the full response is complete. If the model emits a tool call instead of text, you can intercept the tool_calls delta, execute the function locally, and append the result to the message history for the next LLM turn.

Why Latency and Streaming Matter

Conversational AI has a strict latency budget. Research on turn-taking suggests that pauses longer than roughly 800 milliseconds feel unnatural. Every layer of the stack must contribute to hitting that target.

Token-based providers can suffer from variable queue times and cold starts, especially under load. Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, so the first request of a session warms up as quickly as the hundredth. Streaming further compresses perceived latency: the TTS engine can begin speaking the first sentence while the LLM is still generating the second. For best results, use the SSE stream from chat/completions and flush audio chunks to the client as soon as Kokoro returns them.

Cost Predictability with Per-Request Pricing

Voice assistants are inherently multi-turn. A single session can involve a verbose system prompt, a growing chat history, tool results, and intermediate reasoning tokens. On token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale, cost scales with total input and output length. As the conversation deepens, every new turn becomes more expensive because the accumulated context is re-fed into the model. If you add retrieval-augmented generation or agentic planning, input token counts grow even faster.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For voice and agentic workloads where context windows expand across turns, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based billing. You do not need to truncate history aggressively to save money, and you can forecast monthly spend from request volume alone rather than estimating token multipliers.

Exact rates depend on your plan, so review the Oxlo.ai pricing page to compare against your current token-based bill.

Prototyping on the Free Tier

Oxlo.ai offers a free tier at $0 per month with 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, including DeepSeek V3.2. New accounts also receive a 7-day full-access trial. That volume is sufficient to build a voice prototype, test multi-turn sessions, and validate latency before committing to a paid plan. When you scale, the Pro and Premium plans offer 1,000 and 5,000 requests per day respectively, with priority queue access at the Premium level. Enterprise plans add dedicated GPUs and unlimited volume for production assistants with strict SLAs.

Conclusion

Building a voice assistant today is mostly an integration exercise: connect a microphone to a fast transcription service, route text through an LLM with tool access, and stream the result to a speech synthesizer. The hard part is keeping latency low and costs predictable as sessions grow.

Oxlo.ai provides the core inference layer for this stack. With Whisper and Kokoro for audio, a broad catalog of chat models with function calling, streaming responses, no cold starts, and flat per-request pricing, it is a natural backend for voice agents. If you are currently on a token-based provider, the cost advantage on long-context conversations can be substantial, and the OpenAI SDK compatibility means migration is a one-line base URL change.

Start with the free tier, measure your request volume, and scale when you are ready. The infrastructure for your voice assistant is already there.
