title: Using LLM for Text Generation
content:
Today we are building a multi-tone content generator that turns a single topic into three distinct drafts: a technical explanation, marketing copy, and a casual blog summary. This is useful for developer relations teams and product engineers who need to communicate the same feature to different audiences without rewriting the prompt from scratch every time. Instead of managing three separate templates, we will let the model handle the tone shift through a strict system prompt and JSON mode. The result is a small Python utility you can drop into a documentation pipeline or a content calendar workflow.

What you'll need

You need a working Python environment, the OpenAI SDK, and an Oxlo.ai API key. Oxlo.ai is a developer-first inference platform that exposes over 45 models through a fully OpenAI-compatible API. Because it charges a flat rate per request rather than per token, you can stuff long system prompts and detailed examples into every call without watching the meter spin on input length. That makes it a strong fit for structured generation workflows like this one, where consistency matters more than squeezing every token. You will need Python 3.10 or newer, the openai package installed via pip, and a key from the Oxlo.ai portal at https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai also has no cold starts on popular models, so the loop we will write executes without the latency spikes that break interactive scripts.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

The OpenAI SDK was designed to be vendor agnostic. Changing two arguments is all it takes to point your client at Oxlo.ai. I keep the API key in an environment variable in production, but for this tutorial you can paste it directly. We will use llama-3.3-70b as the default workhorse because it follows complex formatting instructions reliably and responds quickly for text generation tasks. Oxlo.ai hosts 45-plus models across seven categories, but this flagship is a safe default when you need predictable JSON output. Create a new file called generate.py and add the following setup block.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

Step 2: Lock down the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between your code and the model. If it drifts, your parser breaks. I treat it as a config file and version it alongside the script. The prompt below forces the model to return a flat JSON object with three specific keys. I also cap each section at 150 words to keep the output predictable and easy to review. Notice that I explicitly forbid markdown code fences. Without that rule, some models wrap JSON in triple backticks, which forces you to strip them before parsing. Add this constant directly below the client setup.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a multi-tone content generation engine.
The user will provide a short topic or feature description.
Respond with a single JSON object containing exactly these keys and no additional text:
- "technical": a precise, detailed explanation suitable for engineers. Use exact terminology.
- "marketing": punchy, benefit-driven copy suitable for a landing page headline and two sentences.
- "casual": a friendly two-paragraph blog summary that a non-technical reader would enjoy.

Keep each string value under 150 words.
Do not wrap the JSON in markdown code fences."""

Step 3: Write the generation function

This function is the only place where we touch the network. I pass the system prompt and the user topic to the chat completions endpoint, then parse the returned string with the standard library json module. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode on compatible models, so setting response_format reduces the chance of stray prose breaking the parser. Streaming is available if you need it, but for a batch generator we want the full object in one shot. Place this function under the system prompt.

def generate_content(topic):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Topic: {topic}"},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Batch process a sprint's worth of topics

In practice, you rarely generate copy for just one item. This loop iterates over a list of feature topics, calls the generator for each, and persists the results to a JSONL file. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, the cost per topic stays constant even when your system prompt grows or your topic descriptions get lengthy. For teams running long-context or agentic workloads, that pricing model removes the guesswork from budgeting. You can review the exact tiers at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. If you need multilingual output, you can swap the model string to qwen-3-32b without changing any other logic. Append this block to the bottom of the file.

topics = [
    "Serverless GPU inference with request-based pricing",
    "Deploying vision models for real-time object detection",
    "Long-context agents for automated code review",
    "Embedding pipelines with BGE-Large for semantic search",
]

results = []
for t in topics:
    try:
        draft = generate_content(t)
        results.append({"topic": t, "drafts": draft})
        print(f"Generated for: {t}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Failed for {t}: {e}")

with open("content_drafts.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for r in results:
        f.write(json.dumps(r) + "\n")

Step 5: Add retry logic for missing keys

LLMs can occasionally hallucinate extra keys or omit one entirely. A thin validation layer keeps the pipeline from writing garbage to disk. If the expected keys are missing, we retry once before giving up. This is cheaper on Oxlo.ai than on token-based providers because the retry is just another flat request, not a billable stream of additional tokens. Once this wrapper is defined, replace the generate_content call inside the loop with generate_safe. The script now tolerates the occasional formatting miss without manual intervention.

def generate_safe(topic, max_retries=1):
    required = {"technical", "marketing", "casual"}
    for attempt in range(max_retries + 1):
        draft = generate_content(topic)
        if required.issubset(draft.keys()):
            return draft
        if attempt == max_retries:
            missing = required - set(draft.keys())
            raise ValueError(f"Missing keys after retry: {missing}")
    return draft

# In the batch loop above, change:
# draft = generate_safe(t)

Run it

Save the file, export your OXLO_API_KEY, and run python generate.py from your terminal. The first time you execute the loop you should see four success lines printed to stdout. Open content_drafts.jsonl and inspect the records. Each line is a valid JSON object containing the original topic and the three generated tones. Here is what the output looks like for the first topic when I ran it earlier. Your wording will vary, but the structure should match exactly.

Generated for: Serverless GPU inference with request-based pricing
Generated for: Deploying vision models for real-time object detection
Generated for: Long-context agents for automated code review
Generated for: Embedding pipelines with BGE-Large for semantic search
{
  "topic": "Serverless GPU inference with request-based pricing",
  "drafts": {
    "technical": "Oxlo.ai exposes open-source LLMs through a serverless API where each call incurs a fixed cost regardless of input token count. This architecture abstracts away GPU provisioning and scales to zero, letting engineering teams run inference without managing Kubernetes clusters or predicting token budgets.",
    "marketing": "Stop counting tokens. Start shipping features. Oxlo.ai delivers flat-rate inference on 45-plus open-source models so your costs stay predictable even when your prompts grow.",
    "casual": "If you have ever watched an API bill balloon because someone pasted a huge log file into the prompt, you will appreciate this. Oxlo.ai charges per request, not per word, which makes it a natural fit for long-context tools and agent workflows."
  }
}

Next steps

This generator is already useful as a local script, but it shines when you integrate it into a larger workflow. First, wire it into a CI pipeline that reads a features.md file from your repo on every release, generates the three tones automatically, and opens a pull request with the updated docs. Second, experiment with larger reasoning models on Oxlo.ai. Swapping llama-3.3-70b for kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 can improve nuance on highly technical topics, and because the API is fully OpenAI-compatible, the only line that changes is the model string. The flat per-request pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing means you can test across the catalog without rewriting your budget logic. For production deployments, the Enterprise tier offers dedicated GPUs and guaranteed savings over your current provider.

title: Building Language Models from Scratch
content:
We are going to build an agentic coding partner that generates a working transformer language model from scratch. It runs against Oxlo.ai, so you can feed entire tracebacks and previous file contents into the context without watching a token meter tick. If you want to understand how self-attention and training loops actually work under the hood, this gives you readable, runnable PyTorch code you can step through in a debugger.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai

Step 1: Design the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training signal we provide. I keep it strict because frontier models otherwise drift into high-level theory or recommend external libraries that hide the mechanics. We want a terse implementation partner that returns complete files inside markdown fences and explains tensor shapes only when asked.

I explicitly forbid Hugging Face, transformers, or datasets. The goal is pedagogical: we want to see nn.Linear, torch.softmax, and the indexing operations directly. I also ask for a tiny usage example after each component so we can sanity check dimensions before we wire everything together.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a hands-on ML engineer helping a developer build a transformer language model from scratch in PyTorch.

Rules:
- Output complete, runnable Python scripts inside markdown code fences.
- Use only PyTorch and the Python standard library.
- Keep explanations short. Prioritize code over prose.
- When asked for a component, provide the minimal correct implementation plus a tiny usage example.
- Do not use Hugging Face, transformers, or datasets libraries."""

Step 2: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I use Llama 3.3 70B as the default worker. It is the general-purpose flagship on Oxlo.ai and stays on track through long, multi-turn coding sessions. Oxlo.ai serves it with no cold starts, so the first token appears immediately after you hit enter. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, the only change is the base_url and your API key.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def ask(user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        stream=True,
    )
    return response

Step 3: Build the conversation loop

Next we add streaming and bounded conversation memory. I stream chunks to stdout so I can watch the model generate 300 lines of PyTorch in real time. I also accumulate the full string so we can parse code blocks later.

I cap the rolling history at the last eight turns. This is not a cost decision, because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request regardless of prompt length. It is an accuracy decision: too much clutter causes the model to lose track of the current task. The flat pricing is still useful here, because when we do append a full file or a long traceback to one of those turns, the price does not spike.

import re

history = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
]

def chat(user_input):
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    # Retain system prompt plus last 8 turns to keep context tight
    context = [history[0]] + history[-8:]

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=context,
        stream=True,
    )

    full_text = ""
    for chunk in response:
        delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content or ""
        full_text += delta
        print(delta, end="", flush=True)
    print()

    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": full_text})
    return full_text

Step 4: Extract and save code blocks

The assistant returns markdown. We parse out Python fences and write them to disk automatically. I open the file in append mode so multi-turn sessions accumulate. In practice, you might ask for the attention module in turn one, the MLP and transformer block in turn two, and the training loop in turn three. Each block appends to tiny_gpt.py until you have a complete project.

The re.DOTALL flag matters because code blocks contain newlines. In a production tool you might use a proper markdown parser, but a regex is fine for a personal build script.

def save_code_blocks(text, path="tiny_gpt.py"):
    pattern = re.compile(r"```python\n(.*?)```", re.DOTALL)
    matches = pattern.findall(text)
    if not matches:
        print("No code blocks found.")
        return
    with open(path, "a") as f:
        for block in matches:
            f.write(block.strip() + "\n\n")
    print(f"Saved {len(matches)} block(s) to {path}")

Run it

I start the session with an explicit specification. Concrete hyperparameters prevent the model from hallucinating a distributed training cluster. A 1K-character Shakespeare snippet, 65-character vocabulary, and 100 training steps fit in CPU memory and finish in under a minute. After the call, tiny_gpt.py contains a self-contained script you can run locally.

I then send a follow-up turn asking for a learning rate scheduler. This shows how the agent refines existing code rather than generating monolithic dumps.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    prompt = (
        "Write a minimal GPT language model in PyTorch. "
        "Include: (1) causal self-attention, (2) a 4-layer transformer block, "
        "(3) a training loop on a tiny 1K-character Shakespeare snippet, "
        "(4) inference code that generates 100 tokens. "
        "Use vocab size 65, embedding dim 64, context length 32, batch size 4, 100 training steps."
    )

    reply = chat(prompt)
    save_code_blocks(reply)

    # Follow-up refinement
    follow_up = "Add a cosine learning rate scheduler and print loss every 10 steps."
    reply2 = chat(follow_up)
    save_code_blocks(reply2)

    # Example terminal output:
    # import torch
    # import torch.nn as nn
    # ...
    # Saved 1 block(s) to tiny_gpt.py
    # ...
    # Saved 1 block(s) to tiny_gpt.py

Next steps

Two directions are obvious from here. First, rerun the same prompt against other models on Oxlo.ai, such as qwen-3-32b or deepseek-v3.2, and diff the outputs. Each model has a different bias toward verbosity, math notation, or loop structure, so you can pick the generated style that matches your own codebase.

Second, add tool use. Give the agent a run_python function that executes the generated script, captures tracebacks, and feeds them back into the chat for automatic repair. This turns the script into a true coding agent. Long error traces are painless on Oxlo.ai because the platform uses flat per-request pricing, so stuffing a full stack trace into context does not inflate your bill. For plan details, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Deploying LLM on Cloud Infrastructure
content:
Deploying large language models in production cloud environments introduces a unique set of infrastructure challenges. Unlike traditional microservices, LLMs require specialized GPU hardware, substantial memory bandwidth, and careful orchestration to maintain low latency under unpredictable traffic patterns. Whether you are serving a 7B parameter model for internal tooling or a 70B+ parameter model for customer-facing applications, the gap between a working prototype and a reliable production system is defined by decisions around compute provisioning, scaling strategy, and cost architecture.

Deployment Architectures

Most production LLM deployments fall into one of three patterns: self-hosted inference on dedicated GPU instances, containerized inference orchestrated through Kubernetes, or fully managed API inference. Each pattern carries distinct trade-offs in control, operational overhead, and cost predictability.

Self-hosted deployment on cloud VMs gives you full control over model weights, quantization strategy, and batching configuration. Teams often choose this path when they need custom CUDA kernels, specialized fine-tunes, or strict data residency requirements. However, this approach requires managing NVIDIA drivers, CUDA versions, and inference servers such as vLLM, TGI, or TensorRT-LLM. You also assume responsibility for autoscaling logic, which is nontrivial when GPU nodes take minutes to provision.

Kubernetes-based deployment adds orchestration benefits but introduces complexity. You must configure GPU node pools, manage pod affinity to keep caches warm, and implement custom metrics-based scaling. While tools like KServe and Seldon Core abstract some of this away, the operational burden remains significant for teams without dedicated ML infrastructure engineers.

Managed API inference removes infrastructure ownership entirely. Providers host the model and expose a standard HTTP endpoint. For teams optimizing for speed to market and operational simplicity, this is often the pragmatic choice. The key differentiator among providers is not just model availability but pricing mechanics and latency guarantees.

Compute Planning and Cost Engineering

GPU memory is the primary bottleneck in LLM serving. A 70B parameter model in FP16 requires approximately 140 GB of VRAM just for weights, excluding KV cache and activation overhead. In practice, this means multi-GPU nodes or high-memory accelerators such as NVIDIA A100 or H100 instances. Cloud providers offer these at premium on-demand rates, and reserved capacity often requires long-term contracts.

Beyond hardware, the economic model of inference matters. Token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale scale costs directly with prompt and completion length. For long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or agentic workflows that pass extensive tool schemas and conversation history back and forth, expenses grow linearly with context window utilization. This creates an unpredictable cost curve that complicates budgeting and product pricing.

An alternative is request-based pricing, where each API call incurs a flat fee regardless of input size. For workloads with large prompts, this model decouples cost from token count and can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context workloads. Oxlo.ai operates on this principle, offering a flat per-request rate across its catalog of 45+ open-source and proprietary models. For teams building agents or processing long documents, this shifts cost from a variable scaling tax into a predictable operational line item. You can compare plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Operational Realities

Production inference is not only about throughput. Cold starts, the latency penalty incurred when spinning up an idle model instance, can destroy user experience in interactive applications. Many serverless GPU platforms advertise scale-to-zero economics but impose multi-second initialization delays that render them unsuitable for real-time chat or coding assistants. Oxlo.ai eliminates this variable by keeping popular models warm, ensuring there are no cold starts on its core catalog.

Load balancing across model replicas also requires careful handling. LLM requests are not uniformly sized. A single long-context request can saturate a GPU's memory and compute for seconds, while short queries clear quickly. naive round-robin load balancing can lead to hot spotting and tail latency spikes. Advanced deployments use request routing based on queue depth, estimated token count, or cache affinity. When you self-host, building this router is your responsibility. Managed platforms abstract it, but quality varies based on their underlying scheduling logic.

Memory management is equally critical. The KV cache for long conversations can grow to rival the model weights themselves. Efficient serving requires attention to cache eviction, paging strategies such as vLLM's PagedAttention, or chunked prefill to keep latency bounded. Without these optimizations, throughput collapses as context length increases.

Build Versus Buy

The decision to self-host or use a managed provider should be driven by workload characteristics and team expertise. Self-hosting is defensible when you have steady, predictable traffic that keeps GPU utilization high, or when regulatory constraints require on-premises or VPC-isolated inference. It also makes sense if you are running heavily customized model architectures that managed APIs do not support.

For the majority of product teams, however, managed inference is the faster path to production. Variable traffic patterns make GPU reservation economically inefficient. Maintaining an inference stack diverts engineering hours from core product features. And as model release cycles accelerate, the burden of benchmarking, quantizing, and rolling out new weights every quarter becomes unsustainable.

This is where Oxlo.ai provides a strong middle ground. It is not merely an API wrapper but a developer-first inference platform designed for production workloads. With no cold starts on popular models, fully OpenAI SDK-compatible endpoints, and a catalog spanning general reasoning, code, vision, and embeddings, it eliminates the infrastructure tax without sacrificing model choice.

Integrating Managed Inference

Switching from self-hosted infrastructure to a managed provider should require minimal code changes. Oxlo.ai exposes a standard OpenAI-compatible API at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, which means existing Python, Node.js, or cURL integrations typically only need a base URL and key update.

The following example demonstrates a chat completion request using the OpenAI SDK pointed at Oxlo.ai:

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your-oxlo.ai-api-key"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a systems architecture assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Design a cloud deployment pattern for a long-context RAG pipeline."}
    ],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, and vision inputs, you can migrate complex agentic workflows without architectural rewrites. The platform offers 45+ models across seven categories, including Llama 3.3 70B for general tasks, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for reasoning, Qwen 3 32B for multilingual agents, and Kimi K2.6 for advanced coding and vision workloads.

Pricing is structured around request volume rather than token consumption. The Free plan includes 60 requests per day across 16+ models, with a 7-day full-access trial. For production workloads, the Pro and Premium tiers offer 1,000 and 5,000 requests per day respectively, with priority queue access at the Premium level. Enterprise plans provide dedicated GPUs and custom pricing. Details are available at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Security and Compliance

Moving inference to a third-party provider requires evaluating data handling policies. If you are processing sensitive payloads, verify whether the provider retains logs for model improvement, supports zero-data-retention agreements, and offers private connectivity options. Encryption in transit and at rest is table stakes, but the finer points of data residency and auditability often determine whether a managed service is viable for regulated industries.

For organizations with strict compliance requirements, Oxlo.ai offers Enterprise deployments with dedicated GPU infrastructure. This isolates workloads from multi-tenant environments, provides guaranteed capacity, and supports custom contractual terms. Dedicated hardware removes the noisy-neighbor risk and gives security teams the isolation boundaries they require without forcing the engineering team to build and maintain a full inference stack internally.

Conclusion

Deploying LLMs on cloud infrastructure involves a series of high-stakes decisions around hardware, scaling, and cost mechanics. Self-hosted solutions offer maximum control but demand significant operational investment. Managed APIs reduce that burden, though not all pricing models align with long-context or agentic use cases.

Oxlo.ai addresses this with a request-based pricing structure that flattens costs for large prompts, an OpenAI-compatible API that requires no client-side rewrites, and a broad model catalog that covers reasoning, code, vision, and embeddings. For teams looking to move from infrastructure management to product development, it is a relevant, production-ready option worth evaluating.

title: Introduction to LLM for Beginners
content:
We are going to build a customer support triage agent that reads an incoming ticket, classifies the customer sentiment, and drafts a first-pass reply. This is a solid first project for anyone new to LLMs because it demonstrates the core pattern that powers most AI apps: a system prompt sets the rules, a user message provides the task, and the model returns structured text you can act on. I am using Oxlo.ai as the inference backend because its OpenAI-compatible API lets me keep the standard Python SDK and my existing habits, while its flat per-request pricing means I can paste in long email threads without watching token meters spin.

What you'll need

Before we start, gather the following:

  • Python 3.10 or newer. I developed this on 3.11, but anything from 3.10 upward works.
  • The OpenAI Python SDK. Install it with pip install openai. Because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, every class and method you already know works exactly the same.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai is an inference platform that hosts open-source models like Llama 3.3 70B and DeepSeek V3.2 with request-based pricing. That means one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length, which keeps this agent economical even when users paste lengthy conversation histories. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

Step 1: Set up the client

First, import the SDK and point the base URL at Oxlo.ai. I read the key from an environment variable so I do not hardcode secrets.

# We use the standard OpenAI SDK, but point it at Oxlo.ai's endpoint.
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt defines the agent's role and the exact output schema. I ask for JSON so I can parse the result reliably in the next step.

# The system prompt defines the agent's role and the exact output schema.
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a customer support agent for a SaaS company.
For each user message:
1. Classify sentiment as happy, neutral, or frustrated.
2. Draft a concise, empathetic reply that addresses the issue.
Return ONLY a JSON object with keys 'sentiment' and 'draft_reply'."""

Step 3: Build the triage function

This function sends the ticket to Oxlo.ai and parses the JSON response. I use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows instructions well for classification and drafting.

import json

def triage_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    # Call Oxlo.ai with Llama 3.3 70B for strong instruction following.
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Handle long tickets

Real support threads can get lengthy. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing instead of token-based pricing, I can pass the full conversation history without the cost scaling by word count.

# Long email threads are fine. Oxlo.ai's per-request pricing means
# the cost stays flat no matter how much context you include.
long_ticket = """
Subject: Billing Issue
Message:
I was charged twice on March 1st and again on March 2nd.
I have attached the invoices. Please fix this immediately.
This is the third time I am writing and I am getting frustrated.
"""
result = triage_ticket(long_ticket)
print(result)

Step 5: Add fail-safe parsing

Occasionally the model wraps JSON in markdown fences. I add a small sanitizer so the script does not crash in production.

import re

def safe_triage(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    # Call the model and sanitize any accidental markdown fences.
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    # Strip markdown code blocks if the model included them.
    raw = re.sub(r"^```json\s*|^```\s*|```$", "", raw, flags=re.MULTILINE).strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Run it

I save the complete script as triage.py, export my OXLO_API_KEY, and run python triage.py. Oxlo.ai serves Llama 3.3 70B with no cold starts, so the first request warms up instantly and returns in under a second on my machine. The response_format parameter enforces JSON mode, which keeps the output machine-readable and lets me pipe these results straight into a CRM or helpdesk without extra parsing logic.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Two sample tickets to demonstrate mood detection and tone shifting.
    tickets = [
        "I love the new dashboard. Great work team!",
        "My export failed three times today. This is blocking my client report.",
    ]

    for t in tickets:
        out = safe_triage(t)
        print(f"Sentiment: {out['sentiment']}")
        print(f"Draft: {out['draft_reply']}\n")

Here is exactly what I see in my terminal. Notice how the model shifted from enthusiastic to apologetic based on the sentiment it detected.

Sentiment: happy
Draft: Thanks so much for the kind words. We are thrilled you are enjoying the new dashboard. Let us know if there is anything else we can help with.

Sentiment: frustrated
Draft: I am sorry to hear your export is failing. I understand how critical client reports are. I am escalating this to our engineering team and will update you within the hour.

Wrap-up

That is a working support triage agent in under fifty lines of Python. Two concrete ways to extend it: first, wrap the safe_triage function in a Flask or FastAPI endpoint and connect it to your helpdesk webhook so it runs on every new ticket automatically. Second, add function calling so the agent can query your internal order database before it drafts a reply, giving customers specific status updates rather than generic apologies. Oxlo.ai supports tool use, streaming, and vision, so you can keep building on this same stack as the agent grows. If you want to experiment with stronger reasoning for complex escalation logic, swap the model string to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6 without changing anything else.

title: Integrating LLMs into Chatbots: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Building a production chatbot requires more than sending user messages to a large language model. You need to select the right model, manage conversation state, handle tool use, and control costs as usage scales. This guide walks through the core steps, from API setup to deployment, with concrete code you can run today. We will use Oxlo.ai as the inference provider because its request-based pricing and OpenAI SDK compatibility remove much of the operational friction that complicates long-context chatbot workloads.

Choose the Right Model and Inference Provider

Your provider choice shapes latency, cost structure, and feature availability. Most inference platforms bill by the token, which means every word in your system prompt, chat history, and user input adds to the cost. For chatbots that maintain multi-turn memory or process long documents, token-based billing creates unpredictable spend.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. That makes it significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads compared with token-based alternatives such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale. You can explore the exact tiers on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories. For general chatbot use, start with Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B. If you need deep reasoning or complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 are strong candidates. For high-volume, low-latency bots, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a one-million-token context window with efficient MoE architecture. All popular models have no cold starts, so your first user of the day does not wait for a GPU to spin up.

Set Up Your API Client

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can keep your existing Python, Node.js, or cURL patterns. You only need to change the base URL and API key.

Install the official OpenAI SDK if you have not already:

pip install openai

Then instantiate the client:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your-oxlo.ai-api-key"
)

This is a drop-in replacement. Any code written for OpenAI, Together AI, Fireworks AI, or another compatible provider will run with minimal changes. You can generate your API key from the Oxlo.ai dashboard and start with the Free plan, which includes 60 requests per day across more than 16 models plus a seven-day full-access trial.

Design System Prompts and Conversation Logic

A system prompt defines persona, constraints, and output rules. Keep it explicit but concise. A vague system prompt leads to inconsistent replies, while an overly long one consumes context space you may need for user history.

Structure every request as a list of messages:

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful support agent. Answer in one paragraph. If you do not know the answer, say so."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "How do I reset my password?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages
)

If your frontend needs structured data, enable JSON mode by adding response_format={"type": "json_object"}. This is useful when you want the model to return a JSON object that your UI can parse into buttons or formatted cards without extra regex.

Manage Context and Multi-Turn Memory

Chatbots feel natural only when they remember prior turns. The standard pattern is to append each user message and assistant reply to the messages array and send the full history with every request.

This pattern can become expensive on token-based platforms because you pay for the entire conversation history on every single turn. On Oxlo.ai, the request-based pricing model means the cost stays flat even as the conversation grows, provided it fits within the model's context window. For very long sessions, models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash and Kimi K2.6 offer generous context limits, so you can keep dozens of turns in memory without truncation.

When you do need to trim, summarize older turns into a single system message rather than dropping them entirely. This preserves semantic relevance while keeping the payload size manageable.

Extend with Function Calling and Tool Use

Modern chatbots rarely rely on static knowledge alone. Function calling lets the model invoke external APIs, query databases, or perform calculations. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use across its chat models, using the same schema as the OpenAI API.

Define your tools and pass them in the request:

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Retrieve the status of a customer order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen-3-32b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

If the model returns a tool_calls finish reason, execute the function in your backend, append the result as a new tool message, and send the updated message list back to the model. This loop is the foundation of agentic workflows, and because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, iterative tool-use loops remain cost-predictable even when the message payload grows.

Handle Responses, Streaming, and Structured Output

Perceived latency matters in chat. Enable streaming so tokens arrive as they are generated rather than waiting for the full completion:

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=messages,
    stream=True
)

for chunk in stream:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")

Beyond text, you may want multimodal capabilities. Oxlo.ai offers vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B, which accept image inputs through the chat completions endpoint. If you are building a voice-enabled bot, you can route audio to Oxlo.ai's transcription endpoint (audio/transcriptions) using Whisper Large v3 or Whisper Turbo, and synthesize replies with the speech endpoint (audio/speech) powered by Kokoro 82M text-to-speech.

Deploy, Monitor, and Optimize Costs

Once your chatbot logic is solid, move from prototype to production. Oxlo.ai offers tiered plans that map cleanly to request volume. The Free plan gives you 60 requests per day. The Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day, and the Premium plan offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access. For teams with dedicated latency requirements or high throughput, the Enterprise plan includes custom contracts, dedicated GPUs, and a guaranteed 30% savings versus your current provider.

Because Oxlo.ai pricing is per request, capacity planning is straightforward. If you expect 3,000 user messages per day, you know exactly which plan covers you. There are no surprise spikes from a user pasting a long document or from a busy conversation thread that accumulates thousands of tokens of history. This predictability is especially valuable for bootstrapped products and internal tools where budget variance is a risk.

Monitor your integration by logging request IDs, tracking latency per model, and setting up alerts for error rates. If you need to switch models, the unified OpenAI-compatible endpoint means you can change the model string without rewriting client code.

Integrating an LLM into a chatbot is now a matter of good engineering rather than research. Pick a model that fits your quality and latency requirements, manage conversation state carefully, add tools where they create value, and choose an inference provider that keeps costs predictable at scale. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing, broad model catalog, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility make it a genuinely relevant option for chatbot builders who want to ship fast without rearchitecting their stack or worrying about token counters.

title: Few-Shot Learning with LLMs: Best Practices and Applications
content:
We are going to build a support ticket classifier that reads a customer message and assigns a priority level with a short justification. Few-shot prompting lets us teach the model the labeling standard using just a handful of examples, no fine-tuning required. This approach works best when you have clear categories and a small set of representative samples, which is exactly what most support teams already have in their backlog. The classifier we will ship runs in a single Python file, calls Oxlo.ai through the OpenAI SDK, and returns structured JSON that any downstream tool can consume. Unlike a fine-tuned model, this classifier can be updated in minutes by editing a Python list. That makes it perfect for teams that need to iterate on labeling standards weekly. I use Oxlo.ai here because its flat per-request pricing means I can pack the prompt with long examples without the cost scaling by token count, which is ideal for few-shot workloads.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai

I am running this against Oxlo.ai because the endpoint is a drop-in replacement for the OpenAI SDK. I do not need to rewrite any client code, and the flat per-request pricing keeps costs predictable even when I send long ticket threads as context.

Step 1: Define the schema and few-shot examples

I start by choosing four priority tiers that map to real operational thresholds: Critical, High, Medium, and Low. The key to effective few-shot learning is selecting examples that cover edge cases and show the model the boundary between labels. If every example is obvious, the model will fail on ambiguous tickets that sit between two tiers. I write two examples per tier so the pattern is clear without bloating the context. Each example pairs a raw support message with the exact JSON output I want, including a one-sentence reason. Storing them as dictionaries keeps the code clean and makes it easy to swap in new examples later without touching the prompt logic. I also keep the JSON structure identical across every example so the model learns a rigid format. In production, free-text responses are fragile. By forcing JSON, I can validate the output with a schema checker and feed it directly into a CRM or PagerDuty integration without string parsing.

import json

PRIORITY_LABELS = ["Critical", "High", "Medium", "Low"]

FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES = [
    {
        "ticket": "Our production database is down and the entire checkout flow is failing. We are losing revenue every minute.",
        "output": {"priority": "Critical", "reason": "Complete production outage affecting revenue."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "The admin dashboard loads but all user analytics show blank charts after the latest deploy.",
        "output": {"priority": "Critical", "reason": "Core business functionality is broken post-deploy."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "Users reporting that password reset emails are delayed by 15 minutes instead of seconds.",
        "output": {"priority": "High", "reason": "Authentication flow degraded, affecting user access."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "The CSV export button is missing on the reports page for accounts created before 2023.",
        "output": {"priority": "High", "reason": "Feature unavailable for a specific user segment."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "Can you update the billing address on file? I moved offices last month.",
        "output": {"priority": "Medium", "reason": "Routine account maintenance with no system impact."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "The dark mode toggle does not persist after logout. It resets to light mode every time.",
        "output": {"priority": "Medium", "reason": "UI preference bug, workaround exists."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "Do you have a public roadmap? I would love to know when mobile apps are planned.",
        "output": {"priority": "Low", "reason": "General inquiry, no immediate action required."}
    },
    {
        "ticket": "Found a typo in the footer of the marketing site: 'Privcy' instead of 'Privacy'.",
        "output": {"priority": "Low", "reason": "Cosmetic issue on marketing page."}
    },
]

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt sets the rules, the output format, and the decision criteria. I define each priority tier in plain language so the model does not have to infer the criteria from the examples alone. I also lock the response format to JSON with a strict schema, which makes downstream parsing trivial. I intentionally keep the prompt concise. Long system prompts can dilute the few-shot demonstrations, especially when you are working near the boundary of the model's context window. The definitions below are short enough to fit in memory alongside eight examples and a long ticket. I version my prompts in git alongside the code. If the team decides that data loss belongs in a separate severity track, I can update the definitions and redeploy without retraining anything. If you are running this on Oxlo.ai, you can switch to Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 later without changing the prompt, because the endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket classifier.
Read the user's message and assign exactly one priority: Critical, High, Medium, or Low.
Respond ONLY with a JSON object containing two keys:
- priority: the label
- reason: one sentence explaining why

Definitions:
- Critical: production outage, data loss, or security breach.
- High: major feature broken or significant customer segment affected.
- Medium: partial issue, workaround exists, or non-urgent account change.
- Low: general question, cosmetic bug, or feature request.
"""

Step 3: Assemble messages and classify

With the examples and prompt ready, I build the message array. I place the system prompt first, then alternate user and assistant messages for each example. This creates a dialogue pattern that the model continues when it sees the new ticket. Some practitioners put all examples after the system prompt in a single user message, but I have found that alternating roles produces cleaner continuations. The model treats each assistant message as the correct completion for the user message above it, which is exactly the behavior we want. The order of examples matters. I randomize or stratify them so the model does not latch onto a false pattern, like assuming every other ticket is Critical. I keep the temperature low at 0.1 so the model stays close to the demonstrated style rather than getting creative. I use Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai because it handles instruction following and JSON formatting reliably. The function returns a parsed dictionary, so the rest of my application never has to deal with raw strings. In a real deployment, I wrap the API call in a retry loop and fall back to a default priority if the model returns malformed JSON. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so the retry latency is consistent. Because the endpoint supports streaming and function calling, you could extend this later to push results into a webhook or Slack channel with the same client.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    
    for ex in FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES:
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ex["ticket"]})
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": json.dumps(ex["output"])})
    
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ticket_text})
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=128,
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

new_ticket = "Since this morning, all API requests return 502 Bad Gateway. Our mobile app is completely unusable."
result = classify_ticket(new_ticket)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Run it

Running the script against a brand new ticket produces this output. The model generalizes from the few-shot pattern and returns structured JSON that matches our schema exactly. Notice that the reasoning is specific to the input, not copied from the examples. That is the generalization we are after. You can test boundary cases, like a ticket that mentions a bug affecting only one browser, and watch the model downgrade it from High to Medium based on the definitions it saw in the system prompt. I also tested a ticket about a missing export button and received High, which confirms the model is using the criteria rather than keyword matching.

{
  "priority": "Critical",
  "reason": "Complete API outage rendering the mobile app unusable."
}

Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, stuffing the context with eight long examples costs the same as a bare prompt. For a busy queue that processes thousands of tickets, that predictability matters. Token-based billing would make this expensive fast, but on Oxlo.ai you can add as much demonstration context as the model allows without watching the meter run. That is one reason I reach for Oxlo.ai when building classification pipelines that need long context windows. You can see the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Next steps

Try expanding the classifier to extract product area and customer sentiment alongside priority. You could also move the examples to an external vector store and retrieve only the most relevant ones for each ticket, turning this into a dynamic few-shot pipeline that scales without burning context on irrelevant examples. If you need even deeper reasoning, swap the model ID to DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai and let the chain-of-thought reasoning improve the boundary decisions between High and Critical.

title: Zero-Shot Learning with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Zero-shot learning lets a large language model perform a classification or extraction task without any task-specific fine-tuning or labeled training data. You simply describe the desired output schema in natural language, and the model generalizes from its pre-training to produce the correct labels. For engineering teams, this means you can deploy a working classifier on day one, before you have collected thousands of historical examples. In this tutorial, we will build a support ticket triage agent that reads raw customer messages and returns structured category, priority, and sentiment labels, all via the flat-rate Oxlo.ai API. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, long tickets with full error logs cost the same as short ones, which makes it practical to send the entire raw message every time.

What you'll need

Make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed on your machine. You will also need an Oxlo.ai API key, which you can generate at https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier gives you 60 requests per day across more than sixteen models, so you can prototype this classifier without entering a credit card. Finally, install the OpenAI SDK with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with this SDK, so every code block below uses the standard client you already know.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

I like to keep configuration in one place. Initialize the OpenAI SDK against Oxlo.ai's endpoint. This is the only Oxlo.ai-specific line in the entire project. Every subsequent call uses the standard chat.completions interface, so if you are migrating from another provider you only change the base URL and API key. I do not add a custom wrapper; the raw SDK is enough because the API supports streaming, JSON mode, and function calling out of the box. Oxlo.ai hosts over forty-five models, but Llama 3.3 70B is a solid default for English classification because it balances speed and instruction following.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Define the classification schema

Zero-shot classification fails when the model has too much freedom. I constrain the output by defining a strict schema before I write a single line of the prompt. The categories below cover the majority of B2B SaaS support traffic, but you should adapt them to your product. I also require a reasoning field. In production, I surface this reasoning to support managers so they can audit why a ticket was marked Critical without reading the raw text. The schema is plain Python, so you can version control it or load it from a YAML file if your taxonomy changes frequently.

CATEGORIES = ["Billing", "Technical", "Feature Request", "Security"]
PRIORITIES = ["Low", "Medium", "High", "Critical"]
SENTIMENTS = ["Frustrated", "Neutral", "Satisfied"]

SCHEMA = f"""
Return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- category: one of {CATEGORIES}
- priority: one of {PRIORITIES}
- sentiment: one of {SENTIMENTS}
- reasoning: one concise sentence explaining the category choice
"""

Step 3: Craft the system prompt

The system prompt is the entire training signal. I do not include any labeled examples, which is what makes this zero-shot. Instead, I describe the persona, restate the schema, and add guardrails: exactly one category, no outside knowledge, and no markdown formatting. Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai follows these instructions reliably, and if your queue contains multilingual tickets you can swap the model string to qwen-3-32b without changing any other code. Keeping the prompt explicit and short reduces the chance that the model adds conversational filler that breaks the JSON parser downstream.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"""
You are a senior support triage agent.
Read the customer message below and classify it.

Rules:
1. Select exactly one category, one priority, and one sentiment.
2. Do not use prior knowledge about the company; base your decision only on the text provided.
3. Return only valid JSON. No markdown, no code fences, no explanation outside the JSON.

Output schema:
{SCHEMA}
""".strip()

Step 4: Build the classifier function

Now I wrap the inference call in a small function. I set temperature to 0.1 because classification is not a creative task; I want the most likely label, not a surprising one. I also enable JSON mode, which forces the model to emit valid JSON even if its internal monologue wants to add markdown backticks. All the flagship chat models on Oxlo.ai support JSON mode, so you do not need a regex fallback. A small try/except block catches malformed output so that one bad response does not crash an overnight batch job. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, I do not need to stress about the system prompt growing long or the user paste containing a thousand tokens of stack trace. The cost is the same flat rate per request regardless of input length.

import json
from json import JSONDecodeError

def classify_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
            ],
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
            temperature=0.1,
        )
        
        raw = response.choices[0].message.content
        return json.loads(raw)
    except JSONDecodeError:
        return {
            "category": "Unknown",
            "priority": "Medium",
            "sentiment": "Neutral",
            "reasoning": "Failed to parse model output",
        }

Step 5: Batch process a ticket queue

In production, these tickets arrive via email, Slack, or a webhook. For the tutorial, I simulate a queue as a simple Python list. I process them sequentially to keep the script readable, but the latency is low enough that you could run this synchronously inside a FastAPI route. Notice that the loop does not sleep between requests; in my tests the endpoint returns in under a second for short tickets, and because there are no cold starts on popular models, the first request is just as fast as the tenth. If you need higher throughput later, you can add concurrent workers without worrying about input length inflating your bill. That predictability is useful when you are processing large attachments or log dumps that would be expensive on token-based providers.

tickets = [
    "I was charged twice for my Pro subscription this month. Please refund the duplicate charge immediately.",
    "How do I export my data to CSV? The export button on the settings page seems greyed out no matter what I try.",
    "Your platform genuinely changed how our team works. I would love to see a dark mode option in the analytics dashboard.",
    "URGENT: I noticed another user can see my private repository files. This is a serious privacy breach and needs fixing now.",
]

for ticket in tickets:
    result = classify_ticket(ticket)
    print(f"Category : {result['category']}")
    print(f"Priority : {result['priority']}")
    print(f"Sentiment: {result['sentiment']}")
    print(f"Reasoning: {result['reasoning']}")
    print("-" * 40)

Run it

Save everything in a single file named triage.py, set your API key in the environment or paste it directly for local testing, and run python triage.py. When I executed this against Oxlo.ai using Llama 3.3 70B, the model returned the following labels. Your exact wording may differ slightly, but the structure and categories should remain consistent. This level of structured output would normally require a fine-tuned BERT model or a brittle rules engine. With zero-shot prompting and a capable LLM, we get the same result in under fifty lines of Python.

Category : Billing
Priority : High
Sentiment: Frustrated
Reasoning: The customer reports a duplicate charge and requests an immediate refund.
----------------------------------------
Category : Technical
Priority : Medium
Sentiment: Neutral
Reasoning: The customer is asking how to perform an action and notes a potentially disabled UI element.
----------------------------------------
Category : Feature Request
Priority : Low
Sentiment: Satisfied
Reasoning: The customer praises the platform and suggests a new UI theme.
----------------------------------------
Category : Security
Priority : Critical
Sentiment: Frustrated
Reasoning: The customer reports unauthorized data visibility, indicating a potential access control vulnerability.

Next steps

One concrete next step is to wire this classifier into your help desk webhook. You can run it on every new Zendesk, Intercom, or GitHub issue so that by the time a human opens the ticket, it already has a category and priority label attached. If you store the reasoning in a database, you can later audit the model's decisions and spot taxonomy drift.

Another step is to experiment with few-shot prompting on your own historical data. Collect ten examples of correctly labeled tickets and append them to the system prompt. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, you can test whether adding those examples improves accuracy without watching a token meter spin up. If your tickets include massive thread history, you could switch to DeepSeek V4 Flash or Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai to leverage their larger context windows while still paying the same flat per-request price. You can compare plans and request allowances at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Unlocking the Potential of LLMs for Speech Recognition
content:
Speech recognition has undergone a quiet revolution. While classical automatic speech recognition systems relied on carefully engineered acoustic models and pronunciation dictionaries, the frontier now belongs to large language models that process audio natively or operate as powerful post-processors on raw transcripts. For developers building voice-enabled applications, this shift means higher accuracy, richer metadata extraction, and simpler integration paths. It also introduces new infrastructure requirements around context length, multimodal chaining, and cost predictability.

Moving Beyond Classical ASR Pipelines

Classical ASR decomposes speech into phonemes, words, and sentences through staged pipelines. These systems struggle with overlapping speech, domain-specific jargon, and contextual disfluencies. LLM-based approaches, particularly those leveraging encoder-decoder architectures trained on vast multimodal corpora, collapse these stages. Models like Whisper learn acoustic, linguistic, and semantic representations jointly, enabling robust performance across accents, languages, and acoustic environments without brittle domain adaptation.

But the real breakthrough is not just the model architecture. It is the API surface. Modern speech workloads are rarely satisfied with raw text. Developers need diarization, timestamping, summarization, and structured data extraction. An LLM-centric pipeline treats transcription as the first step in a unified reasoning chain rather than a terminal output.

Audio Inference with Oxlo.ai

This is where infrastructure choices determine product velocity. Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first inference platform that hosts Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium alongside more than 45 models across vision, code, and reasoning categories. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, switching from other speech APIs requires only a base URL change.

The platform's request-based pricing model is particularly relevant for audio workloads. Speech files generate long token sequences, and with conventional token-based billing, costs scale linearly with audio duration. On Oxlo.ai, a single API request incurs one flat cost regardless of prompt length, making long-form transcription and agentic audio processing significantly more predictable. You can explore the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

There are no cold starts on popular models, so transcription endpoints remain hot even under sporadic traffic. For applications that process user-generated audio, podcast feeds, or call-center recordings, this eliminates the latency spikes that degrade user experience on serverless inference platforms.

Multimodal Post-Processing and Analysis

Transcription is only half the value. Once audio becomes text, LLMs can perform semantic analysis, entity extraction, sentiment scoring, and action-item generation. Oxlo.ai offers models suited to each stage of this pipeline. You might route audio through Whisper Large v3 for high-accuracy transcription, then pass the resulting text to Llama 3.3 70B for general-purpose summarization, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for complex reasoning over technical content, or Kimi K2.6 for advanced agentic coding and vision tasks if the audio references visual materials.

Because all models share the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, chaining these operations requires no client library fragmentation. You use the same SDK patterns for audio transcriptions, chat completions, and embeddings.

Long-Form Audio and Context Window Economics

Podcasts, lectures, and earnings calls routinely exceed thirty minutes. Feeding these transcripts into an analysis model demands large context windows. Oxlo.ai hosts several models built for this exact workload. DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window and efficient MoE inference, making it ideal for analyzing lengthy transcripts in a single pass. Kimi K2.6 offers a 131K context with advanced reasoning capabilities, while GLM 5 handles long-horizon agentic tasks over extended documents.

On token-based providers, running a 100K token transcript through a reasoning model is prohibitively expensive for many use cases. Oxlo.ai's request-based approach breaks this economic barrier. Whether you are processing a two-minute voice memo or a two-hour deposition, the inference cost structure remains flat per request, which can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context workloads.

Implementation: Transcription and Analysis in One Flow

Here is a concrete, copy-pasteable pattern using the OpenAI Python SDK against Oxlo.ai. This example transcribes an audio file and then extracts structured meeting notes using an LLM.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

# Step 1: Transcribe audio
with open("meeting.mp3", "rb") as audio_file:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-large-v3",
        file=audio_file,
        response_format="text"
    )

# Step 2: Structured analysis via chat completion
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "Extract action items, decisions, and key questions from the transcript. Return valid JSON."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": transcript
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

This pattern highlights the platform's uniformity. The same client handles audio and chat endpoints. You can substitute whisper-turbo for lower latency, or swap llama-3.3-70b for deepseek-r1-671b if the audio contains dense technical reasoning that benefits from chain-of-thought processing.

Operational Considerations for Production Speech Workflows

Deploying LLM-based speech recognition requires attention to a few practical factors. First, hallucinations remain a concern. Whisper models occasionally invent words in low-signal audio or dense jargon. Mitigation strategies include voice activity detection preprocessing and confidence-threshold filtering before downstream LLM analysis.

Second, latency matters for real-time applications. While Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts, end-to-end latency still depends on model size. Whisper Turbo offers a favorable speed-accuracy tradeoff for near-real-time captioning, while Whisper Large v3 is better suited for batch archival transcription.

Third, cost predictability is critical when audio volume fluctuates. Token-based bills scale with audio length, speaker count, and language complexity. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing removes this variability, letting engineering teams forecast infrastructure spend without modeling tokens per second or audio compression ratios.

Conclusion

LLMs have redefined what speech recognition can achieve, turning transcription from a terminal output into the opening move of a broader reasoning workflow. For developers, the priority is an inference backend that delivers high-quality audio models, long-context analysis engines, and pricing that respects the economics of lengthy media.

Oxlo.ai provides exactly that stack. With Whisper variants for transcription, a broad catalog of reasoning models for post-processing, and request-based pricing that stays flat regardless of input length, it is designed for production speech pipelines. If you are building voice-enabled products, start at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and treat audio as just another modality in your LLM architecture.

title: Choosing the Right LLM Model for Your Business Needs
content:
Selecting a large language model for production is no longer about finding the single best benchmark score. The market has fragmented into specialized families optimized for reasoning, coding, vision, long-context retrieval, and agentic tool use. A model that excels at creative writing may stall on structured JSON extraction, and a coding specialist might be cost-prohibitive for high-volume chat. The real task is aligning model capabilities with your business workload, traffic patterns, and cost constraints. Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first inference platform that simplifies this alignment with 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, fully OpenAI SDK compatible infrastructure, and request-based pricing that removes the penalty for long prompts. If you are navigating this landscape, here is how to make the decision without over-engineering your stack.

Map the Task Before the Model

Businesses usually start by asking which model is the smartest, but the better question is what the model must actually do. Workloads generally fall into distinct categories: general-purpose chat and reasoning, software generation, vision understanding, embedding and retrieval, image or audio generation, and autonomous agent orchestration. Each category carries different latency requirements, context length needs, and output format constraints. For example, a customer support bot may need multi-turn conversation memory and function calling, while a documentation analysis pipeline may need to ingest hundreds of pages in a single prompt. Oxlo.ai organizes its catalog into these exact categories, offering LLMs and chat models alongside dedicated endpoints for code, vision, embeddings, audio transcriptions, speech synthesis, and even object detection. Before comparing parameter counts, document your input sizes, expected output lengths, and whether you need tool use or JSON mode. That specification becomes your filter.

Understand the Cost Architecture

Pricing models in the inference market split into two camps: token-based metering and request-based flat rates. Token-based providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, charge proportionally to the tokens you send and receive. This means long-context workloads, large system prompts, and agentic loops with heavy tool context scale in cost linearly, often unpredictably. For businesses running retrieval-augmented generation over large knowledge bases or autonomous agents that maintain lengthy state, token bills can escalate faster than utilization.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this architecture can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives because a 100-token query and a 100,000-token query cost the same. You can explore the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. When forecasting spend, model your worst-case context length, not your average. If your use case involves repeated long inputs, a flat per-request structure provides cost predictability that token-based tiers cannot match.

Match Model Families to Workloads

Once you understand your task and cost model, you can map specific model families to business needs. For deep reasoning and complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash deliver near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, with V4 Flash offering a one-million-token context window. General-purpose workloads often benefit from Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B, which offers strong multilingual reasoning and agent workflow support. For pure coding, Qwen 3 Coder 30B and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast provide focused performance. If you need vision capabilities, Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B handle image inputs. Image generation workloads can use Oxlo.ai Image Pro and Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, or Stable Diffusion 3.5, while audio tasks are covered by Whisper Large v3, Turbo, and Medium, plus Kokoro 82M text-to-speech.

Rather than defaulting to the largest model available, benchmark the smallest model in the relevant family first. The Pro and Premium plans unlock higher daily volumes and priority queue access, while Enterprise plans provide dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction versus your current provider.

Evaluate Infrastructure Overhead

Model performance on paper means little if the serving layer introduces cold starts, compatibility friction, or custom client logic. Many teams underestimate the engineering cost of maintaining separate SDKs for each provider or handling warmup latency on infrequently used models. Oxlo.ai exposes a single base URL, https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, and is fully OpenAI SDK compatible across Python, Node.js, and cURL.     base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain request-based pricing."}],

Popular models also run with no cold starts, so latency remains consistent whether you are sending your first request of the day or your thousandth. This is especially valuable when A/B testing candidates during a pilot. For businesses running production agents or user-facing chat, that consistency directly translates to user experience and operational simplicity.

Validate Before Scaling

The final step is to validate your shortlist against real data. Run your own evaluation set on candidate models, measuring not just accuracy but end-to-end latency, JSON mode adherence, and tool use reliability. Create a golden dataset that includes edge cases for your domain, such as long document summaries, multi-step tool calls, or structured output schemas. Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, vision inputs, and multi-turn conversations, so you can test advanced behaviors without platform limitations. Because the pricing is request-based, you can run large-context test batches without watching token meters tick upward. Start on the Free tier to compare models side by side, then scale to Pro or Premium as your daily volume solidifies. If your workload is mission-critical and high-volume, the Enterprise tier offers custom contracts with unlimited requests and dedicated GPU isolation.

Decision Checklist

Choosing the right LLM comes down to a few concrete variables. Define the task category, estimate your maximum context size, determine whether you need tool use or structured output, and select a pricing model that matches your traffic pattern. If your workloads include long-context retrieval, agentic loops, or unpredictable prompt lengths, request-based pricing provides a structural advantage over token-based billing.

Oxlo.ai delivers 45+ models across reasoning, code, vision, audio, and embeddings, all accessible through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint with no cold starts. title: Multimodal LLMs: Applications and Future Directions
content:
Multimodal large language models have moved from research curiosities to production infrastructure. Systems that once handled text alone now process images, audio, video frames, and structured sensor data within a single context window. For developers, this shift changes how applications are built. A customer support bot can now analyze a screenshot of an error message, a medical imaging pipeline can generate structured reports from radiology scans, and a coding assistant can reason over both repository files and UI mockups. The challenge is no longer whether models can handle multiple modalities, but how to deploy them at scale without cost or latency becoming prohibitive.

What Are Multimodal LLMs?

Multimodal LLMs are foundation models trained to understand and generate content across more than one input or output modality. Early transformers were optimized for text tokens, but modern architectures use vision encoders, audio spectrogram processors, and unified projection layers to map disparate signals into a shared latent space. This allows a single model to perform tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, speech-to-text summarization, and cross-modal retrieval. The result is a more flexible interface between human communication and machine reasoning, reducing the need to chain together separate single-purpose models.

Current Applications

The most immediate impact of multimodal LLMs is in computer vision and document understanding. Developers are building systems where users upload images, diagrams, or PDFs and receive structured JSON extracted via function calling. In healthcare, models process imaging alongside clinical notes. In software engineering, vision-enabled agents navigate user interfaces and generate code from screenshots. Audio modalities are also maturing. Speech recognition pipelines now use large models to transcribe meetings, while text-to-speech systems generate natural narration for interactive applications. Image generation endpoints power marketing creative workflows, and object detection models like YOLOv9 and YOLOv11 provide real-time bounding box inference for robotics and surveillance. The common thread is that modern applications rarely rely on a single modality in isolation.

Why Infrastructure Matters for Multimodal Workloads

Multimodal inputs dramatically increase payload size. A high-resolution image encoded as base64 or processed through a vision encoder can expand a context window by thousands of tokens. An audio file transcribed inline, or a video sequence sampled as frames, compounds the effect. On token-based inference platforms, this translates directly into higher costs per request and unpredictable billing. For production systems, infrastructure must support large context windows, efficient vision projection, and stable throughput without cold starts.
