title: How LLMs Work: A Technical Deep Dive
content:
We're building a reasoning inspector that forces a large language model to externalize its step-by-step logic. It helps engineers understand how transformer inference actually unfolds by capturing and parsing each reasoning stage. I run this on Oxlo.ai because flat per-request pricing removes the penalty for long chain-of-thought traces.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or higher
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the OpenAI SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai's endpoint. I use DeepSeek V3.2 here because it handles reasoning and coding problems with minimal verbosity.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Design the system prompt

To see how the model works, I force it to emit its reasoning inside XML tags before giving a final answer. This simulates the autoregressive process: each token depends on the prior context.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a reasoning engine. When given a problem, explain your thinking step by step inside <thinking> tags. Number each reasoning step like Step 1:, Step 2:, etc. After you finish reasoning, provide your final answer inside <answer> tags. Be thorough. Do not skip steps."""

Step 3: Send a hard problem and capture the raw response

I use a classic multi-step logic puzzle. The model fills the context window token by token, and we capture the full string to inspect the progression.

user_message = (
    "A farmer has a fox, a chicken, and a bag of grain. "
    "He must cross a river in a boat that can only carry him and one item. "
    "If left alone, the fox will eat the chicken, and the chicken will eat the grain. "
    "How does he get everything across safely?"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v3.2",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
)

raw_output = response.choices[0].message.content
print(raw_output)

Step 4: Parse the reasoning trace

Now I split the raw output into discrete steps. This mirrors how we might inspect attention patterns: we want to see which pieces of the prompt influenced which parts of the response.

import re

thinking_match = re.search(r"<thinking>(.*?)</thinking>", raw_output, re.DOTALL)
answer_match = re.search(r"<answer>(.*?)</answer>", raw_output, re.DOTALL)

if thinking_match:
    thinking_text = thinking_match.group(1).strip()
    steps = re.findall(r"Step \d+:.*?(?=Step \d+:|$)", thinking_text, re.DOTALL)
    print("=== REASONING TRACE ===")
    for i, step in enumerate(steps, 1):
        print(f"\n--- Step {i} ---")
        print(step.strip())

if answer_match:
    print("\n=== FINAL ANSWER ===")
    print(answer_match.group(1).strip())

Step 5: Add self-correction to show iterative refinement

Real LLM systems rarely stop at one forward pass. I append the assistant's first response to the message history and ask it to critique itself. This demonstrates how the context window accumulates state across turns.

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": raw_output},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Critique your own reasoning above. Did you miss any edge cases or make an unsafe assumption? Explain."},
]

critique_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v3.2",
    messages=messages,
)

print(critique_response.choices[0].message.content)

Run it

Save the full script as reasoning_inspector.py and execute it. The output below shows how DeepSeek V3.2 structures its reasoning before committing to an answer.

$ python reasoning_inspector.py

<thinking>
Step 1: Identify the constraints. The farmer can take only one item per trip. The fox cannot be left alone with the chicken. The chicken cannot be left alone with the grain.
Step 2: Determine the problematic item. The chicken is the only one that conflicts with both others.
Step 3: Plan the first trip. Take the chicken across first. This leaves the fox and grain together, which is safe.
Step 4: Return alone. The farmer goes back to the original side.
Step 5: Take the fox across. Now the fox and chicken are on the far side, which is a conflict.
Step 6: Leave the fox, bring the chicken back. This prevents the fox from eating the chicken.
Step 7: Take the grain across. Now the fox and grain are on the far side, which is safe.
Step 8: Return alone. The farmer goes back to get the chicken.
Step 9: Take the chicken across. All items are now on the far side with no conflicts.
</thinking>

<answer>
1. Take the chicken across.
2. Return alone.
3. Take the fox across.
4. Bring the chicken back.
5. Take the grain across.
6. Return alone.
7. Take the chicken across.
</answer>

=== REASONING TRACE ===

--- Step 1 ---
Step 1: Identify the constraints. The farmer can take only one item per trip. The fox cannot be left alone with the chicken. The chicken cannot be left alone with the grain.

--- Step 2 ---
Step 2: Determine the problematic item. The chicken is the only one that conflicts with both others.

[... additional steps ...]

=== FINAL ANSWER ===
1. Take the chicken across.
2. Return alone.
3. Take the fox across.
4. Bring the chicken back.
5. Take the grain across.
6. Return alone.
7. Take the chicken across.

Critique: The reasoning is sound, but it assumes the farmer cannot tie up the fox or secure the grain. Those assumptions match the puzzle constraints, so no edge cases were missed.

Wrap-up

This inspector gives you a window into autoregressive generation without needing access to internal attention maps. Two concrete next steps: pipe the parsed steps into a visualization library like Rich to build a terminal UI, or swap in Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2 Thinking on Oxlo.ai to compare how different architectures structure reasoning. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, experimenting with long system prompts and multi-turn critiques stays predictable.

title: Introduction to LLMs for Language Understanding
content:
Today we are building a support ticket language understanding agent. It takes raw customer messages and extracts intent, product mentions, and urgency into structured JSON. If you run a support queue, this lets you route tickets automatically instead of reading every thread manually. We will implement it in plain Python against Oxlo.ai's OpenAI-compatible API.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer installed locally. Install the OpenAI SDK with pip install openai. You also need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai.

Oxlo.ai is a fully OpenAI-compatible inference platform, so the code below works without vendor-specific adapters. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request rather than per token, long ticket threads with pasted logs do not inflate your bill. That makes this kind of extraction work predictable during prototyping and in production. You can start on the free tier and move to a paid plan once you scale beyond the daily request limit.

Step 1: Configure the client

First, we point the OpenAI SDK at Oxlo.ai. The client is a drop-in replacement, so we only change the base URL and API key. In your own code, load the key from an environment variable instead of hardcoding it.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is where we teach the model what language understanding means for our domain. We want valid JSON with three fields: intent, entities, and urgency. I do not use JSON mode here because a well-written prompt with low temperature is usually enough for Llama 3.3 70B, and it keeps the example portable.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a language understanding agent that analyzes customer support tickets.
Read the user message and return a single JSON object with these exact keys:
- intent: one of [billing, technical, account_access, feature_request, other]
- entities: a list of objects with keys {name, type} for products, error codes, or account IDs mentioned
- urgency: one of [low, medium, high, critical]

Rules:
1. Return only the JSON object, with no markdown fences.
2. If no entities are found, return an empty list.
3. Base urgency on explicit words like 'outage', 'broken', 'ASAP', or on whether the user cannot work."""

Step 3: Create the analysis function

Now we wrap the API call in a function that accepts a ticket string and returns parsed JSON. I use Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai because it handles instruction-following reliably for extraction tasks. I set temperature to 0.1 so the output stays deterministic, which matters when we later parse JSON. Oxlo.ai serves this model with no cold starts, so the function feels responsive even when you call it interactively.

import json

def analyze_ticket(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process a batch of tickets

In production, you rarely analyze one ticket at a time. We loop over a list of messages and collect results. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so the loop runs without the latency spikes you sometimes see on serverless endpoints. I wrapped the call in a try block so one malformed response does not kill the entire batch.

tickets = [
    "My dashboard is completely blank after the latest update. This is blocking our deploy.",
    "Can you add CSV export to the reports page? Would save me hours each week.",
    "Invoice #9921 is wrong. I was charged for 2 seats but I only have 1.",
    "URGENT: all our webhooks return 500 since 09:00 UTC. Nothing is syncing.",
]

results = []
for t in tickets:
    try:
        results.append(analyze_ticket(t))
    except Exception as e:
        results.append({"error": str(e), "raw": t})

Step 5: Add basic validation

LLMs can hallucinate keys, return markdown fences, or emit trailing commas. We add a small validation layer that enforces our schema and falls back to a default dict if parsing fails. This prevents one bad response from crashing the pipeline.

def safe_analyze(text: str) -> dict:
    try:
        parsed = analyze_ticket(text)
        # enforce schema
        return {
            "intent": parsed.get("intent", "other"),
            "entities": parsed.get("entities", []),
            "urgency": parsed.get("urgency", "medium"),
        }
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, KeyError):
        return {"intent": "other", "entities": [], "urgency": "medium", "parse_failed": True}

batch_results = [safe_analyze(t) for t in tickets]

Run it

We call our pipeline with the sample tickets and print the structured output. The agent returns data we can feed directly into a dashboard, a SQL database, or a PagerDuty trigger. The output below is exactly what I received when running this script against Oxlo.ai.

for ticket, result in zip(tickets, batch_results):
    print("Ticket:", ticket[:50], "...")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    print()

Example output:

Ticket: My dashboard is completely blank after the latest ...
{
  "intent": "technical",
  "entities": [{"name": "dashboard", "type": "product"}],
  "urgency": "high"
}

Ticket: Can you add CSV export to the reports page? Would ...
{
  "intent": "feature_request",
  "entities": [{"name": "reports page", "type": "product"}, {"name": "CSV export", "type": "feature"}],
  "urgency": "low"
}

Ticket: Invoice #9921 is wrong. I was charged for 2 seats ...
{
  "intent": "billing",
  "entities": [{"name": "#9921", "type": "invoice"}],
  "urgency": "medium"
}

Ticket: URGENT: all our webhooks return 500 since 09:00 UTC ...
{
  "intent": "technical",
  "entities": [{"name": "webhooks", "type": "product"}, {"name": "500", "type": "error_code"}],
  "urgency": "critical"
}

Wrap-up

This pipeline turns unstructured text into structured signals you can act on. If your tickets arrive in multiple languages, swap the model to Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai, which handles multilingual reasoning without any code changes.

For a next step, add a confidence threshold and route only high-urgency tickets to a Slack webhook. You could also compare costs on your current provider against Oxlo.ai request-based pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing, especially if your prompts include long conversation threads.

title: LLMs for Tech Support: Challenges and Opportunities
content:
Tech support teams face a familiar tension. Ticket volumes grow linearly with user base, but headcount rarely keeps pace. Large language models promise to close that gap by handling repetitive L1 and L2 inquiries, yet production deployment introduces engineering constraints that benchmark leaderboard scores do not capture. Context windows balloon as tickets include stack traces, conversation history, and knowledge base articles. Latency matters when a user is waiting for a resolution. Costs scale unpredictably on token-based platforms. The opportunity is real, but only for teams that architect around these challenges.

The Case for LLMs in Tech Support

The economics of human-only support are straightforward and limiting. Hiring, training, and retaining agents scales linearly with volume, and multilingual coverage adds further overhead. LLMs can provide consistent, 24/7 responses in dozens of languages, which makes them attractive for global products. Modern reasoning models can parse complex configuration files, compare them against documentation, and suggest remediation steps that once required specialized engineers. The shift is not theoretical. Support organizations are already embedding models into triage bots, draft generators, and autonomous resolution agents. The question is no longer whether to use LLMs, but how to build systems that remain accurate, fast, and cost-effective when a single ticket contains a hundred thousand tokens of context.

Core Architectural Challenges

Production support pipelines differ from simple chatbots in three critical ways. First, context size. A frustrated user often pastes log files, environment variables, and prior email threads into a single message. Without a model that can ingest the full context in one pass, the system must chunk and summarize, which risks dropping the exact error signature needed for diagnosis. Second, reliability. Hallucinated commands in a support context are dangerous. An agent that instructs a user to delete the wrong directory or modify a production database credential can cause outages. Third, integration. Useful support agents do not just talk. They must query ticket statuses, search internal wikis, and execute runbooks via function calling. Any platform powering this pipeline must expose tool-use primitives, JSON mode for structured responses, and streaming so that users see progress rather than staring at a blank screen. Finally, latency and availability matter. Cold starts on inference endpoints create unacceptable delays when a customer is waiting.

Why Long Context Changes the Economics

The most underappreciated variable in support automation is the cost of context. On token-based platforms, a long ticket with extensive logs and a detailed knowledge base retrieval can consume tens of thousands of input tokens before the model generates a single word of advice. Because pricing scales with input plus output length, these workloads become expensive quickly. Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. As a developer-first AI inference platform, Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale, cost does not scale with input length. For tech support, where every ticket carries a unique payload of history and diagnostics, this structure can be significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads.

The platform also offers models explicitly built for massive context, including DeepSeek V4 Flash with its 1 million token context window and Kimi K2.6 with 131K context and advanced reasoning capabilities. These models can ingest entire documentation sections or lengthy traces in a single pass, reducing the engineering complexity of chunking and re-ranking. There are no cold starts on popular models, which means first responses arrive without the spin-up delays that plague on-demand inference.

Building Reliable Agentic Workflows

Effective support agents do not operate in isolation. They search, validate, and then respond. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversations, which makes it possible to build agentic workflows that interact with internal APIs. For reasoning and agentic tasks, the platform provides several strong candidates. Qwen 3 32B excels at multilingual reasoning and agent workflows. GLM 5, a 744B parameter MoE, targets long-horizon agentic tasks. Minimax M2.5 is tuned for coding and agentic tool use. Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision together in one model.

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, integrating these capabilities requires only a base URL change. Here is a minimal pattern for a support agent that decides whether to search a knowledge base or answer directly:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior support engineer. Search the knowledge base before giving a fix."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "After the v2.4 deploy, all background jobs fail with a Redis timeout. Logs attached..."}
    ],
    tools=[{
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "search_knowledge_base",
            "description": "Query internal documentation",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "query": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["query"]
            }
        }
    }],
    tool_choice="auto",
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

The streaming parameter ensures the user sees tokens as they arrive, which improves perceived latency even when tool calls introduce a brief pause.

Multimodal Capabilities for Modern Support

Text is not the only medium in a support ticket. Users paste screenshots of error dialogs, upload photos of hardware serial numbers, and share screen recordings. A modern support pipeline should handle these natively. Oxlo.ai offers vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B for image understanding, which can parse screenshots and correlate them with documented UI states. For voice workflows, the platform provides Whisper Large v3, Turbo, and Medium for audio transcriptions, plus Kokoro 82M text-to-speech for building outbound voice bots or read-back confirmations. These endpoints, including chat/completions, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech, share the same flat request-based pricing logic where applicable, keeping cost forecasting simple even when the input is an audio file rather than a text prompt.

Integration Pattern: RAG plus Structured Output

A robust support agent typically combines retrieval with generation. You can use embedding models like BGE-Large or E5-Large, available via the embeddings endpoint, to encode internal documentation and past resolutions. Retrieved chunks are then injected into the prompt alongside the user query. title: Using LLMs for Language Translation
content:
We are going to build a document-aware translation agent that preserves terminology, tone, and context across long texts such as markdown documentation, product dashboards, and multilingual notification pipelines. If you run a SaaS app or content platform, this gives you a programmable alternative to brittle string substitution or expensive human-only workflows that still drift between releases. I will walk through the exact Python code I use in production, calling Oxlo.ai through the OpenAI SDK so you can drop this into your backend with only a base URL change.

What you'll need

You will need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an active API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. I recommend creating a virtual environment so your dependencies stay isolated from system packages. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only difference from a standard script is the base URL and the choice of model, which means you can test locally and promote the same code to staging without vendor lock-in.

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I always verify the endpoint with a single call before I add wrappers. The snippet below initializes the client and sends a test sentence to Qwen 3 32B, which handles multilingual reasoning well.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen-3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Translate to Spanish: The API key is invalid."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Lock in tone with a system prompt

A generic model will translate literally and strip your product voice. I define a system prompt that enforces tone, preserves formatting, and blocks literal idiom translation, then wrap it in a reusable function.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a professional translator. Follow these rules:
1. Preserve the original tone: formal stays formal, casual stays casual.
2. Do not translate technical identifiers, brand names, or code snippets.
3. Adapt idioms for the target culture rather than translating literally.
4. Maintain all markdown, HTML tags, or formatting exactly as provided.
5. If the source is ambiguous, choose the most common business context.

Return only the translated text, with no preamble or explanation."""
def translate_text(text: str, target_lang: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Translate the following text into {target_lang}:\n\n{text}"},
        ],
        temperature=0.3,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Step 3: Enforce terminology with a glossary

Production software has proper nouns and UI labels that must stay consistent across releases. I inject a JSON glossary into the user message so the model treats it as a binding term list rather than a suggestion.

import json

def translate_with_glossary(text: str, target_lang: str, glossary: dict) -> str:
    glossary_block = json.dumps(glossary, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
    user_msg = (
        f"Target language: {target_lang}\n"
        f"Terminology glossary (use exactly):\n{glossary_block}\n\n"
        f"Text to translate:\n{text}"
    )
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
        ],
        temperature=0.3,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

Step 4: Translate long documents in chunks

Feeding an entire markdown file at once often corrupts formatting or loses narrative thread. I split the source on double newlines, translate each chunk, and feed a running summary forward so style stays coherent across sections.

def translate_document(chunks: list[str], target_lang: str, glossary: dict) -> list[str]:
    translations = []
    context = "No previous context."
    
    for i, chunk in enumerate(chunks):
        if not chunk.strip():
            translations.append("")
            continue
            
        user_msg = (
            f"Target language: {target_lang}\n"
            f"Previous section summary: {context}\n"
            f"Terminology glossary:\n{json.dumps(glossary, ensure_ascii=False)}\n\n"
            f"Translate this section, keeping it consistent with the summary above:\n\n{chunk}"
        )
        
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="qwen-3-32b",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
            ],
            temperature=0.3,
        )
        
        translated = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
        translations.append(translated)
        context = translated[:200].replace("\n", " ")
        
    return translations

Step 5: Batch short strings to cut latency

UI localization usually means hundreds of short strings like button labels and error messages. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing rather than token-based metering, I batch dozens of labels into a single prompt to keep latency low and costs predictable regardless of total token count. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details.

def translate_batch(strings: list[str], target_lang: str) -> list[str]:
    numbered = "\n".join(f"{i+1}. {s}" for i, s in enumerate(strings))
    user_msg = (
        f"Translate each numbered item into {target_lang}. "
        f"Return a JSON array of strings in the same order. No markdown fencing.\n\n{numbered}"
    )
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
        ],
        temperature=0.2,
    )
    
    result = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if result.startswith("```"):
        result = result.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    parsed = json.loads(result)
    return parsed if isinstance(parsed, list) else parsed.get("translations", [])

Run it

The script below ties the glossary injection and document chunking logic together on a realistic two-paragraph input that mixes product terminology with everyday language. When I run it against Qwen 3 32B, the model respects the locked terms, keeps the formal register, and does not hallucinate translations for brand names. The output block shows exactly what I get back.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    glossary = {
        "Oxlo.ai": "Oxlo.ai",
        "dashboard": "tableau de bord",
        "API key": "clé API"
    }
    
    chunks = [
        "Welcome to Oxlo.ai. Your dashboard shows real-time inference metrics.",
        "If you see an error, check that your API key is valid and try again."
    ]
    
    results = translate_document(chunks, "French", glossary)
    for original, translated in zip(chunks, results):
        print(f"EN: {original}")
        print(f"FR: {translated}")
        print()

Example output:

EN: Welcome to Oxlo.ai. Your dashboard shows real-time inference metrics.
FR: Bienvenue sur Oxlo.ai. Votre tableau de bord affiche les métriques d'inférence en temps réel.

EN: If you see an error, check that your API key is valid and try again.
FR: Si vous voyez une erreur, vérifiez que votre clé API est valide et réessayez.

Wrap-up

From here, you have two solid paths forward that I have shipped on similar projects. First, expose this as an async FastAPI endpoint so your frontend or CLI can request translations on demand. Because Oxlo.ai does not cold-start popular models, p99 latency stays predictable even under load, which matters when you are blocking a user signup flow. Second, add a human-in-the-loop feedback table backed by SQLite or Postgres. When a reviewer overrides a translation, append the before and after pair to your glossary prompt. Over time this becomes a self-improving localization memory without any fine-tuning. If your source content includes screenshots or diagrams with embedded text, swap the model to Kimi K2.6 and pass the images through the same chat completions pipeline using the vision input format. The base URL and SDK stay identical, so the switch is one line.

title: The Intersection of LLMs and Computer Vision: Exploring New Frontiers
content:
We are going to build a visual inspection agent that ingests an image and emits a structured JSON report. It is useful for safety audits, inventory checks, and quality control workflows where you need both computer vision and language reasoning in a single pass. By the end, you will have a drop-in Python script that runs on Oxlo.ai and works with any JPEG or PNG you feed it.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • An active Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai.
  • The OpenAI Python SDK installed: pip install openai.
  • A sample image file such as warehouse.jpg.

Oxlo.ai hosts several vision-capable models, including Kimi K2.6 and Gemma 3 27B, which we can call through the same chat completions endpoint. For this build, we will use Kimi K2.6 because it handles vision, reasoning, and long context in one shot.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint, so we can use the official SDK without custom adapters. We import the client, point the base URL to Oxlo.ai, and read the API key from the environment. I prefer to keep secrets out of source control, so the snippet below expects OXLO_API_KEY to be exported in your shell before you run the script. I also import base64 and json here because we will need them for image encoding and report parsing in later steps.

import os
import base64
import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between us and the model. It tells the agent exactly what schema to return and forbids markdown wrappers. I treat the prompt as an API schema. By enumerating the exact JSON keys and their types, I turn the LLM into a vision backend that returns machine-readable data. This is cleaner than asking for prose and then trying to extract structure later.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a visual inspection agent. Analyze the provided image and produce a structured JSON report with exactly the following fields:
- scene_type: string describing the setting
- objects: list of visible objects with estimated counts
- safety_concerns: list of any potential hazards or policy violations
- recommended_actions: list of concrete remediation steps

Respond with valid JSON only. Do not wrap the output in markdown code fences."""

Step 3: Prepare the image input

Vision models on Oxlo.ai accept images as base64 data URLs inside the chat message. Most vision pipelines blow up in cost on other platforms because high-resolution images encode into thousands of tokens. On token-based providers, a single detailed photograph can consume more prompt tokens than a long document. Oxlo.ai removes that variable with request-based pricing. Whether you send a small thumbnail or a full resolution frame, the cost is the same flat per-request rate. That makes this architecture viable for production video frame sampling or drone inspection feeds where resolution is non-negotiable. You can read more on the pricing page. The helper below reads a local file and returns a base64 string. JPEG works best for photographs, while PNG is fine for diagrams or screenshots.

def encode_image(image_path):
    with open(image_path, "rb") as image_file:
        return base64.b64encode(image_file.read()).decode("utf-8")

image_b64 = encode_image("warehouse.jpg")

Step 4: Call the vision model

We use kimi-k2.6 because it supports vision, advanced reasoning, and a 131K context window. The message array contains our system prompt and a user message that carries both the text instruction and the image block. The payload follows the standard OpenAI vision convention: a list of content blocks where one block has type text and another has type image_url. Oxlo.ai routes this to the underlying vision model exactly like the standard API. I set temperature=0.2 to keep the JSON deterministic. A lower temperature keeps the model focused on the schema instead of getting creative with field names. I have found 0.2 to be the sweet spot for structured vision tasks on Oxlo.ai. If you need more variability in the natural language descriptions inside the JSON values, you could raise it slightly, but for machine parsing, consistency matters more than flair. Oxlo.ai serves this model with no cold starts, so the first request of a session returns as quickly as any subsequent one.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "text",
                    "text": "Generate an inspection report for this image."
                },
                {
                    "type": "image_url",
                    "image_url": {
                        "url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{image_b64}"
                    }
                }
            ]
        }
    ],
    temperature=0.2,
)

raw_output = response.choices[0].message.content

Step 5: Parse the structured report

Parsing is where many demos fall apart. Even with a strict system prompt, some vision models occasionally wrap JSON in markdown fences or add a friendly preamble. The cleaner your system prompt, the less this happens, but I still bake in a sanitizer. We strip triple backticks, drop any json language tag, and then parse with the standard library. If you plan to run this unattended, you could wrap the parse call in a retry loop. If you are processing hundreds of images, I recommend logging the raw response text to a file before parsing. That way, if one image triggers an odd formatting edge case, you can inspect the failure without re-running the inference call.

def parse_report(raw_text):
    cleaned = raw_text.strip()
    if cleaned.startswith("```"):
        cleaned = cleaned.split("```")[1]
        if cleaned.startswith("json"):
            cleaned = cleaned[4:]
    return json.loads(cleaned.strip())

report = parse_report(raw_output)
print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Run it

The script below ties the steps together. Save it as inspect.py, replace warehouse.jpg with any image you want to audit, and run python inspect.py. The agent analyzes the scene and prints a structured report you can pipe into jq or load into a pandas DataFrame. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, your client code looks identical to what you would write for any other OpenAI-compatible provider, but your cost model stays predictable no matter how detailed the image is.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    image_b64 = encode_image("warehouse.jpg")

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k2.6",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "Inspect this workspace and list any safety issues."
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "image_url",
                        "image_url": {
                            "url": f"data:image/jpeg;base64,{image_b64}"
                        }
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        temperature=0.2,
    )

    report = parse_report(response.choices[0].message.content)
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))

Here is what the output looks like for a warehouse shelf image I tested.

{
  "scene_type": "warehouse storage aisle",
  "objects": [

title: Sentiment Analysis using LLMs: Best Practices and Applications
content:
I recently built a sentiment analysis service for a team that was drowning in unstructured user feedback. They needed structured outputs, confidence scores, and reasoning, but did not want to maintain a custom NLP pipeline. In this tutorial, we will build a lightweight Python analyzer that classifies text using an LLM on Oxlo.ai, where a flat per-request price keeps costs predictable even when you feed in long support tickets or detailed product reviews.

What you'll need

An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai, Python 3.10 or newer, and the OpenAI SDK. Install it with pip install openai. Optional: pip install pandas if you prefer DataFrames for the batch step.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

First, I verify that the environment is wired up correctly by making a single call. I point the OpenAI SDK at Oxlo.ai and use llama-3.3-70b because it handles classification tasks reliably with low latency.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

user_message = "The battery life is incredible, but the fan noise is unbearable during video calls."

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a sentiment analysis engine. Reply with exactly one word: positive, negative, neutral, or mixed."},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Lock in the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between your code and the model. I define the exact JSON schema, constrain the sentiment labels, and add a rule for ambiguous or sarcastic text. Keeping this in a constant makes it easy to version and tweak without hunting through function bodies.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment analysis engine. Analyze the user's text and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:

- sentiment: one of ["positive", "negative", "neutral", "mixed"]
- confidence: float between 0.0 and 1.0
- topics: array of up to 3 strings naming specific product aspects mentioned
- reasoning: one concise sentence explaining the classification

Use "mixed" when the text contains both clear praise and clear criticism. If the text is sarcastic, classify by the underlying meaning and set confidence below 0.8. Do not wrap the JSON in markdown code fences."""

Step 3: Analyze a single text

Before I process a batch, I wrap the call in a function that enforces JSON mode. This removes the need to strip markdown and guarantees a parseable response.

import json

def analyze_text(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

review = "The onboarding flow is smooth and the UI is gorgeous, but the export feature crashes every time I try to download a PDF."
result = analyze_text(review)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Step 4: Process a batch of reviews

In production, feedback arrives in bursts. I loop over a list of texts, collect results, and catch any parsing errors so one bad response does not kill the entire job. A small sleep between calls keeps you well within rate limits.

import time

reviews = [
    "Absolutely love the new dark mode. My eyes thank you.",
    "Customer support never answered my ticket. Frustrating.",
    "It is okay. Does what it says, but nothing more.",
    "Fast performance, terrible documentation, and the mobile app feels neglected.",
]

def analyze_batch(texts: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for text in texts:
        try:
            out = analyze_text(text)
            out["source_text"] = text
            results.append(out)
        except Exception as e:
            results.append({
                "source_text": text,
                "error": str(e),
                "sentiment": "unknown",
                "confidence": 0.0
            })
        time.sleep(0.5)
    return results

batch_results = analyze_batch(reviews)
for r in batch_results:
    print(f"{r['sentiment']:10} | {r['confidence']:.2f} | {r['source_text'][:50]}...")

Step 5: Filter and surface insights

Raw JSON is not actionable until you query it. I add a helper that surfaces high-confidence negative items needing immediate attention, and prints a simple distribution summary.

def report(results: list[dict]):
    negatives = [
        r for r in results
        if r.get("sentiment") == "negative" and r.get("confidence", 0) > 0.8
    ]
    print(f"High-confidence negative reviews: {len(negatives)}")
    for item in negatives:
        print(f"  - {item['reasoning']}")

    counts = {}
    for r in results:
        s = r.get("sentiment", "unknown")
        counts[s] = counts.get(s, 0) + 1
    print("\nSentiment distribution:", counts)

report(batch_results)

Run it

Save the full script as sentiment.py, swap in your API key, and run python sentiment.py. You should see output similar to this:

{
  "sentiment": "mixed",
  "confidence": 0.92,
  "topics": ["onboarding", "UI", "export feature"],
  "reasoning": "The review praises the onboarding and UI but reports a critical bug in the export feature."
}

positive   | 0.95 | Absolutely love the new dark mode...
negative   | 0.88 | Customer support never answered...
neutral    | 0.72 | It is okay. Does what it says...
mixed      | 0.85 | Fast performance, terrible document...

High-confidence negative reviews: 1
  - The review expresses frustration due to unanswered customer support.
Sentiment distribution: {'positive': 1, 'negative': 1, 'neutral': 1, 'mixed': 1}

If you want to experiment with deeper reasoning, swap the model to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6 in the analyze_text function. Both are available on Oxlo.ai and work with the same client and prompt.

Wrap-up and next steps

This pipeline is already useful as a CLI tool, but the real value comes from integration. My next step would be to wrap analyze_batch in a FastAPI endpoint and POST review webhooks to it, or schedule a daily job that reads from a CSV and writes structured results into a database. You can also switch to a vision model like kimi-k2.6 and pass screenshots of reviews if your feedback lives in image form rather than plain text.

title: Semantic Role Labeling with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Semantic role labeling (SRL) is the task of mapping natural language sentences to predicate-argument structures, identifying who did what to whom. While traditional pipeline models relied on heavy linguistic annotation and task-specific classifiers, large language models now handle predicate-argument extraction through in-context reasoning and structured generation. For teams building production NLP pipelines, the shift to LLMs introduces new engineering questions around prompt design, output serialization, and inference economics, particularly when labeling spans across long documents or multi-turn agentic workflows.

What Is Semantic Role Labeling

At its core, SRL identifies the roles that constituents play relative to a predicate. In the sentence The chef cooked the soup for the guest, the predicate is cooked, The chef is the Agent, the soup is the Patient, and the guest is the Beneficiary. Traditional frameworks like PropBank and FrameNet established ontologies for these roles, but implementing them historically required training sequential taggers or dependency parsers on annotated corpora. These systems were brittle across domains and required feature engineering for every new genre. LLMs remove much of that scaffolding by encoding broad syntactic and semantic knowledge during pretraining, allowing them to infer roles from plain text instructions rather than hand-tuned feature templates.

Why LLMs Change the Game

Modern LLMs perform SRL in zero-shot or few-shot settings without task-specific fine-tuning. A well-constructed prompt can elicit structured role assignments across diverse predicates, including nominalizations and light-verb constructions that confuse classical taggers. Because context windows now routinely exceed 100K tokens, a single request can carry an entire document, a user query, and a detailed role schema. This is especially useful for document-level SRL, where arguments may be separated by paragraphs and coreference must be resolved implicitly. The bottleneck shifts from model capacity to inference cost and latency, particularly when prompts grow to accommodate full chapters, legal contracts, or medical records.

Architectures for LLM-Based SRL

There are three common patterns for deploying LLMs in SRL pipelines.

Direct prompting with JSON mode. The simplest approach sends a system prompt defining the role taxonomy, followed by the target text, and requests a JSON object containing predicates and their arguments. Constrained decoding ensures valid output syntax, which simplifies downstream parsing and database ingestion.

Function calling and tool use. For applications that integrate SRL into larger agent workflows, function calling lets the model emit structured role annotations as arguments to a registered tool. This is useful when the SRL step must trigger a database lookup, a retrieval-augmented generation pass, or a validation callback before the pipeline continues.

Agentic multi-turn pipelines. Complex documents may require iterative extraction. An agent can perform an initial pass to identify predicates, then issue follow-up requests to resolve ambiguous arguments or cross-sentence coreference. Multi-turn conversations and streaming responses keep latency manageable while breaking a long document into structured reasoning steps without overwhelming a single context window.

Prompt Engineering for Predicate-Argument Structures

The difference between noisy and accurate SRL often comes down to prompt specificity. Rather than asking the model to "label roles," provide explicit definitions and examples in the system message.

System: You are a semantic role labeler. Given a sentence, return a JSON
object with a "predicates" array. Each predicate must include the verb
lemma, its text span, and an "arguments" array. Each argument must include
the role (Agent, Patient, Instrument, Beneficiary, Location, Time), the
text span, and start/end character offsets.

User: The engineer fixed the server with a screwdriver at midnight.

For sentences containing multiple predicates, instruct the model to return all predicates in a single structured object rather than generating free text. JSON mode enforces this contract. If the target domain uses a custom ontology, supply three to five examples in the prompt. Few-shot examples anchor the model to the desired granularity and reduce hallucinated role labels. For sentences with nested or coordinated clauses, explicitly ask the model to preserve token indices so downstream components can reconstruct exact spans.

Infrastructure Considerations for Production SRL

Running SRL in production means sending large prompts to an API, often thousands of tokens per request. On token-based inference platforms, costs scale linearly with input length. Providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale bill per token, so labeling roles in long documents or running iterative agent loops becomes expensive quickly.

Oxlo.ai offers a different model: request-based pricing with one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context SRL and agentic workloads, this can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives because a 10,000-token prompt costs the same as a 100-token prompt. You can pass entire documents, detailed role schemas, and few-shot example galleries without watching the meter run on every input token.

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK. For SRL specifically, model selection depends on your context and reasoning requirements. Qwen 3 32B offers strong multilingual reasoning and agent workflows for cross-lingual corpora. Llama 3.3 70B serves as a reliable general-purpose workhorse. When you need to process entire reports or books in one pass, Kimi K2.6 provides a 131K context window, and DeepSeek V4 Flash supports up to 1M tokens with an efficient MoE architecture. For reasoning-intensive domains like legal or biomedical text, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Kimi K2.5, or Kimi K2 Thinking deliver advanced chain-of-thought reasoning that improves argument boundary detection.

Switching to Oxlo.ai is a drop-in replacement. Change your base URL and API key, and existing OpenAI SDK code continues to work with no refactoring.

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are a semantic role labeler. Return JSON only."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "The committee approved the budget after midnight."
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    stream=False
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, vision, and multi-turn conversations, so you can build everything from simple extractors to autonomous annotation agents. There are no cold starts on popular models, which keeps latency predictable for synchronous pipeline steps. To compare plans, visit the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Evaluation and Iteration

SRL quality is measured with per-role precision, recall, and F1 against a gold standard. When using LLMs, start by evaluating zero-shot performance on a held-out set. If certain roles, such as Instrument or Beneficiary, show low recall, add targeted few-shot examples to the prompt rather than fine-tuning the model. Track token counts separately from accuracy, because a more verbose prompt may improve F1 but destroy your economics on a token-based provider. On Oxlo.ai, the flat per-request pricing insulates your evaluation budget from prompt length, so you can iterate on elaborate instructions and few-shot galleries without cost surprises.

Conclusion

Semantic role labeling has evolved from a pipeline of specialized taggers to a structured generation task for large language models. The engineering challenge is no longer feature extraction but prompt design, output constraint, and inference cost management at scale. For teams running long-context or agentic SRL workloads, Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first platform with flat request-based pricing, broad model selection, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility. Whether you are labeling news articles, legal contracts, or clinical notes, the combination of precise prompting and predictable pricing makes production SRL both feasible and economical.

Customer service is one of the most immediate, high-impact environments for large language models. Support teams manage high volumes of repetitive inquiries, complex escalation paths, and multilingual conversations that demand both speed and accuracy. When implemented well, LLMs can handle tier-1 triage, draft contextual responses, and orchestrate multi-step agentic workflows without human intervention. The challenge is not whether language models can do the work, but how to deploy them without letting infrastructure costs erase the business case.

The Case for LLMs in Customer Service

Modern support centers operate as real-time data pipelines. A single ticket can contain a customer’s purchase history, previous threads, policy documents, and screenshots. LLMs excel at synthesizing this unstructured information into coherent action. They classify intent, extract entities, generate personalized replies, and call external tools to update CRM records or query inventory.

The shift toward agentic AI makes this even more relevant. Rather than generating a static reply, an LLM can reason through a problem, invoke functions to check order status, and decide whether to issue a refund or escalate to a human specialist. Dependency parsing remains a foundational task in natural language processing, converting raw text into directed graphs that encode grammatical relationships between tokens. Classical systems rely on transition-based or graph-based architectures trained on annotated treebanks such as Universal Dependencies. The Mechanics of Dependency Parsing

Relations follow frameworks such as Universal Dependencies, which define labels like nsubj, obj, obl, and amod. Traditional parsers, including arc-eager transition systems or graph-based biaffine attention models, process fixed-context windows and depend heavily on gold annotations. LLMs invert this dynamic. Instead of learning explicit scoring functions over arcs, the model generates the entire tree structure conditioned on a prompt and its pretrained knowledge of grammar, morphology, and cross-lingual syntax.

title: LLMs for Named Entity Recognition: Applications and Best Practices
content:
Named Entity Recognition has evolved from hand-crafted rules and BiLSTM-CRF architectures into a programmable interface supported by large language models. Traditional NER pipelines require extensive labeled datasets, fixed tag schemas, and domain-specific feature engineering. Modern LLMs bypass much of this overhead by extracting entities through zero-shot instructions or a small set of examples. For engineering teams building document intelligence, conversational agents, or knowledge graphs, LLMs offer a flexible alternative that adapts to new entity types without retraining the entire model.

Why LLMs Change NER

The primary advantage of using LLMs for NER is instruction following. A classical CRF or BiLSTM model is bound to the tags it was trained on, typically PER, ORG, LOC, and MISC. If a product team needs to extract proprietary part numbers, biomedical terms, or regulatory clauses, retraining is mandatory. An LLM accepts arbitrary schemas: you can ask it to extract all firmware versions mentioned in a support ticket, or every contractual obligation with its associated deadline. This shifts NER from a static classification problem to a dynamic extraction task.

LLMs also improve disambiguation through broader context. A standalone CRF model processing the token Jordan in a narrow window may tag it as a person. An LLM reading the full paragraph can infer whether the reference is to a person, a country, or a brand. The ability to resolve coreference across long passages reduces fragmentation errors common in sliding-window NER systems.

Prompting Patterns and Structured Output

Reliable NER at scale depends on structured output. Unstructured text responses require brittle regex parsing and are prone to format drift. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode across its chat models, which lets you constrain the model to return valid JSON containing your entity schema.

Below is a minimal example using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai. You only need to change the base URL and select a model.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a precise NER system. Extract entities as JSON "
                "with keys: person, organization, location, date."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Apple Inc. is planning to open a new office in Austin "
                "by March 2026. Tim Cook announced the expansion."
            )
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    temperature=0.1

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, existing Python or Node.js NER pipelines require only a two-line change: point base_url to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and swap the model string.

Long-Context and Document-Level NER

Many real-world NER tasks involve long documents. Legal contracts, clinical discharge summaries, and financial filings often exceed the context limits of older transformer models. When text is broken into chunks, cross-sentence references are lost. An entity introduced on page one and referenced by pronoun on page five becomes untraceable.

Oxlo.ai hosts models specifically suited to long-context NER. DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a 1 million token context window, and Kimi K2.6 supports 131K tokens with advanced reasoning and vision capabilities. For multilingual document sets, Qwen 3 32B provides strong multilingual reasoning. These context windows allow you to pass an entire document in a single request and ask the model to extract entities with global awareness.

This is where request-based pricing becomes a structural advantage. Token-based providers scale cost linearly with input length, which makes long-document NER prohibitively expensive. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so processing a 50,000 token legal brief costs the same as a 500 token email. For organizations running document-level NER at volume, that pricing model can reduce costs significantly for long-context workloads. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

Model Selection for NER Workloads

Not every NER task requires the largest reasoning model. Simple schema extraction from well-formed English text can run efficiently on Llama 3.3 70B or DeepSeek V3.2. For ambiguous domains where entities overlap or require implicit reasoning, such as parsing insurance claims or research citations, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2 Thinking provide deeper chain-of-thought reasoning. If your input is a scanned PDF or screenshot, vision models like Kimi VL A3B or Gemma 3 27B can perform OCR and NER in a single pass.

Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across these categories with no cold starts on popular variants. That means you can route simple NER to a fast model and complex extraction to a reasoning model without managing separate infrastructure or waiting for container spin-up.

Evaluation and Operational Best Practices

Moving NER to LLMs changes how you measure quality. Traditional token-level F1 is less relevant when the model outputs structured JSON. Instead, measure entity-level precision, recall, and F1. A partial match, such as extracting Apple instead of Apple Inc., may be acceptable depending on the downstream application.

To improve consistency, keep temperature low and use constrained decoding via JSON mode. Hallucinations remain a risk: an LLM may invent an entity not present in the source text. Mitigate this by validating extracted strings against the original document, or by adding a secondary verification step. Normalization is equally important. The model may return IBM, International Business Machines, and I.B.M. in different requests. A post-processing layer that maps variants to a canonical knowledge base ID prevents entity duplication in your database.

Because NER often serves as a preprocessing stage in larger pipelines, cost predictability matters. Oxlo.ai request-based pricing makes it straightforward to forecast expenses for agentic workflows where each step triggers an API call.

Integrating NER into Agentic Pipelines

NER is rarely the final deliverable. It usually feeds retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graph construction, or compliance monitoring. You can combine NER with function calling so that extracted entities trigger immediate downstream actions. For example, after extracting a company name and date from a news article, the model can call a search tool to pull stock ticker data.

Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use across its chat models, and its OpenAI-compatible endpoints work with orchestration frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex. If you are already using the OpenAI SDK for tool-based agents, switching to Oxlo.ai requires only updating the client configuration.

Conclusion

LLMs have turned Named Entity Recognition from a rigid classification task into a flexible, instruction-driven API. By choosing the right prompting strategy, enforcing structured output, and selecting models matched to your context length and reasoning requirements, you can build NER pipelines that adapt faster than traditional approaches. Oxlo.ai provides the model diversity, long-context capacity, and flat per-request pricing that make it a strong fit for both ad-hoc extraction and high-volume document processing. With full OpenAI SDK compatibility and no cold starts, you can integrate it into existing codebases today.

title: Dialogue Systems with LLMs: A Comprehensive Overview
content:
Modern dialogue systems have moved beyond rigid slot-filling frameworks and handcrafted intent classifiers. Today, large language models serve as the central reasoning layer for conversational agents, handling open-domain chitchat, task-oriented customer support, and complex multi-step agentic workflows in a single unified architecture. This shift simplifies development but introduces new engineering challenges around context retention, tool integration, and inference cost scaling. Building production-grade dialogue systems now requires a deliberate balance between model capability, retrieval infrastructure, and serving economics.

From Modular Pipelines to End-to-End LLMs

Traditional spoken dialogue systems relied on modular pipelines: automatic speech recognition fed into natural language understanding, which updated a dialog state tracker, triggered a policy manager, and finally generated a response through a natural language generation module. Each component required separate training data, maintenance, and error handling. Cascading failures were common.

LLMs collapsed this stack. A single model can now parse user intent, maintain state across turns, query external APIs, and generate coherent responses. This end-to-end approach reduces system complexity and improves generalization to out-of-distribution user utterances. However, it places enormous pressure on the model's context window and the inference backend. Long conversations accumulate history rapidly, and agentic loops that include tool results can expand prompt length by orders of magnitude.

Retrieval Augmented Generation

For knowledge-grounded dialogue, retrieval augmented generation remains the dominant pattern. Instead of relying solely on parametric knowledge, the system retrieves relevant documents from a vector store and injects them into the prompt. For multi-turn conversations, retrieval must be turn-aware. A user might reference "the second option" from three turns ago, so the retrieval layer needs to account for conversational coreference and evolving intent. Hybrid search combining dense embeddings with keyword matching usually outperforms pure vector search for task-oriented dialogue.

Function Calling and Tool Use

Task-oriented agents require structured interaction with external systems. Function calling lets the model emit JSON schemas to query databases, check calendars, or trigger actions. In dialogue settings, this creates agentic loops: the model generates a function call, the application executes it, and the result returns as a new message in the conversation history. These tool-result messages add tokens quickly. A single booking flow might involve five or six turns, each with a lengthy JSON payload. Inference providers that charge per token can make such interactions prohibitively expensive at scale.

Context Management and Memory

Not every prior turn deserves space in the context window. Production systems implement memory hierarchies: a sliding window for recent turns, a summarization module for older conversation phases, and a key-value store for user-specific facts. When a conversation exceeds the model's context limit, selective summarization or truncation strategies prevent silent data loss. For models with very large context windows, such as those supporting 128K tokens or more, developers can often keep full history in memory, but this only remains economical if the serving layer does not linearly scale cost with input length.

title: LLM vs Traditional Machine Learning: What's the Difference?
content:
What we are building

I built a support ticket triage script that runs a classic TF-IDF classifier and an LLM pipeline side by side. If you are deciding between traditional machine learning and a large language model for text classification, this project shows exactly where each one breaks and where Oxlo.ai fits in.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • pip install openai scikit-learn
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Step 1: Build a traditional ML classifier with scikit-learn

Traditional ML pipelines need labeled data, feature engineering, and a fixed set of output classes. I trained a Logistic Regression model on TF-IDF vectors from nine synthetic support tickets. This is the classic approach: convert text to numbers, then fit a linear separator. The TfidfVectorizer strips common English stop words and caps the vocabulary at fifty terms, which mimics the constraints of a real production system where memory and latency matter. Once the pipeline is fitted, prediction is deterministic and runs locally in a few microseconds. That speed is why teams still deploy TF-IDF or gradient boosted models for high volume, low complexity filtering. The catch is that any concept outside those fifty terms is invisible to the model.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

training_data = [
    ("My payment failed and I got charged twice", "billing"),
    ("How do I reset my password", "account"),
    ("The API returns a 500 error on every request", "technical"),
    ("I want to upgrade my plan", "billing"),
    ("Cannot log in with SSO", "account"),
    ("Latency is over 10 seconds in us-east-1", "technical"),
    ("Refund for last month", "billing"),
    ("Invite team members button is missing", "account"),
    ("Webhook not firing after update", "technical"),
]

texts, labels = zip(*training_data)

traditional_clf = make_pipeline(
    TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_features=50),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)
traditional_clf.fit(texts, labels)

def classify_traditional(text):
    return traditional_clf.predict([text])[0]

Step 2: See where traditional ML falls short

Real tickets are messy. Users describe multiple problems in one sentence, use slang, or paste stack traces. I created three edge cases that blend billing, account, and technical language to see how the classifier behaves. The first ticket mentions a declined card, duplicate subscriptions, and API rate limits. A human reader sees two separate issues, but the vectorizer blends them into a single bag of words.

edge_cases = [
    "My card was declined so I tried again and now the dashboard says I have two subscriptions but the API still shows 429 rate limit errors",
    "I am locked out and also I think someone hacked my account because I see API keys I did not create",
    "Your status page shows green but my integration is down and I need a refund for the downtime",
]

print("Traditional ML results:")
for ticket in edge_cases:
    print(f"  {ticket[:50]}... -> {classify_traditional(ticket)}")

When I ran this block, the classifier forced every ticket into one bucket. The first ticket has equal billing and technical signals, yet the model returned a single label with no confidence score, no summary, and no suggestion for what to do next. That is the fundamental limit of traditional ML on unstructured text. It classifies, but it does not understand.

Step 3: Build the LLM triage agent

Large language models do not need retraining on my nine examples. They reason about intent, detect multiple issues in one message, and can return structured data. I use Oxlo.ai because its request-based pricing means I pay one flat cost per ticket, not per token. When users paste hundred-line log files or forward entire email threads, the price stays predictable. That pricing model flips the economics of agentic workflows: you can stuff as much context as the model allows without watching a meter run on every word. I also do not have to maintain a separate embedding layer or model artifact. The entire reasoning engine is hosted on Oxlo.ai and accessed through the standard OpenAI SDK.

Here is the system prompt I used:

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Read the ticket and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- primary_category: one of [billing, account, technical]
- secondary_category: another category if present, else null
- urgency: low, medium, or high
- summary: one sentence describing the issue
- next_action: what a human should do first

Return only valid JSON, no markdown."""

Now I wire it to Oxlo.ai through the OpenAI SDK. I picked Llama 3.3 70B because it follows system instructions tightly and starts instantly with no cold starts.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_llm(ticket_text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

Notice the difference in code size. The LLM pipeline is shorter than the training script, yet it handles ambiguity out of the box. I did not vectorize anything or tune a regularization parameter.

Step 4: Compare both approaches on real tickets

I ran the same three edge cases through the LLM. Instead of a single label, I got back JSON with dual categories, urgency ratings, and next actions. The model recognized that a refund request embedded inside a technical outage report contains two distinct work streams. It also wrote a one-line summary and suggested a concrete first action, such as checking the account audit log or escalating to the on-call engineer.

print("LLM results via Oxlo.ai:")
for ticket in edge_cases:
    result = classify_llm(ticket)
    print(f"Ticket: {ticket[:50]}...")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    print()

The traditional ML model saw keywords and voted. The LLM read the ticket, inferred context, and produced a mini-workflow. That is the practical gap between statistical pattern matching and generative reasoning.

Run it

Here is the complete script. Save it as triage_compare.py, export your YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY, and run it. The script keeps both pipelines in memory so you can A/B test your own tickets by appending strings to the edge_cases list.

import json
from openai import OpenAI
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

training_data = [
    ("My payment failed and I got charged twice", "billing"),
    ("How do I reset my password", "account"),
    ("The API returns a 500 error on every request", "technical"),
    ("I want to upgrade my plan", "billing"),
    ("Cannot log in with SSO", "account"),
    ("Latency is over 10 seconds in us-east-1", "technical"),
    ("Refund for last month", "billing"),
    ("Invite team members button is missing", "account"),
    ("Webhook not firing after update", "technical"),
]
texts, labels = zip(*training_data)

traditional_clf = make_pipeline(
    TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_features=50),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)
traditional_clf.fit(texts, labels)

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Read the ticket and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- primary_category: one of [billing, account, technical]
- secondary_category: another category if present, else null
- urgency: low, medium, or high
- summary: one sentence describing the issue
- next_action: what a human should do first

Return only valid JSON, no markdown."""

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_traditional(text):
    return traditional_clf.predict([text])[0]

def classify_llm(ticket_text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

edge_cases = [
    "My card was declined so I tried again and now the dashboard says I have two subscriptions but the API still shows 429 rate limit errors",
    "I am locked out and also I think someone hacked my account because I see API keys I did not create",
    "Your status page shows green but my integration is down and I need a refund for the downtime",
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for ticket in edge_cases:
        trad = classify_traditional(ticket)
        llm_result = classify_llm(ticket)
        print(f"Ticket: {ticket[:60]}...")
        print(f"  Traditional ML: {trad}")
        print(f"  LLM (Oxlo.ai):  primary={llm_result['primary_category']}, secondary={llm_result.get('secondary_category')}, urgency={llm_result['urgency']}")
        print()

Expected output looks like this. Your exact JSON may vary slightly depending on model temperature, but the key observation is consistent: the LLM surfaces dual intent while the classifier collapses everything to one label.

Ticket: My card was declined so I tried again and now the dash...
  Traditional ML: billing
  LLM (Oxlo.ai):  primary=billing, secondary=technical, urgency=high

Ticket: I am locked out and also I think someone hacked my acco...
  Traditional ML: account
  LLM (Oxlo.ai):  primary=account, secondary=technical, urgency=high

Ticket: Your status page shows green but my integration is dow...
  Traditional ML: technical
  LLM (Oxlo.ai):  primary=technical, secondary=billing, urgency=high

Wrap-up

Traditional ML is still the right choice when you have a narrow, stable problem and need millisecond latency on commodity hardware. It is deterministic, explainable, and cheap to host at massive scale. For everything else, LLMs remove the feature engineering tax and handle edge cases without retraining. The trade-off is a network round trip and a nondeterministic output, which is why I route simple keyword matches to the old pipeline and send ambiguous tickets to Oxlo.ai. If you are building a tiered system, Oxlo.ai works as the drop-in reasoning layer without rewriting your ingestion code.

Two concrete next steps. First, add Oxlo.ai function calling to the agent so it opens a Jira ticket or Slack thread automatically instead of just returning JSON. Second, swap in qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 to test whether a different architecture changes the urgency ratings on your own data. Both run on the same flat request pricing, so experimentation is cheap. If you are processing thousands of tickets daily, look at the Oxlo.ai Premium plan for priority queueing and higher daily request limits.
