title: The Disadvantages of Using Large Language Models
content:
Large language models have become the default building block for modern AI applications, but treating them as universal tools ignores a growing list of engineering trade-offs. Infrastructure teams know that the hype cycle focuses on capabilities, while production reality is defined by constraints. Uncertain costs, variable latency, hard context limits, probabilistic errors, and integration friction can turn a promising prototype into an operational liability. Understanding these disadvantages is not an argument against using LLMs. It is a prerequisite for using them responsibly in production systems.

Unpredictable Inference Costs

Token-based pricing dominates the inference market. Providers charge per input and output token, which means your bill scales linearly with prompt length, conversation history, and the verbosity of the model. A single long-document summarization task, a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline with chunked context, or an agentic loop with tool schemas and memory can consume tens of thousands of tokens in one request. When user inputs are variable, forecasting spend becomes a statistical modeling exercise rather than a fixed line item.

This unpredictability creates tension between product quality and finance. Engineering teams are forced to trim context windows, limit conversation history, or compress prompts purely to control costs. Agentic architectures, which rely on extensive tool definitions and multi-turn memory, are especially vulnerable to bill shock because every added capability increases token count.

Oxlo.ai replaces token math with request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of how long the prompt is. For long-context and agentic workloads, this model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives because cost does not scale with input length. You can send full documents, maintain extended memory, and expose rich tool definitions without rewriting your budget forecast. Details are available on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Latency and Operational Friction

Latency in LLM APIs comes from more than model size. Cold starts, queue depth, and dynamic batching strategies can inject unpredictable delays between your request and the first streamed token. In a customer-facing chat interface, a multi-second wait for the first response is often indistinguishable from a downtime event. Many serverless inference platforms scale to zero to save GPU resources, leaving early requests to pay the full warm-up cost. That pattern works for batch jobs, but it breaks real-time applications.

Beyond first-token latency, operational friction includes retry storms, rate-limit backoff logic, and provider-specific error handling. Each additional failure mode adds complexity to your client code and observability stack.

Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models and offers streaming responses so you can push tokens to the client immediately. The API is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, which means switching providers does not require rewriting your client logic. In most cases, you change the base URL and API key.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain request-based pricing."}],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

Because the endpoint schema is identical to the OpenAI specification, your existing retry logic, timeout handlers, and streaming parsers continue to work without modification.

Context Window Constraints and Memory Costs

Even when cost is not the primary concern, context windows impose hard architectural limits. Most applications cannot fit an entire codebase, a lengthy legal contract, or a multi-hour conversation transcript into a single prompt. When the input exceeds the model's limit, you must chunk, summarize, or retrieve selectively. Each workaround introduces complexity, latency, and potential information loss. Retrieval-augmented generation is the standard mitigation, but it adds a vector database, embedding pipeline, and ranking layer to your stack.

Long-context models are narrowing this gap, yet under token-based pricing they are often too expensive to use at their full capacity. You are architecturally encouraged to keep inputs short, even when the model could theoretically process more.

Oxlo.ai hosts models built for extended memory, including DeepSeek V4 Flash with a 1 million token context window and Kimi K2.6 with 131K context. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, utilizing those large windows does not trigger a surcharge for every additional sentence. You can experiment with true long-context architectures, reduce your reliance on complex chunking pipelines, and still maintain predictable unit economics.

Hallucinations and Deterministic Limits

LLMs are probabilistic autoregressive systems. They do not retrieve facts from a verified database. They predict the next token based on patterns observed during training. That fundamental mechanism means hallucinations are not bugs to be patched out. They are an inherent property of the technology. In production, this translates to code that looks correct but fails silently, citations that point to nonexistent sources, and reasoning chains that arrive at confident but wrong conclusions.

Scaling model size does not eliminate this problem. Larger models may sound more authoritative, but authority is not accuracy. Mitigation requires engineering discipline rather than model selection alone. You need structured outputs, tool use for external verification, and retrieval systems grounded in authoritative data.

Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling across its chat models, letting you constrain generations to valid schemas and delegate factual lookups to deterministic APIs. Models like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2 Thinking expose advanced chain-of-thought reasoning, which lets you audit the model's path before accepting its conclusion. These features reduce surface area for errors, but no model eliminates the need for application-level validation and human oversight.

Vendor Lock-in and Integration Rigidity

Adopting a proprietary API often means accepting custom SDKs, nonstandard parameters, and inference behaviors that differ subtly from open alternatives. Over time, your codebase accumulates provider-specific logic that makes migration expensive. If pricing changes, model versions deprecate, service quality degrades, or rate limits tighten, you are trapped by sunk integration costs.

Open-weight models reduce some of this risk by giving you portable artifacts, but the inference layer can still lock you in if the serving API is bespoke. A more resilient approach is to build against a standard interface from the start.

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible across Python, Node.js, and cURL. The endpoints follow the same schema as the OpenAI API, including chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech. You can prototype against one provider and move inference to Oxlo.ai without refactoring your data structures, rewriting your streaming logic, or retuning your prompt templates. That compatibility is an insurance policy against provider-specific lock-in.

When to Skip the LLM Entirely

Not every AI task requires a 70 billion parameter language model. Using an LLM for image classification, keyword search, or voice transcription is architecturally wasteful. Specialized models often deliver better accuracy, lower latency, and more predictable behavior at a fraction of the complexity.

For semantic search, embeddings such as BGE-Large and E5-Large on Oxlo.ai provide dense vector representations without invoking a chat model. For image generation, Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Flux.1, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 offer dedicated diffusion pipelines. For real-time object detection, YOLOv9 and YOLOv11 run inference optimized for vision, not language. Routing the right workload to the right model category keeps your stack simpler and your costs proportionate to the task.

Conclusion

Large language models are powerful abstractions, but they are not universal solutions. Unpredictable token costs, cold-start latency, finite context windows, inherent hallucinations, and integration rigidity are constraints that shape how reliable systems are built. The goal is not to avoid LLMs, but to containerize their risks through predictable pricing, standard interfaces, structured outputs, and workload-appropriate model selection.

Oxlo.ai addresses these disadvantages directly. Request-based pricing removes the cost penalty for long prompts and agentic loops. No cold starts keep latency consistent. title: LLM for Natural Language Processing: Applications and Use Cases
content:
Large language models have become the default computational substrate for modern natural language processing. What began with static word embeddings and recurrent architectures has evolved into generalist systems capable of reasoning, code generation, and multi-turn dialogue. For engineering teams shipping NLP pipelines today, the challenge is no longer proving that transformers work. It is selecting the right model, managing context windows that routinely exceed 100,000 tokens, and controlling inference costs that scale unpredictably with input length. The infrastructure decision is now as important as the model choice because a poorly chosen provider can turn a feasible product into a cost center.

Core NLP Applications

Production NLP still relies on fundamental tasks: sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, text summarization, translation, and semantic classification. LLMs handle these through prompt engineering or lightweight fine-tuning rather than task-specific architectures. A single model like Llama 3.3 70B can classify support tickets, extract entities from legal contracts, and summarize research papers without retraining. This consolidation reduces model sprawl but places new demands on inference infrastructure. You need low latency for real-time classification and reliable JSON mode for structured extraction pipelines. Streaming responses matter when building interactive dashboards that process feeds in real time. Platforms that expose chat/completions endpoints with JSON mode, streaming, and multi-turn state make it possible to replace legacy NLP stacks with a unified API rather than maintaining separate services for each task. The result is fewer deployed artifacts and a simpler operational surface.

Advanced Reasoning and Agentic Workflows

Beyond classification, modern NLP applications require multi-step reasoning. Chain-of-thought models such as DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Kimi K2.5, and Kimi K2 Thinking expose intermediate reasoning traces that improve accuracy on complex question answering, policy analysis, and mathematical derivation. Agentic workflows extend this by allowing models to invoke external tools through function calling. A research assistant built on GLM 5 or Minimax M2.5 can parse a user query, generate a search plan, call an embedding or retrieval API, and synthesize a cited answer. These patterns require robust tool-use support and stable multi-turn conversation state. When evaluating providers, verify that function calling is first-class and that cold starts do not break interaction loops. Latency spikes in agentic chains compound quickly across tool calls, so consistent response times are critical for user experience.

Long-Context and Document Intelligence

Enterprise NLP increasingly means document intelligence: analyzing annual reports, parsing medical records, or auditing codebases with contexts that span hundreds of pages. Models such as Kimi K2.6 offer 131K context windows, while DeepSeek V4 Flash supports 1M tokens, enabling single-pass analysis of entire repositories or lengthy transcripts without chunking logic. Traditional token-based pricing penalizes these workloads because every input token incurs cost. For long-context and agentic applications, request-based pricing decouples cost from prompt length, making extensive document analysis economically viable. This structural difference matters when a single prompt contains a full textbook, a complete system log, or a long customer conversation history. Inference platforms that charge per request allow engineers to pass entire documents rather than designing fragile summarization pre-processing steps solely to save money. That freedom changes architectural decisions.

Code and Multimodal NLP

Natural language processing now routinely intersects with code and vision. Qwen 3 Coder 30B and DeepSeek Coder handle code generation, documentation, and bug fixing as structured language tasks. Vision-language models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B process charts, diagrams, and screenshots alongside text, enabling automated form extraction, accessibility alt-text generation, and visual question answering. These multimodal tasks require endpoints that accept image inputs and return structured data. A unified platform offering chat/completions, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and embeddings simplifies architecture by routing diverse NLP tasks through one SDK. Audio models like Whisper Large v3 extend NLP to spoken language, while embedding models such as BGE-Large power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines that feed back into LLM context. title: Advantages and Benefits of Using LLM
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage agent that reads raw customer emails and returns structured JSON with priority, sentiment, a one-line summary, and a draft reply. I shipped this last quarter to replace a manual sorting queue that was delaying our first response time by four hours on average. It is a practical demonstration of the core advantages that make LLMs production-ready: natural language understanding, structured generation, and scalable automation without hand-tuned classifiers.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. We will run every model through Oxlo.ai because its flat per-request pricing keeps costs identical whether the ticket is two sentences or a twenty-message thread. That predictability matters when you are processing hundreds of tickets a day, and the full OpenAI SDK compatibility means we only change the base URL.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

I start by instantiating the client against Oxlo.ai and running a smoke test. I use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows system instructions reliably and starts instantly with no cold starts on Oxlo.ai.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello and confirm you are online."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt acts as the schema and behavior contract. I force raw JSON output so downstream Python can parse the result with json.loads instead of wrestling with regex. I keep the prompt short and explicit. In my experience, verbose prompts encourage the model to add conversational filler before or after the JSON, which breaks the parser.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Analyze the customer email below and respond with a single JSON object containing exactly these keys:
- priority: one of low, medium, high, critical
- sentiment: one of happy, neutral, frustrated, angry
- summary: a 12-word or fewer description of the problem
- draft_reply: a professional, empathetic response the support team can send

Rules:
1. Output only valid JSON. No markdown fences, no explanations.
2. If the customer mentions outage, breach, or legal threat, set priority to critical.
3. Keep draft_reply under 150 words."""

Step 3: Parse a single ticket

I wrap the API call in a small function so the rest of the codebase does not need to know about LLMs. The flat per-request pricing on Oxlo.ai is useful here. Even when a customer forwards a month-long email thread, the cost does not scale with input length, so I pass the entire raw text without counting tokens or truncating early. In production I wrap json.loads in a retry with a stricter prompt, but for this tutorial the direct parse is sufficient because Llama 3.3 70B respects the system prompt consistently on Oxlo.ai.

import json

def triage_ticket(raw_email: str) -> dict:
    client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": raw_email},
        ],
    )
    
    content = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(content)

# Test with a realistic ticket
email = """Subject: WTF is going on??
I have been waiting 3 days for a response to my refund request.
Your billing page is broken and I was charged twice. Fix this now
or I am disputing the charge with my bank."""

result = triage_ticket(email)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Step 4: Batch process with model routing

Not every ticket needs the same reasoning horsepower. I route routine questions to DeepSeek V3.2 and escalate emotionally charged or complex threads to Kimi K2.6. I could use a cheaper classifier for routing, but a keyword check is good enough for a v1 and removes one network hop. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing rather than token-based pricing, sending a long conversation history to the stronger model costs the same flat fee as a short ping. That makes intelligent routing economically viable.

def route_and_triage(raw_email: str) -> dict:
    client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
    
    # Simple keyword router
    escalated = any(k in raw_email.lower() for k in ["angry", "lawsuit", "outage", "breach", "dispute"])
    model = "kimi-k2.6" if escalated else "deepseek-v3.2"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": raw_email},
        ],
    )
    
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

tickets = [
    "How do I reset my password? I cannot find the link.",
    "Your platform leaked our data. Our legal team is involved.",
]

for t in tickets:
    out = route_and_triage(t)
    print(out["priority"], out["summary"])

Step 5: Add a human review buffer

Until the agent has proven itself, I gate critical priority items behind a human review step instead of auto-sending replies. This keeps the tool useful while avoiding liability on day one. The JSON format makes this filter a one-line comparison. I also log the full JSON to SQLite for audit purposes. Regulators and finance teams love an immutable log of why an AI marked something critical, and the structured output makes that trivial.

def process_queue(tickets: list[str]):
    for raw in tickets:
        result = route_and_triage(raw)
        
        if result["priority"] == "critical":
            print("[HUMAN REVIEW REQUIRED]", result["summary"])
        else:
            print("[AUTO-DRAFT]", result["draft_reply"][:60] + "...")

process_queue(tickets)

Run it

Running the script against the angry refund email from Step 3 produces this output. The model correctly flags the legal threat, identifies the sentiment, and generates a reply that buys time without making promises I cannot keep. Notice that the summary is exactly twelve words and the draft reply stays under the 150-word limit, which shows the model is following constraints rather than hallucinating open-ended text.

$ python triage.py
{
  "priority": "critical",
  "sentiment": "angry",
  "summary": "Customer double-billed, demands refund after 3-day silence.",
  "draft_reply": "I sincerely apologize for the delay and the duplicate charge. I have escalated this to our billing team and initiated a full refund. You will see the credit within 2 business days. I will personally follow up tomorrow to confirm."
}

Next steps

Wire the process_queue function into a Slack incoming webhook so critical tickets post to an on-call channel in real time. If you want to run this continuously, deploy it as a FastAPI service and point your helpdesk webhook at it. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing means your bill grows with ticket volume, not with the length of customer rants, which is the right cost model for an ingestion pipeline. Another concrete upgrade is a feedback loop: store every draft_reply that a human edits, then fine-tune a lightweight model on Oxlo.ai with those corrections so the agent gradually matches your team's voice.

title: LLM for Text Generation: A Guide with Oxlo.ai
content:
Today we are building a command-line tool that turns raw meeting notes into polished Markdown reports. It reads a JSON file of bullet points and uses an LLM on Oxlo.ai to produce structured summaries you can paste straight into Notion or GitHub. If your team wastes time reformatting notes, this will give you a reusable generator in under an hour. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request instead of per token, you can feed it long transcripts without watching the cost climb.

What you'll need

Before starting, grab Python 3.10 or newer and install the OpenAI SDK. You will also need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai; the platform is fully OpenAI-compatible, so no extra client libraries are required. I recommend setting your key as an environment variable rather than hard-coding it. If you want to see how the flat request pricing compares to your current provider, check https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

pip install openai
export OXLO_API_KEY="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

I always start by verifying the connection with a minimal ping. This confirms my API key and base URL are correct before I add any logic.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say 'Connection OK'"}],
    max_tokens=10,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Lock in the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training the generator gets. I keep it in a dedicated constant so I can tweak tone and format without touching business logic.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical writer. Your job is to convert raw meeting notes into a structured Markdown report.

Follow these rules:
- Use a level-1 heading for the meeting title.
- List attendees as a bullet list.
- Write a short "Key Takeaways" section.
- Write an "Action Items" section with checkboxes.
- Use professional but concise language.
- Do not invent facts. If the notes are unclear, write 'Details needed'."""

Step 3: Ingest the raw notes

I store notes as a dictionary with three fields: title, attendees, and bullets. A small helper builds the user message payload that the model will actually see.

def build_user_message(notes):
    lines = [
        f"Meeting Title: {notes['title']}",
        f"Attendees: {', '.join(notes['attendees'])}",
        "Raw Notes:",
    ]
    lines.extend(f"- {b}" for b in notes["bullets"])
    return "\n".join(lines)

# Inline test data so the script runs without external files
notes = {
    "title": "Q3 Roadmap Sync",
    "attendees": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
    "bullets": [
        "Discussed migration from legacy auth to OAuth2",
        "Bob to prepare test plan by Friday",
        "Need to evaluate Oxlo.ai for batch inference",
        "Next sync scheduled for July 15",
    ],
}
user_message = build_user_message(notes)
print(user_message)

Step 4: Generate the report

Now I send the conversation to Oxlo.ai. I use the llama-3.3-70b model because it handles long context well and follows Markdown formatting reliably, and I enable streaming so I can watch the output arrive in real time.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
    stream=True,
    temperature=0.3,
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="", flush=True)

Step 5: Save and batch process

Printing to stdout is fine for debugging, but I want a file. This last snippet processes every JSON file in a folder and writes a matching Markdown report to disk.

import json
import pathlib

def generate_report(notes_path, out_dir="reports"):
    pathlib.Path(out_dir).mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    with open(notes_path, "r") as f:
        notes = json.load(f)
    user_message = build_user_message(notes)

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        temperature=0.3,
    )

    report = response.choices[0].message.content
    out_path = pathlib.Path(out_dir) / f"{pathlib.Path(notes_path).stem}.md"
    out_path.write_text(report, encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"Wrote {out_path}")

for fp in pathlib.Path("notes/").glob("*.json"):
    generate_report(fp)

Run it

Create a file named notes.json in your working directory. Populate it with the sample meeting data below. The last bullet intentionally references Oxlo.ai so you can see how the model handles product names without hallucinating extra details.

{
  "title": "Q3 Roadmap Sync",
  "attendees": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"],
  "bullets": [
    "Discussed migration from legacy auth to OAuth2",
    "Bob to prepare test plan by Friday",
    "Need to evaluate Oxlo.ai for batch inference, pricing is flat per request",
    "Carol raised concern about latency in Asia region",
    "Next sync scheduled for July 15"
  ]
}

Execute the script from your terminal. Make sure your environment variable is exported.

export OXLO_API_KEY="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
python generate_report.py

If everything is wired correctly, Oxlo.ai will stream back a complete Markdown report. The output should look similar to this, with accurate headings and properly formatted checkboxes.

# Q3 Roadmap Sync

## Attendees
- Alice
- Bob
- Carol

## Key Takeaways
- The team agreed to migrate from legacy auth to OAuth2.
- Oxlo.ai is being evaluated for batch inference workloads due to its request-based pricing model.
- Latency concerns in the Asia region were raised and need follow-up.

## Action Items
- [ ] Bob: Prepare test plan by Friday.
- [ ] Carol: Investigate Asia region latency options.
- [ ] All: Attend next sync on July 15.

Next steps

The generator works, but it is still stateless. A practical upgrade is to add a memory layer: store generated reports in a SQLite database and use the deepseek-v3.2 model on Oxlo.ai to suggest follow-up emails based on outstanding action items. Because Oxlo.ai does not charge by the token, experimenting with longer prompts for email generation stays cheap.

Another option is to wire the script into a GitHub Action so every commit that adds a notes file automatically generates the report and opens a pull request. You could also switch to the kimi-k2.6 model if you need advanced reasoning to cluster related bullets into thematic sections instead of a flat list.

title: Scaling LLM Inference with Oxlo.ai
content:
Scaling large language model inference from prototype to production introduces a predictable set of engineering constraints. Throughput bottlenecks, latency spikes under load, and ballooning context windows all compound the central question of cost. For teams running agentic systems, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, or multi-turn conversational interfaces, the operational overhead of inference often exceeds the complexity of model training. The infrastructure layer you choose determines whether scaling means linear cost growth or a sustainable expansion of capability. This article examines the architectural and economic dimensions of scaling LLM inference, and where Oxlo.ai fits as a backend for production workloads.

The Cost Problem in Token-Based Scaling

Most hosted inference providers structure pricing around tokens. Input and output tokens are metered separately, which means costs scale directly with prompt length. This model works for simple chat completions, but it creates a nonlinear cost curve for production workloads. Long-context retrieval, code repository ingestion, and agent loops that append tool outputs to a growing conversation history all inflate the input token count. At scale, these inputs can dominate your inference budget.

Providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale all use token-based schemes. Without commenting on their specific rates, the structural reality is identical: longer prompts equal higher costs. For teams building applications with 100K+ context windows or autonomous agents that maintain rolling state, this pricing model imposes a hard constraint on architecture. You are forced to optimize prompts primarily to save money, not to improve accuracy. That tension becomes more severe as you scale from hundreds to millions of requests per month.

A Request-Based Alternative for Predictable Economics

Oxlo.ai approaches the problem with a different unit of account. The platform charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. This request-based pricing removes the input token dimension from your cost function. For long-context workloads, the economic difference is structural. Where token-based bills grow with every additional document chunk or historical message appended to a prompt, Oxlo.ai keeps the cost constant per call.

This predictability changes how you design systems. You no longer need to truncate context windows aggressively or maintain separate summarization layers purely to reduce token counts. The pricing model aligns cost with business value, a single user interaction or agent decision, rather than with an internal resource consumption metric. For high-volume agentic workflows, Oxlo.ai can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives, with the gap widening as context length increases.

Oxlo.ai offers a Free plan at $0 per month with 60 requests per day across 16+ models and a 7-day full-access trial. You can verify current rates on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Model Availability Without Cold Start Penalty

Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, which means your first request of the hour behaves like your thousandth. The platform hosts over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories. Handling Long-Context and Agentic Workloads

Modern scaling challenges are defined by context. Operational Features for Production Workloads

Scaling requires more than raw model access. Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, function calling and tool use, JSON mode, vision inputs, and multi-turn conversations. Endpoints cover chat completions, embeddings, image generations, audio transcriptions, and text-to-speech.

For production monitoring and routing, these features let you build deterministic output pipelines. JSON mode constrains model outputs to valid structured data, reducing post-processing overhead. Function calling enables agentic tool use across the model catalog. Streaming improves perceived latency for end users, even when underlying reasoning steps are complex.

Enterprise plans add dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed cost reduction against your current provider, which is useful for teams moving entire product lines off self-hosted or token-based infrastructure.

Conclusion

Scaling LLM inference demands an infrastructure layer that decouples cost from complexity. Token-based pricing creates a structural conflict between richer context and higher bills, forcing engineering teams to optimize for metering rather than for accuracy. Oxlo.ai removes that conflict with flat per-request pricing, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a broad catalog of over 45 models without cold starts.

If your current infrastructure bill scales with every token you send, it is worth evaluating whether your costs should scale with user value instead.

title: Building a RAG Pipeline with Oxlo.ai
content:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) remains the dominant pattern for grounding large language models in private or domain-specific data. Instead of retraining a model, RAG retrieves relevant document chunks at query time and injects them into the prompt. The result is more accurate, attributable, and cost-effective responses. For developers building production pipelines, the choice of inference provider directly impacts latency, cost, and architectural flexibility. Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first platform with request-based pricing, full OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a broad catalog of embedding and generation models that make it a strong fit for RAG systems.

What makes a RAG pipeline production-ready

A toy RAG demo is easy. A production pipeline requires several components working reliably. First, documents must be parsed and chunked with appropriate overlap so that no semantic boundary is lost. Second, the embedding model must map text into a dense vector space where similarity corresponds to semantic relevance. Third, the vector database must support high-recall approximate nearest neighbor search at low latency. Fourth, the generator must synthesize answers from retrieved context without hallucinating beyond the provided evidence. Finally, the entire pipeline must be observable and cost-predictable. Token-based pricing complicates the last point because every additional chunk in the context window increases cost. Oxlo.ai removes that variable by charging a flat rate per API request regardless of prompt length.

Why Oxlo.ai fits RAG workloads

Oxlo.ai is not merely another inference endpoint. It is an AI infrastructure layer designed for workloads where context length fluctuates.

  • Request-based pricing. Competitors bill by the token, which means longer retrieved contexts directly inflate costs. On Oxlo.ai, a request costs the same whether you send a 500-token prompt or a 50,000-token prompt. For RAG, where you may retrieve ten large chunks to maximize answer quality, this model is significantly cheaper.
  • OpenAI SDK compatibility. You can point your existing Python or Node.js client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and use the same code you already have. This reduces migration friction to zero.
  • Model breadth. Oxlo.ai hosts both embedding models (BGE-Large, E5-Large) and generation models (Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2.6). You can keep both stages on one platform with one API key.
  • No cold starts. Popular models are always warm, so the latency spike of loading weights does not break your retrieval-augmented response time.

Architecture overview

A standard RAG pipeline built on Oxlo.ai follows four stages.

  1. Ingestion. Load raw documents, clean formatting, and split into chunks.
  2. Embedding. Send each chunk to Oxlo.ai's embeddings endpoint to receive a dense vector.
  3. Indexing. Store vectors and metadata in a vector database such as pgvector, Chroma, or Weaviate.
  4. Querying. Embed the user question, retrieve the top-k chunks, inject them into a system prompt, and call an Oxlo.ai chat model.

Because Oxlo.ai uses standard REST and OpenAI SDK shapes, each stage integrates with existing Python tooling without adapters.

Step 1. Generating embeddings with Oxlo.ai

Start by embedding your document chunks. Oxlo.ai provides BGE-Large and E5-Large, both well-regarded for retrieval tasks. The following Python snippet assumes you have already chunked your documents and stored them in a list called chunks.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

def embed_chunks(chunks, model="bge-large"):
    vectors = []
    for chunk in chunks:
        resp = client.embeddings.create(
            model=model,
            input=chunk
        )
        vectors.append(resp.data[0].embedding)
    return vectors

The embeddings.create interface is identical to OpenAI's specification. You batch chunks for efficiency, though the example loops for clarity. The returned vectors are 1024-dimensional floats suitable for cosine similarity search.

Step 2. Storing and retrieving vectors

Once you have vectors, store them. The choice of vector store depends on your existing stack. If you use PostgreSQL, pgvector adds a vector column type and supports ivfflat or hnsw indexes. If you prefer an in-memory option for prototyping, Chroma works immediately. The retrieval logic remains the same: compute the question embedding, then query for nearest neighbors.

import numpy as np

def retrieve(question_embedding, stored_vectors, stored_texts, top_k=5):
    # Cosine similarity via dot product on normalized vectors
    similarities = np.dot(stored_vectors, question_embedding)
    top_indices = np.argsort(similarities)[-top_k:][::-1]
    return [stored_texts[i] for i in top_indices]

In production, replace the NumPy brute-force search with your vector database's approximate nearest neighbor query. The key point is that the embedding and retrieval stages are decoupled, so Oxlo.ai handles the inference while your database handles the indexing.

Step 3. Augmenting the prompt and generating answers

With relevant chunks retrieved, construct the prompt. A clear system message instructs the model to use only the provided context. Oxlo.ai's chat completions endpoint accepts the same message list format as OpenAI's.

def answer(question, contexts, model="llama-3.3-70b"):
    context_block = "\n\n".join(
        f"Context {i+1}:\n{ctx}" for i, ctx in enumerate(contexts)
    )

    messages = [
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a precise research assistant. "
                "Answer the question using only the provided contexts. "
                "If the answer is not present, say you do not know."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"{context_block}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
        }
    ]

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.1
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Notice that the prompt length varies with the number of retrieved chunks. On a token-based provider, this unpredictability makes cost forecasting difficult. On Oxlo.ai, the request still incurs a single flat charge, so you can retrieve generously to improve answer quality without budget shock.

Handling long context without token anxiety

RAG quality often improves when you retrieve more or larger chunks. A financial document RAG pipeline might retrieve five pages of regulatory text to answer a compliance question. Under token-based pricing, those five pages could cost more than the generation itself. Oxlo.ai's request-based model inverts this constraint. Because the price is flat per request, you can experiment with larger context windows, re-ranking pipelines that forward more candidates to the generator, and multi-turn RAG conversations where previous context accumulates. You pay per inference call, not per word. For exact plan details, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Putting it all together

A minimal end-to-end script looks like this.

import openai
import numpy as np

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

CHUNKS = [
    "Oxlo.ai offers flat per-request pricing for open-source LLMs.",
    "RAG pipelines retrieve context to ground LLM responses.",
    "Embeddings convert text into dense vectors for similarity search."
]

def embed(texts, model="bge-large"):
    resp = client.embeddings.create(model=model, input=texts)
    return [d.embedding for d in resp.data]

def retrieve(question_emb, doc_embs, docs, k=2):
    sims = np.dot(doc_embs, question_emb)
    idx = np.argsort(sims)[-k:][::-1]
    return [docs[i] for i in idx]

def generate(question, contexts, model="llama-3.3-70b"):
    prompt = "\n".join(f"- {c}" for c in contexts)
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": "Answer using only the listed contexts."},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Contexts:\n{prompt}\n\nQuestion: {question}"}
    ]
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, messages=messages)
    return resp.choices[0].message.content

# Index
doc_embeddings = embed(CHUNKS)

# Query
q = "How does Oxlo.ai price its API?"
q_emb = embed([q])[0]
relevant = retrieve(q_emb, np.array(doc_embeddings), CHUNKS)
print(generate(q, relevant))

This script is fully executable after you insert an API key. It demonstrates the complete loop: embedding, retrieval, and generation, all through Oxlo.ai.

Next steps for production RAG

A basic pipeline is only the foundation. To harden it, consider these upgrades.

  • Hybrid search. Combine dense vector retrieval with keyword BM25 scoring to handle rare technical terms.
  • Re-ranking. Use a cross-encoder or a larger Oxlo.ai embedding model to re-order the top-k retrieved chunks before generation.
  • Query transformation. Use an Oxlo.ai chat model to rewrite vague user questions into targeted search queries.
  • Agentic RAG. For complex research tasks, let an agent loop over retrieval and generation steps, calling tools to refine searches. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use, so the generator can decide when more context is needed.
  • Evaluation. Measure retrieval hit rate and answer correctness with a labeled dataset. Oxlo.ai's predictable pricing makes it feasible to run large evaluation batches without surprise bills.

Oxlo.ai provides the model diversity and pricing structure that RAG developers need. By keeping embeddings and generation on one flat-rate platform, you simplify infrastructure and remove the cost penalty of long context. If you are migrating from a token-based provider, the OpenAI SDK compatibility means the switch requires only a new base URL and API key.

title: Using LLMs for Code Analysis: Best Practices and Challenges
content:
Developers increasingly use large language models to review code, detect bugs, and explain legacy systems. Unlike traditional static analysis tools that rely on fixed rule sets, LLMs can infer intent, identify subtle logic errors, and suggest idiomatic refactors across languages. However, productionizing code analysis with LLMs introduces distinct challenges. Context windows must accommodate entire modules or repositories, outputs must be structured for downstream tooling, and costs can escalate unpredictably when pricing is tied to token volume. Getting reliable results requires deliberate model selection, prompt engineering, and infrastructure choices that match the workload.

Why Long Context Matters for Code Analysis

Modern software is rarely self-contained. A single React component might import from fifteen local modules, pull types from a shared package, and rely on environment variables defined in a remote config. Static analysis tools can trace these links because they build abstract syntax trees and dependency graphs, but an LLM operating on an isolated function loses that global picture. When you ask a model to find a memory leak, detect a race condition, or assess whether a refactor breaks the public API, it needs to see the callers, the interfaces, and the concurrency primitives used across the repository.

This creates a tension. The most valuable analysis is holistic, yet holistic prompts are large. A comprehensive security review might include the target file, its unit tests, the ORM schema it queries, and the middleware that authenticates its routes. Under token-based pricing, every imported file and comment block inflates the bill. Providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale scale cost with input length, which means repo-level scans become expensive experiments rather than routine pipeline steps. Oxlo.ai removes that friction with flat per-request pricing. Whether you submit a fifty-line utility or a five-thousand-line service with its full dependency context, the API cost is the same. That predictability is essential for agentic workflows that explore codebases iteratively, issuing multiple requests as they map call graphs and cross-reference definitions.

Choosing Models for Depth versus Speed

Code analysis is not a single task. A pre-commit hook that checks for obvious anti-patterns has radically different latency and reasoning requirements than a quarterly audit that hunts for subtle supply-chain vulnerabilities. Treating every request as a reasoning problem wastes compute and slows feedback loops.

For high-frequency, low-latency checks, specialized code models are the right tool. Oxlo.ai hosts Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast, all tuned for programming syntax and diff comprehension. These models excel at inline suggestions, naming-convention checks, and formatting guidance. When the task demands deeper logic, such as reasoning about distributed state, cryptographic misuse, or cross-module deadlock potential, you need models that perform extended chain-of-thought reasoning. Options like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Kimi K2.6, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash are built for this. DeepSeek V4 Flash also brings a one-million-token context window, making it possible to load large legacy modules in a single prompt. For long-horizon agentic tasks that require planning and tool use across many files, GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 provide strong agentic coding capabilities. Because Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories through one endpoint, you can route quick linting to a lightweight coder and route architectural reviews to a heavy reasoning model without maintaining separate provider integrations.

Structuring Prompts and Enforcing Output Formats

Raw prose is difficult to act on. If an LLM returns a paragraph describing a bug, a CI system cannot parse it, an IDE cannot underline it, and a security dashboard cannot count it. Production code analysis pipelines must constrain the model to emit structured, verifiable data.

Start with an explicit system prompt that defines the persona, the scope, and the schema. For example, instruct the model to act as a static analyzer that emits only JSON containing the fields severity, file, line, rule_id, and message. Use clear delimiters to separate files within the prompt. Wrapping each source file in XML tags or markdown code fences reduces ambiguity about which path a line number refers to.

Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling, which lets you enforce schemas at the API level rather than hoping the model follows instructions. Function calling is particularly powerful for agentic analysis: the model can propose a vulnerability, invoke an external tool to verify the file hash or query a vulnerability database, and then refine its answer based on the tool result. Here is a minimal example using the OpenAI SDK with an Oxlo.ai endpoint.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-coder",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a security auditor. Analyze the provided code for OWASP Top 10 risks. "
                "Respond with valid JSON containing a list of findings."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"<file path='src/auth.py'>\n{code}\n</file>"
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    temperature=0.2
)

The example uses a low temperature because code analysis benefits from deterministic, conservative outputs rather than creative generation. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, existing analysis tools require only a base URL change to start experimenting.

Managing Context Windows and Infrastructure Cost

The primary infrastructure challenge in LLM code analysis is economic, not algorithmic. Truncating prompts to save money introduces blind spots. A model that cannot see the transaction wrapper around a database call will miss an injection vector. A model that does not receive the interface definition will approve a refactor that breaks downstream consumers.

When your inference provider charges by the token, every additional context file is a tax on thoroughness. Teams often resort to fragile pre-processing: counting tokens, stripping comments, or guessing which files are relevant. These heuristics save money but degrade analysis quality. Oxlo.ai’s request-based model eliminates that trade-off. The platform is designed to be significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads because the cost per request stays flat regardless of input length. For teams running automated scans across microservices or analyzing legacy monoliths, this can change the economics from selective sampling to comprehensive coverage.

Additionally, Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models. That matters for interactive tools and CI pipelines that need consistent latency at any time of day, not just during peak usage windows.

Reducing Hallucinations through Verification Loops

LLMs are confident generators of plausible but incorrect information. In code analysis, this manifests as citing deprecated APIs, inventing configuration keys, or flagging safe patterns as vulnerabilities because they resemble unsafe idioms in other languages. A hallucinated security finding wastes engineering hours; a hallucinated all-clear creates liability.

Mitigation starts with context grounding. Provide the model with actual dependency manifests, type signatures, and API documentation rather than asking it to rely on training-data memory. Use multi-turn conversations to interrogate initial findings. If the model claims a function lacks input validation, ask it to cite the specific line and propose a patch, then verify that patch against the original source.

Oxlo.ai’s support for multi-turn conversations and function calling makes it straightforward to build feedback loops. The model can emit a tool call to a static analyzer or test runner, receive the result, and update its assessment. This agentic pattern combines the flexibility of LLM reasoning with the rigor of deterministic verification.

Integrating Analysis into CI/CD and Developer Workflows

Analysis that lives only in a chat interface provides temporary value. To earn a permanent place in the software lifecycle, LLM review must integrate into pull-request checks, pre-commit hooks, and build pipelines. That integration demands reliable endpoints, predictable scaling, and minimal client-side refactoring.

Because Oxlo.ai exposes a standard chat/completions endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, it functions as a drop-in replacement for any tool built on the OpenAI SDK. Teams can add an AI review stage to GitHub Actions or GitLab CI by changing a single environment variable. Streaming responses keep IDE plugins responsive, while JSON mode ensures pipeline stages can parse results without brittle regex.

For teams evaluating the approach, the Free tier offers 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, including DeepSeek V3.2 for coding and reasoning, with a 7-day full-access trial. The Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day, and Premium offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access. Enterprise plans add dedicated GPUs and guaranteed savings over existing providers. This tiering makes it possible to prototype on a personal repository and then scale to organization-wide scanning without switching platforms.

Conclusion

LLM-based code analysis is moving from novelty to infrastructure. The teams that succeed will be those that treat the model as one component in a larger system of structured prompts, verification tools, and cost-effective inference. Long-context workloads and agentic exploration are not edge cases; they are the defining patterns of serious code intelligence.

Oxlo.ai’s flat per-request pricing, broad catalog of code-specialized and reasoning models, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility provide a practical foundation for these workloads. By removing the token tax on large prompts and offering deterministic latency without cold starts, the platform lets developers focus on analysis quality rather than prompt accounting. If you are building automated review pipelines or agentic coding tools, start with the infrastructure that rewards thoroughness instead of punishing it. Visit https://oxlo.ai/pricing to compare plans and explore the model catalog.

title: Integrating LLM into Chatbots with Oxlo
content:
Chatbots have moved beyond rigid decision trees into dynamic, context-aware conversational agents. Integrating a large language model (LLM) into a chatbot pipeline is now standard practice, yet developers still encounter friction around API compatibility, context window management, and unpredictable token costs. A production chatbot must maintain state across multi-turn conversations, invoke external tools, and sometimes process images or audio. Building this requires an inference backend that supports diverse modalities, offers predictable billing, and works with existing SDKs.

Architecture of a Modern LLM Chatbot

A robust chatbot architecture consists of four core layers. The interface layer handles user input, whether that is web chat, voice, or messaging platforms. The orchestration layer manages conversation state, routes messages, and applies business logic. The inference layer sends formatted requests to the LLM and parses responses. Finally, the memory layer stores conversation history, user profiles, and retrieval-augmented generation context.

The inference layer is where Oxlo.ai fits. Instead of hosting models yourself or navigating fragmented APIs, you route chat completions through a single endpoint. Oxlo.ai provides fully OpenAI-compatible APIs for chat, embeddings, images, audio, and more. This means your orchestration code can use the official OpenAI Python or Node.js SDK by simply changing the base URL and API key.

Selecting a Model for Your Use Case

Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, so you can match the model to the chatbot's job rather than forcing every task through a single endpoint.

For general-purpose conversational agents, Llama 3.3 70B and GLM 5 offer strong multilingual performance and long-horizon reasoning. If your chatbot performs deep research, complex coding, or multi-step agentic workflows, consider DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Kimi K2.6, or Qwen 3 32B. Kimi K2.6 supports advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision with a 131K context window, making it suitable for technical support bots that analyze screenshots or long log files.

For coding-specific assistants, DeepSeek V3.2, Minimax M2.5, and Qwen 3 Coder 30B provide strong code generation and tool-use capabilities. If you need vision inputs, Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B handle image understanding within the same chat completions format. Because Oxlo.ai uses a uniform OpenAI schema, swapping from Llama to Kimi to DeepSeek is a one-line configuration change.

Implementing the Chat Loop

The simplest integration pattern is a stateful loop that accumulates messages and streams responses to the user. Below is a minimal Python example using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai.

client = openai.OpenAI(

title: LLM Tutorial for Beginners with Oxlo
content:
Most support teams waste hours sorting incoming emails before they can actually solve problems. In this tutorial, we will build a triage agent that reads raw customer messages, scores urgency, summarizes the issue, and drafts a first reply using Oxlo.ai. When you finish, you will have a single Python script that processes tickets end to end.

What you'll need

Before we write code, gather these prerequisites:

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free plan includes 60 requests per day across 16 models, which is plenty for this tutorial.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, so the cost of each API call stays flat no matter how long the customer email is. That makes it practical to feed entire conversation threads into the prompt without worrying about token counts. You can view plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Verify the connection to Oxlo.ai

First, confirm that your environment can reach Oxlo.ai. I always start with a minimal ping so I do not debug connection issues inside complex logic later.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Run the script with OXLO_API_KEY=your_key python triage.py. If you see a greeting, the endpoint is live and you are ready to add behavior.

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the agent's job description. I keep it editable as a constant so I can refine tone or add company-specific rules without touching Python logic.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a support triage agent. Your job is to read a raw customer message and produce three items:
1. urgency: one of low, medium, or high.
2. summary: a one-sentence description of the problem.
3. draft_reply: a polite, helpful first response that acknowledges the issue and sets expectations.

Respond in JSON with exactly these keys: urgency, summary, draft_reply.
"""

I ask for JSON inside the prompt text because we will pair it with JSON mode in the next step. This redundancy improves reliability.

Step 3: Build the triage function

Now we wrap the API call into a reusable function. It takes a customer message string, sends it to Oxlo.ai along with the system prompt, and returns the raw model output.

def triage_ticket(customer_message: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": customer_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

At this stage the function returns a string. That is fine for a quick prototype, but parsing free text is fragile, so we will enforce structured output next.

Step 4: Enforce JSON mode for reliable parsing

Oxlo.ai supports OpenAI-compatible JSON mode. By adding response_format={"type": "json_object"}, we instruct the model to emit valid JSON. We then parse it with the standard library before returning a dictionary.

import json

def triage_ticket(customer_message: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": customer_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

I use llama-3.3-70b here because it follows structured instructions reliably and runs with no cold starts on Oxlo.ai. If you later switch to deepseek-v3.2 for technical tickets, the client code stays identical.

Step 5: Process a batch of tickets

Real queues do not arrive one at a time. We will define a list of three example messages and loop through them. This is where you see the flat per-request pricing shine: one of these emails is a short sentence, another is a long paragraph with nested formatting, yet both cost the same single request on Oxlo.ai.

tickets = [
    "Hi, my invoice for March shows a $49 charge but I expected $29. Can you fix this?",
    "URGENT: Our entire team has been locked out of the dashboard since 9 AM. We have a client demo in 30 minutes and need immediate help restoring access. This is costing us money.",
    "Just wanted to say thanks for the quick turnaround on my last question. Really appreciate it.",
]

for ticket in tickets:
    result = triage_ticket(ticket)
    print(f"Urgency: {result['urgency']}")
    print(f"Summary: {result['summary']}")
    print(f"Draft: {result['draft_reply']}")
    print("-" * 40)

Run it

Save everything in a file named triage.py, export your key, and run:

export OXLO_API_KEY="your_key_here"
python triage.py

Typical output looks like this:

Urgency: medium
Summary: Customer reports an incorrect invoice charge of $49 instead of $29.
Draft: Thanks for flagging this. I have forwarded the discrepancy to our billing team and they will issue a corrected invoice within one business day.

----------------------------------------
Urgency: high
Summary: Entire team locked out of dashboard before critical client demo.
Draft: I understand the urgency and I am escalating this to our on-call engineer immediately. Expect an update within 10 minutes.

----------------------------------------
Urgency: low
Summary: Customer sent a thank-you note with no outstanding issue.
Draft: You are very welcome. We are glad the last fix worked for you. Reach out anytime.

Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the loop runs immediately even if this is your first request of the day.

Next steps

Two concrete ways to extend this agent:

  1. Connect it to a real inbox using an IMAP or webhook listener, and append previous thread history to each request. On Oxlo.ai, longer context does not increase the per-request cost, so giving the model full conversation history is economical compared to token-based providers.
  2. Swap the model to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6 when you need deeper reasoning for complex technical bugs. The client code stays the same because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible.

That is the complete pipeline. You now have a working triage agent running on Oxlo.ai.

title: Revolutionizing Speech Recognition with LLMs
content:
Speech recognition has moved beyond simple phoneme matching. Where traditional automatic speech recognition systems delivered raw text with limited context, modern large language models treat audio as a sequence of meaning, not just sound. This shift enables punctuation inference, speaker diarization hints, semantic formatting, and downstream reasoning, but it also changes how developers should think about inference infrastructure. Audio is inherently high-entropy and variable-length. A thirty-second voice note and a ninety-minute podcast both need reliable, low-latency processing without pricing surprises. That is where the underlying platform matters as much as the model itself.

From Transcription to Comprehension

Early ASR pipelines used acoustic models and language models as separate components. The acoustic layer converted sound to phonemes, and the language layer resolved those phonemes into words. This architecture worked for dictation but failed in noisy environments, multilingual settings, and domains with heavy jargon. End-to-end transformers, particularly OpenAI's Whisper family, collapsed these layers into a single attentive mechanism that maps mel-frequency spectrograms directly to text tokens.

When you route Whisper through an LLM-forward inference platform, you gain more than text. You gain a reasoning interface. The model infers paragraph breaks, identifies question-answer pairs, and maintains context across utterances. For developers building meeting assistants, clinical note tools, or media archives, this means less post-processing and more actionable output from a single API call. The transcription becomes a structured document rather than a flat string.

The Hidden Cost of Audio Inference

Audio content scales in ways that expose the weaknesses of token-based billing. A one-hour stereo recording, once converted to the discrete tokens used by modern speech models, can represent a substantial input sequence. When providers bill by the token, costs rise linearly with audio length and output verbosity. For agentic systems that feed transcription into downstream chat loops, the expense compounds quickly.

Request-based pricing removes this uncertainty. Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-form transcription workloads, this model is significantly more predictable than token-based alternatives. A ninety-minute podcast costs the same per request as a thirty-second reminder, so teams processing archives, call-center logs, or lecture libraries can forecast spend without estimating token counts from variable bitrates and speaking speeds.

Oxlo.ai Audio Infrastructure

Oxlo.ai offers Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium through a fully OpenAI-compatible audio/transcriptions endpoint. These models cover distinct latency and accuracy tradeoffs. Whisper Large v3 delivers the highest accuracy for noisy or accented speech. Whisper Turbo optimizes for real-time or near-real-time pipelines where latency dominates. Whisper Medium provides a balanced profile for batch jobs that need quality without the resource footprint of the largest variant.

The platform exposes these through the standard OpenAI SDK, which means existing Python, Node.js, or cURL integrations require only a base URL change. The endpoint is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. There are no cold starts on popular models, so the first request after a quiet period returns at the same speed as the hundredth. For production voice applications, this consistency eliminates the variability that degrades user experience.

Integrating Speech Recognition with Oxlo.ai

Migration from another OpenAI-compatible provider to Oxlo.ai is intentionally frictionless. Because the API surface matches the OpenAI specification, you point your existing client at Oxlo.ai's base URL, set your API key, and preserve the same request shapes.

Consider a batch transcription workflow in Python:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

audio_file = open("earnings_call.wav", "rb")

transcription = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
    model="whisper-large-v3",
    file=audio_file,
    response_format="json",
    language="en"
)

print(transcription.text)

Beyond simple text, you can leverage JSON mode to enforce structured output. If your application needs speaker labels, timestamps, or segmented paragraphs, you can pipe the transcription into an Oxlo.ai chat model such as Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B in the same request flow. Because the platform supports function calling and tool use, you can also trigger downstream actions directly from transcription content, such as logging calendar events or flagging compliance keywords without leaving the Oxlo.ai ecosystem.

Building Multimodal Workflows

Speech rarely exists in isolation. A customer support ticket might include an audio attachment, a screenshot, and a text description. Oxlo.ai supports vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B alongside its audio pipeline, so you can unify transcription, image understanding, and reasoning in a single provider stack.

Multi-turn conversations further extend this pattern. You might transcribe a user voice message with Whisper, feed the result into Kimi K2.6 or DeepSeek V4 Flash for reasoning, and return a synthesized response via Kokoro 82M text-to-speech, all through Oxlo.ai endpoints. Because billing is request-based, chaining these steps does not introduce hidden token escalations. Each stage is a discrete, predictable call.

Selecting the Right Plan for Audio Workloads

Oxlo.ai offers several tiers that accommodate different audio processing volumes. The Free plan includes 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 models, including options suitable for light transcription testing and prototyping. It also includes a 7-day full-access trial for evaluating higher-tier capabilities.

The Pro plan, at $80 per month, provides 1,000 requests per day across all models. This suits teams running daily batch jobs or moderate conversational agents. The Premium plan, at $350 per month, raises the limit to 5,000 requests per day and adds priority queueing, which matters when you are processing large audio backlogs under time constraints. Enterprise customers can negotiate custom terms with unlimited requests, dedicated GPUs, and guaranteed cost reductions relative to their current provider.

For audio specifically, request-based pricing means that a long podcast or extended interview costs the same as a short clip. You can explore the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Conclusion

LLM-based speech recognition has moved from research novelty to production requirement, but the infrastructure underneath it determines whether the technology is affordable at scale. Token-based billing creates friction for audio because sound is variable, continuous, and token-dense. Oxlo.ai addresses this with request-based pricing, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a suite of Whisper models accessible through a unified audio/transcriptions endpoint.

For developers building voice agents, transcription pipelines, or multimodal applications, the combination of predictable costs and drop-in integration reduces both engineering overhead and financial risk. If your current provider scales pricing with every minute of audio, it is worth evaluating whether a flat per-request model better fits your workload.
