title: Unlocking Zero-Shot Learning with LLMs
content:
Zero-shot classification lets you categorize text into arbitrary labels without collecting training data or fine-tuning a model. In this tutorial, I will walk you through building a CLI tool that takes any passage and a list of candidate labels, then returns the best matches using an off-the-shelf LLM. It is useful for support ticket routing, content moderation, or any situation where your categories change frequently and retraining is not practical.

What you'll need

You will need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. A virtual environment is optional but recommended.

I am using Oxlo.ai because its request-based pricing means a classification call costs the same whether you pass a short headline or a ten-page document. For teams processing long tickets or research papers, that predictability matters. You can compare plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the code below works without vendor-specific adapters. I will use llama-3.3-70b as the default model, but you can switch to qwen-3-32b for multilingual workloads or deepseek-v3.2 for code-heavy text.

Step 1: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training the model gets. It must constrain output to valid labels and enforce JSON so we do not have to parse prose. I also embed a confidence requirement so we can filter uncertain predictions later. Create a new file called classifier.py and add the following.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a zero-shot text classifier. Your job is to classify the user-provided text into one or more of the candidate labels provided by the user.

Rules:
1. Only use labels from the provided candidate list.
2. Return your answer as a JSON object with exactly two keys: "labels" (a list of strings) and "confidence" (a float between 0 and 1).
3. If the text fits multiple labels, include all that apply.
4. Do not explain your reasoning. Return only the JSON."""

Step 2: Build the classify function

Next, add a function that formats the user input, calls Oxlo.ai, and parses the JSON response. I am using llama-3.3-70b because it follows instructions reliably for structured output, but you can swap in qwen-3-32b if you need multilingual labels or deepseek-v3.2 for code-heavy documents. Notice that we pass response_format to force valid JSON, which removes the need for fragile regex parsing and keeps the code maintainable.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a zero-shot text classifier. Your job is to classify the user-provided text into one or more of the candidate labels provided by the user.

Rules:
1. Only use labels from the provided candidate list.
2. Return your answer as a JSON object with exactly two keys: "labels" (a list of strings) and "confidence" (a float between 0 and 1).
3. If the text fits multiple labels, include all that apply.
4. Do not explain your reasoning. Return only the JSON."""

def classify(text: str, labels: list[str], model: str = "llama-3.3-70b") -> dict:
    label_list = ", ".join(f'"{label}"' for label in labels)
    user_message = f"Text: {text}\nCandidate labels: [{label_list}]"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 3: Test with unseen labels

Zero-shot means the model has never seen your specific taxonomy during training. Let us verify it works on three different domains without any examples: a support ticket, a news headline, and a product review. This proves the tool generalizes to labels you invent on the spot. If you need stronger reasoning across overlapping categories, switch the model to kimi-k2.6 in the classify call.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a zero-shot text classifier. Your job is to classify the user-provided text into one or more of the candidate labels provided by the user.

Rules:
1. Only use labels from the provided candidate list.
2. Return your answer as a JSON object with exactly two keys: "labels" (a list of strings) and "confidence" (a float between 0 and 1).
3. If the text fits multiple labels, include all that apply.
4. Do not explain your reasoning. Return only the JSON."""

def classify(text: str, labels: list[str], model: str = "llama-3.3-70b") -> dict:
    label_list = ", ".join(f'"{label}"' for label in labels)
    user_message = f"Text: {text}\nCandidate labels: [{label_list}]"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    examples = [
        (
            "The server returned a 502 Bad Gateway after the latest deploy.",
            ["incident", "feature request", "billing", "general inquiry"]
        ),
        (
            "Federal reserve signals potential rate cut amid slowing inflation data.",
            ["finance", "sports", "technology", "politics", "science"]
        ),
        (
            "The battery lasts two days but the camera struggles in low light.",
            ["hardware", "software", "shipping", "warranty"]
        ),
    ]
    
    for text, labels in examples:
        result = classify(text, labels)
        print(f"Text: {text[:50]}...")
        print(f"Result: {result}")
        print()

Step 4: Batch process a CSV

In production, you will classify a backlog of tickets or survey responses. This script reads input.csv with columns text and labels, where labels is a semicolon-separated string. It classifies each row and writes output.csv with predicted_labels and confidence. You can process thousands of rows without worrying about input length driving up cost on Oxlo.ai, because the platform charges per request rather than per token. That flat pricing is especially helpful when individual records vary wildly in length.

import csv
import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a zero-shot text classifier. Your job is to classify the user-provided text into one or more of the candidate labels provided by the user.

Rules:
1. Only use labels from the provided candidate list.
2. Return your answer as a JSON object with exactly two keys: "labels" (a list of strings) and "confidence" (a float between 0 and 1).
3. If the text fits multiple labels, include all that apply.
4. Do not explain your reasoning. Return only the JSON."""

def classify(text: str, labels: list[str], model: str = "llama-3.3-70b") -> dict:
    label_list = ", ".join(f'"{label}"' for label in labels)
    user_message = f"Text: {text}\nCandidate labels: [{label_list}]"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

def main():
    with open("input.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f_in, \
         open("output.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f_out:
        
        reader = csv.DictReader(f_in)
        fieldnames = reader.fieldnames + ["predicted_labels", "confidence"]
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f_out, fieldnames=fieldnames)
        writer.writeheader()
        
        for row in reader:
            labels = [l.strip() for l in row["labels"].split(";")]
            result = classify(row["text"], labels)
            row["predicted_labels"] = ";".join(result.get("labels", []))
            row["confidence"] = result.get("confidence", "")
            writer.writerow(row)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it

Create a sample input.csv in the same directory. The labels column uses semicolons so commas inside the text do not break parsing. Save the file, then run the script from your terminal.

text,labels
"The checkout page crashes when I apply a discount code.","bug;feature request;account issue"
"Do you offer annual billing for teams?","billing;sales;general"
python classifier.py

You should see output.csv written immediately. When I ran this against Oxlo.ai, the output looked like this:

text,labels,predicted_labels,confidence
"The checkout page crashes when I apply a discount code.","bug;feature request;account issue","bug",0.95
"Do you offer annual billing for teams?","billing;sales;general","billing",0.92

The confidence scores give you a quick way to spot uncertain predictions. Because Oxlo.ai does not charge by the token, the cost of classifying a long crash report is the same as a one-line question. That makes it straightforward to budget for pipelines that process thousands of records per day. If you hit rate limits, the Pro or Premium tiers offer higher daily request quotas with priority queueing.

Next steps

Try swapping llama-3.3-70b for qwen-3-32b if your labels or text are multilingual, or for kimi-k2.6 if you need advanced reasoning across ambiguous categories. You could also add a confidence threshold and route low-confidence predictions to a human reviewer, turning this script into a lightweight active-learning loop. Another concrete step is to expose the classify function as a FastAPI endpoint so other services can call it synchronously over HTTP.

title: Introduction to LLMs: How They Work and Their Applications
content:
Support teams waste hours sorting tickets before they can fix anything. Today I am building a single Python agent that ingests raw customer emails, classifies the issue, drafts a first response, and flags angry threads for human review. The whole thing runs on Oxlo.ai, so we pay per request instead of burning tokens on long email threads.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an Oxlo.ai API key. Head to https://portal.oxlo.ai to grab a key. Install the SDK with pip.

pip install openai

That is it. Oxlo.ai carries 45+ open-source and proprietary models, but for this project we only need one general-purpose model. Because the platform is fully OpenAI-compatible, the SDK works without patches or custom adapters.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I start by pointing the OpenAI client at Oxlo.ai. I use Llama 3.3 70B as the workhorse. It is an autoregressive transformer, which means it generates text by predicting the next token given all previous tokens in the context window. At Oxlo.ai, popular models stay warm with no cold starts, so the first request of the day returns as fast as the hundredth. For this agent, input length varies wildly. A customer might send a single sentence, or they might paste a fifty-line error log. Token-based providers make long inputs expensive, which discourages passing full context. Oxlo.ai's per-request pricing removes that friction, so I can always forward the complete email thread without trimming.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def ask_llama(messages):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.3,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

I keep temperature at 0.3. Lower sampling temperature reduces randomness, which means the model sticks closer to the most probable tokens. That is what we want for classification labels and policy-driven replies, not creative writing.

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the agent's job description. It gets injected into the model's context window alongside the user message. By describing the exact output format, I bias the token probabilities toward structured text without needing JSON mode or regex post-processing. This is in-context learning: the model adapts its behavior at inference time from instructions, not from weight updates. The system message occupies the beginning of the context window. Tokens there influence the hidden state for every subsequent token the model generates. That is why a single sentence like "You are a support triage agent" shifts the entire distribution toward professional, structured output.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent. Your tasks are:
1. Classify the ticket into exactly one category: Billing, Technical, or General.
2. Draft a brief, helpful first response.
3. Assess user sentiment as Calm or Frustrated.
Return your answer in this exact format:
Category: 
Response: 
Sentiment: """

Notice the strict format. LLMs are next-token predictors, so giving them a clear pattern to complete improves reliability. I ask for plain labels separated by newlines because that is easy to split in Python.

Step 3: Build the classifier

Traditional machine learning pipelines would train three separate models for classification, generation, and sentiment analysis. An LLM handles all three from a single text prompt because of broad pre-training on code and natural language, followed by instruction tuning. The model does not contain separate modules for each task. Instead, the same self-attention layers compute relationships across the entire prompt, and the feed-forward layers map those representations to vocabulary tokens. When I ask for a category label, the model predicts the word "Billing" because its training distribution associates the input text with that label. When I ask for a response, it switches into generation mode and produces fluent sentences. Both behaviors emerge from the same weights, prompted by different instructions. I send one request that asks for category, draft, and sentiment together. On Oxlo.ai, that single request costs the same whether the email is fifty words or five hundred, which makes long-context triage cheap.

def process_ticket(raw_email: str) -> dict:
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": raw_email},
    ]

    output = ask_llama(messages)

    lines = [line.strip() for line in output.splitlines() if line.strip()]
    result = {"raw": output, "category": None, "response": None, "sentiment": None}

    for line in lines:
        if line.startswith("Category:"):
            result["category"] = line.replace("Category:", "").strip()
        elif line.startswith("Response:"):
            result["response"] = line.replace("Response:", "").strip()
        elif line.startswith("Sentiment:"):
            result["sentiment"] = line.replace("Sentiment:", "").strip()

    return result

The parser is intentionally simple. If the model drifts from the format, the fields stay None and I fall back to the raw text. In production, I would add a retry loop or switch to JSON mode, but for an introductory build, string parsing keeps the dependencies at zero.

Step 4: Add escalation logic

A classifier is useless without business rules. I wrap the parser with a lightweight policy layer. If the sentiment is Frustrated, or if the category is Billing combined with the word "refund", I set an escalate flag. This mimics the guardrails that keep automation from annoying already angry customers. I also keep the rules versioned in git. When the support team wants to auto-escalate shipping complaints too, I edit the Python file and redeploy. I do not need to retrain or fine-tune the model.

def triage(raw_email: str) -> dict:
    result = process_ticket(raw_email)

    escalate = False
    if result.get("sentiment") == "Frustrated":
        escalate = True
    if result.get("category") == "Billing" and "refund" in raw_email.lower():
        escalate = True

    result["escalate"] = escalate
    return result

I keep the rules in code, not in the prompt. Mixing policy and generation makes the model harder to debug. By separating them, I can change the escalation criteria without altering the system prompt and risking format drift.

Step 5: Run it

I test with two tickets. The first is a routine technical question. The second is a billing complaint with clear frustration. Running both demonstrates how the same LLM application adapts to different content without retraining or context switching.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tickets = [
        "Hi, how do I export my data to CSV? I looked in settings but I do not see a download button. Thanks, Alex",
        "You charged me twice this month. I want a refund NOW. This is the third time I have written and nobody replies. Extremely disappointed.",
    ]

    for text in tickets:
        outcome = triage(text)
        print("---")
        print(f"Category: {outcome['category']}")
        print(f"Sentiment: {outcome['sentiment']}")
        print(f"Escalate: {outcome['escalate']}")
        print(f"Draft Response: {outcome['response']}")
        print(f"Raw Output:\n{outcome['raw']}\n")

I run the script from the terminal. The first ticket returns Technical and Calm, so the agent drafts a precise answer and clears it for automated delivery. The second ticket returns Billing and Frustrated, which flips the escalate boolean to True. Even though the LLM generated an empathetic apology, the policy layer holds it back from sending unsupervised. This combination of generative flexibility and hard-coded guardrails is how most production LLM applications actually ship. Example output:

---
Category: Technical
Sentiment: Calm
Escalate: False
Draft Response: Hi Alex, thanks for reaching out. You can export your data by navigating to Settings > Data > Export and selecting CSV. If the button is missing, try a hard refresh or let us know your browser version so we can investigate.
Raw Output:
Category: Technical
Response: Hi Alex, thanks for reaching out...
Sentiment: Calm

---
Category: Billing
Sentiment: Frustrated
Escalate: True
Draft Response: I sincerely apologize for the repeated charge. I am escalating this to our billing team immediately and they will issue a refund within 24 hours. You will receive a confirmation email shortly.
Raw Output:
Category: Billing
Response: I sincerely apologize...
Sentiment: Frustrated

Because Oxlo.ai uses per-request pricing, this pipeline costs the same for a hundred short tweets as it does for a hundred long email threads with full conversation history attached. That pricing model removes token anxiety and makes it practical to pass entire ticket histories into the context window for richer responses.

Next steps

This agent is already useful, but it is still stateless. Two concrete upgrades come to mind.

First, add memory. Store recent ticket history in a cheap key-value store and prepend it to the messages list. The LLM will recognize returning customers and avoid asking for information they already provided. Because Oxlo.ai does not penalize long inputs, you can include several prior turns without inflating cost.

Second, hook up function calling. Oxlo.ai supports tool use on models like Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 3 32B. You can give the agent real powers: looking up order status, processing refunds, or checking account balances against a live database. That turns a draft generator into an autonomous resolver. If you need deeper reasoning for complex log analysis, swap the model to DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 inside the same client call.

If you want to experiment, start with the free tier at Oxlo.ai. It includes 60 requests per day and access to models like DeepSeek V3.2, which is enough to iterate on this agent for several days without a credit card. When you move to production, the Pro or Premium plans unlock higher daily volumes and priority queueing. You can browse the full model catalog and per-request pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: LLM for Language Understanding: A Deep Dive
content:
Language understanding remains the fundamental capability that separates large language models from earlier generations of NLP systems. While token prediction drives the underlying mechanics, the emergent ability to parse intent, resolve coreference, and reason over implicit meaning enables developers to build semantic search engines, document analyzers, and autonomous research agents. For production systems, however, the practical cost of sending long documents, conversation histories, or multi-page legal contracts to an API can scale unpredictably when pricing is tied to token count. This is where the inference architecture behind Oxlo.ai becomes relevant for teams that treat language comprehension as a core workload rather than an occasional API call.

The Mechanics of Comprehension

Modern LLMs rely on transformer architectures with self-attention mechanisms that encode semantic relationships across positions in a sequence. When a model processes a paragraph, attention heads distribute weight across tokens to resolve pronouns, identify entities, and establish thematic continuity. The effective context window determines how much text can participate in a single inference pass. A model with a 131K context window, such as Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai, can ingest an entire technical manual or codebase in one request and answer questions that require cross-referencing distant sections. Similarly, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window, enabling analysis of books or extended conversation logs without chunking artifacts.

Comprehension quality depends on more than context length. Reasoning depth matters when models must infer unstated assumptions or perform multi-hop logical deductions. DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and GLM 5 are architected for these scenarios, using mixture-of-experts routing to allocate compute toward complex inference paths. For multilingual applications, Qwen 3 32B provides strong cross-lingual reasoning, which is essential when language understanding must operate across mixed-language corpora or non-English source documents.

Core Language Understanding Tasks

Developers deploy LLMs for language understanding across a predictable set of high-value tasks. Sentiment analysis and intent classification require models to read between the lines, distinguishing sarcasm from praise or identifying an implicit refund request inside a verbose customer message. Named entity recognition and relation extraction have shifted from shallow pattern matching to contextual disambiguation, where "Apple" is correctly classified based on surrounding finance terms rather than proximity to fruit vocabulary.

Summarization and synthesis represent another heavy-load use case. Abstractive summarization demands that the model comprehend source material deeply enough to paraphrase and prioritize, not merely extract sentences. Question answering over large corpora, whether through direct prompt injection or retrieval-augmented generation, requires the model to ground responses in provided evidence while rejecting distractors. Semantic search, powered by embedding models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large available through Oxlo.ai's embeddings endpoint, translates language understanding into vector space where conceptual similarity transcends keyword overlap.

The Cost Architecture of Long-Context Understanding

Language understanding workloads are disproportionately input-heavy. A classification job on a legal contract might submit fifty thousand tokens of text to extract a single boolean flag. A multi-turn support agent might maintain a growing message history that increases in length with every back-and-forth. Under token-based pricing, common among providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, these workloads incur costs that scale linearly with prompt length. For teams processing documents, logs, or conversation histories at volume, this pricing model creates a direct penalty for depth of context.

Oxlo.ai inverts this relationship with request-based pricing. Each API call incurs one flat cost regardless of prompt length, so sending a 100K token legal document costs the same as a one-sentence classification query. For long-context and agentic workloads, this architectural choice can yield significant savings, particularly when models with large context windows such as DeepSeek V4 Flash or Kimi K2.6 are used to analyze extensive inputs in a single pass. Teams no longer need to engineer aggressive chunking strategies solely to reduce token bills. You can review the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Implementing Language Understanding with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API, which means existing Python or Node.js applications require only a base URL change. The platform supports JSON mode for structured extraction, function calling for tool-augmented comprehension pipelines, and streaming responses for real-time applications.

title: The Future of Computer Vision: Leveraging LLMs for Innovation
content:
Computer vision is undergoing a fundamental shift. Traditional convolutional pipelines are giving way to unified multimodal architectures where large language models process pixels with the same fluency they handle text. This convergence is not incremental. It is reshaping how machines understand spatial relationships, reason about visual scenes, and generate photorealistic imagery from natural language descriptions. For developers building the next generation of intelligent applications, the question is no longer whether to integrate vision with language, but which inference platform can support the unique demands of multimodal workloads without imposing unpredictable costs.

Multimodal Reasoning Becomes the Default

The boundary between natural language processing and computer vision has dissolved. State-of-the-art vision-language models now embed high-resolution images into latent spaces shared with text tokens, enabling unified reasoning across modalities. These architectures do not merely attach a vision encoder to a language backbone. They train joint representations that allow models to answer complex questions about charts, diagnose issues from mechanical diagrams, and write code from UI screenshots. The result is a single model that can follow nuanced instructions involving both sight and language, reducing the need for hand-engineered perception pipelines.

This shift places new demands on inference infrastructure. Applications need endpoints that support vision inputs, multi-turn conversations, structured JSON outputs, and tool use. They also require low-latency streaming and no cold starts, because visual reasoning is increasingly embedded in real-time user experiences. Oxlo.ai meets these requirements with full OpenAI SDK compatibility, so existing codebases require only a base URL change to access vision-capable models. Developers can iterate without rewriting authentication logic or response parsers.

Agentic Vision and Long-Context Workloads

Vision is becoming agentic. Modern systems do not just classify objects. They plan, navigate, and manipulate environments based on continuous visual feedback. An agent might ingest multiple screenshots of a web application, compare them across conversation turns, and invoke tools to modify the interface. Others process long video sequences, medical imaging stacks, or satellite photography where a single logical task spans thousands of tokens. The agent loops between perception and action, and each loop may carry a heavy visual payload.

These workloads are inherently long-context. When a high-resolution image or a sequence of frames enters a transformer, the token count grows rapidly. Under token-based pricing, which is standard among providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, every pixel effectively adds to the bill. Input costs for a single agent step can exceed the cost of the generated response. Oxlo.ai departs from this model. Its request-based pricing charges one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For vision-heavy and agentic pipelines, this structural difference means costs remain stable even as context expands, making iteration financially predictable.

Generative and Analytical Capabilities

The modern computer vision pipeline is bifurcated into understanding and creation. On the analytical side, developers need vision-language models for interpretation and dedicated object detection models for precise localization. On the generative side, they need text-to-image diffusion models that can produce marketing assets, synthetic training data, or design prototypes. title: LLMs for Language Translation: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Machine translation has moved beyond phrase-based and neural statistical models. Large language models now handle translation as a generative reasoning task, capturing nuance, idioms, and domain-specific terminology that older pipelines flatten into literal equivalents. For engineering teams building localization pipelines, customer-support triage, or cross-lingual content generation, LLMs offer a programmable layer of linguistic intelligence that adapts to context rather than requiring retraining for every new language pair.

Why LLMs Are Reshaping Translation

Traditional MT systems excel on high-resource pairs but struggle with low-resource languages, code-switching, and tonal register. They also require separate engines, bilingual dictionaries, and continuous retraining for each domain. LLMs mitigate these issues through massive pretraining on multilingual corpora and instruction tuning. They infer style, preserve formatting, and resolve ambiguities by leveraging broader world knowledge. A single prompt can instruct an LLM to translate a legal contract into formal Brazilian Portuguese, then rewrite the same source as casual marketing copy, all without swapping model weights. This flexibility reduces infrastructure sprawl and cuts the maintenance overhead of managing bespoke bilingual resources for every target locale.

Architecture and Prompting Strategies

Translation quality depends heavily on prompt design and inference configuration. Zero-shot translation works for high-resource pairs and simple sentences, but few-shot prompting with verified examples improves consistency for technical or creative text. For high-stakes outputs, chain-of-thought reasoning encourages the model to break down ambiguous source segments before generating the target language, reducing hallucinated terminology.

Temperature and top-p sampling deserve attention. Translating poetry or marketing copy may benefit from higher temperature to preserve creative flair, while legal or medical texts should use values close to zero to maximize determinism. Structured output is equally important. By requesting JSON with predefined keys for translated text, detected source language, and confidence flags, you can validate responses programmatically. Function calling extends this further: an LLM can route a German customer ticket to the correct department while returning the translated body in a schema your CRM consumes directly. These patterns require reliable tool-use support and JSON mode, both of which should be first-class features in your inference backend.

Choosing the Right Model

Not every LLM handles multilingual workloads equally. You need models with broad language coverage, strong reasoning, and context windows large enough to ingest entire documents or parallel corpora for in-context learning.

Oxlo.ai hosts several options well-suited to translation pipelines. Qwen 3 32B offers multilingual reasoning and agentic workflow support, making it effective for translation tasks that involve tool use or multi-step verification. Llama 3.3 70B serves as a general-purpose flagship with robust performance across dozens of language pairs. For deep reasoning and complex coding documentation, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash provide extensive context windows and near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, with V4 Flash supporting up to 1 million tokens of context. Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision capabilities alongside a 131K context window, which is useful when translating mixed text and image content. GLM 5, with its 744B MoE architecture, targets long-horizon agentic tasks where translation is one step in a broader automation pipeline. Mistral models round out the catalog for low-latency European language pairs. For teams prioritizing efficiency, DeepSeek V3.2 offers strong coding and reasoning capabilities and is available on Oxlo.ai's free tier, letting you prototype without upfront cost.

Handling Long-Context and Document-Level Translation

Sentence-level translation destroys coherence. Pronouns, terminology, and narrative tone drift when context is truncated. Modern pipelines therefore feed entire chapters, legal briefs, or conversation threads into the model. This demands large context windows and an inference backend that does not penalize you for every additional token.

This is where Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing becomes structurally advantageous. Unlike token-based providers, where cost scales linearly with prompt length, Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per API request. For document-level translation, long-context summarization before translation, or agentic workflows that iterate over lengthy source texts, that pricing model removes the per-token tax on input length. You can pass full documents, include extensive few-shot examples, or maintain multi-turn conversational state without watching metered costs accumulate with every extra paragraph. The result is more coherent output and simpler capacity planning.

Tooling and Integration

A translation pipeline is only as reliable as its plumbing. You need streaming responses to show progress on long documents, JSON mode to enforce output schemas, and function calling to trigger post-processing steps like glossary enforcement or translation memory leverage.

Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. You can drop it into existing Python, Node.js, or cURL workflows with a single line change. That compatibility extends to chat completions, embeddings, and audio transcriptions, so you can unify speech-to-text, translation, and text-to-speech within one provider.

For example, a Python call targeting Qwen 3 32B for Spanish-to-English translation with JSON output looks like this:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Translate the user text to English. Return JSON with keys: translation, source_language."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "El contrato entrará en vigor el próximo mes."}
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

Because the endpoint mirrors the OpenAI SDK, you can reuse existing error handling, retry logic, and schema validation without refactoring your codebase.

Cost Engineering for Translation Workloads

Translation at scale is an economic optimization problem. Token-based billing rewards short prompts and punishes the context windows that produce coherent output. When you translate technical manuals, legal contracts, or chat histories, input tokens often dwarf output tokens, and costs scale unpredictably. A single long document can generate a surprisingly large bill before you reach the target language.

Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing inverts this dynamic. Workloads with long inputs, repeated context, or agentic loops that append conversation history become significantly cheaper because the cost is decoupled from sequence length. To understand exact plan tiers and request allowances, see the pricing page. The free tier includes 60 requests per day and access to models such as DeepSeek V3.2, which is sufficient for prototyping. Paid tiers scale to thousands of requests per day with priority queue access, giving production translation pipelines predictable budgeting without token arithmetic.

Evaluation and Quality Assurance

Automated metrics like BLEU and chrF correlate poorly with human judgments of fluency and adequacy for LLM-generated translations. Modern pipelines instead use LLM-as-judge frameworks, where a separate reasoning model evaluates faithfulness, terminology consistency, and register appropriateness against a rubric. You can implement this as a second API call that consumes the source and target texts, returning a structured quality score.

Embedding models also help. By computing semantic similarity between source embeddings and back-translated target embeddings via BGE-Large or E5-Large, you can catch meaning drift that n-gram metrics miss. A/B testing different models on held-out test sets is also essential. Because Oxlo.ai provides 45-plus models across a single endpoint, you can route production traffic to Llama 3.3 70B for general content, Qwen 3 32B for Asian language pairs, and DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for reasoning-intensive legal text, all while using identical SDK code. Centralized access simplifies benchmarking and lets you optimize for latency, cost, and quality without managing multiple provider accounts.

Conclusion

LLMs have turned translation from a static mapping problem into a context-aware reasoning task. Success depends on selecting models with genuine multilingual strength, engineering prompts that preserve document-level coherence, and choosing infrastructure that does not tax long-context inference. Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first platform with request-based pricing, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a broad catalog of models optimized for everything from rapid prototyping to high-volume document translation. If you are building the next generation of localization infrastructure, the economics and flexibility of per-request billing merit serious consideration. Start prototyping on the free tier and scale when your pipeline is ready.

title: Mastering Transfer Learning with LLMs
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage agent that adapts a general-purpose LLM to your private classification taxonomy without retraining. By retrieving labeled historical examples and injecting them into the prompt, we transfer domain knowledge to the model at inference time. This is the cheapest path to production-grade classification, and we will run it entirely on Oxlo.ai.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • pip install openai numpy
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • A handful of labeled support tickets. We will mock these in code so you can run the tutorial immediately.

Step 1: Seed the knowledge base with labeled examples

Transfer learning needs a source domain. I will start with a hard-coded list of past tickets mapped to internal categories. In production, this would be your CRM export or data warehouse query. These examples are the only task-specific data the model will see.

labeled_examples = [
    {"ticket": "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month.", "category": "Billing"},
    {"ticket": "The webhook fires twice on every push event.", "category": "Bug"},
    {"ticket": "How do I migrate from v1 to v2 of the REST API?", "category": "Integration"},
    {"ticket": "My invoice shows the wrong VAT rate.", "category": "Billing"},
    {"ticket": "SDK crashes when parsing null fields in the response.", "category": "Bug"},
    {"ticket": "Do you support OAuth 2.0 PKCE for mobile apps?", "category": "Integration"},
]

Step 2: Embed the examples with Oxlo.ai embeddings

To find relevant examples quickly, we turn each ticket into a dense vector. Oxlo.ai hosts the BGE-Large embedding model, which we access through the same OpenAI-compatible client and API key. Keeping the stack unified means one client, one base URL, and one set of credentials.

from openai import OpenAI
import numpy as np

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def get_embedding(text):
    resp = client.embeddings.create(
        model="bge-large",
        input=[text]
    )
    return np.array(resp.data[0].embedding)

# Index all examples
for ex in labeled_examples:
    ex["embedding"] = get_embedding(ex["ticket"])

print(f"Indexed {len(labeled_examples)} examples.")

Step 3: Build the similarity retriever

At inference time we compute cosine similarity between the new ticket and our indexed history. For a prototype that lives in memory, pure NumPy is enough. The top three matches become our few-shot context.

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

def retrieve_examples(query_text, k=3):
    query_vec = get_embedding(query_text)
    scored = [
        (cosine_similarity(query_vec, ex["embedding"]), ex)
        for ex in labeled_examples
    ]
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
    return [ex for _, ex in scored[:k]]

Step 4: Write the system prompt

The model needs guardrails. I keep the prompt short and strict so the output is easy to parse downstream. The categories must match our internal taxonomy exactly, or the routing logic will break.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a support ticket triage agent. "
    "Your job is to classify each incoming ticket into exactly one of these categories: "
    "Billing, Bug, Integration. "
    "Respond with only the category name and no extra punctuation or explanation. "
    "Base your decision on the pattern shown in the examples."
)

Step 5: Assemble the few-shot prompt and call the LLM

Here is where the transfer happens. We prepend the retrieved examples as user and assistant turns, which acts like a lightweight adapter layer on top of the foundation model. Oxlo.ai serves Llama 3.3 70B with no cold start, and because pricing is per request rather than per token, adding extra context examples does not inflate the cost of each call. That makes iterating on prompt length free from token arithmetic.

def classify_ticket(ticket_text):
    examples = retrieve_examples(ticket_text, k=3)
    
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    
    # Inject few-shot examples as user/assistant turns
    for ex in examples:
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ex["ticket"]})
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": ex["category"]})
    
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": ticket_text})
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

# Test
new_ticket = "I keep getting 401 errors after rotating my API key."
print(classify_ticket(new_ticket))

Run it

Let us test the pipeline on a ticket that is not in the original set. I will print the retrieved examples so you can see why the model chose the label it did.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unseen = "Since rotating my API key, every request returns 401 Unauthorized."
    
    print("Retrieved examples:")
    for ex in retrieve_examples(unseen, k=3):
        print(" -", ex["category"] + ":", ex["ticket"][:60] + "...")
    
    print("\nPredicted category:", classify_ticket(unseen))

When I run this, the output looks like this:

Retrieved examples:
 - Integration: Do you support OAuth 2.0 PKCE for mobile apps?...
 - Bug: SDK crashes when parsing null fields in the response....
 - Billing: My invoice shows the wrong VAT rate....

Predicted category: Integration

Wrap-up and next steps

This pipeline is already useful, but it is just a starting point. You can swap Llama 3.3 70B for Qwen 3 32B if your tickets arrive in multiple languages, or for DeepSeek V3.2 if you need stronger reasoning over long error logs. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, expanding the few-shot window to ten or twenty examples does not change your unit cost. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plan details.

Two concrete next steps: persist your embedding index in a vector database so the knowledge base scales beyond memory, and add a confidence threshold that falls back to a human reviewer when the top similarity score is below 0.75. If you want to experiment without cost, the Oxlo.ai free tier includes 60 requests per day, which is enough to prototype this entire flow.

title: Unlocking LLM Potential for Content Generation
content:
Content generation has moved beyond simple autocomplete. Modern pipelines rely on long-context reasoning, structured output, and multi-step agentic workflows that ingest style guides, retrieval-augmented generation context, prior conversation history, and even visual assets. For engineering teams building these systems, the underlying inference layer determines whether a pipeline is fast, affordable, and maintainable. The right platform should remove infrastructure friction so developers can focus on prompts, orchestration, and evaluation rather than token counters and cold-start latency.

The Architecture of Modern Content Pipelines

A production content pipeline is rarely a single prompt. It is usually a chain of stages: ingestion, enrichment, drafting, revision, and formatting. Each stage can require different context lengths. A style guide alone might run thousands of tokens. When you add few-shot examples, retrieval-augmented generation context, and conversation memory, input length balloons quickly. This is where infrastructure choices separate proof-of-concepts from production systems. If your provider bills by the token, every extra paragraph in the prompt directly increases cost. If your provider suffers from cold starts, latency undermines real-time editing experiences. You need an inference layer that treats long context as a feature, not a premium, and that offers the endpoints necessary for multimodal content. Beyond text, modern pipelines may generate images through endpoints like images/generations, produce audio via audio/speech, or transcribe source material through audio/transcriptions. A unified platform simplifies this stack.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. title: Unlocking LLM Potential for Part-of-Speech Tagging
content:
Part-of-speech tagging remains a foundational task in natural language processing, but the tools used to solve it are shifting. For decades, the state of the art relied on hidden Markov models, conditional random fields, and later, fine-tuned transformer encoders. These approaches excel on clean, well-studied corpora, yet they struggle with contextual ambiguity, low-resource languages, and domain-specific text that diverges from standard grammar. Large language models offer a compelling alternative. With broad pretraining and in-context learning capabilities, modern LLMs can perform zero-shot and few-shot POS tagging with high accuracy, often resolving ambiguities that confuse static taggers. The barrier to adoption is not model capability, but infrastructure economics. When tagging requires sending long contexts, extensive few-shot examples, or entire documents to resolve edge cases, token-based billing turns routine inference into a significant cost center. Oxlo.ai addresses this directly with request-based pricing that decouples cost from input length, making long-context LLM tagging economically viable.

Why LLMs Are Being Used for POS Tagging

Traditional POS taggers are fast and deterministic, yet their performance depends heavily on the quality and domain of their training data. Out-of-vocabulary words, rare syntactic constructions, and informal text found in social media or clinical notes frequently produce errors. LLMs mitigate these issues through massive pretraining on diverse corpora and the ability to condition predictions on broad context windows.

A single word like "run" can function as a noun or a verb depending on its surroundings. While contextual embeddings in fine-tuned models help, they are limited by fixed architectures and local context windows. LLMs can leverage paragraph-level or document-level context to make more informed decisions. This is particularly valuable in low-resource languages, where annotated training data for specialized taggers is scarce. A model such as Qwen 3 32B, available on Oxlo.ai, brings strong multilingual reasoning capabilities that extend to syntactic analysis without requiring language-specific fine-tuning.

Furthermore, organizations increasingly want unified NLP pipelines. Rather than maintaining separate models for POS tagging, named entity recognition, and syntactic parsing, teams can prompt a single LLM to produce structured linguistic annotations in one pass. This simplifies deployment and reduces the surface area for model versioning and dependency management.

The Cost and Context Problem

The practical challenge of LLM-based POS tagging is not accuracy, but cost structure. Most inference providers bill per token. Because POS tagging benefits from surrounding context, a single token of interest may require sending an entire sentence, paragraph, or few-shot prompt containing dozens of examples. In token-based economies, the cost of analyzing a long document scales linearly with its length.

This dynamic penalizes exactly the workflows where LLMs add the most value. Tagging a full legal brief, a book chapter, or a multilingual conversation transcript demands long input sequences. Few-shot prompting, which significantly improves tagging consistency, adds even more tokens. Over thousands of documents, these costs accumulate rapidly. For teams building agentic systems that iteratively analyze and re-tag text, per-token pricing creates unpredictable budgets and forces artificial truncation of context.

How Oxlo.ai Request-Based Pricing Changes the Economics

Oxlo.ai approaches inference pricing differently. Instead of metering every input and output token, Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per API request. For POS tagging workloads, this means the cost to tag a short sentence is the same as the cost to tag a long paragraph, provided both fit within a single request. When your pipeline needs to send extensive context, multiple few-shot examples, or lengthy documents to resolve syntactic ambiguity, request-based pricing prevents costs from scaling with text volume.

This structure is especially relevant for long-context and agentic workflows. If you are processing a large document and need to maintain coherence across sections, you can send large chunks to a model like DeepSeek V4 Flash, which supports a 1M context window, without incurring token-proportional fees. Similarly, multilingual tasks that expand token counts due to subword segmentation, such as those handled effectively by Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6, do not trigger surprise cost spikes on Oxlo.ai.

The platform offers 45+ models across seven categories, fully OpenAI SDK compatible, with no cold starts on popular models. You can experiment on the free tier, which includes access to models like DeepSeek V3.2, and scale to Pro or Premium plans as your tagging volume grows. For detailed plan information, see the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Choosing the Right Model on Oxlo.ai

Not every POS tagging task requires the largest model. Oxlo.ai provides options that let you trade off latency, context length, and reasoning depth.

For general-purpose English text, Llama 3.3 70B offers a strong balance of capability and throughput. When working with multilingual or mixed-language documents, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, making it well suited to cross-lingual tagging tasks.

If your pipeline processes entire reports, books, or conversation logs in a single call, DeepSeek V4 Flash provides an efficient MoE architecture with a 1M context window and near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning. For documents where advanced disambiguation matters, Kimi K2.6 delivers advanced reasoning and agentic coding capabilities across a 131K context window, while Kimi K2.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking offer strong chain-of-thought reasoning for particularly ambiguous syntactic structures.

For teams experimenting before committing resources, DeepSeek V3.2 is available on the free tier and handles coding and reasoning tasks capably. GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 round out the catalog for long-horizon agentic tasks and tool use, respectively, if your POS tagging pipeline is part of a broader linguistic agent.

Implementation: Few-Shot Prompting with JSON Mode

A robust POS tagging pipeline requires structured, parseable output. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, which lets you constrain the model to return valid JSON rather than free text. Combined with the OpenAI SDK, integration requires only a base URL change.

Below is a minimal Python example using few-shot prompting to tag a sentence. The prompt includes examples in the system message, and JSON mode ensures the response can be fed directly into downstream analytics.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a linguistics engine that performs part-of-speech tagging. "
                "Respond in JSON with a list of objects, each containing 'token' and 'tag'. "
                "Use the Penn Treebank tagset. "
                "Examples: "
                "[{'token': 'The', 'tag': 'DT'}, {'token': 'dog', 'tag': 'NN'}]"
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Tag the following sentence: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog."
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

import json
tags = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(tags)

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, existing pipelines written for other providers can be migrated by changing the base URL and model identifier. Streaming responses are also supported, so you can process tags as they arrive rather than waiting for the full JSON payload.

Integrating LLM POS Tagging into Existing NLP Pipelines

Adopting an LLM for POS tagging does not require abandoning existing tooling. Many teams use a hybrid architecture in which a traditional tagger handles unambiguous baseline text, and an LLM is invoked only for ambiguous tokens, out-of-vocabulary terms, or domain-specific passages. This reduces latency and cost while preserving high accuracy.

For real-time applications, Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, allowing your pipeline to begin processing tokens before the generation is complete. If your workflow requires transcription of audio before tagging, the platform also offers audio endpoints via Whisper Large v3 and text-to-speech via Kokoro 82M, enabling end-to-end spoken language processing on the same infrastructure.

When building multi-turn correction workflows, you can leverage the chat completions endpoint to iteratively refine tags based on user feedback or downstream validation rules. The absence of cold starts on popular models means these interactions remain responsive even under variable load.

When to Use an LLM versus a Traditional Tagger

Traditional POS taggers remain the right choice for high-throughput, low-latency processing of short, well-formed sentences in supported languages. If you are tagging millions of clean English tweets with a tight latency budget, a fine-tuned encoder will be faster and more resource efficient.

However, LLM-based tagging becomes advantageous when you face contextual ambiguity, non-standard grammar, low-resource languages, or the need to unify multiple annotation tasks in a single call. Long documents that require cross-sentence context also favor LLMs, provided the inference platform does not penalize you for input length. Oxlo.ai removes that penalty through request-based pricing, making it economically rational to use LLMs precisely in the scenarios where they outperform traditional alternatives.

Conclusion

Part-of-speech tagging is entering a new phase where context and reasoning matter as much as speed. Large language models provide the contextual depth to handle ambiguity, multilingual text, and domain drift, but their adoption in production pipelines depends on infrastructure that aligns cost with value. Token-based pricing discourages the long-context prompting that makes LLM tagging effective.

Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first alternative. With flat per-request pricing, 45+ models including long-context options like DeepSeek V4 Flash and Kimi K2.6, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility, Oxlo.ai makes it practical to deploy LLM-driven POS tagging at scale. Whether you are experimenting on the free tier or running high-volume document analysis, the platform provides the context capacity and pricing structure that linguistic AI workloads require.

title: Semantic Role Labeling with LLMs: A Technical Overview
content:
Semantic role labeling identifies who did what to whom in a sentence. Traditional pipelines rely on PropBank or FrameNet-trained models that break when domain vocabulary shifts. We are going to build an LLM-powered SRL extractor that reads raw sentences and returns structured predicate-argument frames in JSON. This is useful for NLP engineers who need event representations without maintaining a custom transformer model, and for data teams who want to turn unstructured news or support tickets into queryable graphs. I will walk through the exact code I use to get consistent, parseable output from Oxlo.ai.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an API key from Oxlo.ai. Install the SDK with pip and grab your key from the portal.

  • Python 3.10+
  • pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so batching long sentences or documents does not inflate cost the way token-based billing would. You can send a paragraph-length sentence and pay the same as a three-word sentence. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for details. This matters for SRL because legal and medical texts often contain long arguments that would otherwise consume thousands of tokens per request.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the OpenAI SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI API compatible, this is a drop-in replacement. I keep the API key in an environment variable in production, but here it is inline for clarity. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so the first request after import returns immediately. I also import json because we will need to parse structured output later.

import json
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Define the SRL system prompt

The system prompt is the most important part of the build. It constrains the model to emit strict JSON and defines the semantic roles we care about. I treat this as a config file. It tells the model to identify predicates and label arguments as Agent, Patient, Theme, Instrument, Location, or Time. Keeping the instruction set short reduces the chance of hallucinated roles. I explicitly forbid markdown wrapping because LLMs sometimes emit fenced code blocks when asked for JSON. You can extend the role list later if your domain needs Benefactor or Experiencer.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a semantic role labeling engine.
For the input sentence, identify every predicate and its arguments.
Output a single JSON object with this exact structure:
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "verb",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "exact span", "role": "Agent|Patient|Theme|Instrument|Location|Time"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Rules:
- Use the exact words from the sentence for each text span.
- If a role does not apply, omit it.
- Do not wrap the JSON in markdown. Output raw JSON only."""

Step 3: Build the extraction function

Next I write a small wrapper that sends the sentence to Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai and parses the response. I set temperature low to keep the output deterministic. I also strip any accidental markdown fences before parsing. If you prefer a reasoning model for ambiguous sentences, you can swap the model string to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6 without changing any other code. The helper returns a native Python dictionary, so downstream code does not need to touch raw text. I do not add retry logic here yet; we will handle that in the next step.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a semantic role labeling engine.
For the input sentence, identify every predicate and its arguments.
Output a single JSON object with this exact structure:
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "verb",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "exact span", "role": "Agent|Patient|Theme|Instrument|Location|Time"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Rules:
- Use the exact words from the sentence for each text span.
- If a role does not apply, omit it.
- Do not wrap the JSON in markdown. Output raw JSON only."""

def label_sentence(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=1024,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1]
    if raw.endswith("```"):
        raw = raw.rsplit("\n", 1)[0]
    return json.loads(raw.strip())

# Quick sanity check
if __name__ == "__main__":
    test = "The engineer deployed the hotfix to production last night."
    print(json.dumps(label_sentence(test), indent=2))

Step 4: Add batch processing and a fallback model

For production use I process multiple sentences in a loop. If Llama 3.3 70B returns malformed JSON on a tricky passive construction, I fall back to Qwen 3 32B, which handles multilingual and complex syntactic reordering well. Both models are available on Oxlo.ai with the same client and base URL. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, running a second model on the same input costs the same flat rate as the first, not double the tokens. The fallback keeps the pipeline robust without adding billing surprises. In practice I see the fallback trigger on long coordinate structures and embedded clauses.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a semantic role labeling engine.
For the input sentence, identify every predicate and its arguments.
Output a single JSON object with this exact structure:
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "verb",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "exact span", "role": "Agent|Patient|Theme|Instrument|Location|Time"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
Rules:
- Use the exact words from the sentence for each text span.
- If a role does not apply, omit it.
- Do not wrap the JSON in markdown. Output raw JSON only."""

def label_sentence(text: str, model: str = "llama-3.3-70b") -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=1024,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1]
    if raw.endswith("```"):
        raw = raw.rsplit("\n", 1)[0]
    return json.loads(raw.strip())

def label_with_fallback(text: str) -> dict:
    try:
        return label_sentence(text, model="llama-3.3-70b")
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return label_sentence(text, model="qwen-3-32b")

sentences = [
    "The chef cooked the meal in the kitchen.",
    "The meal was cooked by the chef in the kitchen.",
    "Investors acquired the startup for fifty million dollars.",
]

for s in sentences:
    result = label_with_fallback(s)
    print(f"Sentence: {s}")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    print()

Run it

Save the script as srl.py and run it from your terminal. You should see structured JSON for each sentence with predicates and arguments extracted. Here is the output I get from Oxlo.ai using the exact code above. The spans use exact substring matches from the input, which makes it easy to highlight them in a UI later.

$ python srl.py
Sentence: The chef cooked the meal in the kitchen.
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "cooked",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "The chef", "role": "Agent"},
        {"text": "the meal", "role": "Patient"},
        {"text": "in the kitchen", "role": "Location"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Sentence: The meal was cooked by the chef in the kitchen.
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "cooked",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "The meal", "role": "Patient"},
        {"text": "by the chef", "role": "Agent"},
        {"text": "in the kitchen", "role": "Location"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Sentence: Investors acquired the startup for fifty million dollars.
{
  "frames": [
    {
      "predicate": "acquired",
      "arguments": [
        {"text": "Investors", "role": "Agent"},
        {"text": "the startup", "role": "Patient"},
        {"text": "for fifty million dollars", "role": "Theme"}
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Wrap up

This pipeline gives you production-ready SRL without training data or managing infrastructure. Two concrete next steps: pipe the JSON frames into a graph database like Neo4j to build searchable event graphs, or use the labeled output as synthetic training data to fine-tune a smaller model on Oxlo.ai for even lower latency. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, you can feed it long documents or run large batch jobs without watching token meters spin up. Sign up at https://portal.oxlo.ai to get an API key and try it against your own text.

title: Sentiment Analysis with LLMs: Best Practices and Use Cases
content:
This tutorial walks through building a batch sentiment analysis pipeline that turns raw customer feedback into structured JSON. It scores polarity, confidence, and reasoning so support and product teams can prioritize issues without reading every ticket. I built this on Oxlo.ai because the flat per-request pricing keeps long prompts predictable, which matters when you are stuffing full support threads into the context window.

What you'll need

Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. You will also need a CSV file named feedback.csv with at least a text column. Install the SDK with pip install openai.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

The OpenAI SDK is a drop-in client for Oxlo.ai. Point the base URL at the Oxlo.ai endpoint, load your key, and pick a model. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it follows instructions reliably for classification work.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"  # from https://portal.oxlo.ai
)

MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The prompt is the contract. I force JSON output with a strict schema so parsing never fails. The model must return sentiment, a confidence score between 0.0 and 1.0, and a one-sentence rationale.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment analysis engine. Analyze the user feedback and respond ONLY with a JSON object in this exact schema:

{
  "sentiment": "positive" | "neutral" | "negative",
  "confidence": float between 0.0 and 1.0,
  "reasoning": "one sentence explaining why"
}

Rules:
- sentiment must be exactly one of the three allowed strings.
- confidence should reflect how unambiguous the text is.
- Do not include markdown, explanations, or code fences outside the JSON."""

Step 3: Build the analyzer function

Wrap the API call in a helper that catches malformed JSON and retries with a simpler prompt if needed. I keep temperature low for deterministic classifications and strip any accidental markdown fences from the output.

def analyze_sentiment(text: str) -> dict:
    """Call Oxlo.ai to classify a single piece of feedback."""
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=256,
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    
    # Some models may wrap JSON in markdown fences. Strip them.
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process a batch of feedback

I use the standard library csv module so there are no extra dependencies. Read the file, analyze each row, and append results. I add a small sleep to stay polite on rate limits, though Oxlo.ai has no cold starts so the loop moves fast.

import csv
import time

def process_csv(input_path: str, output_path: str):
    results = []
    
    with open(input_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            text = row.get("text", "").strip()
            if not text:
                continue
            
            try:
                analysis = analyze_sentiment(text)
                analysis["original_text"] = text
            except Exception as e:
                analysis = {
                    "sentiment": "error",
                    "confidence": 0.0,
                    "reasoning": str(e),
                    "original_text": text,
                }
            
            results.append(analysis)
            time.sleep(0.2)  # polite rate limiting
    
    with open(output_path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(
            f, fieldnames=["original_text", "sentiment", "confidence", "reasoning"]
        )
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(results)
    
    print(f"Wrote {len(results)} results to {output_path}")

Step 5: Aggregate and export results

After classification, we need a summary. This script prints a distribution and surfaces the highest-confidence negative comments for immediate triage.

from collections import Counter

def summarize(output_path: str):
    sentiments = []
    negatives = []
    
    with open(output_path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            sentiments.append(row["sentiment"])
            if row["sentiment"] == "negative":
                negatives.append((float(row["confidence"]), row["original_text"]))
    
    counts = Counter(sentiments)
    total = sum(counts.values())
    
    print("Sentiment distribution:")
    for s, c in counts.items():
        print(f"  {s}: {c} ({c/total:.1%})")
    
    print("\nTop negative feedback (by confidence):")
    for conf, text in sorted(negatives, reverse=True)[:3]:
        print(f"  [{conf:.2f}] {text[:100]}...")

Run it

Create a small feedback.csv in the same folder.

text
"I love the new dashboard. It saves me hours every week."
"The export button is broken again. This is the third time."
"Login works fine. Nothing special to report."

Then execute the pipeline.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_csv("feedback.csv", "results.csv")
    summarize("results.csv")

Expected output in your terminal:

Wrote 3 results to results.csv
Sentiment distribution:
  positive: 1 (33.3%)
  negative: 1 (33.3%)
  neutral: 1 (33.3%)

Top negative feedback (by confidence):
  [0.95] The export button is broken again. This is the third time...

Wrap-up and next steps

This pipeline is already useful, but two upgrades make it production-grade. First, swap in Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 if your feedback is multilingual. Second, replace the CSV files with a small FastAPI endpoint that accepts webhooks from your CRM and writes results to a database. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing means those longer support threads with ten messages of history still cost one flat request, so you can afford to send full context without surprise bills. You can explore the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Building Chatbots with LLMs: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Building a production-ready chatbot requires more than prompting a language model. You need to select the right model, architect a robust context layer, and choose an inference backend that scales economically as your usage grows. This guide walks through the practical steps, from selecting an LLM to deploying a system that handles streaming responses, tool use, and long conversational memory.

Choose Your Foundation: Model and Provider

Selecting a model is your first architectural decision. General-purpose chatbots need strong reasoning and broad knowledge, while specialized agents may prioritize coding, multilingual support, or vision capabilities. Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories. For general tasks, Llama 3.3 70B serves as a reliable flagship. For multilingual agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B provides strong reasoning across languages. If your bot solves complex coding problems or performs deep reasoning, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 are solid choices. Kimi K2.6 also brings a 131K context window and vision support for agentic coding tasks.

Your pricing model is equally important. Token-based billing scales linearly with input length, which becomes expensive when chatbots ingest long system prompts, documentation, or conversation history. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing. Each API call costs the same regardless of prompt length, which makes it significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads. You can explore the structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can integrate it without rewriting your client code. Point your existing Python or Node.js application to the Oxlo.ai base URL and swap models as needed.

Design the Conversation Architecture

A chatbot is stateless by default. The LLM sees only the messages you send in the current request. Your application must maintain a message array with roles: system, user, and assistant.

The system prompt defines behavior. Be explicit about tone, constraints, and available tools. A vague system prompt produces inconsistent results. For example, instead of saying "be helpful," specify "You are a technical support assistant. Answer in one paragraph. If you do not know the answer, say so."

Structure your message history as an ordered list. Pass the full history on every request, or implement a truncation strategy. Keep in mind that with token-based providers, longer histories increase cost linearly. With Oxlo.ai, the per-request pricing model removes this penalty, letting you pass richer context without worrying about token count.

Implement Core Features with Code

Modern chatbots need more than text replies. They need streaming, structured output, and tool use. Here is how to implement these using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai.

First, install the SDK:

pip install openai

Then configure the client:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

Streaming reduces perceived latency. Instead of waiting for the full completion, render tokens as they arrive:

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain recursion"}],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")

Function calling lets your chatbot interact with external APIs. Define your tools in the request, and the model will return structured arguments:

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools
)

If you need deterministic output shapes, use JSON mode to constrain the model to valid JSON. This is useful for parsing user intent or returning structured data to your frontend. Oxlo.ai supports streaming, function calling, JSON mode, and vision inputs across its model catalog, so you can build complex agents without switching providers.

Handle Context and Memory

As conversations grow, you will exceed context limits or dilute attention. You have three strategies: truncation, summarization, and vector retrieval.

Truncation drops the oldest messages when you approach a limit. This is simple but loses information. Summarization compresses early turns into a single summary message, preserving key facts while saving space. Vector retrieval stores conversation facts in an embedding database and injects only the most relevant snippets into the current prompt.

For chatbots that maintain very long sessions, model selection matters. Oxlo.ai hosts models like DeepSeek V4 Flash with a 1 million token context window and Kimi K2.6 with 131K context. These windows let you keep extensive history in memory. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, you can utilize these large contexts without the cost escalating with every additional sentence in the prompt.

Add Multimodal Capabilities

Text-only chatbots are no longer the default. Users expect to upload screenshots, diagrams, or documents. Vision-enabled models accept image inputs alongside text, letting your chatbot analyze UI mockups, charts, or handwritten notes.

Oxlo.ai provides vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B. You can pass image URLs or base64-encoded data through the same chat completions endpoint. This keeps your architecture unified. If your use case involves audio, Whisper Large v3 handles transcriptions, while Kokoro 82M provides text-to-speech, allowing you to build voice-enabled assistants on the same platform.

Deploy, Monitor, and Control Costs

Moving from prototype to production requires observability and rate management. Log requests, measure latency, and track failure rates. Use retries with exponential backoff for transient errors.

Cost control is critical. On token-based platforms, an unexpected spike in user activity or a misconfigured system prompt can double your bill. Plans range from a Free tier with 60 requests per day and 16+ free models, to Pro at 1,000 requests per day, and Premium at 5,000 requests per day with priority queue.
