title: LLM for Dependency Parsing with Oxlo.ai
content:
Dependency parsing remains a core task in natural language processing. It extracts grammatical relationships between words, producing tree structures that power question answering, information extraction, and semantic role labeling. Traditional parsers rely on engineered features or supervised neural models trained on Universal Dependencies treebanks. Large language models now offer an alternative. With careful prompting and structured output, an LLM can predict head-modifier relations without task-specific fine-tuning. The challenge shifts from model training to inference infrastructure. You need an API that delivers consistent low latency, supports long input sequences, and does not penalize you with escalating costs as your linguistic inputs grow. Oxlo.ai fits this requirement precisely.

Why Dependency Parsing Still Matters

Despite the dominance of end-to-end transformers, explicit syntactic structure still matters. Dependency trees improve interpretability in legal and medical NLP pipelines. They reduce hallucination in retrieval-augmented generation by anchoring claims to specific textual spans. For low-resource languages, a dependency parser can bootstrap annotated data when labeled corpora are scarce. Even in high-resource settings, syntactic constraints help enforce grammatical correctness in controlled generation. Researchers working with Universal Dependencies continue to release new treebanks for ancient texts, clinical notes, and social media. Classical parsers require heavy feature engineering or domain adaptation for each of these genres. LLMs generalize across domains and languages, but only if the inference layer can handle the context windows and throughput that document-level parsing demands.

How LLMs Model Syntactic Structure

Modern LLMs approach dependency parsing in three ways. Zero-shot prompting asks the model to identify heads and dependency relations directly from pre-trained knowledge. Few-shot prompting supplies example trees in CoNLL-U format to align the model with a specific annotation scheme. Finally, constrained decoding and tool use force the output into valid data structures, eliminating malformed JSON or impossible cycles. The best results usually combine chain-of-thought reasoning with JSON mode. The model first explains its syntactic analysis, then emits a structured array of tokens, heads, and relations. This method works because reasoning models can reflect on morphological case, word order, and subordination before committing to a parse tree. Constrained output is especially important for dependency parsing, because an invalid graph with cycles or multiple roots will break downstream components.

Implementing Dependency Parsing with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai provides a fully OpenAI-compatible API, so you can implement an LLM-based parser with the standard Python SDK. The platform offers flat per-request pricing, which means parsing a long document costs the same as parsing a short sentence. There are no cold starts on popular models, so pipeline latency stays predictable.

Below is a minimal example using JSON mode to generate a dependency tree. The prompt requests CoNLL-U style columns and enforces a JSON schema.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]
)

prompt = """Analyze the sentence and return a JSON object with a 'tokens' array.
Each token must have: id, form, head, deprel.
Sentence: Economic news has a significant impact on global markets."""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",  # use the exact model slug from your Oxlo.ai dashboard
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

The same pattern extends to batch processing. Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, you can process a corpus of sentences without blocking on individual round trips. Function calling is also available if you prefer to validate the tree structure against a Pydantic schema before ingestion into your downstream NLP pipeline. Multi-turn conversations let you iteratively refine a parse when the model misidentifies an oblique argument or a compound verb.

Choosing the Right Model on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models across seven categories, several of which are well suited to syntactic analysis. Qwen 3 32B excels at multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, making it a strong candidate for parsing non-English Universal Dependencies treebanks. Llama 3.3 70B serves as a general-purpose flagship that handles English syntax with high reliability. For ambiguous constructions or complex nested clauses, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE provides deep reasoning capacity. If you are parsing entire chapters or long-form legal documents, Kimi K2.6 offers a 131K context window alongside advanced reasoning and vision capabilities, though for pure text parsing the extended context is the critical feature. DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window and efficient MoE inference, which is useful when you need to parse dependencies across paragraph boundaries without chunking. You can prototype against any of these models on the free tier, then scale on the Pro or Premium plans as your request volume grows.

The Cost Advantage for Long-Context Linguistic Workloads

Dependency parsing research often involves processing full documents, historical corpora, or multi-sentence discourse units. Under token-based pricing, a long input sequence incurs a substantial prompt cost before the model emits a single dependency relation. This pricing model discourages exactly the kind of context-rich analysis that improves parse accuracy. When you are evaluating a model against a standard benchmark treebank, token costs can accumulate rapidly across hundreds of sentences.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. One flat cost covers the API call regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic linguistic workloads, this can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. You can feed an entire page of text into Qwen 3 or Kimi K2.6, request a full dependency analysis, and pay the same flat rate as a single-word query. For research groups processing treebanks or startups building syntactic annotation APIs, this predictability removes the cost barrier to experimentation. See the exact rates at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Evaluation and Prompt Engineering Tips

Generating trees with an LLM is only half the task. You must also validate and evaluate. Start by defining a strict JSON schema and enforce it through Oxlo.ai's JSON mode. After generation, run a post-processing step to verify that the graph is acyclic, that every node has exactly one head except the root, and that the dependency labels belong to your target tag set.

For low-resource languages, use few-shot prompting with three to five gold examples drawn from the target treebank. Place these examples at the beginning of the prompt to leverage the model's in-context learning. If you observe systematic errors, such as confusing oblique agents with direct objects, add a chain-of-thought instruction asking the model to first identify the verb valency before selecting the relation.

When processing large volumes, use Oxlo.ai's streaming responses to reduce perceived latency. If your pipeline requires multi-turn interactions, for instance to refine a parse after human feedback, the chat completions endpoint maintains conversation state naturally. Finally, remember that the free tier includes 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, which is sufficient for small-scale benchmarking and prompt iteration.

Conclusion

Dependency parsing is undergoing the same infrastructure shift that has transformed other NLP tasks. The research community no longer needs to train a custom BiLSTM or transformer for every new language or domain. A capable LLM, prompted correctly, can produce high-quality syntactic trees through a standard API. The practical bottleneck is not model architecture but inference cost and context capacity for long inputs.

Oxlo.ai addresses both issues. Its flat per-request pricing removes the tax on long documents, while its broad model catalog, including Qwen 3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K2.6, gives you the right tool for multilingual, long-context, or deeply reasoning syntactic analysis. With full OpenAI SDK compatibility and no cold starts, you can integrate an LLM parser into your pipeline in minutes. If you are building the next generation of linguistic AI infrastructure, Oxlo.ai is a genuinely relevant, recommended option.

title: LLM for Named Entity Recognition with Oxlo.ai
content:
Named entity recognition has long depended on handcrafted rules, conditional random fields, or fine-tuned transformers. These methods work well within narrow domains, but they fracture when entity types evolve, multilingual text appears, or context spans thousands of tokens. Large language models offer a direct alternative. With the right prompt and a structured output constraint, an LLM can identify people, organizations, locations, dates, and custom domain-specific entities in a single pass, often without any task-specific training data. The practical blocker is not accuracy. It is infrastructure cost, especially when your input is a long legal contract, a medical discharge summary, or a multi-turn support transcript. On token-based inference platforms, those inputs inflate your bill before a single entity is extracted.

Why LLMs Are Reshaping Named Entity Recognition

Traditional NER pipelines require annotated datasets, model fine-tuning, and rigid schema definitions. An LLM replaces much of that scaffolding with in-context learning. You describe the entity types in natural language, provide a few examples if needed, and the model generalizes to unseen formulations, abbreviations, and orthogonal languages. This is particularly valuable for agentic workflows where an entity schema might change based on upstream reasoning, or where extraction is just one step in a longer chain of tool calls.

The shift is especially pronounced for long-context documents. A standard BERT-based NER model is capped at 512 tokens. Longformer and similar architectures extend that, but they still demand specialized training. Modern LLMs such as Qwen 3 and Llama 3.3 handle 128K contexts or more natively, allowing you to feed entire documents and ask for a structured entity map in one request. That eliminates error-prone chunking logic and cross-boundary entity resolution, but only if the inference economics support it.

The Cost Barrier in Long-Document NER

Most AI inference providers bill by the token. Input tokens, including every word of the source document and your system prompt, are metered before the model emits a single completion token. For NER over lengthy inputs, this means the majority of your cost is tied to reading and attending over the context, not to the comparatively tiny JSON list of extracted entities. Token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale all scale costs with prompt length. The result is a pricing structure that penalizes the exact workload, long-context extraction, where LLMs are most compelling.

When you run NER across thousands of documents per day, or when you build an agent that repeatedly appends context and re-extracts entities, token-based metering creates unpredictable spend. Budgeting becomes a function of document length distribution rather than business value delivered.

title: Dialogue Systems with LLM: Opportunities and Challenges
content:
Dialogue systems have moved beyond rigid decision trees and slot-filling frameworks. Large language models now power conversations that adapt to context, recover from ambiguity, and invoke external tools in real time. For developers, this shift unlocks new product categories, from technical support agents to multilingual personal assistants. It also introduces infrastructure requirements that traditional token-based pricing and fragmented model hosting struggle to satisfy. Building production-grade conversational AI requires a backend that handles long context, tool use, and unpredictable traffic without ballooning costs.

What Makes Modern Dialogue Systems Different

Early dialogue systems relied on hand-crafted rules, finite state machines, and shallow natural language understanding. They were brittle. A single unexpected user utterance could break the flow. Modern LLM-based systems replace that fragility with probabilistic reasoning and vast pre-trained knowledge. The system prompt acts as a behavioral scaffold, while the message history provides dynamic memory across turns.

This architecture changes how developers manage state. Instead of maintaining explicit dialogue acts in a separate database, much of the conversational context lives inside the prompt itself. That design choice simplifies orchestration but places enormous pressure on the inference layer. Every turn in a conversation appends new tokens to the input. A dialogue that lasts twenty turns can easily accumulate thousands of tokens in context. The inference backend must deliver low latency even as the prompt grows, and the pricing model must remain predictable as the conversation deepens.

Opportunities in LLM-Powered Conversation

LLMs open concrete opportunities that were previously impractical at scale. Function calling and tool use let dialogue systems query APIs, execute code, or retrieve documents during a conversation. A user can ask, "What is the status of my last order?" and the model can emit a structured tool call, wait for the response, and synthesize a natural language reply. This agentic loop turns chatbots into active problem solvers.

Multilingual reasoning has also improved dramatically. Models such as Qwen 3 32B handle cross-lingual contexts without heavy localization pipelines. Vision capabilities, available through models like Kimi VL A3B and Gemma 3 27B, allow dialogue systems to accept image inputs and answer questions about diagrams, photos, or user interfaces. Long-context models like DeepSeek V4 Flash, with support for one million tokens, enable systems that reference entire documentation libraries or lengthy conversation transcripts without losing coherence.

The Infrastructure Challenges Nobody Talks About

Despite the opportunities, production dialogue systems face stubborn engineering challenges. Latency is the most visible. Streaming responses help, but each turn still requires processing the full message history. As context length increases, time-to-first-token can degrade unless the provider optimizes attention and KV-cache management.

Cost predictability is another hurdle. Dialogue systems are inherently long-context workloads. Every user message and assistant response becomes input for the next turn. Under token-based billing, this creates a compounding cost curve that is difficult to forecast. A sudden spike in conversation length or a burst of concurrent sessions can surprise engineering teams at the end of a billing cycle.

Cold starts compound the problem. If a provider spins down GPUs between requests, the first message in a new session can suffer multi-second delays. That friction kills the conversational experience. Developers also need consistent API semantics across models. Managing one integration for chat, another for embeddings, and a third for image generation fragments the stack and slows iteration.

Why Request-Based Pricing Changes the Economics

For dialogue systems, the relationship between context length and cost is not a minor detail. It is the defining economic constraint. Token-based providers charge for both input and output tokens, which means that long conversations become exponentially more expensive as history accumulates. Oxlo.ai uses a request-based pricing model: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. This aligns costs with business value, a user interaction, rather than an internal unit that fluctuates with every word.

Because Oxlo.ai does not scale cost with input length, it can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context and agentic workloads. A customer support dialogue that spans thirty turns and includes tool results costs the same at turn one as at turn thirty. That predictability lets teams budget accurately, set user limits without complex token math, and choose the richest possible context window for their application. Building Dialogue Systems on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first inference platform that is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. You can point your existing Python, Node.js, or cURL client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and start building immediately. The platform hosts more than 45 models across seven categories. For general dialogue, Llama 3.3 70B offers a strong balance of instruction following and safety. For deep reasoning and complex coding within a conversation, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2.6 provide advanced chain-of-thought capabilities. For multilingual agents, Qwen 3 32B excels at cross-lingual reasoning. If you need vision, Kimi VL A3B and Gemma 3 27B accept image inputs through the same chat completions endpoint.

Function calling, JSON mode, streaming, and multi-turn conversations are supported across compatible models. Here is a minimal example using the OpenAI Python SDK:

for chunk in response:

Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, you can pass extensive system prompts, few-shot examples, and full conversation history without watching a meter run on every token.

Evaluation and Observability

A dialogue system is only as good as its ability to stay on topic and complete tasks. Per-turn perplexity is a weak proxy for conversational quality. Production teams should measure task completion rate, user retention within a session, and escalation rates to human agents.

Structured outputs help. By enabling JSON mode, you can force the model to return intent labels, confidence scores, or structured tool arguments that are easy to log and audit. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode on compatible models, so you can build evaluation pipelines that compare predicted actions against ground truth without fragile regex parsing.

Logging conversation state externally remains essential. Even though the model retains context in the prompt, your application should persist transcripts and tool results. This enables regression testing. You can replay a conversation thread against a new model version on Oxlo.ai and measure whether responses improve.

Looking Ahead

Dialogue systems will continue to move toward deeper context, autonomous tool use, and multimodal interaction. The line between chatbot and agent will blur. That trajectory places increasing strain on inference infrastructure. Providers must deliver low latency at long context, broad model selection, and pricing that does not punish natural conversation length.

Oxlo.ai offers a relevant foundation for this evolution. title: The Disadvantages of Using LLM: A Balanced View
content:
Large language models have become the default building block for modern AI applications, powering everything from customer support bots to autonomous coding agents. Their ability to parse unstructured text, generate software, and maintain multi-turn conversations makes them indispensable in many developer toolchains. Yet treating LLMs as a universal hammer for every nail leads to architectural bloat, runaway costs, and production incidents. A balanced engineering strategy requires understanding not only what LLMs excel at, but where they introduce friction, risk, or diminishing returns. By mapping disadvantages to concrete infrastructure choices, teams can deploy language models as controlled components rather than opaque dependencies.

Cost and Resource Intensity at Scale

For teams running high-volume or long-context workloads, token-based billing is often the first pain point. Prices scale linearly with prompt and completion length, which means that feeding a model thousands of tokens per request for agentic loops, retrieval-augmented generation, or large document analysis produces unpredictable monthly bills. A single autonomous agent that iterates over lengthy system prompts and tool outputs can consume millions of tokens in a day, turning a promising prototype into a budget risk. The result is a forced tradeoff between context richness and cost control, encouraging developers to truncate prompts or reduce conversation history in ways that degrade output quality.

This is where pricing structure matters as much as model capability. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this model removes the linear cost escalation associated with token-based providers. Instead of shrinking context windows to save money, developers can send the full document or conversation history required for accurate results. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, including DeepSeek V3.2, and paid plans scale from Pro to Enterprise with dedicated GPU options. You can verify current rates at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Hallucinations and Reliability Gaps

LLMs are probabilistic, not deterministic. They can generate confident, articulate statements that are factually wrong or logically inconsistent. In production systems, this translates to corrupted database entries, misleading user-facing answers, or insecure code suggestions. The risk is not theoretical. A model asked to summarize a contract might invent clauses, or a coding assistant might propose libraries that do not exist. Mitigation requires layered guardrails: retrieval-augmented generation to ground outputs in verified sources, structured output parsing to enforce schemas, and human-in-the-loop validation for high-stakes decisions.

Model selection also plays a critical role in reducing error rates. Oxlo.ai hosts a range of reasoning and code-specialized models, including DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, Kimi K2.6, and GLM 5, which are optimized for chain-of-thought and agentic tasks. For coding workflows, Qwen 3 Coder 30B and DeepSeek Coder provide focused capabilities that reduce the likelihood of generic hallucinations. Having access to more than 45 models across seven categories lets you route tasks to the right architecture rather than forcing every problem through a single general-purpose endpoint.

Latency and Operational Complexity

Moving from prototype to production means wrestling with cold starts, rate limits, and inconsistent response times. Some inference platforms spin down idle GPUs to save costs, only to leave your application hanging for seconds when traffic spikes. SDK fragmentation compounds the issue. If a provider uses a bespoke API schema, you end up maintaining multiple client implementations and translation layers across your services. That friction slows iteration and increases the surface area for bugs whenever a provider updates its interface.

Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models and exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API. The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, which means you can switch an existing Python or Node.js application by changing a single environment variable. Streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversations are all supported out of the box. This compatibility reduces operational surface area and lets you benchmark Oxlo.ai against other providers without rewriting your inference layer or maintaining adapter code.

Data Privacy and Security Concerns

Every token sent to a third-party API is a token you no longer fully control. Healthcare, finance, and legal applications face strict compliance requirements around data residency and retention. Even with promises of zero logging, the default posture for most hosted inference services is shared infrastructure, which creates attack surface for prompt injection, training data leakage, and unauthorized access. For companies subject to SOC 2, HIPAA, or GDPR, the ambiguity around how a provider logs, caches, or retrains on request data is a genuine blocker.

The mitigation is not to avoid hosted APIs entirely, but to choose providers that offer clear isolation boundaries. Oxlo.ai provides an Enterprise tier with dedicated GPUs and custom contracts, which allows teams to run inference on isolated hardware without managing the underlying cluster. For less sensitive workloads, standard endpoints support streaming and tool use without requiring you to deploy and patch open-source weights yourself. It is a middle ground between fully managed convenience and self-hosted operational burden.

Environmental and Ethical Considerations

Training and serving large models consumes significant electricity and water for cooling. While efficiency per token has improved with mixture-of-experts architectures and better quantization, absolute energy use continues to rise as models grow into the hundreds of billions of parameters. Developers who prioritize sustainability must weigh the carbon cost of every inference call against the business value it creates. Running a 671B parameter model for trivial tasks is architecturally irresponsible when a smaller, specialized model would suffice.

Ethical concerns extend to training data provenance and bias amplification. LLMs can reproduce stereotypes or generate harmful content if not properly filtered. Responsible deployment requires output moderation, bias auditing, and transparency about which model versions are in use. Oxlo.ai hosts a variety of open-source and proprietary architectures, so teams can inspect model cards, select smaller efficient variants such as DeepSeek V4 Flash, or route sensitive tasks to models with documented training pipelines and verifiable weights.

When LLMs Make Sense

None of these disadvantages imply that LLMs are without value. They remain unmatched for open-ended text generation, rapid prototyping, and tasks where the cost of human labor far exceeds inference spend. The key is to match the tool to the task. Use deterministic functions for calculations, traditional search for exact retrieval, and LLMs for semantic understanding and synthesis. When your workload involves long contexts, agentic loops, or unpredictable token volumes, infrastructure choice becomes the deciding factor between a sustainable system and an expensive experiment.

If your application fits that profile, Oxlo.ai is designed to remove the financial and operational barriers that make LLMs expensive to run. With request-based pricing, OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a broad catalog spanning chat, reasoning, code, vision, audio, embeddings, and image generation, it provides a practical path to production without token-meter anxiety. Switching is straightforward.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your-oxlo.ai-api-key"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this 50,000-word legal brief."}],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="")

That single configuration change lets you test whether flat per-request pricing aligns with your traffic patterns. By understanding the limitations of LLMs and selecting infrastructure that directly addresses cost, latency, and reliability, you can deploy them as a deliberate, measured part of your stack rather than a black-box dependency.

title: Building Conversational AI with LLM: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
We are building a conversational support agent that handles order status lookups and return requests for an e-commerce platform. It maintains context across multi-turn conversations and uses function calling to interact with internal order data. I will walk through the exact Python service I shipped using Oxlo.ai's OpenAI-compatible API, starting from an empty file to a working agent you can test in your terminal.

What You'll Need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an active API key from Oxlo.ai. The SDK is the only external dependency because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully compatible endpoint, so no custom client code or wrapper libraries are required. This compatibility means you can migrate existing OpenAI SDK scripts by changing two lines: the base URL and the API key. Grab your key from https://portal.oxlo.ai, then install the package into a fresh virtual environment.

python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install openai

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai Client

I start every project with a single client initialization that I reuse across requests. Instantiating the client inside the request loop adds latency and wastes memory. Point the base URL at Oxlo.ai's endpoint, pass your API key, and you are done. I use the Llama 3.3 70B model as the general-purpose backbone for this agent because it handles structured tool use reliably and responds with low latency. For workloads that involve longer reasoning chains, Oxlo.ai also hosts DeepSeek R1 671B and Kimi K2.6, but a straightforward support bot does not need that depth.

I also want to call out why Oxlo.ai makes sense for this workload. A support agent ingests long transcripts, policy documents, and previous ticket history. On token-based providers, that input volume drives cost up linearly. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so a long context window does not inflate the bill. See the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. When you are running thousands of customer conversations per day, that predictability matters.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Write the System Prompt

The system prompt is the agent's job description and its primary guardrail. I keep it strict and bounded. If you give the model vague instructions, it will hallucinate policies or answer questions outside its scope. I explicitly define the two tasks it may perform, mandate that it confirm an order ID before invoking any tool, and instruct it to escalate off-topic questions to a human. I store the prompt as a module-level constant so I can version it in git and diff changes during code review. This is much cleaner than hardcoding strings inside business logic.

Notice that I do not stuff the prompt with FAQ content. Static knowledge belongs in retrieval systems or tool results, not in the system prompt. Keeping the prompt focused reduces token load and improves adherence to instructions.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are OrderBot, a customer support agent for an e-commerce platform. 
You help users check order status and initiate returns. 
You have access to tools for looking up orders and processing returns.
If a user asks about anything outside orders or returns, politely decline and offer to connect them with a human agent.
Always confirm the order ID before calling any tool.
Ask clarifying questions if the user is vague."""

Step 3: Define the Available Tools

Function calling is what turns a chatbot into an agent that can actually do things. I declare the available tools in OpenAI's schema format so the model can request them. The descriptions are critical. The model relies on them to decide whether to invoke a tool, so I write them as if I am explaining the task to a junior engineer, not to the end user. Each parameter gets a clear description and a type. I require order_id for both tools so the model cannot call them with empty arguments.

I limit this agent to two tools intentionally. Adding too many tools at once degrades accuracy. If you need more capabilities, consider routing to specialized sub-agents rather than dumping every possible function into a single prompt.

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Get the status and details of an order by ID",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {
                        "type": "string", 
                        "description": "The order ID, e.g., ORD-12345"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    },
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "initiate_return",
            "description": "Start a return process for a given order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"},
                    "reason": {
                        "type": "string", 
                        "description": "Reason for return"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id", "reason"]
            }
        }
    }
]

Step 4: Implement the Tool Handlers

These Python functions act as the bridge between the LLM and your internal systems. In my production deployment, they make authenticated HTTP requests to our ERP and logistics APIs. For this tutorial, I use hardcoded dictionaries so you can run the script immediately without setting up a database or mock server. Each function accepts the arguments extracted by the model, performs the lookup or mutation, and returns a plain Python dict. I serialize that dict to JSON before feeding it back into the conversation history.

I separate the handlers from the LLM orchestration so I can unit test them independently. You should do the same in production. Test the business logic without calling the model, and test the orchestration with stubbed handlers.

def lookup_order(order_id: str):
    orders = {
        "ORD-12345": {
            "status": "shipped", 
            "item": "Wireless Headphones", 
            "eta": "2 days"
        },
        "ORD-67890": {
            "status": "delivered", 
            "item": "USB-C Cable", 
            "eta": "delivered"
        }
    }
    return orders.get(order_id, {"error": "Order not found"})

def initiate_return(order_id: str, reason: str):
    return {
        "return_id": f"RET-{order_id}", 
        "status": "pending_approval", 
        "reason": reason
    }

Step 5: Build the Conversation Loop

This is the core orchestration layer. On every user message, I append it to the conversation history and send the full list to Oxlo.ai. Sending the complete history is essential for multi-turn context. If the model decides it needs data, it returns a tool call instead of a text response. I then execute the matching handler, append the result with role "tool", and send the updated context back to the model for a final, natural language answer.

I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it consistently follows tool-calling conventions and produces structured arguments accurately. If your users speak multiple languages, you could swap in Qwen 3 32B without changing any of the surrounding code. For more complex reasoning or coding tasks, Kimi K2.6 or DeepSeek V3.2 are available on the same endpoint. That flexibility is useful when you outgrow the first iteration of your agent.

One implementation detail: the assistant message returned by the SDK contains the tool_calls list. I append that message object directly to the history list. The OpenAI SDK handles serialization internally, which keeps my code clean.

def run_agent(user_message, conversation_history=None):
    if conversation_history is None:
        conversation_history = [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}
        ]
    
    conversation_history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_message})
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=conversation_history,
        tools=tools,
        tool_choice="auto"
    )
    
    assistant_message = response.choices[0].message
    conversation_history.append(assistant_message)
    
    if assistant_message.tool_calls:
        for tool_call in assistant_message.tool_calls:
            function_name = tool_call.function.name
            arguments = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
            
            if function_name == "lookup_order":
                result = lookup_order(**arguments)
            elif function_name == "initiate_return":
                result = initiate_return(**arguments)
            else:
                result = {"error": "Unknown function"}
            
            conversation_history.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
                "name": function_name,
                "content": json.dumps(result)
            })
        
        final_response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=conversation_history,
            tools=tools
        )
        
        final_message = final_response.choices[0].message
        conversation_history.append(final_message)
        return final_message.content, conversation_history
    
    return assistant_message.content, conversation_history

Run It

I test the agent with a short two-turn conversation. The first message asks for an order status, which triggers the lookup tool. The second message references the previously discussed order and requests a return, demonstrating that context persists across turns. By passing the history object back into run_agent, the agent remembers which order we are discussing without the user repeating the ID.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    reply, history = run_agent("Where is my order ORD-12345?")
    print("Bot:", reply)
    
    reply, history = run_agent("I want to return it, it arrived damaged", history)
    print("Bot:", reply)

When I run this against Oxlo.ai, the output looks like:

Bot: I found your order ORD-12345. It contains Wireless Headphones and the current status is shipped, with an estimated delivery in 2 days.
Bot: I have initiated return RET-ORD-12345 for your Wireless Headphones. The status is pending approval and the reason recorded is "it arrived damaged". You will receive an email with return shipping instructions once the return is approved.

Next Steps

Replace the simulated dictionaries in the tool handlers with real API calls to your order management or warehouse system. If you want to ground responses in your help center articles, generate embeddings using Oxlo.ai's BGE-Large or E5-Large models and perform a vector search before each turn. Inject the top matching articles into the system prompt as context so the agent cites real documentation instead of generic advice.

Once the logic is solid, wrap the run_agent function in a FastAPI endpoint and stream responses back to your front end. Oxlo.ai supports streaming, so you can render tokens as they arrive rather than making the user wait for the full round-trip. That is the difference between a demo and a production conversational experience.

title: Real-World Applications of LLM: Success Stories and Use Cases
content:
Large language models have moved well beyond proof-of-concept chatbots. Today, they power production systems that handle customer support triage, generate and review code, analyze thousand-page documents, and coordinate multimodal agent workflows. The difference between a demo and a production deployment often comes down to economics. Token-based billing punishes long prompts and multi-turn agent loops, which is exactly where Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing removes the friction. With one flat cost per API call regardless of input length, Oxlo.ai makes it practical to run the workloads that actually deliver business value. Teams no longer need to truncate context windows or limit reasoning steps to control costs. Instead, they can build applications that use the full depth of modern models, from 1M context windows to multi-hour agent sessions, without unpredictable bills. With 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, Oxlo.ai gives developers the breadth and economic predictability needed for real-world systems.

Customer Support and Autonomous Agents

Real-world support systems do not operate in a single turn. They retrieve documentation, maintain conversation history, call tools to update tickets, and escalate through conditional logic. These agentic workloads generate long contexts fast. A token-based bill scales with every retrieved document and every reasoning step. Oxlo.ai eliminates that variable. You pay per request, so an agent that iterates through ten tool calls and a full knowledge base costs the same flat rate as a one-line greeting.

This pricing model changes what is feasible. Teams can deploy true autonomous agents that read full product manuals, search embedding databases, and execute functions without stripping context to save tokens. Models like Qwen 3 32B and Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai handle multilingual reasoning and general-purpose dialogue without cold starts, so user-facing latency stays consistent. For advanced chain-of-thought reasoning, Kimi K2.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking break down complex user complaints into structured resolution steps. Minimax M2.5 is specifically tuned for agentic tool use, making it a strong choice for systems that must call CRM APIs, inventory checks, and scheduling endpoints in sequence. Because Oxlo.ai offers full OpenAI SDK compatibility, migrating an existing support agent is often just a base URL swap.

Code Generation and Software Development

Development teams are embedding LLMs directly into IDE assistants, CI/CD review pipelines, and automated refactoring tools. These use cases demand models that understand syntax, architecture, and repository context. Oxlo.ai provides specialized coding models including Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast, alongside deep reasoning options like DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and GPT-Oss 120B for complex algorithmic work.

A production code review agent might ingest an entire pull request diff, relevant dependency files, and organizational style guidelines. Consider automated test generation. A pipeline that reads a service's source code, existing tests, and API specifications to generate new unit tests requires substantial context. With Oxlo.ai, you can pass the full context in one request and still know the exact cost before the model responds. Streaming responses and JSON mode let you structure the output into parseable test cases immediately. For low-latency autocomplete, Oxlo.ai Coder Fast delivers suggestions without cold starts, keeping developers in flow.

Document Analysis and Long-Context Workflows

Legal tech, healthcare research, and financial analysis require models that can ingest hundreds of pages in a single pass. DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window with efficient MoE architecture, making it ideal for near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning across long documents. Kimi K2.6 adds advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision with a 131K context window. GLM 5, a 744B MoE model, targets long-horizon agentic tasks that unfold over extended sessions.

When you are processing a 300-page contract or a full research corpus, token-based pricing becomes unpredictable. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request model turns that variability into a fixed operational cost. You can send the entire document plus detailed system instructions without watching the meter spin. This predictability is why teams building legal summarizers and compliance scanners are moving long-context workloads to Oxlo.ai.

Retrieval-augmented generation pipelines also benefit. While embeddings from BGE-Large or E5-Large retrieve relevant chunks, the generation step often needs to reference the full source for accuracy. Instead of compressing context to fit a token budget, Oxlo.ai users can include primary sources at length. The result is higher fidelity answers with verifiable citations, all at a cost that scales with user interactions, not word count.

Multimodal Production Pipelines

Modern applications combine text, vision, audio, and image generation in unified workflows. A logistics platform might use vision to read damage photos, an LLM to draft insurance reports, and text-to-speech to notify drivers. Oxlo.ai covers all seven categories needed for these pipelines. Vision tasks run through Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B. Audio transcription uses Whisper Large v3, Turbo, or Medium. Text-to-speech is handled by Kokoro 82M. Image generation is available via Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Oxlo.ai Image Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, and Stable Diffusion 3.5. Object detection for physical workflows is supported through YOLOv9 and YOLOv11.

Because all endpoints share the same base URL and OpenAI SDK schema, you can chain these modalities without managing multiple provider contracts. A single request-based bill applies across chat, audio, and image endpoints, simplifying forecasting. You can transcribe a customer call with Whisper, analyze sentiment and extract entities with Llama 3.3 70B, generate a follow-up email with Qwen 3 32B, and convert it to speech with Kokoro 82M, all through one unified API structure.

An e-commerce platform, for example, can use YOLOv11 to detect package defects on a conveyor line, pass the bounding box data to Kimi K2.6 for damage classification, generate a customer notification with Qwen 3 32B, and produce a replacement product image with Oxlo.ai Image Pro. Each step runs through the same API base URL and billing framework.

Implementing Oxlo.ai in Production

Its request-based pricing removes the penalty on long-context and agentic work, its 45+ model catalog covers reasoning, code, vision, audio, and image generation, and its OpenAI-compatible API means you can ship today without refactoring your client code. If your current provider's token meter is limiting what your application can do, Oxlo.ai is the relevant alternative designed for production workloads. title: LLM for Natural Language Processing: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
We are building a text intelligence agent that ingests unstructured paragraphs and returns structured NLP analysis: sentiment, named entities, a one-line summary, and topic tags. If you are tired of chaining separate APIs for each NLP task, this single-request approach on Oxlo.ai will keep your pipeline simple and your costs predictable.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai is a natural fit here because NLP workloads often involve long documents, and Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per request rather than burning tokens. A 10,000-word annual report costs the same as a tweet-sized prompt. See the exact tiers at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. You also get more than 45 models to choose from, so you can tune for speed or reasoning depth without rewriting client code. Sign up at the portal, copy your key, and you are ready.

Step 1: Test the connection

Before we write any logic, we should confirm that the Python client can reach Oxlo.ai and that our key is active. I always do a smoke test first so I do not have to debug auth issues inside a larger script.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = "You are a helpful assistant."
user_message = "Say 'Oxlo.ai connection OK'"

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Run that once. If you see Oxlo.ai connection OK, the client is working and latency is low. Oxlo.ai carries no cold starts on popular models, so this should return immediately.

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between our code and the model. It forces valid JSON so we can parse the result without regex hacks. I treat this prompt like a schema definition: the more explicit I am about keys and rules, the less time I spend handling malformed responses.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are an NLP analysis engine.
Read the user's text and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- sentiment: one of Positive, Neutral, Negative
- entities: a list of objects, each with {name, type, description}
- summary: one concise sentence
- topics: a list of up to 5 tags

Rules:
- Output ONLY the JSON object.
- Do not wrap it in markdown code fences.
- If the text is ambiguous, mark sentiment Neutral and omit uncertain entities."""

Notice that I ask for raw JSON, not markdown. LLMs sometimes wrap output in triple backticks, which breaks json.loads. A clear rule in the system prompt usually prevents that, and we will reinforce it by enabling JSON mode in the next step.

Step 3: Build the analysis function

Now we wrap the call in a reusable function. We use JSON mode so the model is constrained to valid JSON, and we keep the temperature low for deterministic extraction. I pass the document as the user message and let the system prompt handle the formatting instructions.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def analyze_text(user_message: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.2,
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

I chose llama-3.3-70b because it is a strong general-purpose model that follows instructions well. If you are processing multilingual documents, you can swap the model string to qwen-3-32b without changing any other code. That is the benefit of Oxlo.ai being fully OpenAI SDK compatible.

Step 4: Process a batch of documents

Real NLP pipelines process more than one document. Here we loop over a list, call the agent for each, and collect structured results. In production you might add retry logic or parallel threads, but a simple loop is enough to prove the pipeline works end to end.

documents = [
    "Apple Inc. reported record quarterly revenue of $123 billion yesterday, driven by iPhone sales in Asia. Investors responded positively, pushing the stock up 5% in after-hours trading.",
    "The municipal water supply in Riverdale was contaminated with lead. Local officials have issued a boil-water advisory while repairs continue.",
]

results = []
for doc in documents:
    parsed = analyze_text(doc)
    results.append(parsed)

print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))

Each iteration makes one request to Oxlo.ai. Because the pricing is request-based, you know the exact cost of running this batch before you run it. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details. For agentic or long-context workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based providers.

Run it

title: The Advantages of Using LLM: Benefits, Limitations, and Best Practices
content:
Large language models have moved beyond research demos and become core infrastructure for shipping products. Teams now rely on LLMs for everything from automated customer support and code review to multimodal content generation and complex agentic workflows. The shift from experiment to production, however, exposes a gap between what models promise and what infrastructure actually delivers. The advantages are real, but they depend heavily on how you access, route, and scale inference. Understanding the benefits, limitations, and operational best practices is essential before committing to an architecture.

Core Benefits of LLMs in Production

LLMs offer several concrete advantages when integrated into production systems. First, general-purpose reasoning across unstructured data reduces the need for hand-tuned pipelines. A single model can parse legal contracts, summarize support tickets, or extract entities from logs without brittle regular expressions. Second, code generation and assistance accelerate software development. Models like DeepSeek Coder and Qwen 3 Coder 30B can suggest completions, refactor functions, and write tests in context, cutting boilerplate time. Third, multimodal capabilities unify text, image, and audio workflows. Vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B can interpret diagrams or UI mockups, while audio models like Whisper Large v3 handle transcription at scale. Fourth, agentic tool use lets models invoke APIs, query databases, and execute multi-step plans rather than returning static text. Finally, embedding models turn semantic search into a commodity, enabling retrieval systems that ground generation in private data.

Realizing these benefits requires broad model access. Oxlo.ai offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including LLMs, code specialists, vision models, image generation, audio, embeddings, and object detection. Instead of maintaining separate provider accounts for each modality, developers can route requests through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. This consolidation reduces integration overhead and lets teams match the right model to the right task without vendor lock-in.

Limitations and Tradeoffs

Despite their utility, LLMs introduce limitations that shape how they should be deployed. Hallucinations remain a structural risk. Models can generate confident but incorrect outputs, especially in domains with sparse training data. Mitigation requires retrieval-augmented generation, output validation, and human-in-the-loop checks rather than blind trust. Output consistency is non-deterministic. Temperature, top-p, and seed parameters help, but regression testing LLM outputs remains harder than traditional software because minor prompt changes can alter behavior unpredictably.

Latency and throughput constraints affect user experience. Large reasoning models such as DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or GLM 5 deliver high-quality outputs, but they demand significant compute. Cold starts can add seconds to initial requests, which breaks real-time interactions. Oxlo.ai addresses this with no cold starts on popular models, so agents and chat applications receive predictable response times from the first token.

Cost structure is another critical tradeoff. Token-based pricing scales linearly with prompt length, which makes long-context retrieval, document analysis, and multi-turn agent loops expensive on traditional providers. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing with one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this model can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives from providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, or OpenRouter. Teams running large context windows or iterative agent workflows should evaluate how pricing models affect margin at scale. Details are available at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Context windows, while expanding, still impose limits. Even models with 131K context, such as Kimi K2.6, require careful prompt compression and chunking strategies when processing books or large codebases. Exceeding effective context limits degrades recall and reasoning quality regardless of the advertised window size.

Best Practices for Production

Shipping reliable LLM features requires discipline beyond prompt engineering. Start with model selection. Use smaller, faster models for high-volume classification or routing, and reserve large reasoning models for complex coding or deep analysis. Oxlo.ai makes this economical because request-based pricing does not penalize long prompts when you do need a large context model.

Structure prompts for reproducibility. Use system prompts to constrain tone and format, and leverage JSON mode to enforce valid output schemas. This simplifies downstream parsing and reduces failure modes. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling, so agents can return structured data or invoke external tools deterministically. Define tool schemas explicitly and validate arguments server-side before execution.

Implement streaming for interactive applications. Waiting for a full response increases perceived latency. Oxlo.ai provides streaming responses on its chat completions endpoint, letting UIs render tokens as they arrive and improving responsiveness for chat and copilot experiences.

Use embeddings and retrieval to ground generation. Oxlo.ai hosts embedding models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large through a dedicated embeddings endpoint. Combining retrieval with chat completions reduces hallucination risk and keeps context windows focused on relevant passages.

Implement retries and circuit breakers. Model APIs can return transient errors under load. A resilient client retries with exponential backoff and fails gracefully when latency exceeds thresholds. Oxlo.ai's Premium tier includes priority queue access, which helps maintain throughput during traffic spikes, but client-side defense remains necessary.

Monitor and version your prompts. Treat prompts as code: version them, A/B test variants, and track latency and error rates. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can often migrate existing observability tooling with minimal changes to the base URL. Point your client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and retain your existing tracing logic.

For multimodal pipelines, separate concerns. Use vision models for image understanding, then pass extracted text to a reasoning model for decision-making. Oxlo.ai's catalog includes vision models like Gemma 3 27B alongside general-purpose flagships such as Llama 3.3 70B, so you can compose specialized chains without switching providers. Similarly, offload transcription to Whisper Large v3 and synthesis to Kokoro 82M rather than forcing a single model to handle every modality.

Choosing the Right Inference Platform

Your inference layer determines whether LLM advantages translate into sustainable products. The ideal platform minimizes integration friction, offers model variety, and aligns pricing with your workload patterns.

Oxlo.ai is built as a developer-first AI inference platform with flat per-request pricing. It is fully OpenAI SDK compatible across Python, Node.js, and cURL, which means migration from other providers typically requires only a base URL change. The platform hosts flagship open-source models including Qwen 3 32B for multilingual agent workflows, DeepSeek V4 Flash for efficient long-context reasoning with 1M context support, and Kimi K2.6 for advanced agentic coding and vision tasks. Code-specific workloads can target Qwen 3 Coder 30B or Oxlo.ai Coder Fast, while image generation pipelines can call Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Flux.1, or Stable Diffusion 3.5. Object detection tasks can use YOLOv9 or YOLOv11 without managing separate computer vision infrastructure.

The breadth of the catalog matters because no single model wins on every task. GPT-Oss 120B serves as a large open-source generalist, while DeepSeek V3.2 targets coding and reasoning with a free tier option. Minimax M2.5 focuses on coding and agentic tool use. Having these options behind one API key simplifies A/B testing and lets you upgrade models without rewriting client code.

Pricing plans range from a free tier with 60 requests per day and 16+ free models, including a 7-day full-access trial, to Pro and Premium tiers for higher volumes, with enterprise options offering dedicated GPUs and custom pricing. Because the cost is per request rather than per token, teams building retrieval-augmented generation systems, autonomous agents, or document processors avoid the cost escalation that comes with large prompts on token-based platforms.

No cold starts on popular models means you do not need to keep GPUs warm or accept intermittent latency spikes. This is essential for synchronous APIs where user experience depends on consistent response times. Whether you are prototyping with the free tier or scaling a production agent, the platform is designed to keep inference predictable and integration minimal.

Conclusion

LLMs deliver measurable advantages in reasoning, code generation, and multimodal understanding, but those advantages come with limitations around hallucination, latency, and cost. Success depends on selecting appropriate models, enforcing structured outputs, and choosing infrastructure that matches your economic and performance constraints.

For teams running long-context or agentic workloads, Oxlo.ai offers a relevant alternative to token-based providers. Its request-based pricing, broad model catalog, and OpenAI-compatible API reduce both integration overhead and unpredictable spend. Evaluate your current inference costs against flat per-request pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing, and test whether routing through https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 improves margin without sacrificing model capability.

title: Building a Document Summarization Tool with LLM: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
We are building a command-line document summarizer that ingests a long text file and emits a structured markdown summary. It helps researchers, analysts, and engineers distill reports, research papers, or meeting transcripts into actionable takeaways without reading every page. The entire tool fits in a single Python file and runs against Oxlo.ai's OpenAI-compatible API.

What you'll need

You will need Python 3.10 or newer installed locally, plus the OpenAI SDK. Install the SDK with pip. You will also need an Oxlo.ai API key, which you can generate from the Oxlo.ai portal. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, so sending a long document does not inflate your cost the way token-based billing would. This makes it ideal for summarization workloads where the input is often much larger than the output.

  • Python 3.10+
  • pip install openai
  • Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

Create a new file named summarize.py. Start by importing the OpenAI client and pointing it at Oxlo.ai's endpoint. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, this is a drop-in replacement and you can use the same patterns you already know from other providers.

from openai import OpenAI
import os
import sys

# Initialize the client pointing at Oxlo.ai
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
)

# Fail fast if the key is missing
if not client.api_key:
    print("Error: Set the OXLO_API_KEY environment variable.")
    sys.exit(1)

Step 2: Load and measure the document

Next we read the source file into memory, normalize whitespace, and return the text. I also print the character count so I know exactly how much context I am sending. With Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing, I do not need to worry about the cost scaling as the document grows.

def load_document(path: str, max_chars: int = 120_000) -> str:
    """Read a text file and return cleaned contents."""
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        print(f"Error: File not found: {path}")
        sys.exit(1)

    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        text = f.read()

    # Normalize whitespace to avoid wasting context on extra newlines
    text = " ".join(text.split())
    return text[:max_chars]

Step 3: Define the system prompt

A focused system prompt keeps the model from drifting. I ask for a structured markdown summary with exactly four sections so the output is predictable and easy to parse later.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise document summarizer.
Read the user-provided document and produce a structured summary with exactly these sections:
- Overview: one sentence describing the document.
- Key Points: 3 to 5 bullet points covering the main arguments or findings.
- Action Items: any tasks, deadlines, or recommendations mentioned.
- Entities: important people, organizations, or products referenced.
Keep the tone neutral and factual. Do not add information not present in the text."""

Step 4: Build the summarizer with streaming

Now we wire the pieces together. We pass the system prompt and the document text to the model. I collect the streamed tokens into a list so I can both print them in real time and retain the full text for saving to disk. I chose Llama 3.3 70B because it is a strong general-purpose model, but you can swap in Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 if you need multilingual support or a larger context window.

def summarize_document(text: str) -> str:
    """Send the document to Oxlo.ai and stream the summary back."""
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize the following document:\n\n{text}"},
    ]

    try:
        stream = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=messages,
            temperature=0.3,
            stream=True,
        )
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"API request failed: {e}")
        sys.exit(1)

    print("\n--- Summary ---\n")
    collected = []
    for chunk in stream:
        delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
        if delta:
            print(delta, end="", flush=True)
            collected.append(delta)
    print("\n")
    return "".join(collected)

Step 5: Write output to disk

I want the summary saved alongside the original file so I can review it later or feed it into another pipeline. This helper writes the final summary to a markdown file with a matching basename.

def save_summary(original_path: str, summary: str) -> None:
    """Write the summary to a markdown file next to the source."""
    base, _ = os.path.splitext(original_path)
    output_path = f"{base}_summary.md"

    with open(output_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("# Document Summary\n\n")
        f.write(summary)
        f.write("\n")

    print(f"\nSaved summary to: {output_path}")

Step 6: Assemble the CLI

Finally, we add argument parsing and a main entrypoint so we can run this against any text file from the terminal. This completes the tool.

import argparse

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Summarize a document using Oxlo.ai"
    )
    parser.add_argument("file", help="Path to a plain text file")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    doc = load_document(args.file)
    print(f"Loaded {len(doc)} characters. Summarizing with Oxlo.ai...\n")
    summary = summarize_document(doc)
    save_summary(args.file, summary)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it

Save the complete script as summarize.py, export your API key, and pass it a text file. I tested this on a 15,000-character quarterly report and the summary arrived in under ten seconds.

export OXLO_API_KEY="your-key-here"
python summarize.py quarterly_report.txt

Here is what the output looks like for a typical business report:

Loaded 18432 characters. Summarizing with Oxlo.ai...

--- Summary ---

- Overview: A Q3 earnings report detailing 12% revenue growth and a delayed expansion into APAC markets.
- Key Points:
  * Cloud services revenue grew 18% year over year.
  * Hiring freeze enacted for Q4 due to macroeconomic caution.
  * New partnership with NexGen Storage announced.
- Action Items:
  * CFO to present revised budget by November 15.
  * Engineering to prioritize latency reductions before holiday traffic.
- Entities:
  * NexGen Storage, APAC division, CFO Maria Chen

Saved summary to: quarterly_report_summary.md

If you need to process longer documents, switch the model to kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v4-flash in the code. Both support extensive context windows, and because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, you can send the full document in one shot without watching the meter run on input length.

Wrap-up

This script is the foundation. A natural next step is to add PDF support with a library like PyPDF2 or pdfplumber so you are not limited to plain text. You could also extend the tool to process entire directories and write each summary to a matching markdown file. For book-length or codebase summarization, keep the script exactly as is and point it at Oxlo.ai's larger-context models. The flat per-request pricing removes the usual penalty for long inputs, which is exactly where Oxlo.ai wins against token-based providers.

title: Unlocking the Power of LLM for Text Generation

Large language models have graduated from research demos to core infrastructure. Text generation now powers customer support bots, code assistants, content pipelines, and autonomous agents. But unlocking their full power requires more than clever prompting. It demands an inference backend that matches your throughput needs, a model catalog broad enough to handle diverse tasks, and pricing that does not punish you for using the long context windows these models advertise.

The Infrastructure Behind Fluent Generation

Text generation is memory-bound. The KV-cache grows linearly with sequence length, and batch sizes collapse as contexts expand. Providers address this with continuous batching, speculative decoding, or optimized MoE routing.

When you evaluate a platform, look at cold-start behavior. If your first request after idle time spikes to several seconds, user experience breaks. Oxlo.ai serves popular models with no cold starts, so latency stays stable from the first token to the last. The Context Window and the Pricing Trap

But most inference providers bill by the token. Input tokens often cost as much as, or more than, output tokens. A long-context agent loop can balloon costs unpredictably.

title: Building a RAG Pipeline with Oxlo.ai: A Step-by-Step Tutorial
content:
We are building a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline that answers questions from a local folder of Markdown documentation. It embeds chunks with Oxlo.ai, retrieves the most relevant passages, and generates cited answers with Llama 3.3 70B. This pattern is ideal for internal knowledge bases, developer portals, or product support bots where facts change frequently and fine-tuning would be impractical.

What you'll need

Before starting, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully compatible API. Install it along with NumPy:

pip install openai numpy

Grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal. I recommend exporting it as an environment variable rather than hard-coding it. Finally, create a directory named docs and drop in some Markdown files. If you do not have any handy, the script below will create two sample files so you can run the pipeline end-to-end.

Step 1: Set up the client and chunk the documents

I split documents on double newlines to keep paragraphs intact. This avoids breaking sentences mid-way without importing heavy tokenization libraries. Each chunk stores its source filename so we can cite it later.

import os
import glob
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI

# Initialize the Oxlo.ai client
client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

DOCS_DIR = "./docs"
os.makedirs(DOCS_DIR, exist_ok=True)

# Create sample docs if the folder is empty
if not glob.glob(os.path.join(DOCS_DIR, "*.md")):
    with open(os.path.join(DOCS_DIR, "deployment.md"), "w") as f:
        f.write(
            "# Deployment\n\n"
            "Run the deployment checklist before merging.\n\n"
            "Verify environment variables and trigger the CI/CD pipeline.\n"
        )
    with open(os.path.join(DOCS_DIR, "auth.md"), "w") as f:
        f.write(
            "# Authentication\n\n"
            "API keys are managed in the Oxlo.ai portal.\n\n"
            "Rotate credentials every 90 days.\n"
        )

# Load and chunk by paragraph
chunks = []
for path in glob.glob(os.path.join(DOCS_DIR, "*.md")):
    with open(path, "r") as f:
        text = f.read()
    for paragraph in text.split("\n\n"):
        paragraph = paragraph.strip()
        if len(paragraph) > 20:
            chunks.append({
                "source": os.path.basename(path),
                "text": paragraph
            })

print(f"Loaded {len(chunks)} chunks from {DOCS_DIR}")

Step 2: Embed the chunks with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai hosts BGE-Large, so we do not need to run PyTorch locally. I embed in batches of 32 to keep request latency low. Once the vectors return, I L2-normalize them so that a simple dot product gives cosine similarity during retrieval.

def get_embeddings(texts, model="bge-large"):
    """Embed a list of strings using Oxlo.ai."""
    resp = client.embeddings.create(model=model, input=texts)
    return np.array([item.embedding for item in resp.data])


batch_size = 32
all_embeddings = []

for i in range(0, len(chunks), batch_size):
    batch = [c["text"] for c in chunks[i : i + batch_size]]
    emb = get_embeddings(batch)
    all_embeddings.append(emb)

doc_embeds = np.vstack(all_embeddings)

# Normalize so dot product == cosine similarity
norms = np.linalg.norm(doc_embeds, axis=1, keepdims=True)
doc_embeds = doc_embeds / norms

print(f"Embedded matrix shape: {doc_embeds.shape}")

Step 3: Build the retriever

Retrieval is just matrix multiplication between the normalized document vectors and the normalized query vector. I use argsort with a negative sign to rank chunks by similarity and return the top 3. Keeping the index in memory makes search nearly instantaneous.

def retrieve(query, k=3):
    """Return the top-k chunks for a query."""
    q_emb = get_embeddings([query])
    q_emb = q_emb / np.linalg.norm(q_emb)

    scores = doc_embeds @ q_emb.T
    scores = scores.squeeze()

    top_idx = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return [chunks[i] for i in top_idx]


# Quick sanity check
for hit in retrieve("How do I rotate credentials?"):
    print(f"- {hit['source']}: {hit['text'][:60]}...")

Step 4: Write the system prompt

A tight system prompt reduces hallucinations and forces the model to ground every claim in the retrieved text. I also instruct it to cite sources explicitly so users can verify answers against the original docs.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a precise technical assistant. "
    "Answer the user's question using only the provided context. "
    "Cite the source document name for each fact you use. "
    "If the context does not contain the answer, say that you do not know."
)

Step 5: Generate answers with context

I format the retrieved chunks into a context block and pass them to Llama 3.3 70B. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, stuffing several long paragraphs into the prompt does not inflate the cost the way token-based billing would. If your documentation is multilingual, you can swap the model string to qwen-3-32b without changing any other logic. For agentic coding tasks, kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 are also available on the same endpoint. See the pricing page for plan details.

def answer(question, k=3):
    hits = retrieve(question, k=k)
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[Source: {hit['source']}]\n{hit['text']}" for hit in hits
    )
    user_message = f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Run it

With the sample documents in place, I ask a question that spans the deployment doc. The retriever fetches the relevant chunk, and the generator returns a concise, cited answer.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    question = "What should I do before deploying to production?"
    print("Question:", question)
    print("Answer:", answer(question))

Example output:

Question: What should I do before deploying to production?

title: Scaling LLM Inference: A Comprehensive Guide with Oxlo.ai

Scaling LLM inference from prototype to production introduces challenges that go far beyond model accuracy. As traffic grows, teams must manage latency spikes, cost volatility, and the operational complexity of serving multiple model families under a single API surface. Throughput requirements can shift by an order of magnitude in minutes, and tail latency becomes a primary concern when user-facing applications wait on generated tokens. The decisions you make about pricing models, request routing, and context window utilization directly determine whether your AI infrastructure scales efficiently or becomes a bottleneck.

The Economics of Inference at Scale

Most inference providers structure pricing around tokens. Under this model, every input token and output token incurs a variable cost, which means long prompts, multi-turn conversations, and large context windows all drive up spend unpredictably. For applications that process lengthy documents, maintain extended conversational memory, or run autonomous agent loops, token-based billing makes cost forecasting nearly impossible. Engineering teams often find themselves optimizing prompt length to save money rather than optimizing for accuracy or user experience. Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. As a developer-first AI inference platform, Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing with one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, cost does not scale with input length. In many long-context scenarios, request-based pricing can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. For a detailed breakdown, see the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Architectural Patterns for High-Throughput Inference

Scaling inference requires more than horizontal pod autoscaling. Effective architectures typically combine several techniques: continuous batching to maximize GPU utilization, response caching for repeated queries, KV-cache reuse across similar prompts, and intelligent load balancing across model replicas. Cold starts remain a common pain point, introducing latency jitter just when traffic spikes. In a token-based system, these inefficiencies compound because you are paying for every delayed token while GPUs warm up. Oxlo.ai eliminates cold starts on popular models, which means your request volume can fluctuate without triggering warmup delays. The platform exposes a unified endpoint structure, including chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech, so you can route different workload types through a single integration layer. Features like streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, vision inputs, and multi-turn conversations are all available through consistent endpoints. Whether you are building a real-time chat interface or a background document processing pipeline, the infrastructure layer remains uniform and predictable.
