title: Code Analysis with LLM: Best Practices and Oxlo.ai Integration
content:
Static analysis tools catch syntax errors, but they cannot reason about architecture, intent, or subtle security boundaries. Large language models bridge that gap, yet feeding an entire codebase into an LLM is expensive, slow, and architecturally messy. Token-based billing scales directly with input length, so analyzing a ten-thousand-line pull request or a deeply nested monorepo can inflate costs before a single line of insight is returned. The solution is not to abandon LLMs for code review, but to adopt workflows that maximize context efficiency and pair them with an inference backend that does not penalize long inputs.

The Challenge of Scale

Code analysis differs from chat or summarization because context windows fill quickly. A single file may contain imports, type definitions, configuration, and business logic. Multiply that across dependencies, and even a 128K context window feels small. Traditional approaches split repositories into overlapping chunks, embed them, and retrieve the top-k snippets. This works for simple lookup tasks, but it fails when the bug lives in the interaction between three distant modules. Long-context models have reduced the need for aggressive chunking, yet many providers still charge per token, which discourages developers from passing full files or multi-turn conversation histories.

Best Practices for LLM Code Analysis

Four practical patterns separate toy scripts from production-grade analysis pipelines.

1. Pass full context when the model allows it. If your backend supports a 1M token context window, pass the complete file or the entire diff rather than slicing it. This preserves line numbers, call graphs, indentation, and inline comments in their original positions. The model sees exactly what you see, which reduces hallucinated line references and false positives.

2. Enforce structure with system prompts and JSON mode. Ask the model to return an array of objects with fields such as severity, file_path, line_number, message, and suggested_fix. Structured output removes parsing ambiguity and lets you pipe results directly into CI dashboards or SARIF converters. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling on its chat completions endpoint, so you can lock the response schema without extra wrappers or regex post-processing.

3. Augment the LLM with static metadata. Run a lightweight tree-sitter or LSP pass first to extract function signatures, import graphs, class hierarchies, and call references. Feed that metadata as preamble. The LLM then reasons over a compressed map of the codebase instead of burning tokens on boilerplate or redundant syntax.

4. Use tool use for agentic exploration. Instead of stuffing every file into one massive prompt, give the model a read_file(path) tool. Let it request additional context on demand. Each tool call becomes a new request in a multi-turn conversation. On token-based platforms, this pattern becomes prohibitively expensive because every turn resubmits the full history plus new file contents. On Oxlo.ai, each API call is one flat request, so agentic loops stay predictable and budget-friendly even when the conversation grows.

Matching Models to Code Tasks

Not every analysis job requires the largest reasoning model. Fast lint-level reviews or autocomplete-style suggestions pair well with Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, or Oxlo.ai Coder Fast. These models return low-latency results without overkill.

For deep architectural review, complex bug hunting, or cross-module refactoring, use DeepSeek R1 671B MoE, DeepSeek V4 Flash, or Kimi K2.6. DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a 1M context window and efficient MoE routing, making it ideal for analyzing long build scripts or generated code. Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision support for diagrams or UI mockups embedded in documentation.

When you need long-horizon agentic workflows that span dozens of files, GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 handle tool use and extended reasoning chains. Qwen 3 32B remains a strong default for multilingual codebases where comments and variable names mix languages. The correct choice depends on whether your priority is latency, depth, or autonomy.

Integrating Oxlo.ai for Cost-Efficient Analysis

Oxlo.ai is a developer-first inference platform that charges one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, Oxlo.ai does not scale cost with input size. For code analysis, where a single request can contain thousands of lines of source, dependencies, system prompts, and previous conversation turns, that pricing model can be 10-100x cheaper for long-context workloads.

The platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. You point your existing client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and change the model string. There are no cold starts on popular models, so CI pipelines and IDE plugins get consistent latency from the first request.

Here is a minimal Python example that sends an entire file for security review and enforces JSON output:

import os

    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-r1-671b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are a senior code reviewer. Return findings as JSON."
        },

            "role": "user",

        }

Because Oxlo.ai bills per request, you can pass the full file content without trimming imports or collapsing whitespace to save tokens. If you build an agent that iterates through a repository, appending file contents and tool results to the conversation history, token-based costs compound with every turn. On Oxlo.ai, each turn is still just one flat request.

Oxlo.ai also supports streaming responses, vision input for screenshot analysis, and multi-turn conversations through the same chat/completions endpoint. That means you can stream a code review into an IDE panel, attach a screenshot of a rendered UI for visual bug analysis, or chain tool calls without switching APIs.

The Free plan offers 60 requests per day across 16+ models, including DeepSeek V3.2, which supports coding and reasoning. That is enough to prototype a review bot or a pre-commit hook. When you are ready to scale, the Pro plan provides 1,000 requests per day across all 45+ models, while Premium adds priority queueing at 5,000 requests per day. Enterprise customers can get dedicated GPUs and unlimited volume. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current details.

Getting Started with Oxlo.ai

Track request count, not token count, and upgrade your plan when you need higher daily limits or dedicated throughput.

title: Debugging LLM Issues: Tips and Best Practices
content:
Most production LLM bugs are not model failures. They are prompt misalignment, schema drift, or bad tool calls. In this tutorial, I will build a Prompt Debugger agent that ingests a failed interaction, diagnoses the root cause, and suggests a concrete fix. We will run it against Oxlo.ai so you can replay and verify every suggestion without worrying about token costs.

What you'll need

Before we start, gather the following.

  • Python 3.10 or newer. We use dataclasses and type hints that are fully supported in this version.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so iterating on long prompts or large stack traces does not inflate your bill. You can start on the free tier and upgrade when you move to production.
  • The OpenAI SDK. Install it with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with this client, so no extra adapters are needed.

Step 1: Scaffold the project and connect to Oxlo.ai

I start with a single Python file called debugger.py. The only setup required is pointing the OpenAI client at Oxlo.ai. If you are migrating from another provider, the only change is the base URL and the model string. Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models, so you can keep the same SDK and switch between Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, or Kimi without rewriting your client code. I verify the connection with a cheap call to DeepSeek V3.2 because it is available on the free tier and responds instantly. There are no cold starts on Oxlo.ai, so the first request returns as fast as the hundredth.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

# Verify connectivity with a lightweight health check
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v3.2",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}],
    max_tokens=10
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Model the failure report

Unstructured error reports lead to inconsistent diagnoses. Before I call the model, I define a FailureReport dataclass that enforces a standard schema. It captures the original prompt, the raw response, the expected output, any extra context such as API logs or Pydantic validation errors, and the model that produced the failure. Serializing this to JSON keeps the user message clean and lets me log every case to a file later. Standardization is what makes the agent reliable across different bug types.

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class FailureReport:
    prompt: str
    response: str
    expected: str
    context: Optional[str] = None
    model_used: str = "unknown"

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return json.dumps(asdict(self), indent=2)

report = FailureReport(
    prompt="Extract the invoice_date as YYYY-MM-DD.\n\nText: Received on 12/05/2023.",
    response='{"date": "12/05/2023"}',
    expected='{"invoice_date": "2023-12-05"}',
    model_used="llama-3.3-70b"
)
print(report.to_json())

Step 3: Craft the debugger system prompt

The system prompt is the real product. I do not ask for a generic explanation. I force the model to classify the error into one of four concrete categories, quote the exact offending text, explain the mismatch in a single sentence, and propose a fix. I also lock the output to JSON via the system prompt so the model knows its response will be parsed. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it respects system-level formatting instructions reliably. If you later want to test multilingual error logs, you can swap in Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai with a single line change.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a Prompt Debugger. Your job is to analyze a failed LLM interaction and return a structured diagnosis.

Rules:
1. Identify the error category: prompt_ambiguity, schema_mismatch, instruction_override, or tool_failure.
2. Quote the exact snippet from the prompt or response that caused the failure.
3. Explain the mismatch between the expected and actual output in one sentence.
4. Suggest a concrete fix: rewrite the specific instruction or schema that would correct the output.
5. Respond only in the JSON format requested by the user.
"""

Step 4: Generate structured diagnoses with JSON mode

Now I wire the report into the chat completions endpoint. I set response_format to json_object so Oxlo.ai constrains the output to valid JSON. This eliminates an entire class of parsing bugs. I keep the temperature low at 0.2 because debugging is a reasoning task, not a creative one. The user message explicitly lists the required keys so the model knows the expected schema. Oxlo.ai also supports streaming and function calling, but here we want a single structured object we can validate immediately.

def diagnose(report: FailureReport) -> dict:
    user_message = (
        "Analyze the following failure report and return a JSON object with keys: "
        "category, offending_snippet, explanation, suggested_fix.\n\n"
        f"{report.to_json()}"
    )

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.2,
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

diagnosis = diagnose(report)
print(json.dumps(diagnosis, indent=2))

Step 5: Propose and test a fix

A diagnosis is only useful if we can validate it. I add a second pass that appends the suggested fix to the original prompt as an additional instruction, reruns it through the same model on Oxlo.ai, and checks if the new output matches the expectation exactly. This closes the loop. If the fix fails, I can log the new response and feed it back into the debugger for a second pass. You could also extend this to test multiple candidate fixes in parallel by firing several chat.completions.create calls with different patched prompts. Since Oxlo.ai does not charge by the token, the cost of a parallel batch is easy to predict. You only pay for the number of requests, not the total length of your trace logs. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts, this validation loop feels instant even when you attach thousands of tokens of context.

def test_fix(report: FailureReport, suggested_fix: str) -> dict:
    patched_prompt = (
        f"{report.prompt}\n\n"
        f"Additional instruction: {suggested_fix}"
    )

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "Follow the user's format exactly."},
            {"role": "user", "content": patched_prompt},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )

    new_output = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    return {
        "patched_prompt": patched_prompt,
        "new_output": new_output,
        "matches_expected": new_output == report.expected
    }

result = test_fix(report, diagnosis["suggested_fix"])
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Run it

Here is the complete script and the output I captured when running it live against Oxlo.ai. The scenario is a realistic extraction failure. The original prompt asks for a specific JSON key and date format, but the model returns the wrong key and preserves the original text. The first call identifies a schema mismatch. The second call proves that adding the suggested instruction resolves the issue. Because Oxlo.ai pricing is per request, running this two-step validation pipeline costs the same whether your prompts are fifty tokens or five thousand.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    report = FailureReport(
        prompt="Extract the invoice_date as YYYY-MM-DD.\n\nText: Received on 12/05/2023.",
        response='{"date": "12/05/2023"}',
        expected='{"invoice_date": "2023-12-05"}',
        model_used="llama-3.3-70b"
    )

    print("=== DIAGNOSIS ===")
    diagnosis = diagnose(report)
    print(json.dumps(diagnosis, indent=2))

    print("\n=== FIX TEST ===")
    result = test_fix(report, diagnosis["suggested_fix"])
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

When I run the script, I see the following output.

=== DIAGNOSIS ===
{
  "category": "schema_mismatch",
  "offending_snippet": "{\"date\": \"12/05/2023\"}",
  "explanation": "The model used the key 'date' instead of the required key 'invoice_date' and preserved the original format instead of converting to YYYY-MM-DD.",
  "suggested_fix": "Return strictly valid JSON with the key 'invoice_date' and convert any date to YYYY-MM-DD format before outputting."
}

=== FIX TEST ===
{
  "patched_prompt": "Extract the invoice_date as YYYY-MM-DD.\n\nText: Received on 12/05/2023.\n\nAdditional instruction: Return strictly valid JSON with the key 'invoice_date' and convert any date to YYYY-MM-DD format before outputting.",
  "new_output": "{\"invoice_date\": \"2023-12-05\"}",
  "matches_expected": true
}

Wrap-up and next steps

This agent turns a reactive support ticket into a reproducible test case. Two obvious next steps are to wire it into a CI pipeline so every failed assertion triggers an automatic diagnosis, or to swap in Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai to compare how different model families explain the same failure. If you want to go further, persist the FailureReport objects to SQLite and build a dashboard that tracks which error categories appear most often. Over time, this data will tell you whether your prompt library needs better schema enforcement or whether a particular model family is prone to instruction override. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, sending a 4,000-token failure log costs the same as a one-liner. That makes iterative debugging cheap enough to run on every deploy. You can see how the flat pricing works for your volume at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Building Customer Support Agents with AI
content:
Customer support is moving from scripted chatbots to autonomous agents that can query backends, reference documentation, and hold multi-turn conversations. The difference between a frustrating bot and a useful agent usually comes down to three things: the quality of the underlying model, the precision of its tool use, and the economics of running it at scale. For teams building these systems, inference cost is not an operational footnote. It is an architectural constraint. If your provider charges by the token, every extra paragraph of product documentation, every previous turn in the conversation, and every RAG context chunk directly inflates your bill. That pricing model forces a trade-off between helpfulness and budget. Oxlo.ai removes that trade-off with flat per-request pricing, so your agent can use full context on every single call.

Why AI Agents Are Replacing Traditional Tickets

Traditional ticketing systems force users into rigid forms and long wait times. Modern agents use function calling to look up orders, check inventory, or schedule callbacks in real time. They use retrieval to ground answers in your actual help center, not a static FAQ. The result is a support layer that resolves issues instead of simply collecting them. But this power comes with engineering requirements. Agents need to parse unstructured complaints, maintain conversation state across multiple turns, and sometimes reason over long troubleshooting guides. These workloads are inherently long-context and tool-heavy. A platform that penalizes long inputs will quietly degrade your agent's memory and accuracy as conversations grow.

Anatomy of a Customer Support Agent

A production support agent has four layers.

First, the orchestration layer manages state, routing, and retry logic. It decides when to invoke the model, when to execute a tool, and when to return a final answer.

Second, the retrieval layer fetches relevant articles, past tickets, or account data. Because user queries are vague, you often need to inject large chunks of text to give the model enough signal. Many teams use dense passage retrieval followed by reranking, which can yield five to ten relevant passages per query.

Third, the tool layer exposes functions such as get_order_status, initiate_refund, or create_ticket. The model must decide when to call these and how to map user intent to structured arguments. This requires reliable JSON mode and robust function calling support.

Fourth, the inference layer runs the LLM itself. This layer determines latency, output quality, and your cost structure. For long-context agentic workloads, a request-based provider can change the economics entirely. Oxlo.ai offers 45-plus models across seven categories, all fully OpenAI SDK compatible, with no cold starts on popular models.

The Hidden Cost of Context

Support conversations accumulate context quickly. A single session might include ten back-and-forth turns, each appended to the prompt. If you add RAG retrieval from a knowledge base, plus system instructions, your input tokens can balloon into the tens of thousands. On token-based providers, this means you pay more for every additional turn and every extra document chunk. The usual workaround is to compress or truncate context, but that loses nuance. You might drop the exact error message or the specific policy clause that solves the ticket.

Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing. One API call costs the same regardless of whether you send a one-line greeting or a full conversation history with retrieved documentation. That makes it feasible to give your agent complete context on every turn without watching your per-interaction cost climb linearly.

Building with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, so you can prototype with the same Python or Node.js code you already use. The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. Below is a minimal example of a support agent that uses function calling to check an order before deciding whether to escalate.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Retrieve current status for an order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    },
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "escalate_to_human",
            "description": "Hand off to a human agent",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "reason": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["reason"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a support agent. Be concise. Check orders before escalating."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "I never got my package. Order OX-8842."}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

print(response.choices[0].message)

Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, you can expand the system prompt with detailed routing logic, append long conversation histories, and include retrieved knowledge base articles without watching your per-interaction cost climb. If the model returns a tool call, you simply append the result to the message list and make another request. Each step is one flat charge.

Choosing the Right Model

Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 models across seven categories. For support agents, the right choice depends on your user base and ticket complexity.

  • Llama 3.3 70B works well as a general-purpose backbone. It handles multi-turn dialogue and tool use reliably for English-centric workloads.
  • Qwen 3 32B is a strong pick if you serve multilingual customers. Its reasoning and agent workflow capabilities reduce error rates in non-English conversations.
  • DeepSeek R1 671B MoE excels when the agent must reason through ambiguous policies or complex troubleshooting trees.
  • Kimi K2.6 offers advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision support with a 131K context window. If your support channel includes screenshots or PDFs, this model can parse them inline.
  • DeepSeek V4 Flash provides a 1M context window and efficient MoE architecture for high-volume triage. You can preload an entire product manual and still pay per request.
  • For technical support scripts, Qwen 3 Coder 30B or DeepSeek Coder handle code-specific questions with precision.

Deployment Patterns

Production support agents need more than a smart model. They need predictable behavior and fast feedback loops.

Use streaming responses to show users that the agent is typing. This improves perceived latency even if tool calls take a second to resolve. Oxlo.ai supports streaming on its chat completions endpoint.

Use JSON mode when you need structured output for downstream automation, such as filling a CRM field or triggering a webhook. Enforcing a schema keeps your pipeline stable.

Use multi-turn conversation endpoints to maintain state naturally. With Oxlo.ai, extending the message array does not trigger a higher per-turn cost, so you can keep the full thread intact for better coherence.

Finally, plan for failure. If a tool call times out, your orchestration layer should catch the exception and let the model decide whether to retry or escalate. Because there are no cold starts on popular models at Oxlo.ai, your fallback path stays responsive even during traffic spikes.

Pricing That Scales with Requests, Not Words

Most inference platforms bill by the token. For support agents, that is a misalignment. You want your agent to read everything relevant before responding. You want it to search across long documents and maintain full conversation history. Token-based billing turns those best practices into budget problems. Some teams respond by limiting RAG chunks or summarizing away older turns, which directly hurts resolution rates.

Oxlo.ai flips the model. You pay one flat cost per API request. Request-based pricing can be 10 to 100 times cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context workloads. There are no cold starts on popular models, so your support pipeline stays responsive. You can explore the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Conclusion

Building a customer support agent is no longer a research project. With function calling, retrieval, and modern open-source models, you can deploy systems that resolve tickets end to end. The remaining question is whether your infrastructure bill lets you use those systems to their full potential. Token-based pricing forces you to treat context as a luxury. Oxlo.ai treats it as a baseline. By charging per request instead of per token, Oxlo.ai lets your agent retain full conversation history, search across complete documentation, and reason deeply without inflating your costs. If you are architecting a support pipeline, start with the tools that do not punish you for being thorough. Test your agent on Oxlo.ai and see how flat pricing changes what it is allowed to know.

title: Introduction to LLMs with Oxlo.ai
content:
We're going to build a technical support triage agent that routes developer questions to the right Oxlo.ai model based on complexity. Simple questions get fast answers from Qwen 3 32B, while deep debugging tasks go to Kimi K2.6 for step-by-step reasoning. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, analyzing a two-line error costs the same as processing a thousand-line stack trace, which makes multi-stage agent pipelines practical from day one.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. I recommend exporting your key as OXLO_API_KEY so the client can pick it up cleanly. Create a virtual environment, activate it, and keep credentials out of source control. If you are just experimenting, Oxlo.ai's free tier includes 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, which is plenty for prototyping this pipeline.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

I always verify the API connection before writing business logic. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, which means you can use the official openai Python package without wrappers or custom adapters. This drop-in behavior saves hours when migrating prototypes or integrating with frameworks that expect the standard client. I also import json because the classifier will return structured output later.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Define the system prompts

Good prompts are just configuration that happens to be written in natural language. I define three constants at the top of the file so non-engineers can tune wording without touching the routing code. The classifier prompt must be rigid because it feeds a JSON parser. The support prompts are looser, calibrated to the model they target. Keeping these separate makes it trivial to A/B test different instructions or swap in DeepSeek V3.2 later without refactoring.

CLASSIFIER_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent. Analyze the user question and classify its complexity.
Return valid JSON with keys: 'complexity' ('simple' or 'complex'), 'reason' (string)."""

SUPPORT_PROMPT = """You are a senior developer support engineer. Answer clearly and concisely.
If the user provided code, review it for bugs. Suggest concrete fixes."""

DEEP_REASONING_PROMPT = """You are a principal engineer debugging a critical issue. Think step by step.
Identify root causes, consider edge cases, and provide a detailed remediation plan."""

Step 3: Classify incoming questions with JSON mode

The classifier is the gatekeeper. I use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows system instructions precisely and Oxlo.ai serves it with no cold starts, so the first request after idle time is still fast. I enable JSON mode by passing response_format, which forces the model to emit valid JSON rather than markdown. If you want even more structured control, you could switch the classifier to Kimi K2.6 or enforce a JSON schema, but for a first pass the built-in json_object type is sufficient. This extra call does not blow up the budget because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. One classification request costs the same whether the user message is ten words or ten thousand.

def classify_question(user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": CLASSIFIER_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 4: Answer simple questions with Qwen 3 32B

For the fast path I choose Qwen 3 32B. It handles multilingual reasoning and general developer questions with low latency, which is exactly what you want for FAQs and syntax issues. If your team supports developers in multiple languages, this is a strong default because Oxlo.ai lists it specifically for multilingual workloads. Because Oxlo.ai does not meter input tokens, I can stuff the prompt with relevant documentation snippets or previous chat history without watching a meter spin. The function returns a dictionary with the model name and the answer so the router stays agnostic about how the response was generated.

def answer_simple(user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SUPPORT_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return {
        "model": "qwen-3-32b",
        "answer": response.choices[0].message.content,
    }

Step 5: Handle complex debugging with Kimi K2.6

When the classifier detects ambiguity, concurrency, or infrastructure depth, I escalate to Kimi K2.6. It handles advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision tasks, and it supports a 131K context window on Oxlo.ai. That means you can feed it long stack traces, configuration files, and previous chat history in a single request. For cases where you need even more room, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a 1M context window on the same platform. On traditional token-based hosts, a deep reasoning pass over a long log file can get expensive quickly, but Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing removes that friction. You can pass the entire traceback and still pay the same single request fee.

def answer_complex(user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k2.6",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": DEEP_REASONING_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return {
        "model": "kimi-k2.6",
        "answer": response.choices[0].message.content,
    }

Step 6: Wire the router and return structured results

The support_agent function ties the pipeline together. It calls the classifier, branches on the complexity field, and attaches the triage reason to the final payload. I keep the interface minimal: string in, dictionary out. That makes it easy to wrap this in an HTTP endpoint, a CLI tool, or an async Celery task later. You could also add a timeout or a retry wrapper around the client call if this were production code, but for the tutorial the raw client is enough to see the logic clearly.

def support_agent(user_message):
    classification = classify_question(user_message)
    
    if classification["complexity"] == "simple":
        result = answer_simple(user_message)
    else:
        result = answer_complex(user_message)
    
    result["triage_reason"] = classification["reason"]
    return result

Run it

I test the pipeline with two tickets. The first asks about Python list reversal, which should stay on the fast path with Qwen 3 32B. The second asks about diagnosing a memory leak in a long-running asyncio service, which should trigger Kimi K2.6. Execute the script and inspect the model field in each result to confirm the router is working. Pay attention to the triage_reason field. It surfaces the classifier's logic, which is useful for debugging routing mistakes. If you are on the free tier, these two requests count against your daily limit of 60, leaving plenty of room for iterative testing. Upgrade to a paid plan at https://oxlo.ai/pricing when you need more volume.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    simple_ticket = "How do I reverse a Python list?"
    print(support_agent(simple_ticket))
    
    complex_ticket = (
        "I have a memory leak in a long-running asyncio application using uvloop. "
        "The RSS grows by 50 MB every hour. How do I diagnose it?"
    )
    print(support_agent(complex_ticket))

Example output:

{
  "model": "qwen-3-32b",
  "answer": "You can reverse a Python list in place with .reverse(), or create a reversed copy with slicing: reversed_list = original_list[::-1].",
  "triage_reason": "The question asks for a standard library one-liner with no ambiguity or debugging context."
}
{
  "model": "kimi-k2.6",
  "answer": "1. Confirm the leak is in Python's heap, not just RSS fragmentation, by checking tracemalloc statistics...",
  "triage_reason": "The issue involves long-running infrastructure, an external event loop, and requires root-cause analysis."
}

Next steps

Two directions to take this. First, add a feedback loop. Store every question, classification, and answer in a local SQLite database, then review weekly whether simple questions were incorrectly escalated or complex ones were underserviced. Tuning the classifier prompt is cheaper on Oxlo.ai than on token-based providers because you pay per request, not per token. Second, wire in function calling. Give the agent access to a get_recent_logs tool so it can fetch real error data before answering. Oxlo.ai supports function calling on the same chat/completions endpoint, so the migration is just a messages parameter change. You could also expose the agent via a small FastAPI server and stream responses back to a frontend. Oxlo.ai supports streaming on the chat/completions endpoint, so you can flush tokens to the client as soon as they arrive, which improves perceived latency on deep reasoning passes.

title: LLM for Speech Recognition with Oxlo.ai
content:
Speech recognition has moved past the era of simple audio-to-text converters. Today, the most effective voice applications treat automatic speech recognition (ASR) as an input layer for large language models that correct errors, identify speakers, extract structured data, and trigger agentic workflows. A one-hour recording can easily produce a transcript that feeds a fifteen-thousand-token reasoning chain, which means your infrastructure costs are now tied to context length as much as to audio duration. Oxlo.ai supports this new architecture by offering both the audio transcription models and the reasoning models required for downstream processing, all behind a single API with request-based pricing that does not scale with prompt length.

Why LLMs Are Changing Speech Recognition

Modern ASR systems such as Whisper deliver high-quality transcripts, but raw text is rarely enough for production workflows. Customer support calls contain filler words and false starts. Medical dictations require domain-specific formatting. Podcasts need speaker labels and chapter summaries. Feeding the raw transcript into an LLM lets you clean the text, standardize terminology, and return structured JSON in a single pass.

This pattern also enables real-time agentic behavior. A voice assistant can transcribe user speech, then use function calling to book a calendar slot or query a database before responding. The LLM acts as both a post-processor for the audio stream and a router for business logic. Because these workflows often append the full conversation history to every new turn, context windows grow quickly. The transcription itself becomes a long-context payload that you send repeatedly to the model.

The Hidden Cost of Token-Based Audio Workloads

When you price inference by the token, long transcripts become expensive infrastructure artifacts. A forty-five-minute interview can generate ten thousand words. If you send that transcript through a chain-of-thought reasoning model, or if you maintain it inside a multi-turn agent conversation, your input tokens accumulate on every single request. Token-based providers scale cost directly with input length, which penalizes the exact workloads that make speech recognition valuable.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of how long the prompt is. For long-context and agentic audio workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. Because Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, voice agents and transcription pipelines remain responsive even under variable traffic.

Building an End-to-End Speech-to-Reasoning Pipeline

You can implement this architecture with the OpenAI SDK by pointing the base URL to Oxlo.ai. The pipeline has two stages. First, call the audio/transcriptions endpoint with a Whisper model. Second, pass the resulting text to the chat/completions endpoint with an LLM that supports JSON mode or function calling.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_API_KEY"
)

# Stage 1: Transcribe
with open("earnings_call.wav", "rb") as audio_file:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
        model="whisper-large-v3",
        file=audio_file,
        response_format="text"
    )

# Stage 2: Reason and extract
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "Extract key financial metrics and management quotes as JSON."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": transcript
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

In this example, the transcript length does not affect the price of either API call. Whether the audio is two minutes or two hours, the request to the LLM costs the same flat amount. You can also replace the LLM with a reasoning specialist such as DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for complex coding transcripts, or Qwen 3 32B for multilingual source material. Because Oxlo.ai supports function calling and tool use, you can extend the pipeline so the model schedules follow-up tasks or writes database records based on what was said.

Selecting Models for Speech Workloads on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai hosts more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories. This catalog lets you pair the right transcription backend with the right reasoning frontend.

For transcription, Whisper Large v3 gives maximum accuracy for noisy or accented audio, while Whisper Turbo minimizes latency for real-time captioning. Both are available through the audio/transcriptions endpoint.

For downstream processing, match the LLM to your output requirements. Llama 3.3 70B is a reliable general-purpose workhorse for summarization and formatting. Qwen 3 32B excels at multilingual reasoning and agent workflows when your audio sources include mixed languages. DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash provide deep reasoning for technical or legal transcripts that benefit from chain-of-thought analysis. Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision support, which is valuable when you need to synchronize slides or video with spoken content. GLM 5 handles long-horizon agentic tasks, and Minimax M2.5 specializes in coding and tool use, such as generating executable scripts from verbal instructions.

All of these models are accessible through the same OpenAI SDK client. Switching from a lightweight formatter to a heavy reasoning model is a one-line change, and the platform supports streaming responses, multi-turn conversations, and vision input where the model allows it.

Predictable Pricing for Voice Agents and Long Context

Voice agents are inherently stateful. Each turn typically includes the entire conversation history plus the latest transcript chunk. Under token-based billing, the cost of each turn grows linearly with the conversation length. Over a day of customer service interactions, that compounding effect becomes substantial.

Oxlo.ai flattens this curve. Request-based pricing means a voice agent turn that includes twenty thousand tokens of history costs the same as a turn with two hundred tokens. This structure makes Oxlo.ai a practical backend for agentic workloads that maintain long context windows. Combined with features such as streaming responses, function calling, and multi-turn conversation support, you can build responsive voice applications without token math.

The platform offers a Free plan with 60 requests per day across more than 16 free models, including access to a 7-day full-access trial. This is enough to prototype a complete speech-to-action pipeline. Paid plans scale to thousands of requests per day, and Enterprise customers receive dedicated GPUs with guaranteed savings over their current provider. For exact plan details, see the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Drop-In Integration Without Vendor Lock-In

Because Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI API compatible interface, you can migrate existing speech recognition code by changing two lines: the base URL and the API key. The platform supports Python, Node.js, and cURL. Endpoints include chat/completions, audio/transcriptions, audio/speech, embeddings, and images/generations, so you can unify transcription, synthesis, and reasoning inside one provider.

This compatibility extends to advanced features. JSON mode, function calling, tool use, and streaming responses all follow the same schema you already use. If you have built voice products on token-based providers, moving your long-context workloads to Oxlo.ai can reduce costs without a rewrite.

Speech recognition is now a gateway to reasoning, not just a text output. The pipelines that extract real value from voice combine Whisper-class ASR with LLMs that clean, structure, and act on transcripts. These pipelines generate long contexts by design, which makes infrastructure pricing a critical architectural decision. Oxlo.ai provides the audio models, the reasoning models, and the flat request-based pricing needed to run them economically. With OpenAI SDK compatibility and no cold starts, you can ship voice agents and transcription workflows that scale without surprise costs.

title: Demystifying LLMs: A Beginner's Guide
content:
We are going to build a command-line tutor that explains technical concepts in plain English. If you are new to LLMs, this project will show you exactly how a model turns a prompt into an answer, and you will have a working tool you can actually use. No prior AI experience required.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed on your machine
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai

You can follow along on the Oxlo.ai free tier, which includes access to models like deepseek-v3.2 and llama-3.3-70b. There is no credit card required to start.

Step 1: Set up the client

I always start by proving the wire works. Import the OpenAI SDK, point the base_url to Oxlo.ai, and fire a single question. This is a genuine drop-in replacement. The only difference from OpenAI's own client is two constructor arguments.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is an LLM?"},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

If you see a coherent paragraph explaining large language models, your environment is ready. I keep this snippet in a scratch file so I can test API keys quickly whenever I spin up a new project.

Step 2: Define the system prompt

LLMs do not arrive with a personality. The system prompt is the hidden instruction that shapes every single reply. Think of it as the curriculum for your tutor. We will store it as a constant so it is easy to tweak without hunting through function bodies.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a patient tutor for beginners.
Explain topics in plain English using analogies.
Keep answers under 150 words unless the user asks for detail.
If the user asks something off-topic, gently redirect them to science and technology concepts."""

This string does the heavy lifting. It constrains tone, length, and subject matter without us writing any conditional Python logic. I usually spend more time editing this prompt than I do editing the code, because it is the actual product experience.

Step 3: Build the explainer function

Next, we wrap the API call in a reusable function. Passing the system prompt on every request ensures the model never forgets its role, even if we refactor the rest of the script.

Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, you can make your system prompt as detailed as you want without inflating the cost of each call. That matters when you are experimenting. You are free to iterate on wording and add examples inside the prompt itself.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a patient tutor for beginners.
Explain topics in plain English using analogies.
Keep answers under 150 words unless the user asks for detail.
If the user asks something off-topic, gently redirect them to science and technology concepts."""

def explain_topic(user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(explain_topic("How does a neural network learn?"))

The function returns a plain string. That means you can pipe the result into a web framework, a text-to-speech pipeline, or just print it to the terminal.

Step 4: Add conversation memory

Real chat applications remember context. The mechanism is simple: keep a list of every message, and send the entire list back on every call. The model has no memory of its own. It only sees what you explicitly pass in the messages array.

We start the list with the system prompt. Then we append the user's questions and the model's answers in alternating turns. This pattern, system-user-assistant-user-assistant, is exactly what powers every major chat interface.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a patient tutor for beginners.
Explain topics in plain English using analogies.
Keep answers under 150 words unless the user asks for detail.
If the user asks something off-topic, gently redirect them to science and technology concepts."""

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("Study Buddy is ready. Type 'quit' to exit.")

while True:
    user_input = input("You: ")
    if user_input.lower().strip() == "quit":
        break

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
    )

    assistant_reply = response.choices[0].message.content
    print(f"Study Buddy: {assistant_reply}\n")

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_reply})

Notice that the list grows with each turn. If you ever need to trim context, you can pop old turns from the front of the list after the system prompt. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing makes this kind of iterative experimentation cheap, even as the conversation gets longer.

Run it

Save the script as tutor.py, export your key if you prefer not to paste it directly, and run:

python tutor.py

Here is what a short session looks like on my machine:

You: What is attention in a transformer?
Study Buddy: Think of attention like highlighting sentences in a textbook. When the model reads a sentence, attention lets it focus on the most relevant words, even if they are far apart. It calculates a score for every pair of words, then blends their meanings so the model understands context. This is why modern LLMs can follow long stories and complex instructions.

You: Can you give me another metaphor?
Study Buddy: Imagine a librarian who listens to your question, then instantly knows exactly which books, chapters, and even specific paragraphs to pull from a massive library. Attention is that librarian's ability to zero in on the right information without reading every book cover to cover.

The second answer references the first implicitly because the full conversation history is included in the request. That is the entire magic of stateful LLM interactions.

Next steps

You now have a working mental model of how LLMs process prompts. Two concrete directions to take this:

  1. Structured output. Change the system prompt to request JSON, then add response_format={"type": "json_object"} to the API call. You can use this to generate multiple-choice quiz questions with answers parsed directly into Python dictionaries.
  2. Vision. Swap the model to kimi-k2.6 and pass a base64-encoded image in the messages array. Your tutor can then explain diagrams, screenshots, or textbook pages, not just text.

Both features work through the same OpenAI-compatible client. Because Oxlo.ai exposes dozens of models under one flat per-request pricing model, you can test these variations without re-architecting your code or predicting token costs.

title: Mastering Few-Shot Learning with LLMs
content:
Few-shot learning with LLMs is the practice of steering model behavior by prepending a small set of input-output examples before the actual task prompt. It occupies the practical middle ground between zero-shot prompting, which relies entirely on pre-trained knowledge, and expensive fine-tuning pipelines that require GPU clusters and curated datasets. For engineering teams shipping production features, few-shot prompting offers a fast, reproducible way to boost accuracy without retraining weights. The trade-off is straightforward: every example you add increases prompt length, which directly inflates costs on token-based inference platforms. That cost dynamic makes your choice of infrastructure just as important as your choice of examples.

What Is Few-Shot Learning?

In the context of large language models, few-shot learning refers to in-context learning where the prompt contains N labeled examples, typically one to five, followed by the target input. The model infers the intended pattern, format, and reasoning style from these examples rather than from updated weights. This mechanism works because transformer attention layers can latch onto recurring structures across tokens. A single prompt can therefore act as a temporary training run, with the examples serving as a dynamic, swappable dataset. Because no gradients are computed, switching tasks or updating behavior requires only a text edit, not a training job. The limitation is context window size: examples consume tokens that could otherwise be used for instructions, retrieval context, or conversation history.

Why Few-Shot Prompting Beats Fine-Tuning for Most Teams

Fine-tuning remains the right tool when you need millisecond-level latency reductions, proprietary style embeddings, or extremely high-volume cost amortization. For everything else, few-shot prompting is the pragmatic default. It eliminates data curation overhead. You do not need to build labeling pipelines, validate train-test splits, or manage LoRA adapter versions. Your prompts live in Git, not in a model registry. Iteration cycles shrink from days to minutes. When foundation models update, you are not forced to re-run distillation or fine-tuning jobs. You simply point your inference client at a newer base model and keep your examples. The operational simplicity is hard to overstate for teams that need reliable output formats, classification boundaries, or tone controls without hiring a dedicated machine learning engineer.

Designing Effective Few-Shot Examples

Quality matters more than quantity. Three diverse, well-formatted examples usually outperform ten repetitive ones. Each example should represent a distinct edge case or input distribution present in production. If you are building an entity extractor, include one example with missing fields, one with extra noise, and one with nested structures. Format consistency is non-negotiable. If example one uses JSON, example two must use JSON. If you delimit sections with XML tags, carry that pattern through every shot. Label noise is especially destructive in few-shot settings because the model has no statistical smoothing from a large dataset. One malformed example can corrupt the entire output distribution.

Always version control your example banks separately from application logic. Treat them like configuration files that require pull requests and code review. Place examples in user-assistant message pairs rather than stuffing them into a single system prompt. This preserves role boundaries and makes the pattern easier to parse for models optimized for chat templates. Finally, order matters: place the simplest example first and the most complex last, or alternate input types so the model does not latch onto positional bias.

The Hidden Infrastructure Cost of Few-Shot Prompts

The Achilles heel of few-shot prompting is token count. A rich example with a long document and a detailed JSON response can consume thousands of tokens. Multiply that by four or five shots, add a system prompt and user query, and your input balloons. On token-based providers, this linear cost scaling punishes you for giving the model the context it needs to succeed.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. A 4,000-token prompt containing five detailed examples costs the same as a 200-token greeting. For few-shot pipelines, this changes the design calculus. You can include richer context, broader retrieval documents, and multi-turn tool trajectories without watching token counters. Teams running agentic workloads or long-context retrieval augmented generation with few-shot prefixes often see significant cost reductions compared to token-based billing, because input length no longer drives spend. You can explore exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Choosing the Right Model for Few-Shot Tasks

Not all foundation models handle in-context learning with the same reliability. Oxlo.ai offers a range of options through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, so swapping models is a one-line change.

For general-purpose few-shot extraction and classification, Llama 3.3 70B provides consistent instruction adherence. If your examples require multilingual reasoning or agentic workflows, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for cross-lingual patterns. When your few-shot task involves deep reasoning or complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE excels at multi-step logic. Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision capabilities with a 131K context window, which is ideal when your examples include screenshots or lengthy source documents. For workloads that need massive context, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a 1M context window and efficient MoE architecture, letting you embed entire manuals as few-shot material. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, you can use these large context windows as intended instead of aggressively truncating examples to manage spend.

A Production-Ready Few-Shot Pattern

Here is a concrete pattern you can deploy today. The example uses structured extraction from unstructured messages, a common production task where zero-shot prompts often hallucinate fields or formats. We use the OpenAI SDK pointed at Oxlo.ai, which means the only change from your existing code is the base URL.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

system_prompt = """You extract meeting details into JSON.
Follow the format shown in the examples exactly."""

few_shot_examples = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Email: Let's sync tomorrow at 3pm in Conf Room B about the API migration."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"title": "API migration sync", "date": "tomorrow", "time": "3pm", "location": "Conf Room B", "participants": []}'},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Slack: @sarah and @mike, Q2 planning is moved to Friday 10am over Zoom."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"title": "Q2 planning", "date": "Friday", "time": "10am", "location": "Zoom", "participants": ["sarah", "mike"]}'},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Text: Reminder, architecture review tonight at 7pm in Building 4."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"title": "architecture review", "date": "tonight", "time": "7pm", "location": "Building 4", "participants": []}'},
]

new_input = {
    "role": "user",
    "content": "Calendar invite: Sprint retro on Monday 2pm with the backend team in the main auditorium."
}

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] + few_shot_examples + [new_input],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    stream=False
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

In this pattern, the three examples cover email, Slack, and plain text inputs. They share an identical JSON schema, which trains the model to emit valid JSON even when the input channel changes. The system prompt sets the meta-task, while the user-assistant pairs carry the few-shot signal. Using Oxlo.ai, the cost of this call is predictable. Whether the messages total 500 tokens or 5,000 tokens, the request price does not change. That stability lets you iterate on prompt length without rewriting budget forecasts. You can also enable streaming, function calling, or JSON mode through the same endpoint, so the few-shot pattern integrates cleanly into existing agent architectures.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

First, avoid example contamination. Never pull evaluation data into your few-shot prompt. Your example bank and your test set must be disjoint, or you will overestimate accuracy. Second, do not ignore context limits. Even though Oxlo.ai removes the financial penalty for long prompts, you must still respect each model's maximum context window. Monitor token counts to prevent silent truncation. Third, resist the urge to overfit your prompt. If every example follows the exact same sentence structure, the model may fail on inputs that deviate slightly. Maintain adversarial examples in your evaluation suite. Fourth, keep system prompts active. Few-shot examples guide format and reasoning, but the system prompt still governs tone, safety boundaries, and task framing. Relying on examples alone to override system-level instructions is unreliable. Finally, cache your examples client-side or in a prompt management layer rather than reconstructing them on every request in a way that introduces unnecessary latency.

Putting It All Together

Few-shot learning is one of the highest-leverage techniques available to developers working with LLMs. It requires no training infrastructure, offers same-day iteration cycles, and can push model performance into production-ready territory without touching a single weight. The operational friction has historically been cost: longer prompts mean more tokens, and more tokens mean higher bills on conventional platforms. Oxlo.ai removes that friction with flat, request-based pricing. You can run long-context few-shot prompts on Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, or DeepSeek V4 Flash without token anxiety. content:
Multimodal large language models are no longer experimental curiosities. They are the default interface for applications that need to reason across text, images, audio, and structured data in a single context. Whether you are building a visual agent that inspects screenshots, a documentation pipeline that transcribes meetings and generates diagrams, or an autonomous coding assistant that reads wireframes and writes implementations, the ability to process multiple modalities in one request is now a baseline requirement. Yet the infrastructure behind these models often lags behind their capabilities. Token-based billing, cold starts, and fragmented APIs turn multimodal experiments into expensive engineering sprints. Oxlo.ai addresses this directly with a developer-first inference platform that treats multimodal workloads as first-class citizens.

What Makes a Model Truly Multimodal

A truly multimodal system does not bolt a vision encoder onto a text model as an afterthought. It processes inputs from different channels, text, image, audio, and sometimes video, within a unified latent space so that reasoning can cross boundaries naturally. For developers, this means a single API call can accept a base64-encoded image, a transcript snippet, and a JSON schema, then return structured text or trigger a tool call. The practical impact is shorter pipelines. Instead of chaining a separate OCR service, a summarization model, and a code generator, you send everything to one endpoint and let the model handle alignment. This consolidation reduces latency and error rates, but it also changes how you should think about inference costs. Multimodal inputs, especially high-resolution images and long audio files, expand token counts dramatically.

The Hidden Cost of Multimodal Tokens

Most inference providers bill by the token. That works for short chat prompts, but it breaks down once you start passing screenshots, audio waveforms, or multi-turn agent traces into the context window. A single high-resolution image can consume thousands of tokens. A thirty-minute audio transcription might represent tens of thousands more. When your cost scales linearly with input length, every additional modality becomes a budget risk. Agentic workflows compound the problem because they append tool outputs and observations back into the prompt, inflating context length with every turn. Token-based providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, force you to optimize aggressively by resizing images or truncating audio. title: Unlocking the Potential of LLMs for Tech Support
content:
Tech support teams face a familiar bottleneck. Every ticket requires a human to parse fragmented documentation, reproduce environment-specific bugs, and compose accurate responses. As products grow in complexity and user bases expand globally, this linear scaling model breaks down. Large language models offer a way out, not by replacing engineers, but by augmenting them with reasoning, retrieval, and resolution capabilities that scale horizontally.

From Ticket Queues to Reasoning Pipelines

Traditional support workflows are reactive. A user submits a ticket, waits in a queue, and eventually connects with an engineer who must manually reconstruct the issue from incomplete context. Large language models invert this dynamic. When integrated with ticketing systems and internal knowledge bases, LLMs become reasoning pipelines that preprocess, classify, and often resolve issues before a human engineer reads the first line. They handle high-volume, low-complexity queries autonomously, summarize long threads for senior staff, and maintain consistent tone across multilingual user bases. The result is not a smaller support team, but a team that spends its time on problems that actually require human judgment.

High-Impact Use Cases for LLMs in Support

Automated triage and routing. The first point of friction in any support organization is deciding who should handle a ticket. LLMs can classify incoming requests by product area, severity, and required skill set, then route them to the correct queue. With JSON mode, the model outputs structured metadata that your CRM or ticketing platform can ingest directly, eliminating manual tagging.

Knowledge base synthesis. Most organizations have documentation scattered across wikis, PDFs, READMEs, and closed tickets. An LLM with a long context window can ingest multiple sources simultaneously and generate a coherent, cited answer for the user. This reduces the time engineers spend searching for information and prevents users from receiving contradictory guidance.

Code-aware debugging assistance. Technical support often involves reading stack traces, configuration files, or build logs. Models trained on code, such as Qwen 3 Coder 30B and DeepSeek Coder, can identify root causes in snippets provided by users, suggest fixes, and even generate shell commands or configuration patches. For deeper reasoning, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2 Thinking apply advanced chain-of-thought analysis to complex, ambiguous errors.

Vision-enabled bug reporting. Users do not always describe what they see. Screenshots, screen recordings, and annotated images frequently convey more than paragraphs of text. Vision models like Kimi K2.6, Gemma 3 27B, and Kimi VL A3B can interpret UI glitches, read error dialogs from images, and cross-reference visual symptoms with known issues in the knowledge base.

Agentic resolution with tool use. The most effective support agents do not just answer questions. They take action. By enabling function calling, an LLM can query order databases, verify license keys, restart services through internal APIs, and schedule follow-up tasks. Models such as GLM 5, Minimax M2.5, and Qwen 3 32B support long-horizon agentic workflows that chain multiple tool calls into a complete resolution.

Why Context Length and Tool Use Define Success

Support tickets are messy. A single issue might include a 10,000-line log file, a thread of ten emails, and three related documentation pages. LLMs need to ingest all of this to avoid asking the user for information they have already provided. This is where context length becomes a hard requirement, not a luxury.

Function calling and JSON mode are equally critical. A support LLM that cannot query an internal database or return structured data for a ticketing system is just a chatbot. Real integration requires the model to emit precise tool calls, wait for results, and synthesize answers. Streaming responses keep the user experience responsive while the model reasons over large inputs. Multi-turn conversation support ensures the agent remembers prior clarifications across a long debugging session.

The Pricing Problem with Long-Context Support Workloads

Here is the economic reality that many teams discover only after deployment. Token-based pricing scales linearly with input length. A support agent that ingests a 50,000-token log file, a 20,000-token knowledge base article, and a multi-turn conversation history can consume hundreds of thousands of tokens per ticket. When multiplied across thousands of tickets per day, costs become unpredictable and often prohibitive.

Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. As a developer-first AI inference platform, Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing. One API call costs the same regardless of whether you send a one-line prompt or a 100,000-token context window. For long-context and agentic support workloads, this model can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. Costs remain predictable as you scale, and you are not penalized for giving the model the full context it needs to resolve an issue correctly.

Oxlo.ai offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all fully OpenAI SDK compatible with no cold starts on popular models. You can iterate on Llama 3.3 70B for general queries, switch to DeepSeek R1 671B MoE for complex coding issues, or deploy Kimi K2.6 for agentic coding and vision tasks with 131K context. The platform includes dedicated code models like Qwen 3 Coder 30B and DeepSeek Coder, vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B, and even audio models like Whisper for transcribing customer calls.

Selecting the Right Model on Oxlo.ai

Not every support task needs the same reasoning profile. Oxlo.ai makes it easy to route tickets to the right model without managing multiple provider accounts.

For general-purpose ticket responses and reasoning, Llama 3.3 70B provides a strong balance of capability and speed. If your user base is global, Qwen 3 32B offers multilingual reasoning and agent workflow support. When tickets involve deep debugging or complex code analysis, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Minimax M2.5 excel at chain-of-thought reasoning and tool use. For tickets that include massive log dumps or require synthesizing an entire product manual, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window and efficient MoE inference. GLM 5 handles long-horizon agentic tasks that span multiple tools and steps.

When users attach screenshots or screen recordings, vision models become essential. Kimi K2.6 combines advanced reasoning with vision and a 131K context, making it ideal for analyzing UI bugs alongside technical logs. Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B offer additional vision options for image understanding at different scale points.

Integrating into Your Support Stack

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can drop it into existing Python, Node.js, or cURL workflows by changing a single base URL. This matters for support teams that already have prototype pipelines built against OpenAI APIs and do not want to rewrite their orchestration layer.

Below is a minimal example showing how to query Oxlo.ai with tool use enabled for a support agent that can look up order status and read internal documentation.

    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"

    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[

Conclusion

LLMs are not a substitute for human support engineers, but they extend the capacity of a support team when deployed with the right context and tooling. The difference between a frustrating chatbot and a useful support agent comes down to context, tool access, and economic viability at scale. By choosing a platform that removes the cost penalty for long inputs and provides a broad model catalog under a single OpenAI-compatible API, you can build support systems that understand the problem before suggesting a solution. Oxlo.ai provides that foundation, with predictable pricing and the model diversity to handle everything from simple refunds to complex, multi-modal debugging sessions.

title: Using LLMs for Customer Service
content:
Customer service is one of the first production workloads where large language models move from experiment to infrastructure. Modern support pipelines need more than rigid decision trees. They require context-aware reasoning, multi-turn memory, and the ability to call external tools to resolve tickets without human escalation. The challenge for engineering teams is not deciding whether to use an LLM, but choosing an inference backend that keeps latency low and costs predictable as context windows fill with conversation history, knowledge base articles, and system prompts.

Designing LLM-Powered Support Architectures

A production customer service system typically combines retrieval-augmented generation, stateful multi-turn dialogue, and tool use. When a user opens a ticket, the pipeline must ingest lengthy inputs: previous email threads, order histories, policy documents, and internal wiki pages. Feeding all of this into a single prompt can quickly consume thousands of tokens. Retrieval-augmented generation keeps the model grounded in your internal documentation, but retrieval itself introduces latency. You may need to embed user queries, search a vector store, and then inject the top-k chunks into the prompt. Each chunk adds tokens. If your policy library is large, even a well-curated retrieval set can push prompts past 8,000 or 16,000 tokens. Stateful multi-turn dialogue compounds the issue, because every previous assistant and user message is typically replayed on each API call. For agentic workflows that iterate over several reasoning steps or consult multiple APIs, the input volume compounds across turns. Architecture decisions around context management directly impact both response quality and operational cost. Teams should design for long-context windows from the start, compress historical turns where possible, and reserve detailed documents for retrieval rather than stuffing them into every request. Oxlo.ai supports this architecture with models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash, which offers a 1 million token context window for near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning, and Kimi K2.6 with its 131K context and advanced agentic coding capabilities.

Selecting Models by Support Task

Not every support interaction needs the largest model available. Routing simple refund requests to a heavy reasoning model wastes compute and adds latency. A better approach matches the model to the complexity of the task. For initial triage and multilingual routing, Qwen 3 32B provides strong multilingual reasoning and agent workflow support. Across all of these, Oxlo.ai hosts more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across 7 categories, all accessible through a single endpoint with no cold starts on popular models.

Tool Use and Structured Output

Effective customer service agents do not work in isolation. They query CRMs, check shipping status, and verify account details. Your LLM stack needs the same capability. Function calling and JSON mode let the model decide when to invoke an external tool and return structured data that your backend can act on. JSON mode is equally important for customer service backends. When a model must return a structured update to a ticketing system, strict schema adherence prevents parsing failures. You can enforce JSON output to guarantee that fields like priority, category, and summary are always present and correctly typed. Oxlo.ai exposes these features through a fully OpenAI-compatible API.         "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Retrieve current order status by ID",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }

]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
