title: LLM Tutorial for Beginners
content:
We are going to build a customer support triage agent that reads incoming messages, classifies them by topic and urgency, and drafts a first response. If you are new to LLMs and want to ship something useful today, this tutorial is for you. The final script is under sixty lines of Python and runs against the Oxlo.ai API using the standard OpenAI SDK.

What You'll Need

You need Python 3.10 or newer installed on your machine. You also need the OpenAI Python SDK, which you can install with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with this SDK, so you will not need to learn a new library. Finally, grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal at https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier includes 60 requests per day, which is more than enough to build and test this agent.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai Client

I start every project by isolating the client configuration in its own block. This makes it easy to switch keys or endpoints later without hunting through business logic. Create a new file named support_agent.py and add the following imports and client setup. We import json now because we will parse structured output later. Point the base_url to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and pass your Oxlo.ai API key. If you already have OpenAI SDK experience, the only difference is that single line.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the Agent's System Prompt

The system prompt is the agent's job description. It sets boundaries, defines the output format, and controls tone. I keep it in a constant so non-technical teammates can edit it without touching code. We want three pieces of information back: a category, a priority level, and a short draft reply. I also embed the JSON schema instructions directly in the prompt text. Even though Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode at the API level, the model still needs to know what keys to populate. Keeping the prompt in a constant also makes A/B testing easy, so you can version control the prompt independently and roll back if a change hurts classification accuracy.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a support triage agent for a SaaS company.
Read the customer's message and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:
- category: classify as Billing, Technical, or General.
- priority: classify as High, Medium, or Low.
- draft_reply: write a polite, professional first response of no more than two sentences.

Return only valid JSON. Do not wrap the output in markdown code fences.
"""

Step 3: Build the Triage Function

Now we connect the prompt to a model. I use llama-3.3-70b because it is Oxlo.ai's general-purpose flagship and handles instruction following reliably. You could swap in qwen-3-32b for multilingual tickets or deepseek-v3.2 for coding-heavy support without changing any other code. I set temperature to 0.2 so the classifications stay consistent, and I enable JSON mode via response_format. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing instead of token-based billing, you can make the system prompt as detailed as necessary without inflating costs on every call. That makes iteration cheap, which matters when you are refining agent behavior. I also wrap the call in a try/except block because network calls and JSON parsing can fail. Returning None lets the caller decide whether to retry, fall back to a human, or queue the ticket.

def triage(message: str):
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": message},
            ],
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
            temperature=0.2,
        )
        return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error during triage: {e}")
        return None

Run It

Add a small test harness at the bottom of support_agent.py. I picked three tickets that cover the main categories: a billing urgency, a common technical issue, and general feedback. If you see a parsing error, check that your prompt explicitly forbids markdown fences. Some models are chatty and need that reminder. Run the file with python support_agent.py.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tickets = [
        "I was charged twice this month. Please refund the extra payment immediately.",
        "How do I reset my password? I cannot log in to my account.",
        "Your platform is amazing! Just wanted to say thanks.",
    ]

    for ticket in tickets:
        result = triage(ticket)
        if result:
            print(f"Ticket: {ticket}")
            print(f"Category : {result['category']}")
            print(f"Priority : {result['priority']}")
            print(f"Draft    : {result['draft_reply']}")
            print("-" * 40)

You should see output similar to this:

Ticket: I was charged twice this month. Please refund the extra payment immediately.
Category : Billing
Priority : High
Draft    : We sincerely apologize for the double charge. Our billing team has been notified and will process your refund within one business day.
----------------------------------------
Ticket: How do I reset my password? I cannot log in to my account.
Category : Technical
Priority : Medium
Draft    : You can reset your password by clicking "Forgot password" on the login screen. If you do not receive the email, please check your spam folder.
----------------------------------------
Ticket: Your platform is amazing! Just wanted to say thanks.
Category : General
Priority : Low
Draft    : Thank you so much for the kind words. We truly appreciate you taking the time to share your feedback.
----------------------------------------

Next Steps

This agent is stateless, which is fine for triage but limiting for ongoing threads. A natural next step is to maintain a message history list and pass the full conversation to the model on each turn. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, adding more context history does not increase your cost, so building conversational agents is straightforward. Another solid upgrade is to add function calling so the agent can look up account status or create refund tickets automatically. Oxlo.ai supports tool use across its major chat models, and there are no cold starts on popular models, so the extra capability will not introduce latency. If you move to production, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing for plans with higher daily request limits and priority queuing.

title: Building a Customer Support Agent with LLM
content:
Building a customer support agent that resolves tickets rather than deflecting them requires more than a well-written prompt. You need an inference backend that handles unpredictable context lengths, multi-turn memory, tool calls to your CRM, and streaming responses, all without costs that scale every time a user pastes a long error log. In this guide, we will walk through the architecture, model selection, and implementation patterns for production support agents, and we will show why Oxlo.ai is a strong fit for the inference layer.

Architecture Overview

A production support agent typically follows a loop: ingest the ticket, classify intent, retrieve relevant documentation, decide if a tool call is needed, generate a response, and log the result. The LLM sits at the center of this loop, so latency and context window management directly impact user experience. You will usually embed your knowledge base using embedding models like BGE-Large or E5-Large, both available through Oxlo.ai's embeddings endpoint, and store vectors in any vector database. When a ticket arrives, the system retrieves relevant articles and injects them into the prompt. This retrieval-augmented generation pattern inflates prompt size quickly, which makes inference pricing structure a first-class design constraint.

Model Selection for Support Workloads

Not every turn in a support conversation requires a 70B parameter model. A good architecture pairs lightweight models for intent routing and larger models for complex reasoning or drafting.

For general classification and quick replies, Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai provides a strong balance of speed and accuracy. If your user base is multilingual, Qwen 3 32B handles agent workflows across languages without extra translation layers. When a ticket involves deep reasoning, log analysis, or complex policy interpretation, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 offer advanced chain-of-thought reasoning. For tickets that include code snippets, configuration files, or API logs, Qwen 3 Coder 30B and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast provide syntax-aware responses without invoking a generalist model. If your workflow requires processing screenshots or annotated images, Kimi K2.6 and Kimi VL A3B support vision inputs natively.

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, so you can run embeddings, transcription, and chat from a single provider instead of stitching together multiple APIs.

Function Calling and CRM Integration

Real support agents do not just chat. They look up order statuses, refund policies, and account tiers. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and JSON mode on compatible models, which lets you define schemas for your internal tools and force structured output. The agent loop typically runs until the model decides no more tools are needed. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can implement ReAct-style loops or custom orchestration without platform-specific SDKs.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_order_status",
        "description": "Retrieve current order status by ID",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "order_id": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["order_id"]
        }
    }
}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Where is order #4421?"}],
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)
print(response.choices[0].message.tool_calls)

This code runs unmodified against Oxlo.ai and can be dropped into an existing codebase that already uses OpenAI, Fireworks AI, or Together AI without rewriting your abstraction layer.

Flattening Costs with Request-Based Pricing

Support tickets are inherently long-context workloads. A user might paste a 500-line stack trace, include ten previous messages, or attach a full conversation transcript. Under token-based pricing, every additional line increases cost. If your RAG pipeline returns five large documentation chunks per query, you pay for every token in every chunk. Over a month, this scales linearly with ticket volume and average message length.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For support agents that repeatedly ingest long logs, previous chat history, and large knowledge-base chunks, this model removes the penalty for context. In many long-context and agentic scenarios, request-based pricing can be 10 to 100 times cheaper than token-based alternatives. You can verify current rates on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Implementing Streaming and Tool Use

Users expect near-instant feedback while the agent is thinking or querying a database. Streaming responses let you show partial output or a typing indicator immediately. Oxlo.ai supports streaming on its chat completions endpoint, and popular models have no cold starts, so the first chunk arrives without the spin-up delay common on serverless inference platforms.

Here is a minimal streaming example that also handles forced JSON output for structured ticket tagging:

import json

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=[{
        "role": "system",
        "content": "Tag the ticket with priority and category. Return JSON."
    }, {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "My server keeps returning 502 errors after the latest deploy."
    }],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    stream=True
)

for chunk in stream:
    delta = chunk.choices[0].delta.content
    if delta:
        print(delta, end="")

This pattern works for real-time classification, intermediate reasoning steps, or progressive response rendering in your support UI.

Managing Memory Across Long Tickets

Support threads can span dozens of turns. Instead of sending the entire history to every model call, use a rolling summary of the conversation so far plus the last N raw messages. When an escalation requires the full picture, you can promote the complete thread into a single long-context request. Oxlo.ai models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash support 1M context windows, and Kimi K2.6 handles 131K contexts, so you can pass extensive histories without truncation. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, not per token, summarization and full-context passes are cost-predictable even at scale. This means your escalation logic can be driven by quality needs rather than token budgets.

Scaling from Prototype to Production

During development, the Oxlo.ai free tier offers 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, including options like DeepSeek V3.2, which is sufficient for integration testing and prompt iteration. When you move to production, the Pro and Premium plans provide daily request allotments that map directly to user volume, so your bill is predictable. For teams with dedicated throughput requirements, the Enterprise tier offers custom pricing, dedicated GPUs, and a guaranteed reduction against your current provider.

The key advantage is cost linearity. With token-based providers, a spike in long tickets or a bug that causes users to paste huge logs can double your inference bill overnight. With Oxlo.ai, the cost per interaction is fixed, making budgeting and margin control simpler for support SaaS products. This predictability is especially valuable for platforms that white-label AI to end users, because a single customer pasting a novel-length bug report will not destroy your unit economics.

Conclusion

A production customer support agent needs accurate models, reliable tool use, streaming responses, and context windows that swallow long transcripts without financial penalty. Oxlo.ai delivers all of these through a single, OpenAI-compatible API with flat per-request pricing, no cold starts on popular models, and a catalog that spans fast classifiers to deep reasoning engines. If you are evaluating inference backends for your next support agent, start with the Oxlo.ai free tier and measure the difference in both latency and cost predictability.

title: Demystifying LLM: A Beginner's Guide
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage agent that reads raw customer emails, classifies urgency, extracts the issue type, and drafts a first response. If you are new to LLMs, this is the fastest way to see how a model turns unstructured text into structured decisions without any fine-tuning. By the end, you will have a working Python script that you can plug into a helpdesk queue.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, so you pay per API call rather than by token count. That makes this tutorial cheap to follow even if you paste in long email threads or run the same ticket through multiple models. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

First we confirm the API key and SDK are working. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the only change from a standard OpenAI script is the base_url and your Oxlo.ai key. I start with llama-3.3-70b because it is a solid general-purpose model that responds instantly with no cold starts.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one word."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Design the System Prompt

The system prompt is the agent's job description. It tells the model who it is, what format to use, and what boundaries to respect. We instruct it to return strict JSON so our Python code can parse the result without regex or guesswork. Keeping the prompt explicit reduces hallucinated keys and keeps the output machine-readable.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent.
Analyze the customer message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- urgency: one of low, medium, high, critical
- issue_type: one of billing, technical, account_access, general
- draft_reply: a polite first response under 100 words
- confidence: a float between 0 and 1

Do not include markdown formatting or explanation outside the JSON."""

Step 3: Parse a Single Ticket

Now we write a small function that takes a raw email body, sends it to Oxlo.ai alongside our system prompt, and returns a Python dictionary. I use qwen-3-32b here because it follows structured instructions reliably, even when the input is messy or contains typos. After the call, we run json.loads on the content string. If the model ever returns malformed JSON, you can wrap this in a try/except block and fall back to a safe template.

import json

def triage_ticket(raw_email: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": raw_email},
        ],
    )

    content = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(content)

# Example
email = """Subject: Cannot log in
Hi, I have tried resetting my password three times and I still cannot access my account.
I have a demo in 20 minutes and I am completely locked out. Please help ASAP."""

result = triage_ticket(email)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Step 4: Handle a Long Thread

Real tickets are rarely single messages. They are long threads with quoted history, timestamps, and nested replies. Oxlo.ai offers models with large context windows, and because pricing is per request rather than per token, pasting a ten-message thread does not inflate the cost. We switch to kimi-k2.6 for its 131K context window and advanced reasoning, which helps it extract the true problem from a noisy thread.

long_thread = """Subject: Re: Re: Re: Integration failing
On Tue, support wrote: please try resetting the API key.
On Wed, customer wrote: I did, now I get a 403.
On Thu, support wrote: are you using the sandbox URL?
On Fri, customer wrote: yes, and it worked last week but broke after your update.
Current status: still blocked, launch is Monday."""

def triage_long_thread(thread: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k2.6",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": thread},
        ],
    )
    content = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(content)

result = triage_long_thread(long_thread)
print(result["issue_type"], result["urgency"])

Step 5: Verify with a Reasoning Model

When the first model returns critical urgency, I like to ask a reasoning model to double-check before waking up an on-call engineer. False positives burn team morale, so a second opinion is cheap insurance. We call deepseek-v3.2 to verify the classification. If both models agree on escalate, we route the ticket to a human.

def verify_urgency(raw_email: str, first_pass: dict) -> bool:
    verify_prompt = """You are a senior support manager.
Review the customer message and the junior agent's classification.
Reply ONLY with the word escalate or calm."""

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v3.2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": verify_prompt},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Customer message:\n{raw_email}\n\nJunior classification:\n{json.dumps(first_pass)}"},
        ],
    )

    return "escalate" in response.choices[0].message.content.lower()

# Usage
parsed = triage_ticket(email)
if parsed["urgency"] == "critical" and verify_urgency(email, parsed):
    print("ESCALATED to on-call engineer")
else:
    print("AUTO-REPLY:", parsed["draft_reply"])

Run it

Save the finished script as triage.py, export your key, and run it from your terminal. The script processes the locked-out customer from Step 3, runs the verification gate, and prints the final decision. Here is what the output looks like.

$ export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
$ python triage.py

ESCALATED to on-call engineer

Because Oxlo.ai pricing is per request, running this script twenty times costs the same whether the emails are two sentences or two pages. That predictability matters when you are experimenting with long-context prompts or chaining multiple model calls.

Next steps

Replace the hardcoded email strings with a webhook that reads from your helpdesk inbox, or add a second Oxlo.ai call that uses llama-3.3-70b to rewrite the draft_reply in your company's brand voice. You could also store the structured JSON in a database to build analytics dashboards. If you want to host this without a large upfront commit, the Oxlo.ai free tier gives you 60 requests per day to start, and you can scale up once your daily volume stabilizes.

title: Evaluating the Best API for Long Context Inference
content:
Long context inference has moved from research novelty to production requirement. Agents that iterate over extensive codebases, legal tools that analyze discovery documents, and multimodal pipelines that consume hours of video all depend on APIs that can ingest and reason across 100,000 tokens or more. Yet the infrastructure layer underneath these workloads is still priced and optimized for short chat-style interactions. Choosing the wrong provider for long-context pipelines can inflate costs by orders of magnitude and introduce unpredictable latency that breaks agentic workflows.

The Cost Trap of Token-Based Pricing

Most inference providers, including Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, bill by the token. Input tokens, output tokens, and sometimes cache-write tokens are metered separately. This is transparent for short prompts, but it penalizes the exact workloads that require large context windows. A single agent loop that passes a 50,000 token codebase back to the model can rack up input charges before a single completion token is generated.

Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. As a developer-first AI inference platform, Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives because cost does not scale with input length. Instead of estimating token budgets before every call, teams can ship agents that naturally ingest full documents, conversation histories, or repository context without rewriting prompts to stay under a pricing threshold.

What to Evaluate in a Long Context API

When benchmarking providers, engineers typically look at context window size, but that is only the entry point. The real evaluation criteria include how the provider handles KV-cache memory pressure, whether pricing is deterministic under load, and if the API surface supports the control primitives you need for agentic systems.

Long-context performance is not linear. Attention complexity places heavy demands on high-bandwidth memory, and even optimized kernels can struggle with sustained throughput. A provider that advertises a 128K window but runs on undersized GPU clusters will deliver glacial prefill speeds and truncated outputs under load. You should test not just whether the model accepts the tokens, but whether it retrieves information accurately from the middle and end of the context.

Look for these concrete capabilities:

  • Context window ceiling that exceeds your 99th percentile payload
  • Streaming responses so users see progress on long generations
  • Function calling and JSON mode for structured agent outputs
  • No cold starts on popular models, so the first request after idle time does not timeout
  • OpenAI SDK compatibility so you can switch providers without rewriting client code

Oxlo.ai meets these requirements across its stack. It offers fully OpenAI SDK compatible endpoints, streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversations. There are no cold starts on popular models, which means a 131,000 token prompt does not sit in a warmup queue.

Model Availability and Context Windows

A long context API is only useful if it hosts models that can actually utilize the window. Many providers advertise large context limits but stock only small chat models or quantized variants that degrade on long-range reasoning.

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ open-source and proprietary models across 7 categories. For long-context reasoning, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers an efficient MoE architecture with a 1 million token context window and near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning. Kimi K2.6 supports 131K context with advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision. Qwen 3 32B brings multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, while Llama 3.3 70B serves as a general-purpose flagship for reliable long-document comprehension.

For coding-specific agents, Qwen 3 Coder 30B and DeepSeek Coder are available. For vision workloads that combine images with long text, Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B are supported. This breadth matters because long context is rarely used in isolation. An agent might transcribe a two-hour podcast with Whisper Large v3, embed the result with BGE-Large, and feed the full transcript into Kimi K2.6 for analysis. Oxlo.ai runs all of these categories, LLMs, code, vision, audio, embeddings, and object detection, behind one base URL.

SDK Compatibility and Integration

Switching inference providers should not require a rewrite of your application layer. The OpenAI SDK has become the de facto standard for Python, Node.js, and cURL clients, and any serious alternative must be a drop-in replacement.

Oxlo.ai exposes the standard endpoints: chat/completions, embeddings, images/generations, audio/transcriptions, and audio/speech. The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. Because the platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, migration is a single line change.

For example, a Python client targeting a long-context model with tool use looks like this:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a code review agent."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "<full 100k token repository context>"}
    ],
    tools=[{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "submit_review"}}],
    stream=True
)

The same pattern works for DeepSeek V4 Flash, Llama 3.3 70B, or any other model on the platform. This compatibility removes integration risk when evaluating Oxlo.ai against token-based competitors.

Latency, Cold Starts, and Throughput

Long prompts amplify any latency in the serving path. Prefill time, the phase where the model processes the input context, grows with sequence length. A cold start on a 70B parameter model loading into GPU memory can take tens of seconds, which is unacceptable for synchronous agent steps. Similarly, if the provider does not stream responses, users wait blindly while the model processes a massive attention matrix across thousands of tokens.

Throughput also matters for agentic systems. An agent that reasons over a codebase might issue three to five sequential long-context calls to plan, edit, and verify changes. If each call carries a 30-second cold-start penalty, the interaction becomes unusable. Oxlo.ai delivers streaming responses and eliminates cold starts on popular models. For agentic workloads that chain multiple long-context calls, this predictability is critical. You do not need to build retry loops or keep-alive pings to compensate for initialization delays. The platform also supports multi-turn conversations efficiently, so iterative refinement over a large context does not duplicate preprocessing costs on every round.

Pricing Models and Workload Fit

Not every workload benefits from request-based pricing. A simple classifier that sends 50 tokens and receives 10 tokens might be cheaper on a token-based plan. But long-context inference, by definition, inverts that ratio. When your median input is 20,000 tokens and your output is 500 tokens, token-based billing turns the API into a variable cost that scales with document size.

Oxlo.ai offers several pricing tiers. The Free plan provides 60 requests per day and access to 16+ free models. The Pro plan at $80 per month includes 1,000 requests per day across all models. The Premium plan at $350 per month raises the limit to 5,000 requests per day and adds priority queue access. For teams at scale, the Enterprise tier offers custom unlimited usage, dedicated GPUs, and guaranteed 30% savings compared to your current provider. Because the unit of cost is the request, you can model your infrastructure spend as a fixed operational expense rather than a stochastic function of user behavior.

Conclusion

Evaluating a long context API requires looking past the headline context-window length and examining the economics of the serving layer. Token-based pricing creates a misalignment between provider revenue and user value when inputs grow large. Request-based pricing flips the incentive, making it viable to ship agents and analysis tools that consume entire documents

title: Unlocking LLM Potential for Speech Recognition
content:
Speech recognition has spent decades in the wilderness of hidden Markov models and Gaussian mixture densities. These classical systems worked well enough for short, clean utterances, but they collapse under the weight of real-world audio: overlapping speakers, domain-specific jargon, disfluencies, and hours-long meetings. The recent wave of large language model research from NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Stanford suggests a different path. Instead of treating speech as a standalone acoustic problem, researchers are folding audio directly into LLMs or using LLMs to post-process and correct transcription outputs. The result is recognition that reasons about context, not just sound. For developers building these pipelines, the infrastructure layer matters as much as the model weights. Oxlo.ai provides the audio and language endpoints, plus a pricing model that does not penalize long-form content.

The Limits of Classical ASR

Traditional automatic speech recognition decomposes the problem into an acoustic model, a pronunciation lexicon, and a language model. This pipeline is modular, but fragility accumulates at every handoff. Out-of-vocabulary words, code switching, and spontaneous corrections all degrade accuracy because the language model is too small to carry conversational context. Modern enterprise use cases, medical transcription, legal discovery, and automated meeting notes, require systems that understand what was said, not merely how it sounded. That is where LLMs enter the picture.

How LLMs Reason About Speech

Recent work has demonstrated that LLMs can improve speech recognition in two distinct ways. First, as rescoring engines: a base acoustic model generates n-best hypotheses or lattices, and an LLM selects or rewrites the most contextually coherent transcript. Second, as end-to-end multimodal models: audio encoders project spectrograms or mel-filterbank features into the token embedding space of a foundation model, allowing the LLM to consume speech natively alongside text. Both approaches leverage the core strength of large language models, their ability to resolve ambiguity through context. A word that sounds like "four" versus "for" is disambiguated not by a phoneme dictionary, but by the surrounding paragraph of conversation.

Stanford and Microsoft research groups have shown that even modestly sized LLMs can drastically reduce word error rates when given access to prior conversational turns or domain-specific prompts. NVIDIA has advanced parallel work on efficient audio encoder integration with transformer stacks. The implication is clear: the boundary between speech recognition and natural language understanding is dissolving.

Architectures: From Whisper to Audio LLMs

OpenAI Whisper established the viability of large-scale weak supervision for speech, training encoder-decoder transformers on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio. Whisper remains the practical workhorse for most developers, and it is available through Oxlo.ai as Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, and Whisper Medium via the standard audio/transcriptions endpoint. However, the next generation of research moves beyond encoder-decoder architectures toward decoder-only LLMs augmented with audio adapters.

In these systems, a lightweight adapter module, sometimes just a few transformer layers or a perceiver resampler, bridges a frozen audio frontend to a frozen LLM backbone. The LLM itself sees audio as a sequence of soft prompts. During inference, the model attends across text and audio tokens simultaneously, enabling tasks like timestamped transcription, speaker diarization, and semantic analysis in a single forward pass. The compute cost is higher than Whisper per second of audio, but the accuracy gains on long-context, multi-speaker content can be substantial.

For developers, this means pipelines are becoming simpler but more compute-intensive. A single request may contain tens of thousands of audio-derived tokens plus a lengthy text prompt. Token-based pricing turns this into a budget risk. Oxlo.ai avoids that problem with flat per-request pricing, so a 90-minute earnings call costs the same API fee as a 30-second voice command. You can review the exact structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Building a Hybrid Pipeline

Until fully unified audio LLMs are production-ready, the pragmatic approach is a hybrid pipeline: transcribe with Whisper, then reason with an LLM. Oxlo.ai supports this natively because both model classes share the same OpenAI-compatible SDK and base URL. You do not need to juggle separate providers for audio and text.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

# Step 1: Transcribe long-form audio
audio_file = open("earnings_call.wav", "rb")
transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(
    model="whisper-large-v3",
    file=audio_file,
    response_format="verbose_json",
    timestamp_granularities=["segment"]
)

# Step 2: Extract structured insight with an LLM
completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-r1-671b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are a financial analyst. Read the transcript and extract every forward-looking guidance statement."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": transcript.text
        }
    ],
    temperature=0.1
)

print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

This pattern works because Oxlo.ai offers both endpoints under one roof, with no cold starts on popular models. The transcription step returns rich segment metadata, and the reasoning step can use DeepSeek R1 671B for complex extraction or Llama 3.3 70B for fast, general-purpose analysis. Because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, running a 131K context transcript through Kimi K2.6 for agentic coding analysis costs a predictable flat fee. That predictability is critical when you are batch-processing hundreds of hours of audio.

When Inference Costs Shape Product Decisions

Speech is inherently long context. A one-hour stereo recording at 16 kHz contains over 57 million samples. Even after compression into embeddings or tokens, the resulting sequences are enormous compared to typical chat prompts. Under token-based pricing, long-form audio workloads trigger unpredictable bills that scale with every disfluency, pause, and repeated phrase. This actively discourages developers from building ambitious voice products.

Oxlo.ai inverts that incentive. With request-based pricing, the cost of processing a file is known before you send it. Whether your prompt is 100 tokens or 100,000 tokens, the API call costs the same flat amount. For transcription rescoring, multi-turn meeting summarization, or agentic voice workflows that pass audio context through many tool calls, this model can be radically cheaper than token-based alternatives. The difference is most pronounced on exactly the kind of long-context, agentic speech workloads that LLM research is now enabling.

Looking Ahead

The research frontier is moving quickly. We are seeing early demonstrations of LLMs that handle real-time streaming audio, that perform speaker-specific tool use, and that correct transcription errors by referencing external knowledge bases. As these capabilities mature, they will stop being research demos and become standard infrastructure requirements. Developers will need platforms that offer audio encoders, speech synthesis, and reasoning models through a single, low-latency API.

Oxlo.ai already provides Whisper variants for transcription and Kokoro 82M for text-to-speech, alongside 45+ LLMs and vision models. The unified stack, combined with flat per-request pricing and full OpenAI SDK compatibility, means you can prototype today on Whisper and Llama 3.3 70B, then migrate to DeepSeek V4 Flash or GLM 5 for long-horizon agentic tasks tomorrow without rewriting client code or renegotiating billing logic.

Speech recognition is no longer just about acoustic modeling. It is about reasoning, context, and integration. Oxlo.ai gives you the models and the pricing structure to build that next layer.

title: Unlocking the Potential of LLMs in Computer Vision
content:
We are going to build a visual inventory agent that looks at a photograph of a retail shelf and returns a structured JSON report listing every product it sees, its estimated stock level, and any visible damage. This is for operations teams who currently do manual shelf audits and want to automate the first pass without training a custom computer vision model. Instead of maintaining a separate object detector, OCR service, and rules engine, we will send the image directly to a vision-capable large language model on Oxlo.ai and receive structured data in a single request.

What you'll need

Before writing code, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You also need the OpenAI Python SDK, which Oxlo.ai supports as a drop-in replacement. Install it now.

pip install openai

Next, create an account at https://portal.oxlo.ai and generate an API key. We will pass that key into the client below. For the image source, you can use any publicly accessible URL. If you want to test with local files later, you can base64-encode them and use the same message format.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

Oxlo.ai exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, so the only change from a standard OpenAI script is the base URL. I create the client once and reuse it for every request. There are no cold starts on popular models, so the first call is just as fast as the tenth. The same pattern works in Node.js or cURL if you prefer, but I will use Python here.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Define the system prompt

I keep the system prompt in its own variable so I can version it separately from the request logic. The prompt is intentionally rigid. It tells the model exactly what to look for, how to name the JSON keys, and what to do when it is uncertain. This reduces hallucinated products and keeps the output schema stable across different lighting angles and shelf layouts.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a visual inventory analyst. When given an image of a retail shelf or warehouse rack, do the following:
1. Identify every distinct product visible.
2. Estimate the quantity of each product.
3. Note any visible damage, spills, or disorganization.
4. Return your findings as a JSON object with keys: products, issues, summary.
Be concise and factual. If you cannot identify a product, label it unknown."""

Step 3: Prepare the image payload

The chat completions endpoint accepts a list of content blocks for multimodal input. One block carries the text instruction, and the other carries the image URL. Oxlo.ai follows the same message schema as the OpenAI vision spec, so you do not need to learn a new payload format. I am using a public Unsplash URL here, but in production this would point at your CDN or presigned S3 URL. You can also swap the URL for a base64 data URI if your images are not publicly hosted.

IMAGE_URL = "https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1580913428735-bd3c269d6a82?q=80&w=1000&auto=format&fit=crop"

user_message = [
    {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "Analyze this shelf and return the inventory report."
    },
    {
        "type": "image_url",
        "image_url": {"url": IMAGE_URL}
    }
]

Step 4: Run the vision agent

For the model, I use kimi-k2.6 because it handles vision, reasoning, and long context windows in a single pass. I also enable JSON mode by setting response_format. This tells the model to constrain its output to valid JSON, which removes the need for fragile post-processing regex. Streaming is available if you want progressive text, but for a structured report I prefer to wait for the complete object. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, I do not have to worry about the token cost of a detailed system prompt or a high-resolution image. The price is the same whether the model thinks for fifty tokens or five hundred.

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)

raw_json = response.choices[0].message.content
print(raw_json)

Step 5: Parse the structured report

Once I have the raw JSON string, I parse it with the standard library and walk the structure. I wrap the parse in a try block so a malformed response does not crash the script. In a real deployment, this is where you would push the records to Postgres, trigger a Slack alert, or update an inventory dashboard. I keep the print statements minimal so the logic is easy to transplant into a FastAPI route or a Celery task.

import json

try:
    report = json.loads(raw_json)
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("Failed to parse model output.")
    report = {}

print("Products detected:", len(report.get("products", [])))
for item in report.get("products", []):
    name = item.get("name", "unknown")
    qty = item.get("quantity", "unknown")
    print(f"  - {name}: {qty}")

if report.get("issues"):
    print("Issues flagged:")
    for issue in report["issues"]:
        print(f"  - {issue}")
else:
    print("No issues flagged.")

print("Summary:", report.get("summary", "N/A"))

Run it

Save the complete script below as vision_agent.py, replace the placeholder with your key, and run it. On my machine the end-to-end call completed in under three seconds.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a visual inventory analyst. When given an image of a retail shelf or warehouse rack, do the following:
1. Identify every distinct product visible.
2. Estimate the quantity of each product.
3. Note any visible damage, spills, or disorganization.
4. Return your findings as a JSON object with keys: products, issues, summary.
Be concise and factual. If you cannot identify a product, label it unknown."""

IMAGE_URL = "https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1580913428735-bd3c269d6a82?q=80&w=1000&auto=format&fit=crop"

user_message = [
    {
        "type": "text",
        "text": "Analyze this shelf and return the inventory report."
    },
    {
        "type": "image_url",
        "image_url": {"url": IMAGE_URL}
    }
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)

try:
    report = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
except json.JSONDecodeError:
    print("Failed to parse model output.")
    report = {}

print("Products detected:", len(report.get("products", [])))
for item in report.get("products", []):
    name = item.get("name", "unknown")
    qty = item.get("quantity", "unknown")
    print(f"  - {name}: {qty}")

if report.get("issues"):
    print("Issues flagged:")
    for issue in report["issues"]:
        print(f"  - {issue}")
else:
    print("No issues flagged.")

print("Summary:", report.get("summary", "N/A"))

When I pointed this at a sample warehouse photo, the model returned the following. Your output will depend on the exact image you feed it.

Products detected: 4
  - Blue plastic storage bin: 12
  - Cardboard box (medium): 8
  - Cleaning spray bottle: 3
  - Unknown yellow container: 1
Issues flagged:
  - One cardboard box shows water damage on lower left corner.
Summary: Stock levels appear adequate for standard SKUs. Flag damaged box for QA review.

Next steps

The obvious extension is batch processing. Drop a hundred images into a folder, loop over them with concurrent.futures, and collect reports. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, a 4K image from an industrial camera costs the same as a compressed thumbnail. You do not get penalized for high resolution the way token-based vision APIs do. Check the exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Another useful upgrade is a two-stage pipeline. Let kimi-k2.6 handle the vision parsing, then pass the raw JSON summary to qwen-3-32b or llama-3.3-70b for root-cause analysis or natural language narrations for non-technical stakeholders. Since every model on Oxlo.ai shares the same base URL and SDK, swapping models is a one-line change.

title: Transfer Learning with LLMs: Best Practices and Applications
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage classifier that adapts a general LLM to your internal taxonomy through in-context transfer learning. Instead of fine-tuning weights for weeks, we teach the model with curated examples embedded directly in the prompt. It is useful for any engineering team that needs accurate routing today without building a training pipeline.

What you'll need

Grab Python 3.10 or newer. You will also need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, so loading long prompts with dozens of examples does not inflate your cost the way token-based metering does. That makes few-shot transfer learning practical from day one. Finally, install the OpenAI SDK.

pip install openai

Step 1: Build your example bank

Transfer learning at the inference layer lives or dies by the quality of your labeled data. We create a JSONL file where each line is a support ticket paired with its category and priority. These examples act as our training set, except we never backpropagate. We simply present them to the model at query time. I have found that a small set of clean, diverse examples outperforms a large noisy corpus, so curate carefully. Save the following as tickets.jsonl.

import json

examples = [
    {"text": "I was charged twice for my Pro subscription this month.", "category": "Billing", "priority": "High"},
    {"text": "The API returns a 504 timeout every time I batch more than 500 requests.", "category": "Performance", "priority": "Critical"},
    {"text": "How do I rotate my API key?", "category": "Account Access", "priority": "Medium"},
    {"text": "Your Python SDK example for streaming is outdated.", "category": "API Integration", "priority": "Low"},
    {"text": "My team cannot access the dashboard after the SSO update.", "category": "Account Access", "priority": "High"},
    {"text": "Latency spikes to 2 seconds on the embeddings endpoint after 9 AM UTC.", "category": "Performance", "priority": "Critical"},
    {"text": "Do you offer annual billing with a discount?", "category": "Billing", "priority": "Low"},
    {"text": "The webhook payload schema changed without notice.", "category": "API Integration", "priority": "Medium"}
]

with open("tickets.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for ex in examples:
        f.write(json.dumps(ex) + "\n")

Step 2: Create the transfer prompt

The system prompt is where the general model becomes a domain-specific classifier. We declare the allowed categories and priorities, enforce JSON output, and reserve a slot for dynamic examples. Keeping the instructions terse and the schema explicit reduces hallucination. I use a Python template string so we can swap the example block on every call.

SYSTEM_TEMPLATE = """You are a support triage agent.
Your job is to classify incoming tickets and assign priority.

Rules:
- Category must be one of: Billing, Performance, Account Access, API Integration.
- Priority must be one of: Low, Medium, High, Critical.
- Respond ONLY with a JSON object containing keys "category" and "priority".

Here are examples of correctly classified tickets:

{examples}
"""

Step 3: Wire the Oxlo.ai client

We initialize the OpenAI-compatible client against Oxlo.ai. I chose llama-3.3-70b for this build because it handles long context windows and instruction following reliably. Oxlo.ai carries several strong alternatives, including qwen-3-32b and deepseek-v3.2, but Llama 3.3 70B is a safe default for classification tasks that demand strict JSON obedience. With Oxlo.ai you pay one flat rate per request, so the prompt length does not affect cost. That means we can pass a full page of examples without worrying about input token charges. The helper below formats the prompt and requests a structured JSON response.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def classify_ticket(ticket_text, examples):
    formatted = "\n\n".join(
        f"Ticket: {ex['text']}\nCategory: {ex['category']}\nPriority: {ex['priority']}"
        for ex in examples
    )
    system_prompt = SYSTEM_TEMPLATE.format(examples=formatted)
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Classify this ticket: {ticket_text}"},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 4: Add example selection

Injecting the entire example bank into every request bloats the prompt and dilutes attention. We need a selector that surfaces only the most relevant tickets. A lightweight keyword overlap scorer works well enough for a prototype and avoids adding vector database dependencies. It tokenizes the incoming ticket and the candidate examples, then ranks by intersection size. The top three matches get baked into the system prompt. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, you could experiment with larger candidate pools on every call without watching token costs climb. If you later move to semantic search, you will appreciate that Oxlo.ai offers embedding models like BGE-Large under the same request-based plan.

def select_examples(ticket_text, bank, k=3):
    words = set(ticket_text.lower().split())
    scored = []
    for ex in bank:
        ex_words = set(ex["text"].lower().split())
        overlap = len(words & ex_words)
        scored.append((overlap, ex))
    scored.sort(reverse=True, key=lambda x: x[0])
    return [ex for _, ex in scored[:k]]

def classify(ticket_text):
    bank = []
    with open("tickets.jsonl") as f:
        for line in f:
            bank.append(json.loads(line))
    relevant = select_examples(ticket_text, bank, k=3)
    return classify_ticket(ticket_text, relevant)

Run it

Now we exercise the full pipeline. We load the bank, score the candidates for an unseen ticket, and fire the request to Oxlo.ai. The model returns a structured classification that you can feed directly into a CRM or alerting system. If the model misclassifies, your first debugging step should be the example bank, not the LLM. Add a ticket that closely resembles the failure and rerun. This is the same iterative loop as traditional fine-tuning, except each iteration costs exactly one request. Below is the end-to-end script and the output I received on a sample billing ticket.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    new_ticket = "My invoice shows the wrong billing address and I need a refund."
    result = classify(new_ticket)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

# Example output:
# {
#   "category": "Billing",
#   "priority": "High"
# }

Next steps

Replace the keyword matcher with Oxlo.ai's embeddings endpoint. Embed your example bank once, then retrieve semantically similar tickets at runtime for far better recall than keyword overlap. You can also wrap the classifier in a FastAPI service. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, your endpoint will stay responsive even under load. For teams currently on token-based providers, the cost predictability here is worth noting. A long prompt with twenty examples and a detailed system message costs the same as a one-line greeting. That structure removes the penalty for rich context, which is exactly what transfer learning through prompting needs.

title: LLM Model Comparison: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Selecting the right large language model for a production workload is no longer a simple choice between a single closed-source flagship and an open-source alternative. The current landscape includes dozens of generalist chat models, mixture-of-experts reasoning engines, vision-language variants, and specialized coding agents, each with distinct context limits, latency profiles, and pricing mechanics. For engineering teams, the decision is less about finding the single "best" model and more about matching architectural requirements to the correct capability tier while keeping infrastructure costs predictable. A rigorous comparison framework evaluates models across reasoning depth, context window, multimodal support, and cost structure rather than relying on surface-level benchmark marketing.

Evaluation Criteria for Production LLMs

Before comparing specific weights and architectures, define the dimensions that actually affect your pipeline. Capability tier separates models optimized for casual chat from those tuned for extended chain-of-thought reasoning or tool use. Context length determines whether you can ingest entire codebases, research papers, or multi-turn agent histories in a single request. Latency and availability matter for user-facing applications, while API compatibility dictates how quickly you can swap models without rewriting client logic. Finally, cost architecture is often the decisive factor: token-based billing scales linearly with input and output length, which can make long-context retrieval and agentic loops prohibitively expensive. Oxlo.ai addresses this directly with request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length, alongside 45-plus models across seven categories, full OpenAI SDK compatibility, and no cold starts on popular weights.</

title: Unlocking Language Understanding with LLMs
content:
We are going to build a structured language understanding pipeline that turns raw, unstructured customer feedback into predictable JSON. If you run support, product, or analytics, this gives you entity extraction, sentiment scoring, and intent classification without training or hosting your own model. The entire thing runs against Oxlo.ai, so you get flat per-request pricing and zero cold starts on popular models.

What you'll need

Before you start, make sure you have the following ready.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • The official openai Python SDK. Install it with pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with 60 requests per day, which is plenty for testing.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, so the cost per feedback ticket stays flat even when the input is long. That matters when you start feeding entire chat transcripts or long email threads into the model. You can view the latest plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I start by creating the client. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only difference from other providers is the base URL and API key. This means you can use the official Python SDK without learning a new interface or rewriting existing code. I pick Llama 3.3 70B as the default workhorse because it follows structured instructions consistently and handles mixed content well. Keep your API key in an environment variable in production, but for this tutorial I leave it as a placeholder so the code is readable. If you already have OpenAI client code, migration is a single line change.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

# Quick connectivity check
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract. It tells the model exactly what to extract and how to format the JSON. I keep the schema flat so it maps directly to a SQL table or a Pydantic model downstream. I also explicitly forbid markdown wrappers because they break naive JSON parsers. Spending time here pays off. A tight prompt reduces hallucinated keys and keeps latency low. The rules section is short but critical. It forces the model to infer intent from the underlying goal rather than surface keywords, which is the difference between a naive keyword matcher and a real language understanding layer.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a language understanding engine. Analyze the user message and return a single JSON object with these keys:

- language: ISO 639-1 code of the input language
- sentiment: one of positive, neutral, negative
- intent: one of refund_request, feature_question, bug_report, complaint, praise, other
- entities: array of objects with keys "text" and "label" (label is one of product, person, location, date, price)
- summary: one sentence summarizing the core issue
- urgency: low, medium, or high

Rules:
1. Output ONLY valid JSON. No markdown, no explanation.
2. If no entities are present, return an empty array.
3. Infer intent from the underlying goal, not just keywords."""

Step 3: Build the analyzer with JSON mode

Now I wrap the call in a reusable function. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, so setting response_format={"type": "json_object"} forces valid JSON and removes fragile regex cleanup. I set temperature to 0.1 because we want deterministic extraction, not creative writing. The function returns a native Python dictionary, which means you can immediately feed it into Pandas, a database, or a CI check. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it is reliable for agent-like tasks that must follow output schemas exactly. If you prefer, you can swap this to DeepSeek V3.2 for stronger coding-oriented reasoning without changing any other logic.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def analyze_feedback(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process multilingual batches

Feedback arrives in many languages, and translating everything to English first adds latency and cost. I swap the model to Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai for a batch of mixed-language tickets. Qwen handles dozens of languages natively and is particularly strong at agent workflows and multilingual reasoning. Because the Oxlo.ai API is fully OpenAI-compatible, switching models is a single string change. No new client, no new authentication logic, and no vendor-specific payload formats. On token-based providers, a long German or Chinese ticket could cost significantly more than a short English one. On Oxlo.ai, every request in this batch costs the same flat amount.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

def analyze_multilingual(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

tickets = [
    "I was charged twice for my subscription last month and I need my money back immediately.",
    "¿Cómo puedo exportar los informes a Excel? No encuentro el botón.",
    "Die App stürzt jedes Mal ab, wenn ich ein Foto hochlade. Seit Version 4.2.",
]

results = [analyze_multilingual(t) for t in tickets]

Step 5: Validate and fallback

Production pipelines need guardrails. I add a small validator that checks for required keys. If any are missing, or if JSON parsing fails, I retry once with the heavier Kimi K2.6 model, which excels at advanced reasoning and agentic coding on Oxlo.ai. This fallback pattern is cheap on Oxlo.ai because you pay per request, not per token. A retry on a long ticket costs the same as a retry on a short one. That predictability makes it easy to budget for failure modes without surprise overages. I also like that Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so this retry fires instantly instead of waiting for a container to warm up.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

REQUIRED_KEYS = {"language", "sentiment", "intent", "entities", "summary", "urgency"}

def safe_analyze(text: str) -> dict:
    try:
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": text},
            ],
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
            temperature=0.1,
        )
        data = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

title: LLM Applications in Customer Support
content:
Customer support generates massive volumes of unstructured text, from chat transcripts and email threads to error logs and internal wiki pages. Large language models can parse, reason, and act on this data far faster than rule-based systems, but production deployments face a familiar constraint: cost scales with context length. When every customer conversation includes prior ticket history, product documentation, and tool outputs, token-based billing inflates operational expenses. Oxlo.ai addresses this directly with request-based pricing, one flat cost per API call regardless of input size, making it a practical backbone for support teams running long-context and agentic workloads.

Automating Ticket Triage and Routing

Most support queues still rely on keyword matching or manual sorting. An LLM can replace this with semantic understanding, classifying intent, extracting structured entities such as order IDs or severity levels, and routing tickets to the correct team. For this to integrate cleanly into existing CRMs and helpdesk software, the model must output valid JSON. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode across its chat models, allowing you to constrain outputs to structured schemas for routing decisions. Function calling extends this further by letting the model query external APIs, for example, to look up a customer’s plan tier or recent order status before deciding whether to escalate.

Intelligent Conversational Agents

Modern support bots need to do more than answer FAQs. They must maintain multi-turn conversational state, reference long conversation histories, and invoke tools to perform actions such as issuing refunds or scheduling callbacks. Oxlo.ai provides streaming responses, function calling, and multi-turn conversation support through a fully OpenAI-compatible API. You can drop the Oxlo.ai base URL into your existing Python or Node.js client and point it at models like Llama 3.3 70B for general dialogue, or DeepSeek R1 671B MoE when the user presents a complex reasoning or coding problem. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, adding extra tool context or system prompts to improve accuracy does not increase your unit cost.

Real-Time Agent Assist and Response Generation

Human agents often spend minutes searching knowledge bases while a customer waits. An LLM running alongside the agent can ingest the full ticket thread, internal documentation, and past resolutions to suggest replies in real time. This requires large context windows. Models available on Oxlo.ai such as Kimi K2.6 with 131K context, and DeepSeek V4 Flash with 1M context, can hold entire conversation histories and product manuals in a single prompt. On token-based platforms, passing this volume of text on every inference would multiply costs. With Oxlo.ai, the price remains a flat per-request rate, so you can afford to give the model complete context rather than truncating history to save tokens.

Sentiment Analysis and Escalation Detection

LLMs can classify emotional tone and urgency in real time, flagging conversations for supervisor intervention before churn occurs. This works best when the model evaluates the full thread rather than isolated messages. Small classifiers often miss sarcasm or shifting sentiment across multiple turns, whereas a general-purpose LLM captures nuance. You can run lightweight models for this task or use the same endpoint that powers your chatbot, keeping architecture simple. Oxlo.ai offers models ranging from efficient MoE variants to large reasoning engines, so you can match throughput and latency requirements without maintaining separate infrastructure.

Multilingual Support at Scale

Global support teams face translation delays and inconsistent quality. Multilingual models like Qwen 3 32B handle reasoning and agent workflows across dozens of languages without requiring separate translation layers. This reduces pipeline complexity and preserves intent, because the model reasons in the source language rather than translating back and forth. For teams serving diverse markets, deploying a single multilingual endpoint on Oxlo.ai simplifies operations and ensures that context, such as prior ticket history, stays attached to the conversation regardless of language.

Why Request-Based Pricing Matters for Support Workloads

Support is inherently long-context. A single API call might include a system prompt, retrieval-augmented generation context from a knowledge base, the last ten messages of a chat, and a structured tool result. Under token-based billing, every token in that payload adds to the bill. Competitors such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale scale costs with input length, which means complex agentic loops or detailed ticket histories become expensive to maintain.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For support teams, this means you can pass full conversation histories, large knowledge-base chunks, and detailed tool outputs without watching costs rise linearly. Oxlo.ai notes that this model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context workloads. The predictability also simplifies budgeting. Instead of estimating token counts per ticket type, finance teams can forecast based on request volume, which maps directly to customer contact rates. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details.

Implementing Customer Support LLMs with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. You can use the Python client, Node.js client, or cURL without rewriting your integration. The platform offers 45+ open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, including chat, code, vision, and embeddings, with no cold starts on popular models.

Below is a minimal example using the OpenAI Python SDK to generate a structured routing decision for an incoming support ticket. The same client configuration powers chat completions, function calling, and streaming.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": (
                "You are a support triage assistant. "
                "Read the ticket and return JSON with keys: "
                "department, priority, and summary."
            )
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Subject: CSV upload fails with 502 error. "
                "Body: Customer on Enterprise Plan v2.1 reports that "
                "CSV uploads over 50 MB trigger a 502 Bad Gateway. "
                "They need this resolved by end of day."
            )
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

result = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(result)

For tickets that include screenshots of error messages, you can switch to a vision-capable model such as Kimi VL A3B or Gemma 3 27B by changing the model identifier and including image URLs in the messages payload. If the ticket requires deep reasoning, for example, diagnosing a complex API integration from log files, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 provide advanced chain-of-thought reasoning. Because Oxlo.ai does not charge by token, you can include verbose logs or lengthy documentation in the prompt without cost surprises.

Choosing the Right Model for Each Support Task

Different support workflows demand different capabilities. Oxlo.ai organizes its catalog into seven categories so you can select the right tool without vendor lock-in.

  • General chat and triage: Llama 3.3 70B offers a strong balance of instruction following and latency for conversational agents.
  • Complex reasoning and coding: DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and Kimi K2 Thinking excel at chain-of-thought reasoning for technical tickets involving code or system architecture.
  • Long-context review: DeepSeek V4 Flash supports 1M context for analyzing extensive logs or multi-year customer histories, while Kimi K2.6 provides 131K context with advanced reasoning and vision.
  • Multilingual: Qwen 3 32B handles multilingual agent workflows without separate translation pipelines.
  • Vision: Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B process screenshots and diagrams attached to tickets.
  • Embeddings: BGE-Large and E5-Large power retrieval-augmented generation pipelines that feed context into your chat completions.

Conclusion

LLMs are becoming standard infrastructure for customer support, but deployment economics often limit their effectiveness. Token-based billing discourages teams from providing the full context that makes models accurate. Oxlo.ai removes that friction with flat per-request pricing, an OpenAI-compatible API, and a broad catalog of models suited for everything from quick chat replies to million-token log analysis. For engineering teams building the next generation of support tools, Oxlo.ai offers a developer-first platform where long-context and agentic workloads are first-class citizens, not cost prohibitions.

title: Evaluating LLMs for Language Translation
content:
Machine translation has moved well beyond statistical phrase tables and rigid rule-based systems. Modern large language models now handle low-resource languages, code-switching, and domain-specific terminology through in-context learning, making them viable replacements for legacy translation pipelines. However, moving from prototype to production requires more than prompting a chat model. You need reproducible evaluation criteria, the right inference backend, and cost controls that do not collapse once you move from single sentences to full documents. This post breaks down how to evaluate LLMs for translation workloads and why your choice of inference provider shapes what is economically feasible.

Why Translation Strains Inference Infrastructure

Translation is not a single-turn chat task. Production pipelines often ingest entire documents, preserve formatting, and carry megabytes of context across multiple passages. A single legal contract or technical manual can easily exceed 50,000 tokens when you include system prompts, style guides, and few-shot examples. Under token-based billing, every additional paragraph increases cost linearly. If you are running agentic workflows that chunk, translate, and reconcile sections iteratively, those costs compound quickly.

Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. As a developer-first inference platform, Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale, your bill does not scale with input length. For long-context document translation and agentic workloads, this can make Oxlo.ai significantly cheaper. You can pass full pages of source text, glossary constraints, and prior paragraphs for coherence without watching the meter run on every token.

Quality Metrics Beyond BLEU

Before you optimize infrastructure, you need a rigorous evaluation framework. The most common automated metric is BLEU, which measures n-gram overlap between model output and a reference translation. It is fast and widely reported, but it penalizes valid paraphrasing and rewards lexical memorization. For a more nuanced view, COMET uses neural embeddings to score semantic similarity, while chrF++ weights character n-grams more heavily, making it more robust for morphologically rich languages.

Automated scores are necessary for rapid iteration, yet they do not replace human judgment. Set up a blind evaluation protocol where bilingual reviewers rate fluency and adequacy on a Likert scale. Track error categories: mistranslation, omission, hallucination, and terminology inconsistency. If you are translating into a low-resource language, consider back-translation as a sanity check. The goal is to build a benchmark dataset specific to your domain so that model selection is data-driven, not hype-driven.

Model Selection for Multilingual Pipelines

Not every flagship model excels across all language pairs. Your choice should align with the source language, target language, and task complexity. Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all fully OpenAI SDK compatible with no cold starts.

For multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B offers strong cross-lingual performance. GLM 5, a 744B parameter mixture-of-experts model, is built for long-horizon agentic tasks and handles extended contexts well. If you need to translate entire reports in a single pass, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window and delivers near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning. Kimi K2.6 provides advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision
