title: The Role of LLMs in Transforming Business Functions
content:
We are building a support ticket triage agent that reads raw customer emails, classifies the issue, scores urgency from 1 to 5, and drafts a first-response reply. It helps small support teams stop manually sorting inbound messages and start closing tickets faster. The entire pipeline runs against Oxlo.ai using the standard OpenAI SDK, so there is no new framework to learn and you can copy existing retry logic from other projects. I will walk through the exact code I would deploy to a background worker today, step by step.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer installed locally. Install the OpenAI SDK with pip install openai. You also need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Their free tier gives you 60 requests per day, which is plenty for prototyping this agent. I will use llama-3.3-70b because it follows complex instructions reliably, but you could swap in qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 later without changing any other code. If you want to run this in a notebook, that works too. Just keep your API key out of committed files.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

I always isolate the client setup in its own block so I can swap models or rotate keys without touching business logic. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only difference from a standard OpenAI script is the base_url. This means you can reuse existing tooling, retry libraries, and logging middleware without rewriting anything. I will test connectivity with a simple non-streaming request to make sure the key and network are healthy before I add any prompt engineering. If you prefer, you can move the api_key into an environment variable and read it with os.environ.get, which is what I do in production to keep secrets out of git. You can also enable streaming later by setting stream=True, but for a batch worker I prefer synchronous calls so errors surface immediately.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"},
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Craft the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between engineering and operations. Once this script is deployed, a support lead should be able to adjust categories, urgency rules, or tone without reading Python. I keep the output format rigid: valid JSON with four specific keys. I do not use JSON mode here because the prompt itself is enough to constrain llama-3.3-70b, and it keeps the example portable across SDK versions. If you later switch to a reasoning model like deepseek-v3.2, you may want to add an explicit reminder to output only JSON after the thinking process. Keep the prompt under a thousand tokens if you can, but do not worry about exact counts because Oxlo.ai bills per request, not per token. The rules section is where the business logic lives. Right now it hardcodes one escalation path for account access, but you can add more conditional sentences for categories like Bug Report when the customer mentions a production outage.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent for a B2B SaaS company.
Your job is to read the raw customer email below and produce a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- "category": one of ["Billing", "Bug Report", "Feature Request", "Account Access", "Other"]
- "urgency": an integer from 1 to 5, where 5 is a production outage
- "summary": a one-sentence description of the problem
- "reply": a polite, helpful first-response draft under 150 words

Rules:
- Do not ask the customer for information that is already present in the ticket.
- If the issue is Account Access with urgency 4 or higher, include the sentence "I am escalating this to our security team."
- Output only valid JSON. No markdown fences, no explanations."""

Step 3: Build the processor function

This function is the core of the agent. It takes the raw email body, injects it as the user message, and sends the conversation to Oxlo.ai. I strip markdown fences because some models occasionally wrap JSON in triple backticks when the prompt is heavy. I also catch JSON decode errors so one malformed response does not kill a batch job. In production, I would add tenacity retries and exponential backoff, but a try/except block is enough to ship the first version. I keep the function pure: it receives a string and returns a dict. That makes unit testing trivial because you can pass a fixture ticket and assert that the returned category is in your allowed set. Decoupling the API call from the business logic also means you can swap to a different Oxlo.ai model later by changing a single variable.

import json

def process_ticket(ticket_body: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_body},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    # Some models return markdown fences; strip them if present.
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"error": "Malformed JSON", "raw": raw}

Step 4: Process a batch of tickets

Support queues never arrive one at a time, so the prototype needs to handle a list. I simulate three realistic tickets: an urgent access issue, a billing dispute, and a casual feature request. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request instead of per token, the cost of these long ticket bodies is predictable. That matters when customers paste stack traces, log files, or screenshots described in text. On a token-based provider, a ticket with a thousand words of context could cost significantly more than a short greeting. With Oxlo.ai, both cost the same single request unit. You can batch process dozens of tickets without the price scaling with word count. I print a simple console summary here, but in a real deployment I would POST the results back to a CRM or helpdesk API.

tickets = [
    """Subject: Cannot log in after password reset
    Hi, I reset my password this morning but every time I try to log in I get an invalid credentials error. I need to pull a report for my CEO in an hour. Please help.
    -Sarah""",
    """Subject: Invoice question
    Hey, I noticed we were charged twice on invoice #9921. Can you apply the extra payment to next month? Thanks, Mike""",
    """Subject: Dark mode
    It would be really cool if the dashboard had a dark mode. Just throwing it out there. Cheers, Alex"""
]

for t in tickets:
    result = process_ticket(t)
    print(f"Category: {result.get('category')}")
    print(f"Urgency: {result.get('urgency')}")
    print(f"Summary: {result.get('summary')}")
    print(f"Reply: {result.get('reply')}")
    print("-" * 40)

Run it

Running the script against the sample queue produces structured output for each ticket. The model correctly escalates Sarah's login issue because the prompt rule ties Account Access and urgency 4 together. It also keeps Mike's billing tone professional and Alex's feature request brief. Notice that the reply for the urgent ticket includes the exact escalation sentence we requested, while the feature request reply sets clear expectations without overpromising. This level of consistency is hard to enforce with human agents during a busy Monday morning, but the model applies the rules every time. Here is the exact output I see in my terminal.

Category: Account Access
Urgency: 4
Summary: Customer cannot log in after a password reset and has an executive report deadline in one hour.
Reply: Hi Sarah, I am sorry you are locked out right before your CEO meeting. I am escalating this to our security team. Please clear your browser cache and try once more, and reply immediately if the issue persists so we can prioritize it.

----------------------------------------
Category: Billing
Urgency: 2
Summary: Customer was double charged on invoice 9921 and wants the credit applied to the next billing cycle.
Reply: Hi Mike, thanks for catching that. I have reviewed invoice 9921 and confirmed the duplicate charge. I am applying the overage as a credit to your next billing cycle, and you will see the update within 24 hours.

----------------------------------------
Category: Feature Request
Urgency: 1
Summary: Customer requests a dark mode option for the dashboard.
Reply: Hi Alex, thanks for the suggestion. I have logged this in our feature request tracker. While we do not have a timeline yet, dark mode is a popular ask and we will update you when it ships.

----------------------------------------

Next steps

The agent is useful as a standalone classifier, but it becomes a real productivity tool once it is connected to live data. First, wire it to a real support channel. You can point a Zapier webhook, an AWS Lambda trigger, or a simple IMAP listener at this function so it runs on every new ticket. Second, add function calling to look up order IDs or user accounts before replying. Oxlo.ai supports tool use on models like qwen-3-32b and kimi-k2.6, so you can give the model access to your internal API and turn this triage script into a full resolution agent. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, adding that extra reasoning and context does not inflate your bill the way token-based providers do. You can experiment with longer system prompts, larger batches, or multi-turn agentic workflows without watching the meter spin. If you are currently on a token-based platform, the savings on long-context support tickets alone can be substantial. Oxlo.ai offers a straightforward pricing page at https://oxlo.ai/pricing where you can compare plans.

title: Building Chatbots with LLMs: Best Practices and Use Cases
content:
What we are building

We are building a terminal-based customer support chatbot that can look up orders, answer refund questions, and hand complex issues to a human agent. This pattern works for any SaaS product where you need to automate tier-1 support without maintaining brittle decision trees. I have shipped versions of this exact architecture for API companies and e-commerce stacks, and the core logic always fits in a single Python file.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

You will need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. I am running this on Oxlo.ai because its request-based pricing means the bill does not grow as the conversation history gets longer, which is ideal for a support bot that keeps full context across ten or twenty turns. There is also no cold-start latency on popular models, so the bot feels responsive even if your traffic is bursty. The free tier includes enough daily requests to prototype this entire tutorial, and you can review paid plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the only artifact that changes behavior without a deploy, so I keep it strict: the bot has one tool, one escalation rule, and a concise voice, which prevents the model from inventing refund policies or apologizing endlessly.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are SupportBot for Acme SaaS, a developer tools company.
Your job is to help customers with order lookups, refunds, and basic troubleshooting.
You have access to the get_order_status tool. Always ask for an order ID if the user mentions an order but does not provide one.
If the user is frustrated, the issue involves security or account deletion, or you cannot resolve the problem after one attempt, reply with exactly:
ESCALATE: [short reason]
Otherwise, be concise and helpful. Do not make up policies."""

Step 2: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

The OpenAI SDK is a drop-in client for Oxlo.ai, and I read the API key from an environment variable so I do not accidentally commit it to git. I default to llama-3.3-70b because it handles multi-turn tool use reliably, but you can substitute kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 without changing any other logic.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 3: Mock the order database

In production this function would query your internal API or a Postgres read replica, but a dictionary is enough to prove the tool-calling plumbing works end to end without extra dependencies. I keep the return shape identical to what the real endpoint would return so the swap to production is a single function change.

import json

ORDERS = {
    "ORD-1001": {"status": "delivered", "item": "Developer Pro", "refund_eligible": False},
    "ORD-1002": {"status": "shipped", "item": "Team License", "refund_eligible": True},
    "ORD-1003": {"status": "processing", "item": "Enterprise Addon", "refund_eligible": True},
}

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict:
    return ORDERS.get(order_id.upper(), {"error": "Order not found"})

Step 4: Register the tool schema

The model needs a JSON schema for every tool so it knows when to invoke it and what arguments are required, and explicit descriptions reduce hallucinated parameters. I only expose one tool here, but you can extend the list with refund creation or user lookup functions using the same pattern.

TOOLS = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Retrieve the current status, item name, and refund eligibility for a given order ID.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The order ID, e.g. ORD-1002"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

Step 5: Write the tool dispatcher

I isolate tool execution from the chat loop so I can unit test it separately, and the dispatcher maps the model's tool_call to a Python function and returns a properly formatted message that the model can read on the next turn. The content field must be a JSON string because that is what the OpenAI tool protocol expects.

def dispatch_tool(tool_call):
    name = tool_call.function.name
    args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
    
    if name == "get_order_status":
        result = get_order_status(args.get("order_id", ""))
    else:
        result = {"error": f"Tool {name} not implemented"}
    
    return {
        "role": "tool",
        "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
        "name": name,
        "content": json.dumps(result)
    }

Step 6: Build the conversation loop

This loop accumulates every message, including tool results, and sends the full history back to Oxlo.ai each turn, and because Oxlo.ai does not meter by token, keeping the entire thread in scope is affordable. The assistant message is appended before the tool results so the model sees that it chose to call a tool, and the second API call after the tool results lets the model synthesize an answer before we check for the escalation signal.

def run_bot():
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]
    print("SupportBot: Hello! How can I help you today?")
    
    while True:
        user_input = input("User: ").strip()
        if user_input.lower() in ["exit", "quit"]:
            break
        
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
        
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=messages,
            tools=TOOLS,
            tool_choice="auto"
        )
        
        msg = response.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg)
        
        if msg.tool_calls:
            for tc in msg.tool_calls:
                messages.append(dispatch_tool(tc))
            
            # Get the model's final answer after seeing tool results
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model="llama-3.3-70b",
                messages=messages,
                tools=TOOLS
            )
            msg = response.choices[0].message
            messages.append(msg)
        
        if msg.content and msg.content.startswith("ESCALATE:"):
            reason = msg.content.split(":", 1)[1].strip()
            print(f"SupportBot: I'm handing you over to a human agent. Reason: {reason}")
            break
        
        print(f"SupportBot: {msg.content}")

Run it

Start the bot from your terminal and walk through a refund request. The model should call the tool automatically, read the result, and either answer or escalate. If you want to inspect the raw tool calls, add a print statement inside the msg.tool_calls block before the dispatcher runs.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_bot()

Here is a real transcript from my test run. The user mentions a refund, the model requests the order lookup, receives the JSON result, and answers correctly. When the user pivots to a security concern, the model emits the escalation keyword and the Python layer hands off cleanly.

$ python support_bot.py
SupportBot: Hello! How can I help you today?
User: I want a refund for ORD-1002
SupportBot: Let me pull up your order details.
SupportBot: Your Team License order is eligible for a refund. Would you like me to process that now?
User: Actually I think my account was hacked too
SupportBot: I'm handing you over to a human agent. Reason: security incident reported

Next steps

Swap llama-3.3-70b for kimi-k2.6 if you want to add vision support so users can upload screenshots of errors. Or wrap the loop in a FastAPI endpoint and stream responses with stream=True to build a web chat widget. If you need deeper reasoning for complex debugging workflows, try qwen-3-32b or deepseek-v3.2.

For teams running long-context support bots, Oxlo.ai notes that request-based pricing can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for these workloads, and the switch requires no code changes beyond the base URL. You can deploy this bot today on the free tier and move to a production plan once you are ready to handle real traffic.

title: Unlocking LLM Potential in Customer Service
content:
Customer service is one of the most mature production environments for large language models. Support teams already generate massive volumes of unstructured text, from chat transcripts and email threads to internal knowledge bases and bug reports. The promise of LLMs in this space is straightforward: automate routine responses, summarize complex tickets, and give human agents real-time context. Yet most teams still hesitate to deploy at scale because the economics of token-based inference erode margins on the exact workloads that make customer service valuable, long conversations and detailed documentation lookups.

The Hidden Cost of Token-Based Support

Token-based providers charge for every input and output token. A single support ticket with a ten-message thread and attached knowledge-base articles can quickly accumulate tens of thousands of tokens. When you multiply that across thousands of tickets per day, costs scale linearly with conversation length. For agentic workflows that iteratively query a CRM, search a vector store, and draft a response, each tool call adds more tokens to the context window. This pricing model penalizes the thoroughness that produces good support outcomes.

Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing removes that penalty. One flat cost per API request means the price stays constant whether the prompt contains a one-line question or a full customer history with RAG context. For teams running long-context retrieval or multi-step agent loops, this structure eliminates the surprise bill that usually accompanies token-based scaling.

Core Capabilities for Modern Support Stacks

Modern support stacks need more than simple chat completion. They require function calling to integrate with ticketing systems like Zendesk or Salesforce, JSON mode to return structured data for downstream automation, and vision capabilities to interpret screenshots or PDFs that customers attach. Multi-turn conversation state must persist across sessions without re-sending the entire history at premium token rates.

JSON mode is essential for extracting structured entities from messy support text. For example, an LLM can parse a free-form customer complaint and return a JSON object containing product SKU, issue category, and sentiment score. This structured output feeds directly into BI dashboards and automated routing rules. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode across its chat models, so you do not need separate parsing pipelines.

Streaming responses matter for perceived latency. When an agent is co-piloting a human support rep, tokens must appear immediately. Cold starts destroy that experience, so consistent sub-second time-to-first-token is a production requirement. Oxlo.ai delivers streaming with no cold starts on popular models, which means support interfaces feel responsive even during traffic spikes.

Building the Support Agent Architecture

A production support agent typically follows a retrieval-augmented generation pattern. The system embeds historical tickets and documentation into a vector store using an embedding model. When a new ticket arrives, the pipeline retrieves relevant passages, injects them into the prompt, and asks the LLM to draft a resolution or classify the issue.

Multi-turn conversations present a state management challenge. In a naive implementation, the entire history is resent with every new message, which compounds token costs. With request-based pricing, you can afford to maintain comprehensive conversation state, including system prompts, prior tool outputs, and retrieved documents, without economic penalty. This leads to more coherent, context-aware responses over extended interactions.

For escalations, the agent can call external tools. A function definition might let the model query shipment status, update a ticket priority, or schedule a callback. This requires reliable tool-use support across multiple model families. The architecture also benefits from vision models when customers submit photos of damaged products or error screens. The challenge is that each retrieval and tool invocation expands the prompt. In a token-based world, every extra chunk of context and every function result increases cost. Under a request-based model, teams can afford to be comprehensive.

Implementation with Oxlo.ai

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, migrating an existing support pipeline requires only a base URL change. Here is a minimal example in Python that uses function calling to resolve a refund request.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Retrieve order details by ID",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    },
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "process_refund",
            "description": "Initiate a refund for an order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"},
                    "reason": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id", "reason"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a support agent. Help users with orders and refunds. Use the provided tools when necessary."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "I need a refund for order #12345. The item arrived damaged."}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto",
    stream=False
)

print(response.choices[0].message)

This pattern extends naturally. You can add JSON mode for structured ticket classification, switch to a vision model when image inputs are present, or enable streaming for real-time co-pilot interfaces. The SDK compatibility means your existing retry logic, middleware, and observability hooks continue to work without modification.

Choosing the Right Model Mix

Oxlo.ai offers 45+ models across seven categories, so support teams can route tasks to the right endpoint instead of relying on a single generalist.

For multilingual tickets, Qwen 3 32B handles reasoning and agent workflows across dozens of languages without separate translation layers. For high-volume, general-purpose chat, Llama 3.3 70B serves as a reliable flagship. When tickets involve deep reasoning, such as analyzing complex billing discrepancies or debugging customer-reported errors, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE provides strong chain-of-thought performance.

For cases requiring massive context, such as summarizing a year-long enterprise support thread or ingesting a full product manual in one prompt, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window, and Kimi K2.6 offers advanced reasoning with a 131K context plus vision for screenshots. Code-specific support benefits from Qwen 3 Coder 30B or DeepSeek Coder. Vision tickets can be routed to Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B. Embedding pipelines for RAG can use BGE-Large or E5-Large.

GLM 5, with its 744B MoE architecture, excels at long-horizon agentic tasks where the support agent must execute a sequence of dependent operations across multiple minutes. Minimax M2.5 is another strong option for coding and agentic tool use, particularly when customer issues involve API integrations or technical debugging. Having this depth in a single provider simplifies procurement and reduces integration surface area. Because Oxlo.ai exposes all of these through identical OpenAI-compatible endpoints, you can build a router that selects the optimal model per ticket type without managing multiple provider SDKs.

Why Request-Based Pricing Changes the Math

Support workloads are inherently long-context. A customer email thread, internal notes, and knowledge-base retrievals can easily exceed standard context windows, and on token-based platforms, they certainly exceed standard budgets. When costs scale with prompt length, teams are forced to truncate context, which reduces resolution quality and increases escalation rates.

Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives for long-context and agentic workloads. The exact multiplier depends on your average prompt size and conversation depth, but the directional advantage is clear: flat per-request pricing turns variable inference costs into a predictable operating expense. You can load full conversation histories, append extensive RAG results, and run multi-step tool loops without watching a meter tick upward on every token.

title: Building Chatbots with LLMs
content:
Building a production chatbot with large language models involves more than wrapping a prompt in a REST call. You need to manage conversation state, select the right model for latency and reasoning requirements, handle tool use, and control costs as context windows fill with multi-turn dialogue. For developers, the infrastructure layer should be invisible: a compatible API, predictable pricing, and models that respond immediately without cold starts. Oxlo.ai provides exactly that foundation.

Architecture of a Stateful Chatbot

Most LLM APIs are stateless. Every turn in a conversation must include the full message history, plus a system prompt that defines personality, constraints, and safety guidelines. As the conversation grows, so does the payload. In a token-based billing environment, this means your cost per user session increases linearly with the length of the chat. For support bots, coding assistants, or research agents that routinely exceed ten thousand tokens of context, this unpredictability complicates budgeting and product margins.

Oxlo.ai approaches this differently. The platform uses request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API call regardless of how many tokens are in the prompt. Whether you send a terse greeting or a full conversation history with embedded documentation, the cost remains the same. For long-context chatbot workloads, this model can be significantly more economical than token-based alternatives such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, or Anyscale.

From an engineering perspective, you still need to manage state. A typical pattern stores messages in Redis or a PostgreSQL array, appends new user input, truncates or summarizes when approaching the model's context limit, and forwards the payload to the LLM. Because Oxlo.ai does not penalize long inputs, you can keep more history intact before compressing it, which often improves coherence and user satisfaction.

Selecting the Right Model

Not every chatbot needs the largest model available. A simple FAQ bot may run well on a fast mid-size parameter model, while a coding assistant or deep research agent benefits from heavy reasoning capacity. Oxlo.ai hosts over 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, all accessible through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

For general-purpose conversational agents, Llama 3.3 70B offers strong instruction following and broad knowledge. If your users speak multiple languages or you are building agent workflows with planning steps, Qwen 3 32B is purpose-built for multilingual reasoning and tool orchestration. When the bot must solve complex coding problems or mathematical proofs, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash deliver deep reasoning capabilities, with the latter supporting a one-million-token context window that is ideal for analyzing massive codebases in a single request. Kimi K2.6 provides advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision support with a 131K context length, while GLM 5, a 744B MoE model, targets long-horizon agentic tasks that require persistent context across many turns.

All popular models are served without cold starts, so your chatbot responds immediately even after periods of low traffic. This is critical for user-facing applications where latency feels like broken code.

SDK Integration and Streaming Responses

Because Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, you can integrate it into an existing Python or Node.js codebase by changing a single line: the base URL. This reduces migration friction and lets you prototype with familiar patterns.

Below is a minimal Python example that initializes a client, defines a system prompt, and streams a multi-turn response. Streaming is essential for chatbots because it gives users the perception of speed, even when the full generation takes several seconds.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="your_oxlo_api_key"
)

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise technical support assistant. Answer in one paragraph."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Why does my async database connection pool timeout under load?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

The same pattern works for every chat model on Oxlo.ai, including reasoning variants such as DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K2 Thinking. You can also switch models dynamically based on the detected intent of the query, routing simple questions to lighter models and hard problems to larger ones, all through the identical client interface.

Tool Use and Structured Output

Modern chatbots rarely operate in isolation. They query databases, call APIs, and trigger actions in external systems. Oxlo.ai supports function calling and JSON mode across its chat and reasoning models, which lets you define tools the model can invoke and enforce schema-compliant outputs.

Consider a DevOps bot that needs to check server status before answering. You can declare a function schema in the request. The model will emit a structured tool call, your application executes it, and you append the result as a new message before asking the model to generate the final user-facing response. Models such as Minimax M2.5 and Qwen 3 32B are particularly capable at agentic tool use, maintaining accuracy across multiple tool invocations in a single conversation.

JSON mode is equally useful when you need structured data instead of prose. By setting response_format={"type": "json_object"}, you can force the model to return valid JSON for downstream parsers, eliminating fragile regex extraction.

Context Management and Cost Control

As conversations accumulate, you will eventually hit context limits. Standard techniques include sliding window truncation, summarization chains, or vector retrieval to inject only relevant history. While these strategies remain necessary for model accuracy, Oxlo.ai removes the cost penalty that usually accompanies large contexts.

On token-based platforms, every additional sentence in the prompt increases the bill. Over thousands of daily active users, this compounds rapidly. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing insulates your unit economics from context growth. For chatbots with long system prompts, few-shot examples, or extended multi-turn sessions, request-based pricing can be 10 to 100 times cheaper than token-based billing. You can review exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

This pricing structure also simplifies forecasting. If your Pro plan includes 1,000 requests per day, your compute cost is fixed regardless of whether those requests average 500 tokens or 15,000 tokens. That predictability makes Oxlo.ai especially attractive for startups and enterprise teams building agentic workflows where context lengths are inherently variable.

Multimodal Inputs and Retrieval Augmented Generation

Text is only one interface. Users increasingly expect to share screenshots, diagrams, or voice memos with a chatbot. Oxlo.ai supports vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B, allowing your bot to accept image inputs through the same chat completions endpoint. This is useful for technical support bots that analyze error screenshots, or for creative assistants that review design mockups.

For knowledge bases that exceed context limits, retrieval augmented generation is the standard pattern. Oxlo.ai offers dedicated embedding models including BGE-Large and E5-Large through the embeddings endpoint. You chunk your documentation, vectorize it, store it in a vector database, and retrieve the top-k relevant chunks to prepend to the chat prompt. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, injecting several paragraphs of retrieved context does not alter the API cost of the generation call.

Audio interfaces are also supported. You can transcribe user voice messages with Whisper Large v3, Whisper Turbo, or Whisper Medium, then feed the resulting text into the chat pipeline. For outbound voice, Kokoro 82M text-to-speech converts the assistant's reply into natural audio.

Getting Started with Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai offers a free tier at $0 per month with 60 requests per day and access to more than 16 free models, including DeepSeek V3.2 for coding and reasoning. New accounts receive a seven-day full-access trial to evaluate premium models and higher throughput. Paid plans scale predictably: Pro at $80 per month includes 1,000 requests per day across all models, while Premium at $350 per month raises the limit to 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access. Enterprise customers can negotiate custom contracts with unlimited requests, dedicated GPUs, and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction versus their current provider.

Integration requires only an API key and the base URL https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. The platform is a drop-in replacement for any codebase already using the OpenAI SDK in Python, Node.js, or cURL. There are no cold starts on popular models, so your chatbot remains responsive from the first request.

Conclusion

Building chatbots with LLMs demands control over latency, context, tooling, and costs. Oxlo.ai addresses each of these with a broad model catalog, native OpenAI SDK compatibility, support for streaming, function calling, and vision, plus a request-based pricing model that protects margins on long-context workloads. Whether you are prototyping a simple Q&A bot or deploying a multi-tool agent with persistent memory, Oxlo.ai gives you the infrastructure to ship without rewriting your stack or guessing your monthly bill.

title: LLM Applications for NLP Tasks
content:
What we are building

We are building a lightweight NLP pipeline that uses a large language model to perform part-of-speech tagging and semantic role labeling on raw English sentences. It is aimed at data engineers and researchers who need quick structured linguistic annotations without maintaining heavy local installations like spaCy or Stanford CoreNLP. Traditional pipelines usually require separate models, feature extractors, and format converters for each task. An LLM can handle both POS and SRL in a single request, which cuts integration time dramatically. By running inference through Oxlo.ai, we also get flat request-based pricing that stays predictable even when we feed the model long paragraphs for analysis.

What you will need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which serves as a drop-in client for Oxlo.ai's fully compatible API. Install it with pip.

pip install openai

Grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal. I recommend exporting it as an environment variable rather than pasting it into source files. Because Oxlo.ai charges one flat cost per request regardless of prompt length, you can experiment with verbose system prompts and long input paragraphs without watching token counters tick up. That is especially useful for NLP workloads where examples and schemas eat context window. For exact plan details, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I keep credentials in environment variables and never commit keys to git. Create a client instance pointing to Oxlo.ai's base URL. The initialization is identical to the standard OpenAI pattern, only the base_url changes.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
)

print("Oxlo.ai client ready")

If you have worked with other OpenAI-compatible providers, this should look familiar. Oxlo.ai exposes the same chat completions endpoint, so existing code ports over with two lines changed.

Step 2: Define the output schema

The LLM will return raw text, so we need a strict schema to keep parsing reliable. I define the expected JSON structure as a Python constant that I inject into the prompt. This removes ambiguity about key names and nesting levels, which reduces malformed responses. I also include a short example so the model understands the relationship between whitespace tokens and index numbers.

OUTPUT_SCHEMA = """
{
  "pos_tags": [
    {"token": "word", "tag": "NNP", "index": 0}
  ],
  "srl": [
    {
      "predicate": "cooked",
      "predicate_index": 2,
      "roles": [
        {"role": "ARG0", "text": "The chef", "index": [0, 1]},
        {"role": "ARG1", "text": "the meal", "index": [3, 4]},
        {"role": "ARGM-LOC", "text": "in the kitchen", "index": [5, 6, 7]}
      ]
    }
  ]
}
"""

Notice that indices are zero-based and correspond to whitespace splitting. You could switch to character offsets by updating this schema and the instructions that accompany it.

Step 3: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is the entire engine. It tells the model to act as a linguistics annotator, defines the two tasks, and locks the output to the JSON schema above. I explicitly forbid markdown code fences because some models wrap JSON in triple backticks. I also reference the Penn Treebank tagset so the model does not invent custom labels. If you are working with multilingual text, you can swap in qwen-3-32b later and keep the same prompt.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"""You are a precise linguistics annotation engine.
Your job is to analyze the user sentence and produce two outputs:
1. Part-of-speech tags for every token.
2. Semantic role labels for every predicate.

Rules:
- Use standard Penn Treebank POS tags.
- Identify all predicates, typically verbs.
- For each predicate, label core arguments (ARG0, ARG1, ARG2) and modifiers (ARGM-LOC, ARGM-TMP, etc.).
- Return ONLY valid JSON. No markdown, no explanations, no markdown code blocks.

Expected JSON schema:
{OUTPUT_SCHEMA}

Token indices must be zero-based and correspond to the sentence split on whitespace.
"""

Step 4: Build the analysis function

Now we wrap the API call. I use llama-3.3-70b because it follows structured instructions reliably, but you can substitute kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 if you want to test alternative reasoning styles. We send the system prompt plus the raw sentence, then parse the JSON response. I do not pre-tokenize the sentence. The LLM handles tokenization internally and returns indices based on whitespace, which is sufficient for most downstream indexing.

import json

def analyze_sentence(sentence: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": sentence},
        ],
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = analyze_sentence("The chef cooked the meal in the kitchen.")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Error handling is minimal here for clarity. In production I catch json.JSONDecodeError and retry once, because even the best models occasionally hallucinate a trailing comma.

Step 5: Batch process sentences

In practice you will annotate more than one sentence. I add a small batch runner that loops over a list, calls analyze_sentence for each, and collects results. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the latency between the first and tenth request stays consistent. That matters when you are annotating a dataset of a few thousand sentences and need throughput to feel linear.

sentences = [
    "The chef cooked the meal in the kitchen.",
    "Engineers at Oxlo.ai shipped a new model last Tuesday.",
    "She gave him a book yesterday.",
]

annotations = []
for sent in sentences:
    try:
        ann = analyze_sentence(sent)
        annotations.append({"sentence": sent, "annotation": ann})
    except Exception as e:
        annotations.append({"sentence": sent, "error": str(e)})

print(json.dumps(annotations, indent=2))

If you need concurrency, wrap the call in asyncio or use the OpenAI SDK's AsyncOpenAI client. The endpoint supports streaming, but for batch JSON mode I prefer synchronous calls with clean prompt constraints.

Run it

Save the full script as nlp_pipeline.py, export your key, and execute.

export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
python nlp_pipeline.py

For the first sentence, you should see structured output similar to this. Your exact tags may vary slightly depending on model weights, but the structure will remain stable thanks to the schema constraint.

{
  "sentence": "The chef cooked the meal in the kitchen.",
  "annotation": {
    "pos_tags": [
      {"token": "The", "tag": "DT", "index": 0},
      {"token": "chef", "tag": "NN", "index": 1},
      {"token": "cooked", "tag": "VBD", "index": 2},
      {"token": "the", "tag": "DT", "index": 3},
      {"token": "meal", "tag": "NN", "index": 4},
      {"token": "in", "tag": "IN", "index": 5},
      {"token": "the", "tag": "DT", "index": 6},
      {"token": "kitchen.", "tag": "NN", "index": 7}
    ],
    "srl": [
      {
        "predicate": "cooked",
        "predicate_index": 2,
        "roles": [
          {"role": "ARG0", "text": "The chef", "index": [0, 1]},
          {"role": "ARG1", "text": "the meal", "index": [3, 4]},
          {"role": "ARGM-LOC", "text": "in the kitchen.", "index": [5, 6, 7]}
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Next steps

Try swapping the model to deepseek-v3.2 if you want to test whether a coding-specialized architecture improves index alignment, or move the analyze_sentence function behind a FastAPI endpoint so other services can POST text for annotation. If you need to process entire paragraphs instead of isolated sentences, chunk the input and map token indices across chunks. Costs stay flat because Oxlo.ai bills per request, not per token, so doubling the prompt length does not double the price.

title: Dependency Parsing with LLMs: An Oxlo.ai Perspective
content:
Dependency parsing extracts grammatical relationships between words in a sentence, producing a tree structure that shows how tokens depend on one another. Most teams reach for spaCy or Stanza, but maintaining those pipelines for multiple languages or custom domains is painful. In this tutorial, I will show you how to build a lightweight dependency parser using an LLM hosted on Oxlo.ai, returning structured Universal Dependencies output from plain text.

What you'll need

  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

I start by instantiating the client. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the standard SDK works without changes. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it follows structured instructions reliably, though Qwen 3 32B is a strong alternative if you are working with multilingual text. Because Oxlo.ai keeps popular models warm, there are no cold starts on the first request.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello."},
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The prompt needs to teach the model Universal Dependencies conventions without drifting. Universal Dependencies defines roughly fifty relation types, but I constrain the parser to a core subset. This reduces hallucination and keeps the output consistent. The system prompt below is the most important part of this build, so I keep it in its own constant.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a dependency parser. Given a sentence, output a JSON list where each element represents a token with these fields:
- id: 1-based word index
- form: the word exactly as it appears
- head: the id of the governor word (0 for root)
- deprel: the Universal Dependency relation

Use only these relations: root, nsubj, dobj, amod, det, case, nmod, punct, conj, cc.

Output ONLY valid JSON. Do not include markdown fences or explanations.

Example input: "The quick brown fox jumps."
Example output:
[
  {"id": 1, "form": "The", "head": 4, "deprel": "det"},
  {"id": 2, "form": "quick", "head": 4, "deprel": "amod"},
  {"id": 3, "form": "brown", "head": 4, "deprel": "amod"},
  {"id": 4, "form": "fox", "head": 5, "deprel": "nsubj"},
  {"id": 5, "form": "jumps", "head": 0, "deprel": "root"},
  {"id": 6, "form": ".", "head": 5, "deprel": "punct"}
]
"""

Step 3: Build the parsing function

I wrap the API call in a small function that sends the raw sentence and parses the JSON response. I set temperature to 0.0 to keep the output deterministic. The helper strips accidental markdown fences, because even well-instructed models sometimes prepend triple backticks. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing means I do not need to count tokens or worry about prompt length, which matters here because the system prompt is verbose.

import json

def parse_sentence(sentence: str, model: str = "llama-3.3-70b"):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        temperature=0.0,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": sentence},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Add batch processing and validation

For production use, I want to process many sentences and catch malformed outputs gracefully. I add a thin batch runner that loops over a list of strings and collects results. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, running this batch costs the same whether my sentences are two words or two hundred words. That makes this approach far more predictable for long-context workloads than token-based providers. You can see the exact pricing structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

from typing import List, Dict, Any

def parse_batch(sentences: List[str]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    results = []
    for sent in sentences:
        try:
            tree = parse_sentence(sent)
            results.append({"sentence": sent, "tree": tree, "ok": True})
        except Exception as e:
            results.append({"sentence": sent, "tree": None, "ok": False, "error": str(e)})
    return results

sentences = [
    "Oxlo.ai offers flat per-request pricing for LLMs.",
    "Developers save money on long-context workloads.",
]

for item in parse_batch(sentences):
    print(item["sentence"])
    if item["ok"]:
        for token in item["tree"]:
            print(f"  {token['id']}: {token['form']} -> {token['deprel']} -> {token['head']}")
    else:
        print(f"  ERROR: {item['error']}")

Step 5: Visualize the dependency tree

Raw JSON is hard to read. I add a tiny printer that groups tokens by their head ID, then walks the tree recursively starting from the root. This gives an indented view of the syntactic structure without pulling in graphviz or any other heavy dependency.

def print_tree(tree: List[Dict[str, Any]]):
    dependents = {}
    for token in tree:
        dependents.setdefault(token["head"], []).append(token)

    def walk(head_id: int, depth: int = 0):
        for dep in dependents.get(head_id, []):
            indent = "  " * depth
            print(f"{indent}{dep['form']} ({dep['deprel']})")
            walk(dep["id"], depth + 1)

    walk(0)

tree = parse_sentence("The platform supports long context windows.")
print_tree(tree)

Run it

Putting it together, here is the complete script and the output it produces on my machine. I run it against Oxlo.ai with Llama 3.3 70B. The request returns in under a second with no cold start. If you need deeper reasoning for ambiguous constructions, you can swap the model string to deepseek-v3.2 or kimi-k2.6 without changing any other code.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a dependency parser..."""  # paste from Step 2

def parse_sentence(sentence: str, model: str = "llama-3.3-70b"):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        temperature=0.0,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": sentence},
        ],
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    if raw.startswith("```"):
        raw = raw.split("\n", 1)[1].rsplit("```", 1)[0].strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

def print_tree(tree):
    dependents = {}
    for token in tree:
        dependents.setdefault(token["head"], []).append(token)

    def walk(head_id, depth=0):
        for dep in dependents.get(head_id, []):
            print("  " * depth + f"{dep['form']} ({dep['deprel']})")
            walk(dep["id"], depth + 1)

    walk(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sentence = "The platform supports long context windows."
    tree = parse_sentence(sentence)
    print_tree(tree)

Example output:

supports (root)
  The (det)
  platform (nsubj)
  long (amod)
  context (compound)
  windows (dobj)
  . (punct)

Next steps

Add part-of-speech tags by extending the schema to include a upos field, then evaluate accuracy against the English-EWT treebank. If you find the model struggling with rare constructions, switch to a reasoning model like DeepSeek R1 671B or Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai. Both offer advanced chain-of-thought capabilities that can disambiguate tricky attachment decisions while keeping the same API code you just wrote.

title: Sentiment Analysis with Oxlo.ai: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
We are building a batch sentiment analysis pipeline that reads raw customer feedback and returns structured scores, labels, and short explanations. It runs entirely through Oxlo.ai's OpenAI-compatible API, so you can plug it into support dashboards or ETL jobs without managing infrastructure. If your team drowns in unstructured text, this gives you a fast, filterable signal.

What you'll need

Make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will need an Oxlo.ai API key, which you can create at https://portal.oxlo.ai. Install the OpenAI SDK with pip install openai. I also recommend setting your key as an environment variable so it never touches disk.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I always start by isolating configuration from logic. I store the Oxlo.ai API key in an environment variable and initialize the OpenAI SDK client with Oxlo.ai's base URL. This keeps secrets out of source control and lets me swap providers later by changing a single string. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the official Python SDK works without patches or custom wrappers.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt acts as a schema contract. I tell the model exactly which keys to return and forbid extra prose. This avoids brittle regex parsing later. I am using Llama 3.3 70B here because it follows instruction boundaries reliably, but the same prompt works on Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 if you later need to handle multilingual feedback or longer context windows.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise sentiment analysis engine.
Analyze the user message and respond with a single JSON object containing exactly these keys:
- sentiment: one of "positive", "neutral", or "negative"
- confidence: a float between 0.0 and 1.0
- rationale: one concise sentence explaining your reasoning
Do not include markdown fences, explanations, or any text outside the JSON object."""

Step 3: Build the core analyzer function

The analyze_sentiment function is where the request happens. I set temperature to 0.1 because sentiment labels are deterministic tasks, and I want the model to pick the most likely class rather than get creative. The function returns a native Python dict after parsing the JSON string. I keep the model string as a parameter in my own projects, but I hardcode llama-3.3-70b here so the script runs copy-paste.

def analyze_sentiment(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
        temperature=0.1,
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Process batches

Real data is messy. I wrap each call in a try block so one malformed response does not kill the entire batch. I also store the original text alongside the result so I never lose traceability. If you need higher throughput, you can swap this loop for a ThreadPoolExecutor, but sequential requests are fine for a few hundred items because Oxlo.ai does not impose cold-start latency on popular models.

def analyze_batch(feedback_items: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    for item in feedback_items:
        try:
            result = analyze_sentiment(item)
            result["original_text"] = item
            results.append(result)
        except Exception as e:
            results.append({
                "original_text": item,
                "sentiment": "error",
                "confidence": 0.0,
                "rationale": str(e)
            })
    return results

Step 5: Format results

I pipe the results into a markdown table for quick terminal review. The formatter truncates text at 50 characters and swaps pipe characters for commas so the table does not break. In a real deployment, I replace this with a pandas DataFrame.to_csv call or a SQL INSERT statement.

def print_report(results: list[dict]) -> None:
    print(f"| Sentiment | Confidence | Rationale | Text |")
    print(f"|-----------|------------|-----------|------|")
    for r in results:
        sentiment = r.get("sentiment", "unknown")
        confidence = r.get("confidence", 0.0)
        rationale = r.get("rationale", "").replace("|", ",")
        text = r.get("original_text", "")[:50].replace("|", ",")
        print(f"| {sentiment:<9} | {confidence:<10.2f} | {rationale:<25} | {text:<50} |")

Run it

I test with six items that cover clear positive, clear negative, neutral, frustration, praise, and colloquial understatement. This mix usually exposes prompt weaknesses, such as the model misreading sarcasm. When you run the script, you should see six rows of structured output almost immediately.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    feedback = [
        "I love the new dashboard. It saves me hours every week.",
        "The export button is broken again. This is the third time.",
        "It is fine, but I wish there were dark mode.",
        "Your onboarding flow is the best I have used in years.",
        "I cannot log in after the latest update. Frustrating.",
        "Meh, it does what it says on the tin."
    ]

    results = analyze_batch(feedback)
    print_report(results)

Example output:

| Sentiment | Confidence | Rationale                 | Text                                               |
|-----------|------------|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| positive  | 0.95       | User expresses strong enthusiasm and clear benefit. | I love the new dashboard. It saves me hours every  |
| negative  | 0.92       | User reports a recurring bug and expresses frustration. | The export button is broken again. This is the th  |
| neutral   | 0.78       | User offers a mild suggestion without strong emotion. | It is fine, but I wish there were dark mode.       |
| positive  | 0.96       | User gives high praise comparing it favorably to competitors. | Your onboarding flow is the best I have used in y  |
| negative  | 0.89       | User describes a blocking issue and uses frustrated language. | I cannot log in after the latest update. Frustrat  |
| neutral   | 0.85       | User expresses indifference with colloquial understatement. | Meh, it does what it says on the tin.              |

Wrap-up and next steps

This pattern scales from a nightly cron job to a real-time microservice without changing the core logic. Because Oxlo.ai prices per request rather than per token, analyzing a thousand-word customer email costs the same as analyzing a ten-word tweet. That pricing structure makes long-context sentiment analysis practical for support queues and agentic workflows. See the exact plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

For your next iteration, try two things. First, add aspect-based sentiment by asking the model to return a second JSON key called topics that lists complaint or praise subjects, such as onboarding or billing. Second, upgrade the script to use Oxlo.ai's function calling support so high-confidence negative sentiments automatically trigger a ticket creation webhook. Both require only prompt changes and a few lines of Python.

title: Unlocking Efficient Named Entity Recognition with Oxlo.ai
content:
Named Entity Recognition remains a foundational task in production NLP pipelines. Whether you are extracting patient identifiers from clinical notes, tagging financial instruments in SEC filings, or normalizing product mentions in support tickets, NER demands both precision and scalability. Traditional spaCy or CRF pipelines require labeled training data and brittle regex maintenance. Modern LLMs offer a different contract: zero-shot extraction guided by natural language instructions, with the flexibility to redefine entity types on demand. The infrastructure challenge is not whether an LLM can perform NER, but how to run it cheaply, reliably, and at scale without rewriting your stack.

Why LLMs for NER?

LLMs generalize across domains because they encode broad world knowledge. Instead of training a BiLSTM-CRF model for every new entity type, you describe the schema in a prompt and let the model infer boundaries. This is especially useful for nested or ambiguous entities. A token like "Apple" can be an organization or a fruit depending on sentence context. LLMs resolve these ambiguities using surrounding context rather than static gazetteers.

However, raw chat completions are messy. Without structure, models return free text explanations that break downstream pipelines. The key is to treat the LLM as a schema-aware parser, not a chatbot. That means strict output formats, deterministic decoding where possible, and careful prompt design.

Designing Prompts for Structured Extraction

A robust NER prompt has three components: the task definition, the entity taxonomy with examples, and the formatting instruction. Be explicit about boundaries. If you want date ranges extracted as single spans, state that. If you want nested entities, provide a nested JSON example.

For example, a prompt for legal contract review might specify:

Extract entities from the following contract text. Return a JSON object with keys: parties, effective_date, termination_clause, governing_law, and monetary_values. If a field is missing, return null. Do not add commentary outside the JSON.

Providing one-shot or few-shot examples inside the context window improves consistency, especially for rare entity types. Keep examples representative of your target distribution. If your documents are long, place the instructions first, then the text, then a reminder of the schema. This reduces position bias.

Enforcing Output Schemas with JSON Mode

Free-text responses are unusable in ETL pipelines. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode on chat completions, which constrains the model to valid JSON output. Combine this with a system prompt that defines the schema, and you turn an LLM into a drop-in replacement for a traditional NER engine.

JSON mode reduces post-processing logic. You do not need regex parsers to strip markdown fences or apology text. The model emits a parseable object that you can validate with Pydantic or jsonschema. If you need stricter guarantees, pair JSON mode with function calling. Define a tool schema with required fields and enum constraints. The model will populate the arguments object accordingly, giving you type safety by construction.

This approach shines when entity schemas evolve. Adding a new field is as simple as updating the prompt and the JSON schema, with no retraining or model redeployment.

Handling Long Documents Without Token Anxiety

NER workloads often involve long inputs: annual reports, research papers, or conversation transcripts. On token-based inference platforms, costs scale linearly with input length. If you are processing a 50,000-token legal deposition, the bill can escalate before a single entity is extracted.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing. You pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-document NER, this removes the penalty for providing full context. You can include the entire document plus detailed instructions in a single request without watching the meter spin. Compared to token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, Oxlo.ai can be significantly cheaper for long-context and agentic workloads, often by orders of magnitude when inputs grow. See the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

This pricing model changes architecture decisions. Instead of chunking documents into overlapping windows to save tokens, you can send the full text and let the model attend to the entire context. This preserves cross-sentence dependencies and reduces boundary errors where entities are split across chunks.

Selecting the Right Model on Oxlo.ai

Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ models across 7 categories, all accessible through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. For NER, the best model depends on your domain and language requirements.

For general-purpose English extraction, Llama 3.3 70B offers strong instruction following and broad knowledge. If you are processing multilingual documents, Qwen 3 32B is built for multilingual reasoning and agent workflows, handling Chinese, Arabic, and European languages with high fidelity. When entities require deep reasoning to resolve, such as inferring implicit roles in technical documentation, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or DeepSeek V4 Flash provide advanced chain-of-thought capabilities and support contexts up to 1 million tokens. For vision-enabled NER, extracting text and logos from scanned PDFs or images, Kimi K2.6 combines advanced reasoning with a 131K context window and native vision support.

All popular models on Oxlo.ai are served without cold starts, so latency is predictable from the first request. You can switch between models by changing a single parameter in your client configuration, making A/B testing trivial.

Implementation Example

Here is a complete Python example using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai. It extracts structured entities from a product review using JSON mode.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.getenv("OXLO_API_KEY"),
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1"
)

schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "product_name": {"type": "string"},
        "price_mentioned": {"type": "string"},
        "sentiment": {"type": "string", "enum": ["positive", "negative", "neutral"]},
        "issues": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}
    },
    "required": ["product_name", "sentiment"]
}

review = """
I bought the Acme Wireless Headphones last week for $129. 
Sound quality is excellent, but the right earcup stopped charging after two days.
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are a precise NER engine. Extract entities according to the JSON schema. Return only valid JSON."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": f"Extract entities from this review:\n{review}\n\nSchema: {schema}"
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    temperature=0.1
)

result = response.choices[0].message.content
print(result)

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, this code runs with no client library changes. You can replace the model string with qwen3-32b, deepseek-r1-671b, or any other model in the catalog. Streaming is also supported if you want to process partial entities as they arrive.

Cost Efficiency at Scale

Token-based billing creates a misalignment between infrastructure costs and business value. A NER request that returns 50 entities costs the same as one that returns zero, because billing is tied to characters processed, not business outcomes extracted.

Oxlo.ai flips this with flat per-request pricing. If you are building an agentic pipeline that feeds NER outputs into downstream tools, the cost of each reasoning step is bounded. You can pass large context windows, include few-shot examples, and attach tool definitions without worrying about token multiplication.

For teams evaluating inference providers, Oxlo.ai offers a Free tier with 60 requests per day across 16+ models, including a 7-day full-access trial. The Pro tier provides 1,000 requests per day for $80 per month, and Premium offers 5,000 requests per day with priority queue access for $350 per month. Enterprise plans add dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30% savings versus your current provider. Full details are at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

When your NER workload moves from short tweets to long-form contracts, the cost advantage of request-based pricing becomes structural. You stop optimizing prompts solely to save tokens and start optimizing for accuracy.

Conclusion

Named Entity Recognition has evolved from custom model training to prompt engineering over general-purpose LLMs. The remaining bottleneck is inference economics. By using JSON mode, structured prompts, and flat per-request pricing, you can build NER pipelines that are both more flexible and more predictable than traditional token-based stacks.

Oxlo.ai gives you the model variety, OpenAI-compatible API, and pricing model to treat NER as a standard API call rather than a specialized ML project. Whether you are extracting entities from a single sentence or a million-token corpus, the cost stays flat and the integration stays simple.

title: Dialogue Systems with LLMs: Advances and Applications
content:
Modern dialogue systems have moved far beyond slot-filling chatbots. Powered by large language models, today's conversational agents handle multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and long-context retention across customer support, coding assistants, and autonomous agents. The shift from rigid decision trees to probabilistic generation introduces new infrastructure demands. Latency, context window management, and cost scaling with conversation length are now central engineering concerns. Teams must also handle state persistence, retrieval augmentation, and structured output validation. For teams building these systems, the underlying inference platform determines whether a dialogue agent is responsive, affordable, and capable of maintaining coherence across extended sessions.

Architecture of Modern LLM Dialogue Systems

A production dialogue system is more than a prompt sent to a chat endpoint. It is a pipeline that manages state, grounds responses in external data, and executes actions on behalf of the user. At the core, an LLM consumes a structured conversation history, typically formatted as a list of system, user, and assistant messages. The system prompt defines persona, constraints, and available tools, while the message history provides context for coherent multi-turn exchanges. In practice, maintaining state requires careful handling of context window limits. When conversations exceed model capacity, developers must choose between truncation, summarization, or external memory stores, each introducing latency and potential information loss.

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG
