title: Conversational AI Tutorial for Beginners
content:
We are going to build a working customer support agent that answers questions about a fictional electronics shop, remembers conversation history, and looks up mock order status. If you have never built a conversational AI app before, this tutorial will give you a complete script you can run and extend in under an hour.

What you'll need

Before we start, grab the following items.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed on your machine.
  • The OpenAI Python SDK. Install it with pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key. Sign up at https://portal.oxlo.ai and create a key from the dashboard. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with the OpenAI SDK, so the code below works without any adapter libraries.

I also recommend creating a fresh virtual environment so dependencies stay clean.

Step 1: Create the client

First, we instantiate the OpenAI client pointing at Oxlo.ai. I like to verify the connection with a single-turn request before adding any complexity. We will use Llama 3.3 70B, Oxlo.ai's general-purpose flagship, because it is reliable for straightforward instructions.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say hello like a support agent."}
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Run the script. If you see a friendly greeting, your environment and API key are configured correctly.

Step 2: Write the system prompt

The system prompt is where we define the agent's personality, tone, and guardrails. Keeping it editable makes later tuning easy. Our fictional store is called QuickGadget. The agent should stay concise, polite, and never invent policies.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a customer support agent for QuickGadget, an online electronics store.
Your job is to answer questions about store hours, return policies, and order status.
Be concise and friendly. If you do not know something, say so and offer to escalate.
Current store hours: 9am to 6pm Pacific, Monday through Saturday.
Return policy: items may be returned within 30 days with the original receipt."""

Store this variable at the top of your file. Every request we send to Oxlo.ai will include it as the first message in the array.

Step 3: Build the chat loop

A support conversation is not a single question and answer. The model needs to see the full history so it can resolve follow-ups like "What about Friday?" or "How do I start a return?" We maintain a Python list called messages, append each user turn and assistant reply, and send the entire list every time. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat, request-based pricing rather than charging per token, you can pass a long conversation history without worrying about input length driving up cost. That makes it a strong fit for support bots where context accumulates quickly.

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("QuickGadget Support Agent (type 'exit' to quit)")
while True:
    user_input = input("\nCustomer: ")
    if user_input.lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
        break

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages
    )

    reply = response.choices[0].message.content
    print(f"Agent: {reply}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

Try running this. Ask about store hours, then ask a follow-up question. The agent will remember the context because the full thread is included in every API call.

Step 4: Add a tool for order lookups

Answering policy questions is useful, but a real support agent needs to act on data. We will give our agent a mock order database and teach it to call a Python function when the user asks about an order. For tool use, I switch to Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai because it is explicitly tuned for agent workflows and function calling. Oxlo.ai hosts this model with no cold starts, so the first request after idle time is just as fast as the tenth.

We define the tool schema in OpenAI format, then update the loop so that when the model requests a tool call, we execute the function, append the result as a tool message, and ask the model to generate the final reply. The SDK handles the JSON schema, and Oxlo.ai's endpoint parses it the same way OpenAI does.

import json

MOCK_ORDERS = {
    "ORD-1001": {"status": "shipped", "item": "Wireless Headphones"},
    "ORD-1002": {"status": "processing", "item": "USB-C Cable Pack"},
}

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str:
    order = MOCK_ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if not order:
        return "Order not found. Please double-check the ID."
    return f"Order {order_id} ({order['item']}) is currently {order['status']}."

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Retrieve the status of a customer order by ID.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The order ID, for example ORD-1001."
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

print("QuickGadget Support Agent (type 'exit' to quit)")
while True:
    user_input = input("\nCustomer: ")
    if user_input.lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
        break

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="qwen-3-32b",
        messages=messages,
        tools=tools,
        tool_choice="auto"
    )

    assistant_message = response.choices[0].message

    if assistant_message.tool_calls:
        messages.append({
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": assistant_message.content or "",
            "tool_calls": [tc.model_dump() for tc in assistant_message.tool_calls]
        })

        for tc in assistant_message.tool_calls:
            if tc.function.name == "get_order_status":
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
                result = get_order_status(args["order_id"])
                messages.append({
                    "role": "tool",
                    "tool_call_id": tc.id,
                    "content": result
                })

        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="qwen-3-32b",
            messages=messages,
            tools=tools
        )
        assistant_message = response.choices[0].message

    reply = assistant_message.content
    print(f"Agent: {reply}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

The loop now handles the full tool lifecycle. When the user mentions an order ID, Qwen 3 32B emits a structured tool call, we run the lookup, and the model synthesizes a natural sentence from the result.

Run it

Save the file as support_agent.py, export your key with export OXLO_API_KEY=..., and run python support_agent.py. The agent will prompt you for input. Try asking about store hours, then immediately ask about an order. Here is a sample conversation from my terminal.

QuickGadget Support Agent (type 'exit' to quit)

Customer: What are your store hours?
Agent: Our store hours are 9am to 6pm Pacific, Monday through Saturday.

Customer: Can I return a keyboard I bought 10 days ago?
Agent: Yes, you can return it within 30 days with the original receipt.

Customer: Where is order ORD-1001?
Agent: Order ORD-1001 (Wireless Headphones) is currently shipped.

Customer: thanks
Agent: You're welcome. Let us know if you need anything else.

If the agent ever sounds off, tweak the system prompt and rerun. Because Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, the loop feels instant even when you restart the script repeatedly.

What to build next

You now have a conversational skeleton that you can harden into production. Two concrete directions to explore next.

First, replace the MOCK_ORDERS dictionary with a real database query or an internal API call. The tool structure stays identical. You only change the body of get_order_status, which means your agent can start touching real business data within minutes.

Second, add a second tool that lets the agent escalate to a human, for example by sending a Slack message or an email when sentiment turns negative or the user explicitly asks for a manager. Models like Kimi K2.6 on Oxlo.ai excel at advanced reasoning and agentic coding, so they can handle multi-tool sessions and long context windows without losing track of the goal. If you later want to accept screenshots of broken items, you can upgrade the same script to a vision model such as Kimi VL A3B because Oxlo.ai exposes them through the same chat completions endpoint.

Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request rather than per token, long support threads with full history and multi-turn tool use remain predictable. You can see the exact cost structure at https://oxlo.ai/pricing. That predictability matters when you are debugging and iterating on agent behavior, because you can run dozens of long conversations without surprise fees.

title: Building Conversational AI with LLMs: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Last week I shipped a conversational support agent for a small e-commerce stack. It handles order lookups and return policy questions without hallucinating details it does not know. Here is exactly how I built it on Oxlo.ai using their OpenAI-compatible API.

What you'll need

Before we start, grab Python 3.10 or newer and install the SDK with pip install openai. You will need an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. A free Oxlo.ai account gives you 60 requests per day, which is plenty to test this build. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request instead of per token, you can stuff the context window with long system prompts and multi-turn history without watching metered costs climb. See the exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Verify the connection

I always start with a smoke test. There is no point debugging prompt logic if the endpoint or key is misconfigured. I store the key in an environment variable instead of hardcoding it. This script calls Llama 3.3 70B through Oxlo.ai and asks for a fixed string. Because the Oxlo.ai endpoint is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, the only difference from a standard client is the base URL and key. If you see "Connection OK", you are ready to build. Oxlo.ai serves popular models with no cold starts, so this should return immediately.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "Say 'Connection OK' and nothing else."}
    ]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Lock down the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between you and the model. It defines the persona, the available capabilities, and the guardrails. I keep it in a top-level variable so product managers can edit it later without touching Python logic. The key constraint here is telling the agent to only use tool results or explicit context, never to invent order numbers or tracking details. A tight system prompt is the cheapest guardrail you can deploy.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a customer support agent for an online electronics store.
You can help users with:
- General return policy questions (returns accepted within 30 days with receipt)
- Order status lookups (you have access to a lookup_order function)
- General product questions

Rules:
- Only use information from the provided context or tool results.
- If you do not know something, say so clearly.
- Do not make up order numbers, tracking numbers, or prices.
- Be concise but polite.
"""

Step 3: Add conversation memory

An agent without memory is just a fancy autocomplete. I use a module-level list to hold the message history. In production you would swap this for Redis or Postgres, but a Python list is enough to prove the concept. Every turn appends both the user message and the assistant reply, so the model sees the full thread on the next request. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, growing this history does not inflate your bill the way token-based providers do.

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

def chat(user_input):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages
    )
    
    reply = response.choices[0].message.content
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

Step 4: Define the order lookup tool

Real support requires real data. I define a mock orders database and expose it to the model through the standard OpenAI tools schema. Oxlo.ai supports function calling on Llama 3.3 70B, so the SDK format works without changes. Keeping the data layer separate means the LLM reasons about orders instead of hallucinating them. The JSON schema in the tools list is the only mapping layer between natural language and your Python functions.

import json

ORDERS = {
    "ORD-1001": {"status": "shipped", "item": "Mechanical Keyboard", "eta": "Dec 10"},
    "ORD-1002": {"status": "processing", "item": "Webcam 4K", "eta": "Dec 12"}
}

def lookup_order(order_id: str):
    return ORDERS.get(order_id, {"error": "Order not found"})

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Retrieve order status and estimated delivery date",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "Order ID such as ORD-1001"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

Step 5: Build the agent loop

Now I wire memory and tools together. The loop sends the user message to the model. If the model returns a tool call, I execute the local Python function, append the result back into the message list, and ask the model to generate the final answer. This two-pass pattern, sometimes called reasoning then acting, keeps the model grounded in facts. The tool_choice="auto" parameter lets the model decide whether to call a function or answer directly. I append the tool results with role "tool" so the model knows they came from an external system, not from the user. This replaces the simple chat function from Step 3.

messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}]

def run_agent(user_input):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    
    # First pass: decide if a tool is needed
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        tools=tools,
        tool_choice="auto"
    )
    
    message = response.choices[0].message
    
    if message.tool_calls:
        # Append the assistant's tool request to history
        messages.append({
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": message.content or "",
            "tool_calls": [
                {
                    "id": tc.id,
                    "type": tc.type,
                    "function": {
                        "name": tc.function.name,
                        "arguments": tc.function.arguments
                    }
                } for tc in message.tool_calls
            ]
        })
        
        # Execute each tool call and append results
        for tc in message.tool_calls:
            if tc.function.name == "lookup_order":
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
                result = lookup_order(args["order_id"])
                messages.append({
                    "role": "tool",
                    "tool_call_id": tc.id,
                    "content": json.dumps(result)
                })
        
        # Second pass: generate the natural language answer
        final = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=messages,
            tools=tools
        )
        reply = final.choices[0].message.content
    else:
        reply = message.content
    
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
    return reply

Run it

Here is how I test the finished agent locally. Notice how the second question references the keyboard from the first turn. That happens because the shared messages list preserves context across calls. If the agent ever feels too verbose, you can add "Keep answers under two sentences" to the system prompt and rerun without touching the loop logic.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("User: Where is my order ORD-1001?")
    print("Agent:", run_agent("Where is my order ORD-1001?"))
    print()
    print("User: Can I return the keyboard if I do not like it?")
    print("Agent:", run_agent("Can I return the keyboard if I do not like it?"))

Expected output:

User: Where is my order ORD-1001?
Agent: Your order ORD-1001 for the Mechanical Keyboard has shipped and is estimated to arrive by Dec 10.

User: Can I return the keyboard if I do not like it?
Agent: Yes, you can return the keyboard within 30 days with a receipt. Since it is part of order ORD-1001, it qualifies as long as you are within the return window.

Wrap-up and next steps

This agent works, but it is still a local script. The next concrete step is to replace the ORDERS dictionary with a real database query or HTTP call to your existing order management system. After that, wrap the run_agent function in a FastAPI endpoint so your frontend or support chat widget can reach it. You should also add a small evaluation suite of ten common user questions so you can regression test prompt changes.

If you need stronger reasoning for complex escalation logic, try swapping the model to kimi-k2.6 or deepseek-v3.2 on Oxlo.ai without changing any client code. Because Oxlo.ai offers flat per-request pricing, adding long system instructions or multi-turn context for agentic workflows stays predictable. Check the latest model list and pricing at https://oxlo.ai/pricing and start building.

title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using LLM
content:
We are building an LLM fit-checker that scores a business task on the core trade-offs of using a large language model: flexibility versus consistency, speed versus depth, and cost versus accuracy. It helps teams stop guessing about where LLMs actually help and where they create liability. I will walk through a complete Python implementation you can run today against Oxlo.ai.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

Step 1: Bootstrap the client and schema

I start by pinning the Oxlo.ai client and a JSON schema so the evaluator stays structured. I default to llama-3.3-70b because it follows system instructions tightly.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

EVALUATION_SCHEMA = {
    "task_summary": "string",
    "recommended": "bool",
    "confidence": "1-10",
    "advantages": ["string"],
    "disadvantages": ["string"],
    "mitigations": ["string"],
    "risk_level": "low|medium|high"
}

Step 2: The system prompt

The system prompt forces the model to act as a skeptical engineering lead. It must return only JSON.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a pragmatic engineering lead evaluating whether a given task is a good fit for a large language model.

Analyze the user's task description and return a single JSON object matching this schema:
- task_summary: a one-sentence summary of the task
- recommended: true if an LLM is a strong fit, false otherwise
- confidence: integer 1-10
- advantages: list of specific LLM strengths for this task
- disadvantages: list of specific LLM weaknesses or risks for this task
- mitigations: list of concrete ways to reduce the risks
- risk_level: "low", "medium", or "high"

Rules:
- Be specific. Avoid generic statements like "LLMs are fast." Instead say "LLMs can draft first-pass documentation in seconds, reducing writer overhead."
- Flag hallucination risk whenever the task involves precise facts, numbers, or compliance requirements.
- Flag cost and latency risks when the task requires long context or iterative reasoning.
- Output ONLY valid JSON. No markdown fences, no commentary.
"""

Step 3: Evaluate a task

This function calls Oxlo.ai with JSON mode enabled and parses the result.

def evaluate_task(task_description: str, model: str = "llama-3.3-70b"):
    user_message = f"Task to evaluate:\n{task_description}"
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Cross-model validation

LLMs disagree. I run the same task through kimi-k2.6 to see if its reasoning weights surface different risks, then compare. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, adding a second or third model for validation does not inflate cost as prompts grow. You can verify the exact rate on the pricing page.

def compare_evaluations(task: str):
    models = {
        "generalist": "llama-3.3-70b",
        "reasoning": "kimi-k2.6",
        "multilingual_coding": "qwen-3-32b",
    }
    
    results = {}
    for label, model_id in models.items():
        results[label] = evaluate_task(task, model=model_id)
    
    return results

Step 5: Render the report

Finally, format the structured results into a readable markdown report.

def print_report(task: str, results: dict):
    print(f"# LLM Fit Report: {task[:50]}...\n")
    
    for label, data in results.items():
        print(f"## {label.upper()} ({data.get('confidence', 'N/A')}/10 confidence)")
        verdict = "Proceed" if data.get("recommended") else "Avoid"
        print(f"**Verdict:** {verdict}  ")
        print(f"**Risk:** {data.get('risk_level', 'unknown')}\n")
        
        print("**Advantages:**")
        for a in data.get("advantages", []):
            print(f"- {a}")
        
        print("\n**Disadvantages:**")
        for d in data.get("disadvantages", []):
            print(f"- {d}")
        
        print("\n**Mitigations:**")
        for m in data.get("mitigations", []):
            print(f"- {m}")
        
        print("\n---\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    task = (
        "Read customer support emails, identify refund requests, "
        "calculate the refund amount from the order history in the email thread, "
        "and approve or escalate based on company policy."
    )
    
    findings = compare_evaluations(task)
    print_report(task, findings)

Run it

Save the script as llm_eval.py, export your key, and run it.

export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
python llm_eval.py

Example output for the refund-processing task:

# LLM Fit Report: Read customer support emails, identify refund re...

## GENERALIST (7/10 confidence)
**Verdict:** Avoid  
**Risk:** high

**Advantages:**
- LLMs excel at parsing unstructured email text and extracting intent.
- Can classify sentiment and urgency instantly at scale.

**Disadvantages:**
- Hallucination risk on arithmetic: the model may miscalculate refund totals.
- Policy interpretation requires exact rule matching, which LLMs approximate.

**Mitigations:**
- Use the LLM only for intent classification, not calculation.
- Route all refund amounts to a deterministic calculator.

---

## REASONING (6/10 confidence)
**Verdict:** Avoid  
**Risk:** high

**Advantages:**
- Strong chain-of-thought reasoning can map complex email threads to policy clauses.
- Can generate explicit rationale for audit trails.

**Disadvantages:**
- Reasoning increases latency and token consumption.
- Even with reasoning, numeric precision is not guaranteed without tool use.

**Mitigations:**
- Pair the LLM with a Python interpreter tool for exact math.
- Keep a human in the loop for approvals above a threshold.

---

## MULTILINGUAL_CODING (7/10 confidence)
**Verdict:** Avoid  
**Risk:** high

**Advantages:**
- Capable of extracting entities from mixed-language email threads.
- Can suggest policy clauses from a knowledge base quickly.

**Disadvantages:**
- Coding-oriented token distribution does not guarantee financial accuracy.
- May invent order IDs or amounts if the email thread is ambiguous.

**Mitigations:**
- Validate every extracted order ID against the CRM before calculation.
- Use the LLM for triage, not for final approval.

Wrap-up

This evaluator gives you a repeatable, evidence-based way to decide where LLMs earn their place and where they create technical debt. Two concrete next steps: integrate the script into your design-review CI so every new feature gets an LLM risk score, or extend it to test actual Oxlo.ai model outputs against a golden dataset using deepseek-v3.2 for code-centric evaluations. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, running large evaluation suites over long contexts stays predictable. Check the pricing page to see how flat pricing affects workload costs.

title: LLM vs Traditional Machine Learning: Understanding the Difference
content:
We are going to build a support ticket classifier that routes incoming text to Billing, Technical, or Account teams. A traditional machine learning approach would need labeled datasets, feature engineering, and model retraining every time categories change. We will skip all of that and use a large language model hosted on Oxlo.ai to classify tickets from natural language instructions alone. If you run a support queue and do not want to maintain a separate ML pipeline, this is for you.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which you can install with pip.

pip install openai

Finally, grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, so experimenting with a few dozen tickets will not scale in cost with input length the way token-based providers do. You can see the exact structure on the pricing page.

Step 1: Configure the client

In a traditional machine learning project, the first step is usually loading pandas, scikit-learn, and a serialized model from disk. You would also need to recreate the exact vectorization pipeline used during training, match dependency versions, and ensure the production environment has the same Python runtime. With an LLM, we skip the heavy infrastructure and instantiate a single client. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, this requires only a base URL change and an API key. There are no model files to version, no CUDA drivers to align, and no pickle files that break across Python upgrades. I will use the Llama 3.3 70B model as our classifier engine because it handles instruction following reliably and is available on Oxlo.ai with no cold starts, so the first request is as fast as the hundredth.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

Step 2: Write the system prompt

Traditional ML classifiers learn from thousands of labeled examples. You would spend hours cleaning the text, handling stop words, building a vocabulary, converting everything to TF-IDF vectors or sentence embeddings, then fitting a logistic regression or Random Forest. If you wanted a calibrated confidence score, you would add Platt scaling or isotonic regression. The equivalent step here is writing a clear system prompt. The prompt defines the categories, the output schema, and the decision rules. It also asks the model to report its own confidence, which removes the need for a separate calibration layer. If the business logic changes later, you edit the prompt and redeploy. You do not need to collect new data, re-label historical tickets, or manage a training pipeline.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket classifier.
Your job is to read the user's ticket and return a JSON object with two keys:
  - category: one of ["Billing", "Technical", "Account"]
  - confidence: a float between 0.0 and 1.0

Rules:
- Billing: payment failures, refunds, invoice questions, or charge disputes.
- Technical: bugs, crashes, integration errors, or API failures.
- Account: password resets, user provisioning, role changes, or plan upgrades.

If the ticket spans multiple categories, pick the dominant one.
Be conservative. If you are unsure, set confidence below 0.7."""

Step 3: Build the classifier function

Now we perform inference. In a traditional pipeline, this step would involve loading a vectorizer from disk, transforming the raw string into numerical features, running the model forward pass, and mapping the output index back to a human label. You would also need to handle out-of-vocabulary words that never appeared in training. With Oxlo.ai, we send the raw text and the prompt to the model over HTTPS. I use JSON mode so the response is parseable without fragile regex. The function below takes raw ticket text and returns a Python dict. This single API call replaces the inference server, vectorizer, label encoder, and calibration step you would need in a traditional scikit-learn pipeline. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, the cost is the same whether the ticket is two sentences or two paragraphs.

def classify_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Add confidence guardrails

A traditional classifier outputs a probability distribution across labels. Those probabilities are useful for escalation logic, and production systems often threshold at 0.5 or 0.7 to flag uncertain predictions. We can get the same behavior by asking the LLM to self-evaluate confidence in the prompt. If the model reports a score below 0.7, we route the ticket to a human instead of auto-assigning it. This keeps the automation honest and prevents the LLM from forcing a category when the text is ambiguous. It also mirrors the production guardrails you would wrap around any ML service, giving you a clear audit trail for why a ticket was escalated.

def route_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    result = classify_ticket(ticket_text)
    category = result.get("category", "Unknown")
    confidence = result.get("confidence", 0.0)

    if confidence < 0.7:
        return {
            "action": "escalate",
            "reason": f"Low confidence ({confidence}) for predicted category {category}",
            "ticket": ticket_text,
        }

    return {
        "action": "route",
        "category": category,
        "confidence": confidence,
        "ticket": ticket_text,
    }

Step 5: Process a batch of tickets

Traditional models suffer from concept drift. When your product changes or you add a new feature, the vocabulary in your tickets shifts and model performance degrades. You would need to collect new labeled data, retrain, validate, and redeploy. With this LLM approach, you simply edit the prompt. To prove the point, let us process three realistic tickets that use different wording, lengths, and edge cases. Notice that we never trained on these examples. The model generalizes from the definitions in the system prompt, which is the fundamental difference between LLMs and traditional supervised learning. You can add a new category tomorrow by updating the prompt, not by retraining a model.

TICKETS = [
    "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month. Can you reverse the second charge?",
    "The OAuth redirect throws a 500 error after the latest release. None of our users can log in.",
    "Please add Marco to our workspace and give him admin rights.",
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for t in TICKETS:
        decision = route_ticket(t)
        print(json.dumps(decision, indent=2))
        print("---")

Run it

Save the complete script as ticket_classifier.py, export your key, and execute it. You should see structured routing decisions in under a second per ticket because Oxlo.ai serves popular models without cold starts. If you want to try a different reasoning style, you can swap the model string to qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 without changing any other logic. That is another advantage over traditional ML, where switching architectures is a major project.

export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
python ticket_classifier.py

Here is the output I got on my first run:

{
  "action": "route",
  "category": "Billing",
  "confidence": 0.95,
  "ticket": "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month. Can you reverse the second charge?"
}
---
{
  "action": "route",
  "category": "Technical",
  "confidence": 0.92,
  "ticket": "The OAuth redirect throws a 500 error after the latest release. None of our users can log in."
}
---
{
  "action": "route",
  "category": "Account",
  "confidence": 0.89,
  "ticket": "Please add Marco to our workspace and give him admin rights."
}

Wrap-up

We built a working ticket classifier in about fifty lines of Python. There was no data labeling, no feature engineering, no hyperparameter tuning, and no model training loop. That is the core difference between LLMs and traditional machine learning. The LLM is pre-trained on broad language understanding, so you program it with instructions and examples in the prompt rather than by updating model weights. You trade compute at training time for compute at inference time, and you gain flexibility in return.

If you want to take this further, wire the script into a webhook that ingests real tickets from your help desk and writes the routing decisions into Slack or Zendesk. You could also A/B test this LLM classifier against your existing traditional model on a held-out dataset to measure accuracy and latency side by side. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing makes those experiments predictable, because long ticket descriptions do not inflate your bill the way token-based pricing would. Check the pricing page to see how the costs compare for your volume.

title: Unlocking the Power of LLM for Natural Language Processing
content:
Natural language processing has moved from academic research to production-critical infrastructure. Large language models now handle translation, summarization, classification, entity extraction, and multi-step agentic reasoning with accuracy that seemed impossible five years ago. Yet the real bottleneck for most engineering teams is not model capability. It is the inference layer: unpredictable costs, cold starts, and token-based billing that scales linearly with prompt length. If you are building NLP pipelines today, the model you choose matters, but the platform serving that model matters just as much.

Why LLMs Changed NLP Forever

Before the current generation of large language models, NLP pipelines were fragmented. Engineers trained or fine-tuned separate models for sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, question answering, and summarization. Each task required curated datasets, custom architectures, and expensive retraining when distributions shifted.

LLMs collapsed these silos into a single interface. Through in-context learning and instruction tuning, one model can perform dozens of NLP tasks with only prompt engineering or minimal fine-tuning. This unification accelerated product development, but it also concentrated computational load at inference time. Instead of running a small DistilBERT model on a CPU, you are now sending large contexts to a 70B-parameter model over an API. That shift makes inference pricing and latency central to system design, not an afterthought.

The Hidden Cost of Token-Based Inference

Most inference providers bill by the token. Input tokens and output tokens are metered separately, and costs grow with every character you send. For standard chat this is manageable. For production NLP it is a constraint. Long-document Q&A, retrieval-augmented generation with large chunk sizes, and agent loops that carry full conversation history all inflate the input side of the equation. Providers like Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale use this token-based model, which means your bill scales directly with prompt length.

Oxlo.ai takes a different approach. The platform charges one flat cost per API request regardless of how many tokens are in the prompt. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can be significantly cheaper because cost does not scale with input length. You can pass full documents, maintain extended conversation buffers, and return structured JSON without constantly calculating token budgets. If you want to see how this fits your workload, check the details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Matching the Model to the Task

NLP is not a single problem. Classification, generation, code synthesis, and multilingual understanding place different demands on a model. Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories, so you can route tasks to the right architecture instead of forcing every request through a generalist endpoint.

For reasoning and chat, Llama 3.3 70B serves as a strong general-purpose flagship, while DeepSeek R1 671B MoE handles deep reasoning and complex coding. Qwen 3 32B excels at multilingual agent workflows, and Kimi K2.6 brings advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision support with a 131K context window. If you need efficient long-context processing, DeepSeek V4 Flash offers a 1M context window with near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning.

For code-centric NLP, Qwen 3 Coder 30B, DeepSeek Coder, and Oxlo.ai Coder Fast provide specialized completions. Vision-language tasks such as document understanding can use Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B. For retrieval and clustering pipelines, embedding models like BGE-Large and E5-Large are available through the embeddings endpoint. Audio transcription with Whisper Large v3 and text-to-speech with Kokoro 82M round out the stack for multimodal applications.

Drop-In Infrastructure with OpenAI SDK Compatibility

Switching inference providers should not require a client rewrite. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, which means you can point your existing Python, Node.js, or cURL code to a new base URL and keep the same request shapes.

The base URL is https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. The platform supports streaming responses, function calling, JSON mode, vision inputs, and multi-turn conversations. There are no cold starts on popular models, so latency stays predictable. Below is a minimal example that sends a structured entity extraction request and streams the result:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise NLP assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Extract all named entities from the following text..."}
    ],
    stream=True,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

for chunk in response:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

Because the endpoint shape is identical, you can migrate gradually. Route experimental traffic to Oxlo.ai, compare latency and output quality, and scale up without touching your application logic.

Designing NLP Pipelines That Scale

Production NLP rarely involves a single prompt. It is usually a pipeline: ingest a document, chunk it, embed it, retrieve relevant passages, synthesize an answer, and validate structured output. Agentic systems add tool calls and multi-step reasoning loops. Each step can carry thousands of tokens of context.

Under token-based pricing, every extra sentence in your prompt or every additional retrieved paragraph adds marginal cost. Engineering teams start compressing prompts, truncating history, or limiting retrieval depth to control spend. These optimizations often hurt accuracy.

With Oxlo.ai, the flat per-request pricing removes that tension. You can send full documents in one call, maintain complete conversation history across agent steps, and retrieve generously without watching a meter spin. The free tier offers 60 requests per day across more than 16 models, including a seven-day full-access trial, which makes it easy to prototype without a credit card. When you move to production, the Pro and Premium plans provide daily request allotments for all models, with priority queue access at the Premium level. Enterprise plans add dedicated GPUs and custom pricing.

Getting Started

Building modern NLP applications requires more than a capable model. It requires an inference layer that respects your budget, scales with your context windows, and does not force you to redesign your client code. Oxlo.ai provides 45+ models, request-based pricing that favors long-context workloads, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility.

Start with the free tier to test Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, or DeepSeek V4 Flash on your own data. Point your existing client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, enable streaming or JSON mode, and observe how flat per-request pricing changes the way you design prompts. For detailed plan information, visit https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: LLM for Text Generation: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
We are going to build a batch documentation generator that reads raw Python function signatures and writes Markdown docstrings with usage examples. It helps engineering teams keep internal library documentation current without manual editing. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per API request instead of per token, you can feed entire modules into the context window without the cost scaling with input length. This matters when you are documenting legacy codebases where every function carries twenty lines of type annotations and inline comments.

What you'll need

Before starting, make sure you have the following ready. You do not need any heavy frameworks. The goal is a single file you can drop into any repository and run immediately.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally.
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai.
  • A directory of .py files containing function stubs you want to document.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

I always verify the connection before building logic around it. There is nothing worse than debugging a file parser when the real problem is a misconfigured base URL. Create a file named docgen.py and initialize the OpenAI-compatible client pointing at Oxlo.ai. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it handles technical syntax reliably, supports long context, and has no cold starts on Oxlo.ai. Run this snippet on its own. If you see OK printed to your terminal, the backend is ready and you can move on.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say OK"}],
    max_tokens=10
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Lock down the system prompt

The system prompt is the only prose we write by hand. It forces the model to emit strict Markdown, skip conversational fluff, and include type annotations. Without these constraints, the model tends to add preamble like "Certainly, here is the documentation" which breaks automated pipelines. I keep it as a module-level constant so tuning it does not require touching business logic. You can tweak the tone or add a section for raised exceptions later by editing just this string.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical documentation generator.
You receive a Python function signature and docstring.
You output Markdown containing:
1. A heading with the function name.
2. A description paragraph.
3. An Args table with types and descriptions.
4. A Returns description.
5. A Python code block showing realistic usage.
Do not include introductory phrases like "Here is the documentation".
Output only the Markdown."""

Step 3: Generate docs for one function

Now we write the wrapper that sends a single function to Oxlo.ai. I enable streaming so long docstrings render in real time instead of blocking until the full payload is ready. This also lets you interrupt generation early if the model goes off format. The function appends every delta content chunk into a list and joins them at the end. I avoid string concatenation in a loop because Python lists are cheaper for accumulation.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical documentation generator.
You receive a Python function signature and docstring.
You output Markdown containing:
1. A heading with the function name.
2. A description paragraph.
3. An Args table with types and descriptions.
4. A Returns description.
5. A Python code block showing realistic usage.
Do not include introductory phrases like "Here is the documentation".
Output only the Markdown."""

def generate_docs(function_code: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Document this function:\n\n{function_code}"},
        ],
        stream=True,
    )
    
    collected = []
    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
            collected.append(chunk.choices[0].delta.content)
    return "".join(collected)

Step 4: Batch process an entire directory

A real tool reads from disk and writes to disk. This step globs all Python files in a source directory, extracts top-level function definitions with a regex, and writes one Markdown file per input file into an output folder. In production you might prefer the ast module, but a regex keeps the tutorial self-contained and avoids extra dependencies. The extract_functions helper looks for def statements followed by triple-quoted docstrings. It is naive, but it works for the common case of module-level functions. If your codebase uses nested classes, you can swap this out for ast.parse later without touching the Oxlo.ai integration. The batch_generate function creates the output directory if it does not exist, then iterates over every .py file. For each function found, it calls generate_docs and collects the Markdown. A horizontal rule separates multiple functions in the same file so the resulting Markdown is still readable in any renderer.

import re
from pathlib import Path
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical documentation generator.
You receive a Python function signature and docstring.
You output Markdown containing:
1. A heading with the function name.
2. A description paragraph.
3. An Args table with types and descriptions.
4. A Returns description.
5. A Python code block showing realistic usage.
Do not include introductory phrases like "Here is the documentation".
Output only the Markdown."""

def generate_docs(function_code: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Document this function:\n\n{function_code}"},
        ],
        stream=True,
    )
    
    collected = []
    for chunk in response:
        if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
            collected.append(chunk.choices[0].delta.content)
    return "".join(collected)

def extract_functions(file_path: Path) -> list[str]:
    text = file_path.read_text()
    pattern = r"(def\s+\w+\([^)]*\)(?:\s*->\s*[^:]+)?:\s*(?:\"\"\"[\s\S]*?\"\"\")?)"
    return re.findall(pattern, text)

def batch_generate(src_dir: Path, out_dir: Path):
    out_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for py_file in src_dir.glob("*.py"):
        funcs = extract_functions(py_file)
        if not funcs:
            continue
        
        md_blocks = []
        for func in funcs:
            md_blocks.append(generate_docs(func))
        
        out_file = out_dir / f"{py_file.stem}.md"
        out_file.write_text("\n\n---\n\n".join(md_blocks))
        print(f"Wrote {out_file}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    batch_generate(Path("./src"), Path("./docs"))

Step 5: Sanity check with a hardcoded function

Before pointing the script at a real codebase, I test with one hardcoded stub. This isolates prompt issues from file system bugs and confirms the Markdown format is correct. The resize_image function below has typed arguments, a default value, and a return type, which exercises most of the prompt requirements. If the output skips the Args table or invents types that do not exist, you know the system prompt needs tightening before you burn through a batch of requests. Replace the bottom of docgen.py with this block.

TEST_FUNCTION = '''def resize_image(
    src_path: str,
    dst_path: str,
    width: int,
    height: int,
    maintain_aspect: bool = True
) -> bool:
    """Resize an image on disk and save it to a new path."""
'''

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(generate_docs(TEST_FUNCTION))

Run it

Save everything in docgen.py, replace YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY with your actual key, create a src folder with a few Python files, and run python docgen.py. The script streams Markdown to memory and writes it to the docs directory. You should see one .md file appear for every .py file that contained at least one function definition. Here is the output I received when I passed the resize_image stub through Oxlo.ai. Notice the model inferred reasonable descriptions from the parameter names and types alone, and generated a usage example that respects the default argument.

### resize_image

Resizes an image located at `src_path` and saves the result to `dst_path`.

| Arg | Type | Description |
|-----|------|-------------|
| src_path | str | Path to the source image file. |
| dst_path | str | Path where the resized image will be saved. |
| width | int | Target width in pixels. |
| height | int | Target height in pixels. |
| maintain_aspect | bool | If True, preserves the original aspect ratio. Defaults to True. |

**Returns:** `bool` indicating success or failure.

```python
ok = resize_image(
    src_path="input.jpg",
    dst_path="output.jpg",
    width=1920,
    height=1080,
    maintain_aspect=True
)
```

Wrap-up and next steps

You now have a working documentation generator that runs on Oxlo.ai. Because the platform uses request-based pricing, you can scale this to an entire monorepo without costs ballooning as context length grows. That is a significant departure from token-based providers, where pasting a thousand lines of context for a single request can become expensive. Two concrete next steps. First, rerun the pipeline with deepseek-v3.2 or qwen-3-32b to compare how different architectures handle technical language. Each model has its own formatting quirks, so you may find one produces cleaner tables. Second, wire the script into a Git pre-commit hook so documentation regenerates automatically on every push. If you are moving from a token-based provider, check https://oxlo.ai/pricing to see how flat-rate pricing changes the math for long-context workloads.

title: Code Analysis with LLM
content:
Today we are building a dead-simple code review CLI that feeds a Python file to an LLM and returns a structured analysis of bugs, complexity, and style issues. It is the kind of tool I hook into a pre-commit check when I want a second pair of eyes without spinning up an entire CI pipeline. We will run it on Oxlo.ai because their per-request pricing, detailed on their pricing page, means a 300-line file costs the same as a 10-line snippet. That flat cost removes the incentive to shrink or fragment code before review, which is exactly what you want when hunting for cross-function bugs.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which Oxlo.ai uses as a drop-in client because its API is fully compatible. Install it with pip. Grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal at https://portal.oxlo.ai. Finally, keep a messy Python file handy so we have something to analyze. I will use a deliberately flawed script later in the tutorial, but you can point the finished tool at any module you have on disk.

  • Python 3.10+
  • pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from the portal
  • A Python file you want reviewed

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

We instantiate the OpenAI SDK but point it at Oxlo.ai's base URL. This is the only change you need to make to a standard OpenAI client. I keep my key in an environment variable so it does not leak into shell history or source control. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so the first request after a break returns just as fast as the tenth.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"),
)

Step 2: Lock down the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between your code and the model. I force the model to return raw JSON with specific keys so we can pipe the output into linters, CI dashboards, or SARIF converters later. Without this constraint, the model drifts into markdown prose and breaks parsers. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and function calling, but for this tutorial we will achieve structure through prompt engineering alone. That keeps the script free of extra dependencies and works across every model on the platform, from DeepSeek to Kimi to Llama.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a senior staff engineer performing a concise code review.
Analyze the provided Python file and return a single JSON object with exactly these keys:

- summary: a one-sentence overall verdict.
- issues: a list of objects, each with severity (low, medium, high), line_number (int or null), and description (string).
- refactoring_suggestions: a list of strings describing concrete improvements.

Be terse. Focus on correctness, security, and performance. Do not wrap the JSON in markdown fences."""

Step 3: Read and package the source file

Next we read the file from disk and package it into a user message. I prepend a short instruction reminding the model that the code follows, which reduces the chance it hallucinates context from earlier turns. Since this is a single-shot tool, we do not need conversation history. I also read with explicit UTF-8 encoding to avoid platform-specific defaults mangling comments or type hints. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request instead of per token, we can pass the entire file without pre-counting characters, truncating docstrings, or stripping comments. That is a real cost advantage when you are analyzing legacy modules that stretch past a few hundred lines, and it means you catch bugs that hide in the boilerplate competitors might tell you to omit.

def analyze_file(filepath: str) -> dict:
    with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        code = f.read()

    user_message = f"Review the following Python file and return JSON.\n\n{code}"

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v3.2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return raw

Note that we are using deepseek-v3.2 here. Oxlo.ai carries several code-capable models, including kimi-k2.6 for advanced agentic coding and llama-3.3-70b for general purpose work, so you can swap IDs without changing any other logic.

Step 4: Call the model and parse the response

The raw response is a JSON string, but it sometimes comes with trailing commentary or leading whitespace. We strip it and parse with the standard library. If the model ever emits malformed JSON, we fall back to printing the raw text so the user can still see the analysis. I avoid pulling in Pydantic or similar libraries here so the script stays lightweight and portable. You could add retry logic around the API call, but Oxlo.ai serves these requests without cold starts, so transient latency is already minimal and a simple try-except keeps the codebase readable.

import json

def analyze_file(filepath: str) -> dict:
    with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        code = f.read()

    user_message = f"Review the following Python file and return JSON.\n\n{code}"

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v3.2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"error": "Failed to parse JSON", "raw": raw}

Step 5: Add a CLI wrapper

To make this usable from the terminal, we wire in argparse and pretty-print the results. I stick with the standard library rather than Click or Typer so you can copy the entire script into a utils folder and run it without creating a virtual environment or resolving dependency trees. I also add a small guard so missing environment variables fail fast with a clear message instead of a cryptic HTTP 401 traceback.

import argparse

def main():
    if not os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY"):
        raise SystemExit("Error: set the OXLO_API_KEY environment variable.")

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LLM-powered code review")
    parser.add_argument("filepath", help="Python file to analyze")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    result = analyze_file(args.filepath)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run it

Create a file named example.py with a deliberate bug so we can verify the tool catches it. Here is a small script with an unsafe SQL string concatenation and a redundant list copy.

# example.py
import sqlite3

def get_user(username):
    conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + username + "'"
    cursor.execute(query)
    return cursor.fetchone()

def process(items):
    new_list = []
    for i in range(len(items)):
        new_list.append(items[i])
    return new_list

Now run the analyzer from the same directory:

export OXLO_API_KEY="sk-oxlo.ai-..."
python analyzer.py example.py

You should see output similar to this:

{
  "summary": "The code contains a SQL injection vulnerability and an inefficient loop pattern.",
  "issues": [
    {
      "severity": "high",
      "line_number": 7,
      "description": "Unsafe string concatenation in SQL query enables injection attacks."
    },
    {
      "severity": "medium",
      "line_number": 12,
      "description": "Redundant manual loop copies a list instead of using list(items) or slicing."
    }
  ],
  "refactoring_suggestions": [
    "Use parameterized queries with cursor.execute(query, (username,)).",
    "Replace the process() loop with return list(items)."
  ]
}

Because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, passing a 200-line file with a long system prompt does not inflate the cost. That pricing model makes this kind of whole-file analysis practical for daily use. If you want to experiment, deepseek-v3.2 is available on the free tier, so you can test the loop without worrying about metered tokens.

Next steps

Two concrete ways to extend this. First, pipe git diff into the prompt instead of an entire file so the reviewer focuses only on what changed in the current branch. Second, add a severity filter so the CLI exits with a non-zero code when any high issue appears, which lets you block commits in a pre-commit hook. Both are straightforward additions to the script we just built on Oxlo.ai.

title: RAG Pipeline Tutorial
content:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is the dominant design pattern for grounding large language models in proprietary or rapidly changing data. Rather than fine-tuning a model on your internal documents, you store them in a searchable vector index and inject the most relevant passages into the prompt at inference time. This keeps answers current, reduces hallucinations, and avoids the expense of retraining. In this tutorial, you will build a minimal but production-ready RAG pipeline using Python, ChromaDB, and Oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai offers a fully OpenAI-compatible API for both embeddings and chat completion, with request-based pricing that remains flat regardless of how much retrieved context you pack into the prompt.

What is RAG and Why Build It

RAG bridges the gap between static model weights and dynamic knowledge. A base model only knows what it saw during pre-training. When you need answers from last quarter's sales reports, a private codebase, or an internal knowledge base, RAG retrieves the relevant text and presents it as context. The model then synthesizes an answer grounded in that evidence. This pattern is now standard for internal help desks, legal research tools, and software documentation agents. The core requirement is a reliable inference backend that can handle both embedding creation and long-context generation without unpredictable scaling costs. Oxlo.ai satisfies both requirements through a single, drop-in API.

Architecture Overview

A production RAG pipeline has four stages. First, you ingest source documents and split them into chunks that fit within your embedding model's input limit. Second, you vectorize those chunks using an embedding model and store the vectors alongside the raw text in a vector database. Third, at query time, you embed the user's question, perform a similarity search against the index, and retrieve the top-k chunks. Fourth, you feed those chunks into a chat model as system or user context and stream back an answer. Oxlo.ai provides the embedding and chat models for stages two and four, while ChromaDB, pgvector, or Weaviate can handle stage three. Because Oxlo.ai exposes standard OpenAI SDK endpoints, you can swap it into an existing pipeline with only a base URL change.

Step 1 - Chunking and Embedding

Document chunking is more art than science. For this tutorial, use a simple sliding-window splitter that respects a maximum character length. Aim for chunks between 256 and 512 tokens with a small overlap to preserve context across boundaries. Once chunked, you need to vectorize the text. Oxlo.ai hosts high-performance embedding models including BGE-Large and E5-Large, accessible through the familiar OpenAI embeddings interface.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY")
)

def split_text(text: str, chunk_size: int = 512, overlap: int = 50):
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap
    return chunks

def get_embedding(text: str):
    response = client.embeddings.create(
        model="bge-large",
        input=text
    )
    return response.data[0].embedding

The returned vectors are dense float arrays suitable for cosine similarity search. You can process batches of chunks in parallel to speed up ingestion, but even sequential processing is sufficient for small knowledge bases.

Step 2 - Vector Storage

For the vector store, ChromaDB is the quickest way to get started locally. It handles distance calculations and metadata filtering out of the box. In production, you might migrate to pgvector inside Postgres or a managed service, but the interface remains conceptually identical: add vectors, then query with a new vector to get the nearest neighbors.

import chromadb

chroma_client = chromadb.Client()
collection = chroma_client.create_collection(name="knowledge_base")

def index_chunks(ids, chunks, embeddings):
    collection.add(
        ids=ids,
        documents=chunks,
        embeddings=embeddings
    )

Make sure your IDs are deterministic or UUID-based so you can update documents later without duplicating entries. You can also store metadata such as source filenames to support citation in the final output.

Step 3 - Retrieval

When a user submits a query, embed it using the same model and search the collection. A top-k value between 3 and 5 is usually sufficient for short answers, though complex legal or technical queries may benefit from retrieving 10 or more chunks and then re-ranking with a cross-encoder. For now, perform a direct similarity search.

def retrieve_context(query: str, n_results: int = 4):
    q_embedding = get_embedding(query)
    results = collection.query(
        query_embeddings=[q_embedding],
        n_results=n_results
    )
    return results["documents"][0]

The returned strings are your evidence. Pass them directly into the generation stage. If you need source attribution, store page numbers and titles alongside each chunk in ChromaDB and surface them in your application layer.

Step 4 - Generation with Long Context

This is where Oxlo.ai differentiates itself for RAG workloads. Token-based providers scale cost with every token in the prompt,

title: Building a Document Summarization Tool with LLM
content:
I built a small CLI tool that turns long, unstructured documents into structured executive summaries. It reads any plain text file, splits it into overlapping chunks if needed, and uses an LLM to extract key points, obligations, and entities. If you process reports, transcripts, or legal text regularly, this saves hours of manual reading and gives you a consistent format you can scan in seconds.

What you'll need

Before running the script, make sure you have the following ready on your machine.

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed and available in your PATH.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key. You can grab one from the Oxlo.ai portal. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with daily requests, so you can test this pipeline without an upfront credit card.
  • The OpenAI SDK. Install it with pip install openai. Oxlo.ai is fully compatible with this SDK, so no custom client libraries are required.
  • A text file to test with, such as a long report, meeting transcript, or contract saved as document.txt in your working directory.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client and load the document

We start by initializing the OpenAI-compatible client pointing at Oxlo.ai. Swapping the base_url and api_key is the only change needed from a standard OpenAI setup. I prefer reading the key from an environment variable so it never sits in the script.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

def load_document(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return f.read()

raw_text = load_document("document.txt")
print(f"Loaded {len(raw_text)} characters")

At this point you should see the character count printed. If the file is large, that confirms we are working with the full text and not a truncated buffer.

Step 2: Chunk long text with overlap

Even models with large context windows benefit from focused sections. I split the text into 4,000 character chunks with 200 characters of overlap so no sentence gets cut in half at a boundary. This overlap keeps pronouns and references grounded across chunk boundaries.

def chunk_text(text: str, chunk_size: int = 4000, overlap: int = 200) -> list[str]:
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunks.append(text[start:end])
        start = end - overlap
    return chunks

chunks = chunk_text(raw_text)
print(f"Split into {len(chunks)} chunks")

If your document is under a few thousand characters, this returns a single chunk and the pipeline still works. For a twenty-page transcript, expect five to eight chunks. You could skip chunking entirely if you use a model like DeepSeek V4 Flash with its 1 million token context, but I find that chunking reduces lost-in-the-middle problems and keeps each summary tightly focused.

Step 3: Define the system prompt

A vague prompt produces vague summaries. I force the model to return a rigid structure so downstream parsing is easy. This prompt is the core instruction set for every chunk, and it intentionally forbids fluff like "Here is the summary".

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a precise document summarizer.
Read the provided text and produce exactly the following:
1. Main Point: one sentence describing the primary purpose of this section.
2. Key Details: three to five bullet points covering obligations, findings, or terms.
3. Entities: a bullet list of people, organizations, dates, and monetary values mentioned.
Be concise. Do not add introductory phrases like 'Here is the summary'.
"""

Keeping the output structured makes the final synthesis step more reliable. The model has less freedom to drift into narrative prose, which means the second pass has cleaner inputs to work with.

Step 4: Summarize each chunk via Oxlo.ai

We iterate over the chunks and call Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai for each one. Because Oxlo.ai uses flat per-request pricing, the cost is identical whether a chunk is 500 characters or 4,000 characters. That removes the usual token anxiety when feeding long context, and it makes budgeting for this pipeline straightforward. You can see the exact plan details at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

def summarize_chunk(text: str, index: int) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": f"Chunk {index + 1}:\n{text}"},
        ],
        temperature=0.2,
        max_tokens=1024,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

chunk_summaries = [summarize_chunk(c, i) for i, c in enumerate(chunks)]
print(f"Received {len(chunk_summaries)} partial summaries")

I set the temperature low because summarization is an extraction task, not a creative one. The max_tokens value gives enough room for a structured response without running away. If you need faster iteration during testing, swap in DeepSeek V3.2, which is available on Oxlo.ai and works well for concise reasoning tasks.

Step 5: Synthesize the final summary

Partial summaries often repeat themes or lack cross-section context. We feed all of them into Kimi K2.6 in a single request to produce a coherent executive brief that covers the entire document. This map-reduce pattern scales well because the first stage is embarrassingly parallel, and the second stage is one concentrated reasoning call.

def synthesize(summaries: list[str]) -> str:
    combined = "\n\n---\n\n".join(
        [f"Section {i+1}:\n{s}" for i, s in enumerate(summaries)]
    )

    merge_prompt = (
        "You are given partial summaries from consecutive sections of one document. "
        "Produce a unified executive summary with these sections:\n"
        "- Overall Purpose: one paragraph\n"
        "- Key Points: bullet list\n"
        "- Action Items or Risks: bullet list\n"
        "- Notable Entities: bullet list\n"
        "Be factual. Do not invent details not present in the source."
    )

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="kimi-k2.6",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": merge_prompt},
            {"role": "user", "content": combined},
        ],
        temperature=0.2,
        max_tokens=2048,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

final_summary = synthesize(chunk_summaries)
print(final_summary)

Kimi K2.6 handles the aggregation step cleanly because it excels at reasoning over multiple sources and maintaining consistency across long inputs. If you prefer, Qwen 3 32B is another solid option on Oxlo.ai for multilingual documents.

Run it

Save the full script as summarize.py, place document.txt in the same directory, export your key, and run the file. The pipeline loads the text, chunks it, calls Oxlo.ai for each section, then merges everything into a final brief.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raw_text = load_document("document.txt")
    chunks = chunk_text(raw_text)

    print(f"Processing {len(chunks)} chunks via Oxlo.ai...")
    chunk_summaries = [summarize_chunk(c, i) for i, c in enumerate(chunks)]

    print("\n=== FINAL SYNTHESIZED SUMMARY ===\n")
    print(synthesize(chunk_summaries))

With a sample six-page service agreement, the output looks like this:

Processing 3 chunks via Oxlo.ai...

=== FINAL SYNTHESIZED SUMMARY ===

Overall Purpose:
This agreement establishes a twelve-month software licensing arrangement between Acme Corp and the client, including support terms and data handling procedures.

Key Points:
- License is non-exclusive and non-transferable.
- Support hours are limited to business days, 9 AM to 5 PM EST.
- Data retention period is ninety days post-termination.
- Automatic renewal clause applies unless sixty days written notice is given.

Action Items or Risks:
- Review automatic renewal language before the end of term.
- Confirm data export procedures prior to termination.
- Ensure compliance with the ninety-day retention limit for sensitive records.

Notable Entities:
- Acme Corp
- Effective date: January 1, 2025
- Annual fee: $48,000
- Support tier: Business Plus

Wrap-up and next steps

The tool works end to end, but it is still a local script. A concrete next step is to wrap the pipeline in a FastAPI endpoint so other services can POST a document and receive JSON. Another improvement is to replace the text loader with PyPDF2 or pdfplumber so you can drop PDFs directly into the input folder without manual conversion.

If you run this pipeline frequently, compare your current token-based bill against Oxlo.ai flat per-request pricing. For long-context summarization workloads, the savings are often significant because input length does not affect the cost per call. You can check the latest plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing and scale up when you are ready.

title: Scaling LLM Inference: Best Practices and Innovations
content:
Scaling large language model inference from prototype to production requires more than wrapping a model in an endpoint. Engineering teams must balance throughput, latency, and cost while supporting increasingly complex workloads, from high-volume chat to multi-step agent pipelines. The right infrastructure decisions determine whether an application remains responsive under load or collapses under token costs. This post examines practical techniques for scaling inference, and where Oxlo.ai fits into a production stack.

Optimize Throughput with Batching and Scheduling

Throughput bottlenecks usually appear at the serving layer. Continuous batching, also called inflight batching, keeps the GPU saturated by dynamically grouping incoming requests instead of waiting for each sequence to finish before starting the next. The scheduler iteratively adds new requests to the current batch as soon as slots free up, which increases token generation throughput without adding proportional latency to individual users.

Priority queues matter when workloads mix real-time user requests with background jobs. Oxlo.ai offers a priority queue on its Premium tier, so critical traffic gets served first even during traffic spikes. Because Oxlo.ai maintains no cold starts on popular models, you do not waste GPU cycles on warmup overhead when scaling from zero to peak load. You pay per request, not per token, so aggressive batching strategies that increase prompt size do not inflate your bill. This lets you optimize for hardware utilization instead of token economy.

Reduce Latency with Speculative Decoding and Caching

Latency kills user experience. Two proven techniques are KV cache reuse and prefix caching. When a model processes a long prompt, storing the key-value attention states avoids recomputing them on subsequent turns. For applications with static system prompts, retrieved document chunks, or few-shot examples, prefix caching cuts time-to-first-token dramatically because the model only computes the delta between turns.

Speculative decoding uses a smaller draft model to predict multiple tokens ahead, which the larger target model verifies in parallel. When implemented correctly, it can reduce end-to-end latency by a meaningful factor without changing outputs. Oxlo.ai hosts long-context models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash with a 1 million token context window and Kimi K2.6 with 131K context. On these models, efficient cache management is not optional. Because Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, you can leverage full context windows for retrieval-augmented generation and document analysis without the cost volatility of token-based meters. You are free to pass lengthy legal contracts, codebase contexts, or conversation histories as needed.
