title: Hands-on LLM Tutorial: Getting Started with Oxlo
content:
We're going to build a support ticket triage agent that reads a raw customer message, classifies urgency, extracts the core issue, and drafts a first-response reply. It runs on Oxlo.ai's flat per-request API, so pasting in long conversation threads or log files does not inflate the cost. The whole pipeline is under sixty lines of Python and uses the standard OpenAI SDK, which means zero client-side refactoring if you are migrating from another provider.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an API key from Oxlo.ai.

pip install openai

Grab your key from the Oxlo.ai portal. If you want to see how the request-based pricing works for high-volume workloads, check the pricing page.

Step 1: Configure the client

Point the OpenAI SDK at Oxlo.ai. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI API compatible, the only change from a standard setup is the base_url and your Oxlo.ai API key. I am using Llama 3.3 70B because it follows structured instructions reliably for agent workflows, and there are no cold starts on popular models so the first request is as fast as the hundredth.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The prompt is the entire logic of the agent. I force JSON output so downstream code never has to guess.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent. Read the customer's message and produce a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- urgency: one of "low", "medium", "high", or "critical"
- issue_summary: a one-sentence description of the problem
- draft_reply: a polite, helpful first response under 150 words

Rules:
1. Output ONLY valid JSON. No markdown fences, no explanations.
2. If the customer mentions a security breach or outage, set urgency to "critical".
3. Keep the draft_reply empathetic and actionable."""

Step 3: Build the triage function

This function sends the raw ticket to Oxlo.ai and returns the model's raw text. One API call equals one flat request, regardless of how long the customer message is. That pricing model matters when users paste long threads that would rack up input tokens elsewhere.

def triage_ticket(user_message: str) -> str:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

Step 4: Parse and validate the output

Llama 3.3 70B is reliable, but I still wrap the parse in a fallback so one malformed response does not crash the pipeline.

import json

def parse_triage(raw: str) -> dict:
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {
            "urgency": "medium",
            "issue_summary": "Parse error: agent returned non-JSON.",
            "draft_reply": "We have received your message and a human will review it shortly."
        }

Run it

Here is a realistic ticket and the full script to process it.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ticket = (
        "Hi, I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month. "
        "I attached the invoice but I need the extra $79 refunded immediately. "
        "This is the second time this has happened and it is blocking my quarterly budget review."
    )

    raw = triage_ticket(ticket)
    result = parse_triage(raw)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Typical output looks like this:

{
  "urgency": "high",
  "issue_summary": "Customer was double-charged $79 for the Pro plan and needs an immediate refund.",
  "draft_reply": "I sincerely apologize for the duplicate charge. I have escalated this to our billing team for an immediate refund of $79. You should see the reversal within 1-2 business days, and I will personally email you the confirmation once it processes."
}

Wrap-up

The agent is now a single function you can drop into a FastAPI endpoint, a Slack bot, or an email webhook. If your tickets start including long debug logs or stack traces, switch the model to DeepSeek V3.2 or Qwen 3 32B on Oxlo.ai. Both handle extended context without the per-token cost penalty. For tickets that include screenshots, swap to Kimi K2.6 and pass image URLs in the messages list using the exact same client.

title: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs): Explained
content:
We are going to build a support ticket triage agent that reads a customer message, classifies it by category and urgency, and drafts a first response. This is useful for small teams who want to cut response times without hiring extra staff. Along the way, you will see how a large language model actually works through code rather than theory.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • The OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. The free tier gives you 60 requests per day, which is plenty for prototyping. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing if you need more volume.

You will also want to pick a model. I recommend starting with Llama 3.3 70B for general English tasks, or Qwen 3 32B if you expect multilingual tickets. Oxlo.ai hosts both behind the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so switching is a one-line change.

Step 1: Connect to Oxlo.ai

At its core, an LLM is a function that consumes a list of messages and predicts the next tokens. The messages array lets us separate instructions from user input. When you call chat.completions.create, the backend converts your messages into a prompt, runs inference on a GPU cluster, and returns the generated text. Oxlo.ai handles the cluster management and scaling, so you do not wait for cold starts on popular models.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "My order has not arrived."},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

The system role steers behavior, while the user role carries the actual request. Keeping them separate makes debugging easier, because you can log the system prompt once and focus on how the user input changes.

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the cheapest performance lever you have. It acts as a configuration file that tells the model who it is and what rules to follow. I keep it in a module-level constant so I can version it in git. The more explicit you are about constraints and output shape, the less you have to fix in post-processing.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent for an online electronics store.
Analyze the customer's message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- category: one of [shipping, billing, returns, product_question]
- urgency: one of [low, medium, high]
- sentiment: one of [frustrated, neutral, happy]

Rules:
- Output valid JSON only. No markdown code fences.
- Do not hallucinate tracking numbers, refund amounts, or store policies."""

Notice that I ban markdown fences. Without that rule, some models wrap JSON in triple backticks, which breaks json.loads. A good system prompt anticipates the failure modes you have seen before.

Step 3: Classify the ticket

Raw text is hard to parse reliably. JSON mode constrains the model to emit valid JSON, which turns the LLM from a chatbot into a structured data extractor. Without response_format, the model might prepend a friendly sentence like "Here is the JSON you requested:" before the object. That is fine for humans but annoying for code. JSON mode suppresses that prose and guarantees syntactically valid output.

import json

def classify_ticket(client, user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

# Example usage
ticket = "I was charged twice for my last order and I need this fixed immediately."
result = classify_ticket(client, ticket)
print(result)

I still wrap json.loads in a try block in production, because no guardrail is perfect. If your tickets are highly ambiguous, swap the model string to deepseek-v3.2. It is tuned for coding and reasoning, and because Oxlo.ai is request-based, the longer thinking time does not inflate your bill.

Step 4: Draft the reply

Classification and generation are separate concerns, so I split them into two calls. This follows the same pattern you would use with human staff: one person tags the ticket, another writes the response. With LLMs, this multi-step pipeline improves reliability because each prompt is simpler and more focused.

On traditional token-based platforms, this architecture gets punished because you pay for the full prompt twice. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing removes that penalty, so you can decompose tasks without watching the meter. Each call costs the same whether your system prompt is fifty words or five hundred.

def draft_reply(client, classification, original_message):
    prompt = f"""Customer message: {original_message}
Classification: {json.dumps(classification)}

Write a short, empathetic reply. Acknowledge the issue and set expectations.
Do not invent policies or tracking numbers. Keep it under 80 words."""

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful support agent."},
            {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

reply = draft_reply(client, result, ticket)
print(reply)

Run it

Copy the complete script below into app.py, replace YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY with the key from your portal, and run python app.py. The first call returns structured data you can write to a database or CRM. The second call returns text you can show to a human reviewer or send directly to the customer.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent for an online electronics store.
Analyze the customer's message and return a JSON object with exactly these keys:
- category: one of [shipping, billing, returns, product_question]
- urgency: one of [low, medium, high]
- sentiment: one of [frustrated, neutral, happy]

Rules:
- Output valid JSON only. No markdown code fences.
- Do not hallucinate tracking numbers, refund amounts, or store policies."""

def classify_ticket(client, user_message):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

def draft_reply(client, classification, original_message):
    prompt = f"""Customer message: {original_message}
Classification: {json.dumps(classification)}

Write a short, empathetic reply. Acknowledge the issue and set expectations.
Do not invent policies or tracking numbers. Keep it under 80 words."""

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful support agent."},
            {"role": "user", "content": prompt},
        ],
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

    customer_message = (
        "I ordered a mechanical keyboard three days ago and the status still says pending. "
        "I needed it for a trip tomorrow. This is really frustrating."
    )

    classification = classify_ticket(client, customer_message)
    print("Classification:", json.dumps(classification, indent=2))

    reply = draft_reply(client, classification, customer_message)
    print("\nDraft reply:\n", reply)

When I run this, I see something like the following:

Classification: {
  "category": "shipping",
  "urgency": "high",
  "sentiment": "frustrated"
}

Draft reply:
I'm sorry to hear your order is still pending, especially with your trip tomorrow. I completely understand the frustration. I'm escalating this to our logistics team now and you will receive an update within the next two hours.

Next steps

Make the agent stateful by appending every exchange to a messages list and passing the full history back on the next request. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, you can keep a long context window full of history without the cost scaling with every extra word. This is where flat pricing really wins against token-based providers for long-context and agentic workloads.

After that, add tool use. You could define a lookup_order function and let the model decide when to call it. Oxlo.ai supports function calling on models like Qwen 3 32B and Kimi K2.6, so the upgrade is just another parameter in the same API. You get the benefit of open-source weights and OpenAI-compatible ergonomics, with a pricing model that stays predictable as you scale.

title: Deploying LLM Models: A Step-by-Step Guide
content:
Deploying LLM models into production requires more than calling a chat endpoint from a notebook. You need to select the right infrastructure, manage model versioning, handle scaling, and control costs without sacrificing latency. Whether you are building a customer-facing agent, a coding assistant, or an internal knowledge base, a systematic deployment workflow separates prototypes from reliable systems.

Define your deployment target and infrastructure model

Start by deciding where the model will live. The three common patterns are self-hosted infrastructure on bare metal or cloud VMs, containerized inference with tools like vLLM or TGI on Kubernetes, and fully hosted API services. Self-hosted deployments give you complete control over weights, quantization, and scheduling, but they also require you to manage GPU drivers, batching logic, and autoscaling. Containerized inference improves consistency, yet you still own capacity planning, node pools, and cold-start latency. You must also handle security patching, network isolation, and model weight updates, which can consume engineering hours that would otherwise go toward product features.

A hosted inference platform removes that operational burden. Oxlo.ai provides managed endpoints for more than 45 open-source and proprietary models with no cold starts on popular architectures. Instead of maintaining container registries and CUDA environments, your team can focus on application logic. If you need to iterate quickly or support variable traffic without over-provisioning GPUs, a hosted route reduces operational surface area while preserving full model fidelity.

Select a model architecture that matches your workload

One size does not fit all. A general-purpose flagship such as Llama 3.3 70B works well for broad chat and completion tasks, while DeepSeek R1 671B MoE excels at deep reasoning and complex coding. For multilingual agent workflows, Qwen 3 32B is a strong candidate. If your pipeline processes long documents, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1 million token context window, and Kimi K2.6 offers 131K context alongside advanced reasoning and vision. For coding-specific endpoints, consider Qwen 3 Coder 30B or DeepSeek V3.2. Vision tasks can route to Gemma 3 27B or Kimi VL A3B, and image generation can use Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Flux.1, or Stable Diffusion 3.5. For retrieval-augmented generation, you can generate embeddings through BGE-Large or E5-Large, while audio pipelines can leverage Whisper Large v3 for transcription and Kokoro 82M for text-to-speech.

Oxlo.ai organizes its catalog into seven categories, including LLMs, code models, vision, image generation, audio, embeddings, and object detection. This breadth lets you deploy a heterogeneous system where each task hits a specialized endpoint, rather than forcing every request through a single generalist model. You avoid the complexity of downloading, quantizing, and serving multiple weights yourself.

Integrate with your application stack

Standardizing on a single SDK simplifies retries, error handling, and streaming parsers. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so you can keep your existing Python, Node.js, or cURL patterns and change only the base URL and API key. That compatibility extends to chat completions, embeddings, image generations, audio transcriptions, and text-to-speech. In Node.js, the same pattern applies: instantiate the client with the Oxlo.ai base URL, then call chat.completions.create with identical parameters.

Here is a minimal Python example that streams a chat completion:

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain request-based pricing."}],
    stream=True
)

for chunk in response:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

Because the endpoint shape is identical to the OpenAI specification, you do not need to rewrite JSON mode parsers, function calling handlers, or vision input formatters. The same client code can switch between models by updating the model string, which makes A/B testing and model upgrades trivial.

Configure features for production reliability

Production workloads demand more than text generation. You will likely need structured outputs, tool use, multi-turn conversation state, and multimodal inputs. Enable JSON mode when you want schema-constrained responses that feed directly into downstream business logic. When JSON mode is enabled, the model is constrained to valid JSON, which eliminates brittle regex extraction and reduces post-processing code. Use function calling to let models invoke external APIs, calculators, or retrieval systems. For agentic systems that reason across turns, ensure your backend persists message history and handles context window management.

Oxlo.ai supports these features across its chat/completions endpoint. Vision inputs use the same message list format, so you can pass base64-encoded images or public URLs without adopting a separate client. If your product requires speech or image synthesis, you can call the audio and image generation endpoints using the same SDK and authentication layer. Streaming is available on supported models, which reduces perceived latency for user-facing interfaces.

Optimize cost structure for your traffic pattern

Most hosted providers bill by the token. Under token-based pricing, long system prompts, multi-turn agent memory, and large document context all inflate costs linearly. If your workload includes any of these patterns, token metering can become the dominant line item in your infrastructure budget.

Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic workloads, this model can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives because your cost does not scale with input size. You can pass full documents, maintain longer conversation history, and build tool-heavy agents without constantly compressing context to save money. Predictable per-request costs also simplify budgeting. You can forecast monthly spend from request volume alone, without modeling average token counts per user session. Oxlo.ai offers a free tier with 60 requests per day across 16+ models, and paid plans scale to dedicated GPU clusters for enterprise workloads. See the pricing page for current plan details.

Implement monitoring and fallback strategies

Once live, treat your LLM layer like any other critical service. Track request latency, error rates, and per-model usage. Log prompt templates and output schemas so you can detect drift or regressions when model weights update. Export logs to your existing observability stack, whether that is Datadog, Grafana, or a custom ELK cluster, so your LLM infrastructure is visible alongside your databases and application servers. Set up circuit breakers and retries with exponential backoff to handle transient failures.

Because Oxlo.ai exposes many model families through a unified API, you can implement graceful degradation without maintaining multiple client libraries. If your primary model experiences elevated latency, fail over to another endpoint in the same category, such as routing from Llama 3.3 70B to Qwen 3 32B or DeepSeek V3.2. Premium plans include a priority queue for more predictable latency during traffic spikes. Keep request IDs for end-to-end tracing, and tag traffic by feature flag so you can isolate problematic deployments quickly.

Deploying LLMs is an infrastructure decision as much as a modeling one. By selecting a compatible hosted platform, matching model architectures to tasks, and aligning your cost model with real usage patterns, you move from prototype to production without managing GPU clusters. Oxlo.ai provides OpenAI-compatible endpoints, flat request-based pricing, and a broad catalog of open-source models so you can focus on building applications rather than operating inference infrastructure.

title: Building a Customer Support Agent with AI
content:
Customer support is the most common production workload for LLM agents, but a usable system is more than a chat wrapper. You need retrieval to ground answers in your documentation, function calling to act on behalf of users, and memory to maintain context across a long thread. Most importantly, you need an inference backend that stays predictable as conversations grow. Token-based scaling makes multi-turn support agents expensive fast, especially when you add RAG context and tool results. Oxlo.ai offers a flat per-request pricing model that removes this penalty, along with full OpenAI SDK compatibility so you can build with familiar tools. This guide walks through the architecture, implementation, and deployment of a support agent that actually works.

Agent Architecture

A production support agent has four layers. The interface layer accepts messages. The reasoning layer, powered by an LLM, decides what to say or do. The retrieval layer fetches relevant documentation, past tickets, or account data. The action layer executes function calls against your internal APIs.

The reasoning layer is where model choice and inference costs matter most. Support threads often exceed dozens of turns, and each turn includes the full system prompt, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and conversation history. With token-based billing, every additional message increases the cost of the next one. Oxlo.ai charges a flat rate per request, so the cost of a 20-turn escalation is predictable from the first message. This changes how you design memory and context windows.

Selecting Models for Support Workflows

Not every support query needs the same capability. Tier your models.

For routine queries, a fast general-purpose model like Llama 3.3 70B handles classification and simple answers with low latency. For multilingual teams, Qwen 3 32B provides strong multilingual reasoning and agent workflow support. When a user hits a complex bug or asks for a detailed code fix, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 offer advanced chain-of-thought reasoning and agentic coding. If you want to include an entire long ticket history or a large knowledge base in the prompt, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window, and Kimi K2.6 offers a 131K context with vision support for screenshots.

Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, switching from a 4K context summary to a 128K context dump does not change your unit cost. You can select the model based on capability, not token budget. See the exact tiers at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Implementing the Agent Core

Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. You point your client at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1 and use the same chat.completions interface. Below is a minimal but complete agent loop with function calling.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support agent for Acme Corp.
Use the available tools to help users.
Do not make up order IDs or refund amounts."""

def get_order_status(order_id: str):
    # Call your internal API
    return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

tools = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "get_order_status",
            "description": "Get the status of an order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Where is my order 12345?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

message = response.choices[0].message
if message.tool_calls:
    for tool_call in message.tool_calls:
        if tool_call.function.name == "get_order_status":
            args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
            result = get_order_status(args["order_id"])
            messages.append({
                "role": "tool",
                "tool_call_id": tool_call.id,
                "content": json.dumps(result)
            })
    # Send results back to model for final answer
    final = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=messages,
        tools=tools
    )
    print(final.choices[0].message.content)
else:
    print(message.content)

The system prompt defines tone and available tools. The loop checks for tool_calls, executes them, and appends results. Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversations, you can extend this pattern without changing the underlying client logic.

Retrieval and Long-Context Grounding

Hallucinations destroy trust in support agents. The standard fix is RAG: embed your docs and retrieve the top-k chunks. But chunking FAQs often loses nuance. An alternative is to include an entire category or long document directly in the prompt.

With token-based providers, that is a pricing trap. With Oxlo.ai, a request is a request. You can pass a full knowledge base article or a long customer history to DeepSeek V4 Flash or Kimi K2.6 without watching your burn rate scale with word count. This lets you simplify architecture: retrieve once, include the full text, and let the model reason over it.

For embedding retrieval itself, Oxlo.ai offers BGE-Large and E5-Large via the embeddings endpoint, so you can keep the entire pipeline on one platform.

Memory Strategies for Multi-Turn Threads

Support conversations are stateful. A user might reference a refund they asked about three messages ago. You have two options: send the full history or maintain a rolling summary.

Full history is more accurate but explodes token counts on other platforms. On Oxlo.ai, the per-request model makes full-history agents economically viable. If you prefer summaries, you can run a periodic compression call. Even then, the cost is flat per summary request, not proportional to the length of the transcript.

Guardrails and Structured Output

Support agents must not hallucinate refund amounts or invent policies. Use JSON mode to enforce schemas when calling internal APIs. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode, so you can require the model to emit structured arguments before any side-effecting function runs.

You should also validate tool outputs and use a secondary check for sensitive actions. For example, require explicit user confirmation for refunds over a certain threshold, and log every tool call for audit.

Deployment and Scaling

Latency matters. Users will abandon a chat if replies take more than a few seconds. Oxlo.ai has no cold starts on popular models, so your first request of the day returns as fast as your hundredth.

For scaling, the Pro and Premium plans offer predictable daily request volumes. If you need dedicated throughput or custom limits, the Enterprise tier provides dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed cost reduction over your current provider. This is useful when your support agent moves from pilot to handling your entire queue.

Putting It Together

A reliable customer support agent combines solid retrieval, careful tool use, and a pricing model that does not punish long conversations. Oxlo.ai gives you the models, the OpenAI-compatible API, and the flat per-request structure that makes multi-turn agents practical. Whether you are prototyping with Llama 3.3 70B or scaling a complex escalation pipeline with DeepSeek R1 and Kimi K2.6, the platform stays predictable. Build the agent your users actually want to talk to, and let the inference costs scale with requests, not tokens.

title: Introduction to LLM Inference
content:
We are going to build a technical document analysis agent that ingests a long product specification and extracts structured requirements with citations. This is useful for product managers and engineers who need to parse lengthy RFCs or technical docs without reading every line. Because the agent handles long inputs, flat per-request pricing from Oxlo.ai keeps costs predictable regardless of document length.

What you'll need

Python 3.10 or newer installed locally. An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. The OpenAI SDK, which you can install with pip install openai. No other dependencies are required.

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

Before we can send prompts, we need an authenticated client. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the only change from the default SDK setup is the base_url. Once the client exists, every subsequent inference call follows the same request pattern.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Define the system prompt

A system prompt acts as the invariant part of the context window. It defines the agent's role, output rules, and constraints. I keep the instructions specific and assign them to a top-level constant so I can iterate quickly without hunting through function bodies. Notice that I explicitly forbid JSON here. That lets me verify behavior in plain English before I lock down the schema.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical document analyzer. Your job is to read a product specification and extract a structured list of requirements.

Rules:
- Identify each requirement with a unique ID.
- Quote the exact sentence from the document that supports the requirement.
- If a requirement is ambiguous, flag it with "AMBIGUOUS" and explain why.
- Respond in plain text with bullet points, not JSON."""

print("System prompt loaded.")

Step 3: Run a basic inference call

Inference is the act of transmitting a messages payload to a remote model and receiving a generated completion. In this step, I send the system prompt plus a user message containing a short product spec. The response object follows the standard ChatCompletion schema, so accessing the generated text is identical to what you would write for any OpenAI-compatible provider. I use llama-3.3-70b because it is a reliable general-purpose flagship model that follows instructions tightly.

sample_doc = """
Product Spec v1.2 (Internal)
The API gateway must handle up to 10,000 requests per second with a P99 latency under 50ms.
Authentication is required for all endpoints except the health check.
The health check endpoint should return a 200 OK status.
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Analyze this document:\n{sample_doc}"},
    ],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 4: Build multi-turn context

Because the underlying API is stateless, the application layer must manage conversation history. I construct a messages list that includes the prior system prompt, the original user message, and the assistant's response. Then I append a new user question. When this list is transmitted, the model sees the full context and can answer the follow-up about performance requirements without losing track of the original document. This is the core mechanic behind any agentic loop.

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
    {"role": "user", "content": f"Analyze this document:\n{sample_doc}"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": response.choices[0].message.content},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Which requirements are performance related?"},
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 5: Enforce structured output with JSON mode

Consuming unstructured text in downstream tools requires machine-readable output. By setting response_format to json_object and tightening the system prompt, we force the model to emit valid JSON. I switch to qwen-3-32b here because it handles multilingual and structured reasoning tasks well. After the call, Python's standard json library can parse the content string directly into a dictionary. This pattern is how most production inference pipelines bridge LLMs to traditional software.

import json

SYSTEM_PROMPT_JSON = """You are a technical document analyzer. Read the product specification and return a JSON object with a single key "requirements" containing an array of objects. Each object must have keys: "id", "category", "description", "source_quote", and "ambiguous" (boolean)."""

longer_doc = """
System Architecture RFC 44
1. The database layer must use PostgreSQL 15 or newer.
2. All customer PII must be encrypted at rest using AES-256.
3. The search service may optionally use Elasticsearch, but this is not mandatory for MVP.
4. The web tier should auto-scale between 2 and 20 instances based on CPU utilization.
"""

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen-3-32b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT_JSON},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Document:\n{longer_doc}"},
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)

print(json.dumps(json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content), indent=2))

Run it

Putting it all into a single function makes the agent reusable across different documents. I chose deepseek-v3.2 for the final version because it is optimized for coding and reasoning workloads, and it is available on Oxlo.ai's free tier. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request rather than per token, passing in a ten-page specification costs the same as passing in a one-paragraph summary. That makes this agent economical for real-world RFCs that routinely exceed ten thousand tokens.

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a technical document analyzer. Return JSON with a "requirements" array. Each item needs "id", "category", "description", "source_quote", and "ambiguous" (boolean)."""

document = """
API Gateway RFC
The gateway must authenticate every request via OAuth 2.0 except for the public status page.
Rate limiting is set to 1,000 requests per minute per API key.
Logging must include request_id, timestamp, and user_agent for every call.
The caching layer is described as "nice to have" and is not required for launch.
"""

def analyze_document(doc: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v3.2",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": doc},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    )
    return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)

result = analyze_document(document)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Example output:

{
  "requirements": [
    {
      "id": "REQ-001",
      "category": "security",
      "description": "Authenticate every request via OAuth 2.0",
      "source_quote": "The gateway must authenticate every request via OAuth 2.0 except for the public status page.",
      "ambiguous": false
    },
    {
      "id": "REQ-002",
      "category": "performance",
      "description": "Rate limiting set to 1,000 requests per minute per API key",
      "source_quote": "Rate limiting is set to 1,000 requests per minute per API key.",
      "ambiguous": false
    },
    {
      "id": "REQ-003",
      "category": "observability",
      "description": "Logging must include request_id, timestamp, and user_agent",
      "source_quote": "Logging must include request_id, timestamp, and user_agent for every call.",
      "ambiguous": false
    },
    {
      "id": "REQ-004",
      "category": "infrastructure",
      "description": "Caching layer is optional for launch",
      "source_quote": "The caching layer is described as \"nice to have\" and is not required for launch.",
      "ambiguous": true
    }
  ]
}

Wrap-up and next steps

This agent demonstrates the fundamental building blocks of LLM inference: a persistent system prompt, stateless multi-turn message history, and structured output constraints. For a production version, you could swap deepseek-v3.2 for kimi-k2.6 when you need advanced reasoning over longer documents, or add function calling to validate requirements against a live issue tracker. Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing means you can scale this to full-length technical specifications without worrying about token costs. If you want to experiment before committing, start with the free tier at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: The Role of LLMs in Computer Vision: Trends and Opportunities
content:
Computer vision is undergoing a structural shift. For years, the field was defined by task-specific convolutional networks and handcrafted pipelines. Today, large language models are absorbing visual understanding into unified reasoning systems. Models that once processed text alone now interpret charts, navigate user interfaces, and reason across video frames. This convergence is not a marginal improvement. It redefines how developers build perception into applications.

The transition from separate vision and language stacks to a single multimodal layer creates new architectural demands. Inference costs become unpredictable when high-resolution images are encoded as thousands of tokens. Agentic workflows require vision models to call tools and maintain state across long contexts. Production teams need an infrastructure layer that delivers these capabilities without forcing a rewrite of existing code. Oxlo.ai meets this need with a developer-first inference platform that treats vision and language as a unified workload.

Unified Multimodal Reasoning

The latest generation of open models processes images and text within a single forward pass. Dedicated vision models such as Gemma 3 27B and Kimi VL A3B offer strong performance on optical character recognition, spatial reasoning, and visual question answering. Meanwhile, flagship chat and reasoning models have incorporated vision natively. Kimi K2.6 supports advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision with a 131K context window. Qwen 3 32B handles multilingual reasoning and agent workflows across text and image inputs. Llama 3.3 70B serves as a general-purpose backbone for mixed-modal tasks, while GPT-Oss 120B provides a large open-source alternative for deep reasoning over visual content.

This unification simplifies application architecture. Instead of chaining a separate OCR engine, a captioning model, and a text LLM, developers can pass an image directly to a chat completion endpoint and receive structured reasoning in return. Oxlo.ai hosts more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, so a team can experiment with DeepSeek V3.2 for coding and reasoning or compare Kimi K2.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking for chain-of-thought tasks that include embedded figures. Upgrading from text-only to multimodal inference becomes a parameter change rather than a platform migration.

Agentic Vision and Tool Use

Vision becomes significantly more useful when models can act on what they see. Agentic systems use function calling and tool use to move from passive description to active operation. A model might inspect a dashboard screenshot, identify an anomaly, and then invoke an API to roll back a deployment. GLM 5, with its 744B mixture-of-experts architecture, targets long-horizon agentic tasks. Minimax M2.5 specializes in coding and agentic tool use. Qwen 3 32B supports agent workflows that span both text and visual inputs, making it practical for autonomous systems that interact with graphical interfaces.

Oxlo.ai exposes function calling, JSON mode, and streaming responses across compatible models. Because the platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, existing agent frameworks built for tool use require only a base URL change to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. There are no cold starts on popular models, which keeps agent loops responsive even when vision triggers intermittent inference requests. Function calling is supported across compatible chat models, allowing an agent to alternate between visual perception and external action without custom glue code.

Long Context and Video Understanding

Vision workloads are inherently long-context workloads. A single high-resolution image can consume thousands of tokens when encoded for an LLM. Video understanding multiplies this burden across frames. Models such as DeepSeek V4 Flash offer a 1M context window with efficient MoE architecture, making near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning accessible over extended visual sequences. DeepSeek R1 671B MoE provides deep reasoning for complex coding and analysis tasks that may include lengthy technical diagrams or multi-page scanned documentation.

Chain-of-thought reasoning also benefits from extended context. Kimi K2.5 and Kimi K2 Thinking apply advanced chain-of-thought techniques to problems that include visual inputs, such as academic papers with embedded figures or legal documents with redacted scans. Token-based pricing penalizes these use cases. When cost scales with input length, every additional frame or higher-resolution patch directly inflates the bill. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For vision and agentic workloads that feed large images or multi-frame video into the context window, this model can be 10-100x cheaper than token-based alternatives. Providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale scale cost with input tokens, which makes long-context vision expensive at production volume. Oxlo.ai removes that constraint.

Generative Vision and Object Detection

LLMs are not limited to understanding existing images. They increasingly serve as orchestrators for generative pipelines and as front-ends for detection systems. Oxlo.ai offers image generation through Oxlo.ai Image Pro, Oxlo.ai Image Ultra, Flux.1, SDXL, and Stable Diffusion 3.5, accessible via the images/generations endpoint. These can be triggered by an LLM that first reasons over a user request, breaks it into structured constraints, and then delegates creation to a specialized diffusion model. This orchestration pattern, where an LLM plans and a diffusion model executes, reduces manual prompt engineering and keeps control logic inside a familiar chat completions loop.

For structured perception, Oxlo.ai provides object detection through YOLOv9 and YOLOv11. A developer can build a pipeline in which an LLM reads a scene description from a detection endpoint, reasons about the relationships between objects, and returns a JSON plan. With embeddings models such as BGE-Large and E5-Large also available, it is possible to index visual metadata into a vector store and retrieve it with natural language queries. All of these endpoints, from chat to images to embeddings, share the same API key and request-based pricing structure.

Integrating Vision into Production

The practical hurdle for many teams is not model capability but integration friction. Rebuilding a client library or rewriting prompt templates for a new provider slows experimentation. Oxlo.ai is a fully OpenAI API compatible drop-in replacement. The same client works in Python, Node.js, or cURL. Migrating an existing OpenAI vision pipeline requires no dependency changes beyond the base URL and API key.

The following Python example sends an image to a vision-capable chat model and then requests an image generation based on the description. Both operations use the same client configuration.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

# Vision inference: describe an image
vision_response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="kimi-k2.6",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Describe the UI elements in this screenshot."},
                {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/dashboard.png"}}
            ]
        }
    ],
    max_tokens=512
)

description = vision_response.choices[0].message.content
print("Vision output:", description)

# Image generation based on the description
image_response = client.images.generate(
    model="oxlo.ai-image-pro",
    prompt=f"Redesign this interface with a dark theme: {description}",
    n=1,
    size="1024x1024"
)

print("Image URL:", image_response.data[0].url)

Because Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, JSON mode, and multi-turn conversations, this pattern extends naturally to interactive applications. A free tier offering 60 requests per day and access to 16-plus models, including DeepSeek V3.2 on a free tier, lets developers validate a vision pipeline before committing to a paid plan. Pro and Premium plans provide 1,000 and 5,000 requests per day respectively, with Premium adding priority queue access. Enterprise customers receive dedicated GPUs and a guaranteed 30 percent reduction versus their current provider.

Conclusion

The intersection of LLMs and computer vision is no longer experimental. Production systems now rely on models that reason over pixels, generate imagery, and invoke tools based on visual input. The infrastructure supporting these workloads must handle long contexts, multimodal inputs, and unpredictable token volumes without forcing developers to manage cost spikes or rewrite integrations.

Oxlo.ai provides a unified inference layer for this transition. With 45-plus models across vision, chat, reasoning, image generation, object detection, and embeddings, request-based pricing that protects against long-context cost inflation, and full OpenAI SDK compatibility, it offers a direct path from prototype to production. For teams building the next generation of multimodal applications, the platform is available to evaluate at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Zero-Shot Learning with LLMs: Applications and Techniques
content:
We are building a zero-shot support ticket triage agent that reads raw customer messages and classifies them by category and urgency without any training data or fine-tuning. If you run a SaaS and do not have thousands of labeled historical tickets, this lets you start routing conversations immediately using only a carefully written system prompt and an LLM. I shipped this exact setup last quarter for our own internal queue and it cut first-response time in half because urgent issues stopped sitting in the general inbox.

What you'll need

The prerequisites are minimal. You need Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK installed with pip install openai, and an API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. You also need a handful of unlabeled support messages to test against.

I chose Oxlo.ai for this workload because its request-based pricing means a long customer rant does not inflate the cost. With token-based providers, a detailed bug report or an angry paragraph about billing can quickly eat up input tokens. On Oxlo.ai, you pay one flat fee per API request regardless of prompt length, which keeps the triage pipeline predictable. You also get over 45 models to choose from, so you can start with llama-3.3-70b and later test qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 without changing any client code. You can check the latest plans at https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

I started with the simplest possible setup. Oxlo.ai exposes a fully OpenAI-compatible API, so I imported the standard client and pointed base_url to Oxlo.ai. I grabbed my API key from the portal and kept it in an environment variable in production, but for this tutorial I left it as a placeholder you can swap in. I picked llama-3.3-70b as the general-purpose workhorse because it follows structured instructions reliably and Oxlo.ai serves it with no cold starts. That is important for a triage loop where you might process twenty tickets in a burst and cannot afford a thirty-second warm-up.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"  # swap in your key from https://portal.oxlo.ai
)

Step 2: Write the zero-shot system prompt

This prompt is the entire classifier. I deliberately did not include any few-shot examples because the goal is zero-shot generalization. The model must infer the correct category from the task description and the allowed labels alone. I gave explicit constraints: three categories, four urgency levels, and a strict JSON schema. I also added a one-sentence reason field so I could audit decisions later without parsing prose. Keeping the output schema rigid reduces hallucination and makes downstream automation trivial.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket triage agent.
Your job is to read a raw customer message and classify it.

Allowed categories: Billing, Technical, Account.
Allowed urgency levels: Low, Medium, High, Critical.

Return ONLY a JSON object with this exact structure:
{
  "category": "",
  "urgency": "",
  "reason": ""
}

Do not include markdown code fences, commentary, or text outside the JSON."""

Step 3: Build the structured classifier

Next I wrote a small Python function that sends the ticket text to Oxlo.ai. I set response_format to {"type": "json_object"} so the model is mechanically constrained to valid JSON. I kept temperature at 0.1 to reduce creativity. For triage, I want deterministic categories, not poetic flair. I parse the content with json.loads and raise a clear error if the model ever leaks extra tokens and breaks the schema. In three weeks of production use this has not happened with llama-3.3-70b, but I keep the guardrail anyway because malformed JSON should never crash the pipeline.

import json

def triage_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": ticket_text},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    try:
        return json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid JSON from model: {raw}") from exc

Run it

I tested the agent against three fabricated tickets that cover common edge cases: a billing complaint, a vague technical glitch, and an account lockout. I looped over them and printed the structured output. The results came back in under a second with no cold start, which is typical for Oxlo.ai's hot model pool. Notice how the model inferred High urgency for the lockout even though the user never used the word urgent. That is the zero-shot reasoning capability at work.

tickets = [
    "I was charged twice for my Pro plan this month. Please fix this immediately.",
    "The dashboard sometimes goes blank when I click the Reports tab. It started after your last update.",
    "I forgot my password and the reset email never arrives. I am locked out of my account.",
]

for t in tickets:
    result = triage_ticket(t)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

# Example output:
# {
#   "category": "Billing",
#   "urgency": "High",
#   "reason": "Customer was double-charged and explicitly asked for immediate resolution."
# }
# {
#   "category": "Technical",
#   "urgency": "Medium",
#   "reason": "Reported UI bug affects workflow but does not block core access."
# }
# {
#   "category": "Account",
#   "urgency": "High",
#   "reason": "User is completely locked out and cannot recover access via standard reset."
# }

Wrap-up

That is the whole system. You can deploy this as a lightweight script that polls your support inbox every five minutes and posts structured results to a Slack channel or internal dashboard. A concrete next step is to add a routing field to the JSON schema that maps each category to a specific team member, so the agent assigns an owner automatically. Another is to experiment with qwen-3-32b or kimi-k2.6 on Oxlo.ai for multilingual tickets, since both models handle non-English reasoning well and the flat per-request pricing keeps costs predictable even when messages are long.

title: Few-Shot Learning with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Today we are building a support ticket classifier that routes incoming messages to the correct department without any fine-tuning. By embedding a handful of labeled examples directly into the system prompt, we can teach a general-purpose LLM to recognize intent in a single API call. I built this exact pipeline for an internal tool last quarter when we needed to triage tickets faster than any rules engine allowed, and I will show you the runnable Python version using Oxlo.ai.

What you'll need

You need Python 3.10 or newer installed locally. You also need the OpenAI SDK, which you can install with pip install openai. Finally, grab an API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Oxlo.ai is a strong fit for this project because it charges a flat rate per request, not per token. That means you can stuff the context window with long few-shot examples and the cost stays identical on every call. For token-heavy workloads like classification with rich prompts, that structure removes the usual trade-off between accuracy and bill size.

Step 1: Configure the Oxlo.ai client

Import the SDK and instantiate the client with Oxlo.ai's base URL. If you already have OpenAI SDK code in another project, this is the only line you need to change to migrate. I pull the key from an environment variable to avoid accidental commits, but a hardcoded string works for local prototypes. The client reuses HTTP connections under the hood, so creating it once at module level is the right approach.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"),
)

Step 2: Craft the few-shot system prompt

The entire learning happens inside the prompt. I define three routing categories, then provide two concrete examples per category. The model generalizes from these patterns instead of relying on internal knowledge alone. I ask for strict JSON so we do not need regex hacks to parse the response. Because Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, adding more examples does not increase the per-request cost. You can experiment with longer prompts or larger example sets without watching token costs scale. For this build I am using the general-purpose llama-3.3-70b model, though qwen-3-32b is a solid alternative if your tickets arrive in multiple languages, and deepseek-v3.2 offers strong reasoning if your categories are nuanced.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support ticket router.
Classify each incoming message into exactly one category: Billing, Technical, or Account.
Return strictly JSON with keys: category, confidence (0.0 to 1.0), reasoning.

Examples:

Message: "I was charged twice for my subscription this month. Please refund the duplicate."
Category: Billing
Confidence: 0.95
Reasoning: The user explicitly mentions a duplicate charge and requests a refund.

Message: "My API key returns a 401 error even though I copied it correctly."
Category: Technical
Confidence: 0.98
Reasoning: The user is describing an authentication error with an API integration.

Message: "I need to update the credit card on file."
Category: Billing
Confidence: 0.92
Reasoning: The user wants to change payment information.

Message: "I forgot my password and the reset email never arrives."
Category: Account
Confidence: 0.91
Reasoning: The user cannot access their account and is troubleshooting email delivery.

Message: "Can I add two-factor authentication to my profile?"
Category: Account
Confidence: 0.88
Reasoning: The user is asking about security settings for their account.

Message: "The dashboard loads but the export button spins forever."
Category: Technical
Confidence: 0.93
Reasoning: The user reports a UI bug in the application.

Now classify the following message."""

Step 3: Classify a single ticket

Wrap the API call in a small function. I set temperature to 0.1 to keep outputs deterministic and close to the patterns shown in the examples. The function strips any accidental markdown fences from the response and parses the JSON. If parsing fails, it falls back to a safe dict so the pipeline never crashes on a malformed response. I avoid the JSON mode parameter here because the model is already instructed to return JSON inside the system prompt, which gives us more control over the schema.

import json

def classify_ticket(text: str) -> dict:
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        temperature=0.1,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": text},
        ],
    )
    content = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    # Remove markdown code fences if the model adds them
    if content.startswith("```json"):
        content = content[7:]
    elif content.startswith("```"):
        content = content[3:]
    if content.endswith("```"):
        content = content[:-3]
    content = content.strip()
    try:
        return json.loads(content)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return {"category": "Unknown", "confidence": 0.0, "reasoning": "Parse error"}

Step 4: Add confidence checking

In production, not every ticket is a clean fit. I added a simple confidence gate. If the model returns a score below 0.7, the ticket escalates to a human instead of being auto-routed. This prevents a bad prediction from reaching the wrong team and annoying a customer. You could also inspect logprobs for a second opinion, but I have found that asking the model to self-rate inside the JSON is simpler and reliable enough at this scale. This is another spot where Oxlo.ai's flat request pricing helps. You can afford to include a longer reasoning chain in the prompt, which usually improves calibration without inflating your bill.

def route_ticket(ticket_text: str) -> str:
    result = classify_ticket(ticket_text)
    confidence = result.get("confidence", 0.0)
    category = result.get("category", "Unknown")
    if confidence < 0.7 or category == "Unknown":
        return f"ESCALATE: {ticket_text[:60]}... (confidence {confidence})"
    return f"ROUTE TO {category.upper()}: {ticket_text[:60]}... (confidence {confidence})"

Step 5: Batch process the queue

Support tickets rarely arrive one at a time. I added a small batch runner that loops over a list and prints a formatted table. The OpenAI SDK reuses the underlying HTTP connection, so sequential calls are efficient even without explicit concurrency. If you later need higher throughput, you can swap this loop for asyncio or a queue worker without changing the Oxlo.ai client setup.

tickets = [
    "I was charged twice last week and need a refund.",
    "The export button spins forever when I try to download a PDF.",
    "Can I change the email address on my account?",
    "I am not sure about something random vague thing.",
    "My webhook endpoint returns 500 errors after your latest update.",
]

def process_queue(ticket_list: list[str]):
    print(f"{'STATUS':<20} | {'DETAIL'}")
    print("-" * 60)
    for ticket in ticket_list:
        print(route_ticket(ticket))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_queue(tickets)

Run it

Save the script as ticket_router.py, export your key, and run python ticket_router.py. Here is the output I see on a typical run. Your exact confidence numbers may vary slightly, but the categories should be stable because of the low temperature.

STATUS               | DETAIL
------------------------------------------------------------
ROUTE TO BILLING: I was charged twice last week and need a... (confidence 0.95)
ROUTE TO TECHNICAL: The export button spins forever when I... (confidence 0.93)
ROUTE TO ACCOUNT: Can I change the email address on my acc... (confidence 0.91)
ESCALATE: I am not sure about something random vague thing... (confidence 0.42)
ROUTE TO TECHNICAL: My webhook endpoint returns 500 errors... (confidence 0.89)

Wrap-up and next steps

This classifier went from idea to internal tool in an afternoon because few-shot learning removes the need for training pipelines and labeled datasets. If you want to extend it, wire the output into a Slack webhook so routing happens automatically, or swap to kimi-k2.6 on Oxlo.ai to handle full email threads with 131K context. You can sign up for an API key at portal.oxlo.ai and view the flat request pricing at oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Transfer Learning with LLM: Best Practices and Applications
content:
I have shipped a lot of pipelines that needed to adapt a general foundation model to a narrow domain without spinning up fine-tuning infrastructure. In this walkthrough, I will show you how to build a support ticket triage agent that uses few-shot transfer learning on top of Llama 3.3 70B through Oxlo.ai. You will end up with a single Python script that ingests raw support text and returns structured intent labels, confidence scores, and routing reasoning, all derived from a handful of examples embedded directly in the prompt.

What you'll need

Python 3.10 or newer, the OpenAI SDK, and an Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai. Install the SDK with pip install openai. You do not need PyTorch, a GPU, or a training set. This approach works on any machine that can make HTTPS requests.

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai. Because the platform is fully OpenAI compatible, this is a literal drop-in replacement. No custom adapters, no wrapper classes, and no cold starts on Llama 3.3 70B. I keep my API key in an environment variable out of habit.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

Step 2: Encode the task with a few-shot system prompt

Transfer learning usually makes people think of backpropagation and LoRA adapters, but at inference time you can achieve a similar effect by transferring the model's general language understanding to a narrow task through carefully chosen examples. I encode the entire task definition, the label schema, and five diverse demonstrations into the system prompt. The model has already learned syntax, semantics, and customer service tropes during pre-training. My job is to point that knowledge at a specific classification head using nothing but text. I keep the labels tight, the reasoning explicit, and the JSON schema rigid so the output is machine readable.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent for a SaaS platform.
Your job is to read a customer message and classify it into exactly one of these intents:
REFUND_REQUEST, BUG_REPORT, FEATURE_REQUEST, ACCOUNT_RECOVERY, or GENERAL_INQUIRY.

Return a JSON object with three keys:
- intent: the predicted label
- confidence: a float between 0.0 and 1.0
- reasoning: one sentence explaining why you chose this label

Examples:
Message: "I was charged twice for my monthly subscription. Please reverse the second charge."
Output: {"intent": "REFUND_REQUEST", "confidence": 0.98, "reasoning": "The user explicitly requests reversal of a duplicate charge."}

Message: "The export button does nothing when I click it in Chrome."
Output: {"intent": "BUG_REPORT", "confidence": 0.95, "reasoning": "The user describes a non-working UI element in a specific browser."}

Message: "Can you add dark mode to the dashboard?"
Output: {"intent": "FEATURE_REQUEST", "confidence": 0.97, "reasoning": "The user asks for new functionality that does not currently exist."}

Message: "I forgot my password and the reset email never arrives."
Output: {"intent": "ACCOUNT_RECOVERY", "confidence": 0.96, "reasoning": "The user cannot access their account and mentions password reset failure."}

Message: "What are your office hours?"
Output: {"intent": "GENERAL_INQUIRY", "confidence": 0.92, "reasoning": "The user asks for information unrelated to a technical issue or account problem."}

Now classify the user message below. Respond with valid JSON only."""

Step 3: Add structured output and run inference

I wrap the call in a small function so I can reuse it across a batch of tickets. I set response_format to {"type": "json_object"} to force valid JSON, and I keep temperature at 0.1 so the label distribution stays sharp. I use Llama 3.3 70B because its general-purpose reasoning handles few-shot classification reliably, even when the user message contains typos or mixed intents. One practical benefit of running this on Oxlo.ai is the request-based pricing. I can stuff the system prompt with long examples and detailed instructions without watching the cost scale linearly with tokens, which makes iterative prompt engineering affordable.

import json

def classify_ticket(user_message: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

# quick sanity check
test_msg = "I need help merging two accounts into one billing profile."
result = classify_ticket(test_msg)
print(result)

Step 4: Test against a holdout sample

To make this feel like a real project, I run a tiny evaluation set against holdout messages that are semantically close but not identical to the few-shot examples. I also add a guardrail: if the model returns a confidence score below 0.8, I flag the ticket for human review instead of auto-routing it. This is important in production because transfer learning via prompting can fail silently on out-of-distribution inputs. The assert statements act as a cheap contract test on the output schema.

holdout = [
    ("The mobile app crashes every time I open settings on iOS 17.", "BUG_REPORT"),
    ("I want a yearly invoice sent to my finance team automatically.", "FEATURE_REQUEST"),
    ("My coworker left and I need to take over the admin seat.", "ACCOUNT_RECOVERY"),
]

for msg, expected in holdout:
    prediction = classify_ticket(msg)
    assert "intent" in prediction and "confidence" in prediction
    print(
        f"Expected: {expected} | Got: {prediction['intent']} | "
        f"Confidence: {prediction['confidence']}"
    )
    if prediction["confidence"] < 0.8:
        print("  [FLAG] Low confidence. Route to human queue.")

Run it

Save the complete script below as transfer_classifier.py, export your Oxlo.ai API key, and run python transfer_classifier.py. The script should finish in under a second per ticket because Oxlo.ai serves Llama 3.3 70B without cold starts. If you see a JSON decode error, check that your account has access to the model tier you are requesting.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support triage agent for a SaaS platform.
Your job is to read a customer message and classify it into exactly one of these intents:
REFUND_REQUEST, BUG_REPORT, FEATURE_REQUEST, ACCOUNT_RECOVERY, or GENERAL_INQUIRY.

Return a JSON object with three keys:
- intent: the predicted label
- confidence: a float between 0.0 and 1.0
- reasoning: one sentence explaining why you chose this label

Examples:
Message: "I was charged twice for my monthly subscription. Please reverse the second charge."
Output: {"intent": "REFUND_REQUEST", "confidence": 0.98, "reasoning": "The user explicitly requests reversal of a duplicate charge."}

Message: "The export button does nothing when I click it in Chrome."
Output: {"intent": "BUG_REPORT", "confidence": 0.95, "reasoning": "The user describes a non-working UI element in a specific browser."}

Message: "Can you add dark mode to the dashboard?"
Output: {"intent": "FEATURE_REQUEST", "confidence": 0.97, "reasoning": "The user asks for new functionality that does not currently exist."}

Message: "I forgot my password and the reset email never arrives."
Output: {"intent": "ACCOUNT_RECOVERY", "confidence": 0.96, "reasoning": "The user cannot access their account and mentions password reset failure."}

Message: "What are your office hours?"
Output: {"intent": "GENERAL_INQUIRY", "confidence": 0.92, "reasoning": "The user asks for information unrelated to a technical issue or account problem."}

Now classify the user message below. Respond with valid JSON only."""

def classify_ticket(user_message: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        temperature=0.1,
    )
    raw = response.choices[0].message.content
    return json.loads(raw)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    holdout = [
        ("The mobile app crashes every time I open settings on iOS 17.", "BUG_REPORT"),
        ("I want a yearly invoice sent to my finance team automatically.", "FEATURE_REQUEST"),
        ("My coworker left and I need to take over the admin seat.", "ACCOUNT_RECOVERY"),
    ]

    for msg, expected in holdout:
        prediction = classify_ticket(msg)
        assert "intent" in prediction and "confidence" in prediction
        print(
            f"Expected: {expected} | Got: {prediction['intent']} | "
            f"Confidence: {prediction['confidence']}"
        )
        if prediction["confidence"] < 0.8:
            print("  [FLAG] Low confidence. Route to human queue.")

Example output:

Expected: BUG_REPORT | Got: BUG_REPORT | Confidence: 0.94
Expected: FEATURE_REQUEST | Got: FEATURE_REQUEST | Confidence: 0.91
Expected: ACCOUNT_RECOVERY | Got: ACCOUNT_RECOVERY | Confidence: 0.89

Next steps

First, collect twenty real labeled examples from your own support queue and replace my synthetic few-shot prompts. You will see accuracy climb because the transferred knowledge anchors on vocabulary and sentence structures that actually match your users. If you notice confusion between two labels, add a contrasting example that shows the boundary case. Second, if you start hitting rate limits or need sub-second latency at scale, upgrade from the Free tier to Pro on Oxlo.ai and consider switching the model to DeepSeek V3.2 or Qwen 3 32B for faster inference on long system prompts.
