title: Optimizing LLM Deployment for Tech Support
content:
Tech support teams are increasingly routing customer tickets through large language models to summarize conversations, suggest resolutions, and execute agentic workflows. These workloads generate unusually long prompts. A single ticket can include system logs, prior thread history, knowledge base excerpts, and image attachments. Under traditional token-based inference, costs scale linearly with every character in that context window. For teams handling thousands of tickets daily, this pricing model turns a promising efficiency gain into an unpredictable line item. Optimizing deployment starts with choosing infrastructure that aligns pricing with actual support patterns, not just model capability.

The Context Bloat Problem in Support Pipelines

Support tickets are not short chat messages. A typical enterprise ticket may contain a subject line, a user description, a long stack trace, environment metadata, and several rounds of back-and-forth. When an LLM processes this, the entire thread is usually submitted as context so the model maintains state. In a token-based billing environment, every ticket refresh adds to the meter. Multi-turn conversations compound the problem because each new user message appends the full history.

Teams often respond by truncating logs or summarizing history manually, but that introduces friction and can strip away the signal needed for accurate diagnosis. A more sustainable approach is to decouple cost from context length so engineers can send the full payload without budget anxiety.

Model Routing and Task Segregation

Not every support interaction requires a frontier-scale model. The most cost-efficient deployments use a routing layer that matches task complexity to model size. A lightweight classifier can handle intent detection, sentiment analysis, and routing. A mid-size model can draft initial responses. Only escalations involving deep reasoning or complex code review need the largest parameters.

Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories, which makes this tiered approach practical without managing multiple providers. For fast triage, Qwen 3 32B handles multilingual reasoning and agent workflows with low latency. For general-purpose responses, Llama 3.3 70B works well. When a ticket involves deep reasoning or complex coding, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 are available on the same endpoint. Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, switching models is a single parameter change.

title: Revolutionizing Content Generation with LLMs
content:
I built a content pipeline that turns a one-line topic into a full technical article, complete with social assets and SEO metadata. It runs entirely on Oxlo.ai's request-based API, so I can feed it long transcripts or style guides without watching the token meter spin. If you are a developer who ships docs, blog posts, or changelog entries, this saves hours of drafting time.

What you'll need

  • Python 3.10 or newer.
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai.
  • The OpenAI SDK: pip install openai.

Step 1: Instantiate the Oxlo.ai client

I start by importing the OpenAI SDK and pointing it at Oxlo.ai. Because the platform is fully OpenAI-compatible, this is a literal drop-in replacement. I pull the key from an environment variable and run a one-line sanity check so I know the connection is alive before I build any logic around it.

from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

# Sanity check
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Confirm client is connected"}],
    max_tokens=10
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the creative contract for the whole pipeline. It forces the model to return distinct stages: a brief first, then the article body, then metadata. I keep it in a module-level constant so I can tune tone per project without touching the orchestration code. This makes the output predictable enough to parse by eye or with simple string checks.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a senior technical content strategist writing for developers.

Rules:
1. First output a brief with Title, Angle, and 3 Key Takeaways.
2. Then output the article body in Markdown with H2 sections.
3. Include a code snippet or comparison table when relevant.
4. End with a TL;DR of no more than 2 sentences.

Tone is plain, practical, and direct. No filler."""

Step 3: Generate the content brief

I never let the model write a thousand words without a plan. This function asks for a title, angle, and three key takeaways. The brief acts as a guardrail. If the angle is wrong, I catch it here instead of rewriting an entire article. I use Llama 3.3 70B because it follows structured instructions reliably at this stage.

def generate_brief(topic):
    user_message = (
        f"Topic: {topic}\n\n"
        f"Produce only the brief: Title, Angle, 3 Key Takeaways."
    )
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
        max_tokens=500,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

brief = generate_brief("How request-based pricing changes LLM cost forecasting")
print(brief)

Step 4: Draft the full article

With the brief locked in, I feed it back into the context and ask for the Markdown body. I explicitly request code snippets and comparison tables, since this pipeline targets a technical audience. Because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, I can pass the full brief plus a long style guide without the cost scaling with input length.

def draft_article(topic, brief):
    user_message = (
        f"Topic: {topic}\n\n"
        f"Brief:\n{brief}\n\n"
        f"Now write the full article body in Markdown. "
        f"Include a code example or table if it helps explain the concept."
    )
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
        max_tokens=1500,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

article = draft_article("How request-based pricing changes LLM cost forecasting", brief)
print(article)

Step 5: Generate promotion and metadata assets

Finally, I generate the distribution layer. I pass a truncated version of the article and ask for a social post, SEO keywords, and a meta description. Truncation keeps the model focused on summarization rather than regurgitation. I bump the temperature slightly here because creativity matters more for marketing copy than for the technical body.

def generate_assets(article_text):
    user_message = (
        f"Article excerpt:\n{article_text[:1500]}\n\n"
        f"Produce:\n"
        f"- One social post under 280 characters\n"
        f"- 3 SEO keywords\n"
        f"- One meta description under 160 characters"
    )
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
        temperature=0.8,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

assets = generate_assets(article)
print(assets)

Run it

I wire the stages together in a small CLI block. Executing end to end takes about ten seconds on Oxlo.ai because popular models have no cold starts. Here is the driver script, followed by what the output looks like when I run it with a real topic.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    topic = "Building agentic workflows with Qwen 3 on Oxlo.ai"

    print("=== BRIEF ===")
    brief = generate_brief(topic)
    print(brief)

    print("\n=== ARTICLE ===")
    article = draft_article(topic, brief)
    print(article)

    print("\n=== ASSETS ===")
    print(generate_assets(article))

title: Unlocking LLM Potential for Tech Support
content:
Tech support teams face a familiar tension. Ticket volumes grow linearly, but staffing budgets rarely keep pace. Customers expect instant, accurate answers drawn from sprawling product documentation, error logs, and years of historical case data. Large language models offer a genuine escape from this trap, but only if the underlying inference stack is built for the messy realities of support work. Long contexts, unpredictable query lengths, and tight cost controls make infrastructure choice every bit as important as model selection.

Why Traditional Tech Support Struggles at Scale

Traditional support organizations rely on static knowledge bases and rigid scripted chatbots. These systems work until a customer describes an edge case or attaches a 2,000-line stack trace. Human agents then spend the majority of their time reading thread history, cross-referencing documentation, or manually searching through logs. Escalation chains add hours to resolution times. The result is predictable: high agent churn, ballooning operational costs, and frustrated customers. LLMs can ingest entire conversation threads, documentation corpora, and structured log files in a single prompt, but unlocking that capability requires an inference provider that does not penalize you for every extra token of context.

What LLMs Actually Change

Modern LLMs shift the paradigm from keyword retrieval to semantic reasoning. A support bot can now accept a screenshot of an error via vision input, transcribe a voice description of symptoms through audio transcription, query an internal ticket system via function calling, and synthesize a fix from dozens of pages of API documentation. This moves the bottleneck away from information retrieval and squarely onto inference infrastructure. If your provider bills per token, every additional line of documentation, every turn of conversation history, and every log file append directly inflates your cost. The economics of the stack become the ceiling on the quality of the support experience.

The Infrastructure Problem Everyone Ignores

Most inference platforms bill per token. For tech support, that is a structural mismatch. A single troubleshooting session might include a 10,000-token system prompt stuffed with product documentation, a multi-turn conversation history, and a 5,000-token stack trace. On token-based providers, you pay for every single token on every single turn. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API call regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic support workloads, this can be significantly cheaper than token-based alternatives. You can include full documentation, extensive conversation history, and detailed logs without watching metered tokens drain your budget. The result is better answers because the model sees the full picture, not a truncated version.

Choosing the Right Model for the Job

Not every support query needs the same level of reasoning. Oxlo.ai hosts 45+ models across seven categories, all accessible through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint at https://api.oxlo.ai/v1.

For general troubleshooting and multilingual tickets, Qwen 3 32B offers strong reasoning and native agent workflow support. For complex coding issues or deep reasoning tasks, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE and DeepSeek V4 Flash excel at analyzing large codebases and log dumps. DeepSeek V4 Flash also supports a 1M context window, making it ideal for support bots that need to ingest entire wiki archives or lengthy error trails in one shot. For agentic coding, vision tasks, and architectural diagram analysis, Kimi K2.6 handles 131K context and processes screenshots of UI errors. For fast, cost-sensitive triage, Llama 3.3 70B provides a reliable general-purpose flagship response. When you need structured output for ticket creation or escalation logic, JSON mode and function calling are available across compatible models. Because Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, your support bot responds immediately even during traffic spikes.

Building the Integration

A support agent is only useful if it can act. Function calling lets the LLM query internal tools: looking up a customer ID, checking service status, or searching a vector store. Below is a minimal Python example using the OpenAI SDK pointed at Oxlo.ai. It defines a tool to fetch ticket history and requests a JSON response for downstream processing.

import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_ticket_history",
        "description": "Retrieve recent support tickets for a user",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "user_id": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["user_id"]

}]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a senior support engineer. Be concise. Use the ticket history tool when needed."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "User u-8842 reports a 500 error on the checkout API since 09:00 UTC."}
    ],
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto",
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

This is especially valuable for agentic support bots that iterate over tools and maintain state across multiple turns. from datetime import datetime

# Point the client at Oxlo.ai and swap in your API key
client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")

# Llama 3.3 70B is a solid general-purpose model for tool use
MODEL = "llama-3.3-70b"

# Lock "today" so the refund math is reproducible
TODAY = datetime(2025, 2, 1)

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt is the only training the agent receives, so it needs to spell out the persona, policy, and workflow. Copy the block below into your file and edit the policy section to match your actual business rules.

# This prompt is the entire "training" for the agent. Be explicit.
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a concise support agent for an electronics store.
Your job is to help customers with order status and refund requests.

Policy rules you must follow:
1. Always verify the order ID before discussing details.
2. Refunds are only allowed within 30 days of purchase.
3. If a refund is denied, explain the policy calmly and offer a repair option.
4. Never make up order details. Use the provided tools.
5. Keep responses under three sentences when possible."""

Step 3: Mock the order database and tool schemas

Real agents need real data. Since this tutorial focuses on the LLM layer, I mocked the database with a plain Python dictionary. The tool schemas tell the model exactly when to look up an order and when to attempt a refund.

# Mock database: in production, replace this with a real API or SQL lookup
ORDERS = {
    "ORD-1001": {"item": "Wireless Headphones", "status": "delivered", "purchased": "2024-12-01", "price": 79.99},
    "ORD-1002": {"item": "Mechanical Keyboard", "status": "delivered", "purchased": "2025-01-20", "price": 129.99},
    "ORD-1003": {"item": "USB-C Dock", "status": "shipped", "purchased": "2024-06-10", "price": 49.99},
}

# Tool schemas are standard OpenAI format. Oxlo.ai parses them exactly.
TOOLS = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Retrieve current status and details for a given order ID.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "The order ID, e.g. ORD-1001"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    },
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "initiate_refund",
            "description": "Start a refund for an order if it is within the allowed window.",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {"type": "string", "description": "The order ID to refund"}
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

Step 4: Implement the tool handlers with policy checks

LLMs can misread dates, so I hardcode the 30-day refund limit in Python rather than trusting the prompt alone. If the order is too old, the handler returns a denial and the model explains it politely to the customer.

def lookup_order(order_id: str):
    """Return order details or a clear error."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if not order:
        return {"found": False, "error": "Order ID not found."}
    return {"found": True, "order": order}

def initiate_refund(order_id: str):
    """Enforce the 30-day policy in code, not just in the prompt."""
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if not order:
        return {"success": False, "error": "Order ID not found."}
    purchased = datetime.strptime(order["purchased"], "%Y-%m-%d")
    # Hard guardrail: reject anything older than 30 days
    if (TODAY - purchased).days > 30:
        return {"success": False, "eligible": False, "reason": "Outside 30-day refund window."}
    return {"success": True, "refund_amount": order["price"], "method": "original payment"}

def handle_tool_call(tool_call):
    """Route the model's tool request to the correct local function."""
    name = tool_call.function.name
    args = json.loads(tool_call.function.arguments)
    if name == "lookup_order":
        return lookup_order(**args)
    elif name == "initiate_refund":
        return initiate_refund(**args)
    return {"error": "Unknown tool"}

Step 5: Build the agent loop

This function sends the user message to Oxlo.ai, appends any tool calls to the conversation history, executes the local functions, and sends the results back. The loop continues until the model returns a final text response instead of another tool call.

def run_agent(user_message: str):
    """Main loop: call the model, handle tools, repeat until final answer."""
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
    ]

    while True:
        # Fire the request to Oxlo.ai
        response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=MODEL,
            messages=messages,
            tools=TOOLS,
            tool_choice="auto",
        )
        message = response.choices[0].message

        if message.tool_calls:
            # Append the assistant's tool request to history
            messages.append({
                "role": "assistant",
                "content": message.content or "",
                "tool_calls": [
                    {
                        "id": tc.id,
                        "type": tc.type,
                        "function": {
                            "name": tc.function.name,
                            "arguments": tc.function.arguments,
                        },
                    }
                    for tc in message.tool_calls
                ],
            })
            # Execute each tool and append the result
            for tc in message.tool_calls:
                result = handle_tool_call(tc)
                messages.append({
                    "role": "tool",
                    "tool_call_id": tc.id,
                    "content": json.dumps(result),
                })
        else:
            # Final text response
            return message.content

Run it

At the bottom of support_agent.py, call run_agent with a couple of test messages. The first order is outside the refund window, and the second is inside it. Save the file and run it.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Scenario A: old order, should be denied
    print(run_agent("I want a refund for ORD-1001. It never worked."))
    print("---")
    # Scenario B: recent order, should be approved
    print(run_agent("Can I return ORD-1002? It is the wrong color."))

Run the script from your terminal:

python support_agent.py

The first message asks for a refund on ORD-1001, which our mock database shows was purchased on December 1, 2024. Because that is well beyond the 30-day window hardcoded in our tool handler, the model receives a denial from the function and explains the policy to the user. The second message targets ORD-1002, a recent purchase from January 20, 2025, so the tool handler returns a success payload and the model confirms the refund amount and timeline. When I ran this against Oxlo.ai, the output looked like the following. Your exact wording may vary slightly, but the policy outcomes will be identical because the tool handlers enforce them.

Order ORD-1001 is outside our 30-day refund window, so I cannot process a return. I can offer a repair option instead. Let me know if you would like to proceed.
---
I have initiated a refund of $129.99 for order ORD-1002. The funds will return to your original payment method within 5 to 7 business days.

Notice how the agent stayed concise and did not hallucinate policy exceptions. That is the result of combining a clear system prompt with hardcoded guardrails in the tool layer. Because Oxlo.ai bills per request rather than per token, a long customer rant or a lengthy order transcript does not inflate your cost. You simply pay for the turn, which makes budgeting for a support queue straightforward. See https://oxlo.ai/pricing for current plan details.

Next steps

Swap the mock dictionary for a real database connection or internal API. If you expect heavy traffic, put the agent behind a small FastAPI endpoint and stream responses back to your help-desk UI using Oxlo.ai's streaming support. You could also switch to kimi-k2.6 for longer context windows when customers paste in weeks of back-and-forth history, still paying the same flat per-request rate on Oxlo.ai.

title: Building Chatbots with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
Building a production chatbot with large language models requires more than wrapping a prompt in a REST call. You need to manage conversation state, select the right model for latency and capability, handle tool use, and control costs as context windows fill with multi-turn history. The difference between a prototype and a reliable conversational agent often comes down to infrastructure decisions around context management and inference pricing. This guide walks through the core engineering choices for building chatbots that remain responsive and cost-effective at scale.

Architecture Fundamentals

A typical LLM chatbot has three layers: the interface, the orchestration layer, and the inference backend. The orchestration layer maintains message history, applies a system prompt, and formats user input into the chat template expected by the model. Every turn appends new messages to a growing array. Without active management, this array eventually exceeds the model's context limit or introduces latency and cost overhead. Most implementations use a sliding window to retain the most recent N messages, or they summarize older turns into a compressed system prompt. You should also separate static instructions, such as personality definitions and safety guidelines, from dynamic content like retrieval-augmented generation context and user messages. This separation lets you cache static portions and reduce redundant computation. Finally, consider the inference backend's context window limits. A backend that supports very long contexts without penalizing input length gives you more freedom to keep history intact.

Choosing the Right Model

Model selection depends on your chatbot's domain, languages, and reasoning requirements. For general customer support or open-domain conversation, a strong multilingual model like Qwen 3 32B or Llama 3.3 70B provides low latency and broad knowledge. If the chatbot performs complex coding assistance or multi-step agent workflows, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 offer advanced chain-of-thought reasoning and a 131K context window. For vision-enabled bots that process user-uploaded images, Kimi VL A3B or Gemma 3 27B handle image inputs alongside text. When you need efficient reasoning with an extremely long context, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports 1M tokens and near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning in a mixture-of-experts architecture.

title: Semantic Role Labeling with LLMs: Opportunities and Challenges
content:
Semantic role labeling is the task of identifying the predicate-argument structure in text. Given a sentence like "The chef cooked the soup in the kitchen," SRL identifies "chef" as the agent, "soup" as the patient, and "kitchen" as the location. For years, this required specialized linguistic pipelines or fine-tuned models such as PropBank-trained BERT variants. Today, large language models can perform SRL through prompt-based extraction, turning a classical NLP chore into a generic reasoning task. This shift reduces pipeline complexity, but it introduces new infrastructure considerations for teams running SRL at scale.

What Is Semantic Role Labeling and Why It Still Matters

SRL maps sentences to predicate-argument structures, typically following frameworks such as PropBank or FrameNet. The goal is to identify who did what to whom, where, when, and why. In the sentence "The committee approved the funding after weeks of debate," an SRL system labels "committee" as the agent (ARG0), "funding" as the patient (ARG1), and "after weeks of debate" as a temporal modifier (ARGM-TMP).

This is not an academic exercise. SRL underpins information extraction, event detection, question answering, and agentic tool use. When a support agent asks, "Which customer reported which issue and when?", the backend system is effectively querying SRL structures. Frame-based semantic parsing also helps large language models ground actions in structured environments, making SRL a quiet workhorse in modern AI infrastructure.

How LLMs Change the SRL Pipeline

Classical SRL pipelines combine part-of-speech taggers, dependency parsers, and token classifiers. These components are brittle across domains and require annotated data for each new predicate type. LLMs invert this logic. A model such as Qwen 3 32B or Llama 3.3 70B can read a sentence and emit structured role assignments without task-specific fine-tuning, provided the prompt defines the target frame.

The real change is flexibility. A single LLM can switch between PropBank-style roles, custom frame definitions, or multilingual schemas within the same session. With JSON mode and function calling, the output can be constrained to valid structures that downstream systems consume directly. This collapses what used to be a five-stage pipeline into one API request.

Prompt Engineering for Structured Extraction

Reliable SRL with LLMs depends on precise prompting and schema enforcement. You should define the predicate, expected arguments, and any constraints on role labels. Instead of asking for a free-text analysis, supply a JSON schema and use the model's structured output capability.

Below is a minimal example using the Oxlo.ai API, which is fully OpenAI SDK compatible. The example uses DeepSeek V4 Flash, a model with a one-million-token context window and efficient MoE architecture, making it suitable for long-document SRL.

from openai import OpenAI
import json

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_API_KEY"
)

schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "predicate": {"type": "string"},
        "arguments": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "role": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "enum": ["ARG0", "ARG1", "ARG2", "ARGM-LOC", "ARGM-TMP", "ARGM-MNR"]
                    },
                    "text": {"type": "string"}
                },
                "required": ["role", "text"]
            }
        }
    },
    "required": ["predicate", "arguments"]
}

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek-v4-flash",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",
            "content": "You are a precise semantic role labeler. Extract predicate-argument structures according to PropBank guidelines. Respond with valid JSON only."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "The acquisition will expand the company's presence in Asian markets by 2026."
        }
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"}
)

result = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))

Setting a low temperature, ideally between 0.0 and 0.2, reduces variability in role assignments. You should also validate the output with a library such as Pydantic before passing it to downstream logic. If you are processing multilingual documents, Qwen 3 32B provides strong multilingual reasoning and can maintain role consistency across mixed-language inputs.

Opportunities: Zero-Shot Reasoning and Long Context

The most immediate opportunity is zero-shot generalization. An LLM trained on broad corpora can infer roles for rare predicates or emerging jargon without retraining. This is valuable in legal, biomedical, and financial domains where new events and entities appear constantly.

Long-context models extend this from sentences to documents. Kimi K2.6 supports 131K tokens, and DeepSeek V4 Flash handles up to one million tokens. With these context windows, you can label roles across an entire earnings call transcript or a contract in a single pass. Cross-sentence coreference becomes easier because the model sees the full text at once, rather than relying on error-prone chunking and stitching logic. For agentic workflows, GLM 5 and Minimax M2.5 offer strong tool use and reasoning that can integrate SRL output directly into action pipelines.

Challenges: Consistency, Hallucination, and Cost at Scale

LLM-based SRL is not without problems. Role labels can drift across similar sentences. A model may label "the chef" as ARG0 in one instance and as ARGM-MNR in another, breaking downstream analytics. Hallucinated predicates are another risk: the model may invent a role or misidentify the verbal head in a complex clause.

Cost and latency are the primary infrastructure barriers. SRL on long documents consumes large numbers of input tokens. On token-based providers, this scales linearly with document length, making batch processing of archives or real-time processing of live streams expensive. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, charging one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context SRL workloads, this can reduce inference costs significantly compared to token-based alternatives. The platform also offers no cold starts on popular models, which keeps latency predictable for synchronous pipelines.

Implementation Notes for Production Engineers

When moving from prototype to production, treat the LLM as a noisy parser, not an oracle. Implement a validation layer that checks role names against an allowed vocabulary and verifies that every predicate has at least one core argument. If you process documents longer than the target model's context window, use semantic chunking at paragraph boundaries rather than fixed token cuts, and propagate entity mentions across chunks with a resolution pass.

Oxlo.ai supports streaming responses, which lets you start validating partial JSON as soon as tokens arrive. For workloads that require deep reasoning over ambiguous syntax, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE provides chain-of-thought reasoning that can disambiguate nested clauses before emitting the final structured result. If you need a smaller, faster model for high-volume traffic, DeepSeek V3.2 offers strong coding and reasoning capabilities and is available on the Oxlo.ai free tier.

Monitor your request patterns. Because Oxlo.ai prices by the request, you can send a full document with surrounding instructions in a single call without worrying about incremental token costs. This encourages simpler architectures: one request per document, not a chain of summarization, chunking, and labeling calls.

Where Oxlo.ai Fits

Semantic role labeling is moving from specialized NLP pipelines into general-purpose LLM inference. The infrastructure you choose should support long inputs, structured outputs, and predictable costs. Oxlo.ai provides 45+ models across seven categories, including the long-context and reasoning models most relevant to SRL, with full OpenAI SDK compatibility. You can drop the same code you use for OpenAI into Oxlo.ai by changing the base URL to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1.

Request-based pricing means that labeling a one-million-token document with DeepSeek V4 Flash costs the same as labeling a short sentence. For teams building document understanding pipelines, agentic systems, or event extraction backends, this pricing model removes the penalty for using full context. You can explore the structure on the Oxlo.ai pricing page or start with the free tier, which includes 60 requests per day and a 7-day full-access trial across 16+ models.

title: LLM-Driven Dependency Parsing: A Deep Dive
content:
Dependency parsing remains one of the foundational tasks in natural language processing, mapping syntactic relationships between words to reveal sentence structure. Traditional methods rely on specialized taggers and transition-based or graph-based parsers that demand significant feature engineering and language-specific training data. Large language models now offer an alternative path, treating parsing as either a sequence-to-sequence translation problem or a structured prediction task over natural language prompts. For engineering teams building modern NLP stacks, the shift toward LLM-driven parsing raises important questions about inference cost, output structure, and latency. Oxlo.ai provides an inference platform designed for exactly these workloads, with request-based pricing and full OpenAI SDK compatibility that simplifies integration into syntactic analysis pipelines.

What Is Dependency Parsing?

In dependency parsing, the goal is to identify a directed graph between words in a sentence where each word except the root is a dependent of exactly one head word. Linguists and engineers typically work within frameworks such as Universal Dependencies, which defines a standardized inventory of relations including nsubj, dobj, amod, and nmod. These directed arcs encode not only grammatical roles but also semantic cues that downstream applications rely on. Named entity recognition, relation extraction, semantic role labeling, and question answering systems all benefit from accurate parse trees. Evaluating parser quality typically involves Unlabeled Attachment Score and Labeled Attachment Score, metrics that reward both correct head selection and correct relation classification. Traditional parsers optimize these directly through arc-factored or second-order features. LLMs do not explicitly optimize for UAS or LAS during pretraining, yet their implicit grasp of grammar often yields competitive scores, especially when guided by careful prompting.

Why LLMs Change the Game

The primary advantage of using LLMs for dependency parsing is their ability to generalize across languages and domains without task-specific architectures. A model such as Qwen 3 32B or Llama 3.3 70B can process sentences in dozens of languages and infer syntactic structure even when faced with informal or noisy input that would break traditional pipelines. Instead of maintaining separate models per language, teams can prompt a single model with instructions like "Return the dependency tree for the following sentence as a JSON array." This unified approach reduces model sprawl and deployment complexity. However, it introduces new engineering constraints. Output must conform to strict schemas to be usable in downstream databases or visualization tools. Token costs on traditional providers scale with prompt length, which is problematic because parsing workloads often involve highly variable input lengths, from short queries to multi-sentence paragraphs. Oxlo.ai addresses this through flat per-request pricing, making it possible to parse long documents without watching token meters climb.

Architectures for LLM-Driven Parsing

There are several practical architectures for integrating LLMs into dependency parsing workflows.

Zero-shot prompting is the simplest entry point. You provide the sentence and a system prompt describing the desired output format, such as a list of tuples containing token index, head index, and dependency relation. Because LLMs have seen vast amounts of text during pretraining, they often produce linguistically plausible trees without any fine-tuning.

Few-shot in-context learning improves consistency. By embedding two or three exemplar sentences with their corresponding CoNLL-U or JSON representations inside the prompt, you anchor the model to the exact annotation style your pipeline expects. This reduces format drift and improves accuracy on low-resource languages or technical domains.

Structured generation is the critical production requirement. Raw text completions from an LLM may miss brackets, use incorrect keys, or hallucinate relations. Using JSON mode or function calling guarantees that the output parses cleanly into your application logic. Another emerging technique is constrained decoding, where the inference engine restricts the next token distribution to ensure valid output grammar. While not all APIs expose logits-level control, JSON mode achieves a similar outcome at the application layer by forcing the model to produce parseable objects. For maximum reliability, you can combine JSON mode with Pydantic validation on the client side, retrying only on schema failures rather than re-prompting from scratch. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode and streaming responses across its 45-plus models, so you can enforce schemas while receiving tokens incrementally.

For teams with proprietary annotated treebanks, fine-tuning remains an option, though it demands significant compute and data curation. In most cases, a well-engineered prompt with structured output constraints on a capable generalist model delivers sufficient accuracy at a fraction of the operational cost.

title: Named Entity Recognition with LLMs: Best Practices and Applications
content:
Named entity recognition has moved well beyond BIO tagging and pipeline-based spaCy models. Large language models can perform zero-shot entity extraction across domains, adapt to custom schemas without retraining, and resolve coreference across long passages. For engineering teams, the challenge is no longer whether an LLM can identify a person or organization. It is how to extract structured entities reliably, at scale, without letting inference costs scale linearly with every additional paragraph of context.

Traditional NER systems require annotated corpora, feature engineering, and retraining for each new entity type. LLMs collapse that workflow into a single prompt. A carefully written instruction can extract standard entities like people, locations, and organizations, or domain-specific concepts like drug names, legal clauses, and financial instruments. The flexibility is significant, but it introduces new engineering constraints around prompt stability, output formatting, and context window economics.

Prompt Engineering for Structured Extraction

The difference between a demo and a production NER pipeline is usually the prompt. Vague instructions like "extract all entities" produce inconsistent results. Production prompts should define the target schema explicitly, specify how to handle overlapping or nested entities, and provide formatting rules that remove ambiguity.

Few-shot prompting remains one of the most reliable ways to improve accuracy. Include two or three examples of raw text paired with the desired entity list, formatted in the exact structure you expect in production. If your application needs to distinguish between a company name and a product name, show the model concrete boundary cases. This reduces hallucination and stabilizes output across heterogeneous inputs. Pay special attention to entity boundaries. An LLM might include trailing punctuation or drop possessive suffixes unless your examples explicitly show where spans begin and end.

For applications that require strict schema compliance, JSON mode is essential. Instead of parsing free text, you can instruct the model to return a structured object with arrays of entities, confidence scores, or source offsets. Oxlo.ai supports JSON mode across its LLMs, which means you can enforce type constraints directly at the API level and skip brittle regex post-processing. When combined with a low temperature setting, JSON mode turns a generative model into a predictable extraction engine.

Handling Long Documents and Context Windows

Many high-value NER workloads involve long inputs. Legal contracts, clinical discharge summaries, earnings transcripts, SEC filings, and research papers routinely exceed ten thousand tokens. Extracting entities from these documents in a single pass preserves cross-sentence coreference and reduces error propagation from segmentation logic.

The infrastructure cost of long-context NER is a genuine concern on token-based platforms. When pricing scales with input length, a single long document can cost as much as dozens of short chat queries. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, which means you pay one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. For long-context and agentic NER workloads, this can make a substantial difference in monthly spend compared to token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale. You can send an entire contract or patient record without watching the meter run on every token.

If a document exceeds the context window of your chosen model, use a sliding window with overlap and merge entities across chunks. Track entity identity with embedding-based clustering or deterministic string matching in a downstream deduplication step. When possible, prefer models with larger context windows so you can minimize chunking logic and preserve global context.

JSON Mode and Function Calling

Reliable NER pipelines do not parse bullet points from prose. They consume structured data. Below is a minimal example using the OpenAI SDK with Oxlo.ai to extract entities into a validated JSON schema.

)

    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "entities": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "text": {"type": "string"},
                    "label": {"type": "string", "enum": ["PERSON", "ORG", "GPE", "PRODUCT"]},
                    "start": {"type": "integer"},
                    "end": {"type": "integer"}
                },
                "required": ["text", "label", "start", "end"]
            }
        }
    },
    "required": ["entities"]
}

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a precise NER engine. Extract entities exactly as they appear in the text."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Apple Inc. is planning to open a new office in Austin by January 2026."}
    ],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
    temperature=0.1
)

import json
result = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
print(result)

Because Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, existing NER code written for other providers runs with a single line changed, the base URL. The platform also supports function calling and tool use, which lets you route extracted entities directly into downstream actions such as database inserts, web searches, or validation functions without intermediate parsing logic. This is especially powerful for agentic pipelines where extraction triggers an immediate external lookup or enrichment step.

Model Selection for NER Workloads

Not every NER task requires the largest model. Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 open-source and proprietary models across seven categories, so you can match capacity to complexity and budget.

For general-purpose English NER, Llama 3.3 70B provides strong accuracy and low latency. If your data is multilingual, Qwen 3 32B handles mixed-language documents and agent workflows well. When entities require deep reasoning to disambiguate, such as nested corporate subsidiaries or ambiguous pronoun resolution across sections, DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or Kimi K2.6 offer advanced chain-of-thought reasoning. For extremely long documents, DeepSeek V4 Flash supports a 1M context window and efficient MoE inference, letting you process entire books or codebases in one request. GPT-Oss 120B is another strong open-source option for large-scale extraction tasks.

title: Sentiment Analysis with LLMs: A Comprehensive Guide
content:
What we are building

We are building a lightweight Python CLI that classifies product reviews into Positive, Negative, or Neutral and returns a calibrated confidence score. This is useful for support teams and product managers who need structured signal from unstructured text without managing a separate NLP pipeline or worrying about token accounting on every request. Because we are running inference on Oxlo.ai, we get flat per-request pricing that stays predictable even when reviews are long, plus instant startup with no cold starts on models like Llama 3.3 70B.

What you'll need

Make sure you have Python 3.10 or newer installed. You will also need the OpenAI SDK, which Oxlo.ai supports as a drop-in replacement. Install it with pip.

pip install openai

Finally, grab an API key from the Oxlo.ai portal. Oxlo.ai is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, so the only code change is setting the base_url to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. If you are migrating from a token-based provider, you can keep your existing OpenAI client patterns and simply swap the base URL and model identifiers. The flat per-request pricing is worth noting here, because sentiment analysis on long-form reviews, multi-turn support tickets, or agentic summaries does not balloon in cost as input length grows. You pay per inference call, which makes budgeting for batch jobs straightforward.

Step 1: Set up the Oxlo.ai client

I keep secrets in environment variables. Export OXLO_API_KEY from the Oxlo.ai portal, then initialize the client exactly as you would for the standard OpenAI SDK. The only difference is the base_url pointing to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1. Using the OpenAI SDK against Oxlo.ai means you get streaming, function calling, and JSON mode support out of the box without learning a new interface. That compatibility is useful when your sentiment tool eventually needs to call a secondary API to look up order IDs.

For this project I am using Llama 3.3 70B because it handles classification tasks with low verbosity and high reliability. Oxlo.ai hosts more than 45 models, but for English sentiment classification this one hits the sweet spot of speed and accuracy. If you later need to process multilingual data, switching to Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 is a one-line change with the same client.

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OXLO_API_KEY"],
)

Step 2: Lock down the system prompt

The system prompt is the contract between your code and the model. I treat it like a schema definition. The model must return exactly two keys, sentiment and confidence, with no markdown fences and no conversational filler. This keeps downstream parsing trivial and prevents brittle regex hacks. I keep the allowed labels constrained to three options. Expanding the taxonomy is easy, but start small so you can measure accuracy before adding granular emotions like frustration or delight.

I have found that Llama 3.3 70B respects this instruction consistently on Oxlo.ai. If your dataset includes mixed languages or heavily sarcastic text, Qwen 3 32B is a strong alternative available on the same endpoint.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a sentiment analysis engine.
Classify the user's review into exactly one of these labels: Positive, Negative, or Neutral.
Respond with a single JSON object containing two keys:
- "sentiment": the label
- "confidence": a float between 0.0 and 1.0
Do not include markdown, explanations, or any text outside the JSON object."""

Step 3: Write the analysis function

Now wrap the API call in a small function that injects the user review and parses the JSON response. I keep the interface simple: string in, dictionary out. The function returns a native Python dictionary, so you can immediately access result["sentiment"] or result["confidence"] in conditional logic. This keeps the integration clean whether you are writing to a database or emitting metrics.

In a production service you would add retries, timeout handling, and schema validation, but for a shipped internal tool this level of rigor is enough to get started. The strip() call removes any leading whitespace that occasionally leaks through. If you see malformed JSON on edge cases, you can add a lightweight sanitization step or switch to a model with stronger instruction following. On Oxlo.ai, I rarely see markdown fences from Llama 3.3 70B when the prompt explicitly forbids them, but it is worth logging raw outputs during your first test run so you can spot outliers.

import json

def analyze_sentiment(user_message: str):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_message},
        ],
    )

    raw = response.choices[0].message.content.strip()
    return json.loads(raw)

Step 4: Run a batch over multiple reviews

Real data rarely arrives one review at a time. Here is a short list of raw strings representing typical product feedback. We loop through them and print structured results. Notice that the last review is longer and angrier than the others. On a token-based provider, that extra length would increase cost. On Oxlo.ai, the price is the same flat rate per request, which simplifies cost forecasting for support queues where ticket length varies wildly.

If you move from a toy script to a production pipeline, wrap the loop in asyncio or a ThreadPoolExecutor to send requests concurrently. Oxlo.ai does not cold start popular models, so concurrency scales without the latency spikes that can derail batch jobs on other platforms.

reviews = [
    "The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked all day without plugging in.",
    "Shipping was late and the box was damaged. Not impressed with the service at all.",
    "It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special, but nothing wrong either.",
    "I tried to return the item and customer support never responded. Worst experience ever.",
]

for text in reviews:
    result = analyze_sentiment(text)
    print(f"Review: {text[:60]}...")
    print(f"Result: {json.dumps(result, indent=2)}")
    print()

Run it

Put the pieces together in a single file, export your key, and run python sentiment.py. You should see clean JSON for each review. You can redirect this output to a file or pipe it into jq for quick inspection. The JSON structure is stable enough to feed directly into a pandas DataFrame if you want to calculate mean confidence by category.

Here is what the output looks like on my end using Llama 3.3 70B through Oxlo.ai.

Review: The battery life on this laptop is incredible. I worked all da...
Result: {
  "sentiment": "Positive",
  "confidence": 0.94
}

Review: Shipping was late and the box was damaged. Not impressed with...
Result: {
  "sentiment": "Negative",
  "confidence": 0.91
}

Review: It is a laptop. It turns on. Nothing special, but nothing wro...
Result: {
  "sentiment": "Neutral",
  "confidence": 0.78
}

Review: I tried to return the item and customer support never respond...
Result: {
  "sentiment": "Negative",
  "confidence": 0.96
}

If the output feels too cautious or you need deeper reasoning for sarcastic text, try Kimi K2.6 or DeepSeek V3.2. Both are available on the same Oxlo.ai base URL, so the only change is the model string. This is useful when you move from a simple polarity classifier to a more nuanced emotion detection pipeline.

Wrap-up and next steps

This script is a working foundation you can run today. Two concrete ways to extend it: first, persist results to a SQLite database and trend sentiment over time by product category or release version. Second, wire the script into a webhook so negative reviews above a confidence threshold trigger a Slack alert for your support team in real time. Both extensions benefit from Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing, because monitoring long support threads or detailed feedback forms does not inflate costs as input length grows.

Because Oxlo.ai exposes fully OpenAI-compatible endpoints, you can also adopt this pattern in Node.js, Go, or any other language with an OpenAI client by changing the base URL. The infrastructure stays simple even as the use case grows. If you want to see how the pricing model works for your volume, check https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Unlocking Dialogue Systems with LLMs
content:
Building dialogue systems used to mean handcrafting intent classifiers, slot taggers, and rigid state machines. Large language models changed the rules. A single LLM can now handle natural language understanding, context tracking, and response generation in one pass. The result is more fluid conversations, but also new engineering constraints. Stateful, multi-turn interactions inflate prompt lengths. Agentic flows require reliable function calling. Multimodal inputs demand vision and audio models running alongside text backends. Even a simple customer support bot can accumulate thousands of tokens of policy documentation and conversation history within a few exchanges. The model matters, yet the inference platform matters just as much. If your provider penalizes long contexts with token-based metering, every extra turn in the conversation becomes a tax on user experience.

What Makes a Dialogue System Actually Work?

A production dialogue system is more than a chat loop. It needs turn management, context grounding, error recovery, and often external tool integration. In classical pipelines, these were separate modules. Modern LLMs collapse many of these layers into a single generative step, but the underlying requirements remain. You still need to maintain conversation state, inject system instructions, and format user context so the model stays coherent across turns.

Retrieval-augmented generation adds another layer. When a dialogue system pulls in knowledge base articles, product manuals, or past ticket transcripts, the prompt grows fast. The inference platform must ingest that context without choking on cost or latency. The backend becomes a core architectural component. Latency determines how natural the interaction feels. Context window size dictates how much history you can keep in working memory. Support for structured output and function calling determines whether the system can reliably trigger external actions. When you evaluate infrastructure for dialogue, look beyond raw model benchmarks. Check whether the platform offers consistent uptime, low latency, and economic viability for long prompts that grow with every user turn.

The Hidden Cost of Long Conversations

Dialogue is inherently stateful. Every turn appends tokens to the context. A system prompt, a retrieval-augmented knowledge base, and ten turns of back-and-forth can quickly push prompt lengths into the tens of thousands of tokens. Under token-based pricing, costs scale linearly with that length. For agentic workloads that iterate over plans, query results, and user clarifications, the bill compounds fast.

Truncation might seem like an easy fix, but dropping early turns destroys pronoun resolution, user preferences, and task constraints. Compressing history through summarization adds another model call and risks information loss. A pricing model that accommodates long contexts lets you preserve fidelity.

This is where pricing structure becomes an architectural decision. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing: one flat cost per API request regardless of prompt length. Unlike token-based providers such as Together AI, Fireworks AI, OpenRouter, Replicate, and Anyscale, Oxlo.ai does not charge more when your dialogue history grows. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can make the platform significantly cheaper. You can keep more turns in context, provide richer system prompts, and avoid aggressive truncation strategies that degrade conversation quality. The predictability also simplifies budgeting. You know exactly how much a thousand user sessions will cost without estimating average turns per session.

Designing for State and Memory

Effective dialogue systems need memory. Short-term memory lives in the context window. Long-term memory usually relies on external stores, but the context window still determines how much recent history the model can attend to in a single inference call. Oxlo.ai hosts models with substantial context capacities. Kimi K2.6 offers a 131K context window. DeepSeek V4 Flash supports 1M tokens. GLM 5, a 744B MoE model, targets long-horizon agentic tasks that span many reasoning steps. These windows let you retain full conversation transcripts, detailed personas, or lengthy retrieved documents without truncation.

Some teams attempt to manage cost by summarizing conversation history every few turns. This introduces latency and can strip out nuanced instructions or emotional tone. With Oxlo.ai, keeping the full transcript in context is economically viable, so you can prioritize accuracy over compression.

However, large contexts are only useful if the model is ready when you need it. Oxlo.ai offers no cold starts on popular models, which means your dialogue endpoint responds immediately even after idle periods. This is critical for interactive applications where users expect sub-second replies. Combined with streaming responses, you can start rendering text to the user while the model is still generating, improving perceived latency across long replies.

Tool Use and Agentic Turn-Taking

Most useful dialogue systems do more than talk. They schedule meetings, query databases, run code, or browse the web. This requires the model to emit structured calls, pause for results, and incorporate those results into the next turn. Reliable function calling and JSON mode are therefore non-negotiable features.

Oxlo.ai provides both, across a catalog that includes models specifically suited for agentic workflows. Qwen 3 32B is built for multilingual reasoning and agent workflows. Minimax M

title: Conversational AI Tutorial
content:
We are going to build a conversational customer support agent that remembers context across multiple turns and can look up order status from a backend. This is the same architecture I use for production assistants that need to hold long conversations without rewriting client code. I run it on Oxlo.ai because the flat per-request pricing keeps long chat histories predictable, and the fully OpenAI-compatible API means the agent drops into existing stacks without friction.

What you'll need

Before we start, make sure you have the following ready:

  • Python 3.10 or newer installed locally
  • The OpenAI Python SDK: pip install openai
  • An Oxlo.ai API key from https://portal.oxlo.ai

I also recommend setting your API key in an environment variable rather than hardcoding it, but for this tutorial I will keep it explicit so the flow is obvious.

Step 1: Initialize the Oxlo.ai client and conversation store

Every request goes to Oxlo.ai through the OpenAI SDK. I keep a global messages list so the agent retains context across turns. Without this, the model would treat every message as a fresh conversation and forget the user's order ID from one line to the next. This is where flat per-request pricing matters, because appending history does not increase the cost of each subsequent call. On token-based providers, long threads can get expensive quickly, but Oxlo.ai charges the same flat rate per request regardless of how much context you send.

from openai import OpenAI
import json
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key=os.environ.get("OXLO_API_KEY", "YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
)

messages = []

Step 2: Define the system prompt

The system prompt sets the agent's personality and guardrails. I keep it specific: the agent should ask for an order ID when needed, use the lookup tool, and never hallucinate tracking details.

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a support agent for a direct-to-consumer electronics store.
Your job is to answer questions and look up order status.
If a user asks about an order, use the lookup_order tool with the exact order ID provided.
Do not guess order statuses. If you do not know something, say so.
Be concise but friendly."""

Step 3: Add a tool definition and mock backend

Real agents need to do more than generate text. They need to take action. I define a lookup_order Python function and register its JSON schema in the tools list so the model can request it. The schema tells the model exactly what arguments to provide. The mock database is just a dictionary for demonstration, but you can swap in a real API or SQL query without touching the agent logic.

MOCK_ORDERS = {
    "ORD-1001": {"status": "shipped", "item": "Wireless Headphones", "eta": "2 days"},
    "ORD-1002": {"status": "processing", "item": "USB-C Hub", "eta": "5 days"},
}

def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    order = MOCK_ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if not order:
        return json.dumps({"error": "Order not found"})
    return json.dumps(order)

TOOLS = [
    {
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
            "name": "lookup_order",
            "description": "Retrieve the current status and ETA for a customer order",
            "parameters": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "order_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "description": "The order identifier, for example ORD-1001"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["order_id"]
            }
        }
    }
]

Step 4: Build the turn handler

This function appends the user's message to history, calls Llama 3.3 70B on Oxlo.ai with the tool schema attached, and checks if the model wants to invoke a function. If it does, I run the local Python function, append the result as a tool message, and send the updated history back for the final assistant reply. This two-pass pattern is standard for agentic workflows. The first request decides what action to take, and the second request generates the human-friendly answer based on the tool result. Because Oxlo.ai uses per-request pricing, the extra tool-resolution call stays cheap even as the conversation history grows. You could run fifty turns with full context and still pay the same flat rate per request. I rebuild the assistant message manually as a plain dict to avoid serialization issues when I mix SDK objects with my own tool result dictionaries.

def chat(user_input: str) -> str:
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="llama-3.3-70b",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}] + messages,
        tools=TOOLS,
        tool_choice="auto",
    )
    
    msg = response.choices[0].message
    assistant_msg = {
        "role": msg.role,
        "content": msg.content,
    }
    if msg.tool_calls:
        assistant_msg["tool_calls"] = [
            {
                "id": tc.id,
                "type": tc.type,
                "function": {
                    "name": tc.function.name,
                    "arguments": tc.function.arguments,
                }
            }
            for tc in msg.tool_calls
        ]
    messages.append(assistant_msg)
    
    if msg.tool_calls:
        for tc in msg.tool_calls:
            if tc.function.name == "lookup_order":
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
                result = lookup_order(args["order_id"])
                messages.append({
                    "role": "tool",
                    "tool_call_id": tc.id,
                    "name": tc.function.name,
                    "content": result,
                })
        
        second_response = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="llama-3.3-70b",
            messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT}] + messages,
        )
        final_msg = second_response.choices[0].message
        messages.append({
            "role": final_msg.role,
            "content": final_msg.content,
        })
        return final_msg.content
    
    return msg.content

Step 5: Add the interactive loop

With the core logic working, I wrap it in a simple terminal loop so you can hold a real conversation. The loop runs until you type exit, passing each line through the chat function and printing the reply. I use Llama 3.3 70B here because it handles tool use reliably, but you can switch to Qwen 3 32B or Kimi K2.6 by changing the model string with no other code changes. Oxlo.ai exposes all of them through the same endpoint, so testing different models is just a one-line edit.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Support agent ready. Type 'exit' to quit.")
    while True:
        user_input = input("\nUser: ").strip()
        if user_input.lower() in ("exit", "quit"):
            break
        reply = chat(user_input)
        print(f"Agent: {reply}")

Run it

Save everything into a file named support_agent.py, export your key, and run it:

export OXLO_API_KEY="your-key-here"
python support_agent.py

Here is a sample session against the mock data:

Support agent ready. Type 'exit' to quit.

User: Hi, can you check my order?
Agent: Hello! I'd be happy to help you check on your order. Could you please provide your order ID?

User: It's ORD-1001
Agent: Your order ORD-1001 for Wireless Headphones has been shipped and is expected to arrive in 2 days.

User: What about ORD-9999?
Agent: I wasn't able to find an order with ID ORD-9999. Please double-check the ID and try again.

User: exit

Next steps

Swap the MOCK_ORDERS dictionary for a real database call or an internal REST API. You can also add more tools such as initiate_return or escalate_to_human, and the same two-pass loop will handle them. If you want to expose this agent to users, wrap the loop in a FastAPI endpoint or connect it to a Slack bot. The flat per-request pricing on Oxlo.ai means you can keep long context windows and multi-turn agent loops in production without costs scaling with every extra token. For details on request limits and plans, see https://oxlo.ai/pricing.

title: Building Conversational AI with LLM
content:
Conversational AI has evolved from rigid decision trees to fluid, context-aware dialogues powered by large language models. Modern applications expect more than text completion. They require multi-turn memory, tool integration, and streaming responses that feel instantaneous. For developers, the challenge is not only prompt engineering but also managing inference costs as context windows grow and agentic loops multiply. The infrastructure you choose directly impacts latency, pricing predictability, and how naturally your assistant maintains state across a conversation.

Core Architecture for Conversational LLMs

At the heart of any conversational system is a stateful loop: user input, context assembly, inference, response parsing, and state update. Unlike single-shot completions, conversations accumulate history. Your backend must maintain a message array, typically formatted as OpenAI-style chat messages with system, user, and assistant roles.

A minimal but robust pattern looks like this:

  1. System prompt: Defines persona, constraints, and available tools.
  2. Message history: Ordered array of previous turns.
  3. Context window management: Truncation or summarization when limits approach.
  4. Response post-processing: Validation, logging, and state persistence.

Because context grows with every turn, token-based billing can escalate quickly. This is where pricing models matter. Oxlo.ai uses request-based pricing, meaning one flat cost per API call regardless of how many tokens precede the current prompt. For long-running conversations, this removes the penalty associated with replaying full message history on every turn.

Memory and Context Management

Short-term memory is bounded by the model's context window. When conversations exceed thousands of tokens, you must either truncate early turns or compress them into summaries. A common approach is to keep the last N messages verbatim and summarize older content into a running memory string injected into the system prompt.

Long-term memory often requires external retrieval. Vector stores, knowledge graphs, or simple key-value caches let an assistant recall facts across sessions. When building this layer, consider that every retrieved document adds tokens to the input. Under token-based pricing, retrieval-augmented generation in conversational loops becomes expensive. With Oxlo.ai, stuffing retrieved context into a request does not alter the per-request cost, making retrieval-heavy dialogue economically viable.

Tool Use and Function Calling

Truly useful conversational agents do not reason in isolation. They call APIs, query databases, and execute code. Function calling lets an LLM emit structured JSON to invoke tools, then resume the conversation with the results.

Oxlo.ai supports function calling across its chat models, including Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen 3 32B, and DeepSeek V3.2. Because the platform is fully OpenAI SDK compatible, you can point your existing client at Oxlo.ai with a single configuration change.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1",
    api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY"
)

tools = [{
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "description": "Retrieve current weather for a location",
        "parameters": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "location": {"type": "string"}
            },
            "required": ["location"]
        }
    }
}]

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant with weather tools."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "Do I need an umbrella in Seattle?"}
]

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="llama-3.3-70b",
    messages=messages,
    tools=tools,
    tool_choice="auto"
)

If the model returns a tool call, your application executes the function, appends the result to messages, and sends a follow-up request. Each turn is a single API request. On token-based platforms, the accumulated tool outputs and history inflate costs linearly. Oxlo.ai's flat per-request pricing keeps these agentic loops predictable.

Streaming and Latency

Perceived latency matters in conversation. Waiting for a full response to render creates a sluggish experience. Streaming lets tokens arrive incrementally, letting you display text as it generates.

Oxlo.ai supports streaming through the standard OpenAI SDK interface. Set stream=True and iterate over chunks. The platform also advertises no cold starts on popular models, which means first-token latency remains consistent whether you are prototyping at midnight or serving traffic during peak hours.

stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3-32b",
    messages=messages,
    stream=True
)

for chunk in stream:
    if chunk.choices[0].delta.content:
        print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content, end="")

Consistent latency and streaming support are baseline expectations for production conversational AI. Oxlo.ai meets these without requiring custom SDKs or vendor-specific wrappers.

Model Selection for Dialogue

Not every conversation requires the largest model. Routing simple chitchat to a smaller, faster model and escalating complex reasoning to a heavyweight variant is a proven cost and latency optimization.

Oxlo.ai offers more than 45 models across seven categories. For conversational AI, consider these tiers:

  • Fast, general dialogue: Llama 3.3 70B or Qwen 3 32B, both strong in multilingual reasoning and agent workflows.
  • Deep reasoning and coding: DeepSeek R1 671B MoE or DeepSeek V4 Flash, the latter offering a 1M context window for near state-of-the-art open-source reasoning.
  • Vision-enabled assistants: Kimi K2.6 supports advanced reasoning, agentic coding, and vision with a 131K context window, letting users upload images mid-conversation.
  • Free tier experimentation: DeepSeek V3.2 provides solid coding and reasoning capabilities at no cost within the free plan limits.

Because Oxlo.ai exposes all models through a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, swapping models requires changing only the model parameter.

Cost Efficiency at Scale

The economics of conversational AI shift dramatically with context length. A customer support agent that processes long ticket histories, or a coding assistant that ingests entire repositories, generates input token counts in the tens of thousands. Under token-based billing, every turn replays that history and multiplies costs.

Oxlo.ai's request-based pricing is built for this. One flat cost per API request means that adding more context, retrieved documents, or tool results does not increase the inference fee. For long-context and agentic workloads, this can yield significant savings compared to token-based providers. You can explore the exact structure on the Oxlo.ai pricing page.

Predictable pricing also simplifies capacity planning. Instead of estimating average tokens per user message, you budget by requests per day, which aligns more naturally with user session metrics.

Putting It Together

A production conversational agent combines these elements into a loop: receive input, hydrate context, optionally retrieve memory, call the LLM, handle tool requests, stream the response, and persist state.

With Oxlo.ai, the implementation stays standard. You keep using the OpenAI SDK patterns your team already knows. The difference is in the economics and the breadth of open-source models available under one key. Whether you are building a SaaS copilot, a support bot, or an autonomous research agent, the infrastructure should not force you to choose between rich context and manageable bills.

Here is a skeletal integration that ties streaming, tools, and context together:

import json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.oxlo.ai/v1", api_key="YOUR_OXLO_API_KEY")
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}]

def chat(user_input):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user_input})
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v3.2",
        messages=messages,
        tools=tools,
        stream=True
    )

    reply = ""
    for chunk in response:
        delta = chunk.choices[0].delta
        if delta.content:
            reply += delta.content
            print(delta.content, end="")
        elif delta.tool_calls:
            # Handle tool execution and recurse
            pass

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})

This pattern scales. Because Oxlo.ai charges per request, you can maintain longer message histories and richer system prompts without watching token meters spin.

Conclusion

Building conversational AI in 2025 means architecting for memory, tools, streaming, and cost control. The LLM is only one component. The inference platform underneath determines whether your agent can sustain long context windows, execute multi-step tool workflows, and remain economically viable as usage grows.

Oxlo.ai provides a developer-first option with flat per-request pricing, full OpenAI SDK compatibility, and a broad catalog of open-source models. If your conversational workloads involve long contexts or agentic loops, it is worth evaluating how request-based billing changes your unit economics. Start with the free tier, point your existing client to https://api.oxlo.ai/v1, and measure the difference in both latency and cost.
